Riya buys 25 packets of gulal, pink to yellow in the ratio 3 to 2. A pink packet costs 15 rupees and a yellow packet costs 20 rupees. How much does she spend altogether?
Think of the ratio as equal boxes: 3 parts for pink and 2 parts for yellow.

spec.note: All the boxes together: 25 packets

beats.say: First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 2 make 5 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 2 is 5. So the 25 packets are shared into 5 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 25 divided by 5 is 5, so each part is 5 packets. Careful: we divide by all 5 parts, not by one of the ratio numbers on its own.
Pink has 3 parts: 3 times 5 is 15 packets. Yellow has 2 parts: 2 times 5 is 10 packets.
Now the money. There are 15 pink packets at 15 rupees each. Which sum gives their cost?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 15 pink packets costs 15 rupees. 15 lots of 15 is 15 times 15.

beats.say: 15 times 15 is 225 rupees for pink. And 10 yellow packets at 20 rupees each cost 10 times 20, which is 200 rupees.
Add the two costs: 225 plus 200 is 425.
So Riya spends 425 rupees altogether.
Check the sharing: 15 plus 10 is 25, the whole amount. The shares are right.
So the plan: use the ratio to find how many of each kind, multiply each kind by its own price, then add the two costs.
Ananya has 76,482 rupees in her piggy bank. Her father asks: the place value of the 7 is how many times the face value of the 8?
Look at the chart. The 7 is in the ten-thousands column. What is it worth there?

ask.ifNot: Count the columns from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. So this 7 means 7 ten-thousands, and that is 70,000.

beats.say: 7 times 10,000 is 70,000. That is the place value of the 7.
Now the face value of 8. In this number the 8 sits in the tens column, so its place value is 80. But face value is just the digit as it looks, so it is simply 8.
How many times 8 is 70,000? Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: How many times means divide. And we divide by the face value of the 8, which is 8, not by 80.

beats.say: Here is a neat way to divide by 8: halve, halve again, and halve once more. That works because 2 times 2 times 2 is 8.
70,000 halved is 35,000. Halve again: 17,500. And once more: 8750.
So 70,000 divided by 8 is 8750. Careful: dividing by 80, the place value of the 8, would give a much smaller answer.
Check by multiplying back: 8750 times 8 is 70,000. It works.
So Ananya should say 8750 times.
So remember: place value depends on the column, and face value is just the digit. Find both, then divide.
Meera's tablecloth is 90 centimetres by 60 centimetres. She cuts a piece, 30 centimetres by 20 centimetres, out of one corner. How much cloth is left?

board.text: Piece cut from a corner: 30 cm × 20 cm

beats.say: How do we find the area that is left?

ask.ifNot: Cutting a piece out makes the cloth smaller. So we take the area of the piece away from the area of the whole cloth.

beats.say: First the whole cloth, 90 times 60. 9 times 6 is 54, and the two zeros go on the end: 5400 square centimetres.
Now the piece. 30 times 20 is 600 square centimetres.
Take it away. 5400 minus 600 is 4800 square centimetres.
Careful not to subtract the sides first. That would give 60 by 40, which is only 2400. It slices off a whole strip, not just one corner.
Check by putting the piece back. 4800 plus 600 is 5400, the whole cloth.
So when a piece is cut out, work out both areas first, and then subtract the areas, never the sides.
Arjun's team has 11 players. In each match, every player scores an average of 35 runs, and they play 18 matches. The principal gives one certificate for every 50 runs. How many certificates?

board.text: 11 players × 35 runs, 18 matches; 1 certificate per 50 runs

beats.say: Start with one match. How many runs does the whole team score in a match?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 11 players makes 35 runs. 11 lots of 35 is 11 times 35.

beats.say: 10 players make 350 runs, and 1 more player makes it 385 runs in a match.
They play 18 matches, so we want 385 times 18. 18 is 2 less than 20, so find 385 times 20 and take off 385 times 2.
385 times 20 is 7700. And 385 times 2 is 770.
7700 minus 770 is 6930. The team scores 6930 runs in all.
Now the certificates, one for every 50 runs. 100 runs earn 2 certificates, and 6930 is 69 hundreds with 30 left over.
69 hundreds earn 69 times 2, which is 138 certificates. And 30 runs are still left.
30 runs are left over. Do they earn one more certificate?

choices: No, a certificate needs a full 50
ask.ifNot: A certificate is given only for a complete 50 runs. 30 is not a full 50, so it earns nothing.

beats.say: So 138 certificates are given out.
Check: 138 certificates use up 6900 runs, and the 30 spare runs make 6930. Notice 6930 is in the choices too, but that is the runs, not the certificates.
So multiply up to the total, divide by 50, and here the left over runs are simply dropped.
Arjun has a square sheet of side 20 centimetres. He cuts a 4 centimetre square from each corner and folds up the sides to make a tray. We want the area of the flat base.

board.text: A 4 cm square is cut from each corner

beats.say: When the flaps fold up, the flat middle is the base. So first we need to know how long the base is.

board.text: Base = the middle that stays flat

beats.say: Look along one edge of the sheet. There is a corner cut at both ends. How long is the base along that edge?

ask.ifNot: One corner takes 4 off the left end, and another takes 4 off the right end. 20 minus 4, and minus 4 again, leaves 12.

beats.say: That is the trap. Take off 4 only once and you get 16. But there is a corner at each end, so it is 20 minus 4 minus 4, which is 12.
The sheet was a square, so the very same thing happens the other way. The base is a square, 12 by 12.
12 times 12 is 144. The base is 144 square centimetres.
Let's check that every bit of the sheet is counted. The whole sheet is 20 times 20, 400. The four corners are 4 times 16, which is 64.
Each flap is 12 by 4, which is 48, and four of them make 192. Then 144 plus 64 plus 192 is 400, the whole sheet.
So when corners are cut from a sheet, each side of the base loses the cut twice. Then the base is just length times breadth.
Meera plays 5 rounds: plus 6, minus 9, plus 4, minus 3, plus 5. Her friend Deepa finished on minus 2. How many more points does Meera have than Deepa?
Collect Meera's gains: 6, 4 and 5 make 15. And her losses: 9 and 3 make 12.
Gains of 15, losses of 12. What is Meera's total?

ask.ifNot: This time the gains are bigger than the losses, by 3. So Meera's total is above 0.

beats.say: 15 minus 12 is 3. Meera finishes on 3 points.
Meera has 3 and Deepa has minus 2. How many more points does Meera have?

ask.ifNot: Deepa is below 0 and Meera is above it. From minus 2 up to 0 is 2 points, and then from 0 up to 3 is 3 more.

beats.say: 2 points to climb up to 0, then 3 more to reach Meera. 2 plus 3 is 5. Meera has 5 more points.
As a subtraction it is 3 minus minus 2. Taking away a negative is the same as adding, so it becomes 3 plus 2.
The slip to avoid is 3 take away 2, which gives 1. That would be right if Deepa had plus 2, but she is below 0.
Find the total first. Then, for scores on opposite sides of 0, add their distances from 0.
At the school fair, the ring toss costs 3 rupees to enter, and then 4 rupees for each ring. Rohan spent 31 rupees. How many rings did he toss?
Let x be the number of rings. Which number gets multiplied by x?

ask.ifNot: The 4 rupees is paid again for every ring, so it is 4 times x. The 3 rupees is paid just once, to get in.

beats.say: 3 to enter, plus 4 x for the rings, equals 31.
The 3 is added on, so to undo it we take 3 from both sides. That leaves 4 x equals 31 minus 3, which is 28.
Nearly there. 4 x means 4 times x. What undoes times 4?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So we divide both sides by 4.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide by 4.
28 divided by 4 is 7. Rohan tossed 7 rings.
Check. 7 rings at 4 rupees is 28 rupees. Add the 3 to enter, and he spent 31. It works.
Once only, or every time? The every time number goes with the letter. The once only number comes off first.
Riya has a big square of 625 tiles. She takes a small square out of one corner, and 576 tiles are left. We want the side of the square she can make from the tiles she took out.

board.text: 625 tiles − a small square = 576 tiles. Its side?

beats.say: First, how many tiles did she take out? Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: She started with 625, and 576 are still there. The missing tiles are the difference between those two numbers.

beats.say: 625 minus 576. Let's count up. From 576, 24 more gets us to 600. Then 25 more gets us to 625.
24 and 25 make 49. So she took out 49 tiles.
Now those 49 tiles make a new square. The question asks for its side, not the number of tiles. Which number times itself makes 49?

ask.ifNot: 49 is how many tiles are in the whole square. The side is the number that, multiplied by itself, makes 49. Think of the 7 times table.

beats.say: 7 times 7 is 49. So the new square has 7 tiles on each side.
Check that no tile has gone missing. The 576 left, plus the 49 taken out, make 625.
The trap is to stop at 49. That is how many tiles there are. The side is its square root.
So: subtract to find what was removed, then take the square root to find the side.

Suresh buys 30 cricket balls at 45 rupees each, and pays 150 rupees for a banner and 75 rupees for carry bags. He sells 24 balls at 70 rupees each and gives the other 6 away. Profit or loss, and how much?
He only sold 24 balls. But how many balls did he pay for?

ask.ifNot: The wholesaler was paid for every ball Suresh took, even the 6 he later gave away. So the cost is for all 30.

beats.say: 30 times 45 is 1350 rupees for the balls.
Add the banner and the bags. 1350 plus 150 is 1500, and 75 more makes 1575 rupees spent.
Now the money in. Only the 24 balls he sold count here. 24 times 70 is 1680 rupees.
1575 rupees went out and 1680 rupees came in. Is that a profit or a loss?

ask.ifNot: Compare the two amounts. More money came in than went out, and that is a profit.

beats.say: It is a profit. 1680 minus 1575 is 105 rupees.
The trap is forgetting the banner and the bags. That gives 1680 minus 1350, which is 330, one of the choices.
Check: 1575 spent, plus 105 profit, makes 1680, the money he took in.
So pay for everything that was bought, earn only on what was sold, and take one total from the other.
Sameer starts at minus 8. Round 1, he climbs 12. Round 2, he slides down 5. Round 3, he climbs twice the distance he slid in Round 2.

board.text: Start −8: up 12, down 5, up twice the slide

beats.say: Round 1, up 12. Minus 8 plus 12 is 4. 8 of those steps bring us up to 0, and then 4 more above it.
Round 2, down 5. 4 minus 5 is minus 1. 4 of those steps take us down to 0, and then 1 more below it.
Round 3: he climbs twice the distance he slid down in Round 2. How far is that climb?

ask.ifNot: Look back at Round 2. The slide was 5 metres, and twice 5 is 10. It is the slide we double, not the place where he is standing.

beats.say: Twice 5 is 10, so in Round 3 he climbs 10 metres.
Up 10 from minus 1. Minus 1 plus 10 is 9. Sameer finishes at plus 9.
Check with totals. Up 12, up 10 and down 5 is 17 up overall. And minus 8 plus 17 is 9. It matches.
The trap here was the word twice. It doubles the slide of 5, not Sameer's position.
So: keep track of the position after every round, and read carefully what each round's move depends on.
Ravi puts 5000 rupees in a bank at 6 per cent simple interest a year, for 3 years. With just the interest he buys cricket balls at 150 rupees each. How many can he buy?

board.text: ₹5,000 at 6% a year for 3 years. A ball costs ₹150.

beats.say: 6 per cent a year means every 100 rupees earns 6 rupees in a year. So how many hundreds are in 5000? 5000 divided by 100 is 50.
Each of those 50 hundreds earns 6 rupees. 50 times 6 is 300. So 1 year brings 300 rupees of interest.
The money stays for 3 years. 300 times 3 is 900. So the interest is 900 rupees.
He spends only the interest on balls that cost 150 each. Which sum tells us how many balls?

ask.ifNot: Only the interest is being spent, and that is 900 rupees. Each ball uses up 150 of it, so we count how many 150s fit into 900.

beats.say: 2 balls cost 300. And 900 is 3 lots of 300, so that is 3 lots of 2 balls: 6 balls.
Check by multiplying. 6 balls at 150 each is 900, which uses up the interest exactly.
Notice his 5000 is still safe in the bank. The question only let him spend the interest, so only the interest gets divided.
So: 1 year's interest, times the years, and then share that interest out by the price of 1 ball.
Ravi's family set aside 5,000 rupees for Diwali shopping. They bought crackers, sweets and decorations, and shared what was left between 2 charity boxes.
What do we need to find first?

ask.ifNot: Only the leftover money is shared. And we cannot know the leftover until we know what the three things cost altogether.

beats.say: Add the crackers and the sweets first. 2,475 plus 1,368 is 3,843.
Now the decorations. 3,843 plus 957 is 4,800. So they spent 4,800 rupees.
Take that from the 5,000 they set aside. 5,000 minus 4,800 leaves 200 rupees.
Careful: 200 is one of the choices, but that is the whole leftover. It still has to be split between the 2 boxes.
200 divided by 2 is 100. Each charity box gets 100 rupees.
Check it. 2 boxes of 100 make 200, and 200 plus the 4,800 they spent is 5,000. Every rupee is accounted for.
So follow the story in order: total the spending, find what is left, then share it out.
Riya's grandfather uses 375 millilitres of milk for each cup of chai. He sold 48 cups on Monday and 64 on Tuesday. Milk comes in 5 litre packets. What is the smallest number of packets he needs?

board.text: 375 ml a cup; 48 + 64 cups; milk in 5 litre packets

beats.say: First the cups. 48 plus 64 is 112 cups.
Each cup takes 375 millilitres. 100 cups take 37,500, and the other 12 cups take 4500. Altogether that is 42,000 millilitres.
The milk is in millilitres, but the packets are in litres. How do we change millilitres into litres?

ask.ifNot: 1 litre holds 1000 millilitres. So we count how many thousands there are, and that means dividing by 1000.

beats.say: 42,000 divided by 1000 is 42. He needs 42 litres of milk.
Now the 5 litre packets. 8 packets hold 40 litres, and that leaves 2 litres still needed.
8 packets give 40 litres, but he needs 42. How many packets must he buy?

ask.ifNot: 8 packets leave him 2 litres short, and the shop does not sell part of a packet. So he has to buy one more whole packet.

beats.say: 8 packets and 1 more is 9 packets.
Check: 9 packets hold 45 litres, which covers the 42 he needs. 8 packets would not.
So get the total, change it into the packet's unit, divide, and go up to the next whole packet when some is still needed.
The ages of Kavya and Karan are in the ratio 3 to 5. Karan is 15 years old, and we want Kavya's age.
A ratio keeps its order. Kavya is named first and Karan second. So which number of the ratio belongs to Karan?

ask.ifNot: Match the names with the numbers, in order. Karan comes second, so Karan gets the second number, 5.

beats.say: So Kavya's age is 3 equal parts, and Karan's age is 5 of the same parts. Look at the two bars.
Karan's 5 parts make 15 years. How do we find the size of one part?

ask.ifNot: The 15 years are Karan's, and Karan has 5 parts. So we share 15 into 5 equal parts.

beats.say: 15 divided by 5 is 3. So one part is 3 years.
Kavya has 3 parts, so we take 3 lots of 3. 3 times 3 is 9. So Kavya is 9 years old.
Let us check. Divide both ages by 3. 9 gives 3, and 15 gives 5. That is our ratio, 3 to 5.
One part first, then the parts you need. That works for every ratio like this one.
Two ages today: 47 for Arjun and 9 for Riya. The question takes us back 6 years and asks for the gap between them.
The word ago means we go back in time, so both ages get smaller. 6 years ago Arjun was 47 minus 6, which is 41.
Riya was 6 years younger too. 9 minus 6 is 3.
So back then they were 41 and 3. What is the gap between those two ages?

ask.ifNot: For a gap, take the smaller age away from the bigger one: 41 minus 3.

beats.say: 41 minus 3 is 38. The difference 6 years ago was 38 years.
Now look at today's ages. 47 minus 9 is also 38. The very same gap!
That is no accident. Both of them grew older by the same 6 years, so the gap between them did not change.
Next time you can go straight there. The difference in ages never changes, so just subtract today's ages. The answer is 38.
Which is greater, 5 over 6 or one third? Let's find out.
Let's draw them as two bars, both the same length. One has 6 pieces with 5 shaded, and the other has 3 pieces with 1 shaded.
Is it fair to compare the tops, 5 and 1, straight away?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, the bigger top always wins
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Sixths and thirds are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. 3 goes into 6, so we can turn the thirds into sixths.
For one third, the bottom was multiplied by 2, so the top must be too. 1 times 2 is 2, so one third is 2 over 6. And 5 over 6 stays as it is.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all sixths. Which is greater, 5 over 6 or 2 over 6?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 5 pieces is more than 2 pieces.

beats.say: 5 is more than 2, so 5 over 6 is the greater fraction.
The picture agrees. The bar for 5 over 6 has more of it shaded.
So to compare fractions: make the pieces the same size, then compare the tops.
Siya buys 11 stickers, and each one costs 25 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 11 stickers costs 25 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 11 and 25 would mix up stickers and rupees. We need 11 lots of 25 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 11 lots of 25. That is a times sum.
11 is 10 and 1. So work out 10 lots first, then 1 more lot.
10 lots of 25 is 250. And 1 more lot is just 25.
Add the two parts. 250 and 25 make 275.
So the total cost is 275 rupees.
Does that make sense? 11 stickers must cost a lot more than one, and 275 is a lot more than 25. Yes.
The plan: number of things, times the price of each.
Siddharth buys 12 erasers, and each one costs 15 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 12 erasers costs 15 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 12 and 15 would mix up erasers and rupees. We need 12 lots of 15 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 12 lots of 15. That is a times sum.
12 is 10 and 2. So work out 10 lots first, then the other 2 lots.
10 lots of 15 is 150. And 2 times 15 is 30.
Add the two parts. 150 and 30 make 180.
So the total cost is 180 rupees.
Does that make sense? 12 erasers must cost a lot more than one, and 180 is a lot more than 15. Yes.
The plan: number of things, times the price of each.
11 x, plus 10, plus 8 x, minus 3. That is a lot to say! Let's tidy it up, so it says the same thing in fewer pieces.
Some of these pieces belong together. The ones with an x are one family. The plain numbers are another family. Which two are from the same family?

ask.ifNot: Look for the letter. 11 x and 8 x both have an x, so they are one family. 10 has no x at all.

beats.say: First the x family. 11 lots of x and 8 more lots of x make 19 lots of x.
Now the plain numbers. Careful: the sign in front of a number belongs to that number. So this is 10 minus 3, which is 7.
So we have 19 x and 7. Here is where many people slip. Can we join those two into one piece?

ask.ifNot: 19 x means 19 lots of a hidden number. 7 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: So the short form is 19 x plus 7. Same value, fewer pieces.
Good mathematicians check. If x were 1, the long one would be 11 plus 10 plus 8 minus 3. That is 26. The short one is 19 plus 7, and that is 26 too.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own number. That gave us 19 x plus 7.
Isha has 5 bags of rice. Each bag weighs 8 kilograms 500 grams. We want the weight of all the bags, in grams.

board.text: 5 bags, each 8 kg 500 g. Total in grams?

beats.say: Each bag's weight mixes two units, kilograms and grams. What is a good first step?

ask.ifNot: Kilograms and grams are mixed up here. If we turn one bag into grams first, the rest is one easy multiplication.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. So 8 kilograms is 8000 grams.
Now add on the 500 grams. One bag weighs 8500 grams. Careful: 8500 is one of the choices, but that is only one bag.
There are 5 bags, so we need 8500 times 5. Let's do it in two easy parts.
First the thousands. What is 8000 times 5?

ask.ifNot: Work out 8 times 5 first. Then put the three zeros back on the end.

beats.say: 8000 times 5 is 40000. And 500 times 5 is 2500.
Put the two parts together. 40000 plus 2500 makes 42500. So the 5 bags weigh 42500 grams.
The plan to remember: change everything into the small unit first, then multiply.
Aditya has 36 marbles and gives away 4 over 6 of them. We want to know how many are left.
Let's draw the 36 marbles. The bottom number is 6, so we share them into 6 equal groups.
How many marbles are in each group?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 36 marbles equally into 6 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 36 divided by 6.

beats.say: 36 shared into 6 equal groups gives 6 in each. So one group is 6 marbles.
The top number is 4, so 4 groups go to the friend. 4 times 6 is 24 marbles.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 24?

ask.ifNot: 24 is how many marbles went to the friend. Aditya started with 36, so what is left is 36 take away 24.

beats.say: 36 take away 24 leaves 12. Aditya keeps 12 marbles.
Let's check with the picture. 2 groups were not given away, and 2 times 6 is 12. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
We want the average of these five numbers: 44, 26, 51, 56, 48.
Think of the average as levelling out. We pile everything together, then give each number the same share.
First the total. We add one number at a time. 44 plus 26 is 70. Add 51 to get 121.
Keep going. Add 56 to get 177, and 48 more makes 225.
The total is 225. Now, what do we divide it by?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers in the list. There are 5 of them, so the total is shared 5 ways.

beats.say: 225 divided by 5 is 45, because 5 times 45 is 225.
So the average is 45.
Does it look sensible? The smallest number is 26 and the biggest is 56, and 45 sits between them. An average always does.
Two steps every time: find the total, then share it by the count.
The average of 4 numbers is 58. We know 3 of them: 71, 56, 72. We must find the missing one.
An average is a fair share. It is as if every one of the 4 numbers were 58. That tells us the total.
So how do we find the total of all 4 numbers?

ask.ifNot: If each of the 4 numbers were 58, the total would be 4 lots of 58. So we multiply.

beats.say: 58 times 4 is 232. All 4 numbers together make 232.
Now add the 3 numbers we know. 71 plus 56 is 127, and 72 more makes 199.
The missing number is whatever is left. 232 minus 199 is 33.
The missing number is 33.
Check: 199 plus 33 is 232, and 232 divided by 4 is 58. It works.
Turn the average into a total first. The missing number is the total minus the rest.
The average of 4 numbers is 49. Then a new number, 59, joins them. What is the new average?

board.text: Average of 4 numbers is 49. A new number 59 joins.

beats.say: We do not know what the 4 numbers are. But we do not need to! Their total is enough.
4 numbers with an average of 49 add up to the same as 4 lots of 49. 49 times 4 is 196.
Now the new number joins the pot. 196 plus 59 is 255.
We must share the new total. How many numbers are there now?

ask.ifNot: There were 4 numbers, and 1 more joined. 4 plus 1 is 5. Forgetting to count the new one is the classic slip.

beats.say: There are 5 numbers now. 255 divided by 5 is 51, because 5 times 51 is 255.
The new average is 51.
The new number, 59, is bigger than the old average, 49. So it pulled the average up a little. That makes sense.
Go through the total every time. Find it, add the new number, and share it among one more.
Neha buys 5 rulers, and each ruler costs 5 rupees. Neha hands over 50 rupees. We want to know how much money comes back.

board.text: 5 rulers at Rs.5 each. Pays Rs.50. Change = ?

spec.note: 5 rulers at Rs.5 each, then the change

beats.say: Look at the bar. The whole bar is the money Neha paid. The rulers take up part of it, and the change is the piece at the end. What do we need to find first?

ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper wants money for all 5 rulers, not just one. So first we find what all of them cost together.

beats.say: We need 5 lots of 5. 5 times 5 is 25.
So the whole bill is 25 rupees. That much stays with the shopkeeper.
Neha paid 50 rupees, and the bill is 25 rupees. How do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is the money left over after the bill is paid. So we take the bill away from the money paid.

beats.say: Take the bill away from the money paid. 50 take away 25 leaves 25.
So Neha gets 25 rupees back.
Let's check. The bill, 25, plus the change, 25, makes 50. That is exactly what Neha paid.
So for change, there are two steps. First find the whole bill, then take it away from the money paid.
Find the H C F of 35 and 28. H C F means highest common factor: the biggest number that divides both 35 and 28 exactly.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 28?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 28, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. These numbers have only a few factors, so we list every factor of each one. Then we look for the biggest number in both lists.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 35: 1 times 35 and 5 times 7. So the factors of 35 are 1, 5, 7 and 35.
Do the same for 28. The pairs are 1 times 28, 2 times 14 and 4 times 7. That gives the factors of 28: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14 and 28.
Now look along both lists. Which is the biggest number that is in both of them?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 7. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 7. Careful: 28 is in its own list, but it does not divide 35, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 7, so the H C F is 7.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 35 divided by 7 is 5, and 28 divided by 7 is 4. Nothing is left over either time.
That is the whole method. Write both lists of factors, look for the numbers in both, and the biggest of those is the H C F.
The ages of Sahil and Neha are in the ratio 5 to 6. Neha is 12 years old, and we want Sahil's age.
A ratio keeps its order. Sahil is named first and Neha second. So which number of the ratio belongs to Neha?

ask.ifNot: Match the names with the numbers, in order. Neha comes second, so Neha gets the second number, 6.

beats.say: So Sahil's age is 5 equal parts, and Neha's age is 6 of the same parts. Look at the two bars.
Neha's 6 parts make 12 years. How do we find the size of one part?

ask.ifNot: The 12 years are Neha's, and Neha has 6 parts. So we share 12 into 6 equal parts.

beats.say: 12 divided by 6 is 2. So one part is 2 years.
Sahil has 5 parts, so we take 5 lots of 2. 5 times 2 is 10. So Sahil is 10 years old.
Let us check. Divide both ages by 2. 10 gives 5, and 12 gives 6. That is our ratio, 5 to 6.
So the plan is: use the age you know to find one part, then multiply by the parts you need.
Two ages today: 27 for Arjun and 28 for Riya. The question jumps 10 years ahead and asks what the ages add up to then.
The word after means we go forward in time, so ages go up. After 10 years Arjun will be 27 plus 10, which is 37.
Now Riya. What do we do with Riya's age?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everybody. Riya also grows 10 years older, so we add 10 to 28 as well.

beats.say: Riya grows older as well. 28 plus 10 is 38.
Now we add the two new ages. 37 plus 38 is 75.
So after 10 years, their ages will add up to 75.
Here is a quick check. Today they add up to 55. Each of them gains 10 years, so we add 10 twice. We reach 75 again.
So when time passes, everyone in the sum grows older. Two people means the years are added twice.
Two ages today: 40 for Siya and 34 for Aditya. The question takes us back 10 years and asks for the gap between them.
The word ago means we go back in time, so both ages get smaller. 10 years ago Siya was 40 minus 10, which is 30.
Aditya was 10 years younger too. 34 minus 10 is 24.
So back then they were 30 and 24. What is the gap between those two ages?

ask.ifNot: For a gap, take the smaller age away from the bigger one: 30 minus 24.

beats.say: 30 minus 24 is 6. The difference 10 years ago was 6 years.
Now look at today's ages. 40 minus 34 is also 6. The very same gap!
Here is why. Every birthday adds 1 year to both of them, so the gap between two ages never changes.
Next time you can go straight there. The difference in ages never changes, so just subtract today's ages. The answer is 6.
Isha buys 10 pens, and each one costs 10 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 10 pens costs 10 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 10 and 10 would mix up pens and rupees. We need 10 lots of 10 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 10 lots of 10. That is a times sum.
10 times 10 is 100. So the total cost is 100 rupees.
Does that make sense? 10 pens must cost a lot more than one, and 100 is a lot more than 10. Yes.
So when every item costs the same, the total is the number of items times the price of one.
Neha pays 60 rupees for the book, then sells it at a profit of 10 percent. We want the selling price.
Percent means out of every 100. 10 out of 100 is one tenth. So 10 percent of a number is the number divided by 10.
60 divided by 10 is 6. So the profit is 6 rupees.
Now, the selling price. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: A profit means Neha gets more money back than was paid. So the 6 is added to the cost.

beats.say: A profit means selling for more than the cost. So add the profit to the cost.
60 plus 6 is 66. So the selling price is 66 rupees.
Careful with the trap. 6 is only the profit. The question asks for the selling price, which is 66.
So find the profit first, then add it to the cost.
Three signs in one sum: a divide, a plus and a times. The trick is knowing where to start.
One of these three signs has to wait until the very end. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times both go before plus. So the plus is the one that waits until the end.

beats.say: Dividing and multiplying go before adding. So we box 20 divided by 2, and we box 4 times 2.
First box. 20 divided by 2 is 10, because 2 times 10 is 20.
Second box. 4 times 2 is 8.
Put each answer where its box was, with the plus still in between.
Now the plus gets its turn. 10 plus 8 is 18.
Careful with the trap. Do not add in the middle first. The plus joins the two boxes, so it comes last.
The rule: do the dividing and the multiplying first. The adding comes last.
One of these numbers has digits that add up to 11. Digit sum just means we add the digits together.

board.text: Which number has a digit sum of 11?

beats.say: Let us try the first one, 3420. What do its digits add up to?

ask.ifNot: Add them one at a time: 3 plus 4 plus 2 plus 0. That makes 9.

beats.say: 3 plus 4 plus 2 plus 0 makes 9. That is less than 11, so not this one.
Next, 6036. 6 plus 0 plus 3 plus 6 makes 15. That is more than 11, so not this one.
Then 1046. 1 plus 0 plus 4 plus 6 makes 11. There it is, 11!
Next, 2181. 2 plus 1 plus 8 plus 1 makes 12. That is more than 11, so not this one.
So the number with a digit sum of 11 is 1046.
A tip for next time: a zero adds nothing, so you can skip over it. And check every choice, so nothing surprises you.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a plus and a times.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus, even though the plus is written first. So we begin with 6 times 7.

beats.say: Times goes before plus, so put a box round 6 times 7.
6 times 7 is 42. So 42 goes where the box was, and the rest stays the same.
One job left, the adding. 43 and 42 make 85.
Careful with the trap here. Adding 43 and 6 first, just because they come first, gives a different number. The 6 belongs to the times.
So remember: times first, then the plus.
Here is our question. What is one third of 24?
A picture helps. These are 24 counters, and the bottom number, 3, says share them into 3 equal groups.
What do we do to the 24 first?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number, 3, tells us how many equal groups to make. Sharing into 3 equal groups means dividing by 3.

beats.say: 24 divided by 3 is 8. So each group holds 8.
The top number is 1, so we take just 1 of those groups.
There it is. One third of 24 is 8.
Let's check our groups were fair. 3 groups of 8 should give back 24, and 3 times 8 is 24. They were.
So, for a fraction of an amount: divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top. When the top is 1, the dividing does it all.
The ages of Karan and Ananya are in the ratio 4 to 5. Ananya is 25 years old, and we want Karan's age.
A ratio keeps its order. Karan is named first and Ananya second. So which number of the ratio belongs to Ananya?

ask.ifNot: Match the names with the numbers, in order. Ananya comes second, so Ananya gets the second number, 5.

beats.say: So Karan's age is 4 equal parts, and Ananya's age is 5 of the same parts. Look at the two bars.
Ananya's 5 parts make 25 years. How do we find the size of one part?

ask.ifNot: The 25 years are Ananya's, and Ananya has 5 parts. So we share 25 into 5 equal parts.

beats.say: Share 25 into 5 equal parts and each part is 5. One part is 5 years.
Karan has 4 parts, so we take 4 lots of 5. 4 times 5 is 20. So Karan is 20 years old.
Let us check. Divide both ages by 5. 20 gives 4, and 25 gives 5. That is our ratio, 4 to 5.
So the plan is: use the age you know to find one part, then multiply by the parts you need.
Riya is 26 and Rohan is 11. We want the difference in their ages, but 3 years ago.
The word ago means we go back in time, so both ages get smaller. 3 years ago Riya was 26 minus 3, which is 23.
Rohan was 3 years younger too. 11 minus 3 is 8.
So back then they were 23 and 8. What is the gap between those two ages?

ask.ifNot: For a gap, take the smaller age away from the bigger one: 23 minus 8.

beats.say: 23 minus 8 is 15. The difference 3 years ago was 15 years.
Now look at today's ages. 26 minus 11 is also 15. The very same gap!
Here is why. Every birthday adds 1 year to both of them, so the gap between two ages never changes.
So remember: the gap between two people's ages stays the same, in the past, today and for ever. Here it is 15.
Here is 85844. Two digits are marked: the 8 in the ten-thousands place and the 8 in the hundreds place. We must compare what they are worth.

board.text: In 85844: (8 in ten-thousands) is ? times (8 in hundreds)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 8 in the ten-thousands place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 8 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 80000.

beats.say: The ten-thousands place is worth 10000, and 8 times 10000 is 80000.
Now the 8 in the hundreds place. That seat is worth 100, so 8 times 100 is 800.
Now, how many times. That asks how many lots of 800 fit into 80000. Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 800 fit into 80000, and that is a division.

beats.say: A neat trick: cross off the same number of zeros from both. Here that is 2 zeros from each, leaving 800 divided by 8.
8 times 100 is 800. So 800 divided by 8 is 100.
So the 8 in the ten-thousands place is worth 100 times the 8 in the hundreds place.
Good mathematicians check. 800 times 100 takes us back to 80000.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second.
Look at the signs here. A minus, then a times, then a plus.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 4 times 7.

beats.say: Times is the boss here. It goes before plus and minus, so put a box round 4 times 7.
4 times 7 is 28. Write 28 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 44 take away 28.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 44 take away 28 is 16.
And now the plus. 16 plus 2 is 18.
Did you spot the trap? Going left to right from the very start would mean taking away before multiplying, and that gives a different number.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a minus.
So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus. So 27 times 2 is our first job. The 15 has to wait.

beats.say: Times always goes before plus and minus. This time it is also first in line, so we start on the left.
27 times 2. 20 times 2 is 40, and 7 times 2 is 14. Together that makes 54.
So 54 goes where the box was. The minus 15 is still there.
Now the minus. 54 take away 15 is 39.
Careful with one thing. The 15 is not part of the times. It is only taken away after the multiplying is done.
So remember: times first, then plus or minus.
Which is greater, 2 over 6 or 7 over 8? Let's find out.
A picture first. Two equal bars: the top one cut into 6 with 2 shaded, the bottom one cut into 8 with 7 shaded.
Can we just compare the top numbers, 2 and 7?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, the bigger top always wins
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Sixths and eighths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 6 and 8 both go into, and the smallest one is 24.
For 2 over 6, the bottom was multiplied by 4, so the top must be too. 2 times 4 is 8, so 2 over 6 is 8 over 24.
And for 7 over 8, the bottom was multiplied by 3, so the top must be too. 7 times 3 is 21, so 7 over 8 is 21 over 24.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all twenty-fourths. Which is greater, 8 over 24 or 21 over 24?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 21 pieces is more than 8 pieces.

beats.say: 21 is more than 8, so 21 over 24 is greater. And 21 over 24 is just 7 over 8 cut into smaller pieces.
The picture agrees. The bar for 7 over 8 has more of it shaded.
So to compare fractions: make the pieces the same size, then compare the tops.
Here is our equation. 2 x, minus 9, equals 5. The x is a hidden number, and we are going to find it.
2 x means 2 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 2, then took away 9, and got 5.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance. To find x we work backwards, and undo the last thing first. Which was done last?

ask.ifNot: Read it from left to right. First x was multiplied by 2. After that came the minus 9. So the minus 9 was last, and we undo it first.

beats.say: We undo taking away by adding. So I add 9 to both sides, and the balance stays level.
Now the left side is just 2 x. And 5 plus 9 makes 14. So 2 times x is 14.
Don't stop here! 14 is in the list of answers, but it is what 2 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2. 2 times 7 is 14, so 14 divided by 2 is 7.
That means x is 7. We found the number that was hiding.
Good mathematicians always check. 2 times 7 is 14, and 14 minus 9 is 5. Both sides match.
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
The ages of Meera and Vivek are in the ratio 2 to 3. Vivek is 6 years old, and we want Meera's age.
A ratio keeps its order. Meera is named first and Vivek second. So which number of the ratio belongs to Vivek?

ask.ifNot: Match the names with the numbers, in order. Vivek comes second, so Vivek gets the second number, 3.

beats.say: So Meera's age is 2 equal parts, and Vivek's age is 3 of the same parts. Look at the two bars.
Vivek's 3 parts make 6 years. How do we find the size of one part?

ask.ifNot: The 6 years are Vivek's, and Vivek has 3 parts. So we share 6 into 3 equal parts.

beats.say: Share 6 into 3 equal parts and each part is 2. One part is 2 years.
Meera has 2 parts, so we take 2 lots of 2. 2 times 2 is 4. So Meera is 4 years old.
Let us check. Divide both ages by 2. 4 gives 2, and 6 gives 3. That is our ratio, 2 to 3.
One part first, then the parts you need. That works for every ratio like this one.
5 over 8 of 72. That little word, of, means we are taking a part of the 72.
A picture helps. This bar is all 72, and the bottom number, 8, says cut it into 8 equal parts.
So what is our first job with the 72?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number, 8, tells us how many equal parts to make. Sharing into 8 equal parts means dividing by 8.

beats.say: 72 divided by 8 is 9. So each part is worth 9.
Now the top number, 5. It tells us how many of those parts to take. So what is 5 over 8 of 72?

ask.ifNot: One part is 9, and the top number says take 5 of them. So we need 5 times 9.

beats.say: 5 parts of 9. 5 times 9 is 45.
There it is. 5 over 8 of 72 is 45.
Let's check our parts were fair. 8 parts of 9 should give back 72, and 8 times 9 is 72. They were.
So, for a fraction of an amount: divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top number.
Look at 83233. We want to compare two digits: the 3 in the thousands place and the 3 in the units place.

board.text: In 83233: (3 in thousands) is ? times (3 in units)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 3 in the thousands place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 3 sits in the thousands place, so it is worth 3000.

beats.say: The thousands place is worth 1000, and 3 times 1000 is 3000.
Now the 3 in the units place. That seat is worth just 1, so this 3 is worth 3.
How many times means: how many lots of 3 fit into 3000? Which sum finds that?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 3 fit into 3000, and that is a division.

beats.say: We need the number that, times 3, makes 3000. That number is 1000, because 1000 times 3 is 3000.
So the 3 in the thousands place is worth 1000 times the 3 in the units place.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second.
Here x stands for 2 and y stands for 4. Let's find what 2 x plus 4 y comes to.
Before we swap anything: when x is 2, what is 2 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 2 x means 2 times x. Here that is 2 times 2.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its own number. 2 x becomes 2 times 2. And 4 y becomes 4 times 4.
We do the times first. 2 times 2 is 4. And 4 times 4 is 16.
Now we have two parts: 4 and 16. What do we do with them?

ask.ifNot: Look at the sign between 2 x and 4 y. It is a plus. So the two parts are added.

beats.say: 4 plus 16 is 20. So 2 x plus 4 y is worth 20.
So the plan is: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. The answer is 20.
Here is our story. Isha has 36 marbles, and three quarters of them go to a friend. How many does Isha keep?
Let's draw the 36 marbles. The bottom number is 4, so we share them into 4 equal groups.
So how many marbles does one group hold?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 36 marbles equally into 4 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 36 divided by 4.

beats.say: 36 shared into 4 equal groups gives 9 in each. So one group is 9 marbles.
Isha gives away 3 of those groups. 3 times 9 is 27 marbles.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 27?

ask.ifNot: 27 is how many marbles went to the friend. Isha started with 36, so what is left is 36 take away 27.

beats.say: 36 minus 27 is 9. So Isha has 9 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. Just 1 group was not given away, and one group is 9 marbles. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
Here is our story. Riya has 48 marbles, and two thirds of them go to a friend. How many does Riya keep?
Let's draw the 48 marbles. The bottom number is 3, so we share them into 3 equal groups.
How many marbles are in each group?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 48 marbles equally into 3 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 48 divided by 3.

beats.say: 48 shared into 3 equal groups gives 16 in each. So one group is 16 marbles.
Riya gives away 2 of those groups. 2 times 16 is 32 marbles.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 32?

ask.ifNot: 32 is how many marbles went to the friend. Riya started with 48, so what is left is 48 take away 32.

beats.say: 48 minus 32 is 16. So Riya has 16 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. Just 1 group was not given away, and one group is 16 marbles. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
Here is our equation. 2 x, plus 10, equals 24. The x is a hidden number, and we are going to find it.
When a number sits next to x, it means times. So x was multiplied by 2, then someone added 10, and the answer was 24.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the plus 10. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 10, we take away 10.

beats.say: So 10 comes off. But if we did that on one side only, the balance would tip. So we do it to both sides.
Now the left side is just 2 x. And 24 minus 10 makes 14. So 2 times x is 14.
Don't stop here! 14 is in the list of answers, but it is what 2 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2. 2 times 7 is 14, so 14 divided by 2 is 7.
So x equals 7. The mystery is solved.
Let's check. Put 7 in place of x. 2 times 7 is 14, and 14 plus 10 is 24. It works!
Every equation like this works the same way. Undo the last thing first, and keep both sides level.
Here are 2 bags of sugar, and each one weighs 5 kilograms 750 grams. Our job is to find the total weight in grams.

board.text: 2 bags, each 5 kg 750 g. Total in grams?

beats.say: We want grams at the end. Right now each bag is in kilograms and grams. Where shall we begin?

ask.ifNot: Kilograms and grams are mixed up here. If we turn one bag into grams first, the rest is one easy multiplication.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. So 5 kilograms is 5000 grams.
Now add on the 750 grams. One bag weighs 5750 grams. Don't stop here, though. 5750 is just one bag, and it is sitting in the choices to catch us.
There are 2 bags, so we need 5750 times 2. That is doubling. Let's do it in two easy parts.
First the thousands. What is 5000 times 2?

ask.ifNot: Work out 5 times 2 first. Then put the three zeros back on the end.

beats.say: 5000 times 2 is 10000. And 750 times 2 is 1500.
Put the two parts together. 10000 plus 1500 makes 11500. So the 2 bags weigh 11500 grams.
The plan to remember: change everything into the small unit first, then multiply.

board.text: Rectangle: length 15 cm, width 11 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 15 centimetres long and 11 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 11 rows of 15, so we multiply 15 by 11.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 11 rows of squares, and 15 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
15 times 11 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 11 into 10 and 1.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 15 times 10 is 150. And 15 times 1 is 15. Now we put the two parts together. What is 150 plus 15?
Add them up: 150 plus 15 is 165.
So the area is 165 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 165 squares shared into 11 rows gives 15 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.
Here is 95448. Two digits are marked: the 4 in the hundreds place and the 4 in the tens place. We must compare what they are worth.

board.text: In 95448: (4 in hundreds) is ? times (4 in tens)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 4 in the hundreds place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 4 sits in the hundreds place, so it is worth 400.

beats.say: The hundreds place is worth 100, and 4 times 100 is 400.
Now the 4 in the tens place. That seat is worth 10, so 4 times 10 is 40.
Now, how many times. That asks how many lots of 40 fit into 400. Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 40 fit into 400, and that is a division.

beats.say: A neat trick: cross off the same number of zeros from both. Here that is 1 zero from each, leaving 40 divided by 4.
40 divided by 4 is 10.
So the 4 in the hundreds place is worth 10 times the 4 in the tens place.
Good mathematicians check. 40 times 10 takes us back to 400.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second. And notice: each seat is worth 10 times the seat on its right.
Look at the signs here. A minus, then a times, then a plus.
Where do we begin?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 3 times 5.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding and taking away. So we box the 3 times 5. It goes first.
3 times 5 is 15. Write 15 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 63 take away 15.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 63 take away 15 is 48.
One job left, the plus. 48 and 1 make 49.
The trap in this sum is the minus at the front. It looks like the place to start, but the times must go first.
The rule: multiply first. Then add and take away in order, from left to right.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a plus.
So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus. So 7 times 7 is our first job. The 4 has to wait.

beats.say: Times always goes before plus and minus. This time it is also first in line, so we start on the left.
7 times 7 is 49.
So 49 goes where the box was. The plus 4 is still there.
Now the plus. 49 plus 4 is 53.
Careful with one thing. The 4 is not part of the times. It is only added on after the multiplying is done.
So remember: times first, then plus or minus.
We have to divide 104 in the ratio 3 to 5, and find the smaller share.
A ratio of 3 to 5 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One share gets 3 parts and the other gets 5.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One share has 3 parts and the other has 5. Put them together, so add: 3 plus 5.

beats.say: 3 plus 5 is 8. There are 8 equal parts.
Now share 104 into 8 equal parts. 104 divided by 8 is 13. So one part is 13.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the smaller share. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The smaller share goes with the smaller number of the ratio. Of 3 and 5, that is 3.

beats.say: 3 parts of 13 each. 3 times 13 is 39. So the smaller share is 39.
Let us check. The other share is 5 parts, which is 65. And 39 plus 65 is 104. Nothing is lost.
So for sharing in a ratio: add to count the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for the share you want.
Here is our equation. 7 x, plus 17, equals 101. The x is a hidden number, and we are going to find it.
When a number sits next to x, it means times. So x was multiplied by 7, then someone added 17, and the answer was 101.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the plus 17. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 17, we take away 17.

beats.say: So 17 comes off. But if we did that on one side only, the balance would tip. So we do it to both sides.
On the left, only 7 x is left. On the right, 101 minus 17 is 84. So 7 x equals 84.
Don't stop here! 84 is in the list of answers, but it is what 7 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 7, we divide by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7. 7 times 10 is 70. That leaves 14, and 7 times 2 is 14. So 84 divided by 7 is 10 and 2 more, which is 12.
So x equals 12. The mystery is solved.
Let's check. Put 12 in place of x. 7 times 12 is 84, and 84 plus 17 is 101. It works!
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Find the H C F of 35 and 14. H C F means highest common factor: the biggest number that divides both 35 and 14 exactly.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 14?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 14, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. These numbers have only a few factors, so we list every factor of each one. Then we look for the biggest number in both lists.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 35: 1 times 35 and 5 times 7. So the factors of 35 are 1, 5, 7 and 35.
Now 14. Its pairs are 1 times 14 and 2 times 7. So the factors of 14 are 1, 2, 7 and 14.
Now look along both lists. Which is the biggest number that is in both of them?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 7. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 7. Careful: 14 is in its own list, but it does not divide 35, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 7, so the H C F is 7.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 35 divided by 7 is 5, and 14 divided by 7 is 2. Nothing is left over either time.
So the plan for an H C F like this one: list the factors of each number, find the ones in both lists, and take the biggest. Your turn next!
Which is greater, 3 over 6 or 4 over 7? Let's find out.
Here they are as two bars of the same length. The first is cut into 6 pieces with 3 shaded. The second is cut into 7 pieces with 4 shaded.
Is it fair to compare the tops, 3 and 4, straight away?

choices: Yes, the bigger top always wins
No, the pieces are different sizes
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Sixths and sevenths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 6 and 7 both go into, and the smallest one is 42.
For 3 over 6, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 7 as well: 3 times 7 is 21. That makes 21 over 42.
And for 4 over 7, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 6 as well: 4 times 6 is 24. That makes 24 over 42.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all forty-seconds. Which is greater, 21 over 42 or 24 over 42?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 24 pieces is more than 21 pieces.

beats.say: 24 is more than 21, so 24 over 42 is greater. And 24 over 42 is just 4 over 7 cut into smaller pieces.
The picture agrees. The bar for 4 over 7 has more of it shaded.
Keep this plan. Same bottom number first, and only then compare the tops.
Here are 4 bags of sugar, and each one weighs 3 kilograms 500 grams. Our job is to find the total weight in grams.

board.text: 4 bags, each 3 kg 500 g. Total in grams?

beats.say: The answer has to be in grams, but each bag is given in kilograms and grams. So what shall we do first?

ask.ifNot: Kilograms and grams are mixed up here. If we turn one bag into grams first, the rest is one easy multiplication.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. So 3 kilograms is 3000 grams.
Now add on the 500 grams. One bag weighs 3500 grams. Don't stop here, though. 3500 is just one bag, and it is sitting in the choices to catch us.
There are 4 bags, so we need 3500 times 4. Let's do it in two easy parts.
First the thousands. What is 3000 times 4?

ask.ifNot: Work out 3 times 4 first. Then put the three zeros back on the end.

beats.say: 3000 times 4 is 12000. And 500 times 4 is 2000.
Put the two parts together. 12000 plus 2000 makes 14000. So the 4 bags weigh 14000 grams.
Two steps did it: one bag into grams, then times the number of bags. You can use that every time.
Two ages today: 35 for Tara and 31 for Dev. The question jumps 4 years ahead and asks what the ages add up to then.
The word after means we go forward in time, so ages go up. After 4 years Tara will be 35 plus 4, which is 39.
Now Dev. What do we do with Dev's age?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everybody. Dev also grows 4 years older, so we add 4 to 31 as well.

beats.say: Dev grows older as well. 31 plus 4 is 35.
Now we add the two new ages. 39 plus 35 is 74.
So after 4 years, their ages will add up to 74.
Here is a quick check. Today they add up to 66. Each of them gains 4 years, so we add 4 twice. We reach 74 again.
So when time passes, everyone in the sum grows older. Two people means the years are added twice.
Here x stands for 2 and y stands for 1. Let's find what 3 x plus 4 y comes to.
Before we swap anything: when x is 2, what is 3 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 3 x means 3 times x. Here that is 3 times 2.

beats.say: Each letter has its own number, so be careful not to mix them up. x is 2, so 3 x is 3 times 2. y is 1, so 4 y is 4 times 1.
We do the times first. 3 times 2 is 6. And 4 times 1 is 4.
Now we have two parts: 6 and 4. What do we do with them?

ask.ifNot: Look at the sign between 3 x and 4 y. It is a plus. So the two parts are added.

beats.say: 6 plus 4 is 10. So 3 x plus 4 y is worth 10.
Remember: a number next to a letter always means times. Multiply each part, then add the parts. That gave us 10.
Here are 2 bags of wheat, and each one weighs 2 kilograms 750 grams. Our job is to find the total weight in grams.

board.text: 2 bags, each 2 kg 750 g. Total in grams?

beats.say: We want grams at the end. Right now each bag is in kilograms and grams. Where shall we begin?

ask.ifNot: Kilograms and grams are mixed up here. If we turn one bag into grams first, the rest is one easy multiplication.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. So 2 kilograms is 2000 grams.
Now add on the 750 grams. One bag weighs 2750 grams. Careful: 2750 is one of the choices, but that is only one bag.
There are 2 bags, so we need 2750 times 2. That is doubling. Let's do it in two easy parts.
First the thousands. What is 2000 times 2?

ask.ifNot: Work out 2 times 2 first. Then put the three zeros back on the end.

beats.say: 2000 times 2 is 4000. And 750 times 2 is 1500.
Put the two parts together. 4000 plus 1500 makes 5500. So the 2 bags weigh 5500 grams.
Two steps did it: one bag into grams, then times the number of bags. You can use that every time.
Here x stands for 6 and y stands for 4. Let's find what 4 x plus 4 y comes to.
First, what does 4 x turn into when x is 6?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 4 x means 4 times x. Here that is 4 times 6.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its own number. 4 x becomes 4 times 6. And 4 y becomes 4 times 4.
We do the times first. 4 times 6 is 24. And 4 times 4 is 16.
Now we have two parts: 24 and 16. What do we do with them?

ask.ifNot: Look at the sign between 4 x and 4 y. It is a plus. So the two parts are added.

beats.say: Add them up. 24 plus 16 makes 40. That is our answer: 40.
So the plan is: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. The answer is 40.
Riya has 3 bags of flour. Each bag weighs 5 kilograms 500 grams. We want the weight of all the bags, in grams.

board.text: 3 bags, each 5 kg 500 g. Total in grams?

beats.say: Each bag's weight mixes two units, kilograms and grams. What is a good first step?

ask.ifNot: Kilograms and grams are mixed up here. If we turn one bag into grams first, the rest is one easy multiplication.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. So 5 kilograms is 5000 grams.
Now add on the 500 grams. One bag weighs 5500 grams. Careful: 5500 is one of the choices, but that is only one bag.
There are 3 bags, so we need 5500 times 3. Let's do it in two easy parts.
First the thousands. What is 5000 times 3?

ask.ifNot: Work out 5 times 3 first. Then put the three zeros back on the end.

beats.say: 5000 times 3 is 15000. And 500 times 3 is 1500.
Put the two parts together. 15000 plus 1500 makes 16500. So the 3 bags weigh 16500 grams.
The plan to remember: change everything into the small unit first, then multiply.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a plus.
So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus. So 22 times 9 is our first job. The 10 has to wait.

beats.say: Times always goes before plus and minus. This time it is also first in line, so we start on the left.
22 times 9. 20 times 9 is 180, and 2 times 9 is 18. Together that makes 198.
So 198 goes where the box was. The plus 10 is still there.
Now the plus. 198 plus 10 is 208.
Careful with one thing. The 10 is not part of the times. It is only added on after the multiplying is done.
So remember: times first, then plus or minus.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a plus and a times.
So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: It is tempting to start on the left. But multiplying always goes before adding, so 8 times 2 is our first job.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding. So we box the 8 times 2. It goes first.
8 times 2 is 16. Write 16 in its place, and copy the rest just as it was.
One job left, the adding. 41 and 16 make 57.
Careful with the trap here. Adding 41 and 8 first, just because they come first, gives a different number. The 8 belongs to the times.
The rule: multiply before you add, wherever the times sign sits.
Look at 94863. Our job is to find what the 9 in the ten-thousands place is really worth.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands.

board.text: From right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands

beats.say: Our 9 sits in the ten-thousands place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands. The ten-thousands place is worth 10000.

beats.say: To get the place value, we multiply the digit by the worth of its seat. That is 9 times 10000.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 9 times 10000 is 90000. So this 9 is worth 90000.
Careful: 9 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 90000.
A quick check: 90000 is 9 followed by 4 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So remember: find the seat, then multiply the digit by what the seat is worth.
This is 16378. Let us find out how much the 1 in the ten-thousands place stands for.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands.

board.text: From right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands

beats.say: Our 1 is in the ten-thousands seat. What is the ten-thousands place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands. The ten-thousands place is worth 10000.

beats.say: To get the place value, we multiply the digit by the worth of its seat. That is 1 times 10000.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 1 times 10000 is just 10000. So this 1 is worth 10000.
Careful: 1 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 10000.
A quick check: 10000 is 1 followed by 4 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So the plan is: find the seat, then multiply the digit by the worth of that seat.
Look at 77726. We want to compare two digits: the 7 in the thousands place and the 7 in the hundreds place.

board.text: In 77726: (7 in thousands) is ? times (7 in hundreds)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 7 in the thousands place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 7 sits in the thousands place, so it is worth 7000.

beats.say: The thousands place is worth 1000, and 7 times 1000 is 7000.
Now the 7 in the hundreds place. That seat is worth 100, so 7 times 100 is 700.
Now, how many times. That asks how many lots of 700 fit into 7000. Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 700 fit into 7000, and that is a division.

beats.say: A neat trick: cross off the same number of zeros from both. Here that is 2 zeros from each, leaving 70 divided by 7.
70 divided by 7 is 10.
So the 7 in the thousands place is worth 10 times the 7 in the hundreds place.
Check by multiplying back: 700 times 10 is 7000. It works.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second. And notice: each seat is worth 10 times the seat on its right.
Find the H C F of 105 and 120. H C F means highest common factor: the biggest number that divides both 105 and 120 exactly.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 105?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 105, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: So how do we find it? Listing every factor would take a while. Instead we split each number into prime factors, the building blocks it is made of.
Take 105. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 3, then 5, and 7 is left. So 105 is 3 times 5 times 7.
120 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 120 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 105 and 120 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Ring them on the board. Both lines have a 3 and a 5. The 7 belongs only to 105 and the 2 belongs only to 120, so they stay out.
The middle of the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 3 times 5 is 15. So the H C F is 15.

spec.note: The middle holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 105 divided by 15 is 7, and 120 divided by 15 is 8, with nothing left over. And 7 and 8 share no factor except 1, so nothing bigger works.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.
This time the letter is no mystery: x is 6. So we can find what 5 x, plus 10, minus 8 is worth.
First, what does 5 x turn into when x is 6?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x. Here that is 5 times 6.

beats.say: So the x goes, and 6 takes its place. Now it reads 5 times 6, plus 10, minus 8.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 5 times 6 comes first. The 10 must not be added to the 6.

beats.say: 5 times 6 is 30. So now we have 30, plus 10, minus 8.
Now we go left to right. 30 plus 10 is 40. The sign before the 8 is a minus, so we take it away. 40 minus 8 is 32.
That gives 32. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
Rohan buys 8 books, and each one costs 3 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 8 books costs 3 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 8 and 3 would mix up books and rupees. We need 8 lots of 3 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 8 lots of 3. That is a times sum.
8 times 3 is 24. So the total cost is 24 rupees.
Does that make sense? 8 books must cost a lot more than one, and 24 is a lot more than 3. Yes.
The plan: number of things, times the price of each.
Here is a shop sum. 3 sharpeners at 15 rupees each, and Meera pays with 55 rupees. How much change comes back?

board.text: 3 sharpeners at Rs.15 each. Pays Rs.55. Change = ?

spec.note: 3 sharpeners at Rs.15 each, then the change

beats.say: Look at the bar. The whole bar is the money Meera paid. The sharpeners take up part of it, and the change is the piece at the end. What do we need to find first?

ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper wants money for all 3 sharpeners, not just one. So first we find what all of them cost together.

beats.say: 15 is 10 and 5, so we can do this in two easy bites. First, 3 lots of 10 make 30.
Then 3 lots of 5 make 15.
Put the two bites together. 30 plus 15 makes 45.
So the whole bill is 45 rupees. That much stays with the shopkeeper.
Meera paid 55 rupees, and the bill is 45 rupees. How do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is the money left over after the bill is paid. So we take the bill away from the money paid.

beats.say: Count up from 45 to 55. It is just 10 steps, so 55 take away 45 is 10.
So the change is 10 rupees. That is what Meera gets back.
Let's check. The bill, 45, plus the change, 10, makes 55. That is exactly what Meera paid.
Remember the plan for change: multiply to find the bill, then subtract the bill from the money paid.
Which is greater, two thirds or 4 over 7? Let's find out.
Let's draw them as two bars, both the same length. One has 3 pieces with 2 shaded, and the other has 7 pieces with 4 shaded.
Can we just compare the top numbers, 2 and 4?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, the bigger top always wins
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Thirds and sevenths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 3 and 7 both go into, and the smallest one is 21.
For two thirds, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 7 as well: 2 times 7 is 14. That makes 14 over 21.
And for 4 over 7, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 3 as well: 4 times 3 is 12. That makes 12 over 21.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all twenty-firsts. Which is greater, 14 over 21 or 12 over 21?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 14 pieces is more than 12 pieces.

beats.say: 14 pieces beat 12 pieces. And 14 over 21 is only another name for two thirds, so two thirds is the greater fraction.
And look: two thirds has the smaller top, yet it is the greater fraction. That is why we never compare tops until the pieces match.
So to compare fractions: make the pieces the same size, then compare the tops.
Let's put it on the board. 7 x, minus 9, equals 26. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
7 x means 7 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 7, then took away 9, and got 26.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance. To find x we work backwards, and undo the last thing first. Which was done last?

ask.ifNot: Read it from left to right. First x was multiplied by 7. After that came the minus 9. So the minus 9 was last, and we undo it first.

beats.say: We undo taking away by adding. So I add 9 to both sides, and the balance stays level.
Now the left side is just 7 x. And 26 plus 9 makes 35. So 7 times x is 35.
Careful: 35 is one of the choices, but 35 is 7 x, not x. So, what undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 7, we divide by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7. 7 times 5 is 35, so 35 divided by 7 is 5.
That means x is 5. We found the number that was hiding.
Good mathematicians always check. 7 times 5 is 35, and 35 minus 9 is 26. Both sides match.
Every equation like this works the same way. Undo the last thing first, and keep both sides level.

board.text: Rectangle: length 24 cm, width 11 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Here is our rectangle. It is 24 centimetres long and 11 centimetres wide, and we want its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 11 rows of 24, so we multiply 24 by 11.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 11 rows, with 24 in every row. So the area is length times width.
24 times 11 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 11 into 10 and 1.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 24 times 10 is 240. And 24 times 1 is 24. Now we put the two parts together. What is 240 plus 24?
240 plus 24 makes 264.
There it is: the area is 264 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 264 squares shared into 11 rows gives 24 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.
Karan buys 4 stickers, and each one costs 15 rupees. We want the total cost.
Every one of the 4 stickers costs 15 rupees. Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Adding 4 and 15 would mix up stickers and rupees. We need 4 lots of 15 rupees, and lots of means multiply.

beats.say: We need 4 lots of 15. That is a times sum.
4 times 15. 4 times 10 is 40, and 4 times 5 is 20. Together that makes 60.
So the total cost is 60 rupees.
Does that make sense? 4 stickers must cost a lot more than one, and 60 is a lot more than 15. Yes.
The plan: number of things, times the price of each.
Riya pays 500 rupees for the bicycle, then sells it at a loss of 25 percent. We want the selling price.
Percent means out of every 100. 25 out of 100 is one quarter. To find a quarter, halve the number, then halve it again.
Half of 500 is 250. Half of 250 is 125. So the loss is 125 rupees.
Now, the selling price. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: A loss means Riya gets less money back than was paid. So the 125 is taken away from the cost.

beats.say: A loss means selling for less than the cost. So take the loss away from the cost.
500 take away 125 is 375. So the selling price is 375 rupees.
Careful with the trap. 125 is only the loss. The question asks for the selling price, which is 375.
So find the loss first, then take it away from the cost.
We are adding two fractions. 8 over 10, plus 1 over 10.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 10 equal pieces. The first has 8 shaded, and the second has 1.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all tenths. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, lots of children slip here. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, tenths. Adding more tenths does not change their size, so the bottom stays 10.

beats.say: So adding is just counting. 8 pieces, and 1 piece more, is 9 pieces.
Can we make 9 over 10 simpler? No number except 1 goes into both 9 and 10, so it is already as simple as it can be.
So 8 over 10 plus 1 over 10 is 9 over 10.
Quick check with the picture. Count the shaded pieces in the first two bars: 8 and 1 make 9. It matches.
Remember it like this. Same size pieces? Just count them: add the tops, and the bottom stays as it is.

board.text: Rectangle: length 25 cm, width 3 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Here is our rectangle. It is 25 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide, and we want its perimeter.
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 25 plus 3 is 28.
Careful: 28 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two widths, so we double it. 2 times 28 is 56.
There it is: the perimeter is 56 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 25, 3, 25, 3. Together they make 56.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.
Kavya has 2 bags of sugar. Each bag weighs 3 kilograms 500 grams. We want the weight of all the bags, in grams.

board.text: 2 bags, each 3 kg 500 g. Total in grams?

beats.say: We want grams at the end. Right now each bag is in kilograms and grams. Where shall we begin?

ask.ifNot: Kilograms and grams are mixed up here. If we turn one bag into grams first, the rest is one easy multiplication.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. So 3 kilograms is 3000 grams.
Now add on the 500 grams. One bag weighs 3500 grams. Don't stop here, though. 3500 is just one bag, and it is sitting in the choices to catch us.
There are 2 bags, so we need 3500 times 2. That is doubling. Let's do it in two easy parts.
First the thousands. What is 3000 times 2?

ask.ifNot: Work out 3 times 2 first. Then put the three zeros back on the end.

beats.say: 3000 times 2 is 6000. And 500 times 2 is 1000.
Put the two parts together. 6000 plus 1000 makes 7000. So the 2 bags weigh 7000 grams.
So when kilograms and grams are mixed, make it all grams first. Then multiply by the number of bags.
Let's put it on the board. 5 x, plus 6, equals 61. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
5 x means 5 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 5, then added 6, and got 61.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the plus 6. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 6, we take away 6.

beats.say: And the rule of the balance is: what we do to one side, we do to the other. So I write minus 6 under both.
On the left, only 5 x is left. On the right, 61 minus 6 is 55. So 5 x equals 55.
