Don't stop here! 55 is in the list of answers, but it is what 5 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 5. 5 times 10 is 50, and one more 5 makes 55. So 55 divided by 5 is 11.
That means x is 11. We found the number that was hiding.
Let's check. Put 11 in place of x. 5 times 11 is 55, and 55 plus 6 is 61. It works!
Every equation like this works the same way. Undo the last thing first, and keep both sides level.
This time the letter is no mystery: x is 3. So we can find what 7 x, plus 8, minus 1 is worth.
Look at 7 x. The 7 and the x are side by side. When x is 3, what does that mean?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 7 x means 7 times x. Here that is 7 times 3.

beats.say: So the x goes, and 3 takes its place. Now it reads 7 times 3, plus 8, minus 1.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 7 times 3 comes first. The 8 must not be added to the 3.

beats.say: 7 times 3 is 21. So now we have 21, plus 8, minus 1.
Now we go left to right. 21 plus 8 is 29. The sign before the 1 is a minus, so we take it away. 29 minus 1 is 28.
That gives 28. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
We are adding two fractions. 6 over 12, plus 2 over 12.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 12 equal pieces. The first has 6 shaded, and the second has 2.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all twelfths. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, lots of children slip here. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, twelfths. Adding more twelfths does not change their size, so the bottom stays 12.

beats.say: So we only count the pieces. 6 pieces and 2 pieces make 8 pieces.
We are not done yet: 8 over 12 can be made simpler. What is the biggest number that goes into both 8 and 12?

ask.ifNot: Try the times tables. 4 goes into 8, and 4 goes into 12, and nothing bigger goes into both.

beats.say: So we divide the top and the bottom by 4. 8 divided by 4 is 2, and 12 divided by 4 is 3.
So 6 over 12 plus 2 over 12 is two thirds, in its simplest form.
Quick check with the picture. Count the shaded pieces in the first two bars: 6 and 2 make 8. It matches.
So when the bottom numbers match: add the tops, keep the bottom, and then make it simpler if you can.
Dev has 72 marbles and gives away 1 over 8 of them. We want to know how many are left.
Let's draw all 72 marbles as one long bar. The bottom number is 8, so we cut it into 8 equal parts.
How many marbles are in each part?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 72 marbles equally into 8 parts. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 72 divided by 8.

beats.say: 72 shared into 8 equal parts gives 9 in each. So one part is 9 marbles.
Dev gives away 1 of those parts, so 9 marbles go to the friend.
Careful now. Read the question again: it asks how many are left. So what do we do with the 9?

ask.ifNot: 9 is how many marbles went to the friend. Dev started with 72, so what is left is 72 take away 9.

beats.say: 72 minus 9 is 63. So Dev has 63 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. 7 parts were not given away, and 7 times 9 is 63. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
We need 2 over 8 of 96. Let's work it out together.
A picture helps. This bar is all 96, and the bottom number, 8, says cut it into 8 equal parts.
So what is our first job with the 96?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number, 8, tells us how many equal parts to make. Sharing into 8 equal parts means dividing by 8.

beats.say: 96 divided by 8 is 12. So each part is worth 12.
Now the top number, 2. It tells us how many of those parts to take. So what is 2 over 8 of 96?

ask.ifNot: One part is 12, and the top number says take 2 of them. So we need 2 times 12.

beats.say: 2 parts of 12. 2 times 12 is 24.
There it is. 2 over 8 of 96 is 24.
Let's check our parts were fair. 8 parts of 12 should give back 96, and 8 times 12 is 96. They were.
Here is the plan to keep. Share into the bottom number of groups, then take the top number of them.

board.text: Rectangle: length 15 cm, width 9 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 15 centimetres long and 9 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Imagine an ant walking round the rectangle until it is back where it started.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 15 plus 9 is 24.
Don't stop at 24. That is just one length and one width, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 24 is 48.
So the perimeter is 48 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 15, 9, 15, 9. Together they make 48.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.

board.text: Rectangle: length 16 cm, width 4 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 16 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 4 rows of 16, so we multiply 16 by 4.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 4 rows of squares, and 16 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
16 times 4 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 16 into 10 and 6.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 10 times 4 is 40. And 6 times 4 is 24. Now we put the two parts together. What is 40 plus 24?
40 plus 24 makes 64.
So the area is 64 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 64 squares shared into 4 rows gives 16 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.
Look at this one. 5 x, minus 8, equals 7. Our job is to find the number that x stands for.
5 x means 5 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 5, then took away 8, and got 7.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the minus 8. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo minus 8, we add 8.

beats.say: So 8 goes on. But if we did that on one side only, the balance would tip. So we do it to both sides.
On the left, only 5 x is left. On the right, 7 plus 8 is 15. So 5 x equals 15.
Don't stop here! 15 is in the list of answers, but it is what 5 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 5. 5 times 3 is 15, so 15 divided by 5 is 3.
So x equals 3. The mystery is solved.
Good mathematicians always check. 5 times 3 is 15, and 15 minus 8 is 7. Both sides match.
So the plan is to work backwards. First undo the adding or taking away. Then undo the times.
Here is our story. Ananya has 90 marbles, and two thirds of them go to a friend. How many does Ananya keep?
Let's draw all 90 marbles as one long bar. The bottom number is 3, so we cut it into 3 equal parts.
How many marbles are in each part?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 90 marbles equally into 3 parts. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 90 divided by 3.

beats.say: 90 shared into 3 equal parts gives 30 in each. So one part is 30 marbles.
The top number is 2, so 2 parts go to the friend. 2 times 30 is 60 marbles.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 60?

ask.ifNot: 60 is how many marbles went to the friend. Ananya started with 90, so what is left is 90 take away 60.

beats.say: 90 take away 60 leaves 30. Ananya keeps 30 marbles.
Let's check with the picture. Just 1 part was not given away, and one part is 30 marbles. It matches.
The plan: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top, and then check what the question is really asking for.
Two ratios are equal here. 4 to 7 is the same as 8 to x. Our job is to find x.
Equal ratios are made by multiplying both numbers by the same number. So look at the two first numbers, 4 and 8.
What was 4 multiplied by to become 8?

ask.ifNot: Say the 4 times table until you reach 8. 4 times 2 is 8.

beats.say: 4 times 2 is 8. So the multiplier is 2.
Careful here. We do not add anything. The second number, 7, must be multiplied by the very same 2.
7 times 2 is 14. So x is 14.
Let us check. 4 to 7 became 8 to 14. Both numbers were multiplied by 2, so the two ratios are equal.
So with equal ratios, find the multiplier from the pair you know, then use it on the other pair.
Vivek has 70 books and splits them into two groups, in the ratio 3 to 4. We want the larger group.

board.text: Vivek shares 70 books in the ratio 3 : 4

beats.say: A ratio of 3 to 4 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One group gets 3 parts and the other gets 4.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One group has 3 parts and the other has 4. Put them together, so add: 3 plus 4.

beats.say: 3 plus 4 is 7. There are 7 equal parts.
Now share 70 into 7 equal parts. 70 divided by 7 is 10. So one part is 10.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the larger group. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The larger group goes with the larger number of the ratio. Of 3 and 4, that is 4.

beats.say: 4 parts of 10 each. 4 times 10 is 40. So the larger group is 40 books.
Let us check. The other group is 3 parts, which is 30. And 30 plus 40 is 70. Nothing is lost.
Three small steps every time. Count the parts. Find one part. Multiply by the parts you need.
Here 3 to 6 equals 6 to x. One number is hiding behind the x. Let us find it.
Equal ratios are made by multiplying both numbers by the same number. So look at the two first numbers, 3 and 6.
What was 3 multiplied by to become 6?

ask.ifNot: Say the 3 times table until you reach 6. 3 times 2 is 6.

beats.say: 3 times 2 is 6. So the multiplier is 2.
Careful here. We do not add anything. The second number, 6, must be multiplied by the very same 2.
6 times 2 is 12. So x is 12.
Let us check. 3 to 6 became 6 to 12. Both numbers were multiplied by 2, so the two ratios are equal.
Remember: whatever one number is multiplied by, its partner is multiplied by the same.
We are hunting for the number whose digits add up to 20. Here are the four to choose from.

ask.ifNot: Digit sum is just what it says. Take each digit of the number and add them all together.

beats.say: First, what does 'digit sum' ask us to do?
So we test the numbers one at a time. A tip: a zero adds nothing, so you can skip straight over any zeros.
Try 6516. 6 plus 5 plus 1 plus 6 makes 18. That is too small, so we cross it out.
Take 5052. 5 plus 0 plus 5 plus 2 makes 12. Not 20 either, so out it goes.

ask.ifNot: Go one digit at a time: 8, 0, 5, 7. Keep a running total as you go.

beats.say: Now 8057. Add its digits yourself before I do. What do you get?
8 plus 0 plus 5 plus 7 makes 20. We have found it!
Let's make sure of the others. First 8296. 8 plus 2 plus 9 plus 6 makes 25, which is too big. Cross it out.
So the number with a digit sum of 20 is 8057.
Digit sum means add the digits, nothing more. Test each choice calmly and cross out the ones that miss.
Let's write the number down: 26051. We want the place value of the 6 sitting in the thousands place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. So that is where our 6 lives.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called thousands, so each one in it stands for 1000.

beats.say: A digit in the thousands column counts thousands. So what is each one in that column worth?
Our digit says there are 6 of those. 6 times 1000 makes 6000.
Careful: 6 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 6000. The 3 zeros are there because 3 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 20000 plus 6000 plus 50 plus 1. There is our 6000, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 6 in the thousands place is 6000.
So, find the column, then multiply the digit by what the column is worth. That works for any number.
Here is our number, 46180. The question points at the 8 in the tens place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens. There is our 8.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called tens, so each one in it stands for 10.

beats.say: A digit in the tens column counts tens. So what is each one in that column worth?
So the 8 means 8 lots of 10. That is 80.
Careful: 8 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 80. The zero on the end is there because 1 more place sits to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 40000 plus 6000 plus 100 plus 80. There is our 80, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 8 in the tens place is 80.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Let's write the number down: 31471. We want the place value of the 3 sitting in the ten-thousands place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. There is our 3.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called ten-thousands, so each one in it stands for 10000.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the ten-thousands place?
Our digit says there are 3 of those. 3 times 10000 makes 30000.
Careful: 3 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 30000. The 4 zeros are there because 4 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 30000 plus 1000 plus 400 plus 70 plus 1. And look, 30000 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 3 in the ten-thousands place is 30000.
The plan every time: find the digit's column, see what that column is worth, and multiply.
Let's write the number down: 81615. We want the place value of the 1 sitting in the thousands place.
Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. Careful, this number has more than one 1. We want the one in the thousands column.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called thousands, so each one in it stands for 1000.

beats.say: A digit in the thousands column counts thousands. So what is each one in that column worth?
We have just 1 of them. 1 times 1000 is 1000.
Careful: 1 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 1000. The 3 zeros are there because 3 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 80000 plus 1000 plus 600 plus 10 plus 5. There is our 1000, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 1 in the thousands place is 1000.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Let's write the number down: 54827. We want the place value of the 2 sitting in the tens place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens. So that is where our 2 lives.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called tens, so each one in it stands for 10.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the tens place?
So the 2 means 2 lots of 10. That is 20.
Careful: 2 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 20. The zero on the end is there because 1 more place sits to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 50000 plus 4000 plus 800 plus 20 plus 7. There is our 20, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 2 in the tens place is 20.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Here is our number, 26004. The question points at the 4 in the units place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
The units place is the very last column, on the right. There is our 4.

ask.ifNot: The units column counts single ones. So each one in that column is worth just 1.

beats.say: The units column is the smallest of them all. What is each one in that column worth?
We have 4 ones. 4 times 1 is just 4.
Here is something neat. In the units place, the place value and the face value are the same: 4.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 20000 plus 6000 plus 4. There is our 4, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 4 in the units place is 4.
The plan every time: find the digit's column, see what that column is worth, and multiply.
Here is our number, 68748. The question points at the 8 in the thousands place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. Careful, this number has more than one 8. We want the one in the thousands column.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called thousands, so each one in it stands for 1000.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the thousands place?
We have 8 of them. So 8 times 1000 is 8000.
Careful: 8 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 8000. The 3 zeros are there because 3 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 60000 plus 8000 plus 700 plus 40 plus 8. And look, 8000 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 8 in the thousands place is 8000.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Here is our number, 37814. The question points at the 8 in the hundreds place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds. There is our 8.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called hundreds, so each one in it stands for 100.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the hundreds place?
So the 8 means 8 lots of 100. That is 800.
Careful: 8 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 800. The 2 zeros are there because 2 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 30000 plus 7000 plus 800 plus 10 plus 4. And look, 800 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 8 in the hundreds place is 800.
So, find the column, then multiply the digit by what the column is worth. That works for any number.
Here is our number, 83710. The question points at the 7 in the hundreds place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds. There is our 7.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called hundreds, so each one in it stands for 100.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the hundreds place?
We have 7 of them. So 7 times 100 is 700.
Careful: 7 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 700. The 2 zeros are there because 2 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 80000 plus 3000 plus 700 plus 10. And look, 700 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 7 in the hundreds place is 700.
So, find the column, then multiply the digit by what the column is worth. That works for any number.
Here is 88510. We are comparing two digits: the 8 in the ten-thousands place, and the 5 in the hundreds place.

ask.ifNot: It is 8 in the ten-thousands column, so it stands for 8 lots of 10000. That makes 80000.

beats.say: Here they are in the chart. Start with the 8 in the ten-thousands column. What is it worth?
8 times 10000 is 80000. So that 8 is worth 80000.
Now the 5 in the hundreds place. 5 times 100 is 500.

ask.ifNot: 'How many times' asks how many lots of 500 fit into 80000. Fitting in means dividing the place values, not taking away.

beats.say: Now for the words 'how many times'. Which sum answers that?
80000 divided by 500 is 160.
Good mathematicians check. 160 times 500 is 80000, just as it should be.
So the 8 in the ten-thousands place is worth 160 times the 5 in the hundreds place.
The plan: find each place value first, then divide. Never just divide the digits as they look.
Here is our number, 29916. The question points at the 1 in the tens place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens. And there sits our 1.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called tens, so each one in it stands for 10.

beats.say: A digit in the tens column counts tens. So what is each one in that column worth?
We have just 1 of them. 1 times 10 is 10.
Careful: 1 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 10. The zero on the end is there because 1 more place sits to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 20000 plus 9000 plus 900 plus 10 plus 6. There is our 10, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 1 in the tens place is 10.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
This is 87298. One of its digits, the 8 in the units place, has a value for us to find.
The units place is the very last column, on the right. Careful, this number has more than one 8. We want the one in the units column.

ask.ifNot: The units column counts single ones. So each one in that column is worth just 1.

beats.say: The units column is the smallest of them all. What is each one in that column worth?
We have 8 ones. 8 times 1 is just 8.
Here is something neat. In the units place, the place value and the face value are the same: 8.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 80000 plus 7000 plus 200 plus 90 plus 8. And look, 8 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 8 in the units place is 8.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
One of these four numbers has a digit sum of 10. Let's find out which.

ask.ifNot: Digit sum is just what it says. Take each digit of the number and add them all together.

beats.say: First, what does 'digit sum' ask us to do?
So we test the numbers one at a time. Add slowly, one digit at a time, and nothing can go astray.

ask.ifNot: Go one digit at a time: 3, 3, 4. Keep a running total as you go.

beats.say: Start with 334. Add its digits yourself before I do. What do you get?
3 plus 3 plus 4 makes 10. There it is!
Let's make sure of the others. First 666. 6 plus 6 plus 6 makes 18. That is too big, so we cross it out.
Then 369. 3 plus 6 plus 9 makes 18. Not 10 either, so out it goes.
And last, 977. 9 plus 7 plus 7 makes 23, which is too big. Cross it out.
So the number with a digit sum of 10 is 334.
Digit sum means add the digits, nothing more. Test each choice calmly and cross out the ones that miss.
This is 92203. One of its digits, the 2 in the thousands place, has a value for us to find.
Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. Careful, this number has more than one 2. We want the one in the thousands column.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called thousands, so each one in it stands for 1000.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the thousands place?
We have 2 of them. So 2 times 1000 is 2000.
Careful: 2 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 2000. The 3 zeros are there because 3 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 90000 plus 2000 plus 200 plus 3. And look, 2000 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 2 in the thousands place is 2000.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Here is our number, 72816. The question points at the 7 in the ten-thousands place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. So that is where our 7 lives.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called ten-thousands, so each one in it stands for 10000.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the ten-thousands place?
Our digit says there are 7 of those. 7 times 10000 makes 70000.
Careful: 7 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 70000. The 4 zeros are there because 4 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 70000 plus 2000 plus 800 plus 10 plus 6. And look, 70000 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 7 in the ten-thousands place is 70000.
The plan every time: find the digit's column, see what that column is worth, and multiply.
Let's write the number down: 30578. We want the place value of the 3 sitting in the ten-thousands place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. So that is where our 3 lives.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called ten-thousands, so each one in it stands for 10000.

beats.say: A digit in the ten-thousands column counts ten-thousands. So what is each one in that column worth?
Our digit says there are 3 of those. 3 times 10000 makes 30000.
Careful: 3 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 30000. The 4 zeros are there because 4 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 30000 plus 500 plus 70 plus 8. There is our 30000, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 3 in the ten-thousands place is 30000.
So, find the column, then multiply the digit by what the column is worth. That works for any number.
Here is our number, 77441. The question points at the 4 in the hundreds place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds. Careful, this number has more than one 4. We want the one in the hundreds column.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called hundreds, so each one in it stands for 100.

beats.say: A digit in the hundreds column counts hundreds. So what is each one in that column worth?
Our digit says there are 4 of those. 4 times 100 makes 400.
Careful: 4 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 400. The 2 zeros are there because 2 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 70000 plus 7000 plus 400 plus 40 plus 1. And look, 400 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 4 in the hundreds place is 400.
The plan every time: find the digit's column, see what that column is worth, and multiply.
6 pencils, and every one costs 3 rupees. How much does Siya pay altogether?
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one pencil, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 6 pencils costs 3 rupees. That is 3 rupees, 6 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: Same price, 6 times, so it is a times sum. 6 times 3 is 18.
So the total cost is 18 rupees.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 18 rupees, in lots of 3 rupees, gives 6 pencils. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. Now you try one!
Vivek buys 5 books at 8 rupees each, and hands over 65 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 5 books at Rs.8 each. Pays Rs.65.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 65 rupees pays for the books, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the books
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 5 books, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 5 books at 8 rupees each: that is 5 times 8. 5 times 8 is 40.
Careful: 40 is only the cost, not the answer. Vivek paid 65. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 40 away from 65.

beats.say: 65 take away 40 leaves 25.
So Vivek gets 25 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 40 plus 25 is 65. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
Isha pays 120 rupees for a book. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 15 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 120 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 120 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 120 divided by 10 is 12.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 12 is 6.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 12 plus 6 makes 18. That is the profit.
So the profit is 18 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 120 plus 18 is 138. So the selling price is 138 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 138 is 18 more than 120. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Rohan is sharing out 72 marbles in the ratio 3 is to 5. Our job is to find the larger group.

board.text: 72 marbles in the ratio 3 : 5. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 72 to share. The ratio is 3 is to 5. And the question only wants the larger group.
A ratio of 3 is to 5 means this. One side gets 3 equal parts, and the other gets 5 parts of the very same size. Here they are as two bars.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 3 and 5 together make 8 parts.

beats.say: 3 and 5 make 8. That means the 72 is spread over 8 equal parts.
Careful with this next step, it is the one that trips people up. What is one part worth?

ask.ifNot: The 72 fills all 8 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 72 by 8.

beats.say: 72 divided by 8 is 9. Now we can write 9 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 9

beats.say: The larger group has 5 of these parts. 5 times 9 is 45.
So the larger group has 45 marbles. There it is!
Let's check. The smaller group is 3 times 9, which is 27. And 27 plus 45 is 72, just what we started with.
So, to share in a ratio: count the parts, find what one part is worth, then take as many parts as you need.
54 is being shared out in the ratio 2 is to 7. We are after the smaller share.

board.text: Divide 54 in the ratio 2 : 7. Smaller share = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 54 to share. The ratio is 2 is to 7. And the question only wants the smaller share.
A ratio of 2 is to 7 means this. One side gets 2 equal parts, and the other gets 7 parts of the very same size. Here they are as two bars.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 2 and 7 together make 9 parts.

beats.say: 2 and 7 make 9. That means the 54 is spread over 9 equal parts.
Here comes the turning point. Which sum tells us what a single part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 54 fills all 9 parts, not just the 7 parts of one bar. So we divide 54 by 9.

beats.say: 54 divided by 9 is 6. Now we can write 6 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 6

beats.say: We want the smaller share, and that is 2 parts. 2 times 6 makes 12.
So the smaller share is 12. There it is!
Let's check. The larger share is 7 times 6, which is 42. And 12 plus 42 is 54, just what we started with.
That is the whole method. Total parts first, then one part, then the share the question asks for.
Kavya is sharing out 49 toffees in the ratio 2 is to 5. Our job is to find the larger group.

board.text: 49 toffees in the ratio 2 : 5. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Before any sum, let's be sure what we know. The total is 49. The ratio is 2 is to 5. And we want the larger group only.
Let's draw the ratio. 2 is to 5: one bar with 2 equal parts, and one bar with 5. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 2 and 5 together make 7 parts.

beats.say: 2 and 5 make 7. That means the 49 is spread over 7 equal parts.
Now for the step where slips happen. How do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 49 fills all 7 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 49 by 7.

beats.say: 49 divided by 7 is 7. Now we can write 7 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 7

beats.say: The larger group has 5 of these parts. 5 times 7 is 35.
So the larger group has 35 toffees. There it is!
Let's check. The smaller group is 2 times 7, which is 14. And 14 plus 35 is 49, just what we started with.
That is the whole method. Total parts first, then one part, then the share the question asks for.
The ages of Kavya and Karan are in the ratio 4 is to 7. Karan is 56 years old, and we want Kavya's age.
Look at the order carefully. Kavya is named first, so Kavya goes with the 4. Karan is second, and goes with the 7.
As bars: Kavya's age is 4 equal parts, and Karan's is 7 parts of the same size. We know Karan's whole bar is 56 years.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: So how do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 56 years belong to Karan alone, and Karan's bar has 7 parts. So we divide 56 by 7.

beats.say: 56 divided by 7 is 8, so each part is 8 years. Notice we did not add 4 and 7 this time, because 56 is not the total of both ages.

spec.note: Each piece is 8 years

beats.say: Kavya has 4 of these parts. 4 times 8 is 32.
So Kavya is 32 years old.
Check. Take 32 is to 56, and divide both by 8. We get 4 is to 7, the ratio in the question.
Here is the plan to keep. Find one part from the age you know, then take as many parts as the other person has.
Diya is 39 years old and Nikhil is 20. We want the sum of their ages after 10 years.

board.text: Diya is 39, Nikhil is 20. Sum after 10 years = ?

beats.say: Read the last part again: after 10 years. So we don't add the ages they have today. We add the ages they will have then.
Here is a bar for each of them. In 10 years, each bar grows by a piece of 10.

spec.note: Both bars grow by the same piece

beats.say: Who gets older in those 10 years?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everybody. Diya gets 10 years older, and so does Nikhil.

beats.say: Diya will be 39 plus 10, which is 49. Nikhil will be 20 plus 10, which is 30.
Now add the two new ages. 49 plus 30 is 79.
So after 10 years, their ages add up to 79.
Here is a quick check. Today they add up to 59. Two people each gain 10 years, so the sum gains 20. And 59 plus 20 is 79.
The slip to avoid is adding the 10 only once. Two people means the years are added two times.
Arjun is 47 years old and Riya is 42. The question asks for the difference in their ages 7 years ago.

board.text: Arjun is 47, Riya is 42. Difference 7 years ago = ?

beats.say: Difference means the gap between the two ages: how much older one of them is than the other.
Think about this before any sum. 7 years ago, was the gap between them bigger, smaller, or the same as today?

ask.ifNot: Both of them were 7 years younger then. They step back together, so the gap between them does not move.

beats.say: Here is a fact worth keeping: the gap between two ages never changes. Every year, both people get exactly one year older.

spec.note: The extra piece is the gap between them

beats.say: So we only need the gap today. Arjun's bar is Riya's bar plus an extra piece. 47 minus 42 is 5.
Don't just take my word for it. Go back 7 years: Arjun was 47 minus 7, that is 40. Riya was 42 minus 7, that is 35.
And 40 minus 35 is 5. The very same gap!
So 7 years ago, the difference in their ages was 5 years.
The 7 years was only there to tempt us into extra sums. For a difference in ages, past or future, just subtract the ages you are given.
Arjun is at the shop, buying 15 sharpeners. Each one costs 7 rupees. Let us find the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one sharpener, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 15 sharpeners costs 7 rupees. That is 7 rupees, 15 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 15 is 10 and 5. So we do it in two easy bites. 10 times 7 is 70.
And 5 times 7 is 35.
Put the two bites together. 70 plus 35 makes 105. So 15 times 7 is 105.
So Arjun pays 105 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 105 rupees, in lots of 7 rupees, gives 15 sharpeners. It fits.
Remember it like this: price of one, times the number you buy, is the total cost. Your turn next!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 6 books at 3 rupees each, and Siya pays with 43 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 6 books at Rs.3 each. Pays Rs.43.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 43 rupees pays for the books, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the books
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 6 books, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 6 books at 3 rupees each: that is 6 times 3. 6 times 3 is 18.
Careful: 18 is only the cost, not the answer. Siya paid 43. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 18 away from 43.

beats.say: From 43, take off the 18. That leaves 25.
So Siya gets 25 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 18 plus 25 is 43. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
Isha pays 250 rupees for a tablet. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 250 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 250 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 250 divided by 10 gives 25.
20 per cent is 2 lots of 10 per cent. 2 times 25 is 50. That is the loss.
So the loss is 50 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 250 take away 50 is 200. So the selling price is 200 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 200 is 50 below 250. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Now you try one!
10 rulers, and every one costs 20 rupees. How much does Nikhil pay altogether?
Let us lay it out like a shop bill. One ruler costs 20 rupees, and there are 10 of them.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 10 rulers costs 20 rupees. That is 20 rupees, 10 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: Same price, 10 times, so it is a times sum. 20 times 10 is easy: 20 tens are 200.
So the total cost is 200 rupees.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 200 rupees, in lots of 20 rupees, gives 10 rulers. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. You can do the next one yourself!
Riya buys 5 books at 8 rupees each, and hands over 55 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 5 books at Rs.8 each. Pays Rs.55.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 55 rupees pays for the books, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the books
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 5 books, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

Careful: 40 is only the cost, not the answer. Riya paid 55. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 40 away from 55.

beats.say: 55 take away 40 leaves 15.
So Riya gets 15 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 40 plus 15 is 55. It works.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!
Aditya pays 250 rupees for a bag. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 10 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 250 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 10 per cent. But 10 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 250 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 out of every 100 is one tenth. To find a tenth, divide by 10. 250 divided by 10 is 25. That is the profit.
So the profit is 25 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 250 plus 25 is 275. So the selling price is 275 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 275 is 25 more than 250. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
7 notebooks, and every one costs 9 rupees. How much does Siddharth pay altogether?
Let us lay it out like a shop bill. One notebook costs 9 rupees, and there are 7 of them.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 7 notebooks costs 9 rupees. That is 9 rupees, 7 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: Same price, 7 times, so it is a times sum. 7 times 9 is 63.
So the total cost is 63 rupees.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 63 rupees, in lots of 9 rupees, gives 7 notebooks. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. Your turn next!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 8 crayons at 12 rupees each, and Ananya pays with 101 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 8 crayons at Rs.12 each. Pays Rs.101.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 101 rupees pays for the crayons, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the crayons
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 8 crayons, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 8 crayons at 12 rupees each: that is 8 times 12. 12 is 10 and 2. So we do it in two easy bites. 10 times 8 is 80.
And 2 times 8 is 16.
Put the two bites together. 80 plus 16 makes 96. So 8 times 12 is 96.
Careful: 96 is only the cost, not the answer. Ananya paid 101. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 96 away from 101.

beats.say: Count up from 96 to 101. That is 5 more.
So Ananya gets 5 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 96, plus the change, 5, should make the 101 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Now you try one!
The toy costs Aarav 150 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 40 per cent. What is the selling price?
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 150 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 40 per cent. But 40 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 150 rupees.

First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 150 divided by 10 gives 15.
40 per cent is 4 lots of 10 per cent. 4 times 15 is 60. That is the profit.
So the profit is 60 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 150 plus 60 is 210. So the selling price is 210 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 210 is 60 more than 150. It fits.

Nikhil is at the shop, buying 15 stickers. Each one costs 12 rupees. Let us find the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one sticker, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

And 5 times 12 is 60.

board.text: 4 notebooks at Rs.3 each. Pays Rs.17.

choices: the total cost of the notebooks

The toy costs Aditya 200 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 30 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 200 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 30 per cent. But 30 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 200 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 200 divided by 10 is 20.

Meera has 2 bags of lentils, and each bag weighs 10 kilograms 750 grams. We want the weight of all the bags together, in grams.

15 crayons, and every one costs 6 rupees. How much does Siya pay altogether?
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one crayon, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 15 crayons costs 6 rupees. That is 6 rupees, 15 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: Same price, 15 times, so it is a times sum. 15 is 10 and 5. So we do it in two easy bites. 10 times 6 is 60.
And 5 times 6 is 30.
Put the two bites together. 60 plus 30 makes 90. So 15 times 6 is 90.
So Siya pays 90 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 90 rupees, in lots of 6 rupees, gives 15 crayons. It fits.

Careful: 50 is only the cost, not the answer. Vivek paid 100. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 50 away from 100.

beats.say: 100 take away 50 leaves 50.
So Vivek gets 50 rupees back.

Isha pays 150 rupees for a watch. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 30 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 150 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 30 per cent. But 30 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 150 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 150 divided by 10 is 15.
30 per cent is 3 lots of 10 per cent. 3 times 15 is 45. That is the profit.
So the profit is 45 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 150 plus 45 is 195. So the selling price is 195 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 195 is 45 more than 150. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Now you try one!
Here is a rectangle, 18 centimetres long and 12 centimetres wide. We want its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides takes you along the edges, and that is the perimeter, the walk around. For the space inside we count rows of squares: length times width.

beats.say: Picture little squares, 1 centimetre each way. Every row holds 18 of them, and there are 12 rows. 12 rows of 18 is 18 times 12.
Split 12 into 10 and 2. 18 times 10 is 180, and 18 times 2 is 36. Together that makes 216.
So the area is 216 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we are counting little squares, not measuring along a line.
Check by undoing it. 216 shared into 12 rows gives 18 in each row, and that is our length. It fits.
Remember: area means the space inside, so multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the walk around the edge.

Find the H C F of 91 and 52. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 91 and 52 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both 91 and 52: that is our target. To find it, we split each number into its prime factors.
Take 91. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 7, and 13 is left. So 91 is 7 times 13.
52 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 52 is 2 times 2 times 13.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 91 and 52 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have a 13. The 7 belongs only to 91 and the 2 belongs only to 52, so they stay out.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share: just the 13. So the H C F is 13.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 91 divided by 13 is 7, and 52 divided by 13 is 4, with nothing left over. And 7 and 4 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.
Find the H C F of 33 and 55. H C F stands for highest common factor: the biggest number that divides both 33 and 55 exactly.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 33?

choices: No, it has to fit into 33
ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 33, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. We break each number into prime factors, the building blocks that cannot be split any further.
Take 33. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 3, and 11 is left. So 33 is 3 times 11.
Take 55. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 5, and 11 is left. So 55 is 5 times 11.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 33 and 55 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Let's ring them. Both lines have an 11. The 3 belongs only to 33 and the 5 belongs only to 55, so they stay out.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share: just the 11. So the H C F is 11.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 33 divided by 11 is 3, and 55 divided by 11 is 5, with nothing left over. And 3 and 5 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
Remember the three moves: split into primes, ring what is shared, multiply. And the H C F is never bigger than the smaller number.
We need the H C F of 6 and 8. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both of them with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 6?

choices: No, it has to fit into 6
ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 6, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. We break each number into prime factors, the building blocks that cannot be split any further.
Take 6. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, and 3 is left. So 6 is 2 times 3.
8 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 8 is 2 times 2 times 2.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 6 and 8 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Ring them on the board. Both lines have a 2. Careful: 8 has three 2s, but 6 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share: just the 2. So the H C F is 2.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 8 divided by 2 is 4, with nothing left over. And 3 and 4 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.

choices: No, it has to fit into 4
ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 4, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. We break each number into prime factors, the building blocks that cannot be split any further.
4 is even, so 2 comes out first. That leaves 2, so 4 is 2 times 2.
6 is even, so 2 comes out first. That leaves 3, so 6 is 2 times 3.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 4 and 6 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 4 divided by 2 is 2, and 6 divided by 2 is 3. Both divide exactly, and 2 and 3 have nothing more in common.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.

That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.
Find the H C F of 50 and 40. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

50 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 50 is 2 times 5 times 5.

Arjun has 104 marbles and shares them into two groups, in the ratio 3 is to 5. We want to know how many are in the larger group.

board.text: 104 marbles in the ratio 3 : 5. Larger group = ?

beats.say: First, what are we given? A total of 104, and a ratio, 3 is to 5. And what are we asked for? Just the larger group.
Let's draw the ratio. 3 is to 5: one bar with 3 equal parts, and one bar with 5. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 3 and 5 together make 8 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 5 is 8. So the whole 104 is cut into 8 equal parts.
Careful with this next step, it is the one that trips people up. What is one part worth?

ask.ifNot: The 104 fills all 8 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 104 by 8.

beats.say: 104 divided by 8 is 13. So every single part is worth 13 marbles.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 13

beats.say: We want the larger group, and that is 5 parts. 5 times 13 makes 65.
So the larger group has 65 marbles. There it is!
Let's check. The smaller group is 3 times 13, which is 39. And 39 plus 65 is 104, just what we started with.
That is the whole method. Total parts first, then one part, then the share the question asks for.
Here is a proportion. 5 is to 3, equals 20 is to x. Two ratios that are equal, with one number, x, in hiding.
Before any sum, look at what is given. The first ratio is whole: 5 is to 3. The second has its first number, 20, and a gap where x sits.
Compare the two first numbers, 5 and 20. What happened to 5 to turn it into 20?

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 5 times 4 gives 20, so it was multiplied by 4.

beats.say: 20 divided by 5 is 4. So the first number was multiplied by 4.
For the two ratios to stay equal, what must we do to the second number, 3?

ask.ifNot: Whatever was done to the first number must be done to the second. 5 was multiplied by 4, so 3 is multiplied by 4 as well.

beats.say: 3 times 4 is 12. Careful: we multiply here. Adding would break the ratio.
That makes x equal to 12.
Let's check. Divide 20 and 12 by 4, and we get 5 and 3 again. The two ratios match.
So in a proportion, find what the first number was multiplied by, then do the very same to the second.
We have to divide 28 in the ratio 2 is to 5, and find the smaller share.

board.text: Divide 28 in the ratio 2 : 5. Smaller share = ?

beats.say: Before any sum, let's be sure what we know. The total is 28. The ratio is 2 is to 5. And we want the smaller share only.
Let's draw the ratio. 2 is to 5: one bar with 2 equal parts, and one bar with 5. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 2 and 5 together make 7 parts.

beats.say: 2 plus 5 is 7. So the whole 28 is cut into 7 equal parts.
Here comes the turning point. Which sum tells us what a single part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 28 fills all 7 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 28 by 7.

beats.say: 28 divided by 7 is 4. So every single part is worth 4.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 4

beats.say: We want the smaller share, and that is 2 parts. 2 times 4 makes 8.
So the smaller share is 8. There it is!
Let's check. The larger share is 5 times 4, which is 20. And 8 plus 20 is 28, just what we started with.
Remember the three moves. Add the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for the share you want.

Here is our story. 51 marbles, split into two groups in the ratio 1 is to 2. How many marbles land in the larger group?

board.text: 51 marbles in the ratio 1 : 2. Larger group = ?

beats.say: First, what are we given? A total of 51, and a ratio, 1 is to 2. And what are we asked for? Just the larger group.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 1 and 2 together make 3 parts.

beats.say: 1 and 2 make 3. That means the 51 is spread over 3 equal parts.
Now for the step where slips happen. How do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 51 fills all 3 parts, not just the 2 parts of one bar. So we divide 51 by 3.

beats.say: 51 divided by 3 is 17. Now we can write 17 on every piece of both bars.

So 34 marbles are in the larger group.
Let's check. The smaller group is just 1 part, which is 17. And 17 plus 34 is 51, the number we started with.
Remember the three moves. Add the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for the share you want.
This says 2 is to 9, equals 6 is to x. So the second ratio is the first one in disguise, and x is its missing number.

Find the H C F of 30 and 70. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 30 and 70 exactly.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number that goes into both 30 and 70. The plan: break each number into prime factors, its building blocks.
Take 30. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, then 3, and 5 is left. So 30 is 2 times 3 times 5.
70 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 70 is 2 times 5 times 7.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 30 and 70 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Let's ring them. Both lines have a 2 and a 5. The 3 belongs only to 30 and the 7 belongs only to 70, so they stay out.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 5 is 10. So the H C F is 10.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 30 divided by 10 is 3, and 70 divided by 10 is 7, with nothing left over. And 3 and 7 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
Remember the three moves: split into primes, ring what is shared, multiply. And the H C F is never bigger than the smaller number.

beats.say: The opposite of plus 5 is minus 5. So we take away 5, and we do it on both sides so the balance stays level.
On the left, plus 5 and minus 5 cancel each other out. On the right, 17 minus 5 leaves 12.
Now 2 x is 2 lots of x. How do we get from 2 lots down to just one?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2.
12 divided by 2 is 6. So x equals 6. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 6 back in place of x. 2 times 6 is 12, and 12 plus 5 is 17. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added or taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Look at this equation. 8 x, plus 20, equals 100. We want the x all on its own, so we can see what it is.
The two sides balance, like a see-saw. We want the 8 x alone on its side. What do we clear away first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 8 x has a plus 20 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: To undo plus 20, we take away 20. And to keep the balance level, we do it to both sides.
The left side is now just 8 x. The right side is 100 minus 20, which is 80.
Now 8 x is 8 lots of x. How do we get from 8 lots down to just one?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 8, we divide by 8.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 8.
80 shared into 8 equal parts gives 10 each. So x equals 10. Found it!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 10 back in place of x. 8 times 10 is 80, and 80 plus 20 is 100. It works.
Two moves, every time. Undo the plus or minus first, then undo the times. And always do the same to both sides.
Here is our equation. 2 x, minus 6, equals 10. Somewhere behind that x a number is hiding, and we are going to find it.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 2 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 2 x has a minus 6 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: To undo minus 6, we add 6. And to keep the balance level, we do it to both sides.
The left side is now just 2 x. The right side is 10 plus 6, which is 16.
Now 2 x is 2 lots of x. How do we get from 2 lots down to just one?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2.
16 shared into 2 equal parts gives 8 each. So x equals 8. Found it!
Let's check it. With 8 in place of x, 2 times 8 is 16. Then 16 minus 6 gives 10, just as the equation says.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added or taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Look at this one. 42 minus 2 times 2, plus 3. Before we work anything out, we need to decide where to start.
Where shall we start?

ask.ifNot: Starting from the left with 42 minus 2 is the natural thing to try. But times is stronger than plus and minus, so 2 times 2 has to go first.

beats.say: Times comes before plus and minus, so this pair goes first. I'll underline it. 2 times 2 is 4.
So 2 times 2 turns into 4, and the rest of the line comes down unchanged.
Two signs left, a minus and a plus. Which pair goes next?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equally strong, so neither jumps the queue. We simply go from left to right, and 42 minus 4 is on the left.

beats.say: Left to right, so 42 minus 4 first, and that is 38. Watch out: we are taking away 4 only, not 4 and 3 together.
Last step. 38 plus 3 makes 41. That is our answer.
So here is the plan for a line like this. Hunt for times and divide and do those first. Then do the plus and minus, from left to right.
Look at this one. 30 divided by 3, plus 2 times 3. Before we work anything out, we decide what goes first.
The plus sits in the middle. What must we work out before we can use it?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times are both stronger than plus. So both of those pairs are worked out first, and the plus waits in the middle until they are done.

beats.say: Divide and times both come before plus. Let's take them one at a time. 30 divided by 3 is 10.
And the other pair: 2 times 3 makes 6.
Now we write the line again with those two answers in place. It has shrunk to 10 plus 6.
At last the plus gets its turn. 10 plus 6 is 16. That is our answer.
Here is the trap. Working along from the left, one step at a time, is like wrapping a bracket round the first part. That gives 36, which belongs to a different sum.
Remember it like this. Times and divide go first, wherever they sit. Plus and minus wait their turn, then go from left to right.
Look at this line. 29 times 7, plus 11. Short, but it still has an order to follow.
Have a look at the two signs. Where do we start?

ask.ifNot: 7 plus 11 looks like the easier bit, so it is tempting. But times is stronger than plus, so 29 times 7 has to go first.

beats.say: I'll underline 29 times 7, because times goes before plus. To make it easier, we break 29 into 20 and 9.
20 times 7 is 140, and 9 times 7 is 63. Put them together and we get 203.
So 29 times 7 has turned into 203, and the plus 11 is still waiting at the end.
And 203 plus 11 is 214. That is our answer.
Here is why the order matters. Doing 7 plus 11 first is like putting a bracket round them, and that gives 522. A different sum, so a different answer.
That is the whole trick. Before you work anything out, look at the signs. Times and divide first, then plus and minus in order.
Look at this one. The square root of x, plus 10, makes 22. Our job is to find x itself.
The root of x is not alone on the left. Something is sitting next to it. What should we move out of the way first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 10 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: Plus 10 is undone by minus 10. Whatever we do on the left, we do on the right as well.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 22 minus 10 gives us 12.
Careful, this is where many people stop! 12 is the square root of x, not x. So how do we get x from 12?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 12 times 12, not 12 times 2.

beats.say: Picture a square of tiles, 12 rows with 12 tiles in each row. The side of the square is the root. All the tiles together are x.
12 times 12 is a big one, so we split it. 12 times 10 is 120, and 12 times 2 is 24.
Add them up: 120 plus 24 makes 144. So x equals 144.
Let's check it. The square root of 144 is 12, and 12 plus 10 is 22. It fits perfectly.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!

Neha is at the shop, buying 7 pens. Each one costs 5 rupees. Let us find the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one pen, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 7 pens costs 5 rupees. That is 5 rupees, 7 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 7 times 5 is 35.
So Neha pays 35 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 35 rupees, in lots of 5 rupees, gives 7 pens. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. Your turn next!
Nikhil buys 5 markers at 9 rupees each, and hands over 50 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 5 markers at Rs.9 each. Pays Rs.50.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 50 rupees pays for the markers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the markers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 5 markers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 5 markers at 9 rupees each: that is 5 times 9. 5 times 9 is 45.
Careful: 45 is only the cost, not the answer. Nikhil paid 50. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 45 away from 50.

beats.say: Count up from 45 to 50. That is 5 more.
So Nikhil gets 5 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 45 plus 5 is 50. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
Riya pays 50 rupees for a toy. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 10 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 50 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 10 per cent. But 10 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 50 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 out of every 100 is one tenth. To find a tenth, divide by 10. 50 divided by 10 is 5. That is the profit.
So the profit is 5 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 50 plus 5 is 55. So the selling price is 55 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 55 is 5 above 50. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Find the H C F of 40 and 70. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 40 and 70 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both 40 and 70: that is our target. To find it, we split each number into its prime factors.
Take 40. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 three times, and 5 is left. So 40 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 5.
Take 70. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, then 5, and 7 is left. So 70 is 2 times 5 times 7.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 40 and 70 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Ring them on the board. Both lines have a 2 and a 5. Careful: 40 has three 2s, but 70 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 5 is 10. So the H C F is 10.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 40 divided by 10 is 4, and 70 divided by 10 is 7, with nothing left over. And 4 and 7 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.
Find the H C F of 16 and 56. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 16 and 56 exactly.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number that goes into both 16 and 56. The plan: break each number into prime factors, its building blocks.
Take 16. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 three times, and 2 is left. So 16 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 2.
56 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 56 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 7.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 16 and 56 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have three 2s. Careful: 16 has four 2s, but 56 has only three 2s. So only three 2s are shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 2 times 2 is 8. So the H C F is 8.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 16 divided by 8 is 2, and 56 divided by 8 is 7, with nothing left over. And 2 and 7 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
So the plan for any H C F: break both numbers into primes, keep only the primes they share, and multiply those. Your turn next!
Find the H C F of 21 and 49. H C F stands for highest common factor: the biggest number that divides both 21 and 49 exactly.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 21?

choices: No, it has to fit into 21
ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 21, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. We break each number into prime factors, the building blocks that cannot be split any further.
Take 21. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 3, and 7 is left. So 21 is 3 times 7.
Take 49. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 7, and 7 is left. So 49 is 7 times 7.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 21 and 49 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Ring them on the board. Both lines have a 7. Careful: 49 has two 7s, but 21 has only one 7. So only one 7 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share: just the 7. So the H C F is 7.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 21 divided by 7 is 3, and 49 divided by 7 is 7. Both divide exactly, and 3 and 7 have nothing more in common.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.

beats.say: So how do we find it? We split each number into its prime factors, the smallest building blocks it is made of.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

7 x, plus 18, equals 95. Someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 7, then added 18, and got 95. Let's work backwards and find that number.
The two sides are worth the same, like a level see-saw. To get x alone we undo things, last one first. The plus 18 was done last. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners: each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 18, we take away 18.

beats.say: And here is the rule of the balance: whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So 18 comes off both sides.
On the left, plus 18 and minus 18 cancel each other out. On the right, 95 minus 18 makes 77.
It is tempting to stop here and say 77. But that is 7 x, and we want just x. 7 x means 7 times x. What undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 7, we divide by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7.

Good mathematicians always check. Put 11 back in place of x. 7 times 11 is 77, and 77 plus 18 is 95. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added. Then undo the times. Your turn next!

Which is greater, one quarter or 1 over 6? Let's find out.
Here they are as two bars of the same length. The first is cut into 4 pieces with 1 shaded. The second is cut into 6 pieces with 1 shaded.

No, the pieces are different sizes

We are adding two fractions. 10 over 12, plus 4 over 12. And we must give the answer in its simplest form.

beats.say: So we only count the pieces. 10 pieces and 4 pieces make 14 pieces.

beats.say: So we divide the top and the bottom by 2. 14 divided by 2 is 7, and 12 divided by 2 is 6.

So when the bottom numbers match: add the tops, keep the bottom, and then simplify if you can.

Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 300 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 300 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
25 per cent is one quarter, because 4 lots of 25 make 100. To find a quarter, halve it, then halve it again. Half of 300 is 150.
And half of 150 is 75. So 25 per cent of 300 is 75 rupees. That is the loss.

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 300 take away 75 is 225. So the selling price is 225 rupees.

So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Your turn next!

beats.say: 48 take away 36 leaves 12. Aarav keeps 12 marbles.
