To place brackets, work backwards from the answer, and build the number you need from the ones that are there.
Three letters, but only a is given. b is built from a, and c is built from b. So we find them in that order.
b first. a minus 1 is 17 minus 1, which is 16. Half of 16 is 8. So b is 8.
Then c is b plus 3. 8 plus 3 is 11.
Now the squares. What does a squared mean, when a is 17?

ask.ifNot: Squared means the number times itself. So 17 squared is 17 times 17, not 17 times 2.

beats.say: 17 times 17 is 289. 11 times 11 is 121. And 8 times 8 is 64.
So we have 289, minus 121, plus 64. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are done from left to right. Adding 121 and 64 first would take away too much.

beats.say: 289 minus 121 is 168. Then 168 plus 64 is 232.
So: find the letters in order, square each one, then work from left to right. The answer is 232.
16000 rupees is invested for 18 months, at 8 per cent per annum. We want the simple interest.

board.text: Rs.16000 for 18 months at 8% per annum

beats.say: Per annum means every year. 8 per cent means every 100 rupees earns 8 rupees in one year. And 16000 is 160 hundreds.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.8 in 1 year

beats.say: So one year earns 160 times 8. 16 times 8 is 128, so 160 times 8 is 1280 rupees.
The rate is for a year, but the money is invested for 18 months. How long is 18 months?

ask.ifNot: A year has 12 months. 18 months is 12 months and 6 more. That is 1 year, and half a year.

beats.say: Careful, that is the trap here: the 18 is months, not years. The first year earns 1280. The extra 6 months is half a year, so it earns half of 1280, which is 640.
1280 plus 640 is 1920. So the simple interest is 1920 rupees.
Check with the formula. The time must be in years, and 18 months is 1.5 years. 16000 times 8 times 1.5, divided by 100, is 1920.
So always check the time. If it is in months, turn it into years before you use the yearly rate.

board.text: six hundred hundreds = how many tens?

beats.say: Six hundred hundreds. That sounds like a tongue twister, so let's turn it into numbers.

ask.ifNot: Times 100 puts 2 more zeros on the end. 600 with 2 more zeros is 60,000.

beats.say: Six hundred is 600, and one hundred is 100. So six hundred hundreds means 600 lots of 100. What is 600 times 100?
600 times 100 is 60,000. Two more zeros on the end.

ask.ifNot: Each ten is a group of 10. To see how many groups of 10 fit into a number, we divide it by 10.

beats.say: Careful: 60,000 is the whole amount, not the number of tens. How do we find how many tens are inside it?
Dividing by 10 takes one zero off the end. 60,000 becomes 6000.
Check by going back: 6000 tens is 6000 times 10, which is 60,000. That is our six hundred hundreds.
So 6000 tens form six hundred hundreds. Turn the words into a number first, then ask how many tens fit in.

board.text: place value = face value, in every place?

beats.say: We want a digit whose place value and face value are the same, wherever it sits. Face value is the digit as it looks. Place value is what it is worth in its column.
Let's test 9. Put it in the tens place. Now it is worth 9 times 10, which is 90, but its face is still 9. Not the same.

ask.ifNot: 1 in the tens column means one ten. That is worth 10, not 1.

beats.say: Now try 1 in the tens place. Is its place value the same as its face value?
1 in the tens place is worth 10, but its face value is 1. So 1 does not work either.
Now zero. Put 0 in the tens place, the hundreds place, the thousands place. 0 times 10 is 0. 0 times 100 is 0. 0 times 1000 is 0.
Zero times anything is zero. So the place value of 0 is always 0, and its face value is 0 as well. They match in every column.
So the digit is 0.
In the units place every digit matches its face value. But only zero keeps them equal everywhere.

board.text: The place value is odd. Which place?

beats.say: A digit has an odd place value. Which column could it be sitting in? Let's try a digit, say 7, in different columns and see.

ask.ifNot: 70 ends in 0, and any number ending in 0 can be halved exactly. So it is even.

beats.say: In the tens place, 7 is worth 7 times 10, which is 70. Is 70 odd or even?
Even. In fact anything times 10 ends in 0, so a place value in the tens column is always even.
Hundreds and thousands tell the same story. 700 and 7000 both end in zeros, so they are even too.
But in the units place, 7 is worth just 7. No zero on the end, and 7 is odd.
Careful: the digit itself must be odd too. A 4 in the units place is worth 4, which is even. But the units place is the only one where odd is possible at all.
So a digit with an odd place value must be in the units place.
Tens, hundreds and beyond always end in zero, so they are always even. Odd place values live only in the units place.
Here is 69512. We need two special digits: the one with the greatest place value, and the one with the least.
Place value depends on the column. The column furthest left is worth the most, and the column furthest right is worth the least.

ask.ifNot: 9 is the biggest digit to look at, but it sits in the thousands. The 6 is in the ten-thousands, so the 6 is worth more.

beats.say: So which digit has the greatest place value?
The 6 is worth 60000. The 9 is only worth 9000. Don't let the big 9 fool you.
And the least place value is in the units column. That is the 2, worth just 2.
The question asks for the difference between the digits themselves. 6 minus 2 is 4.
So the difference is 4.
Greatest place value means furthest left. Least means furthest right. The size of the digit does not decide it.
Here is 76025. We are comparing the place value of the 6 with the place value of the 2.

ask.ifNot: Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. So the 6 means 6 thousands.

beats.say: Here they are in the chart. The 6 sits in the thousands column. What is it worth?
6 times 1000 is 6000. And the 2 is in the tens column, so it is worth 2 times 10, which is 20.

ask.ifNot: Dividing the digits, 6 by 2, forgets their columns. We must divide the place values: 6000 by 20.

beats.say: Now, how many times 20 is 6000? Which sum tells us?
6000 divided by 20. Cross one zero off each to make it easy: 600 divided by 2 is 300.
Check it: 300 times 20 gives back 6000. It works.
So the place value of the 6 is 300 times the place value of the 2.
Two place values first, then one division. Dividing the digits alone would have given 3, and missed by a long way.
Four numbers, each with two 8s. In just one of them, one 8 is worth a thousand times the other 8.

ask.ifNot: Each column is one more times 10. We need times 10 three times over to reach 1000, so the 8s are 3 columns apart.

beats.say: Here is the key. Each step to the left makes a digit worth 10 times more, and 10 times 10 times 10 is 1000. So how far apart must the two 8s be?
So we just hunt for two 8s that are 3 columns apart. In 68815 the 8s are side by side, only 1 apart. Out.
65818 has one 8 in the hundreds and one in the units. That is 2 apart. Out.
81586 has one 8 in the ten-thousands and one in the tens. Count the steps between them: 3. This looks right!
Check with the real values. The first 8 is worth 80000 and the other is worth 80. 80000 divided by 80 is 1000.
And in 85168 the 8s are 4 apart, which would be ten thousand times. So that one is out too.
So the number is 81586. The digit is the same both times, so only the gap between the columns matters.
Four numbers, and each has more than one 3. We want the one where one 3 is worth a hundred times another 3.

ask.ifNot: One step left is times 10. Two steps is times 10 and times 10 again, which is times 100. So 2 columns apart.

beats.say: Each column to the left is worth 10 times more, and 10 times 10 is 100. So how far apart must the 3s be?
134639: its 3s are in the ten-thousands and the tens. That is 3 apart. Too far.
752339: the two 3s are next door to each other. Only 1 apart.
863135: one 3 in the thousands, one in the tens. 2 apart. Promising!
Check with the values. The first 3 is worth 3000, the other is worth 30. 3000 divided by 30 is 100.
And 307638 has one 3 in the lakhs place and one in the tens, 4 apart. Out.
So the number is 863135. To be 100 times bigger, the same digit must sit exactly 2 columns to the left.
Here is a five digit number with two stars in it. Both stars hide the same digit, and we are going to find it.
First, look at where the stars sit. Which two places are they in?

ask.ifNot: Count the places from the right. The 9 is in the ones, the 1 is in the tens. Then come the two stars, in the hundreds and the thousands.

beats.say: Let's call the hidden digit d. In the thousands place it is worth 1000 times d. In the hundreds place it is worth 100 times d.
We are told the difference between those two values is 5400. So 1000 d, minus 100 d, equals 5400.
1000 lots of d, take away 100 lots of d, leaves 900 lots of d. So 900 d equals 5400.
900 d means 900 times d. What undoes times 900?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 900, we divide by 900, and we do it to both sides.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 900. 5400 divided by 900 is 6.
Let's check. A 6 in the thousands place is worth 6000. A 6 in the hundreds place is worth 600. 6000 minus 600 is 5400. It works.
So when the same digit sits in two places, write each place value using a letter, subtract, and solve. The digit is 6.
This number has two stars, and the same digit hides behind both. Let's find out which digit it is.
The same digit is worth different amounts in different places. So, where are the two stars?

ask.ifNot: Count from the right: 2 is in the ones, then a star in the tens, 8 in the hundreds, and the other star in the thousands.

beats.say: Call the digit d. In the thousands place it is worth 1000 times d. In the tens place it is worth 10 times d.
The question says the difference between those values is 6930. So 1000 d, minus 10 d, equals 6930.
1000 lots of d, take away 10 lots of d, is 990 lots of d.
Now d is being multiplied by 990. How do we get d on its own?

ask.ifNot: 990 d means 990 times d, and divide is what undoes times. So we divide both sides by 990.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide by 990. 990 times 7 is 6930, so d equals 7.
Check it. A 7 in the thousands place is worth 7000, and a 7 in the tens place is worth 70. 7000 minus 70 is 6930. Just right.
So the repeated digit is 7. The trick was to write both place values with one letter, then solve a small equation.
Two stars again, hiding the same digit. But this time we are not told the digit. We are asked what the difference between its two place values could be.
Start with the places. Where do the two stars sit?

ask.ifNot: From the right: 4 is in the ones, a star in the tens, 8 in the hundreds, and the other star in the thousands.

beats.say: Let's try the easiest digit, 1. Then the two place values are 1000 and 10, and the difference is 990.
If the digit were 2, we would get 2000 minus 20. That is just 2 lots of 990. So the difference is always the digit times 990.
So the right choice must be in the 990 times table. 540 is smaller than 990, so it is out. Have a think: which of the others could it be?
2 times 990 is 1980, so 1880 just misses. 3 times 990 is 2970, and 4 times is 3960, so 3030 is skipped too.
Now try the biggest digit, 9. 9 times 990 is 8910. That is one of our choices!
Check with the digit 9. In the thousands place it is worth 9000, and in the tens place 90. 9000 minus 90 is 8910.
So the difference can be 8910. When you do not know the digit, try 1 first and look for the pattern.

board.text: digits 1, 5, 0, 8: greatest number, then its successor

beats.say: Two jobs here. First build the greatest number from the digits 1, 5, 0 and 8. Then find its successor.

ask.ifNot: The thousands place is worth the most, so it deserves the biggest digit we have. That is 8.

beats.say: For the greatest number, the biggest digit should go where it is worth the most: the thousands place. Which digit goes first?
Then the next biggest in the hundreds, and so on down: 8, 5, 1, 0. That gives 8510.
Now, successor. That is simply the number that comes next when we count. So we add 1.
Careful: the successor does not have to use our four digits. 8511 has two 1s, and that is fine. It is just the next number.
So the answer is 8511.
Greatest number: biggest digits first. Successor: add 1. Two small steps.
We build the greatest odd number from 5, 8, 0, 7 and 4, and then look at its middle digit.

ask.ifNot: A number is odd when its units digit is odd. The other digits make no difference.

beats.say: Whether a number is odd is decided by one digit only. Which one?
So the last digit must be odd. Our odd digits are 5 and 7.

ask.ifNot: The units place is worth the least. So we give it the smaller odd digit, 5, and keep the 7 for a place that is worth more.

beats.say: We want the number as big as possible. So which odd digit should we spend on the units place?
With 5 at the end, arrange the rest from biggest to smallest: 8, 7, 4, 0. That makes 87405.
Compare it with putting 7 last, which gives 85407. That is smaller, so 87405 wins.
Now the middle. There are 5 digits, so the middle one is the third: 4.
Decide the last digit first, using the smaller odd digit. Then line the others up, biggest first.
First we build the smallest even number from 2, 7, 3, 9 and 6. Then we find what its 7 is worth.
Even means the last digit is even. Our even digits are 2 and 6, so one of them must go last.

ask.ifNot: The front place is worth the most, so the smallest digit should go there to keep the number small. That means the 6 goes last.

beats.say: For the smallest number, the 2 is precious. Where is it most useful?
So 6 goes at the end, and the others go from smallest to biggest: 2, 3, 7, 9. That makes 23796.
Check the other choice. Ending in 2, the smallest we could make is 36792, and that is bigger.
Now find the 7. Count from the right: units, tens, hundreds. The 7 is in the hundreds place.
7 hundreds: 7 times 100 is 700.
Careful: 'hundreds' is only the name of the place. The place value is the number, 700.
Build the number first, then read the place. Two questions hiding in one.

board.text: 2-digit even numbers with an odd tens digit

beats.say: We are counting 2 digit numbers that are even, and have an odd digit in the tens place. Let's count the choices for each place.
The tens digit must be odd: 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. That is 5 choices.

ask.ifNot: The even digits are 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8. Do not forget 0: it is even too. That makes 5.

beats.say: The number must be even, so the units digit is even. How many choices are there for it?
0, 2, 4, 6, 8. Five choices, and zero is one of them.
Each tens digit can pair with every one of those. Take tens digit 1: we get 10, 12, 14, 16, 18. That is 5 numbers.
The same happens for 3, 5, 7 and 9. So 5 tens digits, with 5 numbers each: 5 times 5 is 25.
So there are 25 such numbers.
Count the choices for each place, then multiply. No need to write out all 25.
Four digits, 7, 0, 3 and 9, each used once. How many different 4 digit numbers can we make? Let's fill the places one at a time, from the left.

ask.ifNot: 0 cannot go first, because then the number would really have only 3 digits. So only 7, 3 or 9 can lead. 3 choices.

beats.say: Start with the thousands place. How many of our digits are allowed there?
Zero cannot lead, so the thousands place has 3 choices.
One digit is used up, so 3 are left for the hundreds, and zero is welcome now. Then 2 are left for the tens, and 1 for the units.
Multiply the choices. 3 times 3 is 9, times 2 is 18, times 1 is still 18.
Let's check one group. Starting with 7 we get 7039, 7093, 7309, 7390, 7903 and 7930: 6 numbers. The same for 3 and for 9.
So 18 different numbers can be formed.
Go place by place from the left, count the choices, and multiply. Just remember that zero can never lead.
Digits 2, 5, 0 and 8, each used once. We want the 4 digit numbers that are less than 5000.

ask.ifNot: 0 cannot lead a 4 digit number. And with 5 in front the number is at least 5000, which is not less than 5000. Only 2 works.

beats.say: The thousands digit decides whether a number is below 5000. Which of our digits can go there?
So every one of our numbers starts with 2.
The digits 5, 0 and 8 fill the other three places. 3 choices for the hundreds, then 2 for the tens, then 1 for the units.
Six numbers, and even the biggest, 2850, is well below 5000.
So 6 numbers can be formed.
Deal with the place that has a rule first. Here that was the thousands place. Then count the rest and multiply.
Here is a queue. Anay is 10th from the front, Vinay is 8th from the end, and 5 people stand between them. How long is the whole queue?

board.text: Anay 10th from front, Vinay 8th from end, 5 between

beats.say: Let's build the queue in three parts. First part: everyone from the front up to Anay. How many people is that, counting Anay?

ask.ifNot: Anay is the 10th person in line. So from the front up to Anay there are exactly 10 people, with Anay as the last of them.

beats.say: So the front part holds 10 people. The back part works the same way: from Vinay to the end there are 8 people, Vinay included. And 5 stand in the middle.
Now, how do we get the whole queue from these three parts?

ask.ifNot: Look at the bar. The three parts sit side by side with no overlap. Nobody is counted twice, so the queue is all three added together.

beats.say: 10 plus 5 is 15, and 15 plus 8 is 23. There are 23 people in the queue.
Quick check, person by person. 9 ahead of Anay, then Anay, 5 more, Vinay, and 7 behind. That makes 23 again.
So for a queue question, draw the line, mark the parts, and ask yourself whether anyone is counted twice before you add.
We want the 23rd even number before 105. Let's start walking backwards from 105 and see what happens.
105 is odd, so the 1st even number before it is 104. Then come 102, 100 and 98. What is the jump each time we step back?

ask.ifNot: Even numbers are 2 apart. Going backwards, each one is 2 less than the one before.

beats.say: Minus 2, every time.
Now, the trap. 104 is already the 1st one. To reach the 2nd we step back once. To reach the 3rd, twice.
So how many steps back from 104 take us to the 23rd?

ask.ifNot: Look at the table. The steps are always 1 fewer than the position, because 104 itself is number 1. So the 23rd needs 22 steps.

beats.say: 22 steps, and each step is 2. 22 times 2 is 44.
Start at 104 and go back 44. 104 minus 44 is 60. So the 23rd even number before 105 is 60.
Test the idea on one we know. The 3rd is 2 steps back from 104: 104 minus 2 times 2 is 100. And 100 is third in our list.
So: find the first one, take 1 fewer steps than the position, and step back.
Q is some odd number. We want the gap between the even number just before it and the even number just after it.
We are not told Q, so let's try one. Say Q is 7. Which even numbers sit on either side of 7?

ask.ifNot: Odd and even numbers take turns. So the even numbers are right next door to 7: one step back is 6, one step on is 8.

beats.say: There they are on the number line. 6, then 7, then 8. One step up to reach Q, and one more step to go past it.
So the difference is 8 minus 6, which is 2.
Was that just luck with 7? Try another odd number, 13. Its even neighbours are 12 and 14, and 14 minus 12 is 2 again.
It always works. The even number before is Q minus 1, and the one after is Q plus 1. From one to the other is 2 steps.
Careful not to say 1. That is the gap from Q to one neighbour. We wanted the gap from neighbour to neighbour.
When a question uses a letter for a number, try a real number or two. The pattern usually jumps out.
K is an even number, and we want the 12th odd number before it. We don't know K, so let's try it with a real number first.
Pretend K is 30, just to see the pattern. The odd numbers before 30 are 29, 27, 25, and so on.
How far back is each one? 29 is 1 back from K. 27 is 3 back. 25 is 5 back.
1, 3, 5. What kind of numbers are those steps back?

ask.ifNot: 1, 3, 5: they start at 1 and jump in 2s. Those are the odd numbers themselves.

beats.say: So the 12th odd number before K is K, minus the 12th odd number. Now we only need to know the 12th odd number.
Each odd number is 1 less than its even partner. The 1st even is 2 and the 1st odd is 1. The 2nd even is 4 and the 2nd odd is 3.
The 12th even number is 2 times 12, which is 24. So what is the 12th odd number?

ask.ifNot: Each odd number is 1 less than its even partner. The 12th even is 24, so the 12th odd is 23.

beats.say: 24 minus 1 is 23. So the 12th odd number before K is K minus 23.
Check with our pretend K of 30: 30 minus 23 is 7. And 11 steps of 2 back from 29 also lands on 7. It works.
The trap is K minus 24: that is the 12th even number before K. The odd ones sit 1 closer, so the answer is K minus 23.
Three numbers add up to 1478, but three digits are hiding behind the letters A, B and C. Let's set the sum out in columns.

spec.note: Three rows added; the bottom row is the total

beats.say: With a sum like this, which column do we start with?

ask.ifNot: We add from the right, because any carry moves to the left. So the units column comes first, just as in an ordinary sum.

beats.say: Units column: 8, plus B, plus 1, must end in 8. Now 8 plus 1 is 9, so 9 plus B has to end in 8.
Which digit, added to 9, gives a number ending in 8?

ask.ifNot: 9 plus a small digit cannot end in 8, so the total has to go past 10. Try the biggest digit there is: 9 plus 9 does end in 8.

beats.say: So B is 9. And 8 plus 9 plus 1 is 18: we write the 8 and carry 1 to the tens.
Tens column: 4, plus 2, plus C, plus the carried 1, must end in 7. But 4 plus 2 plus 1 is already 7. So C adds nothing at all: C is 0.
Hundreds column: A plus 3 plus 5 must make 14. 3 plus 5 is 8, and 8 plus 6 is 14. So A is 6.
So A is 6, B is 9 and C is 0.
Let's check with the whole sum. 648 plus 329 plus 501 is 1478. It works.
For a missing-digit sum, go column by column from the right, and never forget the carry.
A subtraction with two digits hidden, P and Q. We want P plus Q, so first we must find each one.

spec.note: Top row take away the middle row gives the bottom row

beats.say: Start on the right, as always. Units: 3 minus 2 is 1, and the answer shows 1. Good, nothing was borrowed there.
Tens column: P minus 6 has to give 8. Can a single digit, take away 6, leave 8?

choices: No, so the tens must borrow
ask.ifNot: A single digit is at most 9, and 9 minus 6 is only 3. So to reach 8, the tens column must borrow 1 from the hundreds.

beats.say: With the borrow, the top of the tens column becomes 10 plus P. And that, minus 6, is 8. So 10 plus P is 14, and P is 4.
Now the hundreds. Careful: the 8 lent 1 to the tens, so it is only 7 now. And 7 minus 5 is 2, so Q is 2. Forget the borrow and you would get 3.
Thousands: 9 minus 4 is 5, which matches. So the whole sum reads 9843 minus 4562 equals 5281.
And the question asked for P plus Q. 4 plus 2 is 6.
Column by column from the right. And when a column cannot be done, look for a borrow: it changes the column next door too.
Two lists of 10 numbers each. Natural numbers start at 1. Whole numbers start at 0. We want to know how much bigger one total is than the other.

board.text: First 10 natural numbers and first 10 whole numbers

beats.say: The first 10 natural numbers are 1 up to 10. What are the first 10 whole numbers?

ask.ifNot: Whole numbers begin at 0. Count 10 of them starting from 0, and you stop at 9, not at 10.

beats.say: Let's write both lists, one under the other.
Now look before you add. The numbers 1 to 9 are in both lists. They add the same amount to both totals, so they cannot make any difference.
So what is left over? In the natural list, the 10. In the whole list, the 0.
The difference between the two totals is just 10 minus 0, which is 10.
If you like, check by adding. 1 up to 10 makes 55, and 0 up to 9 makes 45. And 55 minus 45 is 10.
So before adding two long lists, look for what they share. Often only the ends are different.
We add two odd numbers and look at the last digit of the answer. One of these four digits can never turn up there.

board.text: odd + odd: which last digit is impossible?

beats.say: Let's try a few and watch what happens. 1 plus 7 is 8. 3 plus 3 is 6. 5 plus 5 is 10.
Look at those answers: 8, 6 and 10. What kind of numbers are they?

ask.ifNot: Check each one: 8, 6 and 10 can all be split into two equal halves. So they are all even.

beats.say: That is no accident. Every odd number is some pairs with one left over. Add two odd numbers and the two leftovers pair up, so the sum is always even.
And even numbers can only end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
Now look at our four choices. Which one is not on that list?

ask.ifNot: 0, 6 and 8 are all on the list of even endings. 5 is the odd one out.

beats.say: 5 is an odd digit, so it can never be the last digit of odd plus odd.
The rule to keep: odd plus odd is always even. Then just look for the odd digit.
Here is a little number machine: 2 X plus 11. X can be any counting number we like. The question asks what kind of number can never come out.
When a question says any number, try a few small ones. With X as 1 we get 13. With 2 we get 15. With 3 we get 17.
Look at 13, 15 and 17. What do they have in common?

ask.ifNot: Look at the last digits: 3, 5 and 7. None of these numbers can be shared into 2 equal groups. They are all odd. And 15 is 3 times 5, so they are not all prime.

beats.say: Is that just luck? No. 2 times any whole number is always even. That is what even means.
And 11 is odd. An even number plus an odd number is always odd.
So 2 X plus 11 is odd every single time. That means it can never be even.
And the other choices? 13 and 17 are prime, so it can be prime. And every answer we got was a whole number. So those can happen.
So the plan: try a few small numbers, spot the pattern, then ask why the pattern must always hold.
The first 25 even numbers, added up, minus the first 25 odd numbers, added up. That sounds like a lot of adding!

board.text: Sum of first 25 evens − sum of first 25 odds = ?

beats.say: Before we do all that work, let's hunt for a short cut. Try a tiny version: just the first 3 of each, lined up in pairs.
Pair them up: 2 with 1, 4 with 3, 6 with 5. How much bigger is each even number than its odd partner?

ask.ifNot: 2 minus 1 is 1. 4 minus 3 is 1. 6 minus 5 is 1. Each even number is just 1 more than its partner.

beats.say: So with 3 pairs, the evens should win by 3. Let's see: 2 plus 4 plus 6 is 12, and 1 plus 3 plus 5 is 9. 12 minus 9 is 3. Yes!
Our real question has 25 pairs, and each pair gives the evens 1 extra. So what is the difference?

ask.ifNot: Every pair gives the evens 1 extra. There are 25 pairs, so 25 extras. The big numbers never need adding at all.

beats.say: 25 lots of 1 is 25. The difference is 25.
If you do add them the long way, the evens come to 650 and the odds come to 625. And 650 minus 625 is 25. Same answer, far more work.
When two lists pair up neatly, compare them pair by pair instead of adding everything.
In how many ways can 28 be written as a sum of two odd numbers?

board.text: 28 = odd number + odd number. How many ways?

beats.say: Notice what it wants. Not one sum, but a count: how many different pairs of odd numbers add up to 28.
The secret of counting is to go in order. Start with the smallest odd number, 1. 1 plus what makes 28? 27, and 27 is odd. That is our first pair.
Next odd number, 3. 3 plus 25. Then 5 plus 23. See the pattern? One side goes up by 2, and the other comes down by 2.
Keep going the same way. 7 plus 21. 9 plus 19. 11 plus 17. 13 plus 15.
The next one would be 15 plus 13. Should we count it?

choices: yes, it is a new pair
yes, and go on up to 27 + 1
ask.ifNot: 15 plus 13 uses the same two numbers as 13 plus 15, only swapped round. It is the same pair, so we stop here.

beats.say: So we stop, and count the lines on the board. 7 pairs, so 7 ways.
A quick check. Our first numbers were 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13: every odd number below 14, which is half of 28. That is 7 numbers.
Careful: 14 is a tempting answer. But pairs like 2 plus 26 use even numbers, so they do not count.
So to count ways, list them in order, smallest first, and stop when the pairs begin to repeat. That gave us our 7.
We are adding 5 two-digit numbers, and we want the biggest carry that could ever happen.
To make the carry as big as possible, which two-digit numbers should we pick?

ask.ifNot: A carry grows when a column adds up to a lot. So we want the biggest digit in every place, and the biggest two-digit number is 99.

beats.say: So take 99, five times. Units column first: five 9s. 9 times 5 is 45. We write the 5 and carry the 4.
Tens column: five 9s again is 45, plus the carried 4 makes 49. Write the 9 and carry 4 into the hundreds.
Both times, the carry was 4. It cannot be beaten, because no digits are bigger than 9s.
The full sum agrees. 99 times 5 is 495, and that 4 at the front is the last carry.
Don't be tempted by 9. That is the biggest digit, not the biggest carry. A carry is how many tens spill over into the next column.
For any biggest-carry question, fill every place with 9s and add up one column.
Two numbers. Their difference is 17638, and one of them is 4905. We need to find the other.
Is 4905 the bigger number or the smaller one? Think about how large the difference is.

ask.ifNot: If 4905 were the bigger number, the gap between the two could never be more than 4905. But the gap is 17638. So 4905 must be the smaller one.

beats.say: Picture two bars. The larger number is the smaller one with the difference stuck on the end.
So we add. Here is a neat way: 4905 is just 95 short of 5000. Add 5000 first, and we get 22638.
We added 95 too many, so take the 95 back off. 22638 minus 95 is 22543. That is the other number.
Check it against the question. 22543 minus 4905 should be 17638, and it is.
The word difference tempts us to subtract. That gives 12733, but then the gap between 12733 and 4905 is far smaller than 17638.
So first decide which number is the bigger one. Smaller number plus the difference gives the larger number.
Add the difference of 7369 and 2418 to their sum. Let's find the result.

board.text: Add the difference of 7369 and 2418 to their sum

beats.say: This sentence is a little tangled, so let's untangle it. It wants two things made first, a difference and a sum. Then those two are added together.
Start with the difference. Which operation finds a difference?

ask.ifNot: The difference is how far apart two numbers are. We find it by subtracting the smaller from the bigger.

beats.say: 7369 minus 2418. Work column by column from the ones, and regroup at the hundreds. We get 4951.
Now their sum. 7369 plus 2418. Remember to carry 1 from the ones column. That gives 9787.
Last step: add the difference to the sum. 4951 plus 9787 is 14738.
Now look closely at our lines. In one we took 2418 away, and in the other we added 2418. What do you think happens to the 2418 overall?
It cancels out! Taking 2418 away and adding it back leaves nothing. So all that remains is 7369, two times. And 2 times 7369 is 14738.
Isn't that neat? The difference of two numbers plus their sum is always twice the bigger number. It makes a fast check.
Here is 469571. We are going to swap its 5 and its 6, and see how the number changes.
First, where are they? The 6 is in the ten-thousands place. The 5 is in the hundreds place.
Swap them. Now the 5 is in the ten-thousands place and the 6 is in the hundreds place: 459671.

ask.ifNot: Look at the ten-thousands place, the bigger of the two columns. It went down from 6 to 5. So the whole number went down.

beats.say: Before we subtract anything: is the new number bigger or smaller?
The ten-thousands place lost 1, so the number dropped by 10000. The hundreds place gained 1, so it rose by 100. Overall it fell by 9900.
Check by subtracting the whole numbers. 469571 minus 459671 is 9900.
So the new number is less by 9900.
When two digits swap, only their two columns change. The bigger column tells you whether the number went up or down.
5 consecutive numbers have an average of 24, and we want the smallest one.
Consecutive numbers come one after another, like 3, 4, 5. Let's try a small set first: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. They add up to 15, and 15 divided by 5 is 3.
The average is 3. Where does 3 sit in that list?

ask.ifNot: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The 3 has two numbers before it and two after. It is the middle one.

beats.say: That always happens with consecutive numbers: the small ones and the big ones balance around the middle. So in our question, the middle number is 24.
The middle is 24, and there are 5 numbers. How far below 24 is the smallest?

ask.ifNot: With 5 numbers, two sit before the middle and two sit after. So the smallest is only 2 steps below 24, not 5.

beats.say: So the five numbers are 22, 23, 24, 25, 26.
24 minus 2 is 22. The smallest number is 22.
Check: 22 plus 23 plus 24 plus 25 plus 26 is 120, and 120 divided by 5 is 24. Just what the question said.
For an odd count of consecutive numbers, the average is the middle one. Then just count out from the middle.
7 consecutive odd numbers have an average of 31. We want the largest of them.
Consecutive odd numbers jump by 2 each time, like 1, 3, 5. Let's see where the average hides in that small set.
1 plus 3 plus 5 is 9, and 9 shared among 3 is 3. So where does the average sit?

ask.ifNot: The average of 1, 3 and 5 is 3, and 3 is the one in the middle.

beats.say: Same here. With 7 numbers, the middle one is the 4th, and it is 31. Three numbers sit before it, and three after.
From 31 we take 3 more jumps to reach the largest. How far above 31 is that?

ask.ifNot: These are odd numbers, so each step is a jump of 2, not 1. 3 jumps of 2 make 6.

beats.say: 3 jumps of 2 is 6. So we go 31, then 33, 35, 37.
31 plus 6 is 37. The largest number is 37.
Check the balance. The smallest is 31 minus 6, which is 25. And 25 plus 37 is 62, exactly two lots of 31.
The average of evenly spaced numbers is the middle one. Count the jumps from the middle, and remember each jump here is 2.
Five even numbers in a row add up to 80. We want the fourth one.
Even numbers in a row go up in steps of 2, so they are spread evenly around the middle one. That makes the middle number their average. How do we find it?

ask.ifNot: An average is the total shared among how many numbers there are. Here that is 80 shared among 5.

beats.say: 80 divided by 5 is 16. So the middle number, the third one, is 16.
Now step out from the middle in 2s. Going down: 14, then 12. Going up: 18, then 20.
Which one is the fourth number?

ask.ifNot: Count along from the left: 12 is first, 14 second, 16 third, and then 18 is the fourth.

beats.say: The fourth number is 18.
Let's check that they really add to 80. 12 plus 14 plus 16 plus 18 plus 20. Yes, 80.
When numbers are evenly spaced, find the middle one by dividing the total by the count. Then step outwards.
6 years hence, Sumit will be 17. Hence is an old word for from now. And we are asked how old he was 8 years ago.
Notice something. We are told about the future, and asked about the past. But nobody has told us his age today.
So what should we find first?

ask.ifNot: Both clues are counted from today: 6 years from now, and 8 years ago. So today's age is the bridge between them.

beats.say: Today's age, plus 6 more years, makes 17. So today he is 17 minus 6, which is 11.
Now go back 8 years. Which number do we take the 8 away from?

ask.ifNot: 8 years ago is counted from today, and today he is 11. So it is 11 minus 8.

beats.say: 11 minus 8 is 3.
So 8 years ago, Sumit was 3 years old.
Check by walking forward in time. He was 3. 8 years later he is 11, and that is today. 6 more years and he is 17. It all fits.
The trap was 17 minus 8, which jumps straight over today. In age questions, find the age now first, then move forward or back.
The ages of Disha and Nisha add up to 25 years today. What did their ages add up to 4 years ago?

board.text: Sum of their ages 4 years ago = ?

beats.say: Here is a puzzle. We don't know Disha's age, and we don't know Nisha's age. Only the total. Do you think it can still be done?
It can. We don't need each age, only how the total changes. Here is a bar for each girl, with the last 4 years marked off.

spec.note: Today the two bars add up to 25 years

beats.say: Going back 4 years, how much smaller is the sum of their ages?

ask.ifNot: Count the people. Disha was 4 years younger, and Nisha was 4 years younger too. That is 4 and 4, 8 years in all.

beats.say: Two girls, each 4 years younger. 2 times 4 is 8.
So take 8 away from the total. 25 minus 8 is 17.
Four years ago, their ages added up to 17 years.
Let's try it with real ages. Say Disha is 12 and Nisha is 13, which makes 25. Four years ago they were 8 and 9, and 8 plus 9 is 17.
The trap is taking the 4 away only once. When time moves, it moves for everyone, so multiply the years by the number of people.
In 2020, the ages of Mr Joshi, his wife and his son added up to 100 years. What will they add up to in 2028?
First, how much time goes by? From 2020 to 2028 is 8 years.
Here is the family as three bars. In those 8 years, every one of them has 8 more birthdays.

spec.note: In 2020 the three ages add up to 100

beats.say: So by how much does the sum of their ages grow?

ask.ifNot: Count the people: Mr Joshi, his wife and his son. All 3 of them get 8 years older, and 3 times 8 is 24.

beats.say: 3 people, 8 years each. 3 times 8 is 24.
Add that to the old total. 100 plus 24 is 124.
In 2028, their ages will add up to 124 years.
Look at the bars to check. Three extra pieces of 8: 8 plus 8 plus 8 is 24. And 100 plus 24 is 124.
The trap is adding the 8 only once. Every person gets older, so multiply the years by the number of people.
4 years from now, the ages of Vijay and Vinay will add up to 67 years. What did their ages add up to 5 years ago?

board.text: 5 years ago: sum of their ages = ?

beats.say: We have to travel in time twice. First from the future back to today. Then from today back into the past. Here is our time line.
First jump: from 4 years ahead, back to today. By how much does the sum of their ages drop?

ask.ifNot: There are two people, and each of them is 4 years younger today than in 4 years' time. 2 times 4 is 8.

beats.say: 2 times 4 is 8. So today their ages add up to 67 minus 8, which is 59.
Second jump: from today, back 5 years. How much does the sum drop this time?

ask.ifNot: Again there are two people. Each was 5 years younger, and 2 times 5 is 10.

beats.say: 2 times 5 is 10. And 59 minus 10 is 49.
So 5 years ago, their ages added up to 49 years.
Check with one big jump. From 4 years ahead to 5 years ago is 9 years. Two people, so the sum drops by 18. And 67 minus 18 is 49.
So in age questions, come back to today first. And remember that every year counts once for each person.
In 2015, the ages of Aman and Suman added up to 87 years. Aman celebrated his 37th birthday in 2005. In which year was Suman born?

board.text: Aman turned 37 in 2005. Suman born in ?

beats.say: That is a lot of years flying about! So let's make a plan. Aman's age in 2015, then Suman's age in 2015, then Suman's year of birth.

board.text: Plan: Aman in 2015, Suman in 2015, birth year

beats.say: Aman was 37 in 2005. So how old was he in 2015?

ask.ifNot: From 2005 to 2015 is 10 years. So Aman was 10 years older than 37, which is 47.

beats.say: 2015 minus 2005 is 10 years. And 37 plus 10 is 47. So Aman was 47 in 2015.
Now both facts are about 2015. Together they were 87, and Aman was 47. So Suman was 87 minus 47, which is 40.
Suman was 40 years old in 2015. So how do we find the year Suman was born?

ask.ifNot: Suman's age of 40 belongs to the year 2015. So we count 40 years back from 2015.

beats.say: Suman was born in 1975.
Check. Someone born in 1975 is 40 in 2015. And 40 plus 47 is 87. It fits.
The trap was mixing years: Aman's 37 belongs to 2005, but the 87 belongs to 2015. Bring every fact to the same year before you combine them.
A school starts the year with 1005 students. During the year 13 leave and 42 join. At the end, 1000 pass the final exam. How many did not pass?

board.text: 1000 passed. How many did not pass?

beats.say: The exam comes at the end of the year. So what must we know before we can answer?

choices: the number of students at the end
ask.ifNot: Only students who are in the school at the end can sit the exam. So first we need the number of students at the end of the year.

beats.say: Follow the story in order. 13 students left, so the number goes down. 1005 minus 13 is 992.
Then 42 joined, so the number goes up. 992 plus 42 is 1034. That is the school at the end of the year.
Now split those 1034 students into two groups: the ones who passed, and the ones who did not.
How do we find the missing piece of the bar?

ask.ifNot: The whole bar is 1034 and one piece of it is 1000. Take the piece we know away from the whole.

beats.say: So 34 students did not pass.
Check. 1000 who passed and 34 who did not make 1034, the school at the end of the year.
The trap was 1005 minus 1000, which forgets the children who left and joined. In a story sum, follow the story in order.
Three bags of oranges. We know three totals, so let me write them down in short.
Look at the first two lines. All three bags hold 27, and the first and second together hold 13. Which bag can we find from that?

ask.ifNot: The 13 covers the first and second bags. Take those away from all 27 oranges, and what is left must be in the third bag.

beats.say: So the third bag holds 27 minus 13, which is 14 oranges.
We can use the same idea again. The second and third bags hold 19, so the first bag holds 27 minus 19. That is 8.
Careful now. The question does not want one bag. What is it asking for?

choices: the first and third bags together
ask.ifNot: Read the last line of the question again. It asks how many oranges in all in the first and the third bags.

beats.say: So we add the first bag and the third bag. 8 plus 14 is 22.
Let's check with the second bag. The first two hold 13, so the second has 13 minus 8, which is 5. And 5 plus 14 is 19, just as the question said.
So when you know the whole and a part, subtract to find the missing part. The answer is 22 oranges.
In a class there are 11 fewer boys than girls. There are 42 girls. What is the strength of the whole class?

board.text: Boys are 11 fewer than girls. Girls = 42.

beats.say: Strength just means how many students there are altogether, boys and girls. We know the girls. We don't yet know the boys.
Look at the bars. There are 11 fewer boys than girls. So how many boys are there?

spec.note: The boys' bar is shorter by 11

ask.ifNot: Fewer means a smaller number. The boys' bar is shorter than the girls' bar by 11, so we subtract.

beats.say: 42 minus 11 is 31. There are 31 boys.
Are we finished? Not yet! 31 is only the boys, and the question asks for the whole class. This is where many children stop too soon.
Girls and boys together: 42 plus 31 is 73.
The class has 73 students.
Check. 73 students, take away the 42 girls, leaves 31 boys. And 31 is 11 fewer than 42. Good.
So first find the group you don't know, then answer what was really asked. And remember, fewer means subtract.
A and B stood in an election. A received 275 votes, and B won by a majority of 35 votes. How many votes were cast altogether?

board.text: A got 275 votes. B won by 35 votes.

beats.say: Won by a majority of 35 means B got 35 more votes than A. Here it is as two bars.

spec.note: B has 35 more votes than A

beats.say: So how many votes did B get?

ask.ifNot: B is the winner, so B has more votes than A. 35 more than 275 means we add.

beats.say: 275 plus 35 is 310. B got 310 votes.
Careful now. 310 is only B's votes. The question asks for all the votes cast, A's and B's together.
So 585 votes were cast in the election.
Check with the bars. Two pieces of 275 make 550. Add the extra 35, and we get 585.
So always read what the question wants at the end. Here it was the total, so we needed both bars.
In this account, 600 rupees was spent. But by mistake it was entered as income, as money coming in. The balance shows 15000 rupees, and we must put it right.

board.text: Spent Rs.600, but entered as income

beats.say: Here is the 600 in a little table: what should have happened to it, and what really happened.
Spending makes a balance go down. So the 600 should have been taken away. Instead it was added, and the balance went up.
To put it right, how many times must we take 600 away?

ask.ifNot: Taking 600 away once only removes the mistaken adding. The 600 that was really spent still has to come off after that.

beats.say: First, undo the mistake. Take away the 600 that should never have been added. 15000 minus 600 is 14400.
Careful, here is the trap: we are not finished. 14400 is the balance before any spending. The 600 that was really spent must still come off.
14400 minus 600 is 13800. So the correct balance is 13800 rupees.
Check: the mistake pushed the balance 600 the opposite way, so it is out by 2 lots of 600, which is 1200. And 15000 minus 1200 is 13800. It agrees.
So when an entry is written the opposite way round, the fix is double: once to undo it, and once to do it properly.
This time 600 rupees came in as income. But by mistake it was written as spending. The balance shows 15000 rupees, and we must put it right.

board.text: Income Rs.600, but entered as spending

beats.say: Here is the 600 in a little table: what should have happened to it, and what really happened.
Income makes a balance go up. So the 600 should have been added. Instead it was taken away, and the balance went down.
So will the correct balance be more than 15000, or less?

ask.ifNot: The 600 was money coming in, but the account treated it as money going out. So the balance shown is too small, and the correct one is bigger.

beats.say: First, undo the mistake. Put back the 600 that should never have been taken away. 15000 plus 600 is 15600.
Careful, here is the trap: we are not finished. 15600 is the balance before the income is counted. The 600 that really came in must still be added.
15600 plus 600 is 16200. So the correct balance is 16200 rupees.
Check: the mistake pushed the balance 600 the opposite way, so it is out by 2 lots of 600, which is 1200. And 15000 plus 1200 is 16200. It agrees.
So when an entry is written the opposite way round, the fix is double: once to undo it, and once to do it properly.
In a class of 40, 18 students have been to Delhi and 15 have been to Kashmir. 6 have been to both. How many have been to neither place?
Two overlapping groups, so let's draw two overlapping circles. The 6 children who have been to both places sit in the middle.
If we simply add the 18 and the 15, what happens to those 6 children in the middle?

ask.ifNot: The 6 are inside the Delhi 18, and inside the Kashmir 15 as well. So adding the two counts them two times.

beats.say: Let's add anyway, and then put it right. 18 plus 15 is 33, with the middle 6 counted twice.
Take the 6 away once, so every child is counted just one time. 33 minus 6 is 27. So 27 children have been to at least one place.
27 children are somewhere inside the circles, and the class has 40. How do we find the ones outside?

ask.ifNot: The children outside the circles are the rest of the class. So take the 27 inside away from all 40.

beats.say: 40 minus 27 is 13.
So 13 students have been to neither Delhi nor Kashmir.
Check by filling in the circles. Delhi only is 18 minus 6, which is 12. Kashmir only is 15 minus 6, which is 9. And 12, 6, 9 and 13 add up to 40.

spec.note: 13 students are outside both circles

beats.say: So with two overlapping groups: add them, take the overlap away once, then subtract from the whole class.
A class has 30 students, and every one speaks Hindi or Marathi, or both. 21 speak Hindi, and 5 speak both. How many speak only Marathi?

board.text: 30 students. Each speaks Hindi, Marathi or both.

beats.say: Two circles again. And notice: every student speaks at least one language, so nobody stands outside the circles.

spec.note: All 30 students are inside the circles

beats.say: The whole Hindi circle holds 21 students. Careful: that 21 already includes the 5 in the middle who speak both.
So which students are left outside the Hindi circle?

choices: the ones who speak only Marathi
ask.ifNot: Everyone speaks Hindi or Marathi. A student who is not in the Hindi circle must be in the part for Marathi only.

beats.say: So take the Hindi circle away from the whole class. 30 minus 21 is 9.
And we do not subtract the 5 again. They were already inside the 21. Taking them away twice is the trap in this question.
So 9 students speak only Marathi.
Check by filling in the circles. Hindi only is 21 minus 5, which is 16. Then 16, 5 and 9 add up to 30, the whole class.
So draw the circles, and ask what each number really covers. The 21 covered the whole Hindi circle, middle and all. That is how we reached 9.
Siya saves 1 rupee on the 1st, 2 rupees on the 2nd, and so on, right through February 2022. How much has she saved by the end?

board.text: February 2022: 1 + 2 + 3 + ... up to the last day

beats.say: First, how many days did February 2022 have?

ask.ifNot: February has 29 days only in a leap year, and leap years divide exactly by 4. 2022 does not, so that February had 28 days.

beats.say: So we need 1 plus 2 plus 3, all the way up to 28.
Adding 28 numbers one by one would take ages. Here is a lovely trick: pair the first with the last. 1 plus 28 is 29. Then 2 plus 27 is 29 as well.
Every pair makes 29. With 28 numbers, how many pairs are there?

ask.ifNot: Each pair uses up 2 numbers. So 28 numbers make half as many pairs, and half of 28 is 14.

beats.say: 14 pairs, each worth 29. For 14 times 29, do 14 times 30, which is 420, then take away one 14. That leaves 406.
So Siya saved 406 rupees. And notice the calendar mattered: one extra day in the month would have changed the total.
To add a long run of numbers, pair up the two ends. Every pair has the same total, so you only multiply.
Four players join a chess tournament. Each player plays one game against every other player. How many games are played in all?

board.text: 4 players. Each pair plays one game. Games = ?

beats.say: Let's give the players names: A, B, C and D. A game needs two players, so we are really counting pairs.
Start with A. A plays B, A plays C, A plays D. That is 3 games.

board.text: A plays B, C, D: 3 games

beats.say: Now B. Careful: B against A is already on our list. So how many new games does B have?

ask.ifNot: B's game against A is already counted. B's new games are against C and against D, which makes 2.

beats.say: B has 2 new games, against C and D. C has only 1 new game, against D. And D? Every one of D's games is already listed.

board.text: B plays C, D: 2 new games

beats.say: Add them up. 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 6. So 6 games are played in all.
Check another way. Each of the 4 players plays 3 games, and 4 times 3 is 12. But that counts every game twice, once for each player in it. Half of 12 is 6.
The trap is that 12. A against B and B against A are the same game. So list the pairs in order, and never count one twice.
At a meeting, 13 people all shake hands with each other. How many handshakes happen in all?

board.text: 13 people. Everyone shakes hands with everyone.

beats.say: 13 is a lot of people, so let's try a tiny meeting first, with 3 people: A, B and C. The handshakes are A with B, A with C, and B with C. That makes 3.

board.text: 3 people: AB, AC, BC make 3 handshakes

beats.say: Here is a quicker way to count the same thing. Each of the 3 people shakes 2 hands, and 3 times 2 is 6. But 6 is double the real 3, because each handshake got counted by both people in it.
Back to our 13 people. How many hands does each person shake?

ask.ifNot: Nobody shakes their own hand! So each person shakes hands with the 12 other people.

beats.say: 13 people, 12 handshakes each. 13 times 12 is 156.
Is 156 the number of handshakes?

choices: no, each one was counted twice
ask.ifNot: When A shakes hands with B, we counted it once for A and once again for B. One handshake, counted two times.

beats.say: So we halve it. 156 divided by 2 is 78.
There were 78 handshakes.
We can check by counting new handshakes person by person. The first person shakes 12 hands, the next has 11 new ones, then 10, and so on down to 1. Added up, that is 78 as well.
So for handshakes, or games between pairs: multiply each person by the others, then halve, because every pair was counted twice.
This one is all in words, so let's turn it into numbers. How many 15s make up twelve hundreds?
What number is twelve hundreds?

ask.ifNot: Twelve hundreds means 12 lots of 100. That is 12 with two zeros written after it.

beats.say: 12 times 100 is 1200.
How many 15s fit into 1200? Let's get there in easy steps. Two 15s make 30.
30 goes into 120 4 times. So 15, which is half of 30, goes into 120 8 times.
And 1200 is 10 times as big as 120, so we need 10 times as many 15s. That is 80 of them.
Now look at the choices. None of them says 80. Which one means the same as 80?

ask.ifNot: 8 on its own is far too few: 8 fifteens only make 120. We found 80, and 80 is 8 lots of 10, which we call 8 tens.

beats.say: 80 is 8 tens. So 8 tens of fifteens make up twelve hundreds.
Turn the words into numbers, divide, and then match your answer to the way the choices are written.
A multiplication with stars where some digits should be. The top number starts with 5 and ends in 7. The answer ends in 61. Let's be detectives.
Start with the very last digit. The answer ends in 1, and that 1 comes from 7 times the last digit of the bottom number.
7 times which digit ends in 1?

ask.ifNot: Go through the 7 times table until the answer ends in 1. You get there at 7 times 3, which is 21.

beats.say: So the bottom number is 43. We write the 1 and carry the 2 from that 21.
Now the first row of working. It is the top number times 3, and it has 5 and 8 in the middle. So 3 times the hidden digit, plus the carried 2, must end in 8.
3 times which digit, plus 2, ends in 8?

ask.ifNot: We need 3 times the digit to end in 6, so that adding 2 gives 8. And 3 times 2 is 6. So the hidden digit is 2.

beats.say: So the top number is 527. Check that row: 527 times 3 is 1581, with 5 and 8 in the middle, just as the puzzle shows.
Now finish the multiplication. 527 times 40 is 21080, and adding the 1581 gives 22661.
So the product is 22661.
With star puzzles, start from the last digit and let each clue unlock the next one.
We want only the units digit of a product: all the odd numbers from 16 to 25, multiplied together.

board.text: Odd numbers from 16 to 25, multiplied. Units digit = ?

beats.say: First, which numbers are they? 17, 19, 21, 23 and 25.
Multiplying all of that would give a giant number. But we only need its last digit. Which number in the list is the special one for last digits?

ask.ifNot: Look at 25. It ends in 5, and multiplying by a 5 does something very predictable to the last digit.

beats.say: Watch what 5 does to odd numbers. 5 times 3 is 15. 5 times 7 is 35. 5 times 9 is 45.
What do all of those answers end in?

ask.ifNot: 15, 35, 45. Look at the last digit of each one. It is always 5.

beats.say: An odd number times 5 always ends in 5. It could end in 0 only if an even number joined in, and every number in our list is odd.
So this whole product ends in 5.
Let's check with last digits only. 7 times 9 is 63, so keep the 3. 3 times 1 is 3, 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 times 5 is 45. It ends in 5.
For a units digit question you never need the whole product. Follow the last digits, and look out for a 5.
One amoeba, and the number doubles every 20 minutes. We want to know how many there are after 2 hours.

board.text: Doubles every 20 minutes. Start: 1. After 2 hours?

beats.say: First we need to know how many times it doubles. 2 hours is 120 minutes. How many lots of 20 minutes is that?

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps of 20 on the number line: 20, 40, 60, 80, 100, 120. That is 6 jumps.

beats.say: 120 divided by 20 is 6. So the amoebas double 6 times.
Now we double, starting from 1. 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8. That is 3 doublings so far.
Keep going: 16, then 32, then 64. Count the arrows: 6 doublings altogether.
So after 2 hours there are 64 amoebas.
Careful: doubling is not adding 2 each time, and it is not 6 times 2. Every step doubles everything that is already there, so it grows faster and faster.
So first count how many doublings there are. Then double, step by step, that many times.
A factory makes 1720 boxes every day. What is its total production in the month of July?

board.text: 1720 boxes every day. Total in July = ?

beats.say: One number seems to be missing. To find the total for July, what else do we need to know?

ask.ifNot: July is one of the long months, with 31 days. On your knuckles, July lands on a knuckle, and knuckle months have 31.

beats.say: So the factory makes 1720 boxes, 31 times over. That is 1720 times 31. A big sum, so let's break the 31 into 30 and 1.
First the 30 days. 1720 times 3 is 5160. Put a zero on the end for times 30, and we have 51600.
Now the 1 extra day: 1720 more boxes. This is the day children forget!
Add the two parts. 51600 plus 1720 is 53320.
So in July the factory makes 53320 boxes.
Check. Take one day's boxes off our answer: 53320 minus 1720 is 51600, exactly the 30 days we began with.
The trap is to use 30 days and stop at 51600. So know your months, and split a hard multiplication into easy pieces.
A chain of containers: cups fill a bottle, bottles fill a jug, jugs fill a bucket. We want to know how many cups go into 2 buckets.

board.text: 1 bottle = 4 cups, 1 jug = 3 bottles, 1 bucket = 7 jugs

beats.say: The trick with a chain is to turn everything into cups, one link at a time. A jug is 3 bottles, and each bottle is 4 cups. So how do we find the cups in a jug?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 3 bottles holds 4 cups. That is 3 lots of 4, so we multiply.

beats.say: 3 times 4 is 12. One jug holds 12 cups.
A bucket is 7 jugs, and each jug is 12 cups. 7 times 12 is 84. One bucket holds 84 cups.
Are we finished? Read the last line of the question once more.

ask.ifNot: 84 cups fill one bucket. But the question asks about 2 buckets, so there is one more step to go.

beats.say: 2 buckets hold 2 times 84, which is 168 cups.
Written in one line, it is 4 times 3 times 7 times 2. Every link in the chain is a multiplication.
In a chain like this, change one link at a time. And read the end of the question again before you stop.
Two secret numbers multiply to give 108. Then one is doubled and the other is tripled. What is the new product?
Doubling one number makes the product 2 times as big. Tripling the other makes it 3 times as big again. So altogether, how many times bigger is the new product?

ask.ifNot: The two changes multiply, they do not add. Twice as big, and then 3 times as big again, is 2 times 3. That is 6 times as big.

beats.say: Let's see that on the board. The new product is 2 times the first number, times 3 times the second.
In a multiplication we can shuffle the order. Bring the 2 and the 3 to the front, and what is left is first times second, our old product.
So the new product is 6 times 108.
6 times 100 is 600, and 6 times 8 is 48. Together that makes 648.
Let's test it with real numbers. 12 times 9 is 108. Double the 12 to get 24, triple the 9 to get 27, and 24 times 27 is 648 as well.
So when numbers in a product are scaled up, the product is scaled by both, multiplied together.
A three-digit number ending in 6, times a two-digit number ending in 9. The other digits are hidden. Which of these four could be the product?
We cannot multiply hidden digits. But one digit of the answer we can know for sure. Which one?

ask.ifNot: The last digit of a product comes only from the last digits of the two numbers. And those we can see: 6 and 9.

beats.say: 6 times 9 is 54. So the product must end in 4.
That knocks out 5417, which ends in 7, and 86996, which ends in 6.
Two are left, and both end in 4. So now think about size. How big could the product possibly get?
Use the biggest numbers that fit the pattern: 996 and 99. 996 times 99 is 98604. That has five digits.
So a six-digit number like 357604 is far too big. Cross it out.
Only 5104 is left. And it really can happen: 176 times 29 is 5104.
For star products, check the last digit first. Then check the size.
Stars hide most of the digits. We know one number ends in 7 and the other ends in 4. Let's see which of the four choices can be their product.
Only the last digits are showing, 7 and 4. What do they tell us about the product?

ask.ifNot: When we multiply, the units digit of the answer comes from the units digits alone. So 7 and 4 fix the last digit of the product.

beats.say: 7 times 4 is 28, so the product ends in 8. 35271 ends in 1, so it is out.
The other three all end in 8, so we need another test: size. The smallest numbers that fit are 107 and 14, and 107 times 14 is 1498.
So is 1398 possible?

ask.ifNot: The smallest the product can ever be is 1498. And 1398 is below that, so it cannot happen.

beats.say: Cross out 1398. Now the other end: the biggest numbers that fit are 997 and 94, and 997 times 94 is 93718. So 104978 is too big.
Only 16448 is left, and it does work: 257 times 64 is 16448.
Two tests for a hidden product: the last digit, and then the smallest and biggest it could be.
A bundle of 5 rupee notes, numbered from 40801 to 40901. Two steps: count the notes, then multiply by 5.

ask.ifNot: Try it with small numbers. Notes 1 to 3 are 3 notes, but 3 minus 1 is only 2. We must add 1, to count the first note as well.

beats.say: So how many notes are there, from 40801 to 40901?
40901 minus 40801 is 100. Then add 1 for the first note, 40801 itself. That makes 101 notes.
This is the trap in the question. Subtracting counts the steps between the notes, and there is always one more note than steps.
Now the money. 100 notes of 5 rupees make 500 rupees, and 1 more note makes 505.
So the bundle holds 505 rupees.
Counting from one number to another: subtract, then add 1, because both ends are in the bundle.
The same girls are lined up in two different ways. With 26 in a row, the 21st row is not full. We want to know how many more girls would fill it.

board.text: 18 in a row: 30 rows. 26 in a row: 21st row is short

beats.say: First, how many girls are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: 30 rows with 18 girls in each is 30 lots of 18. So we multiply.

beats.say: 18 times 30 is 540. There are 540 girls.
Now put 26 in each row. 20 full rows use 26 times 20, which is 520 girls.
So 540 is 20 full rows, with 20 girls left over. Those 20 girls stand in the 21st row.
The 21st row has 20 girls in it, but a full row has 26. How many more girls are needed?

ask.ifNot: 20 is how many girls are already standing in that row. The question asks how many more it needs to reach 26.

beats.say: 26 minus 20 is 6. So 6 more girls are needed.
Check: with 6 more girls there would be 546, and 26 times 21 is 546. Every row full.
Find the total, divide to see what is left over, and then read carefully: does the question want the leftover, or what is missing?
A 10 metre wire is cut into 7 equal parts, each a whole number of centimetres. We want the smallest piece that could be left over.

board.text: 10 m wire, 7 equal parts, whole centimetres

beats.say: The parts are measured in centimetres. So first, how many centimetres is 10 metres?

ask.ifNot: One metre is 100 centimetres. So 10 metres is 10 lots of 100.

beats.say: 10 times 100 is 1000 centimetres of wire.
To waste as little as possible, each part should be as long as possible. So let's see how many 7s fit in 1000. 7 times 100 is 700, which leaves 300.
7 times 40 is 280, which leaves 20. And 7 times 2 is 14, which leaves 6.
So each part is 100 plus 40 plus 2, that is 142 centimetres, and 6 centimetres are left over.
Could we make each part 143 centimetres and waste even less?

ask.ifNot: 7 parts of 143 centimetres would need 1001 centimetres, and the wire is only 1000 long. So 142 is the longest each part can be.

beats.say: So the least that can be left over is 6 centimetres.
A leftover is a remainder. Change to the small unit, divide, and the remainder is what is left.
12.5 kilograms of sweets are shared equally among 25 students. 17 of them are girls and the rest are boys. How much does each boy get?

board.text: 12.5 kg of sweets shared equally by 25 students
17 girls, the rest boys. Each boy gets = ?

beats.say: Read one word again: equally. So does a boy get more than a girl, less, or the same?

ask.ifNot: Equally means every student gets the same amount, whether a boy or a girl.

beats.say: So each boy gets the same as any other student. That means the 17 girls is extra information. We don't need it at all.
Now the sharing. 12.5 kilograms among 25 is awkward, so let's change to grams. 1 kilogram is 1000 grams, so 12.5 kilograms is 12500 grams.
Among how many students do we share the 12500 grams?

ask.ifNot: The sweets went to all 25 students, not only to the boys. So we share among 25.

beats.say: 125 divided by 25 is 5. So 12500 divided by 25 is 500.
Each boy gets 500 grams of sweets.
Check. 25 students with 500 grams each: 25 times 500 is 12500 grams, which is our 12.5 kilograms.
Two things to keep. Watch for the word equally. And don't be afraid to leave a number unused when the question does not need it.
A mystery number is divided by 11. We are given clues about the quotient and the remainder, and we have to rebuild the number.
Let's name each piece. The divisor is 11. The quotient is equal to the divisor, so it is 11 as well.
The remainder is 2 less than the divisor. So what is the remainder?

ask.ifNot: 2 less than the divisor means the divisor take away 2. The divisor is 11, so that is 11 minus 2.

beats.say: 11 minus 2 is 9. The remainder is 9.
Now build the number back up. Any division can be undone like this: divisor times quotient, plus the remainder.
So we need 11 times 11, plus 9. 11 times 11 is 121, and 121 plus 9 is 130.
The trap is to use 2 as the remainder. Read it again: the remainder is 2 less than the divisor, and that is 9.
To rebuild a number after a division: divisor times quotient, plus remainder.
3000 is divided by a mystery number. The quotient is 76 and 36 is left over. We have to find the divisor.
Write the division the other way round. The number is the divisor times the quotient, plus the remainder.
The 36 left over is not part of the equal groups. So what do the equal groups add up to?

ask.ifNot: The remainder is what is left after the groups are made. Take it away from 3000, and what remains is exactly the groups.

beats.say: 3000 minus 36 is 2964. So the mystery number times 76 is 2964.
Now, how many 76s make 2964? Try 40 of them. 76 times 40 is 3040, which is just a little too much.
How much too much? 3040 minus 2964 is 76. Exactly one 76 too many! So we need one fewer than 40, which is 39.
The divisor is 39. And it fits the whole story: 39 times 76, plus 36, is 3000.
One more sense check. A remainder is always smaller than the divisor, and 36 is smaller than 39. So 36 itself could never be the divisor.
To find a divisor: take the remainder off first, then divide by the quotient.
We want the greatest three-digit number that 57 divides exactly. So it must be in the 57 times table, and it must not go past 999.
Let's get close to 999 quickly. 57 times 10 is 570. That is too small, so we need more 57s.
Double it: 57 times 20 is 1140. What does that tell us?

choices: Too far: it has four digits
ask.ifNot: 1140 has four digits, so it has gone past 999. Our number is somewhere between 10 lots and 20 lots of 57.

beats.say: So we step back from 1140, one 57 at a time. 1140 minus 57 is 1083. Still four digits.
Step back again. 1083 minus 57 is 1026. Still too big.
Once more: 1026 minus 57 is 969. Three digits at last!
We took 3 lots away from 20 lots, so that is 17 lots. 57 times 17 is 969, and the next one up, 57 times 18, is 1026.
So the greatest three-digit multiple of 57 is 969.
One trap: a bigger-looking choice is no good unless it is in the 57 times table. So jump close with easy multiples, then step one 57 at a time until you are just under the limit.
We want the smallest four-digit number in the 57 times table. Four-digit numbers start at 1000, so we need the first multiple of 57 that reaches 1000 or more.
Jump close first. 57 times 10 is 570, and double that, 57 times 20, is 1140.
1140 has four digits and it is in the 57 times table. But it is 140 past 1000. Is it surely the smallest?

choices: Not yet: a smaller one may fit
ask.ifNot: The gap of 140 is bigger than 57. So there is room for another multiple of 57 between 1000 and 1140.

beats.say: So step back one 57 at a time. 1140 minus 57 is 1083. Still four digits.
Step back again. 1083 minus 57 is 1026. Still four digits!
And once more: 1026 minus 57 is 969. That has only three digits, so now we have gone too far.
So 1026 is the smallest four-digit multiple. It is 18 lots of 57.
Name the trap: 1140 is a four-digit multiple of 57 too, and it is easy to stop there. Always step back to see whether a smaller one still fits.
A student divided by 24 when he should have divided by 42, and got 91. We want the answer he should have got.

board.text: Divided by 24 instead of 42, and got 91

beats.say: We are not told the number he was dividing. But his working gives it away. How do we get it back?

ask.ifNot: He divided the number by 24 and got 91. To undo a division we multiply, so 24 times 91 gives the number back.

beats.say: 24 times 91. First 24 times 90, which is 2160. Then one more 24 makes 2184.
That is the number he started with. Now do what he should have done, and divide 2184 by 42.
42 times 50 is 2100. That leaves 84, and 84 is 2 more 42s.
50 and 2 make 52. So the correct answer was 52.
Does it make sense that 52 is smaller than 91? Yes. Dividing by a bigger number always gives a smaller answer.
When the divisor has been mixed up, multiply back to find the starting number. Then divide by the right one.
A student was meant to multiply a number by 13. By mistake he divided it by 13, and got a quotient of 11 with remainder 4. What should the answer have been?
It is a little detective story, in two steps. First find the secret number he started with. Then do what he was supposed to do with it.

board.text: Step 1: find the number. Step 2: multiply by 13.

beats.say: We know the divisor, 13, the quotient, 11, and the remainder, 4. How do we rebuild the number?

ask.ifNot: The number is made of 13 groups of 11, and then the 4 that were left over. Left over means we add them back on.

beats.say: 13 times 11 is 143. Add the remainder: 143 plus 4 is 147. The secret number is 147.
We have the number, 147. Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: 147 is only the number he started with. The question asks what he should have got, by multiplying it by 13.

beats.say: So, 147 times 13. Split the 13 into 10 and 3. 147 times 10 is 1470. 147 times 3 is 441. And 1470 plus 441 is 1911.
So the correct answer to his problem was 1911.
Check our secret number. 147 divided by 13: 13 times 11 is 143, with 4 left over. Quotient 11, remainder 4, just as the question said.
So to undo a division: divisor times quotient, plus remainder. Then do what the question really wanted.
A student divided by 18 when he should have divided by 12. He got 71, with 6 left over. What would be left over if he had divided by 12?
First we need the number itself. Which sum gives it back?

ask.ifNot: Divisor times quotient gives the full groups, 18 times 71. Then the 6 that was left over has to be added back on.

beats.say: 18 times 70 is 1260, and one more 18 makes 1278. Add the 6 left over, and the number is 1284.
Now divide 1284 by 12. 12 times 100 is 1200, and that leaves 84.
Does 12 go into 84 exactly?

ask.ifNot: Count up in 12s and you land right on 84 at the 7th step. So it goes in exactly, with nothing left.

beats.say: 12 times 7 is 84. So 1284 is exactly 12 times 107, and nothing is left over.
The remainder is 0.
Notice the remainder changed. It was 6 with 18, but 0 with 12. A remainder belongs to its own divisor, so you cannot carry it across.
Rebuild the number first: divisor times quotient, plus remainder. Then do the division you were really asked for.
Anay types 126 words in 3 minutes. We want to know how many words he types in just half a minute.
3 minutes is a long way from half a minute, so let's use a stepping stone: 1 minute. How do we find the words for 1 minute?

ask.ifNot: The 126 words are spread evenly over 3 minutes. 1 minute is one of 3 equal parts, so we divide by 3.

beats.say: 126 is 120 and 6. 120 divided by 3 is 40, and 6 divided by 3 is 2. So he types 42 words in 1 minute.
Careful now. 42 is one of the choices, but the question does not ask about 1 minute. It asks about half a minute. So what do we do with 42?

ask.ifNot: Half a minute is less time than 1 minute, so he types fewer words, not more. Half the time means half the words.

beats.say: Half of 42 is 21. So Anay types 21 words in half a minute.
Check it. 3 minutes holds 6 half minutes, and 6 times 21 is 126. Exactly what we were told.
So when the numbers do not match up, go through 1. Find what happens in 1 minute, then shrink it or grow it to what you need.
Three numbers multiply together to make 2880. Two of them are 12 and 15, and the third is hiding.
First, squash the two numbers we know into one. 12 times 10 is 120, and 12 times 5 is 60. Together that is 180.
So now 180 times the hidden number is 2880. How do we find a missing factor?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. If 180 times something makes 2880, then 2880 divided by 180 gives that something.

beats.say: 2880 divided by 180. Both end in 0, so knock a 0 off each. That leaves 288 divided by 18.
18 times 10 is 180. Take that from 288 and 108 is left. And 18 times 6 is 108.
10 lots and 6 lots make 16 lots. So the third number is 16.
Check it. 180 times 10 is 1800, and 180 times 6 is 1080. Together that is 2880. It works.
So when a product is known and one factor is missing: multiply the factors you have, then divide the product by that.
72 students, and each one gets 7 chocolates. We want the number of chocolates, counted in dozens.

board.text: 72 students, 7 chocolates each. How many dozens?

beats.say: Two steps here. First, how many chocolates altogether? 72 times 7. Split the 72 into 70 and 2.
70 times 7 is 490, and 2 times 7 is 14. Together, 504 chocolates.
Now we need dozens. What do we do with the 504?

ask.ifNot: A dozen is 12. We want to know how many 12s there are in 504, and that is a division by 12.

beats.say: 504 divided by 12. 12 times 40 is 480. That leaves 24, which is 2 more 12s.
40 and 2 make 42. We need 42 dozens.
Here is a shortcut worth seeing. 72 students is 6 dozens of students. Each gets 7, so we need 6 times 7 dozens. That is 42 straight away.
The trap is to stop at 6. That is the students counted in dozens, not the chocolates.
Find the total first, then change it into the unit the question asks for.
A number should have been multiplied by 53, but it was multiplied by 35. The answer came out 378 too small. What is the number?

board.text: × 35 instead of × 53: the answer is 378 too small

beats.say: Think in lots of the number. 53 lots were needed, but only 35 lots were taken. How many lots went missing?

ask.ifNot: 35 lots were taken where 53 were needed. The missing lots are the gap between 53 and 35, and a gap is found by taking away.

beats.say: 53 minus 35 is 18. So 18 lots of the number are missing.
And those 18 missing lots are exactly the 378 that the answer fell short by.
So the number is 378 divided by 18. 18 times 20 is 360. That leaves 18, which is one more lot. So 21.
Let's check with the whole story. 21 times 53 is 1113. 21 times 35 is 735. And the gap between them is 378.
Careful not to stop at 18. That is how many lots were missing, not the number itself.
When two multiplications of the same number are compared, look at the difference in lots.
A basket has 56 apples. Amey takes out 4 apples at a time and puts 3 oranges in their place, until no apples are left. How many oranges are there at the end?

board.text: 56 apples. Each turn: 4 apples out, 3 oranges in.

beats.say: Each turn is a swap: 4 apples out, 3 oranges in. Watch the first few turns in this table.
The oranges go up by 3 on every turn. So if we know the number of turns, we know the oranges. The turns are the key.
How many turns does it take to remove all 56 apples?

ask.ifNot: Apples leave 4 at a time. So the number of turns is how many times 4 goes into 56.

beats.say: 56 divided by 4 is 14. So Amey makes 14 swaps.
Each of the 14 turns puts in 3 oranges. So how do we find the oranges?

ask.ifNot: 3 oranges go in on every turn, and there are 14 turns. 14 lots of 3 means multiply.

beats.say: 14 times 3 is 42.
So there are 42 oranges in the basket at the end.
Does that make sense? Each swap puts in one fruit fewer than it takes out. 14 swaps, so 14 fewer fruits, and 56 minus 14 is 42. Yes.
So when something happens again and again, first count how many times it happens. Then multiply.
Two odd numbers, next-door neighbours like 5 and 7, add up to 124. We want the smaller one.

board.text: Two consecutive odd numbers add up to 124

beats.say: Start with a simpler idea. If the two numbers were equal, each would be half of 124. What is half of 124?

ask.ifNot: Try 62 and 62. Together they make 124, so 62 is the half we want.

beats.say: 124 divided by 2 is 62. But 62 is even, and our two numbers are odd. So 62 is not one of them: it is the halfway point between them.
Next-door odd numbers are 2 apart. So they sit one step on either side of 62: 61 and 63.
The question wants the smaller of the two. Which is it?

ask.ifNot: 62 was only our halfway marker. The two odd numbers are 61 and 63, and the smaller of those is 61.

beats.say: The smaller number is 61. And the check: 61 plus 63 is 124.
When two numbers are evenly placed around a middle, halve the total to find the middle, then step out to each side.
Two multiples of 9, next-door neighbours in the 9 times table, add up to 153. We want the larger one.

board.text: Two neighbouring multiples of 9 add up to 153

beats.say: Neighbours in the 9 times table are always 9 apart. So the larger one is just the smaller one with an extra 9 on the end. Look at the two bars.

spec.note: Together the two bars make 153.

beats.say: Suppose we take that extra 9 away from the total. What would be left?

ask.ifNot: Without the extra 9, the two bars are exactly the same length. So what is left is two equal parts, each one the smaller multiple.

beats.say: 153 minus 9 is 144. That is two copies of the smaller multiple.
So halve it. 144 divided by 2 is 72, and that is the smaller multiple.
Careful: the question asks for the larger one. Put the 9 back: 72 plus 9 is 81.
Check. 72 is 9 times 8 and 81 is 9 times 9, so they are neighbours in the table. And 72 plus 81 is 153.
So for two neighbours with a known sum: take away the gap, halve, then add the gap back for the bigger one.
Four years from now, Siya will be 3 years older than Diya. Today their ages add up to 35. How old is Siya now?

board.text: In 4 years Siya will be 3 years older than Diya
Now: Siya + Diya = 35 years. Siya now = ?

beats.say: In four years, Siya will be 3 years older than Diya. So how much older is she today?
