beats.say: Check all three clues. 9 is 3 times 3. Last year's 8 is 4 times 2. Next year's 10 is 5 times 2. All of them fit.
Look at 21. It is a multiple of 3, and last year's 20 is a multiple of 4. Tempting! But next year's 22 is not a multiple of 5. Every clue must fit.

board.text: 21: last year 20 fits, next year 22 does not

beats.say: With several clues, use one to make a short list, then test the list against the others.
Ritu and her two brothers are all more than 4 years old. Five years from now their ages will add up to 50. What did they add up to 2 years ago?

board.text: Ritu and her 2 brothers: three children
In 5 years their ages will add up to 50
What did they add up to 2 years ago?

beats.say: We are given a sum in the future and asked for a sum in the past. And there are three children, so every year counts three times.
From 5 years ahead, back to 2 years ago. How many years back is that altogether?

ask.ifNot: First 5 years back to today, then 2 more years back. So 5 plus 2.

beats.say: 5 plus 2 is 7 years back.
Each of the three children was 7 years younger. So the sum was smaller by 3 times 7, which is 21. The trap is to take 7 off only once.
50 minus 21 is 29. So two years ago their ages added up to 29 years.
Check in two steps. Back to today: take off 3 times 5, which is 15, leaving 35. Back 2 more years: take off 3 times 2, which is 6, leaving 29.
And why are we told they are all more than 4 years old? So that we know all three were already born 2 years ago.
So when a sum of ages moves in time, multiply the years by the number of people.
A mother is 5 times as old as her daughter. In 6 years their ages will add up to 60. How old is the daughter now?

board.text: A mother is 5 times as old as her daughter
In 6 years their ages will add up to 60

beats.say: One clue is about today: 5 times as old. The other is about 6 years from now: the sum of 60. We must bring them to the same time.
In 6 years they add up to 60. So what do they add up to today?

ask.ifNot: Both of them will be 6 years older. So today's sum is smaller by 6 for the mother, and by 6 again for the daughter.

beats.say: 60, minus 6, minus 6, is 48. Two people, so the 6 comes off twice. That is the trap here.
Today the daughter is 1 block and the mother is 5 blocks. That is 6 blocks.
6 blocks make 48. 48 divided by 6 is 8. The daughter is one block, so she is 8.

board.text: The daughter is 8 years old now

beats.say: Check: the mother is 5 times 8, which is 40. In 6 years they are 14 and 46, and 14 plus 46 is 60.
So bring the sum to the same time as the other clue. Then use blocks.
The ages of two cousins multiply to give 84. The older one is 5 years older. What do their two ages add up to?

board.text: Two cousins: their ages multiply to give 84
The older is 5 years older. Ages add up to ?

beats.say: We need two numbers that multiply to 84. Let us list the pairs, starting small.
We want the pair that is 5 apart. Which one is it?

ask.ifNot: Find the gap in each pair. 4 and 21 are much too far apart. 14 minus 6 is 8. But 12 minus 7 is 5.

beats.say: 12 minus 7 is 5, and 7 times 12 is 84. So the cousins are 7 and 12.
Now read the question again. It does not ask for either age. It asks what the two ages add up to.
7 plus 12 is 19. So their ages add up to 19.
Pairs like 6 and 14 also multiply to 84, but they are 8 apart, not 5. Both clues must fit.
So list the pairs that multiply to the number, then pick the pair with the right gap.
Kabir's age in months is the same number as his grandfather's age in years. Their ages add up to 78 years. How old is Kabir?

board.text: Kabir's age in months = grandfather's age in years
Their ages add up to 78 years. Kabir = ?

beats.say: A strange clue! Let us try it out. If Kabir were 1 year old, he would be 12 months old. So his grandfather would be 12 years old.
So the grandfather's age is always how many times Kabir's age?

ask.ifNot: Every year of Kabir's age is 12 months. So the number of months is 12 times the number of years.

beats.say: So Kabir is 1 block and his grandfather is 12 blocks. Together that is 13 blocks.
13 blocks make 78 years. 13 times 6 is 78, so one block is 6.
Kabir is one block. So Kabir is 6 years old.
Check: 6 years is 6 times 12, which is 72 months. So his grandfather is 72 years old. And 6 plus 72 is 78.
Careful: 72 is the grandfather's age, and 12 is only the number of months in a year. The question asks for Kabir.
So change both ages to the same unit, see how many times one is of the other, then use blocks.
Tara's age and her uncle's age are in the ratio 2 to 5. Six years ago they were in the ratio 1 to 4. How old is her uncle now?

board.text: Six years ago it was 1 : 4. Uncle now = ?

beats.say: Careful: the 2 and the 5 are not ages. They are parts. So we cannot just take 6 away from them. We need real ages.
Real ages in the ratio 2 to 5 come from multiplying both by the same number. Both must be more than 6, so start at 8 and 20. Then 10 and 25, 12 and 30, 14 and 35.
Take 6 years off each pair. We get 2 and 14, 4 and 19, 6 and 24, 8 and 29.

board.text: 6 years ago: 2 and 14, 4 and 19, 6 and 24, 8 and 29

beats.say: Six years ago the ratio was 1 to 4. So the uncle was 4 times Tara's age. Which pair fits?

ask.ifNot: Multiply the smaller number by 4 and see if you get the bigger one. Only 4 times 6 gives its partner, 24.

beats.say: 4 times 6 is 24. So six years ago Tara was 6 and her uncle was 24.
Come back to today. Tara is 6 plus 6, which is 12. Her uncle is 24 plus 6, which is 30.
So her uncle is 30 years old now.

board.text: Her uncle is 30 years old now

beats.say: Check today's ratio. Divide 12 and 30 by 6 and we get 2 and 5. Yes, 2 to 5.
So list real ages that fit one clue, then test them against the other clue.
Meera had p rupees. She bought 3 pencils, and each one cost q rupees. We want an expression for the money she has left.

spec.note: 3 pencils at ₹q each are paid for out of ₹p

beats.say: First, how much did the 3 pencils cost altogether?

ask.ifNot: One pencil costs q. Three pencils cost q plus q plus q. That is 3 times q, which we write as 3 q.

beats.say: q, and q, and q again. Three lots of q is 3 q rupees. That is what she spent.
Money left is the money she had, take away the money she spent.
She had p and she spent 3 q. Which expression is the money left?

ask.ifNot: The 3 belongs to the pencils, so it sits with q, not with p. Her own money p is counted just once. So it is p minus 3 q.

beats.say: So she has p minus 3 q rupees left.
Test it. Say she had 50 rupees and each pencil cost 10. Three pencils cost 30, and 50 minus 30 leaves 20.
The number of things multiplies the price of one. Then take that from the money she had: p minus 3 q.
A team scored r runs in the first innings. In the second innings it scored 40 runs fewer. We want the total for both innings.

spec.note: Total runs in both innings = ?

beats.say: The second innings was 40 runs fewer than the first. How do we write that?

ask.ifNot: Fewer means less. So we start from the first score, r, and take 40 away from it.

beats.say: Fewer means take away. So the second innings is r minus 40.
Careful: r minus 40 is only the second innings. The question wants the total of both.
Total means add. So we write r, plus r minus 40.
Look at r plus r. What is that?

ask.ifNot: One r and another r make two r's. We write that as 2 r.

beats.say: Two r's make 2 r. The 40 is taken away just once, because only one innings was 40 fewer.
Test it. If the first score was 100, the second was 60. Together that is 160. And 2 times 100, minus 40, is 160 too.
Write each part with the letter, then add. The total is 2 r minus 40.
Four terms here. Some have an a, and some have a b. Simplify means join the ones that belong together.
Which terms belong to the a family?

ask.ifNot: Look at the letter, not the number. 7 a and 2 a both carry an a. Those are like terms.

beats.say: The a family: 7 a, and then minus 2 a. The minus sign in front of 2 a belongs to it. 7 a minus 2 a is 5 a.
Now the b family: 3 b plus b. A b standing on its own, how many b's is that?

ask.ifNot: A letter standing alone is one of that letter. We just do not bother to write the 1. So b means 1 b.

beats.say: b on its own is 1 b. So 3 b plus 1 b is 4 b.
a and b are different hidden numbers, so 5 a and 4 b cannot be joined. They stay side by side.
Test it with a as 1 and b as 1. The long one is 7 plus 3 minus 2 plus 1, which is 9. The short one is 5 plus 4, also 9.
Collect each letter on its own, and keep every sign with its own term. That gave us 5 a plus 4 b.
The odd numbers go 1, 3, 5, 7 and on. We want a rule that gives the odd number in any position. The letter n stands for the position.
Start with something easier: the even numbers. The 1st is 2, the 2nd is 4, the 3rd is 6.
What is the rule for the even number in position n?

ask.ifNot: Each even number is double its position. The 3rd is 6, which is 2 times 3. So the nth one is 2 times n.

beats.say: Each even number is 2 times its position. So the nth even number is 2 n.
Now look at the odd numbers above the even ones. 1 sits above 2. 3 sits above 4. 5 sits above 6. Each odd number is 1 less.
So the nth odd number is 1 less than 2 n. How do we write that?

ask.ifNot: 1 less means take 1 away. So start from 2 n and take away 1.

beats.say: So the rule is 2 n minus 1.
A good rule must fit every position, so we test more than one. For n as 1: 2 times 1, minus 1, is 1. For n as 4: 2 times 4, minus 1, is 7. Both fit.
Here is the trap. 3 n minus 2 also gives 1 when n is 1. But for n as 2 it gives 4, and 4 is not odd. One test is never enough.
So the nth odd number is 2 n minus 1. Double the position, then take away 1.
An isosceles triangle has two equal sides. Here each one is 2 a plus 3 centimetres. The third side is a minus 2 centimetres. We want the perimeter.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. How many sides do we add?

ask.ifNot: Walk all the way round the triangle. You pass every side once, and there are 3 of them. So the equal side is counted twice.

beats.say: So we add all three. 2 a plus 3, then 2 a plus 3 again, then a minus 2.
Gather the a terms first. 2 a, and 2 a, and one more a. That is 5 a.
Now the plain numbers: 3, and 3, and the 2 from a minus 2. What do they come to?

ask.ifNot: The third side is a minus 2, so the 2 is taken away, not added. 3 plus 3 is 6, and 6 minus 2 is 4.

beats.say: 3 plus 3 is 6, and then minus 2 leaves 4. The minus sign travels with its 2.
So the perimeter is 5 a plus 4 centimetres.
Add every side, letters with letters and numbers with numbers. And keep each sign with its own number.
A garden is a rectangle, p metres long and q metres wide. One long side is along a wall. A fence goes round the rest. How long is the fence?

board.text: long sides: p m,   short sides: q m

spec.note: A fence goes on three sides only

beats.say: A rectangle has 4 sides. How many of them need a fence?

ask.ifNot: One long side is along the wall, and the wall does the job there. So the fence runs along the other 3 sides.

beats.say: One long side is the wall. So the fence goes along the other long side, and both short sides.
Now in letters. Which three sides are fenced?

ask.ifNot: The wall takes the place of a long side, and the long sides are p. So only one p is left. Both short sides, q and q, still need a fence.

beats.say: One long side is p. The two short sides are q and q.
q plus q is 2 q. So the fence is p plus 2 q metres.
Try it with numbers. If the garden is 9 metres long and 4 metres wide, the fence is 9 plus 4 plus 4, which is 17 metres.
The whole way round would be 2 p plus 2 q. But the wall saves us one p. So the fence is p plus 2 q.
a is 6 and b is 4. We want the value of 3 a, minus 2 b, plus a b. Three parts, so we take them one by one.
3 a is 3 times 6, which is 18. And 2 b is 2 times 4, which is 8.
Now the last part, a b. Two letters side by side. What does a b mean here?

ask.ifNot: Letters side by side have a hidden times sign between them, just like a number next to a letter. So a b is 6 times 4.

beats.say: a b is 6 times 4, which is 24.
Now put the three parts back, each with its own sign. 18, minus 8, plus 24.
Look at the sign in front of the 8. What do we do with the 8?

ask.ifNot: The sign in front of 2 b is a minus. So the 8 is taken away from the 18.

beats.say: Left to right. 18 minus 8 is 10. Then 10 plus 24 is 34.
So the value is 34. Side by side always means times, for a number with a letter and for two letters.
We are given two rules. The nth odd number is 2 n minus 1. The nth even number is 2 n. How much more is the 30th odd number than the 12th even number?
Can we just take 12 away from 30?

choices: No, find the two numbers first
ask.ifNot: 30 and 12 are only positions, like places in a queue. We need the numbers standing in those places. So we use the rules first.

beats.say: The 30th odd number. Put 30 in place of n. 2 times 30 is 60, and 60 minus 1 is 59.
Notice it is 59, not 60. An odd number is 1 less than double its position. Never 1 more.
The 12th even number. Put 12 in place of n. 2 times 12 is 24.
How much more is 59 than 24? Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: How much more means the gap between the two numbers. We find a gap by taking the smaller from the bigger.

beats.say: 59 minus 24 is 35.
So the 30th odd number is 35 more. Use each rule to find the real number first, then compare.
Anu is x years old. Her father's age is 4 years more than three times Anu's age. We want the sum of their ages after 5 years.

spec.note: Sum of their ages after 5 years = ?

beats.say: First, the father's age now. 4 more than three times x. Which is it?

ask.ifNot: Three times x is 3 x. Then 4 more means add 4 after that. So it is 3 x plus 4.

beats.say: Three times x is 3 x, and 4 more makes 3 x plus 4. That is the father today.
Now jump ahead 5 years. Anu will be x plus 5.
Who else gets 5 years older?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everyone. If Anu is 5 years older, her father is 5 years older as well.

beats.say: The father gains 5 years too. 3 x plus 4, plus 5, is 3 x plus 9.
Now add the two ages. x plus 3 x is 4 x. And 5 plus 9 is 14.
So the sum will be 4 x plus 14. The trap was the 5 years. Two people each grow 5 years older, so the sum grows by 10.
Three numbers come one after another, like 4, 5, 6. The smallest is n. We want the sum of all three.

board.text: three numbers in a row, smallest n

spec.note: Three numbers, one after another

beats.say: If the smallest is n, what is the next number?

ask.ifNot: The next number is always 1 more. After 4 comes 4 plus 1. So after n comes n plus 1.

beats.say: The next is n plus 1. And the one after that is 1 more again: n plus 2.
Now add all three together.
How many n's are there in that sum?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the three numbers has an n inside it. Count them on the board: n, n, and n.

beats.say: Three n's make 3 n. The plain numbers, 1 and 2, make 3. So the sum is 3 n plus 3.
Test it with 4, 5 and 6. Their sum is 15. And 3 times 4, plus 3, is 15 too.
Write each number using n first. Then add the letters and the numbers on their own. That gives 3 n plus 3.
A taxi charges 50 rupees for the first kilometre, and 12 rupees for every kilometre after that. We want the fare for a ride of d kilometres.

spec.note: First km ₹50, then ₹12 for every km after it

beats.say: Try a short ride first. For 2 kilometres: 50 for the first, then 12 for one more. That is 62 rupees.
Now a ride of d kilometres. The first one costs 50. How many kilometres are left at 12 rupees each?

ask.ifNot: The first kilometre has its own price, so it is not charged again at 12. Take that 1 kilometre away from d. That leaves d minus 1.

beats.say: d minus 1 kilometres, at 12 rupees each. That costs 12 times, d minus 1.
Open the bracket. 12 times d is 12 d. 12 times 1 is 12. So that part is 12 d minus 12.
Now add the 50 for the first kilometre. 50 minus 12 is 38.
So the fare is 12 d plus 38 rupees.
Check with our 2 kilometre ride. 12 times 2 is 24, and 24 plus 38 is 62. The same as before!
The trap is to charge 12 for all d kilometres and then 50 on top. The first kilometre is paid for only once. That is why we get 12 d plus 38.
Each box holds m mangoes. Riya has 3 boxes and 5 loose mangoes. Sameer has 2 boxes and 4 loose ones. Then Riya gives one full box to Sameer.

spec.note: Riya gives one full box to Sameer

beats.say: After the box moves, how many boxes does each child have?

ask.ifNot: Riya gives one away, so her 3 boxes become 2. Sameer gets it, so his 2 boxes become 3. The loose mangoes do not move.

beats.say: Riya now has 2 boxes and 5 loose: 2 m plus 5. Sameer has 3 boxes and 4 loose: 3 m plus 4.
How many more does Sameer have? To find how many more, we take Riya's from Sameer's.
Compare the boxes first. 3 m take away 2 m leaves one box, which is m.
Now the loose mangoes. Sameer has 4 and Riya has 5. Who has more loose ones?

ask.ifNot: 5 is more than 4. So in loose mangoes Riya is 1 ahead, and that takes 1 off Sameer's lead.

beats.say: So Sameer is ahead by a whole box, m, but behind by 1 loose mango. Altogether he has m minus 1 more.
Test it. If a box holds 10, Riya has 25 and Sameer has 34. And 34 minus 25 is 9, which is 10 minus 1.
Write what each child has after the move, then subtract. Sameer has m minus 1 more.
The letter n stands for an even number. We want the 5th odd number that comes after it.
Let's try it with a real even number first. Say n is 10. The odd numbers after 10 are 11, 13, 15, 17 and 19.
Look at the very first jump, from 10 to 11. How big is it?

ask.ifNot: 10 is even, and the very next number, 11, is already odd. So the first jump is only 1. After that, the jumps are 2.

beats.say: The first jump is just 1, because the number right after an even number is odd. Then the odd numbers go up in twos.
Count along the list. Which one is the 5th?

ask.ifNot: Point at each one and count: 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th. The 5th in the list is n plus 9.

beats.say: The 5th one is n plus 9.
Check with our 10. The 5th odd number after 10 was 19. And 10 plus 9 is 19.
The trap is to make 5 jumps of 2, which gives n plus 10. But the first jump from an even number is only 1. So the answer is n plus 9.
A wire is bent into a square. Each side is 3 a plus 6 centimetres. Then the same wire is bent into a triangle with three equal sides. How long is each side of the triangle?

spec.note: This wire square is opened out and bent into a triangle

beats.say: The wire is bent into a new shape. What stays the same?

ask.ifNot: Bending does not stretch the wire or cut it. So the whole length stays the same. Only the shape changes.

beats.say: So first we find the whole wire. It goes round the square, and a square has 4 equal sides.
4 times, 3 a plus 6. The 4 multiplies both parts. 4 times 3 a is 12 a. 4 times 6 is 24. So the wire is 12 a plus 24 centimetres long.
The triangle has 3 equal sides, made from this whole wire. How do we find one side?

ask.ifNot: The whole wire is shared equally among the 3 sides of the triangle. Sharing equally means dividing by 3.

beats.say: Share each part by 3. 12 a divided by 3 is 4 a. And 24 divided by 3 is 8.
So each side of the triangle is 4 a plus 8 centimetres.
Same wire, same total length. Find the total first, then share it among the sides of the new shape.
We are told that 2 x plus y is 10. We want 6 x plus 3 y, minus 4. But we do not know x or y on their own!

spec.note: Use this to find 6x + 3y − 4

beats.say: That is fine. Look for the first expression hiding inside the second one. Compare 2 x with 6 x, and y with 3 y.
6 x is how many times 2 x?

ask.ifNot: 2 x, and 2 x, and 2 x make 6 x. That is 3 lots. And y has become 3 y, which is 3 lots too.

beats.say: Both parts are 3 times as big. So 6 x plus 3 y is 3 lots of, 2 x plus y.
And we know that 2 x plus y is 10. So 3 lots of it is 3 times 10, which is 30.
Is 30 our final answer?

ask.ifNot: 30 is only 6 x plus 3 y. The expression we want has a minus 4 at the end. One small step is left.

beats.say: 30 minus 4 is 26.
So the value is 26. We never found x or y. We spotted the whole of 2 x plus y, three times over, and used it as one block.
p stands for an odd number. We want the expression that is always a multiple of 4. The key word is always. It must work for every odd number, not just one.
Let's test with p as 1. p plus 3 gives 4. And 2 p plus 2 gives 4 as well. Both are multiples of 4, so far.
Still with p as 1: 4 p plus 2 gives 6, and 2 p gives 2. Neither is a multiple of 4. Those two are out.
Two are left: p plus 3, and 2 p plus 2. Both gave 4. Can we stop here?

ask.ifNot: Always means every time. One test cannot show that. So we try the next odd number, 3.

beats.say: Try p as 3. p plus 3 is 6. That is not a multiple of 4, so it is out. 2 p plus 2 is 8, and 8 is a multiple of 4.
Why does it always work? 2 p plus 2 is 2 lots of, p plus 1. p is odd, so p plus 1 is even. And double an even number is always a multiple of 4.
So the one that is always a multiple of 4 is 2 p plus 2.
When a question says always, test more than one number. One lucky fit is not proof.
Two moments in this story: three years ago, and now. Ravi is x years old now. Three years ago, Meena was twice as old as Ravi was then. How old is Meena now?

spec.note: Three years ago. Ravi is x years old now.

beats.say: The twice as old was true three years ago. So first: how old was Ravi three years ago?

ask.ifNot: Three years ago he was younger. So take 3 away from his age now. That is x minus 3.

beats.say: Three years ago Ravi was x minus 3.
Meena was twice that. 2 times, x minus 3. The 2 multiplies both parts, so we get 2 x minus 6.
2 x minus 6. Is that Meena's age now?

choices: Yes, that is her age now
ask.ifNot: 2 x minus 6 is how old Meena was three years ago. She has had three birthdays since then. So we must add 3.

beats.say: That was her age three years ago. To reach today, add 3. Minus 6, then plus 3, makes minus 3.
Test it. Say Ravi is 10 now. Three years ago he was 7, and Meena was 14. Today she is 17. And 2 times 10, minus 3, is 17.
Keep track of which moment each age belongs to. Go back, double, then come forward again. Meena is 2 x minus 3.
Rina makes a row of squares with matchsticks. The first square needs 4. Each new square shares a side, so it needs only 3 more. How many for a row of n squares?

board.text: first square: 4,   each new square: 3 more

spec.note: A row of squares made with matchsticks

beats.say: Count some small rows. 1 square needs 4. 2 squares need 4 plus 3, which is 7. 3 squares need 7 plus 3, which is 10.
In a row of n squares, the first one uses 4. How many of the squares are new ones, using 3 each?

ask.ifNot: The first square is already counted with its 4 matchsticks. Take it out of the n squares. That leaves n minus 1 new ones.

beats.say: n minus 1 new squares, with 3 matchsticks each. 3 times, n minus 1, is 3 n minus 3.
Now add the 4 for the first square. 4 minus 3 leaves 1. So it is 3 n plus 1.
Let's check with 3 squares. We counted 10. What does 3 n plus 1 give when n is 3?

ask.ifNot: 3 n means 3 times 3, which is 9. Then add 1.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9, and 1 more is 10. It matches our count.
The trap is 3 n plus 4. That gives 3 to every square and then 4 more. But the first square is counted only once. So the answer is 3 n plus 1.
Anu has 5 k plus 3 rupees. Bala has 3 k plus 11. k can be any whole number from 1 to 10. For how many of those does Anu have more?
Start with k as 1. Anu has 5 plus 3, which is 8. Bala has 3 plus 11, which is 14. Bala is ahead by 6.
Each time k goes up by 1, Anu gains 5 rupees and Bala gains 3. What happens to the gap?

ask.ifNot: Anu gains 5 while Bala gains only 3. So Anu catches up by 2 rupees every time k goes up by 1.

beats.say: Anu catches up by 2 each time. The gap goes 6, then 4, then 2, then 0. So when k is 4 they are level.
Check k as 4. Anu has 5 times 4, plus 3, which is 23. Bala has 3 times 4, plus 11, also 23. Equal.
When k is 4 they have the same. Does 4 count as Anu having more?

ask.ifNot: More means really bigger. When both have 23 rupees, nobody has more. So 4 does not count.

beats.say: After 4, Anu pulls ahead and stays ahead. So she has more when k is 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 or 10.
Count them. That is 6 values.
Find where the two are equal. Then count only the values on the winning side. And equal never counts as more.
A card is 2 a plus 5 centimetres long and a plus 1 wide. A small square, with each side a centimetres, is cut from one corner. We want the perimeter of what is left.

spec.note: A square of side a cm is cut from one corner

beats.say: Start with the whole card, before the cut. Length plus breadth: 2 a plus 5, plus a plus 1, is 3 a plus 6.
The perimeter is double that. 2 times 3 a is 6 a, and 2 times 6 is 12.
Now the cut. Trace the edge with your finger. At the corner, two pieces of the old edge have gone. Each one was a centimetres long.
But the cut also makes new edges, on the inside of the corner. How long are the new edges altogether?

choices: a + a, the same as was lost
nothing, there are no new edges
ask.ifNot: The hole is a square with side a. Two of its sides are now part of the card's edge. So the new edges are a and a.

beats.say: Two edges of a were lost, and two new edges of a appeared. They balance exactly. The distance round does not change.
So the perimeter is still 6 a plus 12 centimetres.
A square notch at a corner swaps two outside edges for two inside edges of the same length. So always trace the edge before you take anything away.
The rule is 4 n minus 1. So the pattern starts 3, 7, 11, 15. We have four numbers to test, and only one of them belongs to the pattern.
See how each term is made. Take a multiple of 4, like 4, 8, 12 or 16. Then take away 1.
So if a number is in the pattern, what must we get when we add 1 to it?

ask.ifNot: Every term is 1 less than a multiple of 4. So adding the 1 back must land us exactly on a multiple of 4.

beats.say: Test each number by adding 1. 44 becomes 45. 45 becomes 46. 46 becomes 47. And 47 becomes 48.
Which of 45, 46, 47 and 48 is a multiple of 4?

ask.ifNot: Count in fours from 44. The next one is 48. So of our four numbers, only 48 is a multiple of 4.

beats.say: 48 divided by 4 is 12, a whole number. So 47 is in the pattern. It is the 12th term.
Watch out for 45. Taking 1 away from it gives 44, which is tempting. But the rule already takes 1 away, so to undo it we add 1.
To test a number against a rule, undo the rule backwards. Here: add 1, then see if 4 divides it exactly. Only 47 passes.
Sana has s rupees. Tara has 20 rupees more than Sana. Then Tara gives 15 rupees to Sana. Who has more now, and by how much?

spec.note: Then Tara gives ₹15 to Sana

beats.say: Tara has 20 more than Sana. So Tara starts with s plus 20.
Tara gives 15 rupees to Sana. Whose money changes?

ask.ifNot: The 15 rupees leave Tara's hand and land in Sana's. So Tara goes down by 15, and Sana goes up by 15.

beats.say: Tara loses 15. s plus 20, minus 15, is s plus 5.
Sana gains 15. So Sana now has s plus 15.
Now compare s plus 15 with s plus 5. Who has more?

ask.ifNot: Both have the same s. On top of that, Sana has 15 and Tara has only 5. So Sana has more.

beats.say: Both have s. Sana has 15 extra and Tara has 5 extra. 15 minus 5 is 10. So Sana has 10 rupees more.
The trap is to take 15 off Tara's lead of 20 and stop there. But the same 15 also lands with Sana. Write both new amounts, then compare. Sana is 10 ahead.
Five whole numbers come one after another. The middle one is m. We want the smallest and the greatest added together.

board.text: five numbers in a row, middle one m

spec.note: Five numbers in a row. The middle one is m.

beats.say: Look at the example: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. The middle is 8. The smallest, 6, is 2 less than 8. The greatest, 10, is 2 more.
So if the middle number is m, what is the smallest?

ask.ifNot: Step back from the middle, one at a time. One step back is m minus 1. Two steps back is m minus 2. That is the smallest.

beats.say: Step out from the middle, both ways. The five numbers are m minus 2, m minus 1, m, m plus 1 and m plus 2.
Add the smallest and the greatest. m minus 2, plus m plus 2.
What happens to the minus 2 and the plus 2?

ask.ifNot: Taking 2 away and then adding 2 brings you back to where you started. Together they make nothing.

beats.say: Minus 2 and plus 2 cancel. All that is left is m and m, which is 2 m.
Check with the example. 6 plus 10 is 16. And 2 times 8 is 16.
When m is in the middle, the two ends are the same distance away, one on each side. So together they make 2 m.
A rectangle has a perimeter of 10 a plus 6 centimetres. Its length is 3 a plus 2 centimetres. We want its breadth.
The perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths. So what is half the perimeter?

ask.ifNot: Cut the trip round the rectangle in half. Half of 2 lengths and 2 breadths is 1 length and 1 breadth.

beats.say: So halve the perimeter. Half of 10 a is 5 a. Half of 6 is 3. One length plus one breadth is 5 a plus 3.
Now take the length away. What is left is the breadth.
We take away the whole length, 3 a plus 2. What happens to the 2?

ask.ifNot: The bracket says the whole length goes. That is the 3 a, and the 2 as well. Both are taken away.

beats.say: Letters first: 5 a minus 3 a is 2 a. Then numbers: 3 minus 2 is 1.
So the breadth is 2 a plus 1 centimetres.
Check by going forwards. Length plus breadth is 5 a plus 3. Double it, and we are back at 10 a plus 6.
To work back from a perimeter: halve it first, then take away the side you know.
A two digit number has tens digit t and ones digit u. Swap the digits to make a second number. We want the sum of the two numbers.

board.text: tens digit t,   ones digit u

spec.note: Swapping the digits makes a second number

beats.say: Try real digits first. Tens digit 4 and ones digit 3 make 43. That is 4 tens and 3 ones.
So with letters, what is the number with tens digit t and ones digit u worth?

ask.ifNot: A digit in the tens place is worth ten times itself. So t in the tens place is worth 10 t. Then add the ones digit, u.

beats.say: The first number is worth 10 t plus u.
Now swap the digits. u moves to the tens place, and t to the ones place. So the second number is worth 10 u plus t.
Add them. For t: 10 t and 1 more t make 11 t. For u: 1 u and 10 u make 11 u.
So the sum is 11 t plus 11 u.
Check with 43 and 34. 43 plus 34 is 77. And 11 times 4, plus 11 times 3, is 44 plus 33, also 77.
Each digit sits in the tens place once and in the ones place once. That is why each one is counted 11 times.
We are told that 3 x plus 2 is 20. We want the value of 3 times, x plus 2, with a bracket.

spec.note: Use this to find 3(x + 2)

beats.say: These two look almost the same. Are they the same thing?

ask.ifNot: With the bracket, the 3 multiplies the x and the 2 as well. Without the bracket, only the x is multiplied.

beats.say: Open the bracket. 3 times x is 3 x. 3 times 2 is 6. So it is 3 x plus 6.
Now compare. We know 3 x plus 2. We want 3 x plus 6. The 3 x part is the same in both.
How much more is 3 x plus 6 than 3 x plus 2?

ask.ifNot: The 3 x is the same in both. So just compare the plain numbers. From 2 up to 6 is 4.

beats.say: It is 4 more. 3 x plus 2 is 20, so 3 x plus 6 is 20 plus 4, which is 24.
We can check by finding x. x must be 6, because 3 times 6, plus 2, is 20. And 3 times, 6 plus 2, is 3 times 8, which is 24.
The trap is to add the whole 6 on to the 20. But the 20 already has a 2 inside it. So we add only 4, and get 24.
A carpenter cuts a long pole into n pieces. Each cut takes 3 minutes. How long does all the cutting take?

board.text: n pieces,   each cut takes 3 minutes

spec.note: Each cut takes 3 minutes. How long is all the cutting?

beats.say: Careful. The time goes with the cuts, not with the pieces. So first we count the cuts.
Picture a stick. 1 cut makes 2 pieces. 2 cuts make 3 pieces.
So how many cuts make n pieces?

ask.ifNot: The cuts are always 1 fewer than the pieces. 2 pieces need 1 cut. 3 pieces need 2 cuts. So n pieces need n minus 1 cuts.

beats.say: n minus 1 cuts, at 3 minutes each. That is 3 times, n minus 1.
Open the bracket. What is 3 times, n minus 1?

ask.ifNot: The 3 multiplies both parts in the bracket. 3 times n is 3 n. And 3 times 1 is 3, so 3 is taken away, not 1.

beats.say: 3 times n is 3 n. 3 times 1 is 3. So the cutting takes 3 n minus 3 minutes.
Check with 2 pieces. That is 1 cut, so 3 minutes. And 3 times 2, minus 3, is 3. It fits.
Count the cuts, not the pieces. There is always one cut fewer. That gives 3 n minus 3.
Three angles lie side by side on a straight line. Two of them are 48 degrees and 67 degrees. We want the third.

ask.ifNot: Angles side by side on a straight line make a half turn together. A half turn is 180 degrees. 360 is for angles all the way round a point.

beats.say: What do the angles on a straight line add up to?
So all three angles together make 180. First, add the two we know.
48 and 67. 40 and 60 make 100. 8 and 7 make 15. So that is 115.

ask.ifNot: 115 is the two angles we were given, added together. The third angle is the piece that is still missing from the straight line.

beats.say: We have 115. Is that our answer?
The third angle is what is left of the 180. Take away 100 first, which leaves 80. Then 15 more, which leaves 65.
So the third angle is 65 degrees.
Check by adding all three: 115 and 65 make 180. One whole straight line.
So for angles on a line: add what you know, then take it away from 180.

board.text: 8 equal slices, 3 eaten. Angle of the rest = ?

beats.say: A pizza is cut from the centre into 8 equal slices, and Ria eats 3. What angle do the remaining slices make at the centre?

ask.ifNot: All the way round a point is a full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees. 180 is only half way round.

beats.say: All the slices meet at the centre, and together they go the whole way round. How many degrees is the whole way round?
360 shared among 8 equal slices. Half of 360 is 180, half of 180 is 90, and half of 90 is 45. So each slice is 45 degrees.

ask.ifNot: There were 8 slices to begin with, and 3 are eaten. 8 take away 3 leaves 5.

beats.say: Ria eats 3 of the 8 slices. How many slices are left?
5 slices are left, and each one is 45 degrees.
5 times 45. 4 slices are half the pizza, which is 180 degrees. One more slice of 45 makes 225.
So the remaining slices make an angle of 225 degrees.
A check: the 3 eaten slices make 135. And 135 and 225 make 360, the whole pizza.
135 is the trap. It is the part that was eaten. Always look at which slices the question asks about.

board.text: Hour hand, 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. Degrees turned = ?

beats.say: How many degrees does the hour hand turn between 3 p.m. and half past 7 the same evening?
The hour hand goes once round the clock, 360 degrees, in 12 hours. So in 1 hour it turns 360 divided by 12, which is 30 degrees.

ask.ifNot: From 3 to 7 is 4 hours. Then there is half an hour more, up to half past 7.

beats.say: How long is it from 3 p.m. to half past 7?

board.text: 3 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. = 4 and a half hours

beats.say: 4 whole hours, and then half an hour.
For the 4 whole hours, the hand turns 4 times 30, which is 120 degrees.
Don't stop there! The hour hand keeps moving during the last half hour. Half an hour gives half of 30, which is 15.
120 and 15 make 135. The hour hand turns through 135 degrees.
The hour hand is slow but steady. 30 degrees for every hour, and 15 for every half hour.

board.text: Facing East. Three-quarter turn anticlockwise. Now?

beats.say: Arjun faces east. He makes a three-quarter turn anticlockwise. Which way does he face now?
A quarter turn takes you from one main direction to the next. A three-quarter turn is 3 of those, one after another.

ask.ifNot: Clock hands go from east down to south. Anticlockwise is the other way, so from east we go up to north.

beats.say: Anticlockwise means the opposite way to clock hands. Starting from east, which direction comes first going anticlockwise?
First quarter turn: east to north.
Second quarter turn, still anticlockwise: north to west.
Third quarter turn: west to south.
So Arjun is facing south.
A neat check: three quarters anticlockwise lands in the same place as one quarter clockwise. And one step clockwise from east is south.
Take quarter turns one at a time, and always check which way round you are going.

board.text: Ladder makes 58° with the ground. With the wall = ?

beats.say: A ladder leans on a wall and makes 58 degrees with the ground. What angle does it make with the wall? Look: the ladder, the wall and the ground make a triangle.

ask.ifNot: Upright meeting level makes a square corner, like the corner of a room. A square corner is a right angle, 90 degrees.

beats.say: The wall stands upright and the ground is level. So what angle do the wall and the ground make?
The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees. The right angle uses 90 of that. So the other two angles share what is left: 90.

ask.ifNot: The two ladder angles make 90 together, and one is 58. So take 58 away from 90. Taking it from 180 forgets the right angle.

beats.say: So the two angles at the ends of the ladder make 90 together. One of them is 58. Which sum finds the other?
90 take away 50 is 40, and 8 more away is 32.
So the ladder makes an angle of 32 degrees with the wall.
Check: 58 and 32 make 90, and the right angle adds 90 more. 180 in all.
In a triangle with a right angle, the other two angles always make 90 together.

board.text: 6:00: angle is 180°. How much smaller at 6:30?

beats.say: At 6 o'clock the hands make a straight line, 180 degrees. By 6:30 the angle is smaller. We want to know how much smaller.

ask.ifNot: The hour hand moves too. In half an hour it goes half of the way from the 6 to the 7.

beats.say: First we need the angle at half past 6. The minute hand has gone half way round, and now it points at the 6. Where is the hour hand?
Halfway between the 6 and the 7. That is the first trap. If it had stayed on the 6, the two hands would be together.
One gap between two numbers is 30 degrees, because 360 shared among 12 gaps is 30. So half a gap is 15.
So at half past 6, the angle between the hands is just 15 degrees.

choices: No, how much smaller it became
ask.ifNot: The question says: by how many degrees has the angle become smaller. So we compare 180 at the start with 15 now.

beats.say: Now read the question again. Does it ask for the angle at 6:30?
The angle went from 180 down to 15. The drop is 180 take away 15, which is 165.
So the angle has become smaller by 165 degrees.
Two traps in one question. The hour hand creeps, and the question asks for the change, not the new angle. Read the last line twice.

board.text: Full turn every 40 seconds. Turn in 15 seconds = ?

beats.say: A lighthouse lamp makes one full turn every 40 seconds, at a steady speed. How many degrees does it turn in 15 seconds?

ask.ifNot: A full turn takes you all the way round, back to where you started. That is 360 degrees.

beats.say: How many degrees is one full turn?
So the lamp turns 360 degrees in 40 seconds.
Find the turn in 1 second first. 360 shared among 40 seconds. Cross a zero off each number: 36 divided by 4, which is 9.

ask.ifNot: Each second gives 9 degrees, and there are 15 seconds. So it is 15 times 9.

beats.say: 9 degrees every second. Now, which sum gives the turn in 15 seconds?
15 times 9. 10 nines are 90, and 5 nines are 45. 90 and 45 make 135.
So the lamp turns through 135 degrees.
Does that make sense? 15 seconds is less than half of 40 seconds. And 135 is less than half a turn, 180. Good.
Find what happens in 1 second, then multiply. That works for anything that turns at a steady speed.
The supplement of an angle is 3 times its complement. We must find the angle. There is a lovely idea hiding in here.

ask.ifNot: Both start from the same angle. One goes up to 90 and the other goes up to 180, which is 90 further. So the supplement is always 90 more.

board.text: Complement: tops the angle up to 90°
Supplement: tops the angle up to 180°

beats.say: Take any angle. Its complement tops it up to 90. Its supplement tops it up to 180. So how much bigger is the supplement than the complement?
180 is 90 more than 90. So the supplement is always the complement, plus 90.
Now use the clue. The supplement is 3 times the complement. Picture the complement as 1 block. Then the supplement is 3 of those blocks.

ask.ifNot: 2 equal blocks make 90, so each block is half of 90. That is 45.

beats.say: The supplement has 2 blocks more than the complement. And we know the extra is 90. So 2 blocks make 90. How big is 1 block?
Half of 90 is 45. So the complement is 45 degrees.
The angle and its complement make 90. So the angle is 90 take away 45, which is 45 as well.
Check. The supplement of 45 is 180 take away 45, which is 135. And 3 times 45 is 135. It works.
The key was one fact: a supplement is always 90 more than the complement of the same angle.

board.text: Lines cross: one angle = 4 × the one beside it. Largest?

beats.say: Two straight lines cross. One angle is 4 times the angle beside it. We want the largest angle.

ask.ifNot: Angles side by side on a straight line make a half turn together. A half turn is 180 degrees. 360 is for all 4 angles round the point.

beats.say: Two angles beside each other at a crossing sit on one straight line. So what do those two add up to?
Now think in parts. Call the smaller angle 1 part. The angle beside it is 4 times as big, so it is 4 parts.

ask.ifNot: 1 part for the small angle and 4 parts for the big one. 1 and 4 make 5 parts.

beats.say: How many parts make the 180?
5 parts make 180, so one part is 180 divided by 5. 5 thirties are 150 and 5 sixes are 30. So 5 times 36 is 180. One part is 36.
36 is the small angle. The big one is 4 parts, 4 times 36. Double 36 is 72, and double 72 is 144.
Opposite angles at a crossing are equal. So the 4 angles are 144, 36, 144 and 36. The largest is 144 degrees.
Check: 36 and 144 make 180, a straight line.
36 is the trap. It is the small angle, and the question wants the largest. And angles beside each other share a straight line, so they share 180, not 360.

board.text: Round a point: 80° and 4 equal angles. Each = ?

beats.say: 5 angles meet at a point and fill the whole turn. One is 80 degrees, and the other 4 are equal. How big is each equal angle?

ask.ifNot: All the way round a point is a full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees. 180 is only half way round.

beats.say: The angles fill the whole turn round the point. How many degrees is that?
First take away the angle we know. 360 take away 60 is 300, and 20 more away is 280.

ask.ifNot: There are 5 angles in all, but the 80 has already been taken out. Only the 4 equal angles share the 280.

beats.say: 280 is left for the equal angles. How many angles share it?
280 shared among 4. 28 divided by 4 is 7, so 280 divided by 4 is 70.
So each of the equal angles is 70 degrees.
Check: 4 times 70 is 280, and 80 more makes 360. A whole turn.
Take away what you know, then share the rest. And share it only among the angles that are still unknown.

board.text: Smaller angle between the hands at 2:40 = ?

beats.say: What is the smaller angle between the hands of a clock at 2:40? Here is the clock.
The 12 numbers cut the full turn of 360 degrees into 12 equal gaps. Each gap is 30 degrees.
At 40 minutes past, the minute hand is on the 8. Measure from the top of the clock, the 12. From the 12 round to the 8 is 8 gaps, and 8 times 30 is 240.

ask.ifNot: 1 degree for every 2 minutes. 40 minutes is 20 lots of 2 minutes. So the hour hand moves 20 degrees.

beats.say: Now the hour hand. At 2 o'clock it is 2 gaps from the top, 60 degrees. But it moves 30 degrees in 60 minutes: 1 degree every 2 minutes. How far does it move in 40 minutes?
20 degrees. So the hour hand is at 60 and 20 more: 80 degrees from the top.
The angle between the hands is the difference. 240 take away 80 is 160.
Is 160 the smaller angle? The two ways round the clock make 360 together, so the other way round is 200. Yes, 160 is the smaller one.
The trap is to leave the hour hand on the 2. From the 2 to the 8 is 6 gaps, which would be 180. But the hour hand has crept 20 degrees closer.
So the smaller angle is 160 degrees.
Measure both hands from the top of the clock, then subtract. And remember that the hour hand never sits still.

board.text: 2:10 to 2:50. Minute hand turn − hour hand turn = ?

beats.say: From 2:10 to 2:50 both hands of a clock keep turning. How many more degrees does the minute hand turn than the hour hand?

ask.ifNot: Both times are in the same hour. From 10 minutes past to 50 minutes past is 50 take away 10, which is 40 minutes.

beats.say: First, how much time passes from 2:10 to 2:50?
40 minutes pass.
The minute hand does a full turn, 360 degrees, in 60 minutes. That is 6 degrees every minute. So in 40 minutes it turns 40 times 6, which is 240.

ask.ifNot: 1 degree for every 2 minutes. 40 minutes is 20 lots of 2 minutes, so the hour hand turns 20 degrees.

beats.say: The hour hand is much slower. It crosses one gap of 30 degrees in 60 minutes. That is 1 degree every 2 minutes. So how far does it turn in 40 minutes?
20 degrees. A small turn, but it counts.

ask.ifNot: How many more asks how far ahead the minute hand is. That is a difference, so we take the smaller turn away from the bigger one.

beats.say: The question says how many more. Do we add the two turns, or subtract?
240 take away 20 is 220. The minute hand turns 220 degrees more.
240 is the minute hand alone and 20 is the hour hand alone. Both are waiting in the choices. Only the difference answers how many more.

board.text: From 12 noon the hour hand turns 75°. Time = ?

beats.say: At 12 noon the hour hand points straight up. Later it has turned exactly 75 degrees. What time is it?

ask.ifNot: 360 degrees shared among 12 hours is 30 degrees for each hour.

beats.say: The hour hand goes right round, 360 degrees, in 12 hours. So how far does it turn in 1 hour?
30 degrees every hour.
So every 30 degrees is 1 hour. How many 30s fit into 75? 30 and 30 make 60. One more 30 would be 90, which is too many. So 2 whole hours.
2 hours use up 60 degrees. 75 take away 60 leaves 15 degrees still to explain.

ask.ifNot: 30 degrees takes a whole hour. 15 is half of 30, so it takes half an hour, and half an hour is 30 minutes. The degrees are not the minutes.

beats.say: 15 degrees is half of 30. So how much time does that last bit take?
Half of the turn, so half of the hour: 30 minutes.
So 2 hours and 30 minutes have passed since 12 noon. The time is 2:30 in the afternoon.
The trap is to read degrees as if they were minutes. The hour hand is slow: 30 degrees for an hour, 15 for half an hour.

board.text: 12:20. Sana says 120°. How far from the true angle?

beats.say: At 12:20 Sana says the angle between the hands is 120 degrees. We have to find how far her answer is from the true angle.
Sana says two things: the minute hand is on the 4, and the hour hand is on the 12. Let's check each. First, each gap on a clock is 360 divided by 12, which is 30 degrees.
At 20 minutes past, the minute hand is exactly on the 4. From the 12 to the 4 is 4 gaps, and 4 times 30 is 120. So far, Sana is right.

choices: No, it has crept towards the 1
ask.ifNot: The hour hand moves all the time. In the 20 minutes since 12 o'clock, it has moved a little way towards the 1.

beats.say: Now the hour hand. Is it exactly on the 12 at 12:20?
How far has it crept? 20 minutes is one third of an hour. In a whole hour the hour hand moves 30 degrees. So it has moved one third of 30, which is 10 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The hour hand has moved towards the minute hand. The two hands are closer together, so the angle is smaller.

beats.say: It has crept 10 degrees towards the 4, where the minute hand is. So is the true angle bigger or smaller than Sana's 120?
The true angle is 120 take away 10, which is 110.
The question asks how far Sana's answer is from the true one. 120 take away 110 is 10.
110 sits in the choices as a trap. It is the true angle, but the question asks for the difference. Sana forgot that the hour hand never waits.
Farhan faces north-east and makes three turns: 90 clockwise, 225 anticlockwise, then 135 clockwise. Where does he end up facing?

ask.ifNot: Two of the turns are clockwise: the 90 and the 135. Add them. 90 and 135 make 225.

beats.say: We could follow every turn. But here is a quicker idea: clockwise and anticlockwise are opposites, so they cancel. How much does he turn clockwise altogether?
90 and 135 make 225, clockwise.
And anticlockwise he turns 225. Look at that! 225 one way, and 225 the other way.

ask.ifNot: Turning 225 one way and then 225 back the other way undoes everything. It is like taking 5 steps forward and 5 steps back.

beats.say: So what do all his turns come to?
The turns cancel, so he ends up facing the way he started: north-east.

board.text: NE → SE, then back 5 steps → W

beats.say: Let's check it the slow way. From north-east, 90 clockwise is south-east. Then 225 anticlockwise is 5 steps back: east, north-east, north, north-west, west.
From west, 135 clockwise is 3 steps: north-west, north, north-east. Home again.
When turns go both ways, add up each direction first. Often a lot of it cancels.
Ravi turns 135 degrees clockwise and then 90 degrees anticlockwise. Now he faces south. Which way was he facing at the start?

ask.ifNot: Rewinding goes backwards through time. The last thing he did was the 90 anticlockwise turn, so that one is undone first.

beats.say: We know where Ravi ends, not where he starts. So we work backwards, like rewinding a film. When you rewind, which turn gets undone first?
To undo a turn, turn the same amount the opposite way. So to undo 90 anticlockwise, we turn 90 clockwise, starting from south.
90 clockwise from south is a quarter turn, and it takes us to west. So between his two turns, Ravi was facing west.

ask.ifNot: Undoing means going the opposite way. He turned clockwise, so we go back anticlockwise.

beats.say: Now undo the first turn, 135 clockwise. Which way do we turn to undo it?
The compass directions are 45 degrees apart, so 135 is 3 steps. Anticlockwise from west: south-west, south, south-east.
So Ravi was facing south-east before he turned.
Check it forwards. From south-east, 135 clockwise goes south, south-west, west. Then 90 anticlockwise from west goes back to south. Yes!
South-west is the trap. You get it by doing the turns again from south, instead of undoing them. Working backwards means last turn first, and the opposite way.

board.text: Facing North. 13 presses of 45° clockwise. Now?

beats.say: A robot faces north. Each press of the button turns it 45 degrees clockwise. Which way does it face after 13 presses?

ask.ifNot: There are 8 compass directions, one step apart. So 8 presses take the robot once all the way round, back to north.

beats.say: Each press of 45 degrees is one step round the 8 compass directions. How many presses bring the robot right back to north?
8 presses make 8 times 45, which is 360 degrees. A full turn. The robot faces north again.
So the first 8 of the 13 presses change nothing. 13 take away 8 leaves 5 presses that matter.

ask.ifNot: Count the presses, not the starting place. North-east, east, south-east, south, south-west. The 5th press lands on south-west.

beats.say: Now count 5 steps clockwise from north. Careful: north is where it starts. The first press takes it to north-east. Where does the 5th press land?
North-east, east, south-east, south, south-west. The robot faces south-west.
South is the trap. You get it if you count north as step 1. North is the start, before any press.
When something goes round and round, throw away the full turns first. Then count what is left.

board.text: 3 angles fill a full turn: first, 2 × first, 3 × first
The largest is what kind of angle?

beats.say: Three angles fill the whole turn round a point. The second is twice the first, and the third is three times the first. What kind of angle is the largest?

ask.ifNot: All the way round a point is a full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees. 180 is only half way round.

beats.say: Read carefully: the angles fill the whole turn round a point. So what do they add up to?
Call the first angle 1 part. Then the second is 2 parts and the third is 3 parts.

ask.ifNot: Add them all: 1 and 2 and 3 make 6 parts.

beats.say: How many parts are there altogether?
6 parts make 360. 6 times 60 is 360, so one part is 60 degrees.
The largest angle is 3 parts. 3 times 60 is 180.

ask.ifNot: Obtuse angles stop just before 180, and reflex angles start just after it. Exactly 180 makes a straight line: a straight angle.

beats.say: 180 degrees. What kind of angle is exactly 180?

board.text: The largest is a straight angle (180°)

beats.say: So the largest of the three is a straight angle.
The three angles are 60, 120 and 180. 120 is obtuse, but it is not the largest. Find every size exactly before you name it.

board.text: Lines cross. 3 of the 4 angles add up to 250°.

beats.say: Two straight lines cross and make 4 angles. Three of them add up to 250 degrees. We want the smallest of the 4 angles.

ask.ifNot: All the way round a point is a full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees. 180 is only half way round.

beats.say: The 4 angles go all the way round the crossing point. So what do all 4 add up to?
360 for all 4, and 250 for three of them. So the angle that was left out is 360 take away 250, which is 110.

ask.ifNot: Angles side by side on a straight line make 180. 180 take away 110 leaves 70.

beats.say: Is 110 the smallest? Find the others before you decide. The angle beside the 110 shares a straight line with it, and a straight line is 180. So how big is it?
180 take away 110 is 70.
Angles opposite each other at a crossing are equal. So the 4 angles are 110, 70, 110 and 70.
So the smallest angle is 70 degrees.
Check the clue. The three that were added are 110, 70 and 70. And they do make 250.
110 was the first number we found, but it was not the answer. Find all 4 angles, then pick the one the question wants.

board.text: An angle is 30° more than its complement.

beats.say: An angle is 30 degrees more than its complement. We want the supplement of this angle. There is a lot to keep track of, so let's go slowly.

ask.ifNot: Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. A square corner is a right angle, and that is 90 degrees.

beats.say: An angle and its complement add up to how much?
The angle is its complement, plus an extra 30. Cut off that extra 30, and two equal pieces are left. Together they make 90 take away 30, which is 60.
Two equal pieces make 60, so each one is 30. That is the complement.
The angle is 30 more than that. 30 and 30 make 60. So the angle is 60 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The last line asks for the supplement of this angle. That is the partner that makes a straight line with it.

beats.say: Now stop, and read the question again. What does it ask for?
The supplement makes 180 with the angle. 180 take away 60 is 120.
So the supplement of the angle is 120 degrees.
We found three numbers: complement 30, angle 60, supplement 120. All three are tempting. Answer the one that was asked.

board.text: P + Q = 90°.   Q + R = 180°.   What is always true?

beats.say: Angles P and Q add up to 90. Angles Q and R add up to 180. We have to find what is always true, whatever the size of P.

ask.ifNot: P and Q are complementary, so they make 90. 90 take away 20 is 70.

beats.say: No sizes are given, so let's choose one ourselves and see what happens. Say P is 20 degrees. P and Q make 90. So what is Q?
Q is 70. Now Q and R make 180. So R is 180 take away 70, which is 110.
So P is 20 and R is 110. R is 90 more than P. But was that just luck? Let's try another size.
This time let P be 40. Then Q is 90 take away 40, which is 50. And R is 180 take away 50, which is 130.

ask.ifNot: 130 take away 40 is 90. So R is 90 more than P, the same as before.

beats.say: P is 40 and R is 130. How much more is R than P this time?
90 again. Here is why. Q is in both pairs. With P it makes 90. With R it makes 180, which is 90 more. So R must be 90 bigger than P.

board.text: Angle R is 90° more than angle P

beats.say: So what is always true is this: angle R is 90 degrees more than angle P.
When a question says whatever the size, test it with two different numbers. A rule that is really true works every time.

board.text: Angle AOB = 70°. Angle BOC = 30°. Angle AOC = ?

beats.say: Angle A O B is 70 degrees. A ray O C makes 30 degrees with O B. Riya says angle A O C must be 100. Is she right?
Riya pictured the ray O C on the far side of O B, away from O A. Then the two angles sit side by side, and we add them. 70 and 30 make 100.

choices: No, it can be on either side of OB
Yes, only on the far side
ask.ifNot: The question only says O C makes 30 degrees with O B. It does not say which side. O C could also lie on the near side, between O A and O B.

beats.say: So 100 is possible. But there is no picture in the question. Is the far side the only place where O C can go?
Put O C on the near side, inside angle A O B. Now the 30 is a slice cut out of the 70. So angle A O C is 70 take away 30, which is 40.

ask.ifNot: Angle B O C is fixed at exactly 30. A ray that is 30 degrees from O B has only two places to go: one on each side of O B.

beats.say: So angle A O C could be 100, or it could be 40. Could it be any size in between as well?
Only two places, one on each side of O B. So there are only two possible answers.
So angle A O C could be 100 degrees or 40 degrees.
Riya's adding was fine. Her slip was the word must. When there is no picture, ask yourself: is there another way to draw it?
A round plate has a diameter of 18 centimetres. What is its radius?
The diameter goes right across the plate, through the centre. The radius only goes from the centre to the edge.

ask.ifNot: The radius is the shorter one. It reaches only halfway across the plate. So we halve the diameter.

beats.say: So to get from the diameter to the radius, do we double or halve?
The radius is half the diameter. Half of 18 is 9.
The radius is 9 centimetres.
Check: 9 and 9 make 18, the full diameter.
Radius to diameter: double. Diameter to radius: halve. Ask yourself which one should be bigger.

board.text: Circle of diameter 12 cm, drawn with a compass.

spec.note: The compass opens from the centre to the circle

beats.say: Kiran wants to draw a circle of diameter 12 centimetres with a compass. How far apart should the needle and the pencil tip be?

board.text: needle: centre.  pencil: on the circle

beats.say: Think about how a compass works. The needle stays at the centre. The pencil travels round on the circle.

ask.ifNot: The gap runs from the centre to a point on the circle. Centre to circle is the radius.

beats.say: So the gap between the needle and the pencil is which part of the circle?
It is the radius. That's the trap: the question gives the diameter, but the compass is set to the radius.
The radius is half the diameter. Half of 12 is 6.
The needle and the pencil tip should be 6 centimetres apart.
If Kiran opened the compass to 12, the circle would come out twice as wide as he wanted.

spec.note: How long is the longest chord?

beats.say: A circle has a radius of 8 centimetres. How long is the longest chord that can be drawn in it?

board.text: Chord: joins two points on the circle

beats.say: A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle. Short ones sit near the edge, longer ones nearer the middle.

ask.ifNot: A circle is widest across its middle. So the longest straight line inside it passes through the centre.

beats.say: Where does the very longest chord pass?
Through the centre. And a chord through the centre is the diameter.
The diameter is twice the radius. 2 times 8 is 16.
The longest chord is 16 centimetres.
The question never says the word diameter. You have to spot that the longest chord is the diameter.

board.text: Circle: radius 6 cm. P is 4 cm from the centre.

spec.note: P is 4 cm from the centre. Where is P?

beats.say: A circle has a radius of 6 centimetres. Point P is 4 centimetres from the centre. Where is P?

board.text: on the circle: exactly 6 cm away

beats.say: Every point on the circle is exactly 6 centimetres from the centre. That is what the radius tells us.

ask.ifNot: The circle is 6 centimetres away from the centre. You have only walked 4, so you are not there yet.

beats.say: Start at the centre and walk towards the circle. After 4 centimetres you stop. Have you reached the circle yet?
Not yet. 4 is less than 6.
So P is closer to the centre than the circle is. P is inside the circle.
Here is the rule. Less than the radius: inside. Equal to the radius: on the circle. More than the radius: outside.
So just compare the distance with the radius. Here 4 is less than 6, so P is inside.

board.text: O is the centre. A and B are on the circle.

spec.note: O is the centre. A and B are on the circle. OA = 7 cm

beats.say: O is the centre of a circle. A and B are two points on the circle. O A is 7 centimetres. How long is O B?

ask.ifNot: A line from the centre to the circle is a radius. A diameter would go right across, and a chord joins two points on the circle.

beats.say: O A joins the centre to a point on the circle. What do we call a line like that?

board.text: OA: a radius.  OB: a radius.

beats.say: O A is a radius. And O B also joins the centre to a point on the circle. So O B is a radius too.
Now the big fact about circles: every radius of the same circle has the same length.
So O B is the same as O A: 7 centimetres.
No sum was needed at all! It doesn't matter where B is on the circle. It is always one radius from the centre.

board.text: 4 circles in a row, each of radius 3 cm, touching.

spec.note: Four touching circles. First centre to last centre = ?

beats.say: Four equal circles, each of radius 3 centimetres, sit in a row, each touching the next. How far is it from the centre of the first to the centre of the last?

board.text: centre to next centre = radius + radius

beats.say: Start small. Take two circles that touch. From one centre you travel a radius to the touching point, then another radius to the next centre.
So neighbouring centres are 3 plus 3, which is 6 centimetres apart.

ask.ifNot: Hold up 4 fingers and count the spaces between them. There is always one gap fewer than the number of things.

beats.say: Now the tricky part. There are 4 centres in the row. How many gaps are there between the first and the last?
That's the trap: 4 circles, but only 3 gaps between their centres.
3 gaps of 6 centimetres. 3 times 6 is 18.
The distance from the first centre to the last is 18 centimetres.
The whole row is longer than that, because half a circle sticks out at each end. Centre to centre, count the gaps.

board.text: 6 bangles in a row, each of radius 4 cm, touching.

spec.note: Each bangle has radius 4 cm

beats.say: Six round bangles, each of radius 4 centimetres, lie in a straight row, each touching the next. How long is the row from end to end?

ask.ifNot: The radius only reaches from the centre to the edge. The full width of a bangle is its diameter, twice the radius.

beats.say: How much of the row does one bangle take up? Its full width, from one side to the other. Which measure is that?
The full width is the diameter. 2 times 4 is 8 centimetres.
The bangles touch, so there are no spaces between them. The row is just 6 bangles, side by side.
6 times 8 is 48.
The row is 48 centimetres long.
This time we want end to end, so every whole bangle counts. If it had asked centre to centre, we would count gaps instead.

board.text: Circle inside a square of side 10 cm, touching all sides.

spec.note: A circle inside just touches all four sides. Radius = ?

beats.say: A circle is drawn inside a square of side 10 centimetres, just touching all four sides. What is the radius of the circle?

ask.ifNot: The circle reaches from one side of the square to the opposite side. So it is exactly as wide as the square.

beats.say: The circle touches the left side and the right side of the square. So how wide is the circle, right across?
The circle is as wide as the square. So its diameter is 10 centimetres.
But the question asks for the radius, not the diameter.
The radius is half the diameter. Half of 10 is 5.
The radius of the circle is 5 centimetres.
A circle that fits snugly in a square has the square's side as its diameter. Then halve for the radius.

board.text: Circle of radius 6 cm fits exactly inside a square.

spec.note: A square fits round it, touching. Perimeter of the square = ?

beats.say: A circle of radius 6 centimetres fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the perimeter of the square?

ask.ifNot: The circle stretches right across the square, from one side to the other. Right across a circle is its diameter.

beats.say: The circle touches opposite sides of the square. So the side of the square is as long as which part of the circle?
The side of the square equals the diameter. 2 times 6 is 12 centimetres.
Careful: the side is 12, not 6. The radius only reaches halfway across the square.
A square has 4 equal sides. 4 times 12 is 48.
The perimeter of the square is 48 centimetres.
Two steps: radius to diameter gives the side, then 4 sides give the perimeter.

board.text: Two touching coins: radius 5 cm and radius 3 cm.

spec.note: Centre to centre, through the point where the coins touch

beats.say: Two coins lie flat and touch each other. One has a radius of 5 centimetres and the other 3 centimetres. How far apart are their centres?

ask.ifNot: Centre to edge is the radius. The big coin has a radius of 5 centimetres.

beats.say: Travel from one centre to the other. First you go from the centre of the big coin out to its edge. How far is that?

board.text: big coin: centre to edge = 5 cm

beats.say: 5 centimetres, one radius of the big coin. Now you are at the point where the coins touch.

board.text: small coin: edge to centre = 3 cm

beats.say: From there you go to the centre of the small coin. That is one radius of the small coin: 3 centimetres.
So the whole trip is 5 plus 3, which is 8.
The centres are 8 centimetres apart.
When two circles touch from outside, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius.

board.text: Same centre: radius 9 cm and radius 5 cm.

spec.note: Two circles with the same centre. Width of the ring = ?

beats.say: Two circles share the same centre. The big one has a radius of 9 centimetres and the small one 5 centimetres. How wide is the ring between them?

board.text: small circle at 5 cm, big circle at 9 cm

beats.say: Walk out from the centre in a straight line. After 5 centimetres you cross the small circle. After 9 centimetres you reach the big circle.

ask.ifNot: The ring is the gap between the 5 centimetre mark and the 9 centimetre mark. To find a gap, we subtract.

beats.say: The ring is the stretch between the two circles. How do we find its width?
9 minus 5 is 4.
The ring is 4 centimetres wide.
Check: 5 centimetres to the small circle, then 4 more across the ring, brings you to 9.
For circles with the same centre, the gap between them is the difference of the radii.
The diameter of a circle is 12 centimetres longer than its radius. What is the radius?
We always know one thing about a diameter. It is made of two radii, end to end.
And the question tells us the diameter is the radius plus 12 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Line one says radius plus radius. Line two says radius plus 12. The second part of each must match.

beats.say: Look at the two lines together. Both start with one radius. So what must the 12 centimetres be?
The extra 12 is the second radius! So the radius is 12 centimetres.
Check: the diameter is 12 plus 12, which is 24. And 24 is 12 more than 12. It fits.
The trap is to halve 12 and say 6. Don't halve just because you see the word diameter. Read what the 12 really is.

board.text: NOT a chord length: 4, 9, 12 or 13 cm?

spec.note: Which length cannot be a chord?

beats.say: A circle has a radius of 6 centimetres. Which of these cannot be the length of a chord: 4, 9, 12 or 13 centimetres?

board.text: Chord: joins two points on the circle

beats.say: A chord joins two points on the circle. Chords can be tiny, near the edge. But there is a limit to how long one can be.

ask.ifNot: A radius starts at the centre, so it is not a chord. The longest chord goes right across through the centre: the diameter.

beats.say: Which chord is the longest one of all?
The diameter. For this circle that is 2 times 6, which is 12 centimetres.
So a chord can be any length up to 12, but never more. 4 fits. 9 fits. 12 is the diameter itself, so it fits too.
But 13 is more than 12. No chord can be longer than the diameter.
So 13 centimetres cannot be a chord of this circle.
Careful with 12: it looks too big next to a radius of 6, but it is exactly the diameter. Compare with the diameter, not the radius.

board.text: Tray 20 cm by 8 cm. Biscuits of radius 2 cm, in rows.

spec.note: Round biscuits of radius 2 cm, in straight rows

beats.say: A tray is 20 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide. Round biscuits of radius 2 centimetres are laid on it in straight rows. What is the most that can fit?

ask.ifNot: 2 centimetres is only the radius, from the centre to the edge. The full width is the diameter, twice that.

beats.say: How much room does one biscuit need? Its full width, in every direction. What is the full width of a biscuit?
Here's the trap: a biscuit takes up its diameter, not its radius. 2 times 2 is 4 centimetres.
Along the 20 centimetre length: 20 divided by 4 is 5. So 5 biscuits fit in a row.
Across the 8 centimetre width: 8 divided by 4 is 2. So there is room for 2 rows.
2 rows of 5 biscuits. 5 times 2 is 10.
The tray holds 10 biscuits.
So: find the full width of one circle, see how many fit each way, then multiply.

board.text: Wire: circle of radius 7 cm, then a square.

spec.note: The same wire is bent into a square. Side = ?

beats.say: A wire is bent into a circle of radius 7 centimetres. Then the same wire is bent into a square. What is the side of the square? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

ask.ifNot: The wire is the curved edge of the circle. The distance round a circle is its circumference.

beats.say: The wire goes once round the circle. So the length of the wire is the circle's what?
The circumference is 2 times pi times the radius.
The 7 underneath and the radius 7 cancel each other. That leaves 2 times 22, which is 44.
So the wire is 44 centimetres long. Now it becomes a square with 4 equal sides.
44 divided by 4 is 11.
The side of the square is 11 centimetres.
Same wire, same length. The circumference of the circle becomes the perimeter of the square.

board.text: Big radius = small diameter. Small radius = 3 cm.

spec.note: Its diameter is the radius of a big circle

beats.say: The radius of a big circle equals the diameter of a small circle. The small circle's radius is 3 centimetres. What is the big circle's diameter?
Lots of radius and diameter words here! Go one step at a time. Start with the small circle. Its diameter is twice its radius.

ask.ifNot: Read the first sentence again: the radius of the big circle equals the diameter of the small circle.

beats.say: The small diameter is 6 centimetres. The question says that this is the same as the big circle's what?
It is the big circle's radius. So the big radius is 6 centimetres.
Careful: don't stop at 6! We want the big circle's diameter, which is twice its radius.
2 times 6 is 12.
The diameter of the big circle is 12 centimetres.
We doubled twice: 3 to 6, then 6 to 12. Label each number as you go, so you always know what it is.

board.text: 3 circles, radius 4 cm, each touching the other two.

spec.note: A, B, C: centres of touching circles of radius 4 cm

beats.say: Three equal circles with centres A, B and C each have a radius of 4 centimetres. Each touches the other two. What is the perimeter of triangle A B C?
Look at one side of the triangle, from A to B. It starts at one centre and ends at the other, passing through the point where the circles touch.

ask.ifNot: From A to the touching point is one radius, 4 centimetres. From there to B is another radius.

beats.say: So how long is the side A B?
One radius and then another: 4 plus 4 is 8 centimetres.
The circles are all the same size, so the other two sides are 8 centimetres as well.
The triangle has 3 sides of 8. 3 times 8 is 24.
The perimeter of triangle A B C is 24 centimetres.
Whenever circles touch, the line between their centres is one radius plus the other radius.

board.text: 10 circles in a rectangle: 2 rows of 5.
Perimeter = 84 cm. Radius of each circle = ?

spec.note: One circle in each square. Perimeter = 84 cm. Radius = ?

beats.say: Ten equal circles sit inside a rectangle in 2 rows of 5, touching each other and the sides. The rectangle's perimeter is 84 centimetres. What is each circle's radius?
Let's measure the rectangle in diameters. The length holds 5 circles, so it is 5 diameters. The width holds 2 circles, so it is 2 diameters.
So length plus width is 5 plus 2, which is 7 diameters.

choices: No, 7 diameters is only half of it
ask.ifNot: The perimeter is two lengths and two widths. One length plus one width is only halfway round.

beats.say: Now, the perimeter is 84. Is 84 equal to those 7 diameters?
That's the trap. Length plus width is half the perimeter. Half of 84 is 42.
So 7 diameters make 42. 42 divided by 7 is 6. Each diameter is 6 centimetres.
One last step: the question asks for the radius. Half of 6 is 3.
The radius of each circle is 3 centimetres.
Check: the length is 5 times 6, which is 30. The width is 2 times 6, which is 12. 30 plus 12 is 42, and double is 84.

board.text: Small circle (radius 3 cm) inside big circle (radius 10 cm).
They touch at one point. Centres are ? apart

spec.note: Both end at the point where the circles touch

beats.say: A small circle of radius 3 centimetres lies inside a big circle of radius 10 centimetres, touching it at one point. How far apart are the two centres?

board.text: touching point, small centre, big centre: one line

beats.say: Stand at the touching point and look inwards. Both centres are straight ahead of you, on one line.

board.text: big centre: 10 cm in.  small centre: 3 cm in.

beats.say: The big centre is 10 centimetres from the touching point. The small centre is 3 centimetres from it. Both in the same direction.

ask.ifNot: Both centres are on the same side of the touching point. One is 3 in and the other is 10 in. The gap between them is the difference.

beats.say: So how far is it from one centre to the other?
10 minus 3 is 7.
The centres are 7 centimetres apart.
Here's the trap. When circles touch from outside, we add the radii. When one is inside the other, we subtract.

board.text: Circles of radius 2 cm, 3 cm, 4 cm in a row, touching.

spec.note: Three touching circles in a row. First centre to last = ?

beats.say: Three circles of radius 2, 3 and 4 centimetres are in a row, centres on one line. The middle one touches the other two. How far is it from the first centre to the last centre?
Let's take the trip in three parts. Part one: from the first centre out to its edge. That is its radius, 2 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: We go in one side of the middle circle and out the other. That is its full width, the diameter, which is twice 3.

beats.say: Part two: we must cross the whole middle circle, from one side to the other. How far is that?
That's the trap: the middle circle is crossed completely, so we need its diameter. 2 times 3 is 6.
Part three: from the edge of the last circle in to its centre. That is its radius, 4 centimetres. We stop at the centre.
Add the three parts. 2 plus 6 plus 4 is 12.
The distance between the first and last centres is 12 centimetres.
Centre to centre: one radius for each end circle, but a whole diameter for any circle in between.

board.text: Circle: circumference 88 cm, fits exactly in a square.

spec.note: Circumference = 88 cm. The circle fits exactly inside a square

beats.say: A circle has a circumference of 88 centimetres. It fits exactly inside a square, touching all four sides. What is the side of the square? Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circle touches opposite sides of the square. So the side of the square equals the circle's diameter. We need the radius first.
Circumference is 2 times 22 over 7 times r. 2 times 22 is 44. So it is 44 times r, divided by 7.
44 times something makes 88. That something is 2.
So r divided by 7 is 2. That means r is 2 times 7, which is 14 centimetres.

choices: No, the side is the diameter
ask.ifNot: The radius only reaches from the centre to one side of the square. The circle stretches right across, so the side is the diameter.

beats.say: The radius is 14. Is that the side of the square?
The side is the diameter: 2 times 14 is 28.
The side of the square is 28 centimetres.
Another trap is sharing 88 among 4 sides. The 88 goes round the circle, not round the square.

board.text: Square sheet of side 14 cm. Circle of radius 7 cm cut out.

spec.note: A circle of radius 7 cm is cut out of this sheet

beats.say: A circle of radius 7 centimetres is cut out of a square sheet of side 14 centimetres. What area of paper is left? Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The paper left is the square with the circle taken away. So we need two areas.
The square: 14 times 14. 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 4 is 56. Together, 196.

ask.ifNot: 2 times pi times the radius is the distance round, the circumference. For the space inside, the radius is used twice.

beats.say: Now the circle. Which rule gives the area of a circle?
Pi times radius times radius: 22 over 7, times 7, times 7. One 7 cancels the 7 underneath, leaving 22 times 7.
22 times 7 is 154.
Take the circle from the square. 196 minus 154 is 42.
The area of paper left is 42 square centimetres.
Careful to take away the circle's area, not its circumference. Area from area, always.

board.text: 5 points on a circle. Every pair is joined.

beats.say: Five points are marked on a circle. Every pair of points is joined by a straight line. How many chords are drawn?
Let's count in order so we don't count any chord twice. Call the points 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.
From point 1, chords go to each of the other 4 points. That is 4 chords.

ask.ifNot: Point 2 can join points 3, 4 and 5. Its chord to point 1 is already drawn, so we don't count it again.

beats.say: Now point 2. It is already joined to point 1. So how many new chords start from point 2?
3 new chords. Then point 3 gives 2 new ones, and point 4 gives just 1. Point 5 is already joined to everyone.
Add them up: 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 10.
10 chords are drawn.
The trap is 5 times 4, which is 20. That counts every chord twice, once from each end. And half of 20 is 10.

board.text: Two trays of side 24 cm: 3 rows of 3, and 4 rows of 4.

spec.note: First tray: 3 rows of 3. Second tray: 4 rows of 4

beats.say: Two square trays each have a side of 24 centimetres. One is filled by 9 plates in 3 rows of 3. The other by 16 plates in 4 rows of 4. How much longer is a plate's radius in the first tray?
First tray: 3 plates fit across 24 centimetres. So each plate is 24 divided by 3, which is 8 centimetres wide.

ask.ifNot: The full width of a round plate, from one side to the other, is its diameter. The radius is half of that.

beats.say: 8 centimetres is the full width of a plate. Is that its radius or its diameter?
It is the diameter. So the radius is half of 8, which is 4 centimetres.
