Second tray: 4 plates across. 24 divided by 4 is 6 centimetres wide, so the radius is half of 6, which is 3.
Now compare the radii. 4 minus 3 is 1.
The radius in the first tray is 1 centimetre longer.
The trap is comparing the diameters, 8 and 6. The question asks about the radii, so halve first, then subtract.

board.text: Wire 132 cm, cut into 3 equal pieces. Each makes a circle.

spec.note: Each piece is bent into a circle. Radius = ?

beats.say: A wire 132 centimetres long is cut into 3 equal pieces. Each piece is bent into a circle. What is the radius of each circle? Use 22 over 7 for pi.
Careful: the whole wire does not make one circle. First cut it. 132 divided by 3 is 44 centimetres for each piece.

ask.ifNot: The wire is bent to make the edge of the circle. The distance all the way round the edge is the circumference.

beats.say: One piece goes once round its circle. So 44 centimetres is that circle's what?
It is the circumference. And circumference is 2 times 22 over 7 times r. 2 times 22 is 44, so that is 44 times r, divided by 7.
44 times r, divided by 7, must give 44. So r divided by 7 is 1, and r is 7.
The radius of each circle is 7 centimetres.
Check: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7. The 7s cancel, and 2 times 22 is 44. That is one piece of wire.
So: cut first, then treat each piece as a circumference and work back to the radius.

board.text: 12 circles in a rectangle: 3 rows of 4.
Area of rectangle = 432 sq cm. Radius = ?

spec.note: One circle in each square. Area = 432 sq cm. Radius = ?

beats.say: Twelve equal circles sit inside a rectangle in 3 rows of 4, touching each other and the sides. The rectangle's area is 432 square centimetres. What is each circle's radius?

board.text: 12 equal little squares fill the rectangle

beats.say: Imagine a little square box drawn round every circle. The 12 boxes fill the rectangle exactly, like tiles.
So the 432 is shared equally among 12 little squares. 432 divided by 12 is 36. Check: 12 times 30 is 360, 12 times 6 is 72, and together they make 432.

ask.ifNot: Area of a square is side times side. Which number times itself makes 36? Try 6 times 6.

beats.say: A little square has an area of 36. How long is its side?
6 times 6 is 36. So each little square has a side of 6 centimetres.

board.text: side of little square = diameter = 6 cm

beats.say: The circle just fits its square. So the side of the square, 6, is the circle's diameter. Don't stop here!
The question asks for the radius. Half of 6 is 3.
The radius of each circle is 3 centimetres.
Check: the rectangle is 4 times 6 long, which is 24, and 3 times 6 wide, which is 18. And 24 times 18 is 432.

board.text: Pond: radius 7 m. Path 7 m wide all round.

spec.note: A path 7 m wide runs all the way round this pond

beats.say: A round pond has a radius of 7 metres. A path 7 metres wide runs all the way round it. What is the area of the path? Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The path is a ring. A ring is a big circle with a smaller circle taken out of its middle.

ask.ifNot: From the centre, go 7 metres to the edge of the pond. Then 7 more metres across the path.

beats.say: The big circle is the pond and the path together. What is its radius?
7 for the pond and 7 more for the path: 14 metres.
Big circle: 22 over 7, times 14, times 14. 14 divided by 7 is 2. So we have 22 times 2 times 14.
22 times 2 is 44. 44 times 14: 44 times 10 is 440, and 44 times 4 is 176. Together, 616.
The pond: 22 over 7, times 7, times 7. One 7 cancels. That leaves 22 times 7, which is 154.
Take the pond out of the big circle. 616 minus 154 is 462.
The area of the path is 462 square metres.
Surprised? The path is as wide as the pond's radius, but its area is 3 times the pond's. Rings on the outside are big!

board.text: Radius doubled: circumference grows by 88 cm.

spec.note: The radius is made twice as long

beats.say: When a circle's radius is made twice as long, its circumference becomes 88 centimetres longer. What was the radius at the start? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

ask.ifNot: The radius is multiplied into the circumference. Make the radius twice as big, and the whole answer is twice as big.

beats.say: Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius. If we double the radius, what happens to the circumference?
It doubles. So the new circumference is the old one, and then the old one again.
Here's the key. The extra part is exactly one old circumference. And the extra part is 88. So the old circumference was 88.
Careful: 88 is not the new circumference. It is the amount it grew, which equals the old one.
Now find the radius. 2 times 22 is 44, so the circumference is 44 times r, divided by 7. 88 divided by 44 is 2.
So r divided by 7 is 2, and r is 2 times 7, which is 14.
The radius at the start was 14 centimetres.
Check: the doubled radius is 28. Its circumference is 44 times 4, which is 176. And 176 minus 88 is 88. It grew by 88.

board.text: 7 points on a circle. Join each to all but its 2 neighbours.

beats.say: Seven points are marked on a circle. Each point is joined to every other point, except the two right next to it. How many chords are drawn?
Stand on one point. There are 7 points in all. You can't join to yourself, and you skip your 2 neighbours. That rules out 3 points.

ask.ifNot: 7 points, and 3 of them are ruled out: yourself and your two neighbours. Take 3 from 7.

beats.say: So how many chords leave your point?
7 minus 3 is 4. Each point sends out 4 chords.
7 points with 4 chords each: 7 times 4 is 28. But wait. Is 28 the answer?
Here's the trap. Every chord has two ends, so we counted each chord twice: once from each end.
So we halve it. Half of 28 is 14.
14 chords are drawn.
Counting from every point is quick, but remember that each line gets counted from both of its ends. Halve at the end.

board.text: 8 equally spaced points on a circle. Every pair is joined.
How many chords are NOT diameters?

beats.say: Eight points are equally spaced round a circle. Every pair is joined by a chord. How many of these chords are not diameters?
Plan: count all the chords, then take away the ones that are diameters.
All the chords. The first point joins 7 others. The next gives 6 new chords, then 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1.

ask.ifNot: A diameter passes through the centre. That happens only when the two points are straight across the circle from each other.

beats.say: That adds up to 28 chords. Now, when is a chord a diameter?
A diameter joins two opposite points. 8 points make 4 opposite pairs. So there are 4 diameters.
Careful: not 8 diameters. Each diameter uses up 2 points, one at each end.
Take the diameters away. 28 minus 4 is 24.
24 of the chords are not diameters.
When a question says not, count everything first, then take away the ones you don't want.

board.text: Small circle inside big circle: touches it at one point
and passes through its centre. Big diameter = 24 cm.

spec.note: A small circle inside touches it and passes through its centre

beats.say: A small circle inside a big circle touches it at one point, and also passes through the big circle's centre. The big diameter is 24 centimetres. How far apart are the centres?
Start with the big circle. Its radius is half of 24, which is 12 centimetres.

board.text: touching point to big centre = 12 cm

beats.say: So from the touching point to the big centre is 12 centimetres. The small circle passes through both of those points.

ask.ifNot: The two points are on opposite sides of the small circle, as far apart as they can be. That full width is its diameter.

beats.say: The small circle stretches from the touching point right across to the big centre. So that 12 centimetres is the small circle's what?
It is the small circle's diameter. And the small centre sits halfway along a diameter.
Half of 12 is 6. So the small centre is 6 centimetres from the big centre.
The centres are 6 centimetres apart.
We halved twice: 24 to 12 for the big radius, then 12 to 6 for the small radius. Each halving had its own reason.

board.text: 3 touching coins. Centres are 7 cm, 8 cm, 9 cm apart.

spec.note: The corners are the centres of the three coins

beats.say: Three coins of different sizes each touch the other two. The distances between their centres are 7, 8 and 9 centimetres. What is the radius of the largest coin?
When two coins touch, the distance between their centres is one radius plus the other radius. So each distance is two radii added.

ask.ifNot: Each coin touches two others. So its radius is part of two of the distances.

beats.say: Add all three distances: 7 plus 8 plus 9 is 24. In that total, how many times is each coin's radius counted?
Twice! So 24 is every radius counted twice. Halve it: the three radii add up to 12.
The two smaller coins have the closest centres: 7 centimetres. So their two radii add up to 7.
All three radii make 12. The two smaller ones make 7. So the largest is 12 minus 7, which is 5.
The radius of the largest coin is 5 centimetres.
Check: the radii are 3, 4 and 5. 3 plus 4 is 7. 3 plus 5 is 8. 4 plus 5 is 9. All three distances match!
The trap is halving the 9. That only works for two equal coins, and these are all different.

board.text: 2 touching tins, radius 7 cm. A tight ribbon round both.

beats.say: Two round tins of radius 7 centimetres stand touching. A ribbon is pulled tight round both: straight across on two sides, and curving round the outer half of each tin. How long is it?
Split the ribbon into easy pieces: two straight parts, and two curved parts.
A straight part runs from one tin across to the other. It is as long as the gap between the centres: one radius plus one radius.
There is a straight part on both sides. 2 times 14 is 28.

ask.ifNot: Half and half make one whole. The two curved parts together are the same as going once round one tin.

beats.say: Now the curves. The ribbon goes round half of one tin and half of the other. What do two half circles make?
One whole circle! Its circumference is 2 times 22 over 7 times 7. The 7s cancel, leaving 2 times 22, which is 44.
Add the straight parts and the curved parts. 28 plus 44 is 72.
The ribbon is 72 centimetres long.
The trap is going right round both tins: 2 times 44, which is 88. The ribbon only hugs the outer half of each tin.

board.text: Hour hand 7 cm long. One day = 24 hours.

spec.note: The tip of the hour hand moves round this circle

beats.say: The hour hand of a clock is 7 centimetres long. How far does its tip travel in one full day of 24 hours? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

board.text: tip moves on a circle of radius 7 cm

beats.say: As the hand turns, its tip draws a circle. The hand is the radius of that circle: 7 centimetres.
Once round is the circumference: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7. The 7s cancel, leaving 2 times 22, which is 44.

ask.ifNot: The minute hand goes round in 1 hour. The hour hand is slow: it creeps from 12 all the way back to 12 in 12 hours.

beats.say: Now think about the clock. How long does the hour hand take to go once round?
12 hours for one round. A day has 24 hours, so the hour hand goes round 24 divided by 12 times: that is 2 rounds.
2 rounds of 44 centimetres. 2 times 44 is 88.
The tip of the hour hand travels 88 centimetres in a day.
Two traps: stopping at one round, or thinking the hour hand goes round every hour. That one is the minute hand!
How many whole numbers are there from 15 to 42, counting both 15 and 42?
Let's try a tiny case first. From 1 to 3 we have 1, 2, 3. That is 3 numbers. But 3 minus 1 is only 2.
So if we only subtract, what do we miss?

ask.ifNot: Subtracting counts the jumps between the numbers. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: Subtracting counts the jumps. So first, 42 minus 15 is 27 jumps.
Then add 1, so that the starting number 15 is counted too. 27 plus 1 is 28.
So there are 28 whole numbers from 15 to 42.
Counting both ends: subtract, then add 1.
Meera is in a queue. She is 7th from the front and 5th from the back. How many children are in the queue?

board.text: 7th from the front, 5th from the back. How many?

spec.note: Meera (M) is 7th from the front and 5th from the back

beats.say: If Meera is 7th from the front, how many children are in front of her?

ask.ifNot: Meera herself is number 7. So the children in front of her are numbers 1 to 6.

beats.say: 6 children are in front. In the same way, she is 5th from the back, so 4 children are behind her.
Now add everyone up: 6 in front, Meera herself, and 4 behind.
So there are 11 children in the queue.
The trap is 7 plus 5, which is 12. That counts Meera twice, once from each end. Take 1 away and we get 11 again.
So the quick rule is: add the two positions, then take away 1.
A straight fence is 40 metres long. A post stands every 5 metres, with one at each end. How many posts are there?

board.text: Fence 40 m. A post every 5 m, and at each end.

beats.say: First count the gaps between the posts. Each gap is 5 metres, so 40 divided by 5 is 8 gaps.
8 gaps. So how many posts?

spec.note: Mark every 5 m along the fence. Count the gaps between the marks

ask.ifNot: Count the marks on the line, starting from 0. Each gap ends with a post, and there is one more post at the very start.

beats.say: The posts stand at 0, 5, 10, and so on up to 40. Count them and you get 9. It is always one more than the gaps.
So there are 9 posts.
Look at your hand: 5 fingers, 4 gaps. In a straight line, the posts are the gaps plus 1.
How many 2-digit numbers end in the digit 5?
A 2-digit number has a tens digit and a ones digit. The ones digit is fixed: it must be 5.
So only the tens digit can change. Can the tens digit be 0?

ask.ifNot: With 0 in the tens place we would just have the number 5. That has only one digit.

beats.say: The tens digit can be 1, 2, 3, and so on up to 9. That is 9 choices.
Let's list them to be sure: 15, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 75, 85, 95.
Count them: 9 numbers.
The trap is saying 10. The number 5 on its own does not count, because it has just one digit.
Riya has 3 different tops and 2 different skirts. An outfit is one top with one skirt. How many outfits can she make?
Take the first top. She can wear it with skirt 1 or with skirt 2. That is 2 outfits from just one top.
The second top can also go with either skirt. And the third top too. So how do we find the total?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 3 tops makes 2 outfits. 3 lots of 2 means we multiply.

beats.say: 3 tops, with 2 outfits each. That is 3 times 2, which is 6.
So Riya can make 6 different outfits.
The trap is adding: 3 plus 2 is 5. But every top pairs with every skirt, so we multiply.
How many even numbers are there from 1 to 30?

board.text: Even numbers from 1 to 30: how many?

beats.say: Even numbers are the ones in the 2 times table: 2, 4, 6, 8 and so on.
Look at the pattern: odd, even, odd, even. What part of all the numbers are even?

ask.ifNot: The numbers take turns: odd, even, odd, even. So every second number is even. That is half.

beats.say: There are 30 numbers from 1 to 30, and half of them are even. 30 divided by 2 is 15.
So there are 15 even numbers.
Check the ends: the last number, 30, is even, so it is counted. And 0 is not in our list.
From 1 up to an even number, exactly half the numbers are even.
A carpenter cuts a long plank into 6 pieces, one cut at a time. How many cuts does he make?
Before any cut, the plank is 1 piece. After 1 cut, there are 2 pieces.
After 2 cuts, how many pieces?

ask.ifNot: Each cut turns one piece into two. So each cut adds just 1 more piece.

beats.say: 2 cuts make 3 pieces. 3 cuts make 4 pieces. The pieces are always one more than the cuts.
So for 6 pieces we need one fewer cut. 6 minus 1 is 5.
The carpenter makes 5 cuts.
Try it with a strip of paper. Cuts are always one fewer than pieces.
How many 2-digit numbers can we make using only the digits 3 and 8? A digit may be used twice.
A 2-digit number has two places: tens and ones. The tens digit can be 3 or 8. That is 2 choices.
The digit may be used again. So how many choices are there for the ones digit?

ask.ifNot: Repeats are allowed. So the ones digit can also be 3 or 8, whatever the tens digit was.

beats.say: 2 choices for the tens, and for each of them 2 choices for the ones. 2 times 2 is 4.
Let's list them: 33, 38, 83 and 88.
So 4 numbers can be made.
The trap is to count only 38 and 83. Read carefully: a digit may be used twice, so 33 and 88 count too.
The pages of a book are numbered 1 to 25. How many digits are printed in all?

board.text: Pages 1 to 25. How many digits printed?

beats.say: Do all the page numbers have the same number of digits?

ask.ifNot: Page 7 has one digit, but page 25 has two. So we need two groups.

beats.say: First group: pages 1 to 9. That is 9 pages with 1 digit each, so 9 digits.
Second group: pages 10 to 25. How many pages? 25 minus 10 is 15, plus 1 because we count both ends. 16 pages.
Careful there: it is 16 pages, not 15. Count on your fingers from 10 to 25 if you are unsure.
Each of those 16 pages has 2 digits. 16 times 2 is 32 digits.
Add the two groups. 9 plus 32 is 41.
So 41 digits are printed.
Split the pages by how many digits they have, count each group, then add.
How many 2-digit numbers have digits that add up to 7?

board.text: 2-digit numbers, digits add up to 7. How many?

beats.say: Let's be organised and go through the tens digit. If the tens digit is 1, the ones digit must be 6. That is 16.
Tens digit 2 needs a 5: that is 25. Then come 34, 43, 52 and 61.
Is that all of them? What if the tens digit is 7?

ask.ifNot: 7 plus 0 is 7. So 70 belongs on our list too. Zero is a digit as well!

beats.say: Yes: 70. But the tens digit cannot be 0, because that would just be the 1-digit number 7.
Count the list: 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61, 70. That is 7 numbers.
Go through the tens digit in order, and you will not miss any or count any twice.
Kiran writes all the numbers from 1 to 40. How many times does she write the digit 3?

board.text: Write 1 to 40. How often is the digit 3 written?

beats.say: A 3 can sit in the ones place or in the tens place. Let's count each place on its own.
Ones place first: 3, 13, 23 and 33. That is 4 times.
Now the tens place. Which numbers have a 3 in the tens place?

ask.ifNot: The tens digit is 3 for every number in the thirties, from 30 up to 39.

beats.say: 30, 31, 32, all the way to 39. That is 10 numbers, so 10 more 3s.
What about 33? It has two 3s. And we counted it in both lists, once for each 3. So that is just right.
Add the two counts. 4 plus 10 is 14.
So she writes the digit 3 a total of 14 times.
Count place by place. Then a number like 33 looks after itself.
30 children stand in a line. Arjun is 12th from the front. What is his position from the back?

board.text: 30 in a line. 12th from the front. From the back?

spec.note: Arjun (A) is 12th from the front. His place from the back = ?

beats.say: First, how many children are behind Arjun? Take away the first 12 children, which includes Arjun. 30 minus 12 is 18.
18 children are behind him. Counting from the back, what is Arjun's position?

ask.ifNot: Count from the back: the 18 children behind him come first. Arjun is the very next one.

beats.say: Those 18 come first, and then Arjun. 18 plus 1 is 19.
So Arjun is 19th from the back.
Check: add his two positions and take away 1, since he was counted twice. 12 plus 19 minus 1 is 30. It fits.
Position from the other end: the total, minus the position, plus 1.
A square garden has sides of 12 metres. Posts go all around it, one at every corner and one every 3 metres. How many posts?

board.text: Square, side 12 m. A post every 3 m all around.

spec.note: A post at every corner, and every 3 m along each side

beats.say: The posts go all the way round, so find the distance around. 4 sides of 12 metres make 48 metres.
Each gap between posts is 3 metres. 48 divided by 3 is 16 gaps.
On a straight fence we would add 1 to the gaps. But this fence goes round in a loop. So how many posts?

ask.ifNot: Walk round the garden. After the last gap you arrive back at the first post. No extra post is needed.

beats.say: In a loop, the last gap ends at the first post again. So the posts and the gaps are equal: 16.
So 16 posts are needed.
Another trap: each side has 5 posts, and 4 times 5 is 20. But that counts every corner post twice. 20 minus 4 is 16 again.
Straight line: gaps plus 1. Closed loop: the same as the gaps.
Anu, Binu and Charu stand in a row for a photo. In how many different orders can they stand?

board.text: Anu, Binu, Charu in a row. How many orders?

beats.say: Think of 3 empty places. Any of the 3 children can take the first place. That is 3 choices.
One child has taken the first place. How many children are left to choose from for the second place?

ask.ifNot: One child is already standing in the first place. So only 2 are left for the second.

beats.say: 2 choices for the second place. Then just 1 child is left for the last place.
Multiply the choices. 3 times 2 times 1 is 6.
Let's check with letters: A B C, A C B, B A C, B C A, C A B, C B A. That is 6.

board.text: ABC ACB BAC BCA CAB CBA

beats.say: So they can stand in 6 different orders.
To arrange things in a row: count the choices for each place, getting smaller each time, and multiply.
A window has 4 small square panes, in 2 rows of 2. Counting squares of every size, how many squares can you see?

board.text: 2 rows of 2 panes. Squares of every size?

spec.note: A window of 4 small panes. Count the squares of every size

beats.say: Start with the small ones. There are 4 small square panes.
Are there any bigger squares hiding?

ask.ifNot: Step back and look at the whole window. It is as wide as it is tall, so it is a square too.

beats.say: The whole window is 1 big square, made of all 4 panes.
What about 2 panes side by side? That shape is longer than it is tall. It is a rectangle, not a square, so we do not count it.
Add them. 4 small and 1 big make 5.
So there are 5 squares in the window.
When counting shapes, go size by size: small ones first, then bigger ones.
16 players enter a knockout tournament. In every match the loser goes out. How many matches are played to find the champion?
Go round by round. In round 1, the 16 players make 8 matches. 8 winners go on.
The 8 winners play 4 matches. Then 4 players play 2 matches. Then the last 2 play 1 match: the final.
Add the rounds. 8 plus 4 plus 2 plus 1 is 15.
Here is a clever shortcut. Each match sends exactly 1 player out. How many players must go out to leave 1 champion?

ask.ifNot: There are 16 players and only 1 champion. Everyone else must lose once. 16 take away 1.

beats.say: 15 players must lose, and each match makes exactly 1 loser. So there are 15 matches. Both ways agree!
So 15 matches are played.
In a knockout, the matches are always one fewer than the players.
How many 2-digit numbers are multiples of 7?
Multiples of 7 are the 7 times table: 7, 14, 21 and so on. But 7 itself has only 1 digit. So the first one we want is 14.
Now the biggest one. 7 times 14 is 98. What about 7 times 15?

ask.ifNot: 98 plus 7 is 105. That has 3 digits, so it is out. 98 is the last one.

beats.say: So our multiples go from 7 times 2 up to 7 times 14.
Now count the multipliers from 2 to 14. From 1 to 14 there are 14 of them. Leave out the 1, and there are 13.
So there are 13 two-digit multiples of 7.
The trap is 14, which forgets that 7 itself is only a 1-digit number. Find the first and the last, then count.
Sunita climbs from the 1st floor to the 4th floor: 48 steps. Every floor has the same number of steps. How many steps from the 1st floor to the 7th?
From the 1st floor to the 4th floor, how many flights of stairs does she climb?

ask.ifNot: Count the climbs: 1st to 2nd, 2nd to 3rd, 3rd to 4th. She starts on the 1st floor, so she does not climb up to it.

beats.say: 1st to 2nd, 2nd to 3rd, 3rd to 4th. That is 3 flights, not 4.
So 48 steps are shared among 3 flights. 48 divided by 3 is 16 steps in each flight.
Now the 7th floor. In the same way, 1st to 7th is 6 flights.
6 flights of 16 steps. 6 times 16 is 96.
So she would climb 96 steps.
Floors are like fence posts, and flights of stairs are the gaps. Always count the gaps.
An ice-cream shop has 4 flavours: mango, chocolate, vanilla and strawberry. Rohan picks 2 different flavours. How many different pairs can he choose?

board.text: 4 flavours: M, C, V, S. Pairs of 2 different ones?

beats.say: Let's list the pairs in order, so that we miss none. Mango can go with chocolate, vanilla or strawberry. 3 pairs.
Next, chocolate. Chocolate with mango is already on the list. So how many new pairs does chocolate make?

ask.ifNot: Chocolate with mango is the same cup as mango with chocolate. The new ones are chocolate with vanilla, and chocolate with strawberry.

beats.say: Chocolate gives 2 new pairs. Then vanilla with strawberry is the last new pair.
Add them. 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 6.
So Rohan can choose 6 different pairs.
The trap is 4 times 3, which is 12. That counts every pair twice. In a cup, the order does not matter, so halve it.
Using each of the digits 2, 0 and 5 exactly once, how many 3-digit numbers can be made?
One of these digits cannot go in the hundreds place. Which one?

ask.ifNot: If 0 goes first, the number is not really a 3-digit number. A 0 at the front counts for nothing.

beats.say: So the hundreds digit is 2 or 5. Start with 2: the other two digits can go as 0 then 5, or 5 then 0. That gives 205 and 250.
Start with 5 and we get 502 and 520.
Count them: 2 numbers and 2 numbers. 2 plus 2 is 4.
So 4 three-digit numbers can be made.
The trap is 3 times 2 times 1, which is 6. That would also count numbers that start with 0. Watch out for 0 at the front.
A big triangle has 2 lines drawn from its top corner down to its base, making 3 small triangles side by side. How many triangles are there, of every size?

board.text: 3 small triangles side by side. Every size?

spec.note: Two lines from the top corner to the base. Count every triangle

beats.say: Let's count size by size. First the small ones: left, middle and right. That is 3.
Can 2 small triangles next to each other make a bigger triangle?

ask.ifNot: Join the left and the middle: the shape still has 3 corners, so it is a triangle. The middle and the right do the same.

beats.say: Left with middle is one. Middle with right is another. That is 2 triangles made of 2 parts.
Left with right? They do not touch, so that is not a shape. And all 3 parts together make the 1 big triangle.
Add them. 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 6.
So there are 6 triangles in the figure.
Count shapes by size: 1 part, 2 parts, 3 parts. Then nothing hides from you.
In a queue, Ravi is 8th from the front and Sana is 15th from the front. How many people stand between them?

spec.note: Places in the queue, from the front. How many stand between them?

beats.say: Between means after Ravi and before Sana. So we want the people in places 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 and 14.
Count those places. How many are there?

ask.ifNot: Point at each one: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. Do not count Ravi's 8 or Sana's 15.

beats.say: There are 6. Now a quick way. 15 minus 8 is 7. But that 7 counts Sana's own place too.
So take 1 away for Sana. 7 minus 1 is 6.
So 6 people stand between them.
For 'between', subtract the positions, then take away 1.
How many numbers from 100 to 200, counting both, end in the digit 0?
Numbers ending in 0 are the tens: 100, 110, 120 and so on, up to 200.
From 100 to 200 is a distance of 100. Each jump is 10, so there are 10 jumps.
10 jumps. So how many numbers?

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 10 gaps need 11 posts, because both ends count.

beats.say: The numbers are the posts, and the jumps are the gaps. 10 plus 1 is 11.
So 11 numbers end in 0.
Whenever both ends are counted, it is the jumps plus 1.
A book's pages are numbered from 1. In all, 129 digits were printed. How many pages does the book have?

board.text: Pages from 1. 129 digits printed. How many pages?

beats.say: Pages 1 to 9 have 1 digit each. So the first 9 pages use up 9 digits.
How many digits are left? 129 minus 9 is 120.
From page 10 onwards, how many digits does each page use?

ask.ifNot: Page 10 and the pages after it are each written with 2 digits.

beats.say: Each page uses 2 digits. So 120 digits make 120 divided by 2, which is 60 pages.
Careful: 60 is only the 2-digit pages. Add back the first 9 pages. 9 plus 60 is 69.
So the book has 69 pages.
Check: 9 digits, then 60 pages of 2 digits is 120 more. 9 plus 120 is 129. It fits.
How many 2-digit numbers have a tens digit bigger than the ones digit? 72 is one, but 27 is not.

board.text: 2-digit numbers with tens digit > ones digit?

beats.say: Go through the tens digits in order. Tens digit 1: the ones digit must be smaller than 1, so only 0. That is the number 10. Just 1 number.
Tens digit 2: the ones digit can be 0 or 1. How many numbers is that?

ask.ifNot: The ones digit can be 0 or 1, giving the numbers 20 and 21.

beats.say: 2 numbers. Do you see the pattern? Tens digit 3 gives 3 numbers, tens digit 4 gives 4, all the way up to tens digit 9, which gives 9.
So we add 1 plus 2 plus 3, all the way up to 9.
A neat way to add: pair 1 with 9, 2 with 8, 3 with 7, 4 with 6. That is 4 tens, which is 40, and the 5 in the middle makes 45.
So there are 45 such numbers.
Do not forget the numbers that end in 0, like 10 and 20. Zero is smaller than every tens digit, so they count.
How many 3-digit numbers have digits that add up to 4?

board.text: 3-digit numbers, digits add up to 4. How many?

beats.say: Let's go through the hundreds digit. It cannot be 0. If it is 1, the other two digits must add up to 3.
That gives 103, 112, 121 and 130. 4 numbers.
Hundreds digit 2: the other two digits must add up to 2. How many numbers?

ask.ifNot: The last two digits can be 0 and 2, or 1 and 1, or 2 and 0. That is 3 ways.

beats.say: They are 202, 211 and 220. 3 numbers.
Hundreds digit 3 gives 301 and 310. And hundreds digit 4 gives just 400.
Add the groups. 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 10.
So there are 10 such numbers.
The easy ones to miss are 400 and the others with zeros in them. Going in order catches them all.
A square board has 9 small squares, in 3 rows of 3. Counting squares of every size, how many are there?

board.text: 3 rows of 3 small squares. Squares of every size?

spec.note: A board of 9 small squares. Count the squares of every size

beats.say: Size by size. The smallest squares first: there are 9 of them.
Next, squares that are 2 wide and 2 tall. How many of those fit on the board?

ask.ifNot: A 2 by 2 square can sit in the top left, top right, bottom left or bottom right. They overlap, and that is fine.

beats.say: There are 4: one snug in each corner of the board. They overlap each other, and that is allowed.

spec.note: A square 2 wide and 2 tall fits in each corner: 4 of them

beats.say: And the biggest: the whole board is 1 square, 3 wide and 3 tall.
Add all the sizes. 9 plus 4 plus 1 is 14.
So there are 14 squares on the board.
The 2 by 2 squares are the ones people miss. Count every size, one at a time.
4 small squares are joined in a row to make a strip. Counting rectangles of every size, small squares too, how many are there?

board.text: A strip of 4 squares. Rectangles of every size?

spec.note: A strip of small squares in a row. Count rectangles of every size

beats.say: A square is a special rectangle, so each small square counts. That is 4.
Now rectangles made of 2 squares side by side. How many are there?

ask.ifNot: Number the squares 1, 2, 3, 4. The pairs are 1 and 2, then 2 and 3, then 3 and 4.

beats.say: 1 with 2, 2 with 3, 3 with 4. That is 3.
Rectangles made of 3 squares: 1 to 3, and 2 to 4. That is 2. And the whole strip is 1 more.
Add them. 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1 is 10.
So there are 10 rectangles in the strip.
Notice the pattern: 4, 3, 2, 1. Each longer size has one fewer place to sit.
At a party, every child gave one card to every other child. In all, 30 cards were given. How many children were there?

board.text: Each child gives a card to every other. 30 cards.

beats.say: Try a small party first. With 3 children, each one gives 2 cards. 3 times 2 is 6 cards.
So the rule is: the number of children, times one fewer than that. We need two neighbouring numbers that multiply to 30.
Which pair of neighbours multiplies to 30?

ask.ifNot: Neighbours are numbers next to each other, like 5 and 6. Multiply each neighbouring pair, and look for the one that makes 30.

beats.say: 6 times 5 is 30. So there were 6 children, and each one gave 5 cards.
So 6 children were at the party.
Careful: 5 is the number of cards each child gave, not the number of children. The children are one more.
And we do not halve here, as we do for handshakes. A card from Anu to Binu is different from a card from Binu to Anu.
Using the digits 0, 1, 2 and 3, with no digit repeated, how many 3-digit even numbers can be made?
An even number ends in an even digit. Here that means it ends in 0 or in 2. Let's take the two cases one at a time.
Case 1: it ends in 0. The hundreds digit can be 1, 2 or 3: 3 choices. Then 2 digits are left for the tens place. 3 times 2 is 6.
Case 2: it ends in 2. The digits left are 0, 1 and 3. How many of them can go in the hundreds place?

ask.ifNot: 0 cannot go first, or the number would not have 3 digits. So only 1 or 3 can go there.

beats.say: Only 1 or 3: that is 2 choices. Then 2 digits are left for the tens place, and one of them is the 0. 2 times 2 is 4.
Add the two cases. 6 plus 4 is 10.
So 10 such numbers can be made.
When 0 is one of the digits, split into cases. Zero is not allowed at the front, so it changes the count.
A temple bell takes 6 seconds to ring 4 times, from the first ring to the last. How long does it take to ring 10 times?
The time passes in the gaps between the rings. How many gaps are there between 4 rings?

ask.ifNot: Tap the table 4 times: ding, ding, ding, ding. There are only 3 waits in between.

beats.say: 4 rings have 3 gaps. So 6 seconds are shared among 3 gaps. 6 divided by 3 is 2 seconds for each gap.
Now 10 rings. In the same way, 10 rings have 9 gaps.
9 gaps of 2 seconds each. 9 times 2 is 18.
So it takes 18 seconds to ring 10 times.
The trap is to share the 6 seconds among the 4 rings. The clock only runs in the gaps between them.
Tara is 9th from the left and Uma is 6th from the right. They swap places, and now Tara is 15th from the left. How many children are in the row?

board.text: Tara: 9th from left. Uma: 6th from right.
After the swap, Tara: 15th from left. How many?

beats.say: After the swap, where is Tara standing?

choices: at the end of the row
ask.ifNot: They swapped. So Tara has moved into the place where Uma used to stand.

beats.say: Tara is in Uma's old spot. We know two things about that one spot: it is 15th from the left, and it is 6th from the right.

board.text: One spot: 15th from left, 6th from right

beats.say: So there are 14 children to its left, and 5 children to its right.
Add them all: 14 on the left, the spot itself, and 5 on the right. 14 plus 1 plus 5 is 20.
So there are 20 children in the row.
The 9 was only there to distract us. We never needed it! The shortcut: 15 plus 6, minus 1 for the spot counted twice.
Aman writes all the numbers from 1 to 100. How many times does he write the digit 1?

board.text: Write 1 to 100. How often is the digit 1 written?

beats.say: Count place by place. Ones place first: 1, 11, 21, 31, and so on up to 91. That is 10 times.
Now the tens place. Which numbers have a 1 in the tens place?

ask.ifNot: Every number in the teens has a 1 in the tens place, and so does 10 itself.

beats.say: 10, 11, 12, up to 19. That is 10 numbers, so 10 more 1s.
The number 11 has two 1s, and it is in both lists, once for each. So that is right.
One more to find: the hundreds place. The number 100 starts with a 1.
Add them. 10 plus 10 plus 1 is 21.
So Aman writes the digit 1 a total of 21 times.
Place by place: ones, tens, hundreds. And do not forget the last number, 100.
How many numbers from 1 to 60 can be divided exactly by 2, or by 3, or by both?

board.text: 1 to 60: divisible by 2 or by 3 (or both)?

beats.say: First the multiples of 2. Every second number is one, so 60 divided by 2 is 30 of them.
Next the multiples of 3. Every third number is one, so 60 divided by 3 is 20 of them.
30 plus 20 is 50. But think of the number 6. Which list is it in?

ask.ifNot: 6 is 2 times 3. So it is a multiple of 2 and also a multiple of 3. We counted it twice!

beats.say: Numbers like 6, 12 and 18 are in both lists. They are the multiples of 6, and there are 60 divided by 6 of them. That is 10.
We counted those 10 twice, so take them away once. 50 minus 10 is 40.
So there are 40 such numbers.
For 'this or that': count each list, add, then take away what is in both.
A flag has 3 stripes in a row. Each is red, green or blue. Stripes that touch must be different colours. How many flags can be made?

board.text: 3 stripes. Red, green or blue. Neighbours differ.

beats.say: Paint one stripe at a time. The first stripe can be any of the 3 colours.
The second stripe touches the first. So how many colours can it be?

ask.ifNot: It cannot match the first stripe. That leaves the other 2 colours.

beats.say: 2 choices for the second. Now the third stripe. It touches only the second one, not the first.
So how many colours can the third stripe be?

ask.ifNot: It only has to differ from the second stripe. It is allowed to match the first, because they do not touch.

beats.say: The third stripe has 2 choices as well. It may even be the same as the first. Multiply: 3 times 2 times 2 is 12.
So 12 different flags can be made.
The trap is 3 times 2 times 1, which is 6. That makes all 3 stripes different, but the rule was only about stripes that touch.
How many numbers are in this list? 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24.
The question asks how many numbers there are. It does not ask how big they are. So we just count them, one by one.
Point at each number as you count. 4 is the 1st. 8 is the 2nd. 12 is the 3rd.
16 is the 4th, and 20 is the 5th. What about 24?

ask.ifNot: After the 5th comes the 6th. 24 is the last number, and it is the 6th one we point at.

beats.say: 24 is the 6th, and it is the last one.
So there are 6 numbers in the list.
Careful: 24 is the last number, not how many there are. Count the numbers, not their size.
Ria writes down the whole numbers from 6 to 10: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10. How many numbers does she write?
Let's count them one at a time, pointing as we go. 6 is the 1st, 7 is the 2nd, 8 is the 3rd.
9 is the 4th. So what is 10?

ask.ifNot: After the 4th comes the 5th. 10 is the last number she writes, and it is the 5th one.

beats.say: 10 is the 5th, and the last.
So Ria writes 5 numbers.
Careful: 10 minus 6 is 4, but there are 5 numbers. When both ends are counted, there is always one extra.
How many whole numbers lie between 10 and 15? We must not count 10 or 15.
Between means after 10 and before 15. Let's write them down: 11, 12, 13, 14.
How many numbers did we write?

ask.ifNot: Count them one by one: 11, 12, 13, 14. The ends, 10 and 15, are left out.

beats.say: 11, 12, 13, 14. That is 4 numbers.
So there are 4 whole numbers between 10 and 15.
A quick check: 15 minus 10 is 5, and we take away 1 because neither end counts. That gives 4.
Anu and Bala stand in a line, one behind the other. In how many different orders can they stand?

board.text: Anu and Bala in a line. How many orders?

beats.say: Let's try it. Anu can stand in front, with Bala behind.
Is there another way?

choices: no, that is the only way
ask.ifNot: The two children can change places. Then Bala is in front and Anu is behind.

beats.say: They swap. Now Bala is in front, with Anu behind.
Are there any more? With 2 children, one is in front and the other is behind. So that is all.
So they can stand in 2 different orders.
To count orders, write each one down. Then you can see that you have them all.
Using the digits 4 and 7 once each, how many different 2-digit numbers can you make?
Put 4 in the tens place and 7 in the ones place. That makes 47.
Now swap the two digits around. Which number do we get?

ask.ifNot: Put 7 in the tens place and 4 in the ones place. That reads 74.

beats.say: 7 first, then 4. That makes 74.
Could we make 44 or 77? Not here: each digit can be used only once.
So we can make 2 different numbers.
With 2 digits used once each, there are 2 numbers: one, and its swap.
5 children stand in a queue. From the front they are Asha, Bina, Chetan, Dev and Esha. Who is 3rd?
The question says: starting from the front. So we begin counting at Asha.
Asha is 1st. Bina is 2nd.
Who comes next, in 3rd place?

ask.ifNot: After Bina, who is 2nd, the next child in the line is Chetan.

beats.say: Chetan is 3rd. After him, Dev is 4th and Esha is 5th.
So Chetan is 3rd in the queue.
For positions, always check which end to start from. Then count along: 1st, 2nd, 3rd.
Ravi is 4th in a queue. How many children are standing in front of him?

board.text: Ravi is 4th. How many in front of him?

beats.say: Let's draw the queue. 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and then Ravi in 4th place.
Which places are in front of Ravi?

ask.ifNot: Ravi is the 4th child himself. He cannot be in front of himself! So it is only the 1st, 2nd and 3rd.

beats.say: The 1st, 2nd and 3rd children are in front. Ravi is the 4th, so we do not count him.
That is 3 children. 4 minus 1 is 3.
So 3 children are standing in front of Ravi.
The number of people in front is always one less than your position.
There are 6 children in a queue. Meena is at the very front. How many children are behind her?

board.text: 6 in a queue. Meena is first. How many behind?

beats.say: Meena is at the front. So every other child in the queue is behind her.
There are 6 children altogether. Is Meena one of the 6?

ask.ifNot: The 6 children in the queue include Meena. So she must not be counted among those behind her.

beats.say: So take Meena away from the 6. 6 minus 1 is 5.
So 5 children are behind Meena.
Check: Meena and the 5 behind her make 6. It fits.
How many even numbers are in this list? 3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 13.
Even numbers can be shared into 2 equal groups. They end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.
Check each one. 3 is odd, so cross it out. 4 is even: keep it. 7 is odd.
8 is even. Now, what about 10?

ask.ifNot: 10 can be shared into 2 groups of 5. A number ending in 0 is always even.

beats.say: 10 ends in 0, so it is even. And 13 ends in 3, so it is odd.
The even numbers are 4, 8 and 10. That is 3 numbers.
To spot an even number, look only at its last digit.
Here are all the orders for Anu, Binu and Charu: A B C, A C B, B A C, B C A, C A B, C B A. In how many is Anu first?

board.text: ABC, ACB, BAC, BCA, CAB, CBA

beats.say: A stands for Anu. So we want the orders that begin with the letter A.
Look at the first letter of each order. Which ones start with A?

ask.ifNot: Look only at the first letter. B A C has an A in it, but it starts with B.

beats.say: A B C starts with A. So does A C B.
The other 4 start with B or C, so Anu is not first in those.
So Anu is first in 2 of the orders.
When a list is given, read exactly what to look for, then check each item.
Count the days from Monday to Thursday, counting both Monday and Thursday. How many days is that?

board.text: Monday to Thursday, counting both. How many days?

beats.say: Let's write the days in order: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday.
The question says to count both Monday and Thursday. So where do we start counting?

ask.ifNot: Both ends count. So Monday itself is day number 1.

beats.say: Monday is 1, Tuesday is 2, Wednesday is 3, Thursday is 4.
So that is 4 days.
When both ends are counted, write the list and count every item, the first and the last too.
7 chairs stand in a row, numbered 1 to 7. Which chair is exactly in the middle?
The middle chair has the same number of chairs on each side of it.
Here is a way to find it. Cross off one chair from each end at the same time. First 1 and 7.
Then 2 and 6. Then 3 and 5.
Which chair is left?

ask.ifNot: We crossed off 1, 2 and 3 from one end, and 7, 6 and 5 from the other. Only one chair is left standing.

beats.say: Chair 4 is left. It has 3 chairs on its left and 3 chairs on its right.
So the middle chair is Chair 4.
To find the middle, cross off from both ends together until one is left.
Rohit's runs in five cricket matches were 34, 52, 47, 25 and 43. In which match did he score the most runs?
Most runs means the biggest number. To compare numbers with two digits, look at the tens digit first.
Which of these numbers has the biggest tens digit?

ask.ifNot: The tens digits are 3, 5, 4, 2 and 4. The biggest is 5, and that belongs to 52.

beats.say: 52 has 5 tens. No other score has that many, so 52 is the biggest.
Now look back at the table. Which match has 52 runs? It is Match 2.
Rohit scored the most runs in Match 2.
Careful: the answer is the match, not the number of runs. Find the biggest number, then read off its label.
Each picture of a book stands for 5 books sold. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday 6, Wednesday 3 and Thursday 5. On which day were the fewest books sold?

board.text: Each picture = 5 books. Fewest books on which day?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 5 books

beats.say: Here are the pictures for each day.
Do we need to work out the number of books for every day?

ask.ifNot: Every picture stands for the same number of books. So the day with the fewest pictures also has the fewest books.

beats.say: Every picture is worth the same. So fewer pictures means fewer books. We only need the smallest number of pictures.
Of 4, 6, 3 and 5, the smallest is 3. That is Wednesday.
Let's check with books. Wednesday's 3 pictures make 15 books. Monday's 4 pictures make 20, which is more.
The fewest books were sold on Wednesday.
Read the word carefully. Fewest means the smallest, not the biggest.
In a tally chart, each bundle stands for 5 and each single stroke stands for 1. The row for parrots has 3 bundles and 2 single strokes. How many parrots?

spec.note: A bundle stands for 5, a single stroke for 1

beats.say: A tally bundle is four strokes with one more drawn across them. That is why a bundle always stands for 5.
So what are 3 bundles worth?

ask.ifNot: Each bundle stands for 5. 3 bundles are 3 lots of 5, and 3 times 5 is 15.

beats.say: 3 times 5 is 15. Or just count in fives: 5, 10, 15.
Now the 2 single strokes. Each one is worth 1, so we add 2. 15 plus 2 is 17.
17 parrots were counted.
Count the bundles in fives, then count on the single strokes.
The children present in Class 4 were: Monday 38, Tuesday 35, Wednesday 40, Thursday 32. How many more children were present on Wednesday than on Tuesday?

board.text: How many more on Wednesday than on Tuesday?

spec.note: How many more on Wednesday than on Tuesday?

beats.say: The table has four days, but we only need two of them. Pick out Wednesday and Tuesday.
We want to know how many more. Which sum finds that?

ask.ifNot: How many more means the gap between the two numbers. To find a gap, take the smaller from the bigger: 40 minus 35.

beats.say: 40 minus 35 is 5.
5 more children were present on Wednesday.
Check by counting up: 35 and 5 more makes 40. Yes.
Two tips: use only the rows the question asks about, and for how many more, subtract.
A bar graph shows samosas sold: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 9, Thursday 15, Friday 11. Which two days have bars of the same height?

board.text: Which two days have bars of the same height?

spec.note: Which two bars have the same height?

beats.say: In a bar graph, the height of a bar shows its number. So equal bars mean equal numbers.
Look along the numbers. Which number appears twice?

ask.ifNot: Read them slowly: 12, 15, 9, 15, 11. The 15 comes up two times.

beats.say: 15 appears twice: once for Tuesday and once for Thursday.
12 and 11 are close, but close is not equal. Those two bars would be a little different.
The bars of the same height are Tuesday and Thursday.
To find equal bars, hunt for a number that shows up twice.
The children of Class 4 each chose one favourite fruit: Mango 14, Banana 6, Apple 9, Guava 5. How many children chose banana or guava?

board.text: How many chose banana or guava?

beats.say: There are four fruits in the table, but the question only asks about two. Banana has 6 children, and guava has 5.
Banana or guava means everyone in either group. So what do we do with 6 and 5?

ask.ifNot: We want the two groups together. Putting groups together means adding.

beats.say: 6 plus 5 is 11.
11 children chose banana or guava.
Each child chose just one fruit, so nobody is counted twice. Pick the rows you need, then add.
Six children got these marks in a spelling test: 14, 18, 9, 20, 12, 17. How many children got more than 15 marks?

board.text: Marks: 14, 18, 9, 20, 12, 17. How many are more than 15?

spec.note: How many marks are more than 15?

beats.say: We check each mark against 15, one at a time. A ring if it is more than 15, and a line through it if not.
14 is less than 15, so cross it out. 18 is more, so ring it. 9 is less, cross it out.
Now 20, 12 and 17. Which of these are more than 15?

ask.ifNot: 20 is more than 15, and so is 17. But 12 is less than 15, so it does not count.

beats.say: 20, ring. 12, cross it out. 17, ring.
Count the rings: 18, 20 and 17. That is 3 children.
Notice that 14 is close to 15, but it is still less, so it does not count.
Go through the list one by one and mark each number. Then count your rings.
Each child in a class chose one favourite game: Cricket 13, Kho-kho 8, Football 7, Carrom 4. How many children are in the class?

spec.note: How many children are in the class?

beats.say: Each child chose one game. How do we find the number of children in the class?

ask.ifNot: Every child is in exactly one of the four groups. So the class is all four groups put together. We add.

beats.say: Let's add smartly. Look for pairs that make a round number. 13 and 7 make 20.
And 8 and 4 make 12.
20 plus 12 is 32.
There are 32 children in the class.
When you add a list, pair up numbers that make tens. It is quicker and safer.
In a tally chart, a bundle stands for 5 and a single stroke stands for 1. Which of the choices shows 23?
Bundles are fives. So we ask how many fives fit into 23. Count in fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25.
How many bundles can we use without going past 23?

ask.ifNot: 5 bundles make 25, which is already more than 23. 4 bundles make 20, and that fits.

beats.say: 4 bundles make 20. That is as close as fives can get.
From 20 up to 23 we need 3 more. Those are 3 single strokes.
So 23 is shown by 4 bundles and 3 strokes.
Careful: 2 bundles and 3 strokes just copies the digits of 23. But 2 bundles are only 10, so that shows 13.
Take out as many fives as you can. What is left is the single strokes.
Each picture of a sun stands for 2 sunny days. January has 5 pictures, February 8, March 6 and April 9. Which month had 16 sunny days?

board.text: Each sun = 2 sunny days. Which month had 16?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 2 sunny days

beats.say: We could work out the days for every month. But here is a shortcut: work backwards from the 16.
Each picture stands for 2 days. How many pictures make 16 days?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many 2s fit into 16. 16 divided by 2 is 8.

beats.say: 16 divided by 2 is 8. So we need 8 pictures.
Now look for the month with 8 pictures. That is February.
February had 16 sunny days.
Check: 8 times 2 is 16. Yes. When a question gives you the total, divide to get back to the pictures.
The heights of five plants in centimetres are: Rose 34, Tulsi 28, Neem 41, Mint 19, Lily 37. Which plant is the second tallest?
Second tallest means: find the tallest, set it aside, and then find the tallest of the rest.
First, which plant is the tallest?

ask.ifNot: Look at the tens digits. Only 41 has 4 tens, so Neem is the tallest.

beats.say: Neem is the tallest at 41. But that is not what we were asked! Set it aside.
Now the rest: 34, 28, 19 and 37. Two of them have 3 tens: 34 and 37. Compare the ones. 7 is more than 4, so 37 wins.
The second tallest plant is Lily.
In order from the tallest, the heights are 41, 37, 34, 28, 19. Lily is second.
For second biggest, find the biggest first, cross it out, then look again.
The side of a bar graph is marked 0, 10, 20, 30, 40. Tuesday's bar ends exactly halfway between 20 and 30. What number does it show?

board.text: The bar ends halfway between 20 and 30. It shows ?

spec.note: Tuesday's bar ends exactly halfway between 20 and 30

beats.say: The bar goes up past 20, but it does not reach 30. So the answer is somewhere between them.
How far apart are the two marks? 30 minus 20 is 10.
The bar stops halfway across that gap of 10. What is half of 10?

ask.ifNot: Half means two equal parts. 10 split into two equal parts gives 5 and 5.

beats.say: Half of 10 is 5. So the bar ends 5 above the 20 mark. 20 plus 5 is 25.
Tuesday's bar shows 25.
Check: 25 is 5 above 20 and 5 below 30. Right in the middle.
When a bar ends between two marks, find the gap, then work out how far across it the bar goes.
In a pictograph, each picture stands for 3 kites. Ravi's row has 5 pictures and Meena's row has 8 pictures. How many more kites does Meena have than Ravi?

board.text: 1 picture = 3 kites. Ravi 5 pictures, Meena 8 pictures.
How many more kites does Meena have?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 3 kites

beats.say: Let's compare the pictures first. Meena has 8 and Ravi has 5. 8 minus 5 is 3, so Meena has 3 more pictures.
Is 3 the answer?

ask.ifNot: The question asks for kites. 3 is the number of extra pictures, and each picture stands for 3 kites.

beats.say: Each extra picture is worth 3 kites. 3 times 3 is 9.
Meena has 9 more kites than Ravi.
Check the long way. Meena has 8 times 3, which is 24 kites. Ravi has 5 times 3, which is 15. And 24 minus 15 is 9.
In a pictograph, always change pictures into the real thing before you answer.
In a pictograph of library books, each picture stands for 5 books. Monday has 4 pictures, Tuesday has 6 and Wednesday has 3. How many books were borrowed altogether?

board.text: 1 picture = 5 books. Mon 4, Tue 6, Wed 3 pictures.

spec.note: Each picture stands for 5 books

beats.say: Every picture is worth the same. So we can count all the pictures first, and change them into books at the end.
4 plus 6 plus 3 is 13 pictures.
13 pictures, and each one stands for 5 books. What do we do now?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 13 pictures stands for 5 books. 13 lots of 5 means we multiply.

beats.say: 13 times 5. 10 fives are 50, and 3 fives are 15. 50 plus 15 is 65.
65 books were borrowed altogether.
Check day by day: 20 books, 30 books and 15 books. 20 plus 30 plus 15 is 65.
13 is only the number of pictures. Always turn the pictures into books.
Each picture stands for 6 eggs. A farmer's chart has 5 pictures for Monday and 3 for Tuesday. He packs all these eggs in boxes of 12. How many boxes does he fill?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 6 eggs. A box holds 12 eggs

beats.say: This has three steps: pictures, then eggs, then boxes. We take them one at a time.
Pictures first. 5 plus 3 is 8 pictures.
Each picture is 6 eggs. 8 times 6 is 48 eggs.
48 eggs go into boxes of 12. How do we find the number of boxes?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many 12s fit into 48. That is a division.

beats.say: Count in twelves: 12, 24, 36, 48. That is 4 twelves. So 48 divided by 12 is 4.
The farmer fills 4 boxes.
A neat shortcut: 2 pictures make 12 eggs, which is 1 box. So 8 pictures fill 4 boxes.
Do not stop at 8 pictures or at 48 eggs. Keep going until you reach what the question asks for.
A sweet shop sold 60 laddoos in four days: Monday 12, Tuesday 18, Thursday 14. The number for Wednesday is smudged. How many were sold on Wednesday?
The whole is 60. Three parts are known and one is hidden. So first find what the three known parts add up to.
12 and 18 make a round 30. Then 14 more makes 44.
The three known days make 44, and the total is 60. How do we find Wednesday?

ask.ifNot: The 60 already holds all four days. Take away the three we know, and Wednesday is what is left.

beats.say: 60 minus 44 is 16.
16 laddoos were sold on Wednesday.
Check: 12 plus 18 plus 16 plus 14 is 60. It fits.
The missing part is the whole, minus the parts you know.
Tickets sold at a mela: on Saturday, 20 adult and 35 child tickets. On Sunday, 28 adult and 30 child tickets. How many more tickets were sold on Sunday than on Saturday?

board.text: Sat: 20 adult, 35 child.   Sun: 28 adult, 30 child.
How many more tickets on Sunday?

spec.note: How many more tickets on Sunday than on Saturday?

beats.say: The question says tickets, and that means all tickets, adult and child together. So we need each day's total first.
Saturday: 20 plus 35 is 55.
Sunday: 28 plus 30 is 58.
Saturday has 55 and Sunday has 58. How many more on Sunday?

ask.ifNot: Take Saturday's total away from Sunday's. 58 minus 55 is 3.

beats.say: 58 minus 55 is 3. So 3 more tickets were sold on Sunday.
The trap is to compare only the adult tickets, 28 and 20. That leaves out the children. Total each day first, then compare.
In a pictograph, each picture stands for 4 children, and Monday's row has 6 pictures. The chart is drawn again with each picture standing for 8 children. How many pictures now?

board.text: Drawn again with 1 picture = 8 children. Pictures = ?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 4 children. Now each must stand for 8

beats.say: The pictures change, but the children do not! So first find how many children there really are.
6 pictures of 4 children each. 6 times 4 is 24 children.
Now each picture stands for 8 children. Will we need more pictures, or fewer?

ask.ifNot: Each new picture holds more children than before. So fewer pictures are needed to show the same 24 children.

beats.say: How many 8s fit into 24? Count: 8, 16, 24. That is 3.
Monday's row will have 3 pictures.
Notice: each picture is now worth twice as much, so we need half as many. Half of 6 is 3.
When the key of a pictograph changes, go back to the real number first.
A full picture stands for 10 coconuts and a half picture for 5. Monday's row has 3 full pictures and 1 half picture. Tuesday's row has 2 full pictures. How many coconuts in all?

board.text: Monday: 3 full and 1 half.    Tuesday: 2 full.

spec.note: Full picture 10 coconuts, half picture 5. Total = ?

beats.say: Monday first. 3 full pictures are 3 times 10, which is 30.
Monday also has a half picture. What do we add for it?

ask.ifNot: A half picture stands for half of 10 coconuts, and that is 5.

beats.say: 30 plus 5 is 35 coconuts on Monday.
Tuesday: 2 full pictures are 2 times 10, which is 20.
Both days together: 35 plus 20 is 55.
55 coconuts were sold on the two days.
A half picture counts for half. Work out each row, then add.
A tally chart of birds uses bundles of 5 and single strokes. Crows: 2 bundles and 3 strokes. Sparrows: 3 bundles and 1 stroke. Pigeons: 1 bundle and 4 strokes. How many birds in all?

board.text: Crows: 2 bundles 3 strokes.  Sparrows: 3 bundles 1 stroke.

spec.note: A bundle is 5, a stroke is 1. How many birds in all?

beats.say: Each bundle is 5 and each stroke is 1. We do one bird at a time. Crows: 2 fives are 10, plus 3 is 13.
Sparrows have 3 bundles and 1 stroke. How many sparrows is that?

ask.ifNot: Count the 3 bundles in fives, then add 1 for the single stroke. That gives 16.

beats.say: 3 fives and 1 more make 16 sparrows.
Pigeons: 1 five and 4 more make 9.
Now add the three birds. 13 plus 16 is 29, and 9 more is 38.
38 birds were counted in all.
Check another way. There are 6 bundles in all, which is 30, and 8 single strokes. 30 plus 8 is 38.
A bundle is never worth 1. Count bundles in fives, then add the strokes.
A bar graph shows kites sold: Monday 14, Tuesday 9, Wednesday 17, Thursday 11. Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's. How many kites were sold on the five days?

board.text: Mon 14, Tue 9, Wed 17, Thu 11. Friday = twice Tuesday.

spec.note: Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's bar

beats.say: Friday's bar is twice as tall as Tuesday's, and Tuesday is 9. So what is Friday?

ask.ifNot: Twice as tall means 2 times as many. 2 times 9 is 18.

beats.say: 2 times 9 is 18. Friday sold 18 kites.
Now add Monday to Thursday. 14 and 11 make 25. 9 and 17 make 26. And 25 plus 26 is 51.
Don't forget Friday! 51 plus 18 is 69.
69 kites were sold altogether.
Two traps here. Twice means times 2, not plus 2. And the total needs all five days.
40 children each chose one favourite game. Cricket was chosen by 16, football by 10 and badminton by 8. All the others chose kabaddi. How many chose kabaddi?

spec.note: Cricket, football, badminton, then kabaddi

beats.say: Everyone chose one game. So the four groups together make 40, and three of the groups are known.
Add the three known groups. 16 plus 10 is 26, and 8 more is 34.
34 children chose the first three games. How many are left for kabaddi?

ask.ifNot: Take the 34 away from all 40 children. 40 minus 34 is 6.

beats.say: 40 minus 34 is 6. So 6 children chose kabaddi.
Check: 16 plus 10 plus 8 plus 6 is 40. Everyone is counted.
Add what you know, then take it away from the whole.
Meera read 12 pages on Monday, 0 pages on Tuesday, 9 on Wednesday and 15 on Thursday. What is the average number of pages she read per day?

board.text: Mon 12, Tue 0, Wed 9, Thu 15. Average per day = ?

spec.note: Average number of pages per day = ?

beats.say: The average is the fair share. If she had read the same number of pages every day, how many would that be?
First the total. 12 plus 0 plus 9 plus 15 is 36 pages.
Now we share the 36 pages over the days. On Tuesday she read nothing. So how many days do we divide by?

ask.ifNot: Tuesday is still a day, even with 0 pages. The question says four days, so we divide by 4.

beats.say: Tuesday counts. A day with 0 pages is still one of the four days. This is the trap.
36 divided by 4 is 9.
The average is 9 pages per day.
Check: 4 days of 9 pages make 36 pages. Yes. A zero still counts when you count how many.
A bar graph shows cups of tea sold: Monday 22, Tuesday 17, Wednesday 25, Thursday 19. Put the days in order from the shortest bar to the tallest bar.

board.text: Order: shortest bar to tallest bar

spec.note: Put the days in order, shortest bar to tallest

beats.say: A shorter bar means a smaller number. So we put the numbers in order, smallest first.
Which number is the smallest?

ask.ifNot: Two of the numbers have just 1 ten: 17 and 19. Of these, 17 has fewer ones. So 17 is the smallest.

beats.say: 17 is the smallest, and that is Tuesday. Next comes 19, which is Thursday.
Then 22, which is Monday. And the biggest is 25, Wednesday.
So the order is Tuesday, Thursday, Monday, Wednesday.
Watch the direction: shortest to tallest means smallest first. And do not just read the days in weekday order.
A school has three clubs. Art: 9 girls and 6 boys. Music: 7 girls and 11 boys. Chess: 5 girls and 12 boys. Which club has the most children?

board.text: Art: 9 girls, 6 boys.    Music: 7 girls, 11 boys.

spec.note: Which club has the most children?

beats.say: Most children means girls and boys together. So we add up each club.
Art: 9 plus 6 is 15.
Music has 7 girls and 11 boys. How many children is that?

ask.ifNot: 7 plus 11. First 7 plus 10 is 17, and then 1 more is 18.

beats.say: Music: 7 plus 11 is 18.
Chess: 5 plus 12 is 17.
Compare 15, 18 and 17. The biggest is 18, so the club with the most children is Music.
Art has the most girls, and Chess has the most boys. But the question asks about all the children. Add up what the question really asks for.
Children chose their favourite fruit: Mango 18, Apple 9, Banana 12, Orange 6, Grapes 3. Which fruit was chosen by exactly twice as many children as orange?

board.text: Which fruit has exactly twice as many as Orange?

spec.note: Which fruit has exactly twice as many as orange?

beats.say: Start with orange. Orange was chosen by 6 children.
What does twice as many as 6 mean?

ask.ifNot: Twice means two times. So twice as many as 6 is 2 times 6.

beats.say: 2 times 6 is 12.
Now find the fruit that 12 children chose. That is banana.
The answer is Banana.
Mango's 18 is three times 6, and Grapes' 3 is half of 6. Only banana is exactly twice.
Hardik played 5 cricket matches. His average score was 32 runs per match. How many runs did he score in the 5 matches altogether?

board.text: 5 matches. Average 32 runs per match. Total = ?

spec.note: Average 32: as if he scored 32 in each of the 5 matches

beats.say: An average of 32 means this: if he had scored the same in every match, it would be 32 each time.
So how do we get the total for the 5 matches?

ask.ifNot: The total is 5 lots of 32. Lots of means we multiply.

beats.say: 5 times 30 is 150, and 5 times 2 is 10. 150 plus 10 is 160.
Hardik scored 160 runs altogether.
Check: 160 shared over 5 matches is 32 each. So the total is the average times the number of matches.
The rainfall in a town, in millimetres, was: Monday 6, Tuesday 10, Wednesday 4, Thursday 12, Friday 8. On how many days was the rainfall more than the average?

board.text: On how many days was it more than the average?

spec.note: On how many days was the rainfall more than the average?

beats.say: There are two jobs here. First find the average. Then count the days that beat it.
Add them up: 6 plus 10 plus 4 plus 12 plus 8 is 40.
There are 5 days. 40 divided by 5 is 8. So the average is 8 millimetres.
Now compare each day with 8. Tuesday's 10 is more. Thursday's 12 is more. Monday's 6 and Wednesday's 4 are less.
What about Friday, with exactly 8?

ask.ifNot: Friday's 8 is equal to the average. Equal is not the same as more than. So Friday is left out.

beats.say: Friday is equal to the average, not more than it. So Friday is out. That is the trap.
The rainfall was more than the average on 2 days.
More than means really bigger. Find the average first, then compare with care.
Ananya's average mark in 4 tests was 18. After the 5th test, her average for all 5 tests became 20. How many marks did she get in the 5th test?

spec.note: Averages shown as equal pieces. Marks in the 5th test = ?

beats.say: Averages hide the real marks. So we turn each average into a total. A total is the average times the number of tests.
4 tests with an average of 18. 4 times 18 is 72 marks.
After 5 tests the average is 20. What is the total for all 5 tests?

ask.ifNot: Now there are 5 tests, not 4. So the total is 5 times 20, which is 100.

beats.say: 5 times 20 is 100 marks.
The total grew from 72 to 100. That jump is the 5th test. 100 minus 72 is 28.
Ananya got 28 marks in the 5th test.
Why so high? The 5th test had to score 20 for itself, and also lift each of the 4 earlier tests by 2. That is 8 extra, and 20 plus 8 is 28.
The trap is to just add 2 to 20. Always change averages into totals first.
A pictograph shows newspapers collected. Class 4A has 7 pictures and Class 4B has 4. Each picture stands for the same number. Class 4A collected 21 more than Class 4B. How many did 4A collect?

spec.note: Class 4A collected 21 more newspapers than Class 4B

beats.say: We are not told what one picture stands for. That is the puzzle. But there is a clue: the 21 more.
Class 4A has 7 pictures and 4B has 4. 7 minus 4 is 3. So 4A has 3 extra pictures.
Those 3 extra pictures are the 21 extra newspapers. So what does 1 picture stand for?

ask.ifNot: 3 pictures stand for 21 newspapers. Share 21 among the 3 pictures: 21 divided by 3 is 7.

beats.say: 21 divided by 3 is 7. Each picture stands for 7 newspapers.
Now Class 4A. It has 7 pictures, each worth 7. 7 times 7 is 49.
Class 4A collected 49 newspapers.
Check: 4B has 4 times 7, which is 28. And 49 minus 28 is 21. It fits.
When the key is missing, use the difference to find what one picture is worth.
Class 4 has 42 children, and 23 of them are girls. 15 children come to school by bus, and 9 of these are girls. How many boys do not come by bus?

board.text: 42 children, 23 girls.    15 by bus, 9 of them girls.
Boys who do NOT come by bus = ?

spec.note: How many boys do NOT come by bus?

beats.say: Lots of numbers! We want boys, so let's find out everything about the boys. First, how many boys are in the class?
42 children, and 23 are girls. 42 minus 23 is 19 boys.
15 children come by bus, and 9 of these are girls. How many boys come by bus?

ask.ifNot: The bus children are girls and boys together. Take the 9 girls away from 15, and 6 boys are left.

beats.say: 15 minus 9 is 6. So 6 boys come by bus.
There are 19 boys, and 6 of them come by bus. The rest do not. 19 minus 6 is 13.
13 boys do not come by bus.
Find all the boys, find the bus boys, then subtract. One group at a time.
Vikram found the average of five numbers to be 20. Then he saw that he had copied one number as 25 when it was really 15. What is the correct average?

board.text: Five numbers: average 20. One copied as 25, not 15.

beats.say: The average came from a total. So first find the total that Vikram used. 5 times 20 is 100.
He wrote 25, but the real number was 15. So what can we say about his total?

ask.ifNot: 25 is 10 more than 15. So he added 10 too many, and his total is 10 too big.

beats.say: 25 minus 15 is 10. His total was 10 too big, so take 10 off. 100 minus 10 is 90.
Now share the correct total among the five numbers. 90 divided by 5 is 18.
The correct average is 18.
Here is the trap: the average does not drop by 10. The 10 is shared among five numbers, so each loses 2. And 20 minus 2 is 18.
Fix the total first. Then find the average again.

A shop sold school bags: Monday 14, Tuesday 18, Wednesday 10. On Saturday it sold as many as Monday and Tuesday together. On Sunday it sold half as many as Saturday. What is the total for these five days?

board.text: Sat = Mon + Tue.    Sun = half of Sat.    Total = ?

spec.note: How many bags on these five days altogether?

beats.say: Two of the five days are hidden behind clues, so we uncover them first. Saturday is Monday and Tuesday together: 14 plus 18 is 32.
Sunday is half of Saturday. What is half of 32?

ask.ifNot: Half means divide by 2. 32 divided by 2 is 16.

beats.say: 32 divided by 2 is 16. So Sunday is 16.
Now Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday together. We already know 14 plus 18 is 32. Add Wednesday's 10 to get 42.
Add all five days. 42 plus 32 is 74, and 16 more is 90.
The shop sold 90 bags altogether.
Work out the hidden days first. Then make sure all five days are in your total.
Four friends have 8, 14, 11 and 7 marbles. They share so that all four have the same number. How many marbles must the friend who had 14 give away?

board.text: Marbles: 8, 14, 11, 7. Share so all four are equal.
How many does the friend with 14 give away?

spec.note: They share so that all four have the same number

beats.say: First we find the equal share. Put all the marbles together, then share them among the 4 friends.
8 and 7 are 15. 14 and 11 are 25. And 15 plus 25 is 40 marbles.
40 marbles among 4 friends. 40 divided by 4 is 10 each.
Is 10 the answer?

choices: no, 10 is what each ends with
ask.ifNot: 10 is the number each friend ends up with. The question asks how many the friend with 14 gives away.

beats.say: The friend with 14 must come down to 10. 14 minus 10 is 4.
That friend must give away 4 marbles.
Check: the friend with 11 gives away 1, so 5 are given away. The friend with 8 needs 2 and the friend with 7 needs 3. That is 5 needed. It balances!
Find the equal share first. Then see how far above it each friend is.
Riya's pictograph has 12 pictures, each standing for 5 stamps. Kabir's has 7 pictures, each standing for 8 stamps. Who has more stamps, and by how many?

board.text: Riya: 12 pictures of 5 stamps.  Kabir: 7 pictures of 8.
Who has more stamps, and by how many?

spec.note: Who has more stamps, and by how many?

beats.say: The two charts use different keys. So we cannot compare the pictures. We must change each chart into stamps.
Riya: 12 times 5 is 60 stamps.
Kabir has 7 pictures of 8 stamps. How many stamps is that?

ask.ifNot: 7 times 8 is 56. Here is a way to remember it: 5, 6, 7, 8. 56 is 7 times 8.

beats.say: Kabir: 7 times 8 is 56 stamps.
Riya has 60 and Kabir has 56. So Riya has more. 60 minus 56 is 4.
Riya has more stamps, by 4.
Riya has more pictures, and Kabir has bigger pictures. Only the stamps settle it. Never compare pictures from charts with different keys.
Class 4A has 20 children with an average mark of 30. Class 4B has 30 children with an average mark of 40. What is the average mark of all 50 children together?

spec.note: Average mark of all 50 children = ?

beats.say: Here is a tempting idea. The averages are 30 and 40, so just pick the middle. Is that safe?

choices: no, the classes are different sizes
ask.ifNot: The middle would be fair only if both classes were the same size. Class 4B has more children, so it pulls the average its way.

beats.say: The middle is the trap. Class 4B is bigger, so it counts for more. To be fair to every child, we use the total marks.
Class 4A: 20 children with an average of 30. 20 times 30 is 600 marks.
Class 4B: 30 children with an average of 40. 30 times 40 is 1200 marks.
Together that is 600 plus 1200, which is 1800 marks for 50 children.
Share 1800 marks among 50 children. 1800 divided by 50 is 36, because 50 times 36 is 1800.
The average mark of all 50 children is 36.
See, 36 is closer to 40 than to 30. The bigger class pulls the average towards itself. Never average two averages: go back to the totals.
On a bar graph, the bottom line stands for 20 books, not 0. Each square above it stands for 5 more books. Saturday's bar is 3 squares tall and Sunday's is 6. How many books in all?

board.text: Bottom line = 20 books. Each square above = 5 more.

spec.note: The bottom line is 20 books. Each square is 5 more books

beats.say: This graph does not start at 0. It starts at 20. So every bar already holds 20 books before we count a single square.
Saturday is 3 squares above 20. 3 times 5 is 15, and 20 plus 15 is 35.
Sunday's bar is 6 squares tall. How many books is that?

ask.ifNot: 6 squares are 6 times 5, which is 30. But the bar starts from 20, so add them: 20 plus 30 is 50.

beats.say: 6 times 5 is 30, and 20 plus 30 is 50. Sunday is 50 books.
Now both days together: 35 plus 50 is 85.
Altogether 85 books were sold.
The starting 20 belongs to each bar, so it is counted once for each day. Always check where a graph's scale begins.
In a class of 40 children, 24 like cricket and 20 like football. 6 children like neither game. How many children like both games?

board.text: 6 like neither. How many like both?

spec.note: 40 children. 6 like neither game

beats.say: First set aside the 6 who like neither game. They are on no list at all. 40 minus 6 leaves 34 children who like at least one game.
Now imagine two lists: a cricket list with 24 names and a football list with 20 names. 24 plus 20 is 44 names.
44 names, but only 34 children. How can that be?

choices: some children are on both lists
ask.ifNot: A child who likes both games is written on the cricket list and on the football list. So that child is counted twice.

beats.say: A child who likes both games is on both lists, and so is counted twice. Each such child makes 1 extra name.
How many extra names are there? 44 minus 34 is 10.
10 children like both games.
Check: cricket only is 24 minus 10, which is 14. Football only is 20 minus 10, which is 10. And 14 plus 10 plus 10 plus 6 is 40.
When two lists have more names than there are children, the extra names are the children on both lists.
The average of five whole numbers is 8. Which of the four statements on the board is certainly true?

board.text: Five whole numbers have an average of 8.
• at least one number is exactly 8
• at least one number is 8 or more
• three of the numbers are more than 8
• none of the numbers is more than 16

beats.say: Certainly true means true for every possible set of five numbers, not just for some. First, the total: 5 times 8 is 40.
To test a statement, we try to break it. One strange set does the job: 0, 0, 0, 0 and 40. It adds up to 40, so its average is 8.
In this set no number is exactly 8. Only one number is more than 8. And 40 is more than 16. So three of the statements are broken.
One statement is left: at least one number is 8 or more. Could all five numbers be less than 8?

choices: no, the total would be under 40
ask.ifNot: If every number were less than 8, five of them would add up to less than 5 times 8. But the total must be exactly 40.

beats.say: Five numbers that are each 7 or less make at most 35. That cannot reach 40. So at least one number must be 8 or more.
That is the statement that is certainly true.

board.text: At least one of the numbers is 8 or more

target.text: At least one of the numbers is 8 or more

beats.say: The numbers cannot all be below their own average. Someone has to be at the average, or above it.

Riya draws a pictograph for kites sold: Monday 12, Tuesday 18, Wednesday 30, Thursday 42. Every picture stands for the same number, only whole pictures, and as few pictures as possible. How many pictures?

board.text: Whole pictures only. Fewest pictures in all = ?

spec.note: Whole pictures only, and as few as possible

beats.say: To draw as few pictures as possible, should each picture stand for a small number of kites, or a large number?

ask.ifNot: If each picture stands for more kites, fewer pictures are needed. So we want each picture to be worth as much as possible.

beats.say: But only whole pictures are allowed. So the number for one picture must divide 12, 18, 30 and 42 exactly, with nothing left over.
Let's test. 2 divides them all. 3 divides them all. And 6 divides them all, because 12, 18, 30 and 42 are all in the 6 times table.
Can we go bigger than 6? The number must divide 12, so the only bigger one to try is 12 itself. Does 12 divide 18 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 12 goes into 18 once, with 6 left over. So 12 does not work, and 6 is the largest number that does.

beats.say: So each picture stands for 6 kites. Now the pictures for each day: 2, 3, 5 and 7.
Add the pictures. 2 plus 3 plus 5 plus 7 is 17.
Riya will draw 17 pictures altogether.
6 is only what one picture is worth. The question asks for the number of pictures. The largest key gives the fewest pictures.
A shop sold school bags: Monday 20, Tuesday 35, Wednesday 25 and Friday 40. Thursday's number is smudged, but it was exactly equal to the average of all five days. What was it?

board.text: Thursday = the average of all five days

spec.note: Thursday is exactly the average of all five days

beats.say: This sounds like a riddle. Thursday is the average, but the average needs Thursday! Here is the way in.
Think of the average as a level. If Thursday is already at that level, it pulls it neither up nor down. So the other four days must level out to the same number.

board.text: Thursday = average of the other four days

beats.say: Add the four known days. 20 plus 40 is 60, and 35 plus 25 is 60. Together that is 120.
What is the average of those four days?

ask.ifNot: There are four known days, so share 120 among 4. 120 divided by 4 is 30.

beats.say: 120 divided by 4 is 30. So Thursday should be 30.
Check with all five days. 120 plus 30 is 150, and 150 divided by 5 is 30. Thursday really is the average.
30 bags were sold on Thursday.
The trap is to divide 120 by 5. That treats Thursday as if it sold nothing. A number equal to the average leaves the average unchanged.
Riya is reading a storybook. The table shows the total pages she had read by the end of each day: Monday 12, Tuesday 30, Wednesday 41, Thursday 65, Friday 80. On which day did she read the most?

board.text: Total pages read by the end of each day:
On which day did she read the most pages?

spec.note: On which day did she read the most pages?
