The digits left are 0, 4 and 7. To keep the number small, write them from smallest to greatest.
So the number is 29047.

spec.note: 9 is in the thousands place

beats.say: Careful: 20479 is even smaller, but its 9 is in the ones place. The rule about the 9 comes first.

board.text: 20479: the 9 is in the ones place

beats.say: Two numbers to find. Each has 4 digits, and no digit may repeat. Then we subtract.

board.text: Greatest − smallest 4-digit number, all digits different

beats.say: For the greatest, start with the biggest digit, 9, and step down: 9, 8, 7, 6. That makes 9876.
For the smallest, the first digit must be 1, because a number cannot start with 0. What is the best digit for the second seat?

ask.ifNot: 0 cannot go first, but it is welcome in the second seat, and it is the smallest digit there is. The 1 is already used.

beats.say: This is the key idea. Zero cannot lead, but it can sit right behind the 1. Then come 2 and 3. So the smallest is 1023.
Now subtract 1023 from 9876. No borrowing is needed: 6 minus 3, 7 minus 2, 8 minus 0, and 9 minus 1.
The difference is 8853.
Watch out for two traps. 1234 forgets that 0 may be used. And 1000 repeats the 0, which is not allowed.
Check by adding back: 8853 plus 1023 is 9876.
In 7,26,935, one digit has a place value that is exactly 10,000 times its face value. Let us find that digit.

board.text: 7,26,935: place value = 10,000 × face value. Which digit?

beats.say: Remember: the face value is the digit itself. The place value is the digit times what its seat is worth.

board.text: place value = face value × worth of the seat

beats.say: So we want the seat that is worth 10,000. Which place is that?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. The fifth seat is worth 10,000.

beats.say: Now count the seats of 7,26,935 from the right: 5 ones, 3 tens, 9 hundreds, 6 thousands, 2 ten-thousands.

spec.note: The ten-thousands place

beats.say: So the digit is 2. Its place value is 20,000, which is 2 times 10,000.
Careful with the neighbours. The 6 is only in the thousands place, and the 7 is in the lakhs place. One seat off gives a different digit.
So: turn the clue into a seat, then count from the right to see who sits there.
This number is written with Indian commas. We want to read it the international way, with millions.
The digits do not change, only the commas. So first take the commas out. There are 8 digits.
The international system groups the digits from the right. How many digits go in each group?

ask.ifNot: The Indian system goes 3, then 2, then 2. The international system keeps it simple: 3 digits in every group.

beats.say: So group in threes from the right. We get 30, then 540, then 3 zeros.
The first group counts millions and the second counts thousands. So we have 30 million and 540 thousand.
In words: thirty million, five hundred forty thousand.

board.text: Thirty million five hundred forty thousand

target.text: Thirty million five hundred forty thousand

beats.say: Careful: the Indian commas make groups of 2 digits. Do not read those groups one by one. Regroup in threes first, then read.
So: drop the commas, regroup in threes from the right, then name the groups.
Rahim gets 3,00,000 rupees, all in 100 rupee notes. We want to know how many notes that is.
Each note is worth 100. Which sum tells us the number of notes?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many hundreds fit into 3,00,000. Finding how many fit is a division.

beats.say: So we divide 3,00,000 by 100.
First count the zeros in 3,00,000. There are 5 of them.
Dividing by 100 takes away 2 zeros, one for each zero in 100. So 5 zeros become 3 zeros.
A 3 with 3 zeros is 3,000. So Rahim gets 3,000 notes.
Check: 3,000 notes of 100 rupees make 3,00,000 rupees. It works.
Careful when you count the zeros in a lakh. 1 lakh has 5 zeros, not 4. Miss one, and the answer comes out ten times too small.
India became independent in the year M C M X L V I I. We want the year 75 years later, in Roman numerals.
Roman numerals are hard to add. So first, we change the year into our own numbers, part by part.

spec.note: The year, part by part

beats.say: C M has a smaller letter in front of a bigger one. C is 100 and M is 1000. So what is C M?

ask.ifNot: A smaller letter in front is taken away. 1000 minus 100 is 900.

beats.say: So M is 1000, C M is 900, X L is 40 and V I I is 7. The year is 1947.
Now add 75 years. 1947 plus 75 is 2022.
Back to Roman letters. 2022 is 2000, 20 and 2.
2000 is M M. 20 is X X. And 2 is I I.
Careful: we crossed the year 2000, so the answer has to start with M M. A numeral starting M C M is still before 2000.
So: Roman to our numbers, do the sum, then back to Roman.
4 Roman numerals to put in order, smallest first. They look alike, so let us find the value of each one.

board.text: XL, LX, XIV, XLIV: smallest first

beats.say: X L has the smaller letter first, so we take away. 50 minus 10 is 40.
Now L X. The bigger letter is first this time. What is L X worth?

ask.ifNot: When the bigger letter comes first, we add. 50 and 10 make 60.

beats.say: L X is 50 plus 10, which is 60. The same letters as X L, but a different number!
X I V is 10, and then I V, which is 4. That makes 14.
X L I V is X L, which is 40, and then I V, which is 4. That makes 44.
Now put the numbers in order: 14, 40, 44, 60.
So in Roman numerals, smallest first: X I V, then X L, then X L I V, then L X.
The trap is X L I V. It begins like X L, so it is 44, and it comes before L X, not after it.
Some number was rounded to the nearest hundred, and the result was 4,700. We want the greatest whole number it could have been.

spec.note: Which numbers round to 4,700?

beats.say: Numbers above 4,700 can round down to it, as long as they are closer to 4,700 than to 4,800.
Halfway between them is 4,750. Which way does the halfway number round?

ask.ifNot: The rule is: 5 or more in the tens place rounds up. 4,750 has a 5 in the tens place, so it rounds up to 4,800.

beats.say: So 4,750 is already too big, because it rounds up to 4,800. That is the trap in this question.
Step back just one. 4,749 has a 4 in the tens place, and 4 is less than 5, so it rounds down to 4,700.

spec.note: 4,749 still rounds down

beats.say: So the greatest whole number is 4,749.
And what about 4,799? It is far too close to 4,800. Only the tens digit matters: 4 or less rounds down, 5 or more rounds up.
So for the greatest number that rounds down: go to the halfway point, then step back one.
38,462 people watched the match. Anil rounds to the nearest thousand and Bina rounds to the nearest ten. How far apart are their answers?

board.text: 38,462: nearest thousand, and nearest ten. Difference?

beats.say: Anil rounds to the nearest thousand. Which digit must he look at to decide?

ask.ifNot: To round to a place, look at the digit just to its right. For thousands, that is the hundreds digit, which is 4.

beats.say: The hundreds digit is 4. That is less than 5, so Anil rounds down to 38,000.
Bina rounds to the nearest ten, so she looks at the ones digit. It is 2, less than 5, so she rounds down to 38,460.
Now the difference: 38,460 minus 38,000 is 460.
Careful: use Bina's rounded number, 38,460, not the number we started with. Otherwise you get 462.
So for each rounding, look one digit to the right. Less than 5, go down. 5 or more, go up.
Two words to know here. The successor of a number is the one just after it. The predecessor is the one just before it.

board.text: Successor of greatest 4-digit + predecessor of smallest

beats.say: The greatest 4-digit number is 9,999. Its successor is 1 more. What is 9,999 plus 1?

ask.ifNot: Adding 1 turns every 9 into a 0 and puts a new 1 in front. So we get 10,000, which has 5 digits.

beats.say: 9,999 plus 1 is 10,000. Every 9 rolls over to 0.
The smallest 4-digit number is 1,000. Its predecessor is 1 less, which is 999.
Now add the two: 10,000 plus 999 is 10,999.
Careful with the two words. Successor goes up one, predecessor goes down one. Mix them up and you add a different pair of numbers.
So: find each special number, take one step the right way, then add.
We are told the successor of a secret number is 20,000. We want the predecessor of that same secret number.

spec.note: 20,000 is the successor

beats.say: The successor is one more than the number. So where is the secret number?

ask.ifNot: 20,000 comes just after the secret number. So the secret number is one step back from 20,000.

beats.say: One step back from 20,000 is 19,999. That is our secret number.
Careful: we are not done! 19,999 is the number itself. The question asks for its predecessor, one more step back.
So from a successor back to the predecessor is always 2 steps. 20,000 minus 2 is 19,998.
Predecessor, number, successor: three neighbours in a row.
We want the greatest 4-digit number whose digits are all different and add up to 10.

board.text: 4 different digits that add up to 10. Greatest number?

beats.say: For a big number, the first digit should be as big as possible. So try 9 first. The other 3 digits must then add up to 1.
Three different digits that add up to 1. Can it be done?

ask.ifNot: 1, 0 and 0 does add up to 1, but the 0 is used twice. The digits must all be different, so 9 cannot go first.

beats.say: So 9 is out. Try 8: the rest must add up to 2. That needs 2, 0, 0 or 1, 1, 0. A digit repeats each time, so 8 is out too.
Now try 7. The rest must add up to 3, and 2, 1 and 0 do it. All different!
Put those digits after the 7, from greatest to smallest. That makes 7210.
Check: 7 plus 2 plus 1 plus 0 is 10, and no digit repeats.
The trap is 9100. Its digits add up to 10, but the 0 is used twice. Read every rule in the question.
In 46,285 the digit 6 is swapped for a 9. By how much does the number grow?

spec.note: Which seat is the 6 in?

beats.say: Count from the right: 5 ones, 8 tens, 2 hundreds. Where is the 6?

ask.ifNot: 5 is in the ones, 8 is in the tens, 2 is in the hundreds, and next comes the 6, in the thousands place.

beats.say: The 6 is in the thousands place, so it is worth 6,000.
A 9 in the same seat is worth 9,000.
Nothing else changed. So the number grows by 9,000 minus 6,000, which is 3,000.
Careful: 9 minus 6 is only 3. But these are 3 thousands, because of the seat the digit sits in.
Check with the whole numbers: 49,285 minus 46,285 is 3,000.
Riya writes every number from 1 to 100. We count how many times her pencil writes the digit 7.

board.text: Numbers 1 to 100: how many times is the digit 7 written?

beats.say: A 7 can be in the ones place or in the tens place. Count each place on its own. First the ones: 7, 17, 27, and so on, up to 97.
That is 10 numbers, so the 7 is written 10 times in the ones place.
Now the tens place. Which numbers have a 7 in the tens place?

ask.ifNot: A 7 in the tens place means the number is in the seventies. That is every number from 70 to 79.

beats.say: From 70 to 79 there are 10 numbers, so that is 10 more sevens.
Here is the trap: 77. It is in both lists! But that is right, because 77 really has two 7s, and both are written.
So the total is 10 plus 10, which is 20.
So when you count a digit, count one place at a time. A number like 77 is counted once in each place.
A number puzzle with 5 seats. Two clues are easy: 3 goes in the ten-thousands place and 0 goes in the hundreds place.
The ones digit is the greatest odd digit. The odd digits are 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9, so the ones digit is 9.
Now the tricky clue: the thousands digit is twice the tens digit. The pairs could be 2 and 1, 4 and 2, 6 and 3, or 8 and 4.
One of those pairs breaks the rule that all 5 digits are different. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Look at what is already in the number: 3, 0 and 9. The pair 6 and 3 would use the 3 a second time.

beats.say: So 6 and 3 is out, because 3 is already in the first seat.
We want the greatest number, so choose the biggest thousands digit that is left. That is 8, with 4 in the tens.
The number is 38049.
Check every clue: 8 is twice 4, the ones digit is 9, 0 is in the hundreds, and 3, 8, 0, 4, 9 are all different.
Careful with 38409. It uses the same digits, but the 0 has slipped out of the hundreds place.

board.text: 38409: 0 is not in the hundreds place

beats.say: We want the smallest 5-digit number that is odd and has no digit repeated. Build it one seat at a time, from the left.

board.text: Smallest 5-digit odd number, all digits different = ?

beats.say: The first seat cannot be 0, so it takes 1. The second seat can take 0, the smallest digit of all.
Next come the smallest digits not used yet: 2, and then 3.
Now the last seat. The number must be odd, and no digit may repeat. Which digit goes there?

ask.ifNot: 4 would make the number even. 1 and 3 are odd, but they are already used. So the smallest odd digit left is 5.

beats.say: Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. But 1 and 3 are taken, so we use 5.
The number is 10235.
Careful: 10234 is the smallest with different digits, but it is even. And 12345 forgets that 0 can sit in the second seat.
Which of these 4 numbers needs the most letters when it is written in Roman numerals? Let us write each one and count.

board.text: 99, 98, 88, 78: which needs the most Roman symbols?

beats.say: First, a question. Is the biggest number always the longest in Roman numerals?

choices: No, some big numbers are short
ask.ifNot: Think of 10. It is just X. But 8 is V I I I, which is much longer. Bigger does not mean longer.

beats.say: 99 is 90 and 9. That is X C and I X. Only 4 letters, thanks to the take away trick.
98 is 90 and 8. That is X C and V I I I, which makes 6 letters.
78 is 70 and 8. That is L X X and V I I I, which makes 7 letters.
88 is 80 and 8. That is L X X X and V I I I, which makes 8 letters. The longest of all!
So the answer is 88.
The lesson: 8s make a numeral long, because an 8 needs 4 letters. 9s and 4s keep it short.
Meena does not know the take away rule. She just adds up all four letters of X L I V. How much bigger is her total than the true value?

board.text: XLIV: Meena adds X, L, I and V. How much too big?

beats.say: First, Meena's way. X is 10, L is 50, I is 1 and V is 5. She adds them all and gets 66.
Now the true value. In X L, the smaller letter X is in front of L. What does that mean?

ask.ifNot: A smaller letter in front of a bigger one is taken away. So X L is 50 minus 10.

beats.say: X L is 50 minus 10, which is 40. And I V is 5 minus 1, which is 4.
So the true value is 40 plus 4, which is 44.
Now compare. Meena's 66 minus the true 44 is 22.
Careful: 66 and 44 are both among the choices, but neither is what the question asks. It asks how much greater.
A neat check: each letter in front was added when it should be taken away, so it counts double. Twice 10 plus twice 1 is 22.
Lots of numbers round to 600 when we round to the nearest hundred. We want to count all of them.

board.text: How many whole numbers round to 600 (nearest hundred)?

spec.note: Which numbers round to 600?

beats.say: Numbers below 600 can round up to it. What is the smallest number that rounds up to 600?

ask.ifNot: A 5 in the tens place is enough to round up, and 550 has a 5 there. Anything smaller rounds down to 500 instead.

beats.say: The smallest is 550, because a 5 in the tens place rounds up.
Numbers above 600 round down while the tens digit is 4 or less. So the greatest is 649. The next one, 650, rounds up to 700.

spec.note: From 550 to 649

beats.say: Now count from 550 to 649. Subtract first: 649 minus 550 is 99.
Careful, this is the trap! Subtracting counts the steps, not the numbers. We add 1 so that both ends are counted.
So 100 whole numbers round to 600.
That makes sense: 50 numbers from 550 to 599, and 50 more from 600 to 649.
A number rounds to 350 to the nearest ten, and to 300 to the nearest hundred. We want the greatest number that does both.
Take the first clue. The numbers that round to 350, to the nearest ten, run from 345 up to 354.
Now the second clue. To the nearest hundred, where does 350 itself go?

ask.ifNot: 350 has a 5 in the tens place, and 5 or more rounds up. So 350 goes up to 400.

beats.say: So 350, and anything above it, rounds to 400 and not 300. Only the numbers below 350 are left.
The numbers that fit both clues are 345, 346, 347, 348 and 349.
The greatest of these is 349.
Check: 349 to the nearest ten is 350. And 349 to the nearest hundred is 300. Both clues fit.
The trap is 354. It is the greatest number that rounds to 350, but it does not fit the second clue.
Sana and Ravi both start with 4,446. Sana rounds 3 times, one step at a time. Ravi rounds just once. Will they end at the same number?

board.text: 4,446: Sana rounds in 3 steps, Ravi rounds once

beats.say: Sana first rounds to the nearest ten. The ones digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so she goes up to 4,450.
Next she rounds 4,450 to the nearest hundred. The tens digit is 5. Which way does she go?

ask.ifNot: 5 or more rounds up. The tens digit is exactly 5, so 4,450 goes up to 4,500.

beats.say: Up to 4,500. Then she rounds that to the nearest thousand. The hundreds digit is now 5, so up again, to 5,000.
Now Ravi. He rounds 4,446 straight to the nearest thousand. The hundreds digit is 4, less than 5, so he goes down to 4,000.
The difference is 5,000 minus 4,000, which is 1,000.
Here is the surprise. Each little rounding pushed Sana's number up a bit, until it tipped over. Rounding in steps can change the answer.
So always round straight from the number you started with. Ravi's way is the proper one.
A printer numbers the pages from 1 to 120. Some page numbers have 1 digit, some have 2 and some have 3. So we count in three groups.

board.text: Pages 1 to 120: how many digits are printed?

beats.say: Pages 1 to 9 have 1 digit each. That is 9 pages, so 9 digits.
Pages 10 to 99 have 2 digits each. How many pages is that?

ask.ifNot: There are 99 pages up to page 99. Take away the first 9 pages, and 90 pages are left.

beats.say: 90 pages with 2 digits each is 180 digits.
Now pages 100 to 120. Careful, this is the trap. 120 minus 100 is 20, but there are 21 pages, because page 100 counts too.
21 pages with 3 digits each is 63 digits.
Add the three groups: 9 plus 180 plus 63 is 252.
So: split the pages into groups by how many digits they have, and count both ends of every group.
Take a 2-digit number, swap its digits, and add the two. The total must be 121. How many numbers can do that?

board.text: Number + its reverse = 121. How many 2-digit numbers?

beats.say: Try one to see what happens. 29 plus 92 is 121. It works! And look at its digits: 2 plus 9 is 11.
Here is why. In the ones column we add the two digits. In the tens column we add the same two digits again. So the total is 11 times the digit sum.
So what must the two digits add up to, for a total of 121?

ask.ifNot: The total is 11 times the digit sum. 11 times 11 is 121, so the digits must add up to 11.

beats.say: The digits must add up to 11. List the pairs: 2 and 9, 3 and 8, 4 and 7, 5 and 6.
Careful, this is the trap. Each pair makes two numbers, like 29 and 92. So 4 pairs give 8 numbers.
So 8 different numbers work.
And why not start with 1? Its partner would have to be 10, and 10 is not a digit.
A number like 2552 reads the same forwards and backwards. We want the greatest 4-digit one whose digits add up to 14.

board.text: Reads the same both ways, digits add up to 14. Greatest?

beats.say: Such a number has a matching outer pair and a matching inner pair.
The 4 digits add up to 14. Each digit is there twice, so one outer digit and one inner digit add up to half of 14, which is 7.
For the greatest number, which digit should be as big as possible?

ask.ifNot: The outer digit sits in the thousands place, the most powerful seat. So make the outer digit as big as you can.

beats.say: The outer digit can be as big as 7. That leaves 0 for the inner digit, and 0 is allowed in the middle.
So the number is 7007.
Check: 7 plus 0 plus 0 plus 7 is 14, and 7007 reads the same both ways.
Two traps here. 6116 fits the clues, but it is smaller. And 7700 adds up to 14, but backwards it is not the same.
In 8,35,264 we count the digits whose place value is more than 100 times their face value.

board.text: 8,35,264: digits with place value > 100 × face value?

beats.say: Place value is face value times the worth of the seat. So this is really about seats: which seats are worth more than 100?
The 2 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 200. That is exactly 100 times 2. Does it count?

choices: No, exactly 100 is not more than 100
ask.ifNot: The question says more than 100 times. The 2 is worth exactly 100 times its face value, and exactly is not more.

beats.say: This is the trap. Exactly 100 times is not more than 100 times. So the 2 is out, and so are the 6 in the tens and the 4 in the ones.
The seats worth more than 100 are the thousands, ten-thousands and lakhs. The digits sitting there are 5, 3 and 8.

spec.note: Seats worth more than 100

beats.say: That is 3 digits.
Check one of them: the 5 is worth 5,000, which is 1,000 times 5. Yes, that is more than 100 times.
So: turn the clue into seats, and read little words like more than very carefully.
Among the Roman numerals from 1 to 39, some are written with exactly 2 letters. We count them in an orderly way.

board.text: Roman numerals 1 to 39: how many use exactly 2 letters?

beats.say: Only 3 letters are used up to 39: I, V and X. Let us sort the 2-letter numerals by their first letter.
Starting with I: I I is 2, I V is 4 and I X is 9. That is 3 numerals.
Starting with V, there is V I, which is 6. Is V V a proper numeral as well?

ask.ifNot: Two fives make 10, and 10 already has its own letter, X. So V is never written twice.

beats.say: So V gives just one numeral, V I. And V X is not allowed either, because V is never used to take away.
Starting with X: X I is 11, X V is 15 and X X is 20. That is 3 more.
Careful: X L has 2 letters too. But X L is 40, and that is outside 1 to 39.
Add them up: 3 plus 1 plus 3 is 7.
So when you count, sort into groups, and check the edges of the range.
We add something to 49,950, and we want its ten-thousands digit to change. What is the smallest number that does it?

spec.note: The ten-thousands digit is 4

beats.say: The ten-thousands digit is 4 now. Counting up, which is the first number with a different ten-thousands digit?

ask.ifNot: As we count up from 49,950, the 4 in front stays until all the other seats are full. It first changes at 50,000.

beats.say: The 4 changes to a 5 the moment we reach 50,000.
So how far is 49,950 from 50,000? Subtract.
Just 50! The number was already very close.
Check: 49,950 plus 50 is 50,000. And adding anything less, like 49, stays below 50,000.
The trap is to think a big seat needs a big number, like 10,000. But the question asks for the smallest.

board.text: 10,000 works, but it is not the smallest

beats.say: Rahul writes a 6-digit number using only the digits 3, 0 and 8. Each must appear at least once. We want the greatest number.

board.text: 6 digits, only 3, 0 and 8, each used at least once

beats.say: At least once. Does that mean a digit can be used more than once?

choices: Yes, as many times as we like
ask.ifNot: At least once means once or more. And we need 6 digits from only 3 kinds, so some digit has to repeat.

beats.say: So digits may repeat. For the greatest number, we want the biggest digit, 8, in as many seats on the left as possible.
But 3 and 0 must each appear once. So they take 2 seats, and 8 fills the other 4.
Now the last two seats. The tens seat is worth more than the ones seat, so the bigger digit, 3, goes in the tens.
The greatest number is 888830.
Careful with 888803. It is very close, but the 3 and the 0 are the other way round, and that makes it smaller.
So: fill the big seats with the big digit, and give the small digits the smallest seats.
Lots of numbers in this story! We take it one step at a time. First, how many pencils does the school buy?

board.text: 15 boxes of 24.  12 teachers keep 8 each.  6 classes.

beats.say: 15 boxes with 24 in each is 15 times 24. 10 times 24 is 240, and 5 times 24 is 120. Together, 360 pencils.
Now the teachers. 12 teachers keep 8 pencils each. How many pencils is that?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 12 teachers keeps 8. So that is 12 lots of 8, not just 12 pencils.

beats.say: 12 times 8 is 96. So the teachers keep 96 pencils.
Take those away. 360 take away 96. Take away 100 to get 260, then give 4 back. 264 pencils are left.
These 264 pencils are shared equally among 6 classes. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: The classes share only what is left after the teachers take theirs. That is 264, so we need 264 divided by 6.

beats.say: Split 264 into 240 and 24. 240 divided by 6 is 40, and 24 divided by 6 is 4.
40 and 4 make 44. So each class gets 44 pencils.
The plan was: find the total, take away what the teachers keep, then share the rest. One step at a time.
Two brackets in this one. Brackets go first, so we deal with them one at a time.
Look inside the first bracket: 10 minus 2 times 3. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, times goes before minus. So 2 times 3 comes first.

beats.say: 2 times 3 is 6, and 10 take away 6 is 4. The first bracket is worth 4.
The second bracket is quick. 7 take away 4 is 3.
Write the sum again, with 4 and 3 in place of the brackets.
Now there is a divide, a plus and a times. Which one waits until the end?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times go before plus. So the plus waits until the end.

beats.say: 48 divided by 4 is 12. And 5 times 3 is 15.
Now the plus. 12 plus 15 is 27.
So: brackets first, with times before minus inside them. Then divide and times. Then plus.
Four sums, and we want the one with the smallest value. We cannot tell just by looking, so we work out all four.
First one. Bracket first: 30 take away 6 is 24. Then 24 divided by 3 is 8, and 8 plus 2 is 10.
Second one: 6 plus 18 divided by a bracket. The bracket, 3 times 2, is 6. Then which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide goes before plus. So 18 divided by 6 comes first.

beats.say: 18 divided by 6 is 3, and 6 plus 3 is 9.
Third one. Bracket first: 3 plus 5 is 8. Then times before minus: 4 times 8 is 32. And 40 take away 32 is 8.
Fourth one. Bracket first: 2 plus 3 is 5. Then 50 divided by 5 is 10, and 10 plus 1 is 11.
Our four values are 10, then 9, then 8, then 11. Which is the smallest?

ask.ifNot: Put them in order from small to big: 8, then 9, then 10, then 11. The smallest is 8.

beats.say: 8 is the smallest, and it came from the third sum.
The trap is the second sum. It comes to 9, which is close, but the third one is smaller still. Always work out every choice.
A train story with lots of numbers. We need two things: how many seats there are, and how many people are on the train now.

board.text: 12 coaches of 72 seats.  598 on, 135 off, 210 on.

beats.say: Seats first. 12 coaches with 72 seats each. 10 times 72 is 720, and 2 times 72 is 144. Together, 864 seats.
Now the passengers. The train starts with 598. Then 135 get off and 210 get on. Which sum shows that?

ask.ifNot: Getting off means fewer people, so take away 135. Getting on means more people, so add 210.

beats.say: People who get off are taken away. People who get on are added.
598 take away 135 is 463. Then 463 plus 210 is 673. So 673 passengers are on the train now.
864 seats and 673 passengers, each in one seat. How do we find the empty seats?

ask.ifNot: Every passenger fills one seat. So take the 673 passengers who are on the train now away from the 864 seats.

beats.say: 864 take away 673. Take away 600 to get 264. Then take away 73 more to get 191.
So 191 seats are empty.
The trap is using the 598 from the first station. People got off and on after that, so we must use the new number, 673.
A shopkeeper story. We need the money he paid, the money he got, and then the gap between the two.

board.text: Buys 9 dozen at 4 rupees each. 12 go bad. Sells at 6 rupees.

beats.say: How many bananas did he buy? 9 dozen is 9 times 12, which is 108.
He paid 4 rupees for each one. 100 times 4 is 400, and 8 times 4 is 32. So he paid 432 rupees.
Then 12 bananas go bad. How many can he sell?

ask.ifNot: The 12 bad bananas are thrown away. So take 12 from 108, which leaves 96 to sell.

beats.say: 108 take away 12 is 96. He sells 96 bananas.
Each one sells for 6 rupees. 90 times 6 is 540, and 6 times 6 is 36. So he gets 576 rupees.
He paid 432 and he got 576. How do we find how much more he got?

ask.ifNot: How much more means the gap. Take what he paid, 432, away from what he got, 576.

beats.say: 576 take away 432 is 144. So he gets 144 rupees more than he paid.
Watch the trap. He paid for all 108 bananas, even the bad ones. But he only sold 96. Keep those two numbers apart.
This looks like a lot of hard multiplying. But there is a clever shortcut hiding in it. Let us hunt for it.
Look at the first part: 25 times 37 times 4. Two of those numbers make a lovely round number. Which two?

ask.ifNot: Try 25 and 4. Four 25s make exactly one hundred, and multiplying by a hundred is the easiest job of all.

beats.say: 25 times 4 is 100. We may multiply in any order, so the first part is 100 times 37.
Now read it in words. It says: 100 lots of 37, take away 99 lots of 37.
If you have 100 lots of something and you take away 99 lots, how many lots are left?

ask.ifNot: 100 take away 99 is 1. So just 1 lot of 37 is left.

beats.say: 100 take away 99 is 1. So just one lot of 37 is left.
And one lot of 37 is 37. No long multiplying needed!
Careful with the trap. It is 99 lots that are taken away, not 100. So the answer is not 0. One 37 is left over.
The key idea: before you multiply big numbers, look for a friendly pair, and look for the same number on both sides of the minus.
500 laddoos go into boxes of 12. Some will be left over, and those are shared among 4 children.

board.text: 500 laddoos in boxes of 12. Left-overs to 4 children.

beats.say: How many full boxes? Let us build up in twelves. 12 times 40 is 480.
One more box makes 492. Another box would make 504, which is more than 500. So there are 41 full boxes.
41 boxes use up 492 laddoos. How many are left over?

ask.ifNot: Take the 492 that are packed away from the 500. That leaves 8.

beats.say: 500 take away 492 is 8. So 8 laddoos are left over.
8 shared equally among 4 children is 8 divided by 4, which is 2. Each child gets 2 laddoos.
Careful with the trap. The children do not share all 500 laddoos. And 8 is not the final answer either. Only the left-overs are shared.
So: find the full boxes, find what is left over, then share that.
Three kinds of bracket, one inside the other, like boxes inside boxes. We open the smallest box first.
Start in the round bracket: 18 plus 12 divided by 3. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, divide goes before plus. So 12 divided by 3 comes first.

beats.say: 12 divided by 3 is 4, and 18 plus 4 is 22. The round bracket is worth 22.
Next, the square bracket. 60 take away 22 is 38.
Careful here. We take the whole 38 away from 100. We do not take away 60 and then 22, one after the other.
Now the curly bracket. 100 take away 38 is 62.
Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: Look at the end of the sum. There is still a divide by 2 waiting outside the brackets.

beats.say: Half of 62 is 31.
So: round bracket, square bracket, curly bracket, and then whatever is waiting outside.
Asha earns money, spends some, and saves the rest. We want to know how many weeks it takes her to save 18,000 rupees.

board.text: Earns 500 a day, 6 days a week. Spends 1,800 a week.

beats.say: First, how much does she earn in a week? 6 days at 500 rupees a day. 6 times 5 is 30, so 6 times 500 is 3,000.
She spends 1,800 of that each week. How much does she save in a week?

ask.ifNot: Saving is what is left after spending. Take 1,800 away from 3,000, and 1,200 is left.

beats.say: 3,000 take away 1,800 is 1,200. So she saves 1,200 rupees every week.
Now, how many weeks to reach 18,000? Which number do we divide 18,000 by?

ask.ifNot: Only the money she saves builds up. So we count how many lots of 1,200 make 18,000.

beats.say: Count up in lots of 1,200. 10 weeks give 12,000. That leaves 6,000 still to save.
5 more weeks give that 6,000, because 5 times 1,200 is 6,000.
10 weeks and 5 weeks make 15 weeks. She needs 15 weeks.
The trap is choosing which number to divide by. It is the saving each week that counts, not the spending, and not the pay for one day.
A long sum with a bracket, some times, a divide, a minus and a plus. We take it in the proper order.
Bracket first. 9 take away 4 is 5.
Now look at the minus and the plus. They cut the sum into three chunks. We work out each chunk on its own.
First chunk: 7 times 8 is 56. Second chunk: 6 times 5 is 30.
Third chunk: 20 divided by 5 times 2. Careful, this is the trap. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times are equal partners, so we go left to right. The divide comes first here: 20 divided by 5.

beats.say: Left to right. 20 divided by 5 is 4, and 4 times 2 is 8.
Now put the three chunks back with their signs. 56 minus 30 plus 8.
Left to right again. 56 take away 30 is 26, and 26 plus 8 is 34.
So: brackets, then times and divide from left to right, then plus and minus from left to right.
A hall full of chairs, and then two things change: the number of rows, and the number of chairs in each row.

board.text: 28 rows of 35 chairs. 15 rows go. 6 more chairs a row.

beats.say: First the rows. 15 rows are taken away from 28. 28 take away 15 is 13 rows.
Now 6 more chairs are added to each row that is left. How many chairs are in one row now?

ask.ifNot: Each row had 35 chairs and gets 6 more. 35 plus 6 is 41.

beats.say: 35 plus 6 is 41. So each row now has 41 chairs.
13 rows with 41 chairs in each. Which sum gives all the chairs?

ask.ifNot: There are 13 rows left, and every one of them has 41 chairs. So we need 13 times 41.

beats.say: 13 times 41. 10 times 41 is 410, and 3 times 41 is 123.
410 plus 123 is 533. So there are 533 chairs in the hall now.
Careful with the trap. The 6 extra chairs go into every one of the 13 rows. It is not just 6 chairs for the whole hall.
So: find the new number of rows, find the new chairs in a row, then multiply.
A farmer packs 1,000 mangoes, first into crates and then into baskets. We need the number of baskets.

board.text: 1,000 mangoes. 25 crates of 2 dozen. Baskets of 50.

beats.say: Each crate holds 2 dozen mangoes. How many is that?

ask.ifNot: A dozen is 12. So 2 dozen is 2 times 12, which is 24.

beats.say: 2 dozen is 2 times 12, which is 24 mangoes in each crate.
Now 25 crates of 24. 20 times 24 is 480, and 5 times 24 is 120. Together, 600 mangoes go into crates.
Take those from the 1,000. 1,000 take away 600 leaves 400 mangoes.
These 400 go into baskets of 50. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: Only the mangoes that are left go into baskets. That is 400, so we need 400 divided by 50.

beats.say: How many fifties are in 400? 2 fifties make 100. So 400 needs 4 times as many, which is 8 fifties.
So he needs 8 baskets.
The plan: mangoes in one crate, mangoes in all the crates, mangoes left, and then the baskets.
We must put one pair of brackets into this sum so that it comes to 14.
First, what is it worth with no brackets? Times first: 4 times 5 is 20. Then 6 plus 20, take away 3, comes to 23.
23 is too big. We want 14. So the brackets must make something smaller. Which part can we make smaller?

ask.ifNot: A bracket round 4 times 5 changes nothing, because times goes first anyway. But a bracket round 5 minus 3 makes the 4 multiply a smaller number.

beats.say: Try it. Bracket first: 5 take away 3 is 2.
Then the times. 4 times 2 is 8.
Then the plus. 6 plus 8 is 14. That is our target!
So the brackets go round 5 minus 3.
A bracket round 6 plus 4 would give 10 times 5, take away 3, which is 47. Far too big.
The key idea: brackets only matter when they change which job goes first.
Riya may put in one pair of brackets, and she wants the smallest value she can get. Let us think like detectives.
With no brackets: 36 divided by 6 is 6, and 3 times 2 is 6. Then 6 plus 6 is 12.
To get less than 12, here is the big idea. What happens when you divide 36 by a bigger number?

ask.ifNot: Share 36 sweets among more children and each child gets fewer. Dividing by a bigger number gives a smaller answer.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number we can make straight after the divide sign. Try a bracket round 6 plus 3. That makes 9.
36 divided by 9 is 4, and 4 times 2 is 8. That is smaller than 12. But can we do better?
Make the bracket longer: 6 plus 3 times 2. Inside it, times goes first. 3 times 2 is 6, and 6 plus 6 is 12.
Now we are dividing by 12. And 36 divided by 12 is 3.
What about a bracket at the front, round 36 divided by 6 plus 3? That gives 9 times 2, which is 18. Bigger, not smaller.
So the smallest value is 3. The key idea: to make a division small, make the number you divide by as big as you can.
Two empty boxes, and each needs a sign. The finished sum must come to 9. We test the choices, and we always follow the order rules.
Try plus then divide first: 12 plus 6 divided by 2. Which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide goes before plus. So 6 divided by 2 comes first.

beats.say: 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 12 plus 3 is 15. Not 9. This is the trap: adding first, from the left, seems to give 9, but that breaks the rule.
Now try minus then divide: 12 minus 6 divided by 2. Again the divide goes first. 6 divided by 2 is 3.
12 take away 3 is 9. That is our number!
A quick check on the other two. 12 divided by 6, plus 2, is 4. And 12 minus 6, plus 2, is 8. Neither is 9.
So the signs are minus, then divide.
When you test signs, work the sum out by the rules, not just from left to right.
We have three signs, plus, minus and times, to use once each. We want the biggest answer we can make.
Times makes numbers grow the most. So where should the times go?

ask.ifNot: 8 and 2 are the biggest pair of neighbours, so multiplying them gives the biggest product. 2 times 3 is only 6, and 3 times 1 is only 3.

beats.say: 8 times 2 is 16. That is far more than 2 times 3, or 3 times 1.
Now the plus and the minus go in front of the 3 and the 1. Which way round is better?

ask.ifNot: Add the bigger number and take away the smaller one. So plus 3, minus 1.

beats.say: Add the bigger one, take away the smaller one. So the sum is 8 times 2, plus 3, minus 1.
Times first gives 16. Then 16 plus 3 is 19, and 19 take away 1 is 18.
Check a rival, with the times in the middle: 8 plus 2 times 3, minus 1. That is 8 plus 6, minus 1, which is only 13.
Careful with a trap. Reading that rival from left to right, as 10 times 3, gives a number that is too big. Times must go first.
So the greatest result is 18. Put the times where the numbers are biggest, add the bigger number, and take away the smaller.
The seller sells half of his mangoes and 2 more. Then he does the same again. In the end 8 are left. How many did he start with?

board.text: Sells half and 2 more, twice. 8 left. Start = ?

beats.say: We know the end of the story, not the beginning. So we work backwards, undoing one sale at a time.
Undo the afternoon. He sold half, and then 2 more, and 8 were left. Which do we undo first?

ask.ifNot: The 2 extra mangoes were sold last, so they go back first. After that we double.

beats.say: Put the 2 back: 8 plus 2 is 10. That 10 is the half he kept, so double it. 10 times 2 is 20.
So there were 20 mangoes after the morning. Now undo the morning in exactly the same way.
Put the 2 back: 20 plus 2 is 22. Then double: 22 times 2 is 44.
Let us check by going forwards. Half of 44 is 22. Selling 22 and 2 more leaves 20.
Half of 20 is 10. Selling 10 and 2 more leaves 8. It matches the story!
The trap is doubling before adding the 2 back. Undo things in the opposite order: the last thing done is the first thing undone. So the start was 44.
Asha and Bela have 60 stickers together. Asha gives Bela 8, and then they have the same number. How many did Asha start with?

board.text: Asha + Bela = 60.  Asha gives 8.  Then equal.

beats.say: Here is something useful. When Asha gives stickers to Bela, no sticker is lost. So the total is still 60.
At the end the two girls have the same number, and 60 altogether. How many does each have?

ask.ifNot: Two equal shares that make 60. Half of 60 is 30, so each girl has 30.

beats.say: 60 shared equally between 2 is 30. So at the end, each girl has 30.
Asha has 30 after giving 8 away. So before she gave them, did she have more than 30, or fewer?

ask.ifNot: She gave 8 away to get down to 30. So before that she had 8 more than 30.

beats.say: Put the 8 back. 30 plus 8 is 38. Asha had 38 stickers at first.
Check. Bela had 60 take away 38, which is 22. After getting 8, she has 30. And Asha, after giving 8, has 30 too. Equal!
So: find what each girl has at the end, then undo the giving. Asha started with 38.
500 oranges go into boxes of 24. The last box will not be full. How many more oranges would fill it?

board.text: 500 oranges, boxes of 24. Last box needs ? more

beats.say: First, the full boxes. 24 times 10 is 240. So 24 times 20 is 480.
One more box would need 504 oranges, and that is more than 500. So 20 boxes are full.
20 full boxes use 480 oranges. How many oranges are left over for the last box?

ask.ifNot: Take the 480 that are packed away from 500. That leaves 20 oranges.

beats.say: 500 take away 480 is 20. So the last box holds 20 oranges.
Is 20 our answer?

choices: No: find how many more make 24
ask.ifNot: Read the question again. It asks how many more oranges are needed to fill the box, and a full box holds 24.

beats.say: A full box holds 24, and this one has 20. 24 take away 20 is 4. He needs 4 more oranges.
Funny thing: there are 20 full boxes, and also 20 oranges left over. Do not mix them up. The question wants the gap up to 24.
So: find the left-overs, then find how many more make a full box.
Four times sums, and we want the greatest. Multiplying all four out would take ages. Let us look for a pattern instead.
Add the two numbers in each pair. 47 and 53. 49 and 51. 48 and 52. 50 and 50. What do you notice?

ask.ifNot: 47 and 53 make 100. 49 and 51 make 100. 48 and 52 make 100. And 50 and 50 make 100 too.

beats.say: Every pair adds up to 100. So the real question is: with the same total, which pair gives the biggest product?
Try it with small numbers that add up to 10. 5 times 5 is 25. 4 times 6 is 24. 3 times 7 is 21.
Which small pair gave the biggest product?

ask.ifNot: 5 times 5 gave 25, the biggest. The closer together the two numbers are, the bigger the product.

beats.say: The closer the two numbers, the bigger the product. And 50 and 50 are as close as can be.
So 50 times 50 is the greatest. 5 times 5 is 25, so 50 times 50 is 2500.
Check the nearest rival. 49 times 50 is 2450, and one more 49 makes 2499. That is just 1 less than 2500.
The trap is picking the pair with the biggest single number, 53. Its partner is small, so that product is the smallest. The winner is 50 times 50.
One empty box. Which sign makes the sum come to 12? We test, and we follow the order rules every time.
Try divide: 6 plus 12 divided by 3 times 2. Which part waits until the end?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times go before plus. So the 6 plus at the front waits until the end.

beats.say: 12 divided by 3 is 4, and 4 times 2 is 8. Then 6 plus 8 is 14. Not 12.
That was the trap. Going left to right from the very start seems to give 12, but the plus must wait its turn.
Now try minus: 6 plus 12 minus 3 times 2. Times goes first. 3 times 2 is 6.
Left to right now. 6 plus 12 is 18, and 18 take away 6 is 12. That is our number!
The other two signs make it far too big. Plus gives 24, and times gives 78.
So the sign in the box is minus.
When you test a sign, work the whole sum out by the rules: times and divide before plus and minus.
Four sums, each with brackets. In one of them the brackets are not really needed. Which one?

board.text: Where can the brackets go without changing the value?

beats.say: Remember what brackets do. They say: do me first. So brackets are not needed when that part would go first anyway.
Look at 12 minus, bracket, 4 times 2. If the brackets were not there, what would go first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before minus. So 4 times 2 goes first, even with no brackets.

beats.say: Times goes first anyway. With brackets or without, it is 12 take away 8, which is 4. The value does not change.
Test another. 12 minus, bracket, 4 plus 2, is 12 take away 6, which is 6. Without brackets we go left to right and get 10. It changed.
Next: bracket 12 minus 4, times 2. That is 8 times 2, which is 16. Without the brackets, times goes first and we get 4. It changed.
Last one. 12 divided by, bracket, 4 plus 2, is 2. Without the brackets, divide goes first and we get 5. It changed too.
So only the first one stays the same.
The key idea: brackets can go when they only wrap a times or a divide that would have gone first anyway.
Rohit buys 10 things, some pencils and some pens, and pays exactly 60 rupees. How many are pens?

board.text: Pencil 4 rupees, pen 9 rupees. 10 things cost 60.

beats.say: Here is a clever way in. Pretend all 10 are pencils, the cheaper ones. 10 times 4 is 40 rupees.
But he paid 60, not 40. That is 20 rupees more.
Where does the extra 20 come from? Each time we swap a pencil for a pen, how much does the bill go up?

ask.ifNot: A pen costs 9 and a pencil costs 4. Swapping one for the other adds the gap, 9 take away 4, which is 5 rupees.

beats.say: A pen costs 5 rupees more than a pencil. So every swap adds 5 rupees.
How many swaps make 20 rupees? 20 divided by 5 is 4. So 4 of the things are pens.
Check. 4 pens cost 36 rupees. The other 6 things are pencils, and they cost 24 rupees.
36 plus 24 is 60. Exactly what he paid.
Careful at the end: 6 is the number of pencils. The question asks for pens, and that is 4.
Kiran should have divided her number by 6. But she multiplied it by 6 instead, and got 432. What should her answer have been?
First we need Kiran's number. She multiplied it by 6 to get 432. How do we go back?

ask.ifNot: Divide undoes times. So to undo multiplying by 6, we divide 432 by 6.

beats.say: Divide undoes times. So we need 432 divided by 6. Split 432 into 420 and 12.
420 divided by 6 is 70, and 12 divided by 6 is 2. So her number was 72.
Is 72 the answer?

ask.ifNot: 72 is only the number she started with. She was supposed to divide it by 6, and that is still to do.

beats.say: Now do what she was meant to do: 72 divided by 6. 60 is 10 sixes, and the other 12 is 2 more sixes.
10 and 2 make 12. Kiran should have got 12.
So we divided by 6 twice: once to undo her slip, and once to do the real job.
In a magic square, every row, every column and both diagonals add up to the same total. One number in Row 3 is missing.

spec.note: Every row, column and diagonal has the same total

beats.say: To find the missing number we need the magic total. Which line can give it to us?

ask.ifNot: Row 3 has a gap, so we cannot add it yet. Row 1 is complete: 9, 2 and 7.

beats.say: Row 1 is 9 plus 2 plus 7, which is 18. So the magic total is 18.
Row 3 must make 18 too. It already has 5 and 3, which make 8. And 18 take away 8 is 10.
So the missing number is 10.
Check with the middle column, which also holds the gap. 2 plus 6 plus 10 is 18. It works there too.
In a magic square, find the total from any full line. Then every gap is just a subtraction.
A number riddle! It is a 2-digit number. Its tens digit is 4. And its two digits add up to 11.

board.text: Tens digit: 4.  The digits add up to 11.

spec.note: The two digits add up to 11

beats.say: The tens digit is 4, so the number is forty-something. We only need the ones digit.
The two digits add up to 11, and one of them is 4. What is the other?

ask.ifNot: 4 plus what makes 11? Take 4 away from 11, and 7 is left.

beats.say: 11 take away 4 is 7. So the ones digit is 7.
Tens digit 4, ones digit 7. The number is 47.
Careful with the order. 74 also has digits that add up to 11, but its tens digit is 7. Ours must have the 4 in the tens place.
Check: 4 plus 7 is 11. In digit riddles, write down the place of each digit before you do anything else.
Here P is a hidden digit. 4 P means a two-digit number: 4 tens and P ones. Careful, it does not mean 4 times P.

spec.note: 4P is a two-digit number. Which digit is P?

beats.say: The number 4 P, plus 25, makes 71. How do we find the number 4 P?

ask.ifNot: Something plus 25 gives 71. To undo the adding, take 25 away from 71.

beats.say: 71 take away 25 is 46. So the number 4 P is 46.
4 P is 46. So which digit is P?

ask.ifNot: P sits in the ones place. The ones digit of 46 is 6.

beats.say: P is the ones digit, so P is 6.
Check by putting it back. 46 plus 25 is 71. It works.
When a letter hides a digit, find the whole number first by working backwards. Then read off the digit in the right place.
A picture puzzle. A star plus a star makes 14. A star plus a moon makes 10. What is the moon worth?

spec.note: What is the moon worth?

beats.say: Which clue should we use first?

ask.ifNot: The first clue has only stars in it. So it can tell us what one star is worth.

beats.say: Two equal stars make 14. So one star is half of 14, which is 7.
Now use the second clue. A star plus a moon is 10, and we know the star is 7.
10 take away 7 is 3. So the moon is worth 3.
Careful: the star and the moon are not equal, so we must not halve the 10. We use the 7 we found.
Check both clues. 7 plus 7 is 14, and 7 plus 3 is 10. Start with the clue that has only one kind of picture.
Four children, three clues. Amit is taller than Bina. Bina is taller than Chetan. Divya is shorter than Chetan. Who is the tallest?
Let's line them up, with the tallest on the left. Clue 1 says Amit is taller than Bina. So Amit goes first.
Clue 2 says Bina is taller than Chetan. Where does Chetan go in our line?

ask.ifNot: Chetan is shorter than Bina. So he stands after her in the line.

beats.say: So far the line is Amit, Bina, Chetan.
Careful with clue 3. It says shorter, not taller. Divya is shorter than Chetan, so she goes at the end.
The tallest is at the front of the line. That is Amit.
For puzzles like this, build one line, a clue at a time. And watch closely for the words taller and shorter.
In this magic square every row adds up to 21. One row has 4, 11 and a missing number.

spec.note: Every row adds up to 21

beats.say: Start with the two numbers we know. 4 plus 11 is 15.
The row must reach 21, and we have 15 so far. What do we work out?

ask.ifNot: 21 is the total of the whole row. The missing number is the gap between 15 and 21.

beats.say: 21 take away 15 is 6. So the missing number is 6.
Here is the slip to watch for. The 21 is the total of the row. It is not another number to add on.
Check: 4 plus 11 plus 6 is 21. It works.
When you know the total and all the parts but one, add the parts you know and subtract from the total.
Two signs have gone missing: 8, something, 4, something, 2, equals 10. We must put the right signs back.
8 is already close to 10, so let's try plus first. 8 plus 4 is 12.
Now we have 12, and we need 10. What should we do with the 2?

ask.ifNot: 12 is 2 more than 10. So we must take the 2 away.

beats.say: 12 take away 2 is 10. So the signs are plus, then minus.
Let's make sure nothing else works. Minus then plus gives 6. Plus then plus gives 14. Times then minus gives 30. None of those is 10.
With missing signs, make a sensible first try, see how far off you are, and then fix it.
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like 353. One of these four numbers is a palindrome. Let's find it.

board.text: Palindrome: the same forwards and backwards

beats.say: The test is simple: write the number backwards and see if it changes. Take the first one. Its digits are 1, 2, 1, 2. Backwards that is 2, 1, 2, 1.
That is a different number, so it is not a palindrome. Now take the digits 1, 2, 2, 1. What do you get when you write them backwards?

ask.ifNot: Start from the last digit and go back: 1, then 2, then 2, then 1. The same as before.

beats.say: It is the same both ways. The first digit matches the last, and the two middle digits match each other.
The other two change as well. 1122 turns into 2211, and 2121 turns into 1212.
So the palindrome number is 1221.
A quick test for a palindrome: the first digit must match the last, the second must match the second from last, and so on.
A magic square with two letters hiding in it, P and Q. Every row, column and diagonal has the same total. We want P plus Q.

spec.note: Every row, column and diagonal has the same total. P + Q = ?

beats.say: First we need the magic total. Which row can give it to us?

ask.ifNot: Rows 1 and 2 each hide a letter. Row 3 is complete, so we can add it.

beats.say: 8 plus 18 plus 4 is 30. So every line adds up to 30.
Row 1 is 16, 2 and P. 16 plus 2 is 18, and 30 take away 18 is 12. So P is 12.
Row 2 is 6, Q and 14. 6 plus 14 is 20, and 30 take away 20 is 10. So Q is 10.
We have P and we have Q. What does the question want?

ask.ifNot: Read the last line of the question again. It asks for P plus Q.

beats.say: 12 plus 10 is 22. So P plus Q is 22. Don't stop at 30: that is the magic total.
Check Q with a diagonal: 16 plus 10 plus 4 is 30. Find the total from a full line, fill the gaps, then answer what was asked.
P is the same hidden digit both times. 3 P is a number in the thirties. P 8 is a number ending in 8. Together they make 82.

spec.note: 3P + P8 = 82: the top two rows add up to the bottom row

beats.say: Write it as a column sum and start with the ones column, just as we always do. In the ones column we add P and 8.
P plus 8 must end in 2, and P is a single digit. Which digit works?

ask.ifNot: 8 plus 4 makes a number that ends in 2. Taking 2 from 8 gives 6, but here the digits are added, not subtracted.

beats.say: 4 plus 8 is 12. That ends in 2, and 1 ten is carried over.
Now test the whole sum with P as 4. The two numbers are 34 and 48. And 34 plus 48 is 82. It works!
So P is 4.
Look at the tens as well. 3 tens and 4 tens and the 1 carried over make 8 tens. Everything fits.
In a letter sum, start with the ones column. It often gives the digit away. Then check the whole sum.
P and Q are digits. The numbers P Q and Q P add up to 77. And P is 1 more than Q. We want the number P Q.

board.text: PQ + QP = 77,  P is 1 more than Q

spec.note: PQ + QP = 77, and P is 1 more than Q

beats.say: Stack them as a column sum. In the ones column we add Q and P. In the tens column we add P and Q. The same two digits each time!
The total is 77. So what is P plus Q?

ask.ifNot: Each column adds P and Q, and each column of the answer shows a 7. So P plus Q is 7.

beats.say: So we need two digits that add up to 7, where one is 1 more than the other.
Which pair of digits is it?

ask.ifNot: 5 and 2 make 7, but they are 3 apart. 4 and 3 make 7 and are just 1 apart.

beats.say: P is the bigger one. So P is 4 and Q is 3, and the number P Q is 43. Careful: not 34.
Check: 43 plus 34 is 77. So the number is 43.
When two letters swap places in a sum, look at one column at a time. Each column tells you what the letters add up to.
I think of a number. I double it and then add 3. The answer is 17. What was my number?

spec.note: Double the number, then add 3. The answer is 17

beats.say: To get back to the start, we undo the steps. Which step do we undo first?

ask.ifNot: Adding 3 was done last. It is like shoes and socks: the last thing on is the first thing off.

beats.say: To undo adding 3, take 3 away. 17 take away 3 is 14. So the doubled number was 14.
Now undo the doubling. How?

ask.ifNot: Doubling means times 2. Halving is what undoes it.

beats.say: Half of 14 is 7. So the number was 7.
Check by going forwards. 7 doubled is 14, and 14 plus 3 is 17. It works.
To find a starting number, work backwards. Undo the last step first, using the opposite move each time.
Isha, Jay, Kiran and Lata each have one pet: a cat, a dog, a parrot and a rabbit. We have three clues, and we want Lata's pet.
Jay has the cat and Kiran has the rabbit. Which pets are left for Isha and Lata?

ask.ifNot: Cross off the cat and the rabbit. The two pets left are the dog and the parrot.

beats.say: Cross off the cat for Jay, and the rabbit for Kiran. The dog and the parrot are left.
Now the last clue. Isha does not have the dog. So Isha must have the parrot.
Only one pet is left, and only one child. So Lata has the dog.
Here is everyone with their pet. Every clue fits.
In a matching puzzle, use the sure clues first and cross things off. A clue that says not is useful once only two choices are left.
A number riddle with three clues. It is a 2-digit number less than 50. It is a multiple of 7. And its digits add up to 6.
Start with the clue that leaves the fewest numbers. The 2-digit multiples of 7 below 50 are 14, 21, 28, 35, 42 and 49.
Now the last clue. Which of these has digits that add up to 6?

ask.ifNot: 4 plus 2 is 6. Check the others: 3 plus 5 is 8, and 2 plus 1 is 3.

beats.say: Add the digits of each. 14 gives 5. 21 gives 3. 28 gives 10. 35 gives 8. 42 gives 6. 49 gives 13.

spec.note: Top: the multiple of 7. Below: its digits added

beats.say: Only 42 has digits that add up to 6. So the number is 42.
Careful: 24 also has digits that add up to 6. But 24 is not in the 7 times table. 42 is, because 7 times 6 is 42.
With several clues, list the numbers that fit one clue. Then let the other clues cross numbers off.
A pencil and an eraser cost 12 rupees together. Two pencils and an eraser cost 19 rupees. How much is the eraser?

spec.note: How much does the eraser cost?

beats.say: Compare the two purchases. What extra thing is in the second one?

ask.ifNot: Both have an eraser. The first has 1 pencil and the second has 2. So the only extra is 1 pencil.

beats.say: The only difference is 1 extra pencil, and the price went up from 12 to 19. So a pencil costs 7 rupees.
A pencil and an eraser cost 12 rupees together, and the pencil is 7. So what do we work out for the eraser?

ask.ifNot: The pencil and the eraser together make 12. Take the pencil's 7 away, and the eraser is left.

beats.say: 12 take away 7 is 5. So the eraser costs 5 rupees.
Check both purchases. 7 plus 5 is 12. And 7 plus 7 plus 5 is 19. Both fit.
When two purchases are nearly the same, look at what is different. The difference in price belongs to the extra thing.
R is a hidden digit in the three-digit number 2 R 5. When that number is multiplied by 3, the answer is 735.

spec.note: R stands for one digit

beats.say: Some number times 3 gives 735. How do we find that number?

ask.ifNot: Dividing undoes multiplying. So divide 735 by 3.

beats.say: Split 735 into 600 and 135. 600 divided by 3 is 200. 135 divided by 3 is 45. So the number is 245.
So 2 R 5 is 245. Which digit is R?

ask.ifNot: R is the middle digit, in the tens place. The tens digit of 245 is 4.

beats.say: R is in the tens place, and the tens digit of 245 is 4. So R is 4.
Check: 245 times 3. 200 threes are 600 and 45 threes are 135. Together that is 735. It works.
To find a hidden digit, find the whole number first by undoing the sum. Then pick out the digit in the right place.
Five children ran a race. We have three clues about the order they finished in. Who came second?
Take the first clue. Dev finished after Farah but before Esha. So the order is Farah, then Dev, then Esha.
Now the second clue. Hari finished between Dev and Esha. What is the order now?

ask.ifNot: Between Dev and Esha means after Dev and before Esha. So Hari slots in right there.

beats.say: Hari slots in between Dev and Esha: Farah, Dev, Hari, Esha.
Gita finished last. So the full order is Farah, Dev, Hari, Esha, Gita.
Now count from the front. Farah is 1st, and Dev is 2nd.
For an order puzzle, write the names in a line and slot each new clue into it. Then just read off the place you want.
On a dice, opposite faces always add up to 7. Neha can see the faces 1, 2 and 3. What do the three hidden faces add up to?

board.text: Opposite faces add up to 7.  She sees 1, 2, 3.

spec.note: Opposite faces always add up to 7

beats.say: Each hidden face is opposite a face she can see. Which face is opposite the 1?

ask.ifNot: The two opposite faces add up to 7. 1 plus what makes 7? It is 6.

beats.say: Opposite 1 is 6. Opposite 2 is 5. Opposite 3 is 4.
Now add the hidden faces. 6 plus 5 plus 4 is 15.
Here is another way to check. All six faces add up to 21. The faces she sees add up to 6. And 21 take away 6 is 15.
The slip here is to add the faces she can see. Read the question: we want the faces she cannot see.
So the hidden faces total 15. Use the rule to find each hidden face, then add them up.
A magic square with many blank boxes. Every row, column and diagonal has the same total. We must find Q.

spec.note: Every row, column and diagonal has the same total. Q = ?

beats.say: We need the magic total, so we need one complete line. Which line is complete?

ask.ifNot: Row 1 hides P, and Row 3 has a blank and Q. But the diagonal from 9 down to 13 has all three numbers.

beats.say: 9 plus 11 plus 13 is 33. So every line adds up to 33.
Row 1 is P, 16 and 9. 16 plus 9 is 25, and 33 take away 25 is 8. So P is 8.
Now we want Q. Which line holds Q and two numbers we know?

ask.ifNot: Row 3 and the last column each have a blank box as well as Q. The diagonal from P to Q is missing only Q.

beats.say: The diagonal is 8, 11 and Q. 8 plus 11 is 19, and 33 take away 19 is 14. So Q is 14.
Here is the whole square filled in. Every row, column and diagonal makes 33.

spec.note: Every line adds up to 33

beats.say: Don't forget the diagonals! When rows and columns have too many blanks, a diagonal may be the line that helps.
A two-digit number ending in 3 is multiplied by a two-digit number ending in 4. We don't know the other digits. Which choice can be the product?
We can't see the hidden digits. But we can still work out the last digit of the product. What is it?

ask.ifNot: The last digit of a product comes only from the last digits of the two numbers. 3 times 4 is 12, so the product ends in 2.

beats.say: 3 times 4 is 12, so the product must end in 2. One choice ends in 7, so we cross it out.
Next, the size. What is the smallest two-digit number that ends in 3?

ask.ifNot: A two-digit number cannot start with 0. So the smallest one ending in 3 is 13.

beats.say: The smallest numbers that fit are 13 and 14. Their product is 182. So 172 is too small.
The largest numbers that fit are 93 and 94. Their product is 8742. So 9872 is too big.
Only one choice is left: 1032. It ends in 2, and it is the right size.
And it really can be made. For example, 43 times 24 is exactly 1032.
Check the last digit, then the smallest and largest products. Those three tests can settle a puzzle without knowing the hidden digits.
P and Q are two different digits. P plus P plus P gives the two-digit number Q P. We want P plus Q.
P plus P plus P is 3 times P. And look at the answer, Q P: its last digit is P again. So 3 times P must end in P.

board.text: 3 × P ends in the digit P

beats.say: There are only nine digits to try. Here is each one, times 3.

spec.note: Top: P.   Below: 3 × P
Top: P.   Below: 3 × P

beats.say: Which answer is a two-digit number that ends in the digit we started with?

ask.ifNot: 15 ends in 5, and it came from 5. The others end in a digit that is different from the one we started with.

beats.say: 5 plus 5 plus 5 is 15. So P is 5. And Q P is 15, so Q is 1.
Careful with the last step. The question wants P plus Q. That is 5 plus 1, which is 6. Not 15, and not just 5.
When a letter puzzle has only a few possible digits, test them all in a tidy table. Then answer exactly what was asked.
A 3-digit riddle. The hundreds digit is double the ones digit. The tens digit is the hundreds digit plus the ones digit. All three add up to 12.
Everything depends on the ones digit. So let's try a ones digit and build the number from it.
Try ones digit 1. The hundreds digit is double that, 2. The tens digit is 2 plus 1, which is 3. But the digits add up to only 6. Too small.
Try ones digit 2. The hundreds digit is double that, 4. So what is the tens digit?

ask.ifNot: The tens digit is the hundreds digit plus the ones digit. That is 4 plus 2.

beats.say: The tens digit is 4 plus 2, which is 6. Now add all three digits: 4 plus 6 plus 2 is 12. Every clue fits!
Put the digits in their places: 4 hundreds, 6 tens, 2 ones. The number is 462.
Careful with the order. The same digits the other way round would not fit, because the hundreds digit must be double the ones digit.
When clues link the digits together, pick one digit to try. Build the rest from it, and test the total.
A farmer has hens and goats. Together they have 10 heads and 28 legs. How many goats are there?
10 heads means 10 animals. Here is a clever trick: pretend that all 10 are hens. Hens have 2 legs, so that would be 20 legs.
But there are 28 legs, which is 8 more than 20. Where do the 8 extra legs come from?

ask.ifNot: A goat has 4 legs and a hen has 2. So every goat brings 2 more legs than we counted.

beats.say: Each goat has 2 more legs than a hen. So 8 extra legs means 8 divided by 2 goats. That is 4 goats.
So the farmer has 4 goats.
Check. 4 goats and 6 hens make 10 animals. The goats have 16 legs and the hens have 12. And 16 plus 12 is 28.
Careful: 6 is the number of hens. The question asks for the goats, and that is 4.
Pretend they are all the same kind, see how many legs are missing, and share the extra legs out. That trick works every time.
The digits of a 2-digit number add up to 9. Swap the two digits, and the new number is 27 more. What is the first number?
After the swap the number gets bigger. So in the first number, which digit is the smaller one?

ask.ifNot: The swap moves the ones digit into the tens place. If the number grows, the ones digit was the bigger one.

beats.say: So we want digits that add up to 9, with the smaller digit in the tens place. That gives 18, 27, 36 and 45.
Swap the digits of each one and subtract. 81 minus 18 is 63. 72 minus 27 is 45. 63 minus 36 is 27. 54 minus 45 is 9.
Only one of them grows by exactly 27. It is 36, which turns into 63.
So the first number is 36.
Careful: 63 is the number after the swap. The question asks for the first number, the smaller one.
List the numbers that fit the first clue, then test each one against the second clue. A short list makes a hard puzzle easy.
A laddoo is hidden in one of three boxes. Each box has a label, but only one of the three labels is true. Where is the laddoo?

board.text: Box 1 says: it is in this box
Box 2 says: it is not in this box
Box 3 says: it is not in Box 1

beats.say: We can't tell which label to trust. So let's test each box in turn, and count how many labels would be true.
Suppose it is in Box 1. Then label 1 is true. Label 2 says it is not in Box 2, and that is true as well. Does Box 1 fit?

ask.ifNot: Only one label may be true. With the laddoo in Box 1, labels 1 and 2 are both true. That is one too many.

beats.say: Box 1 gives two true labels, so it is out. Now suppose it is in Box 3. Label 2 is true, and label 3 is true. Two again, so Box 3 is out.

board.text: in Box 1: labels 1 and 2 are true
in Box 3: labels 2 and 3 are true

beats.say: Now suppose it is in Box 2. Label 1 is not true. Label 2 says it is not in this box, so that is not true either. Label 3 is true.

board.text: in Box 2: only label 3 is true

beats.say: Exactly one true label! That is what the puzzle needs. So the laddoo is in Box 2.
Here are all three tests side by side. Only one row has exactly one true label.

spec.note: Only one label may be true

beats.say: When you can't trust the clues, don't guess. Test each possibility and see which one fits the rule.

board.text: 4 equal sides, no right angles. What is it called?

spec.note: All four sides are equal. No corner is a right angle

beats.say: A shape has four sides, all equal, but none of its angles is a right angle. What is it called?

ask.ifNot: A rectangle only needs its opposite sides equal. The two shapes with all four sides equal are the square and the rhombus.

beats.say: We have two clues. Clue one: all four sides are equal. Which shapes have four equal sides?
So it is either a square or a rhombus.
Clue two: none of its angles is a right angle. A square always has four right angles. So it can't be a square.
What is left is the rhombus. Think of a square that has been pushed over, like a diamond.
So: four equal sides and no right angles means a rhombus.
When a question gives two clues, use both. The first clue narrows it down, and the second one decides.

board.text: Parallelogram: one angle = 70°. Angle next to it = ?

beats.say: One angle of a parallelogram is 70 degrees. We want the angle right next to it.
In a parallelogram, two angles next to each other always add up to 180 degrees. If one is small, its neighbour is big.

ask.ifNot: The equal angle is the one opposite, across the shape. The neighbour is different: together the two must make 180.

beats.say: So how do we find the angle next to 70 degrees?
180 minus 70 is 110.
So the angle next to it is 110 degrees.
Careful: 70 degrees is the angle opposite, not the one next door. Opposite angles are equal. Neighbours make 180.
Check: 70 plus 110 makes 180. It works.

spec.note: Rhombus. Perimeter = 52 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of a rhombus is 52 centimetres. How long is each side?
What is special about a rhombus? All four of its sides are the same length, just like a square.

ask.ifNot: The 52 centimetres is shared equally among 4 sides. Sharing equally means dividing, and there are 4 sides.

beats.say: So 4 equal sides add up to 52. How do we find one side?
52 divided by 4. Half of 52 is 26, and half of 26 is 13.
So each side of the rhombus is 13 centimetres.
Check by walking round: 13, 13, 13 and 13 make 52. It fits.
Remember: a side is always shorter than the whole perimeter. For 4 equal sides, divide the perimeter by 4.

board.text: Square, side 25 cm. Lace all round, ₹3 per cm. Cost = ?

spec.note: Lace all around the edge: ₹3 for every centimetre

beats.say: A square handkerchief has sides of 25 centimetres. Lace goes all around its edge, and costs 3 rupees for every centimetre. What does the lace cost?

ask.ifNot: Lace is stitched along the edge, not spread over the cloth. The distance round the edge is the perimeter.

beats.say: First, how much lace? The lace goes all around the edge. So do we need the area or the perimeter?
A square has 4 equal sides. 4 times 25 is 100. So we need 100 centimetres of lace.
Each centimetre costs 3 rupees. So 100 centimetres cost 100 times 3, which is 300.
The lace costs 300 rupees.
The trap is to stop at one side. 25 times 3 is 75, but that only pays for one edge of the handkerchief.
So: all around means perimeter. Find the length first, then multiply by the price.

board.text: Wire: square of side 18 cm, then a rectangle

spec.note: The same wire makes a rectangle: length = 2 × breadth

beats.say: A wire is bent into a square of side 18 centimetres. Then the same wire makes a rectangle whose length is twice its breadth. What is the rectangle's area?
The wire's length is the square's perimeter. 4 times 18 is 72 centimetres.
Now the rectangle. Its length is twice its breadth. So one length is the same as 2 breadths.

ask.ifNot: Each length counts as 2 breadths. So round the rectangle we have 2, then 1, then 2, then 1. Add those up.

beats.say: Walk round the rectangle: length, breadth, length, breadth. Counting in breadths, how many is that altogether?
2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6. So 6 breadths use up the whole 72 centimetres of wire.
72 divided by 6 is 12. The breadth is 12 centimetres, and the length is twice that: 24.
Area is length times breadth: 24 times 12. 24 times 10 is 240, and 24 times 2 is 48.
240 plus 48 makes 288. The area of the rectangle is 288 square centimetres.
Notice the trap. The square's area is 18 times 18, a different number. Same wire means same perimeter, not same area.
Check the wire: 24 plus 12 is 36, and double 36 is 72. It fits, so 288 it is.

board.text: Garden 20 m by 14 m. Path 2 m wide all round.

spec.note: Garden inside, path all around. Area of the path = ?

beats.say: A garden is 20 metres long and 14 metres wide. A path 2 metres wide runs all around it, on the outside. What is the area of the path?
The path is like a frame round the garden. Here's a neat trick: find the big rectangle with the path, then take away the garden.

ask.ifNot: The path is at both ends of the garden. So the length grows by 2 metres at one end and 2 metres at the other.

beats.say: The path is 2 metres wide at the left end and at the right end. So how long is the big rectangle?

spec.note: 2 m on each side: add 4 m to the length and to the width

beats.say: That's the trap: the path is on both sides, so each measurement grows by 2 and 2. The length is 24 metres and the width is 18 metres.
Big rectangle: 24 times 18. 24 times 10 is 240, and 24 times 8 is 192. Together that is 432.
The garden alone is 20 times 14, which is 280.
Take the garden away from the big rectangle. 432 minus 280 is 152.
So the area of the path is 152 square metres.
For a path all round: add the path's width twice to each side, find the big area, and subtract the inside.

board.text: Floor 6 m by 4 m. Square tiles of side 50 cm.

spec.note: Square tiles of side 50 cm cover the floor

beats.say: A floor is 6 metres long and 4 metres wide. It is covered with square tiles of side 50 centimetres. How many tiles are needed?

ask.ifNot: 1 metre is 100 centimetres. 50 and 50 make 100, so two tiles fit along each metre.

beats.say: Watch the units! The floor is in metres but the tile is in centimetres. How many tiles of 50 centimetres fit along 1 metre?
Two tiles for every metre. Along the 6 metre side we fit 6 times 2, which is 12 tiles.
Along the 4 metre side we fit 4 times 2, which is 8 tiles. So the floor has 8 rows of 12 tiles.
8 rows of 12. 12 times 8 is 96.
The floor needs 96 tiles.
The trap is 6 times 4, which is 24. That counts big squares of 1 metre, and each of those holds 4 tiles. 24 times 4 is 96 again.
So: put everything in the same unit, count the tiles each way, then multiply.

board.text: Square of side 12 cm, cut into 2 equal rectangles.

spec.note: One straight cut makes two equal rectangles

beats.say: A square sheet of paper has sides of 12 centimetres. One straight cut makes two equal rectangles. What is the perimeter of each rectangle?

ask.ifNot: The cut goes through the middle of a 12 centimetre side. So that side is shared into two equal halves.

beats.say: The cut goes through the middle. One side of each piece is still 12 centimetres. What is the other side?
Half of 12 is 6. So each piece is 12 centimetres long and 6 centimetres wide.
Now walk round one piece: 12, 6, 12, 6. That adds up to 36.
The perimeter of each rectangle is 36 centimetres.
Here's a surprise. The square's perimeter is 4 times 12, which is 48, and half of that is 24. But the answer isn't 24!
Why not? The cut makes a new edge of 12 centimetres on each piece. 24 plus that new 12 gives 36.
When you cut a shape, new edges appear. So find the sides of the new piece and add them up.

board.text: How many ALWAYS have 4 right angles?

beats.say: Think about four shapes: square, rectangle, rhombus and parallelogram. How many of them always have four right angles?
The important word is always. Let's test the shapes one at a time. Square first: four right angles, every time. Yes.
Rectangle: four right angles is what makes it a rectangle. Yes, always.

ask.ifNot: Picture the diamond on a playing card. Its four sides are equal, but its corners are not square corners.

beats.say: Now the rhombus. It has four equal sides. But does it always have right angles?
A rhombus can lean over, like a diamond. So, not always.
A parallelogram can lean over too. Not always.
Count the yeses: the square and the rectangle. That makes 2.
When you see the word always, hunt for a shape that breaks the rule. One leaning rhombus is enough to say no.

board.text: Length + 5 cm, width − 5 cm. The area?

spec.note: Length 5 cm longer, width 5 cm shorter. Area?

beats.say: A rectangle is 20 centimetres long and 15 centimetres wide. The length is made 5 centimetres longer, and the width 5 centimetres shorter. What happens to the area?
Area at the start: 20 times 15, which is 300.
Now change the sides. The length grows to 20 plus 5, which is 25. The width shrinks to 15 minus 5, which is 10.
We added 5 to one side and took 5 from the other. Do you think the area stays the same? Have a guess.
Let's find out. The new area is 25 times 10, which is 250.

ask.ifNot: Compare 300 at the start with 250 now. The new number is the smaller one.

beats.say: It changed! 300 has become 250. So what happened to the area?
300 minus 250 is 50. The area decreases by 50 square centimetres.
Here's the trap. Plus 5 and minus 5 keeps the perimeter the same, but not the area. For area, work out both and compare.

board.text: Carpet ₹150 per sq m. Strip ₹40 per m. Total = ?

spec.note: Carpet ₹150 per sq m. Wall strip ₹40 per m

beats.say: A hall is 12 metres long and 9 metres wide. Carpet costs 150 rupees for each square metre. A wooden strip along the walls costs 40 rupees for each metre. What is the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Carpet covers the space inside the room, and space inside is area. The strip along the walls is the one that uses perimeter.

beats.say: Two things to buy, and each uses a different measure. The carpet covers the whole floor. Which measure is that?
Carpet uses area: 12 times 9 is 108 square metres.
Each square metre costs 150 rupees. 100 times 150 is 15,000, and 8 times 150 is 1,200. Together that is 16,200 rupees.
The strip runs along all four walls. That is the perimeter. 12 plus 9 is 21, and double is 42 metres.
Each metre of strip costs 40 rupees. 42 times 4 is 168, so 42 times 40 is 1,680 rupees.
Add the two costs. 16,200 plus 1,680 makes 17,880.
So the total cost is 17,880 rupees.
The trap is using one measure for both. Covering a floor uses area. Going along the edge uses perimeter.

board.text: Field 30 m by 20 m. Posts every 5 m, all round.

spec.note: A post every 5 m, with one at each corner

beats.say: A field is 30 metres long and 20 metres wide. Fence posts go all around it, 5 metres apart, with one at each corner. How many posts are needed?
Posts go all the way round, so first we need the distance round. 30 plus 20 is 50, and double is 100 metres.
The posts are 5 metres apart. 100 divided by 5 is 20. So there are 20 gaps between posts.

choices: Yes, so add one more post
No, it is a closed loop
ask.ifNot: The fence goes round the field and comes back to where it began. So the last gap ends at the very first post.

beats.say: Now the tricky bit. In a straight line of posts you need one extra post at the end. But is this fence a straight line?
Round a loop, the last gap ends at the first post. So no extra post is needed. Posts and gaps are equal in number.
The field needs 20 posts.
Think of a tiny square with a post at each corner. 4 gaps, 4 posts. It is the same idea here.
So: find the distance round, divide by the gap, and for a closed loop that is your number of posts.

board.text: Wire 40 cm, bent into a rectangle. Length > breadth.

beats.say: A wire 40 centimetres long is bent into a rectangle with whole number sides, and the length is greater than the breadth. Find the largest area minus the smallest area.
The wire is the perimeter, 40 centimetres. So length plus breadth is half of that: 20.
Lots of pairs add up to 20. 19 and 1. 18 and 2. 17 and 3. All the way to 11 and 9.
