beats.say: Which number, times itself, makes 225? A clue: 10 times 10 is 100 and 20 times 20 is 400.

ask.ifNot: 225 is between 100 and 400, so the number is between 10 and 20. And 225 ends in 5, so the number ends in 5. That is 15.

beats.say: 15 times 15 is 225. So the number is 15.
One more than 15 is 16.
16 times 16: 16 times 10 is 160, and 16 times 6 is 96. Together, 256.
Careful: add 1 to the number, not to its square. 225 plus 1 is 226, and that is not a square at all.
So: go back to the number, change it, and then square again.
We count every perfect square from 1 to 100, with both ends included.

board.text: How many perfect squares from 1 to 100?

beats.say: The first one is 1 times 1, which is 1. Yes, 1 is a perfect square!
And the last one? Which number, times itself, makes exactly 100?

ask.ifNot: 10 times 10 is 100. So 100 is itself a perfect square, the square of 10.

beats.say: 10 times 10 is 100. So the squares run from the square of 1 up to the square of 10.
Here they all are.
Each number from 1 to 10 gives one square. So there are 10 of them.
Careful: both ends count here, 1 and 100. Miss one and you get 9. And 11 times 11 is 121, which is too big.
51 squared, take away 49 squared. Big numbers, but there is a neat way in.
Start with 51 times 50, which is 2550.
51 times 51 is one more 51 than that. 2550 plus 51 is 2601.
Now 49 times 49. 49 times 50 is 2450. Is 49 times 49 more or less than that?

ask.ifNot: 49 times 49 has one 49 fewer than 49 times 50. So we take 49 away.

beats.say: Now subtract the squares. 2601 minus 2401 is 200.
The trap: 51 minus 49 is 2, and 2 squared is 4. But we must square first, and only then subtract.
A shortcut to enjoy: add the two numbers to get 100, and multiply by their difference, 2. That gives 200 as well.
We divide 48 by something, and the result must be a perfect square. We want the smallest number that works.
Smallest means we test small numbers in order. Dividing by 1 leaves 48, which is not a square.
Divide by 2 and we get 24. Is 24 a square? 4 times 4 is 16 and 5 times 5 is 25. So no.
Now divide by 3. What is 48 divided by 3?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 16 is 48. So 48 divided by 3 is 16.

beats.say: 48 divided by 3 is 16. And 16 is 4 times 4. A perfect square!
So the smallest number to divide by is 3.
Careful: dividing by 12 gives 4, which is a square too. But 12 is not the smallest. That is why we test in order.
We subtract as little as we can from 1000, and we must land on a perfect square.
We need the biggest perfect square below 1000. 30 times 30 is 900. So try the numbers just above 30.
31 times 31: 31 times 30 is 930, and one more 31 makes 961.
32 times 32 is 1024. Can we use that one?

ask.ifNot: We are subtracting from 1000, so the square must be less than 1000. 1024 is above it.

beats.say: 1024 is above 1000. This is the trap: it is nearer, but we cannot reach it by taking away. So our square is 961.
1000 minus 961 is 39.
Check: 1000 minus 39 is 961, which is 31 times 31.
Careful: 31 is the number we squared, not the number to subtract.
We count the whole numbers that lie between 15 squared and 16 squared.

board.text: How many whole numbers between 15² and 16²?

beats.say: First work out the two squares. 15 times 15 is 225, and 16 times 16 is 256.
The numbers between them start at 226 and end at 255.
256 minus 225 is 31. Is that the number of whole numbers in between?

ask.ifNot: The gap of 31 counts every step from 225 up to 256, and the last step lands on 256 itself. So there is one fewer in between.

beats.say: This is the trap. There are 31 steps, but the last step lands on 256, which is an end. So 30 numbers are in between.
Check another way: from 226 to 255 is 255 minus 226, plus 1.
A pattern: between 15 squared and 16 squared there are 2 times 15 numbers. It works for any two neighbours.
The farmer has enough trees for one square, with 5 left over. For the next bigger square he is 20 short. How many trees has he?

board.text: A square with 5 left over; 20 more for the next square

beats.say: Picture his trees on a number line. He is 5 past one perfect square, and 20 short of the next one.
So how far apart are those two squares?

ask.ifNot: From the smaller square up to his trees is 5. From his trees up to the bigger square is 20. Together that is 5 plus 20.

beats.say: 5 plus 20 is 25. We need two neighbouring squares that are 25 apart.
A tip: neighbouring squares differ by the sum of the two numbers. 12 plus 13 is 25, so try 12 and 13.
12 times 12 is 144, and 13 times 13 is 169. And yes, 169 minus 144 is 25!
So his square holds 144 trees, with 5 left over. 144 plus 5 is 149.
Check: 149 plus 20 is 169, the next square. And careful: 144 forgets the 5 left over.
Asha has two square sheets of stamps: 9 rows of 9, and 12 rows of 12. She makes one big square from all of them.

board.text: 9 rows of 9 and 12 rows of 12, made into one square

beats.say: Count the stamps on each sheet. 9 times 9 is 81. And 12 times 12 is 144.
Altogether, 81 plus 144 is 225 stamps.
The big square has 225 stamps. How do we find the number in each row?

ask.ifNot: In a square, the rows and columns are equal. So we need the number that, times itself, makes 225.

beats.say: Try 15. 15 times 10 is 150, and 15 times 5 is 75. Together, 225.
So the big square has 15 stamps in each row.
The trap: 9 plus 12 is 21, but sides cannot simply be added. 21 times 21 is 441, far more stamps than she has.
A riddle with two clues. I am a two-digit perfect square, and my digits add up to 13.

board.text: A two-digit perfect square. Its digits add up to 13.

beats.say: Start with the stronger clue: a two-digit perfect square. There are only 6 of those.
Now test the second clue on each. 1 plus 6 is 7. 2 plus 5 is 7. 3 plus 6 is 9. None of those is 13.
What do the digits of 49 add up to?

ask.ifNot: The digits of 49 are 4 and 9. And 4 plus 9 is 13.

beats.say: 4 plus 9 is 13. That fits!
The last two: 6 plus 4 is 10, and 8 plus 1 is 9. So only 49 works.
Careful: 67 and 94 also have digits that add up to 13. But they are not perfect squares. Both clues must fit.
We want the smallest perfect square that can be divided exactly by 6, and also by 8.

board.text: Smallest perfect square that 6 and 8 both divide

beats.say: It can be divided by 8, so it must be even. So we only test the even squares, in order.
4 and 16 cannot be divided by 6. 36 can, but 36 cannot be divided exactly by 8.
64 is 8 times 8, so 8 divides it. Does 6 divide 64 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 6 times 10 is 60 and 6 times 11 is 66. 64 falls between them, so 6 does not divide it exactly.

beats.say: 64 is out. And 100 is out too, because 6 times 16 is 96 and 6 times 17 is 102.
Now 144. 144 divided by 6 is 24, and 144 divided by 8 is 18. Both are exact!
So the smallest such perfect square is 144.
The trap is 24 or 48. Both 6 and 8 divide them, but they are not perfect squares. Every word of the question counts.
Most numbers have an even number of factors. We count the numbers from 1 to 50 that have an odd number of factors.

board.text: 1 to 50: how many numbers have an odd number of factors?

beats.say: Factors come in pairs. For 12: 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4. That is 3 pairs, so 6 factors. An even count.
Now look at 16: 1 and 16, 2 and 8, and then 4 and 4.
4 and 4 is a pair made of the same number. How many times do we count the factor 4?

ask.ifNot: 4 is just one factor of 16. We do not list it twice. So this pair adds only 1 to the count.

beats.say: So 16 has 5 factors: 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. An odd count! That happens when a factor pairs with itself.
This is the key idea. A number has an odd number of factors only when it is a perfect square.
So we just count the perfect squares up to 50.
There are 7. The next square, 64, is past 50.
Careful: this is not about odd numbers, and not about prime numbers. It is about squares.
A pattern is given, and we use it to add all the odd numbers from 1 to 39. No long adding needed!
Look at the answers: 4, 9, 16. Those are 2 times 2, 3 times 3 and 4 times 4. All squares!
1 plus 3 plus 5 has 3 numbers, and its sum is 3 times 3. So what gets squared?

ask.ifNot: With 3 odd numbers the sum is 3 times 3. With 4 odd numbers it is 4 times 4. So we square how many numbers there are.

beats.say: The sum is the count of odd numbers, times itself. So we need to know how many odd numbers there are from 1 to 39.

spec.note: 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 builds a 4 by 4 square

beats.say: From 1 to 40 there are 40 numbers, and half of them are odd. Half of 40 is 20.
So there are 20 odd numbers, and the sum is 20 times 20, which is 400.
The trap is to square the last number, 39. The pattern squares the count, not the last number.
Check with the pattern: 1, 3, 5, 7 ends in 7, and half of 7 plus 1 is 4. The sum was 4 times 4. It fits.
Two numbers come one after the other, and their squares differ by 37. We want the larger number.

board.text: Two neighbours. Their squares differ by 37. Larger = ?

beats.say: Look for a pattern with small neighbours first. 4 squared is 16 and 5 squared is 25. The difference is 9.
The squares of 4 and 5 differ by 9. How is 9 connected to 4 and 5?

ask.ifNot: 4 plus 5 is 9. The difference of two neighbouring squares is the sum of the two numbers.

beats.say: 4 plus 5 is 9. Try another pair, 5 and 6. 36 minus 25 is 11, and 5 plus 6 is 11. It works again!
So our two neighbours add up to 37. Which neighbours add up to 37? 18 and 19.
Check with the squares. 19 times 19 is 361 and 18 times 18 is 324. They differ by 37.
So the larger number is 19.
Careful: 18 is the smaller one. And 37 is the gap between the squares, not one of the numbers.
144 children stand in a square. Only the children on the outside edge hold a flag. How many is that?

board.text: 144 children in a square. How many on the outside edge?

beats.say: First, the size of the square. 12 times 12 is 144, so each side has 12 children.

spec.note: 12 rows of 12

beats.say: There are 4 sides with 12 children on each. Is the answer 4 times 12, which is 48?

choices: No, the corners get counted twice
ask.ifNot: A child in a corner stands on two sides at once. So 4 times 12 counts each corner child twice.

beats.say: This is the trap. Each corner child belongs to two sides, so 48 counts 4 children twice.
Take away those 4 extra counts. 48 minus 4 is 44.
Check another way. The top and bottom rows have 12 each. The two sides have 10 more each, without the corners.
Or think of the children inside: they make a 10 by 10 square of 100. And 144 minus 100 is 44.
A square floor of 225 tiles. The tiles on both diagonals are red. How many red tiles?

board.text: 225 tiles in a square. Both diagonals are red. How many?

beats.say: First the size. 15 times 15 is 225, so the floor is 15 tiles by 15 tiles.
A diagonal goes from corner to corner, and takes one tile from every row. So each diagonal has 15 tiles.

spec.note: A small floor, 5 by 5

beats.say: Two diagonals of 15 tiles. Is the answer 15 plus 15, which is 30?

choices: No, they share the middle tile
ask.ifNot: 15 is odd, so there is one tile exactly in the middle. Both diagonals pass through it, and 30 counts it twice.

beats.say: Here is the trap. Because 15 is odd, the two diagonals cross on the middle tile. We counted that tile twice.
So take 1 away. 30 minus 1 is 29.
Look at the small floor, 5 by 5. It has 5 plus 5 minus 1 red tiles, which is 9. Count them and see!
Some numbers are the sum of two perfect squares. For example, 13 is 4 plus 9. One of these 4 numbers is not.

board.text: Which is NOT a sum of two perfect squares?

beats.say: The squares small enough to use are 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25.
Test 20. Take away 4, and 16 is left. Both are squares, so 20 can be made.
Test 34. Take away 25. What is left, and is it a square?

choices: 9, but it is not a square
ask.ifNot: 34 minus 25 is 9, and 9 is 3 times 3. So 34 is 25 plus 9, which is two squares.

beats.say: 34 is 9 plus 25. And 29 is 4 plus 25. Both can be made.
Now 21. Take away each square in turn: 20, 17, 12 and 5 are left. None of those is a square.
So 21 cannot be made.
The method: take away one square, and see whether a square is left. Try every square, so that nothing is missed.
Soldiers stand in a square. Then 3 full rows and 3 full columns march away, 69 soldiers in all, and a smaller square is left.

board.text: Square of soldiers. 3 rows and 3 columns leave: 69 go.

beats.say: When 3 rows and 3 columns leave, the square that remains has sides that are 3 shorter.
Is 69 simply 3 rows plus 3 columns of soldiers?

choices: No, some soldiers are in both
ask.ifNot: A soldier in the corner is in a row that leaves and also in a column that leaves. He must not be counted twice.

beats.say: That is the trap, so we go a safer way. The soldiers who left are the big square minus the small square.
Test sides of 12 and 9. 144 minus 81 is 63. Not enough.
Test sides of 13 and 10. 169 minus 100 is 69. That matches!
So at first there were 13 rows of 13, which is 169 soldiers.
Careful: 69 divided by 3 is 23, but a 23 by 23 square would lose far more than 69 soldiers.
In each pair the two numbers add up to 60. Which pair has the greatest product? We can find out without doing all four.
Learn from small numbers first. Take pairs that add up to 10.
5 times 5 is 25, 4 times 6 is 24 and 3 times 7 is 21. What happens as the two numbers move apart?

ask.ifNot: 25, then 24, then 21. The further apart the two numbers are, the smaller the product.

beats.say: The equal pair wins. The further apart the numbers move, the smaller the product gets.
The same happens here. The equal pair is 30 times 30, which is 900.
29 times 31 is 899, just 1 less. And 28 times 32 is 896.
So the greatest product is 30 times 30.
Careful: 33 is the biggest number here, but its partner 27 is the smallest. For the same sum, the square always wins.
Look at the pattern in the question. We use it to find 11111 times 11111 without multiplying.
121. 12321. 1234321. The digits climb up, and then come back down.
11 has two 1s, and its answer climbs to 2. 111 has three 1s, and its answer climbs to 3. How high will 11111 climb?

ask.ifNot: Count the 1s in 11111. There are 5 of them, so the answer climbs to 5.

beats.say: 11111 has five 1s. So the answer climbs to 5 and comes back down.
Now add its digits. Going up: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 make 15.
Coming down: 4, 3, 2 and 1 make 10.
15 plus 10 is 25.
The trap is to stop at 15. The digits come back down too. And look: 25 is 5 times 5, another square!
Kabir's age is a perfect square now. In 9 years it will be a perfect square again. How old is he?

board.text: Age now: a perfect square. In 9 years: a square again.

beats.say: List some perfect squares that could be ages.
Add 9 to each, and see if we land on another square. 1 becomes 10. 4 becomes 13. 9 becomes 18. No luck yet.
Now try 16. What is 16 plus 9, and is it a square?

choices: 25, but it is not a square
ask.ifNot: 16 plus 9 is 25. And 25 is 5 times 5, so it is a perfect square.

beats.say: 16 plus 9 is 25, which is 5 times 5. It works!
Could a bigger age work too? 25 plus 9 is 34. 36 plus 9 is 45. No. After 16, the squares are more than 9 apart.
So Kabir is 16 this year.
Careful: 25 is the age he will reach, not his age now.
We multiply 12 by something to get a perfect square. But the square must be greater than 100. We want the smallest multiplier.
First, what turns 12 into any perfect square? 12 is 2 times 2 times 3. The 3 has no partner.
Multiply by 3, and we get 36, a perfect square. But look at the question again.
36 is a perfect square. Does it answer the question?

choices: No, it is not greater than 100
ask.ifNot: The question wants a perfect square greater than 100. 36 is far below 100.

beats.say: This is the trap. 36 is too small. So we look at bigger multipliers, for a square above 100.
12 times 9 is 108. That is above 100, but 108 is between 100 and 121, so it is not a square.
12 times 12 is 144. A perfect square, and greater than 100!
And nothing smaller works. The only square between 100 and 144 is 121, and 12 does not divide 121.
Anu squares an odd number and subtracts 1. Some number always divides her answer. We want the greatest such number.
Try the first few odd numbers. 3 squared is 9, and 9 minus 1 is 8.
5 squared is 25, minus 1 is 24. 7 squared is 49, minus 1 is 48. 9 squared is 81, minus 1 is 80.
The very first answer is 8. Can a number bigger than 8 divide 8 exactly?

ask.ifNot: A number cannot be divided exactly by something bigger than itself. So nothing above 8 can divide every answer.

beats.say: This is the key idea. The first answer is 8, so our number cannot be more than 8. That rules out 16 and 24.
Does 8 divide them all? 24 is 3 times 8. 48 is 6 times 8. 80 is 10 times 8. Yes!
So the greatest number that always divides her answer is 8.
Careful: 4 divides them all too, but it is not the greatest. And 24 divides some of the answers, but not all.
The year 2025 is 45 times 45, a perfect square. How many years until the next perfect square year?

board.text: 2025 = 45 × 45. Years until the next perfect square = ?

beats.say: Which multiplication gives the next perfect square?

ask.ifNot: Perfect squares come from the counting numbers, one after another. After 45 times 45 comes 46 times 46.

beats.say: The next square is 46 times 46. Build it up. 46 times 45 is one more 45 than 45 times 45. That is 2070.
Then 46 times 46 is one more 46. 2070 plus 46 is 2116.
So the next perfect square year is 2116. That is 91 years after 2025.
Notice: we added 45 and then 46, and 45 plus 46 is 91. Neighbouring squares always differ by the sum of the two numbers.
Careful: 90 is twice 45, which is 1 short. And 46 is the next number to square, not the number of years.
A train leaves Pune station at 17:20 on the 24-hour clock. What is this time on the 12-hour clock?

board.text: 17:20 on the 24-hour clock = ? on the 12-hour clock

beats.say: On the 24-hour clock the hours do not start again after noon. They keep on counting: 13, 14, 15, all the way to 24.
The hour here is 17. Is 17:20 before noon or after noon?

ask.ifNot: Noon is 12 o'clock. 17 is more than 12, so this time comes after noon. That makes it p.m.

beats.say: 17 is more than 12, so it is a p.m. time. To find the hour, take 12 away. 17 minus 12 is 5.
The minutes do not change at all. They stay as 20.
Check: 5 plus 12 is 17. So for any hour bigger than 12, take away 12 and write p.m.
How many days are there altogether in the months of June and July?

board.text: Days in June + days in July = ?

beats.say: First we need the length of each month. Here is a rhyme that helps: 30 days have September, April, June and November.
So how many days does June have?

ask.ifNot: June is in the rhyme: September, April, June and November. Those four months have 30 days each.

beats.say: June is in the rhyme, so June has 30 days.
July is not in the rhyme, and it is not February. So July has 31 days.
Now add them. 30 plus 31 is 61.
June and July have 61 days altogether.
The two months are not the same length, and that is the trap. Know your month lengths, and the adding is easy.
How many days are there in February 2028?
February is the odd one out. It has 28 days in an ordinary year, and 29 days in a leap year.

board.text: February: 28 days, or 29 in a leap year

beats.say: So the real question is: is 2028 a leap year? A leap year is one that divides exactly by 4.
Here is a quick test. Just look at the last two digits, 28. Does 28 divide exactly by 4?

ask.ifNot: 4 times 7 is 28, with nothing left over. So 28 divides exactly by 4, and that means 2028 does too.

beats.say: 2028 divided by 4 is 507, with no remainder. So 2028 is a leap year.
In a leap year, February gets one extra day. So February 2028 has 29 days.
For any February question, test the year first. If it divides by 4, February has 29 days.
A film is 135 minutes long. How long is that in hours and minutes?
An hour is 60 minutes. So we ask: how many full 60s fit into 135? Let's write a little list to help.
How many full hours fit into 135 minutes?

ask.ifNot: 2 hours is 120 minutes, and that fits inside 135. 3 hours would be 180 minutes, which is too many.

beats.say: 120 is the biggest one that fits. So there are 2 full hours.
Now the minutes left over. 135 minus 120 is 15.
So the film is 2 hours 15 minutes long.
Check: 120 plus 15 is 135. Remember, the digits of 135 do not tell you the hours. Only the 60s do.
Today is Wednesday. What day of the week will it be 10 days from today?
The days of the week go round in a circle of 7. After 7 days, it is the same day again.
So split the 10 days into 7 days and some more. 10 minus 7 is 3.
After 7 days it is Wednesday again. Now we count 3 more days. Which day do we count first?

ask.ifNot: Wednesday is today, so it is our starting point. The first day we count is tomorrow, Thursday.

beats.say: Thursday is 1, Friday is 2, Saturday is 3.
So 10 days from today it will be Saturday.
Throw away the full weeks. Then count on the days that are left, starting from tomorrow.
Arjun's school starts at 8:00 a.m. and ends at 1:30 p.m. How long is his school day?

board.text: School: 8:00 am to 1:30 pm. How long?

spec.note: How long is the school day?

beats.say: We cannot just take 8 away from 1, because the clock passes 12 noon on the way. So we go in two jumps, with a stop at noon.
First jump. How long is it from 8:00 a.m. to 12 noon?

ask.ifNot: 12 minus 8 is 4. So it is 4 hours from 8 o'clock to noon.

beats.say: 12 minus 8 is 4. The morning part is 4 hours.
Second jump. From 12 noon to 1:30 p.m. is 1 hour and 30 minutes.
Put the jumps together. 4 hours and 1 hour make 5 hours, and there are 30 minutes as well.
Arjun's school day is 5 hours 30 minutes long.
When a time crosses noon, stop at 12 on the way. Two easy jumps beat one hard subtraction.
Dadi's favourite TV serial starts at a quarter to 7 in the evening. What is this time on the 24-hour clock?

board.text: A quarter to 7 in the evening = ? (24-hour clock)

beats.say: First, what does a quarter to 7 mean?

ask.ifNot: The word to means we have not reached 7 yet. A quarter of an hour is 15 minutes, so it is 15 minutes before 7.

beats.say: 15 minutes before 7 o'clock is 6:45, because 60 minus 15 is 45. So we are still in the hour of 6.
It is evening, so this is 6:45 p.m.
On the 24-hour clock, what do we do with a p.m. hour?

choices: leave the hour as it is
ask.ifNot: After noon, the 24-hour clock keeps counting past 12. So for a p.m. time we add 12 to the hour.

beats.say: 6 plus 12 is 18. The minutes stay as 45.
On the 24-hour clock the serial starts at 18:45.
Two steps: turn the words into a clock time, then add 12 to the hour for p.m.
A train journey from Kanyakumari to Jammu takes exactly 3 days. How many hours is that?
How many hours are there in one full day, with its night?

ask.ifNot: A clock face shows 12 hours, but the hour hand goes round twice in one full day. So a day has 24 hours.

beats.say: One full day, day and night together, has 24 hours.
3 days are 3 lots of 24 hours. So we multiply 3 by 24. Let's do it in two easy pieces.
3 times 20 is 60, and 3 times 4 is 12. 60 plus 12 is 72.
The journey takes 72 hours.
Check by adding: 24 plus 24 is 48, and 24 more is 72. To change days into hours, multiply by 24.
A night bus leaves Bengaluru at 9:30 p.m. The journey to Chennai takes 6 hours 45 minutes. When does the bus reach Chennai?

board.text: Leaves 9:30 pm. Journey 6 hours 45 minutes. Arrives?

beats.say: We add the hours first, and then the minutes. And we watch out for midnight on the way.
What is 6 hours after 9:30 p.m.?

ask.ifNot: Split the 6 hours into 3 and 3. The first 3 take us just past midnight. The next 3 bring us to 3:30, early in the morning, so a.m.

beats.say: 3 hours take us just past midnight, to 12:30 a.m. 3 more hours bring us to 3:30 a.m. It is the next day now.
Now the 45 minutes. First, 30 minutes take us from 3:30 up to 4 o'clock.
We have used 30 of the 45 minutes. 45 minus 30 leaves 15 more.
15 minutes after 4 o'clock is 4:15 a.m. That is when the bus reaches Chennai.
A night bus arrives early in the morning, so a.m. makes sense. Add the hours, then fill up to the next o'clock, then add the rest.
A train leaves Mumbai at 22:40 and reaches Goa at 05:10 the next morning. How long is the journey?

board.text: Leaves 22:40. Reaches 05:10 next morning. How long?

beats.say: The train travels through midnight. So we work in two parts: up to midnight, and after midnight.
Midnight is 24:00. From 22:40, 20 minutes take us to 23:00, and 1 more hour takes us to midnight.
So before midnight the train travels for 1 hour 20 minutes.
And how long is it from midnight to 05:10?

ask.ifNot: Midnight is zero hours. So 05:10 is exactly 5 hours and 10 minutes after midnight.

beats.say: After midnight the train travels for 5 hours 10 minutes.
Add the two parts. 1 hour and 5 hours make 6 hours. 20 minutes and 10 minutes make 30 minutes.
The journey takes 6 hours 30 minutes.
When a journey crosses midnight, do not subtract the two times. Count up to midnight, then count on.
In a certain month, the 5th is a Tuesday. What day of the week is the 23rd of the same month?

spec.note: The 5th is a Tuesday. Which day is the 23rd?

beats.say: The same day comes round every 7 days. So let's hop forward in sevens from the 5th.
5 plus 7 is 12. 12 plus 7 is 19. So the 12th and the 19th are Tuesdays too.
One more hop would land on the 26th, and that is past the 23rd. So we stop at the 19th.
How many days is it from the 19th to the 23rd?

ask.ifNot: Take 19 away from 23. 23 minus 19 is 4.

beats.say: 23 minus 19 is 4. So count 4 days on from Tuesday: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday.
The 23rd is a Saturday.
Hop in sevens to get close. Then count the last few days one by one.
How many days after the 20th of February 2024 is the 5th of March 2024?
To get from February into March, we must know how long this February is. And that depends on the year.
So, is 2024 a leap year?

choices: no, it is an ordinary year
ask.ifNot: Test the last two digits. 4 times 6 is 24, so 2024 divides exactly by 4. It is a leap year.

beats.say: 2024 is a leap year, so this February has 29 days, one more than usual. That is the trap in this question.

board.text: 2024 is a leap year: February has 29 days

beats.say: From the 20th to the end of February: 29 minus 20 is 9 days.
Then 5 more days carry us to the 5th of March. 9 plus 5 is 14.
So the 5th of March is 14 days after the 20th of February.
Whenever a question crosses February, check for a leap year first. Then count to the end of the month, and add on.
Anil practises the tabla for 40 minutes every day. For how long does he practise in one week?
A week has 7 days, and he practises on every one of them. So we want 7 lots of 40 minutes. 7 times 40 is 280.
280 minutes is a lot, so let's turn it into hours. An hour is 60 minutes. Here is a little list to help.
How many full hours fit into 280 minutes?

ask.ifNot: 4 hours is 240 minutes, and that fits inside 280. 5 hours would be 300 minutes, which is too many.

beats.say: 4 hours is 240 minutes. That is the most that fits, so there are 4 full hours.
Now the minutes left over. 280 minus 240 is 40.
Anil practises for 4 hours 40 minutes in one week.
Find the total minutes, take out the full 60s, and what is left is the minutes.
A month has 30 days, and its 1st day is a Saturday. How many Sundays are there in this month?

board.text: Month of 30 days. 1st = Saturday. How many Sundays?

beats.say: The 1st is a Saturday. Which date is the first Sunday?

ask.ifNot: Sunday comes right after Saturday. So if the 1st is a Saturday, the 2nd is a Sunday.

beats.say: Sunday comes right after Saturday, so the 2nd is the first Sunday.
Sundays are 7 days apart. So keep adding 7: the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th.
Look at that last one. Is the 30th inside this month?

ask.ifNot: The month has 30 days, so the 30th is its very last day. It still counts.

beats.say: The 30th is the last day of the month, so it counts. The next Sunday would be the 37th, and there is no such date.
So there are 5 Sundays in this month.
Find the first one, then add 7 again and again until the month runs out.
Kavya's train leaves at 14:10. She wants to be at the station 25 minutes early, and the trip from home takes 35 minutes. What is the latest she can leave home?

board.text: Be there 25 minutes early. Travel takes 35 minutes.

beats.say: We work backwards from the train time. Kavya needs 35 minutes to travel, and then 25 minutes of waiting, all before 14:10.
How much time does she need in all before the train leaves?

ask.ifNot: She must travel for 35 minutes and then still be 25 minutes early. Both come before the train, so we add them.

beats.say: 25 plus 35 is 60 minutes. And 60 minutes is exactly 1 hour.
So she must leave home 1 hour before 14:10. 14 minus 1 is 13, so that is 13:10.
The choices use the 12-hour clock. 13 is more than 12, so it is p.m., and 13 minus 12 is 1.
The latest Kavya can leave home is 1:10 p.m.
Check: leave at 1:10, travel 35 minutes, arrive at 1:45. That is 25 minutes before 2:10, which is 14:10. It works.
When you must be somewhere on time, add up everything that comes first, and count backwards.

board.text: Sides: 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm. What kind of triangle?

spec.note: What kind of triangle is it?

beats.say: A triangle has sides of 5 centimetres, 5 centimetres and 8 centimetres. What kind of triangle is it?
Triangles are named by how many of their sides are equal. So let's compare the 3 lengths.

ask.ifNot: Look at the lengths: 5, 5 and 8. The 5 is there twice, and the 8 is on its own.

beats.say: How many of the sides are equal?
Exactly 2: the pair of 5s. The 8 is the odd one out.
Here are the 3 names. 3 equal sides: equilateral. 2 equal sides: isosceles. No equal sides: scalene.
One choice says these sides cannot make a triangle at all. Let's test. The 2 short sides together must be longer than the long side. 5 plus 5 is 10, and 10 is more than 8. So they do meet.
So it is an isosceles triangle.
To name a triangle by its sides, just count the equal ones.

spec.note: What kind of triangle is it?

beats.say: The angles of a triangle are 35 degrees, 55 degrees and 90 degrees. What kind of triangle is it?
This time we name the triangle by its angles. The trick is to look at the biggest angle.

ask.ifNot: Compare the 3 numbers. 90 is greater than 55, and 55 is greater than 35.

beats.say: Which is the biggest of the 3 angles?
90 degrees. Now the name depends on how the biggest angle compares with 90.

ask.ifNot: An angle of exactly 90 degrees is a square corner, and its name is a right angle.

beats.say: Our biggest angle is exactly 90. What is an angle of 90 degrees called?
A right angle. So this is a right-angled triangle.
And equilateral? That needs 3 equal angles. These 3 are all different.
So to name a triangle by its angles, find the biggest angle and compare it with 90.

board.text: All 3 sides are different. Its name, by its sides = ?

spec.note: All three sides have different lengths

beats.say: All 3 sides of a triangle have different lengths. By its sides, what is the triangle called?
There are 3 names for triangles by their sides. Each name counts the equal sides.
3 equal sides: equilateral. 2 equal sides: isosceles.

ask.ifNot: Isosceles needs 2 equal sides. Right-angled is a name about angles. The name for no equal sides is scalene.

beats.say: Our triangle has no equal sides at all. Which name is left?
Scalene. No 2 sides are the same.
Be careful with right-angled. It is a real triangle name, but it comes from the angles. This question asks for the name that comes from the sides.
So the triangle is a scalene triangle.
A way to remember: a scalene triangle looks a little lopsided, because nothing matches.

board.text: Isosceles: equal sides 9 cm each, third side 6 cm.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides of 9 centimetres each, and a third side of 6 centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter is the walk all the way round the triangle. So we need the length of every side.

ask.ifNot: The question says 2 equal sides of 9 centimetres each. So the 9 comes twice, and the 6 comes once.

beats.say: What are the 3 sides?
9, 9 and 6. The 9 is there twice because it is the equal pair.
Now add them. 9 plus 9 is 18. And 18 plus 6 is 24.
So the perimeter is 24 centimetres.
2 slips to dodge. Adding only 9 and 6 leaves out a side. And multiplying 9 by 6 is not a walk round the triangle at all.
For a perimeter, list all the sides first, then add.

spec.note: Which name describes it best?

beats.say: A triangle has angles of 100 degrees, 40 degrees and 40 degrees. We want the name that describes it best.
The name has 2 parts. One part comes from the biggest angle. The other part comes from how many angles are equal.

ask.ifNot: 100 is more than 90. An angle that is bigger than a right angle is called obtuse.

beats.say: Start with the biggest angle, 100 degrees. A right angle is 90. So is the triangle acute-angled, right-angled or obtuse-angled?
Obtuse-angled, because 100 is more than 90. That is the first part of the name.
Now the second part. Look at the other 2 angles: 40 and 40. They are equal.

ask.ifNot: Scalene means no sides are equal, and equilateral means all 3. For exactly 2 equal sides the name is isosceles.

beats.say: 2 equal angles mean 2 equal sides. What is a triangle with 2 equal sides called?
Isosceles. Put the 2 parts together: it is an obtuse-angled isosceles triangle.
So read the angles twice: once for the biggest one, and once for equal ones.

board.text: Which lengths CANNOT be the sides of a triangle?

beats.say: Here are 4 sets of lengths. 3 sets can be the sides of a triangle. One set cannot. Let's find it.
Think of 3 sticks. Lay the longest one flat. The 2 shorter ones rise up from its ends, and they must meet. They can only meet if together they are longer than the long stick.
So here is the test: add the 2 shorter lengths, and compare with the longest.
A: 3 plus 4 is 7, more than 5. Fine. B: 6 plus 6 is 12, more than 11. Fine, though it is a very flat triangle.
C: 7 plus 8 is 15, more than 14. Fine as well.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sticks together are exactly as long as the long one. They can only meet by lying flat on top of it. No triangle rises up.

beats.say: D: 4 plus 5 is 9, and the longest side is also 9. Can these 3 make a triangle?
They lie flat. Equal is not enough: the 2 short sides must be longer than the long side.

board.text: 4 cm, 5 cm, 9 cm cannot make a triangle

beats.say: So the set that cannot make a triangle is 4 centimetres, 5 centimetres and 9 centimetres.
The trap is the equal case. More than: yes. Only equal to: no.

board.text: Right-angled. One acute angle is twice the other.

spec.note: Right-angled. One acute angle is twice the other.

beats.say: In a right-angled triangle, one of the 2 acute angles is twice the other. We want the smallest angle of the triangle.
A right-angled triangle has one angle of 90 degrees. And all 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180.

ask.ifNot: Take the right angle away from the total. 180 minus 90 leaves 90 for the other 2 angles to share.

beats.say: So how much is left for the 2 acute angles together?
90 degrees, because 180 minus 90 is 90.
One acute angle is twice the other. So think in parts: the small angle is 1 part, and the big one is 2 parts.

ask.ifNot: The small angle is 1 part and the big angle is 2 parts. 1 plus 2 makes 3 parts.

beats.say: How many equal parts share the 90 degrees?
3 parts. So 1 part is 90 divided by 3, which is 30.
The acute angles are 30, and twice 30, which is 60. Check: 30 plus 60 plus 90 makes 180.
The question asks for the smallest angle. That is 30 degrees, not 60.
Parts make a twice as big question easy: count the parts, then share.

board.text: Isosceles: perimeter 40 cm, different side 12 cm.

spec.note: Perimeter = 40 cm. The two sides marked ? are equal.

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 40 centimetres. The side that is different is 12 centimetres. How long is each of the equal sides?
The perimeter is all 3 sides added together. One side is 12, and the other 2 are equal, like twins.

ask.ifNot: The 12 centimetre side is not one of the twins. Take it out of the perimeter first. What is left belongs to the twins.

beats.say: What should we do first?
40 minus 12 is 28. So the 2 equal sides together are 28 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: The 2 sides are equal, and they share 28 between them. So each one gets half of 28.

beats.say: 28 is for both twins together. How long is each one?
Half of 28 is 14. Each equal side is 14 centimetres.
Check: 14 plus 14 plus 12 makes 40. It works.
The trap is to halve 40 straight away. Always take off the odd side first, then share.

board.text: All 3 angles are equal. Sum of any 2 angles = ?

spec.note: All three angles are equal. Add any two of them.

beats.say: All 3 angles of a triangle are equal. We want the sum of any 2 of its angles.

ask.ifNot: The 3 corners of a triangle fit along a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do the 3 angles of a triangle add up to?
180 degrees. And here the 3 angles are equal, so they share 180 fairly.
180 shared among 3 is 60, because 3 times 60 is 180. So each angle is 60 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Read the question once more. It asks for the sum of any 2 of the angles, not for one angle.

beats.say: Is 60 our answer?
The question wants 2 of the angles added together. 60 plus 60 is 120.
So any 2 of the angles add up to 120 degrees.
Always read the last line of a question again before you answer. Here 60 was a step, not the finish.

board.text: Two sides: 7 cm and 10 cm. Third side: a whole number.

spec.note: The third side is a whole number of centimetres

beats.say: 2 sides of a triangle are 7 centimetres and 10 centimetres. The third side is a whole number. How long can it be at the very most?
Picture 2 sticks, 7 and 10 centimetres long, joined at a hinge. The third side stretches between their free ends.

ask.ifNot: End to end in a straight line, the 2 sticks reach 7 plus 10, which is 17 centimetres.

beats.say: Open the hinge until the sticks lie in one straight line. How far apart are the free ends now?

board.text: Third side is shorter than 17 cm

beats.say: 17. But at 17 the sticks lie flat, and a flat line is not a triangle. So the third side must be shorter than 17.

ask.ifNot: It must be less than 17, so 17 itself is not allowed. The next whole number down is 16.

beats.say: The third side is a whole number, less than 17. What is the greatest it can be?
16. Check: 7 plus 10 is 17, and 17 is more than 16, so the triangle closes.
And the 3 in the choices? That is 10 minus 7. It is near the shortest the third side could be, not the greatest.
So: add the 2 sides, then step just below. Equal is never enough.

board.text: Sticks: 3 cm, 5 cm, 7 cm, 10 cm. Pick 3 for a triangle.

beats.say: Jay has 4 sticks: 3, 5, 7 and 10 centimetres. He picks 3 sticks at a time to make a triangle. How many different triangles can he make?
There are 2 jobs here. First, list every way to pick 3 sticks. Then test each pick, because not every pick closes into a triangle.

ask.ifNot: Each time, exactly 1 stick stays behind. There are 4 sticks that could stay behind, so there are 4 ways.

beats.say: Picking 3 sticks out of 4 is the same as leaving 1 stick out. How many ways are there?
4 ways. Here they are, in order.
The test: the 2 shorter sticks together must be longer than the longest. First pick: 3 plus 5 is 8, and 8 is more than 7. A triangle!
Second pick: 3 plus 5 is 8 again, but now the long stick is 10. 8 is less than 10, so the sticks cannot reach.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sticks are exactly as long as the long one, so they can only lie flat along it. This is the trap in the question.

beats.say: Third pick: 3, 7 and 10. 3 plus 7 is exactly 10. Triangle, or not?
Not a triangle. Equal is not enough, so this pick is out too.
Last pick: 5 plus 7 is 12, more than 10. A triangle!
Count the picks that passed: 3, 5, 7 and 5, 7, 10. That makes 2 triangles.
List in order, test every pick, and watch for the one where the short sticks only just equal the long one.

board.text: Isosceles. Top angle = 3 times each of the other two.

spec.note: Isosceles. Find the angle between the equal sides.

beats.say: In an isosceles triangle, the angle between the 2 equal sides is 3 times each of the other 2 angles. How big is that angle?
In an isosceles triangle, the 2 angles at the bottom are equal. Call each of them 1 part.
The angle between the equal sides, at the top, is 3 times as big. So it is 3 parts.

ask.ifNot: Do not forget that there are 2 bottom angles. 3 parts, plus 1 part, plus 1 more part, makes 5.

beats.say: How many equal parts are there in the whole triangle?
5 parts. This is where slips happen: counting only 1 bottom angle gives 4.
All the angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. So 5 parts make 180, and 1 part is 180 divided by 5, which is 36.

ask.ifNot: 1 part is the size of each of the 2 equal angles at the bottom. The top angle is 3 parts.

beats.say: 36 degrees is 1 part. Which angle is that?
So each bottom angle is 36. The top angle is 3 parts, and 3 times 36 is 108.
So the angle between the equal sides is 108 degrees. Check: 108 plus 36 plus 36 makes 180.
Turn times as big into parts, count every part, then share out the 180.

spec.note: Together the three angles make 180°

beats.say: In a triangle, the second angle is 20 degrees more than the first. The third is 20 degrees more than the second. We want the largest angle.
Look at the bars. The second angle is the first plus 20. The third is the first plus 20 plus 20, so it is the first plus 40.
And all 3 angles together make 180 degrees.
Now imagine cutting off the extra bits, the 20 and the 40. What is left is 3 equal bars, each the size of the first angle.

ask.ifNot: Both extras come off, the 20 and the 40. That is 60 in all, and 180 minus 60 leaves 120.

beats.say: The extras are 60 altogether. So what do the 3 equal bars add up to?
120 for 3 equal bars. 120 divided by 3 is 40. So the first angle is 40 degrees.

choices: no, we want the largest angle
ask.ifNot: 40 is the first angle, and it is the smallest. The question asks for the largest, which is the third one.

beats.say: Is 40 our answer?
The second angle is 40 plus 20, which is 60. The third is 60 plus 20, which is 80.
So the largest angle is 80 degrees. Check: 40 plus 60 plus 80 makes 180.
When things grow by equal steps, cut off the extras first. Then share what is left.

board.text: Isosceles: perimeter 50 cm, one side 12 cm.

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has a perimeter of 50 centimetres, and one of its sides is 12 centimetres. What can the other 2 sides be?
Isosceles means 2 sides are equal, like twins. But the question does not say whether the 12 is a twin, or the odd one out. So we must try both.
Case 1: the 12 is a twin. Then the sides are 12, 12 and one more. 12 plus 12 is 24, and 50 minus 24 is 26.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sides together make 24. That is less than 26, so they cannot meet above the long side.

beats.say: Sides of 12, 12 and 26. Can they make a triangle?
They cannot. 24 is less than 26, so the short sides never meet. Case 1 is the trap.
Case 2: the 12 is the odd one out. Then the twins share the rest. 50 minus 12 is 38, and half of 38 is 19.
Sides of 12, 19 and 19. Test them: 12 plus 19 is 31, which is more than 19. The triangle closes.

board.text: Other two sides: 19 cm and 19 cm

beats.say: So the other 2 sides are 19 centimetres and 19 centimetres.
And a pair like 14 and 24 does add up to the right perimeter. But then no 2 sides are equal, so the triangle is not isosceles.
2 checks every time: are 2 sides equal, and can the short sides reach across the long one?

board.text: Which statement about triangles is true?
A: A triangle can have two obtuse angles
B: An equilateral triangle can be right-angled
C: A scalene triangle can have two equal angles
D: A right-angled triangle can be isosceles

beats.say: 4 statements about triangles. Only 1 of them is true. Let's test them one at a time.
We test with 2 facts. The 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. And equal angles always sit opposite equal sides.

ask.ifNot: Each obtuse angle is more than 90. So 2 of them make more than 90 plus 90, and that is already 180.

beats.say: Statement A. An obtuse angle is bigger than 90 degrees. What happens if a triangle has 2 of them?

target.text: A: A triangle can have two obtuse angles

beats.say: Too much! 90 plus 90 is already 180, and there is still a third angle to fit in. So A is not true.

target.text: B: An equilateral triangle can be right-angled

beats.say: Statement B. Every angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees. So it can never hold a 90. Not true.

target.text: C: A scalene triangle can have two equal angles

beats.say: Statement C. 2 equal angles always give 2 equal sides. But scalene means no equal sides at all. Not true.

choices: no, that is not a triangle
ask.ifNot: 90 plus 45 plus 45 is exactly 180, so it is a real triangle. It has a right angle, and it has 2 equal angles.

beats.say: Statement D. Can a triangle have a right angle and 2 equal angles as well? Try 90, 45 and 45.
It works. Fold a square of paper from corner to corner and you are holding exactly this triangle.

board.text: D is true: right-angled and isosceles

beats.say: So the true statement is D: a right-angled triangle can be isosceles.
To test whether a kind of triangle can exist, try to build one with real angles. If you can, it is true.

board.text: A 12 cm straw is cut into 3 whole-number pieces.

spec.note: Three whole-number pieces that can make a triangle

beats.say: Meera cuts a 12 centimetre straw into 3 pieces, each a whole number of centimetres, and makes a triangle. How many different triangles can she make?
The 3 pieces add up to 12. But they must also close into a triangle: the 2 shorter pieces together must be longer than the longest one.

ask.ifNot: If the longest piece is 6, the other 2 share the 6 that is left. They would be exactly as long as the long piece, and lie flat.

beats.say: Could the longest piece be 6 centimetres?
So the longest piece must be shorter than 6, which is half the straw. It can be 5 at most.
Longest piece 5. The other 2 share 7. They can be 2 and 5, or 3 and 4. Not 1 and 6, because then the 6 would be the longest.

ask.ifNot: Neither piece may be longer than 4, and together they must make 8. Only 4 and 4 does that.

beats.say: Longest piece 4. The other 2 share 8, and neither may be longer than 4. What must they be?
4 and 4. So the triangle is 4, 4, 4, an equilateral one.
Longest piece 3? Then 3 pieces of 3 or less make 9 at most. That cannot reach 12. So the list is complete.
Count them: 2, 5, 5 and 3, 4, 5 and 4, 4, 4. That makes 3 triangles.
The secret was to work in order, from the longest piece down. That way nothing is missed, and nothing is counted twice.

board.text: Two sides: 6 cm and 11 cm. Third side: a whole number.
How many different lengths can it have?

spec.note: The third side is a whole number of centimetres

beats.say: 2 sides of a triangle are 6 centimetres and 11 centimetres. The third side is a whole number. How many different lengths can it have?
The third side cannot be too long, and it cannot be too short. Let's find both ends. Think of 2 sticks joined by a hinge.
Open the hinge flat. The free ends are 6 plus 11 apart, which is 17. Flat is not a triangle, so the third side must be shorter than 17.

ask.ifNot: Folded shut, the short stick lies along the long one. The gap between the ends is the difference, 11 minus 6.

beats.say: Now close the hinge, folding the 6 back along the 11. How far apart are the free ends?
5. And folded flat is not a triangle either. So the third side must be longer than 5.
So the third side is a whole number, more than 5 and less than 17. It runs from 6 up to 16.

ask.ifNot: Point at each number once as you count: 6, 7, 8, and so on up to 16. The first number counts too.

beats.say: How many whole numbers are there from 6 to 16?
11. Here is a quick way. From 1 to 16 there are 16 numbers. Take away the first 5, which are not allowed. 16 minus 5 is 11.
So the third side can have 11 different lengths.
2 traps here. Counting 5 and 17, which lie flat. And working out 17 minus 5, which gives 12 and miscounts. Find both ends, leave them out, and count with care.

board.text: Isosceles. One angle is 4 times another.

beats.say: In an isosceles triangle, one angle is 4 times another. The triangle has no obtuse angle. We want its smallest angle.
Call the small angle 1 part. Then the big angle is 4 parts. Isosceles means 2 of the angles are equal. But which 2? And remember, the 3 angles make 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The equal pair could be the 2 small angles, or the 2 big angles. The question does not say, so both must be tried.

beats.say: What could the 3 angles be, in parts?
First case: parts 1, 1 and 4. That is 6 parts. 180 divided by 6 is 30.
So the angles are 30, 30, and 4 times 30, which is 120. But wait.

ask.ifNot: 120 is bigger than a right angle, so it is obtuse. And the question says the triangle has no obtuse angle.

beats.say: What is the matter with 120 degrees here?
It is obtuse, and the question does not allow that. So case 1 is out. This is the trap: 30 looks like an answer, but it is not.
Second case: parts 1, 4 and 4. That is 9 parts. 180 divided by 9 is 20.
The angles are 20, 80 and 80. None is obtuse, and 80 is 4 times 20. Everything fits.
So the smallest angle is 20 degrees.
When a question does not say which angles are equal, try every case. Then use the extra clue to choose.

board.text: Two isosceles triangles, each with an angle of 40°.
Different angle sets. Largest angles: difference = ?

beats.say: 2 triangles are both isosceles, and each has an angle of 40 degrees. But their angles are not the same. We want the difference between their largest angles.
How can 2 isosceles triangles both have a 40 and still be different? Because the 40 can sit in 2 different places.

choices: in the equal pair, or on its own
ask.ifNot: An isosceles triangle has 2 equal angles and 1 other angle. The 40 could be one of the equal pair, or it could be the other one.

beats.say: Where can the 40 degree angle be?
First triangle: 40 is one of the equal pair. The angles are 40, 40 and one more. 40 plus 40 is 80, and 180 minus 80 is 100.
Second triangle: 40 is on its own. The equal pair share what is left. 180 minus 40 is 140, and half of 140 is 70.
Here they are. One triangle is wide and flat. The other is tall and narrow.

ask.ifNot: Take the largest angle from each triangle. In the first it is 100. In the second it is 70.

beats.say: Which 2 angles must we compare?
100 and 70. Their difference is 100 minus 70, which is 30.
So the difference between the 2 largest angles is 30 degrees.
One angle of an isosceles triangle can mean 2 different triangles. Always ask: is it a twin, or the odd one out?

board.text: Isosceles: one side 5 cm, another side 11 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: An isosceles triangle has one side of 5 centimetres and another side of 11 centimetres. We want its perimeter.
A triangle has 3 sides, and we are told only 2. But isosceles means 2 sides are equal. So the third side is a copy of one of the others.

ask.ifNot: The third side must equal one of the 2 sides we know. So it is either another 5 or another 11.

beats.say: What could the third side be?
Try 5 first. The sides would be 5, 5 and 11. Test them: 5 plus 5 is 10. Is 10 longer than 11? It is not.
The 2 short sides cannot reach across the 11. So 5, 5, 11 is not a triangle at all. This is the trap.
So the third side must be 11. The sides are 5, 11 and 11. Test: 5 plus 11 is 16, longer than 11. It closes.

ask.ifNot: A triangle has exactly 3 sides: 5, 11 and 11. Add those 3, no more and no fewer.

beats.say: Now the perimeter. Which sum gives it?
5 plus 11 is 16, and 16 plus 11 is 27. So the perimeter is 27 centimetres.
When a side is missing in an isosceles triangle, try both copies. Keep the one that can really close.

board.text: Sticks of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm, plenty of each.
3 sticks make a triangle. How many different triangles?

beats.say: Aman has plenty of sticks of 3, 4 and 8 centimetres. He uses 3 sticks to make a triangle, and sticks may be the same length. How many different triangles?
The lengths may repeat, so we need an orderly list. First all 3 the same, then 2 the same, then all different.
All the same: 3, 3, 3 and 4, 4, 4 and 8, 8, 8. Equal sticks always close into a triangle. That is 3 so far.
Now 2 the same and 1 different. Take a pair, then add one of the other 2 lengths. That gives 6 picks.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sticks together make 6. That is less than 8, so they cannot reach across the long stick.

beats.say: Test 3, 3, 8. The 2 short sticks make 3 plus 3, which is 6. Does it close?
It does not. And 4, 4, 8 is sneaky: 4 plus 4 is exactly 8, so the sticks lie flat. Out as well.
The other 4 picks all close. 3 plus 3 is 6, more than 4. And when the pair is the longest length, it always closes.

ask.ifNot: 7 is less than 8. The 2 short sticks cannot meet across the 8.

beats.say: Last, all different: 3, 4 and 8. 3 plus 4 is 7. Is that a triangle?
No triangle there. So we have 3 with all sides equal, and 4 with 2 sides equal. 3 plus 4 is 7.
So Aman can make 7 different triangles.
Sort the picks into groups, test each one, and beware of the pick that only just lies flat.

board.text: Largest size the smallest angle can have = ?

beats.say: The 3 angles of a triangle are whole numbers of degrees, and all 3 are different. How big can the smallest angle be?
The 3 angles add up to 180. If one is small, the others are big. To push the smallest angle up, we want all 3 as close together as we can.

ask.ifNot: Equal angles share the 180 fairly. 180 divided by 3 is 60.

beats.say: If all 3 angles were exactly equal, what would each one be?
60 each. But the question says all 3 are different. So 60, 60, 60 is not allowed.

ask.ifNot: If the smallest is 60, the other 2 are both bigger than 60. Then the total is more than 3 times 60, which is more than 180.

beats.say: Can the smallest angle be 60 when the angles are all different?
So the smallest must be less than 60. Try 59. Then the other 2 share 180 minus 59, which is 121.
Can 2 different angles, both bigger than 59, make 121? Yes: 60 and 61.
58 works as well, with 60 and 62. But the question wants the largest size, and 59 beats 58.
So the smallest angle can be 59 degrees at most. The angles are 59, 60 and 61.
To make the smallest of 3 numbers as big as possible, squeeze the numbers close together. That gave us 59.

board.text: Which statement is true for EVERY triangle?
A: Its largest angle is more than 60°
B: It has at least two acute angles
C: Its two smallest angles add up to less than 90°
D: Exactly one of its angles is 60° or more

beats.say: 4 statements. Only 1 of them is true for every triangle there is. Which one?
True for every triangle is a strong claim. If we find even 1 triangle that breaks a statement, that statement is out. So let's hunt for rule breakers.
A good triangle to test with is the equilateral one. Its angles are 60, 60 and 60.

ask.ifNot: In the equilateral triangle the largest angle is 60. That is equal to 60, not more than 60. So it breaks statement A.

beats.say: Statement A says the largest angle is more than 60. Does the equilateral triangle obey?

target.text: A: Its largest angle is more than 60°
C: Its two smallest angles add up to less than 90°

beats.say: It breaks A. It breaks C too: its 2 smallest angles make 60 plus 60, which is 120. That is far more than 90.

target.text: D: Exactly one of its angles is 60° or more

beats.say: Now D: exactly one angle of 60 or more. Try a triangle with angles 40, 70 and 70. It has 2 angles above 60. D is broken.

choices: no, they would use up all 180°
ask.ifNot: 2 angles of 90 or more add up to at least 180. That leaves nothing for the third angle.

beats.say: Only B is left. But can it ever be broken? An acute angle is less than 90. Could a triangle have 2 angles that are 90 or more?
So at most 1 angle can be 90 or more. The other 2 must be acute, every single time.

board.text: B: at least two acute angles

beats.say: So the statement that is true for every triangle is B: it has at least 2 acute angles.
To knock out an always statement, find 1 rule breaker. To keep one, show why it can never be broken.

board.text: 5 equilateral triangles, side 4 cm, joined in a row.

spec.note: Five triangles in a row. Dashed lines are shared sides.

beats.say: 5 equilateral triangles, each with sides of 4 centimetres, are joined in a row, up, down, up, down, up. We want the perimeter of the whole shape.
Perimeter means the outside edge only. A side shared by 2 triangles is inside the shape, so it does not count.
Start by counting every side, as if the triangles were apart. 5 triangles with 3 sides each: 5 times 3 is 15 sides.

ask.ifNot: Look at the dashed lines in the picture. There is 1 join between each pair of neighbours, so 5 triangles have 4 joins.

beats.say: In a row of 5 triangles, how many joins are there between neighbours?
4 joins. Now the important part. At each join 2 sides are hidden, one from each triangle. So 4 joins hide 8 sides.
15 sides, take away the 8 hidden ones. That leaves 7 sides on the outside.

ask.ifNot: Only the 7 outside sides count. 15 counts every side, and 11 takes off each join only once instead of twice.

beats.say: Each outside side is 4 centimetres. So what is the perimeter?
7 times 4 is 28. The perimeter is 28 centimetres.
Check by walking round the picture: 3 sides along one long edge, 2 along the other, and 1 slanted side at each end. That is 7 sides.
When shapes are joined, every shared side disappears twice: once for each shape.

board.text: Sides: 3 consecutive whole numbers, like 5, 6, 7 cm.

spec.note: One example. Find the smallest triangle of this kind.

beats.say: The sides of a triangle are 3 consecutive whole numbers, such as 5, 6 and 7. What is the smallest perimeter such a triangle can have?
Consecutive means one after another, like 5, 6, 7. We want the smallest triangle of this kind, so we start from the smallest numbers.

ask.ifNot: A side cannot be 0 long. So the smallest set starts at 1, and it is 1, 2, 3.

beats.say: What is the smallest set of 3 consecutive whole numbers that could be lengths?
1, 2, 3. But do they close into a triangle? The 2 short sides together must be longer than the long side. 1 plus 2 is 3. Only equal!
Equal means the short sides lie flat along the long one. No triangle. So 1, 2, 3 is out, and its total of 6 is a trap.

choices: yes, so it is a triangle
ask.ifNot: 5 is more than 4. So the 2 short sides can rise up and meet above the long side.

beats.say: Next set: 2, 3, 4. 2 plus 3 is 5. Is that longer than 4?
5 is more than 4, so 2, 3, 4 is a real triangle.
Its perimeter is 2 plus 3 plus 4, which is 9 centimetres.
3, 4, 5 is a triangle too, with a perimeter of 12. But 9 is smaller.
Start small and test each set. The first one that closes is the winner, and here that gave 9.

board.text: Perimeter 30 cm. Each side is a whole number.
Greatest length of the longest side = ?

beats.say: A triangle has a perimeter of 30 centimetres, and each side is a whole number. How long can its longest side be?
We want one side as long as possible. But there is a limit. The other 2 sides together must still be longer than it, or they cannot meet.

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is 30. Take away the 15 centimetre side, and 15 is left for the other 2.

beats.say: Try a longest side of 15. How much is left for the other 2 sides together?
15 is left. So the other 2 sides together are exactly as long as the longest side. They lie flat. 15 does not work.
This is the trap. 15 is exactly half of the perimeter. The longest side has to be less than half.
Try 14. 30 minus 14 leaves 16 for the other 2 sides. And 16 is more than 14.
Can you think of 2 whole numbers that add up to 16, with neither longer than 14?
Here is one pair: 14 and 2. Sides of 14, 14 and 2 make a tall, thin triangle. 8 and 8 would work too.
So the longest side can be 14 centimetres at most.
And 28? That leaves only 2 for both of the other sides, far too little to reach across.
The longest side of a triangle is always less than half of the perimeter. Half of 30 is 15, so the best whole number is 14.

board.text: Right-angled. One angle is 4 times another.
All angles are whole numbers. Smallest angle = ?

beats.say: A triangle is right-angled. One of its angles is 4 times another, and all the angles are whole numbers. We want the smallest angle.
One angle is the right angle, 90 degrees. The other 2 share the rest: 180 minus 90 is 90.
Which 2 angles are linked by 4 times? Perhaps the right angle is 4 times a small angle. Let's test that idea first.

choices: no, it is not a whole number
ask.ifNot: The question says every angle is a whole number of degrees. 22.5 has a half in it, so it is not allowed.

beats.say: 90 divided by 4 is 22.5. Is that allowed?
Not allowed. That clue about whole numbers was there for a reason! So the 4 times link is between the 2 acute angles.
The small acute angle is 1 part, and the other is 4 parts. That is 5 parts, and together they make 90 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Only the 2 acute angles are being shared out. Together they make 90, not 180, and there are 5 parts.

beats.say: So how big is 1 part?
18 degrees. The other acute angle is 4 times 18, which is 72.
Check: 18 plus 72 plus 90 makes 180, and every angle is a whole number.
So the smallest angle is 18 degrees.
Use every clue in a question. Here the whole number clue told us which angles were linked.

board.text: Two sides: 9 cm and 4 cm. Third side: a whole number.
Perimeter is a multiple of 7. Third side = ?

spec.note: The perimeter is a multiple of 7

beats.say: 2 sides of a triangle are 9 centimetres and 4 centimetres. The third side is a whole number, and the perimeter is a multiple of 7. How long is the third side?
2 things must both be true. The sides must make a real triangle. And the perimeter must be in the 7 times table. Start with the triangle.

board.text: Third side: more than 5, less than 13

beats.say: The third side must be shorter than 9 plus 4, which is 13. And it must be longer than 9 minus 4, which is 5.
So the third side is 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12.
The perimeter is 13 plus the third side. So it runs from 13 plus 6, which is 19, up to 13 plus 12, which is 25.

ask.ifNot: Count in sevens: 7, 14, 21, 28. Only 21 lands between 19 and 25.

beats.say: Which multiple of 7 lies from 19 to 25?
21. So the perimeter is 21, and the third side is 21 minus 13, which is 8.
So the third side is 8 centimetres.
Watch the traps. A side of 1 gives a perimeter of 14, and a side of 15 gives 28. Both are multiples of 7, but neither closes into a triangle.
And a side of 7 is tempting. But it is the perimeter that must be a multiple of 7, not the side. The answer stays 8.

board.text: Triangle ABC is isosceles. Angle A = 50°.
Angle B is bigger than A and bigger than C. Angle C = ?

spec.note: Angle A (top) is 50°. Angle B (left) is the biggest. Angle C = ?

beats.say: Triangle A B C is isosceles. Angle A is 50 degrees. Angle B is bigger than angle A, and bigger than angle C. What is angle C?
Isosceles means 2 of the 3 angles are equal, like twins. The puzzle is: which 2?

choices: no, it equals neither of them
ask.ifNot: If B is bigger than A, it is not equal to A. If B is bigger than C, it is not equal to C. So B has no twin.

beats.say: Angle B is bigger than A, and bigger than C. Can B be one of the twins?
B is the odd one out. So the twins must be A and C.
Angle A is 50 degrees, so angle C is 50 degrees as well.
Let's check that B really is the biggest. 50 plus 50 is 100, and 180 minus 100 is 80. Angle B is 80, bigger than 50. It fits.
The trap is to make B and C the twins and share 130 between them, which gives 65. But twins are equal, and B has to be bigger than C.
So angle C is 50 degrees.
In an isosceles puzzle, first work out which 2 angles are the twins. The words of the question tell you.

board.text: Two angles add up to 110°. The bigger is 30° more.

spec.note: These two angles of the triangle add up to 110°

beats.say: 2 angles of a triangle add up to 110 degrees. The bigger one is 30 degrees more than the smaller one. What kind of triangle is it?
To name a triangle we need all 3 angles. So first let's find these 2, using the bars.
Cut the extra 30 off the bigger bar. Now the 2 bars are equal. Together they make 110 minus 30, which is 80.

ask.ifNot: The 2 equal bars share 80 between them. Half of 80 is 40.

beats.say: 2 equal bars make 80. How big is the smaller angle?
40 degrees. And the bigger angle is 40 plus 30, which is 70.
Do not stop here! 40 and 70 are different, so scalene looks tempting. But a triangle has a third angle.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180. The first 2 use 110 of it, so 180 minus 110 is left.

beats.say: The first 2 angles make 110. What is the third angle?
70 degrees. So the angles are 40, 70 and 70.
2 angles are equal, so 2 sides are equal. It is an isosceles triangle.
Never name a triangle from only 2 of its angles. Find the third one first.
A cycle track is 4 kilometres 75 metres long. We want that as one number of kilometres.
The 4 kilometres stay put. The 75 metres must become a part of a kilometre. How many metres make 1 kilometre?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So it takes 1000 metres to make 1 kilometre.

beats.say: 1000 metres make 1 kilometre, so we divide 75 by 1000. The digits slide 3 places to the right.
Careful here. 0.75 kilometres would be 750 metres. Our 75 metres is much less, so a 0 must come after the point: 0.075.
Now join it to the 4 whole kilometres. 4 plus 0.075 is 4.075.
See it in the place chart. The 4 is in the ones, and the 7 and the 5 sit in the hundredths and thousandths.

spec.note: 4 whole kilometres, and 75 m in the thousandths

beats.say: So the track is 4.075 kilometres long.
Remember: metres to kilometres means 3 decimal places. Fill the empty place with a 0.
Meera's bottle holds 1.2 litres. She drinks 350 millilitres. How many millilitres are left?
Can we take 350 away from 1.2 just like that?

choices: no, change litres to ml first
ask.ifNot: The two amounts are in different units. We must make them both millilitres before we subtract.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. So 1.2 litres is 1.2 times 1000, which is 1200 millilitres.
Careful: it is 1200, not 1020. The 0.2 of a litre is 200 millilitres.
She drank the water, so we take it away. 1200 minus 350.
Take away 300 first, which leaves 900. Then take away 50 more. That leaves 850.
So 850 millilitres of water are left.
Check: 850 plus 350 is 1200. It works. Same units first, then subtract.
A new pencil is 14 centimetres 6 millimetres long. After sharpening, it is 12 centimetres 9 millimetres. How many millimetres shorter is it?
The answer is wanted in millimetres. What is a good first step?

ask.ifNot: Mixed units are slippery. Let's write each length in millimetres only, then subtract once.

beats.say: 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. So 14 centimetres is 140 millimetres, and 6 more makes 146.
The same for the short pencil. 12 centimetres is 120 millimetres, and 9 more makes 129.
Now find the gap between 129 and 146. Count up: 1 more gets us to 130, and 16 more gets us to 146.
1 and 16 make 17. So the pencil is 17 millimetres shorter.
Here is the trap to dodge. Taking 6 from 9 mixes up the two pencils: the 9 millimetres belong to the shorter one.
So change everything into the small unit first. Then it is one clean subtraction.
Amma buys 1 kilogram 750 grams of potatoes and 2 kilograms 400 grams of onions. What is the total, in kilograms?
Add the grams first. 750 plus 400 is 1150 grams.
1150 grams is more than 1000 grams. So what is hiding inside it?

choices: nothing, leave it as it is
ask.ifNot: 1000 grams make 1 kilogram. 1150 is more than 1000, so 1 whole kilogram is inside, with some grams left over.

beats.say: 1150 grams is 1 kilogram and 150 grams. That extra kilogram joins the others.
Now the kilograms. 1 plus 2, plus the 1 we carried, makes 4. So the total is 4 kilograms 150 grams.
Last step: write it as a decimal. 150 grams is 150 divided by 1000, which is 0.15 kilograms.
So the vegetables weigh 4.15 kilograms. Watch the place: 0.015 would be only 15 grams.
Remember: when the grams pass 1000, carry a kilogram across.
A fruit seller has 7 dozen bananas. He sells 3 score. How many bananas are left?
Dozen and score are names for numbers. A dozen is 12. So 7 dozen is 7 times 12, which is 84 bananas.
Now the score. How many is 1 score?

ask.ifNot: A score is 20. It is bigger than a dozen.

beats.say: A score is 20. So 3 score is 3 times 20, which is 60 bananas.
He sold 60, so we take them away. 84 minus 60 is 24.
So 24 bananas are left.
Turn the number words into numbers first. After that it is a sum you already know how to do.
A box holds 1 gross of pencils. A teacher gives 2 pencils to each of 54 children. How many pencils remain?
How many is a gross?

ask.ifNot: A gross is 12 dozen. And 12 times 12 is 144.

beats.say: A gross is 12 dozen, and 12 times 12 is 144. So the box starts with 144 pencils.
Each of the 54 children gets 2 pencils. 54 times 2 is 108.
Careful: it is 2 pencils each, not 1. If we forgot that, we would take away only 54.
Now subtract. 144 minus 108. Take away 100 to get 44, then 8 more to get 36.
So 36 pencils remain in the box.
Check: 108 given out, plus 36 left, makes 144. It fits.
A milkman pours 750 millilitres of milk into each of 6 packets. How many litres does he use?
First the total in millilitres. 6 times 700 is 4200, and 6 times 50 is 300. Together, 4500 millilitres.
The question asks for litres. How do we change millilitres into litres?

ask.ifNot: 1000 millilitres make 1 litre. Litres are bigger, so there are fewer of them. We divide by 1000.

beats.say: 1000 millilitres make 1 litre. 4500 divided by 1000 is 4.5.
So the milkman uses 4.5 litres of milk. That is 4 and a half litres.
Does it make sense? Each packet is less than 1 litre, so 6 packets must be less than 6 litres. 4.5 fits nicely.
The plan: multiply first, then change the unit at the end.
Ravi's school is 850 metres from home. He walks there and back on each of 5 school days. How many kilometres is that in the week?

board.text: 850 m to school, there and back, 5 days
How many km in the week?

beats.say: Read it slowly: there and back. How many times does Ravi walk the 850 metres in one day?

ask.ifNot: He walks to school, and then he walks home again. That is the 850 metres twice each day.

beats.say: So in one day he walks 850 times 2, which is 1700 metres.
There are 5 school days, so we need 1700 times 5. 1000 times 5 is 5000, and 700 times 5 is 3500. Together, 8500 metres.
Now change metres into kilometres. 1000 metres make 1 kilometre, so we divide by 1000.
So Ravi walks 8.5 kilometres in the week.
The trap was the walk home. Forget it and you get only half the distance. Always ask: one way, or both ways?
A carpenter cuts a plank 3 metres long into 8 equal pieces. How long is each piece, in centimetres?
The answer is wanted in centimetres. What shall we do first?

ask.ifNot: Cutting into equal pieces is sharing, so we will divide. But first, let's turn the 3 metres into centimetres.

beats.say: 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so 3 metres is 300 centimetres.
Now share 300 among 8 pieces. Halving 3 times is the same as dividing by 8. Half of 300 is 150.
Half of 150 is 75. And half of 75 is 37.5.
So each piece is 37.5 centimetres long.
Check: 8 pieces of 37.5 centimetres make 300 centimetres. And each piece is much shorter than the plank, as it should be.
A stack of 40 equal coins is 6 centimetres tall. How thick is one coin, in millimetres?
The answer is in millimetres, so change the height first. 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres, so 6 centimetres is 60 millimetres.
The 40 coins share that height equally. So which sum gives one coin?

ask.ifNot: The whole stack is 60 millimetres, shared among 40 coins. Sharing means dividing the height by the number of coins.

beats.say: 60 divided by 40. Take a zero off both, and it is 6 divided by 4. 4 goes into 6 once, with 2 left over, and 2 out of 4 is a half.
So one coin is 1.5 millimetres thick.
Check: 40 coins at 1.5 millimetres each make 60 millimetres, which is our 6 centimetres.
Change the unit first, then share. And ask if the answer is sensible: a coin really is about that thin.
Which of these 4 lengths is the greatest? They are written in different ways, so we cannot tell just by looking.

board.text: Greatest: 1.08 km, 1 km 800 m, 1008 m, 10800 cm?

beats.say: What is the fair way to compare them?

ask.ifNot: A big number with a tiny unit can still be a short length. Let's write every length in metres, then compare.

beats.say: First, 1.08 kilometres. 1 kilometre is 1000 metres, so 1.08 times 1000 is 1080 metres.
Next, 1 kilometre 800 metres. That is 1000 plus 800, which is 1800 metres.
1008 metres is already in metres. Now the last one: 10800 centimetres. 100 centimetres make 1 metre, so divide by 100. Only 108 metres!
So in metres we have 1080, 1800, 1008 and 108. Which is the biggest?

ask.ifNot: Look at the hundreds. 1800 has 8 hundreds after its thousand, more than any of the others.

beats.say: 1800 metres is the greatest. That is 1 kilometre 800 metres.
Did you see the trap? 10800 looked huge, but centimetres are tiny. Always compare in the same unit.
One tablet has 250 milligrams of medicine. How many grams are there in a strip of 10 tablets?
First the total in milligrams. 10 times 250 is 2500 milligrams.
Now we need grams. How many milligrams make 1 gram?

ask.ifNot: Milli means a thousandth. So 1000 milligrams make 1 gram.

beats.say: 1000 milligrams make 1 gram, so we divide by 1000. 2500 divided by 1000 is 2.5.
So the strip contains 2.5 grams of medicine.
Careful with the choices. 2500 is the number of milligrams, not grams. And 0.25 grams is just 1 tablet.
Multiply first, then change the unit. And always check which unit the question wants.
A tailor has 5 metres of cloth. He uses 2 metres 35 centimetres for a kurta. How much cloth is left?
Let's write both lengths in centimetres. 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so 5 metres is 500 centimetres.
And 2 metres 35 centimetres is 200 plus 35, which is 235 centimetres.
Now subtract. 500 minus 200 is 300, and 300 minus 35 is 265.
265 centimetres. How do we write that in metres and centimetres?

ask.ifNot: Every 100 centimetres is 1 metre. 265 has 2 hundreds, with 65 left over.

beats.say: 265 is 200 and 65. So 2 metres 65 centimetres of cloth is left.
The trap is 3 metres 65. To take away the 35 centimetres, one of the metres had to be broken into 100 centimetres.
Check: 235 used, plus 265 left, makes 500. It works.
A running track is 4 hectometres long. Sunil runs 5 rounds. How many kilometres does he run?
What does hecto mean?

ask.ifNot: Hecto means a hundred. So a hectometre is a hundred metres.

beats.say: 1 hectometre is 100 metres. So one round is 4 times 100, which is 400 metres.
Sunil runs 5 rounds. 400 times 5 is 2000 metres.
Now change to kilometres. 1000 metres make 1 kilometre, and 2000 divided by 1000 is 2.
So Sunil runs 2 kilometres.
Remember: hecto is a hundred, and kilo is a thousand. Change to metres first, and the rest is easy.
Rina needs 150 laddoos. The shop sells them only in boxes of one dozen. What is the least number of boxes she must buy?

board.text: 150 laddoos. Boxes of 1 dozen. Fewest boxes?

beats.say: A dozen is 12. So we ask: how many 12s do we need to reach 150? Start with 10 boxes: 12 times 10 is 120.
2 more boxes give 24 more laddoos. 120 plus 24 is 144. So 12 boxes hold 144 laddoos.
Rina needs 150, and 12 boxes give 144. Is that enough?

ask.ifNot: 150 minus 144 is 6. She would be 6 laddoos short, and her guests would notice!

beats.say: She cannot buy part of a box. So she needs one whole box more. 12 plus 1 is 13 boxes.
13 boxes hold 156 laddoos, which is enough. So Rina must buy 13 boxes.
When things come in packs, a remainder means one more pack. Round up, so that there is enough.
Arjun walks 2 kilometres 75 metres, then 850 metres, then 1.5 kilometres. How many kilometres in all?
The 3 distances are written in 3 different ways. What is the safest plan?

choices: change all to metres, then add
ask.ifNot: Different units cannot be added as they are. Let's put all of them in metres, add, and change back at the end.

beats.say: 1 kilometre is 1000 metres. So 2 kilometres 75 metres is 2000 plus 75, which is 2075 metres.
Careful: 2075, not 2750. The 75 metres are just 75.
850 metres is already in metres. And 1.5 kilometres is 1.5 times 1000, which is 1500 metres.
Now add. 2075 plus 1500 is 3575. Then 850 more makes 4425 metres.
Back to kilometres: divide by 1000. 4425 divided by 1000 is 4.425.
So Arjun walks 4.425 kilometres in all.
The plan: everything into the small unit, add, then change back.
An empty basket weighs 600 grams. With 12 equal mangoes in it, it weighs 4 kilograms 200 grams. What does one mango weigh?

board.text: Basket 600 g. Basket + 12 mangoes = 4 kg 200 g.

beats.say: First make it all grams. 4 kilograms is 4000 grams, and 200 more makes 4200 grams.
Is 4200 grams the weight of the mangoes?

choices: no, the basket is in there too
ask.ifNot: The scale weighed the basket and the mangoes together. We must take the basket's 600 grams away first.

beats.say: Take the basket away. 4200 minus 600 is 3600 grams. That is the 12 mangoes alone.
Now share 3600 among 12 mangoes. 36 divided by 12 is 3, so 3600 divided by 12 is 300.
So one mango weighs 300 grams.
Check: 12 mangoes weigh 3600 grams, and the basket's 600 makes 4200. It fits.
When something is weighed in a container, take the container away first.
A leaking tap drips 5 millilitres of water every minute. How many litres does it waste in one full day?
Let's climb in steps: a minute, then an hour, then a day. An hour has 60 minutes, and a day has 24 hours.
So how much water drips away in one hour?

ask.ifNot: The tap loses 5 millilitres in every one of the 60 minutes. So we multiply 5 by 60.

beats.say: 5 times 60 is 300. The tap wastes 300 millilitres every hour.
Now a whole day: 300 times 24. 3 times 24 is 72, so 300 times 24 is 7200 millilitres.
Change to litres. 1000 millilitres make 1 litre, so 7200 divided by 1000 is 7.2.
So the tap wastes 7.2 litres in a day. That is more than 7 big bottles of water, from tiny drips!
The trap is to stop at 300, which is only one hour. Go up step by step and you will not miss one.
A snail crawls 3 centimetres 5 millimetres every minute. How many minutes does it take to crawl 2.1 metres?

board.text: 3 cm 5 mm each minute. 2.1 m takes ? minutes

beats.say: Centimetres, millimetres and metres are all mixed up here. Which single unit shall we use for everything?

ask.ifNot: The smallest unit here is the millimetre. If we use it for everything, there are no decimals to worry about.

beats.say: 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. So 3 centimetres is 30 millimetres, and 5 more makes 35 millimetres each minute.
Now the 2.1 metres. 1 metre is 100 centimetres, and each of those is 10 millimetres. So 1 metre is 1000 millimetres.
2.1 times 1000 is 2100 millimetres. Careful, not 210: that would be the centimetres.
So the snail must go 2100 millimetres, at 35 each minute. How many 35s are in 2100? 35 times 2 is 70, and 70 times 30 is 2100.
2 times 30 is 60. So 35 times 60 is 2100, and the snail takes 60 minutes.
