ask.ifNot: Times 0 means zero lots of something. Zero lots of any number, big or small, is nothing at all.

beats.say: Think of 3 times 0 as 3 empty plates: nothing on any of them. Even 1000 empty plates still hold nothing.
So whatever the bracket comes to, the answer will be 0. We do not even need to work the bracket out!
The bracket, times 0, equals 0.
The trap is diving into the bracket, with its half of 14 and all those take aways, and making a slip in there. None of it was needed.
So look before you leap: scan the whole line first. If everything is multiplied by 0, the answer is 0.
A minus, a divide, a plus, and a fraction of a number, all in one line. The order we choose decides the answer.
Which pieces get done before the minus and the plus?

ask.ifNot: Of means times, and times and divide always go before plus and minus. So the two early jobs are 8 divided by 2, and a third of 18.

beats.say: Start with the of. A third of 18 means 18 shared into 3 equal parts, and 18 divided by 3 is 6.
Now the divide. 8 divided by 2 is 4. Write the line again with 4 and 6 in place.
Only minus and plus are left: 20 minus 4 plus 6. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we read from left to right, like a sentence. That means 20 minus 4 comes first.

beats.say: Left to right it is: 20 minus 4 is 16.
And 16 plus 6 is 22. That is our answer.
Name the trap: starting with 20 minus 8 because it is on the left. That 8 belongs to the divide, so it must be halved first.
Check by walking backwards. 22 minus 6 is 16, and 16 plus 4 is 20, right where the line started.
So: of and divide go first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Four number sentences. Three of them are true and one is not, and we are hunting for the one that is not.
Take the first one. Of means times, so we need a fifth of 125. 125 shared into 5 equal parts is 25.
Then 25 divided by 25 is 1, and 1 minus 1 is 0. It says 0, so this one is true.
The next one ends in times 0. Anything times 0 is 0, so it is true whatever the brackets come to.
Now this one, which claims to equal 3. Which pieces do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times go before minus and plus. So the early jobs are 8 divided by 2 times 6, and 3 divided by 9.

beats.say: Left to right: 8 divided by 2 is 4, and 4 times 6 is 24.
3 divided by 9 does not come out whole. It is 3 parts out of 9, which is just a third.
24 plus 27 is 51, and taking away a third leaves more than 50. That is nowhere near 3!
So this sentence is not true. Let's make sure the last one is fine. It starts with a quarter divided by three quarters.
Three quarters is 3 times as big as a quarter. So a quarter divided by three quarters is a third.
Next, divide that third by two quarters. Two quarters is a half, and dividing by a half doubles, so we get two thirds.
Last, two thirds times 4 over 3. On top 2 times 4 is 8, underneath 3 times 3 is 9, so we get 8 over 9, just as it says.
So the one that is not correct is 8 divided by 2, times 6, minus 3 divided by 9, plus 27. It does not equal 3.
Two traps here: stopping at the first sentence that looks odd, and forgetting the question wants the one that is not true. Work every sentence out by the rules.
Only times and divide in this line, no plus or minus at all. Times and divide are equal partners, so we go from left to right.
Start on the left with 5 times 125. 5 times 100 is 500, and 5 times 25 is 125, so together that is 625.
So now the line starts 625 times 15, divided by 625. Do you spot anything?

ask.ifNot: We multiply by 625 and then divide by 625. One undoes the other, like a step forward and then a step back. So only the 15 is left.

beats.say: Times 625 and divided by 625 cancel each other out. That leaves just the 15.
Carry on, left to right. 15 times 3 is 45, so we are left with 45 times 45.
Split one 45 into 40 and 5. 45 times 40 is 1800, and 45 times 5 is 225.
1800 plus 225 is 2025. So the whole line is worth 2025.
Careful with the divide sign: it only belongs to the 625 right after it. The 3 and the 45 are still multiplying, so the answer stays big.
Check the shortcut the long way: 625 times 15 is 9375, and 9375 divided by 625 is 15 again.
So with only times and divide: go left to right, and watch for a times and a divide by the same number, because they cancel.
This one asks us to turn a sentence into an equation. A number, when divided by 7, gives 25.
We don't know the number, so we call it x. Now we translate the sentence, one piece at a time.
The number divided by 7. How do we write that?

ask.ifNot: The number is the thing being divided, so it comes first: x divided by 7. And 7 x would mean 7 times the number.

beats.say: x divided by 7. In the choices the divide is written as a sloping line, like a fraction with x on top and 7 underneath. It means the same thing.
And gives 25 means the result equals 25. So the equation is x divided by 7 equals 25.
Careful with the order. Swap the 7 and the 25, or turn the divide into a times, and the equation describes a different number. Each piece must stay where the sentence put it.
Let's test it. If x divided by 7 is 25, then x is 25 times 7, which is 175. And 175 divided by 7 is 25, just as the sentence says.
So: name the unknown, then translate each phrase in order. Divided by 7 becomes the divide sign and a 7. Gives 25 becomes equals 25.
A short equation. x minus 5 equals 1. Some number, with 5 taken away, leaves 1.
We want x by itself. What undoes minus 5?

ask.ifNot: Minus 5 took 5 away. To get it back, we add 5. Adding undoes subtracting.

beats.say: And to keep the balance level, we add 5 to both sides.
On the left, minus 5 and plus 5 cancel, leaving just x. On the right, 1 plus 5 is 6. So x equals 6.
Careful: a common slip is to take 5 away again, or to work out 5 minus 1 and say 4. We are undoing a minus, so we add.
Check. Put 6 in place of x. 6 minus 5 is 1. It works.
For a one step equation, do the opposite of what was done to x, and do it to both sides.
5 x plus 7 equals 3 x plus 17. Notice that x appears on both sides of the equals sign.
We want all the x terms on one side. Which move does that?

ask.ifNot: Whatever we do, we do to both sides. Taking 3 x from both sides clears the x from the right, and still leaves some on the left.

beats.say: Take 3 x from both sides. On the left, 5 x minus 3 x is 2 x. On the right, the 3 x is gone.
We want the 2 x by itself. So what should we do about the 7 that is added on?

ask.ifNot: Adding 7 is undone by taking 7 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: Take away 7 on the left, and 7 on the right as well. That leaves 2 x equals 17 minus 7, which is 10.
Now 2 x is 2 lots of x. To find just one x, we divide both sides by 2.
10 divided by 2 is 5. So x equals 5.
Check both sides with x as 5. Left: 5 times 5, plus 7, is 32. Right: 3 times 5, plus 17, is 32. Both sides agree.
One trap: 2 x equals 10 is not the end, because that is 2 lots of x. So the plan is to collect the x terms, clear the loose number, then divide.
Rekha is 5 years older than Madhavi, and their ages add up to 25 years. We want both ages.
Let's give the letter x to the younger girl. Who is that?

ask.ifNot: Rekha is 5 years older, so Rekha has the bigger age. The younger one is Madhavi.

beats.say: So Madhavi is x. And Rekha, 5 years older, is x plus 5.
Their ages add up to 25. x and x make 2 x, so 2 x plus 5 equals 25.
We want the 2 x by itself. So what should we do about the 5 that is added on?

ask.ifNot: Adding 5 is undone by taking 5 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: Take away 5 on the left, and 5 on the right as well. That leaves 2 x equals 25 minus 5, which is 20.
Now 2 x is 2 lots of x. To find just one x, we divide both sides by 2.
20 divided by 2 is 10. Madhavi is 10 years old.
Rekha is 5 years older. 10 plus 5 is 15. So Rekha is 15 and Madhavi is 10.
Check. 15 plus 10 is 25, and 15 is 5 more than 10. Careful when you pick the choice: one has the right numbers with the names swapped. Rekha must be the older one.
For two ages: give the letter to the younger, write the older from it, add, and solve.
Here we turn words into an equation. A number, when multiplied by 4, gives 20.
The number is unknown, so let's call it x.
Multiplied by 4. Which piece of maths says that about x?

ask.ifNot: Multiplied means times. So it is x times 4.

beats.say: x times 4. Now the word gives. It tells us what the result is, so it turns into the equals sign.
So what goes on the other side of the equals sign?

ask.ifNot: The sentence says the result is 20. Nothing has been turned upside down, so it is plain 20.

beats.say: x times 4 equals 20. In the choices, the times sign is written as a little star.
Test it with a number. 5 times 4 is 20. So x would be 5, and the equation says exactly what the sentence says.
Careful: the 4 and the 20 must stay where the sentence put them. Swap them and you describe a different number. So translate each phrase in order.
Words into an equation again. A number is subtracted from 15, and we get 4.

board.text: A number is subtracted from 15, we get 4

beats.say: Call the number x. Now the tricky part: subtracted from 15. Try it with a real number. If 3 is subtracted from 15, what do we write?

ask.ifNot: Subtracted from 15 means we start with 15 and take the number away. So the 15 comes first: 15 minus 3.

beats.say: So we start with 15 and take away. With 3 it is 15 minus 3. With our unknown number, it is 15 minus x.
Careful, this is the classic trap. The words name the number first, but the maths puts the 15 first. x minus 15 would mean taking 15 away from the number.
We get 4 means the result equals 4. So the equation is 15 minus x equals 4.
Let's test our equation. Which number, taken away from 15, leaves 4?

ask.ifNot: Count up from 4 to 15, or work out 15 minus 4. Both give 11.

beats.say: 15 minus 11 is 4. So the equation works, with x as 11.
So when you read subtracted from, start with the number that comes after the word from. Then take the other one away.
6 x plus 8 equals 4 x plus 18. Notice that x appears on both sides of the equals sign.
We want all the x terms on one side. Which move does that?

ask.ifNot: Whatever we do, we do to both sides. Taking 4 x from both sides clears the x from the right, and still leaves some on the left.

beats.say: Take 4 x from both sides. On the left, 6 x minus 4 x is 2 x. On the right, the 4 x is gone.
The 8 is added on, so to undo it we take 8 from both sides. That leaves 2 x equals 18 minus 8, which is 10.
Nearly there. 2 x means 2 times x. What undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So we divide both sides by 2.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide by 2.
10 divided by 2 is 5. So x equals 5.
Check both sides with x as 5. Left: 6 times 5, plus 8, is 38. Right: 4 times 5, plus 18, is 38. Both sides agree.
Careful not to stop at 2 x equals 10 and say 10. That is 2 lots of x. Collect the x terms, clear the loose number, then divide.
Here is our equation. y times 6 equals 36 divided by 6. Notice there is a sum waiting on the right hand side.
What should we do first?

ask.ifNot: The right hand side is not finished yet. 36 divided by 6 is a sum we can simply work out. Do that first, and the equation gets much shorter.

beats.say: 36 divided by 6 is 6. So the equation is really y times 6 equals 6.
y times 6 gives 6. What undoes times 6?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 6, we divide both sides by 6.

beats.say: Divide both sides by 6. 6 divided by 6 is 1. So y equals 1.
Does 1 feel like an odd answer? It is fine. 1 times any number leaves it unchanged, so 1 times 6 is 6, and both sides match.
Careful: the slip here is to see 36 and pick it, or to stop at 6. But 6 is the value of the right hand side, not the value of y.
So: tidy each side first, then undo what is being done to the letter.
Here is an expression with three letters: 7 a, plus 3 b, minus c. We know that a is 1, b is 2 and c is 3.
What does 3 b mean, when b is 2?

ask.ifNot: A number written right beside a letter means times. So 3 b is 3 times b, and b is 2.

beats.say: So swap each letter for its number. 7 times 1, plus 3 times 2, minus 3.
Which parts do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times comes before plus and minus. So first work out 7 times 1 and 3 times 2, and only then add and subtract.

beats.say: 7 times 1 is 7, and 3 times 2 is 6. So now we have 7, plus 6, minus 3.
7 plus 6 is 13, and 13 minus 3 is 10.
So the value is 10.
Careful with the lonely c at the end. It has no number in front, so it is just 1 c. We take away 3, once.
Check by going in a different order. 7 minus 3 is 4, and 4 plus 6 is 10 again.
Swap the letters for their numbers, do the times first, then add and subtract from left to right.
Two letters this time. 16 x minus 7 y equals 77. But we are told that x is 7, so only y is unknown.
x is 7. So what does 16 x become?

ask.ifNot: 16 x means 16 times x. A number written next to a letter is multiplying it. So with x as 7, it is 16 times 7.

beats.say: Put 7 in place of x. Careful: only the x becomes 7. The 7 in front of the y stays just as it is.
16 times 7 is 112. So 112 minus 7 y equals 77.
112, take away something, leaves 77. How big is that something?

ask.ifNot: If taking 7 y away from 112 leaves 77, then 7 y is the gap between 112 and 77. That is 112 minus 77.

beats.say: So 7 y equals 112 minus 77, which is 35.
7 y means 7 times y, so we divide both sides by 7. 35 divided by 7 is 5. So y equals 5.
Check. 16 times 7 is 112, and 7 times 5 is 35. 112 minus 35 is 77. It works.
When you are given the value of one letter, put it in straight away. Then you have an ordinary equation in the other letter.
x is 3 and y is 2. We want the value of 3 x, minus 5 y, plus 7.
Start with the 5 y. What does it mean when y is 2?

ask.ifNot: A number written right beside a letter means times. So 5 y is 5 times y, which is 5 times 2.

beats.say: So swap the letters for their numbers. 3 x becomes 3 times 3, and 5 y becomes 5 times 2.
Times first. 3 times 3 is 9, and 5 times 2 is 10. So we have 9, minus 10, plus 7.
Now a puzzle. 9 minus 10: we cannot take 10 from 9 without dipping below zero. What can we do?

choices: Add the 7 first, then take away 10
ask.ifNot: We may not swap a take-away round: 10 minus 9 is a different sum. But the plus 7 is waiting, and adding first is allowed.

beats.say: 9 plus 7 is 16. Then 16 minus 10 is 6.
It is like money. You have 9 rupees, you owe 10, and then you are given 7 more. You end up with 6.
If you know numbers below zero, the straight way works too. 9 minus 10 is minus 1, and minus 1 plus 7 is 6.
The slip to avoid is adding the 10 and the 7 first and taking all of that away. The minus belongs only to the 10.
Swap letters for numbers and do the times first. Then, if a take-away looks stuck, add the plus parts before you subtract.
x is 0 and y is 2. One of these four expressions comes to exactly 10, and we have to find which.

board.text: x = 0, y = 2. Which has the value 10?
A: 3x + 2y   B: 5y + x   C: 3y − x   D: x + y

beats.say: Choice A starts with 3 x, and x is 0. What is 3 times 0?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 0 means 3 lots of nothing. That is still nothing: 0.

beats.say: So in A, the 3 x part is 0. Then 2 y is 2 times 2, which is 4. And 0 plus 4 is 4. Not 10.
B starts with 5 y. What does 5 y mean when y is 2?

ask.ifNot: A number written right beside a letter means times. So 5 y is 5 times y, and with y as 2 that is 5 times 2.

beats.say: 5 times 2 is 10. Then we add x, which adds 0. So B is exactly 10. This one works.
Let's make sure of the other two. C: 3 times 2 is 6, and taking away 0 leaves 6.
And D is 0 plus 2, which is just 2.
Only B reaches 10.
Careful with a 0. Multiplying by 0 wipes that part out completely. But adding or taking away 0 changes nothing at all.
When the choices are expressions, put the numbers into each one and work it out. Then pick the one that hits the target.
Here is a rule that x and y must obey: 2 x, minus 2 y, equals 2. Four pairs are offered, and only one of them obeys the rule.
How can we find out which pair works?

choices: Try each pair in the rule
ask.ifNot: A rule is tested by trying it. Put each pair in place of x and y, and see whether the left side really comes to 2.

beats.say: Pair A: x is 1 and y is 1. 2 times 1 is 2, and 2 times 1 is 2 again. 2 minus 2 is 0, not 2.
Pair B: x is 2 and y is 1. 2 times 2 is 4, and 2 times 1 is 2. 4 minus 2 is 2. That obeys the rule.
Check the last two as well. Pair C: x is 1 and y is 2. That gives 2 minus 4, which drops below zero. So it cannot be 2.
Pair D: x is 4 and y is 2. 2 times 4 is 8, and 2 times 2 is 4. 8 minus 4 is 4. Too big.
So only pair B fits: x is 2 and y is 1.
Now a shortcut. 2 x minus 2 y is double the gap between x and y. If double the gap is 2, what is the gap?

ask.ifNot: Double the gap is 2, so the gap itself is half of 2. That is 1.

beats.say: So x must be exactly 1 more than y. And 2 is 1 more than 1.
Careful with pair C. Its numbers are 1 apart too, but there y is the bigger one. In a take-away, the order matters.
To test a rule, put the numbers in and see. And when both parts are doubled, look at the gap between the letters.
We multiply 4 by the whole bracket, x plus y. What does that come to?
Think of the bracket as a bag holding one x and one y. 4 times the bracket means 4 of those bags.
Count what is inside all the bags. How many x, and how many y?

ask.ifNot: Every bag has one x and one y inside. There are 4 bags, so there are 4 of each: 4 x and 4 y.

beats.say: So the 4 multiplies both things in the bracket: 4 times x, and 4 times y.
4 times the bracket is 4 x plus 4 y.
Careful: the classic slip is to multiply only the first one and write 4 x plus y. The y is in the bracket too, so it gets its 4 as well.
Let's test it with numbers. Say x is 2 and y is 5. The bracket is 7, and 4 times 7 is 28.
Now our answer. 4 times 2 is 8, and 4 times 5 is 20. 8 plus 20 is 28. A match.
And the slip, 4 x plus y, would give 8 plus 5, which is only 13. No match.
A number outside a bracket multiplies everything inside it. Draw the arcs, and nobody gets left out.
a is 2, b is 4 and c is 1. We want the expression that comes to zero.

board.text: a = 2, b = 4, c = 1. Which has the value zero?
A: a + b + c   B: a − b + 2c   C: 2c + 2a − 2b

beats.say: A is all adding: 2 plus 4 plus 1 is 7. Adding these numbers can never bring us down to zero.
B is a, minus b, plus 2 c. With the numbers in, which sum is that?

ask.ifNot: Swap each letter for its number, and keep the signs where they are. 2 c means 2 times c, which is 2 times 1.

beats.say: 2 times 1 is 2. So B is 2, minus 4, plus 2.
2 minus 4 looks stuck, so think of it as in and out. In goes 2, and another 2, which is 4. Out goes 4. Nothing is left: zero.
B gives zero. But look at C before deciding. 2 times 1 is 2, 2 times 2 is 4, and 2 times 4 is 8.
In goes 2 plus 4, which is 6. Out goes 8. We take out 2 more than we put in, so C lands 2 below zero. Close, but not zero.
So the answer is B.
Careful with None of these. It is only right when every other choice has been tried and has missed. Here B hits zero.
Put the numbers in, then compare what goes in with what comes out. Equal amounts in and out means zero.
We have a rule: a equals b times c. We are told a is 15 and b is 5, and we want a plus c.
Put in the numbers we know. a becomes 15, and b becomes 5.
15 equals 5 times c. How do we find c?

ask.ifNot: 5 times c makes 15. To undo times 5, we divide by 5. So c is 15 divided by 5.

beats.say: 15 divided by 5 is 3. So c is 3.
Are we finished?

choices: No, we still need a + c
ask.ifNot: Look back at the question. It asks for a plus c, not just c.

beats.say: Careful: finding c is only half the job. The question wants a plus c. a is 15 and c is 3, so 15 plus 3 is 18.
Check the rule with our numbers. b times c is 5 times 3, which is 15, and that is a. So c is right, and a plus c is 18.
So: put the known values into the rule, find the missing letter, and then answer the question that was asked.
Here is a formula: D equals S times T. We know D is 70 and T is 10, and we want S.
Put the numbers we know into the formula. D becomes 70, and T becomes 10.
70 equals S times 10. Which move finds S?

ask.ifNot: S is being multiplied by 10. To undo times 10, we divide by 10. Multiplying again would only make the number bigger.

beats.say: Divide both sides by 10. 70 divided by 10 is 7. So S is 7.
Careful: the formula has a times sign in it, so it is tempting to multiply 70 by 10. But 70 is already the result of the multiplying. We are working backwards.
Check. Put 7 back in. 7 times 10 is 70, and that is D. It works.
With a formula, put in what you know. If the missing letter is being multiplied, divide to find it.
p is 5 and q is 6. We want the expression that has the same value as 3 p plus q.

board.text: p = 5, q = 6. Which has the same value as 3p + q?

beats.say: What do we need to do first?

choices: Pick the one that looks like 3p + q
ask.ifNot: We are hunting for a match. Before we can match anything, we need the target: the value of 3 p plus q.

beats.say: 3 times 5 is 15, and 15 plus 6 is 21. So 21 is our target.
A: 2 times 5 is 10, and 3 times 6 is 18. 10 plus 18 is 28. Too big.
B: 2 times 5 is 10, 2 times 6 is 12, and then we take away p, which is 5. 10 plus 12, minus 5, is 17. Too small.
C: 5 times 5 is 25. Add q, which is 6, then take away 10. 25 plus 6, minus 10, is 21. A match!
So C has the same value as 3 p plus q.
Careful: C looks nothing like 3 p plus q, and A looks much more like it. Looks do not matter here. Only the value does.
Here is why C works. It has 2 more p than the target, and 2 times 5 is 10. Then it takes that 10 straight back off.
Find the target value first. Then work out each choice and look for the same number.
g is 2 and h is 3. We want the expression whose value is greater than 10.

board.text: g = 2, h = 3. Which has a value greater than 10?
A: 2g + 2h   B: g + h − 3   C: gh − 6   D: 2g + 3h

beats.say: A: 2 times 2 is 4, and 2 times 3 is 6. 4 plus 6 is 10.
A comes to exactly 10. Is that greater than 10?

choices: No, it must be more than 10
ask.ifNot: Greater than 10 means past 10, not on it. 10 is equal to 10, so A just misses.

beats.say: That is the trap in this question. A lands right on 10, and it is the first one you try. So we keep going.
B: 2 plus 3 is 5, and 5 minus 3 is 2. Far too small.
C has g h: two letters side by side. What does g h mean?

ask.ifNot: Letters written side by side are multiplied, just like a number beside a letter. So g h is g times h, which is 2 times 3.

beats.say: So C is 2 times 3, which is 6, minus 6. That is 0.
D: 2 times 2 is 4, and 3 times 3 is 9. 4 plus 9 is 13, and 13 is greater than 10.
So the answer is D.
Work out every choice, then read the question's words with care. Greater than means strictly more.
a is 3, b is 1 and c is 0. We want the value of 3 a, plus 2 b, minus the bracket a plus b, times c.
Swap in the numbers. 3 times 3, plus 2 times 1, minus the bracket 3 plus 1, times 0.
Brackets first. 3 plus 1 is 4. So the last part is 4 times 0.
What is 4 times 0?

ask.ifNot: Times 0 means no lots at all. 4 lots of nothing is nothing. Anything times 0 is 0.

beats.say: So the whole last part disappears: we are taking away 0. Careful, though. Only that part is 0, not the whole expression.
Now the other two parts. 3 times 3 is 9, and 2 times 1 is 2.
9 plus 2 is 11, and taking away 0 changes nothing. The value is 11.
Check the whole line in one go, and it agrees.
Swap letters for numbers. Brackets first, then times, then plus and minus. And when you spot a times 0, that whole piece is 0.
Here the letter p stands for a number below zero: minus 3. We want the value of minus 3 p, plus 2 q, plus 3 r.
Swap in the numbers. Put the minus 3 in a bracket, so that its sign does not get lost.
Take the easy parts first. 2 times 2 is 4, and 3 times 4 is 12.
Now the first part: minus 3, times minus 3. What is it?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 3 is 9. Each minus sign flips the answer to the other side of zero. Two flips bring it back, so it is plus 9.

beats.say: Here is a way to see it. p is a debt of 3. Minus 3 p means taking that debt away 3 times. Lose three debts of 3 and you are 9 better off.
Careful: this is the trap. With only one flip you get minus 9, and the total comes out far too small.
Now add the three parts. 9 plus 4 is 13, and 13 plus 12 is 25.
So the value is 25.
Check by adding in another order: 12 plus 4 plus 9 is 25 again.
Bracket any number below zero when you swap it in. Minus times minus gives plus. Then add up the parts.
Three letters, and two of them stand for numbers below zero. We want the expression that comes to minus 14.

board.text: l = 2, m = −3, n = −1. Which has the value −14?

beats.say: Two sign rules will carry us through. A plus number times a minus number gives a minus. And taking away a minus number is the same as adding.
A: 2 times 2 is 4. 3 times minus 3 is minus 9. And taking away minus 1 adds 1. So 4, minus 9, plus 1: that is minus 4, not minus 14.
Now B, one part at a time. Minus 2 times 2 is minus 4. And 4 times minus 3 is minus 12.
The last part of B takes away 2 n. 2 times minus 1 is minus 2. So what does taking away minus 2 do?

ask.ifNot: Taking away a debt leaves you better off. So taking away minus 2 is the same as adding 2.

beats.say: So B is minus 4, minus 12, plus 2. Down 4 and down 12 is down 16. Then up 2 leaves us at minus 14.
B hits minus 14. A quick look at the others: C is 10, plus 12, plus 1, which is 23. D is minus 2, plus 6, minus 1, which is 3. Both are above zero.
So the answer is B.
The trap is the last part of B. Forget that taking away a minus adds, and you go down 2 instead of up 2, and miss the target.
With numbers below zero, slow down at every sign. Bracket them when you swap them in, and remember that taking away a minus adds.
x and y must obey this rule: 2 x, minus 2 y, equals 6. Four pairs are offered. We could test all four, but let's look for something clever first.
Both parts on the left are doubled: double x, take away double y. That is the same as doubling the gap between x and y.
So double the gap is 6. What is the gap between x and y?

ask.ifNot: Double the gap is 6, so the gap is half of 6. Half of 6 is 3.

beats.say: So x must be exactly 3 more than y.
Now run down the pairs and look at the gaps. A: 6 minus 4 is 2. B: 7 minus 2 is 5. C: 8 minus 6 is 2. D: 6 minus 3 is 3.
Which pair has the gap we need?

ask.ifNot: We need a gap of exactly 3, with x the bigger one. Only 6 and 3 are 3 apart.

beats.say: Now test that pair properly in the rule. 2 times 6 is 12, and 2 times 3 is 6. 12 minus 6 is 6. It works.
So x is 6 and y is 3.
Careful with pair A. It comes to 4, which is close to 6 but not equal. With an equals sign, close does not count.
When both parts of a rule are doubled, halve everything in your head and look at the gap. Then test your pair in the real rule.
x is 9 and y is 2. Three of these expressions come to 14. We want the odd one out: the one that does not.

board.text: x = 9, y = 2. Which is NOT equal to 14?

beats.say: A: 9 plus 2 plus 3 is 14.
A comes to 14. So is A our answer?

choices: No, we want the one that misses 14
ask.ifNot: Read the question again: it asks for the one that is not equal to 14. A hits 14, so A is safe, and we move on.

beats.say: That is the trap in a NOT question. The first choice that hits 14 feels like the answer. Here, hitting 14 means we cross it out.
B: 2 times 2 is 4. Then 9 plus 4 plus 1 is 14 again. Cross it out.
C: 2 times 9 is 18, and 2 times 2 is 4. 18 minus 4 is 14. Cross it out too.
Only D is left. But we never guess, so work it out: 18 plus 4, minus 7, is 15. Not 14.
So D is the one that is not equal to 14.
In a NOT question, work out every choice, cross out the ones that hit the target, and keep the one that misses.
x is 5, y is 3, and z is a number below zero: minus 2. We want the expression equal to 12.

board.text: x = 5, y = 3, z = −2. Which is equal to 12?
C: 4x − 3y + z   D: x + y + z

beats.say: Start with the simplest one, D. 5 plus 3 is 8, and adding minus 2 takes 2 off. That is 6, not 12.
A ends by taking away 2 z. 2 times minus 2 is minus 4. So what does taking away minus 4 do?

ask.ifNot: Taking away a debt of 4 leaves you 4 better off. So taking away minus 4 is the same as adding 4.

beats.say: So A is 10, plus 9, plus 4. That is 23, far past 12.
B: 5 times 5 is 25, and 3 times 3 is 9. Then 2 times minus 2 is minus 4, and adding minus 4 takes 4 off.
25 minus 9 is 16, and 16 minus 4 is 12. That is our target.
And C, to be sure: 20, minus 9, minus 2, is 9. Not 12.
So the answer is B.
Careful with z. Treat it as plus 2 and B comes out too big. The minus sign travels with the number wherever z goes.
Swap in the numbers, brackets round the one below zero. Adding a minus pulls the total down, and taking away a minus pushes it up.
3 times the bracket x plus y. We want to write it without the bracket.
Think of the bracket as a bag holding one x and one y. 3 times the bracket means 3 of those bags.
Count what is inside all the bags. How many x, and how many y?

ask.ifNot: Every bag has one x and one y inside. There are 3 bags, so there are 3 of each: 3 x and 3 y.

beats.say: So the 3 multiplies both things in the bracket: 3 times x, and 3 times y.
3 times the bracket is 3 x plus 3 y.
Careful: the classic slip is to multiply only the first one and write 3 x plus y. The y is in the bracket too, so it gets its 3 as well.
Let's test it with numbers. Say x is 4 and y is 1. The bracket is 5, and 3 times 5 is 15.
Now our answer. 3 times 4 is 12, and 3 times 1 is 3. 12 plus 3 is 15. A match.
And the slip, 3 x plus y, would give 12 plus 1, which is only 13. No match.
Outside the bracket means times everything inside. One arc to each term, every time.
a is 2, b is 3 and c is 1. One of these may come to zero. Let's test them.

board.text: a = 2, b = 3, c = 1. Which has the value zero?
A: a + b + c   B: a − b + 2c   C: 2c + 2a − 2b

beats.say: A: 2 plus 3 plus 1 is 6. It is all adding, so it had no chance of being zero.
B: a, minus b, plus 2 c. That is 2, minus 3, plus 2 times 1.
In goes 2 and another 2, which is 4. Out goes 3. So 1 is left over. Close, but not zero.
Two misses. Is it time to choose None of these?

ask.ifNot: None of these is only safe when every other choice has been tried. C is still waiting, so we test it.

beats.say: C: 2 c, plus 2 a, minus 2 b. 2 times 1 is 2, 2 times 2 is 4, and 2 times 3 is 6.
In goes 2 plus 4, which is 6. Out goes 6. Nothing is left: zero.
There is a neat reason too. Everything in C is doubled. Inside, c plus a is 3 and b is 3, so they cancel. And double nothing is still nothing.
Test every choice before you trust None of these. And to spot a zero, look for what goes in being equal to what comes out.
Here is a formula with three letters: a equals b divided by c. We know a is 3 and b is 18, and we want a plus c.
We cannot add yet, because c is still hiding. So first, put the numbers we know into the formula.
3 equals 18 divided by c. So 18 has been split into equal parts, and each part is 3. How do we find c?

ask.ifNot: Ask how many 3s fit into 18. That is a division: 18 divided by 3.

beats.say: 18 divided by 3 is 6. So c is 6.
Careful: 6 is only c, not the answer. The question asks for a plus c.
a is 3 and c is 6. 3 plus 6 is 9.
Check c in the formula. 18 divided by 6 is 3, and a is 3. It fits.
So when a formula has a missing letter, put in what you know, find the missing one, and then answer what was really asked.
a equals b times c. We know a is 24 and c is one half. We need b minus a.
Put in what we know. 24 equals b times one half.
b times one half means half of b. So half of b is 24. What is b?

ask.ifNot: If half of b is 24, then b is two of those halves. 24 and 24 make 48. Halving 24 gives 12, but that goes the other way.

beats.say: Half of b is 24, so b is 24 times 2, which is 48.
Careful: the trap is to halve 24. But b times one half is 24, so b has to be bigger than 24, not smaller.
Now the question: b minus a. 48 minus 24 is 24.
Check b in the formula. 48 times one half is 24, and a is 24. It works.
Put in what you know, find the missing letter, and then do what the question asks with it.
L equals M times N. We know M is 13 and L is 78, and we must find N.
Put the numbers in place of their letters. 78 equals 13 times N.
13 times some number makes 78. What undoes times 13?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 13, we divide by 13.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 13. N is 78 divided by 13.
Count up in 13s. 13 times 5 is 65, and one more 13 makes 78. So 6 lots of 13 make 78.
So N is 6.
Careful not to add or multiply the 78 and the 13. N has to be small, because 13 times N is only 78.
Check: 13 times 6 is 78, and that matches L.
When a formula says one number times another, you find a missing one by dividing.
169 times 1 over x equals 13. First we find x. Then the question wants 3 x.
169 times 1 over x is the same as 169 divided by x. So 169 divided by x equals 13.
169 is split into x equal parts, and each part is 13. How do we find x?

ask.ifNot: Ask how many 13s fit into 169. That is 169 divided by 13.

beats.say: 13 times 10 is 130, and 13 times 3 is 39. 130 plus 39 is 169, so 13 lots of 13 make 169.
So x is 13.
Careful: x is not the answer yet. The question wants 3 x, which means 3 times x.
3 times 13 is 39.
Check x in the equation. 13 times 13 is 169, so 169 divided by 13 really is 13.
Find the letter first. Then read the question again to see what it really wants.
625 over x equals 25 over 1. First we find x. Then the question wants 4 x.
25 over 1 is just 25. So 625 divided by x equals 25.
625 is split into x equal parts, and each part is 25. How do we find x?

ask.ifNot: Ask how many 25s fit into 625. That is 625 divided by 25.

beats.say: 25 times 20 is 500, and 25 times 5 is 125. 500 plus 125 is 625, so 25 lots of 25 make 625.
So x is 25.
Careful: x is not the answer yet. The question wants 4 x, which means 4 times x.
4 times 25 is 100.
Check x in the equation. 25 times 25 is 625, so 625 divided by 25 really is 25.
Find the letter first. Then read the question again to see what it really wants.
Four letters, each one built from the next, and then an expression that uses them. It looks like a tangle, so we look for the loose end.
We know that a is 6. Which letter can we work out next?

ask.ifNot: To find x we need y, and to find y we need z. But z only needs a, and we know a. So z comes first.

beats.say: z is a plus 6. That is 6 plus 6, which is 12.
y is z plus 1: 12 plus 1 is 13. And x is y minus 2: 13 minus 2 is 11.
Now put them into the expression. x is 11, a is 6, and inside the bracket y times a is 13 times 6.
What do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Brackets always come first. And inside the bracket, the times comes before the minus.

beats.say: Inside the bracket: 13 times 6. 10 sixes are 60 and 3 sixes are 18, so 78. Then 78 minus 3 is 75.
Now we have 11, plus 6 times 75. Careful: times before plus. Adding the 11 and the 6 first is the trap.
6 times 75. 6 times 70 is 420, and 6 times 5 is 30. That makes 450.
Last of all, add the 11. 450 plus 11 is 461.
A quick check on size. 6 times 75 is 450, so the answer has to be a little more than 450. And 461 is.
Start from the letter you know and work along the chain. Then brackets first, times next, and plus last.
It is 9 o'clock. We want the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand.

board.text: Angle between the hands at 9 o'clock = ?

beats.say: First, where are the two hands at 9 o'clock?

choices: Hour hand on 9, minute hand on 12
Hour hand on 12, minute hand on 9
ask.ifNot: On the hour, the long minute hand always points straight up at 12. The short hour hand points at the hour, which is 9.

beats.say: Now, the clock face is a full turn, 360 degrees, shared equally by 12 gaps between the numbers. 12 times 30 is 360, so each gap is 30 degrees.
How many gaps are there from 9 round to 12? Count the hops on the board.

ask.ifNot: Count the hops, not the numbers. 9 to 10 is one, 10 to 11 is two, 11 to 12 is three. So there are 3 gaps.

beats.say: 3 gaps of 30 degrees each. 3 times 30 is 90.
So at 9 o'clock the hands are 90 degrees apart.
That is a right angle, a perfect square corner. You can see it on the clock: one hand straight up, the other straight across.
Careful not to count the numbers 9, 10, 11 and 12 and call it 4. There are four numbers, but only 3 gaps between them.
Another way to see it: from 9 to 12 is a quarter of the clock, and a quarter of 360 is 90.
For clock angles on the hour, each gap is 30 degrees. Count the gaps between the hands and multiply.
We want the complementary angle of 45 and a half degrees. So first, what does complementary mean?
Two angles are complementary when they add up to how much?

ask.ifNot: Complementary angles fit together to make a square corner, and a square corner is 90 degrees. The pair that makes 180 has a different name: supplementary.

beats.say: So 45 and a half, plus our missing angle, makes 90.
Let's subtract in two easy steps. First the whole degrees: 90 minus 45 is 45.
But we still have to take away the extra half. What is 45 minus a half?

ask.ifNot: Taking a half away makes the number smaller, so we drop below 45. Break one whole into two halves: that is 44 and two halves. Take one half away and 44 and a half is left.

beats.say: Careful: this is where it slips. Stopping at 45 forgets the half. One whole is two halves, so 45 minus a half is 44 and a half.
So the complementary angle is 44 and a half degrees.
Check by adding. The two halves make 1 whole. 45 and 44 make 89, and 1 more is 90.
And don't mix up the two words. Taking the angle from 180 would give its supplementary angle, which is a different question.
Complementary means the two angles make 90 degrees. Subtract the whole degrees first, then deal with the half.
We want the supplementary angle of 100 and a half degrees. So first, what does supplementary mean?
Two angles are supplementary when they add up to how much?

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees. The pair that makes 90 is called complementary.

beats.say: So 100 and a half, plus our missing angle, makes 180.
Let's subtract in two easy steps. First the whole degrees: 180 minus 100 is 80.
But we still have to take away the extra half. What is 80 minus a half?

ask.ifNot: Taking a half away makes the number smaller, so we drop below 80. Break one whole into two halves: that is 79 and two halves. Take one half away and 79 and a half is left.

beats.say: Careful: this is where it slips. Stopping at 80 forgets the half. One whole is two halves, so 80 minus a half is 79 and a half.
So the supplementary angle is 79 and a half degrees.
Check by adding. The two halves make 1 whole. 100 and 79 make 179, and 1 more is 180.
Notice the word had to be supplementary here. 100 and a half is already bigger than a square corner, so it can have no complementary angle at all.
Supplementary means the two angles make 180 degrees. Subtract the whole degrees first, then deal with the half.
Two angles are equal, and they are also complementary. We want the size of each one.
Start with the long word. Complementary angles add up to how much?

ask.ifNot: Complementary angles fit together to make a square corner, and a square corner is 90 degrees. The pair that makes 180 has a different name: supplementary.

beats.say: So the two angles together make 90 degrees. And they are equal, so it is the same angle twice.
Two equal angles share 90 degrees. How do we find each one?

ask.ifNot: Sharing equally between two means halving. So we divide the 90 degrees by 2.

beats.say: Half of 90 is 45. So each angle is 45 degrees.
Careful not to answer 90. That is what the two angles make together, not the size of each one.
Picture a square corner cut exactly down the middle. Check: 45 plus 45 is 90.
Turn the word into its number, 90 for complementary. Then two equal angles each get half.
Two angles are equal, and they are also supplementary. We want the size of each one.
Start with the long word. Supplementary angles add up to how much?

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees. The pair that makes 90 is called complementary.

beats.say: So the two angles together make 180 degrees. And they are equal, so it is the same angle twice.
Two equal angles share 180 degrees. How do we find each one?

ask.ifNot: Sharing equally between two means halving. So we divide the 180 degrees by 2.

beats.say: Half of 180 is 90. So each angle is 90 degrees.
Careful not to halve 90 here. That would be for complementary angles. Supplementary angles share 180.
Picture a pole standing straight up on flat ground, with a square corner on each side. Check: 90 plus 90 is 180.
Turn the word into its number, 180 for supplementary. Then two equal angles each get half.
Two angles form a linear pair, and one of them is 90 degrees. We want to know what kind of angle the other one is.

board.text: Linear pair: one angle = 90°. The other is what kind?

beats.say: First the words. A linear pair is two angles side by side on a straight line. What do they add up to?

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn. A full turn is 360 degrees, so the two angles of a linear pair share 180 degrees.

beats.say: So 90, plus the other angle, makes 180.
180 minus 90 is 90. The other angle is 90 degrees too.
And what do we call an angle of exactly 90 degrees?

ask.ifNot: Acute angles are smaller than 90 degrees, and obtuse angles are bigger than 90. Exactly 90 degrees, a square corner, is a right angle.

beats.say: Here are the three names together. Less than 90 is acute. Exactly 90 is right. More than 90, up to 180, is obtuse.
So the other angle is a right angle.

board.text: The other angle is a right angle (90°)

beats.say: It can feel as if the partner must be a different kind. Usually it is: a small acute angle has a wide obtuse partner. But 90 is exactly half of 180, so here both are the same.
Picture a pole standing straight up on flat ground: a square corner on each side. And 90 plus 90 is 180.
For a linear pair, take the angle you know from 180. Then name what you get: acute, right or obtuse.
Two angles sit side by side on a straight line. That is a linear pair. One of them is acute, and we want to know what kind the other must be.

board.text: Linear pair: one angle is acute. The other?

beats.say: First, the key fact. A straight line is a half turn, so the two angles of a linear pair always add up to 180 degrees.

board.text: Linear pair: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: Acute means small: less than 90 degrees. Let's try one. Say the acute angle is 50 degrees. How do we find its partner?

ask.ifNot: The two angles share 180 degrees between them. So the partner is whatever is left when we take 50 away from 180.

beats.say: 180 minus 50 is 130. That is more than 90 degrees, so the partner is an obtuse angle.
Was that just luck? Try an acute angle close to 90, say 80 degrees. Its partner is 180 minus 80, which is 100. Still more than 90.
Here is why it always works. 90 and 90 make 180. If one angle takes less than its 90, the other has to take more than 90 to make up the total.
So the other angle is always obtuse.
The trap is to say acute, because the two angles are a pair. But two acute angles together are less than 180, so they could never fill a straight line.
Remember it this way: on a straight line, a small angle always has a big partner.
We have three pairs of angles, and we are hunting for a supplementary pair. There may not be one at all.
First, what does supplementary mean? What must the two angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 90 degrees is for complementary angles. Supplementary angles fill a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So our test is simple. Add the pair. If the total is exactly 180, it is supplementary.

board.text: Supplementary: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: Pair A. 70 plus 20 is 90. That is a right angle, not a straight line. So A is out.
Pair B. 50 plus 50 is 100. Not 180 either.
Pair C looks tempting, because it has 180 in it. But we need the total to be 180. What is 100 plus 180?

ask.ifNot: Add the two angles together: 100, and 180 more. That goes well past 180.

beats.say: 280. Far too big. So C is out as well.
None of the three pairs adds up to 180. So the answer is: none of these.
It can feel odd to pick none of these. But we tested every pair, so we can be sure.
The method: for supplementary, add the pair and look for 180. Check every choice before you decide.
Three pairs of angles. One of them is a complementary pair, and we are going to find it.
What do complementary angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is for supplementary angles. Complementary angles fit together into one right angle, and a right angle is 90 degrees.

beats.say: So we add each pair and look for exactly 90.

board.text: Complementary: the two angles add up to 90°

beats.say: Pair A. 80 plus 20 is 100. Close, but 100 is not 90. A is out.
Pair B. 70 plus 110 is 180. That pair is supplementary, which is the other word. Easy to mix up! B is out.
Pair C. 50 plus 40. What do we get?

ask.ifNot: Add the tens: 5 tens and 4 tens make 9 tens.

beats.say: 90, exactly. So 50 degrees and 40 degrees are complementary.
A way to remember: C for complementary, C for corner. A corner is a right angle, 90 degrees.
So: add the pair. 90 means complementary, 180 means supplementary.
Two angles add up to 180 degrees. There is a special name for a pair like that.

board.text: Two angles add up to 180°. They are called ...?

beats.say: Here is a pair like that: 120 degrees and 60 degrees. Side by side they make a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.
Two names get mixed up all the time: complementary and supplementary. One goes with 90 degrees, the other with 180. Which is the name for 180?

ask.ifNot: Complementary goes with a corner, 90 degrees. The other word, supplementary, goes with a straight line, 180 degrees.

beats.say: Supplementary. Here is the trick: S for supplementary, S for straight line. And C for complementary, C for corner, which is 90 degrees.
What about the other two choices? Adjacent just means the angles are neighbours, sharing an arm. Their total can be anything.

board.text: Adjacent: next to each other, any total

beats.say: And vertically opposite angles face each other where two lines cross. They are equal, but they need not add up to 180.

board.text: Vertically opposite: across a crossing, equal

beats.say: So two angles with a sum of 180 degrees are called supplementary angles.
Whenever you see a total of 180, think straight line, think supplementary.
Two angles add up to 90 degrees. There is a special name for a pair like that.

board.text: Two angles add up to 90°. They are called ...?

beats.say: Here is a pair like that: 60 degrees and 30 degrees. Together they fill a square corner, and a square corner is a right angle, 90 degrees.
Two names get mixed up all the time: complementary and supplementary. One goes with 90 degrees, the other with 180. Which one goes with 90?

ask.ifNot: Supplementary goes with a straight line, 180 degrees. The other word, complementary, goes with a corner, 90 degrees.

beats.say: Complementary. Here is the trick: C for complementary, C for corner. And S for supplementary, S for straight line, which is 180 degrees.
What about the other two choices? Adjacent just means the angles are neighbours, sharing an arm. Their total can be anything.

board.text: Adjacent: next to each other, any total

beats.say: And vertically opposite angles face each other where two lines cross. They are equal, but they need not add up to 90.

board.text: Vertically opposite: across a crossing, equal

beats.say: So two angles with a sum of 90 degrees are called complementary angles.
Whenever you see a total of 90, think corner, think complementary.
Picture a compass. We want the angle between East and South.
A compass is a full circle. How many degrees are there in a full turn?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is only a half turn, a straight line. All the way round, back to where you started, is twice that.

beats.say: 360 degrees. And the 4 main directions, North, East, South and West, cut that circle into 4 equal parts.

board.text: N, E, S, W: 4 equal parts

beats.say: So each part is 360 divided by 4. That is 90 degrees, a quarter turn.
Now, East and South. Are they next-door neighbours on the compass, or is there another main direction between them?

ask.ifNot: Go round the compass in order: North, East, South, West. East and South come one straight after the other.

beats.say: They are neighbours. So turning from East to South is exactly 1 quarter turn.
The angle between East and South is 90 degrees. A right angle.
Check with the half-way direction, South-East. From East to South-East is 45 degrees, and from South-East to South is another 45. Together, 90.
So for the main compass directions, neighbours are always a quarter turn apart: 90 degrees.
Picture a compass. We want the angle between West and North-East.
North-East is one of the half-way directions. With those included, how many directions are there around the compass?

ask.ifNot: There are 4 main directions, and one half-way direction sits between each pair of them. That makes 4 more.

beats.say: 8 directions, equally spaced around a full turn of 360 degrees.

board.text: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW: 8 directions

beats.say: So each step from one direction to the next is 360 divided by 8, which is 45 degrees.
Now count the steps from West to North-East, the short way, over the top. West to North-West, then to North, then to North-East. How many steps?

ask.ifNot: Count the arrows, not the names. West to North-West is 1, North-West to North is 2, North to North-East is 3.

beats.say: 3 steps of 45 degrees. 3 times 45 is 135. The angle is 135 degrees.
Why the short way? Going round the other way is 5 steps, and 5 times 45 is 225. The angle between two directions is the smaller one.
And a check: 135 plus 225 makes 360, the full turn. The two ways round fit together.
The trap is to say 90, by treating North-East as if it were North. West to North is 90, and then there are 45 more.
So: 45 degrees for every step on the compass. Count the steps, then multiply.
We need the complementary angle of 37 and a half degrees.
Complementary angles are partners. What do the two partners add up to?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is for supplementary angles. Complementary angles fit into one right angle, a square corner, and that is 90 degrees.

beats.say: So our angle and its partner make 90 degrees together. To find the partner, we take 37 and a half away from 90.
Let's do it in two small steps. First the whole part: 90 minus 37 is 53.
Now there is still a half to take away. What is 53 minus a half?

ask.ifNot: Taking away a half makes the number smaller than 53, but not a whole 1 smaller. So it lands between 52 and 53.

beats.say: 52 and a half. So the complementary angle is 52 and a half degrees.
Check by adding the partners. 37 and 52 make 89. The two halves make 1 more. And 89 plus 1 is 90.
Watch out: if you take it away from 180 instead, you are finding the supplementary angle, which is a different partner.
So: complementary means the pair makes 90. Take the angle away from 90, whole part first, then the fraction.
We need the supplementary angle of 98 and a quarter degrees.
Supplementary angles are partners. What do the two partners add up to?

ask.ifNot: 90 degrees is for complementary angles. Supplementary angles fill a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So the partner is 180 take away 98 and a quarter.
Whole part first. From 98 up to 100 is 2, and from 100 up to 180 is 80. So 180 minus 98 is 82.
Now take a quarter from 82. Break 1 whole off the 82: that leaves 81 and 4 quarters. Take 1 quarter away from the 4 quarters. What is left?

ask.ifNot: We had 81 and 4 quarters. One quarter goes, so 3 quarters stay, and the 81 does not change.

beats.say: 81 and three quarters. So the supplementary angle is 81 and three quarters degrees.
Check by adding. 98 and 81 make 179. A quarter and three quarters make 1 whole. And 179 plus 1 is 180.
The slip to watch is 81 and a quarter. The quarter is being taken away, so it cannot just be copied into the answer.
So: supplementary means the pair makes 180. Take away the whole part first, then the fraction.
It is exactly 9 o'clock. We want the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand.

board.text: Angle between the hands at 9 o'clock = ?

beats.say: First, where are the two hands pointing at 9 o'clock?

choices: hour hand at 12, minute hand at 9
hour hand at 9, minute hand at 12
ask.ifNot: At an exact hour, the long minute hand points straight up at 12. The short hour hand points at the hour, which is 9.

beats.say: Now the clock face. It is a full circle, 360 degrees, and the 12 numbers cut it into 12 equal gaps.
So each gap, from one number to the next, is 360 divided by 12. That is 30 degrees.
Now count the gaps between the hands, the short way round. From 9 to 10, 10 to 11, 11 to 12. How many gaps?

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps, not the numbers. 9 to 10 is 1, 10 to 11 is 2, 11 to 12 is 3.

beats.say: 3 gaps of 30 degrees each. 3 times 30 is 90. The angle is 90 degrees.
Check it another way. 3 gaps out of 12 is a quarter of the clock, and a quarter of 360 is 90. The hands make a perfect square corner.
Don't go the long way round, from 12 all the way down to 9. That is 9 gaps. The angle between the hands is the smaller one.
So for any exact hour: count the gaps between the hands, and multiply by 30 degrees.
It is exactly 4 o'clock. We want the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand.

board.text: Angle between the hands at 4 o'clock = ?

beats.say: First, where are the two hands pointing at 4 o'clock?

choices: hour hand at 12, minute hand at 4
hour hand at 4, minute hand at 12
ask.ifNot: At an exact hour, the long minute hand points straight up at 12. The short hour hand points at the hour, which is 4.

beats.say: Now the clock face. It is a full circle, 360 degrees, and the 12 numbers cut it into 12 equal gaps.
So each gap, from one number to the next, is 360 divided by 12. That is 30 degrees.
Now count the gaps between the hands, the short way round. From 12 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4. How many gaps?

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps, not the numbers. 12 to 1 is 1, 1 to 2 is 2, 2 to 3 is 3, 3 to 4 is 4.

beats.say: 4 gaps of 30 degrees each. 4 times 30 is 120. The angle is 120 degrees.
Does that look right? At 3 o'clock the hands make a square corner, 90 degrees. At 4 o'clock they are 1 gap wider, and 90 plus 30 is 120.
The slip here is to count the numbers 12, 1, 2, 3, 4 and get 5. We count the gaps between them, and there are 4.
So for any exact hour: count the gaps between the hands, and multiply by 30 degrees.
Two angles are equal, and they are supplementary. We want the size of each one.
Supplementary tells us the total. What do supplementary angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 90 degrees is the total for complementary angles. Supplementary angles fill a straight line, which is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So the two angles add up to 180. They are equal, so let's call each one x.
x plus x is 2 lots of x. So 2 x equals 180.
2 times x is 180. How do we get x on its own?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 2, we divide by 2, and we do it to both sides.

beats.say: Divide both sides by 2. Half of 180 is 90. So x is 90.
Each angle is 90 degrees, a right angle. Check: 90 plus 90 is 180. Equal, and supplementary.
The trap is to share out 90 instead, which gives 45. But 90 is the total for complementary angles. Supplementary means 180.
So when two equal angles make a total, just halve the total.
Two complementary angles. One is x degrees and the other is x plus x degrees. We need to find x.
What do complementary angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is for supplementary angles. Complementary angles fit into a right angle, which is 90 degrees.

beats.say: So the first angle plus the second angle makes 90. Let's write that down.
Now count the x's on the left. How many are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every x you can see: one outside the bracket, and two inside it.

beats.say: 3 of them. So 3 x equals 90.
3 times x is 90, so we divide both sides by 3. 90 divided by 3 is 30.
Check. The first angle is 30. The second is 30 plus 30, which is 60. And 30 plus 60 is 90. Complementary!
The trap is to forget the first x and write 2 x equals 90. That gives 45, and then the angles would be 45 and 90. Far too much.
So: write the total as an equation, gather the x's, and divide.
Four pairs of angles. Three of them are supplementary, and one is not. We want the odd one out.
What do supplementary angles add up to?

ask.ifNot: 90 degrees is for complementary angles. Supplementary angles fill a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So we add each pair, and look for the one that does not make 180.

board.text: Supplementary: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: Pair A. 70 plus 20 is 90. That is not 180. It looks like our odd one out, but let's check the others to be sure.
Pair B. 40 plus 140 is 180. Supplementary.
Pair C. 70 plus 110. What is the total?

ask.ifNot: Add the two angles carefully: start at 110, and count on 70 more.

beats.say: 180 again. And pair D: 120 plus 60 is 180 as well.
So only pair A does not make 180. 70 degrees and 20 degrees are not supplementary.
Notice the word not in the question. Three pairs pass the test here, and we want the one that does not.
70 and 20 make 90, so they are complementary instead. Add the pair: 90 is complementary, 180 is supplementary.
Two angles side by side on a straight line make a linear pair. This time one of them is obtuse. What kind is the other?

board.text: Linear pair: one angle is obtuse. The other?

beats.say: The key fact first. A straight line is a half turn, so the two angles of a linear pair always add up to 180 degrees.

board.text: Linear pair: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: Obtuse means wide: more than 90 degrees, but less than 180. Let's try one. Say the obtuse angle is 120 degrees. How do we find its partner?

ask.ifNot: Together the two angles make 180 degrees. So the partner is what is left when 120 is taken away from 180.

beats.say: 180 minus 120 is 60. That is less than 90 degrees, so the partner is an acute angle.
Try another, to be sure. An obtuse angle of 100 degrees leaves 180 minus 100, which is 80. Less than 90 again.
Here is why. 90 and 90 make 180. If one angle takes more than its 90, there is less than 90 left for the other.
So the other angle is always acute.
Don't be tempted by obtuse. Two obtuse angles would add up to more than 180, and that is too much for a straight line.
On a straight line, a big angle always has a small partner.
Two angles side by side on a straight line make a linear pair. One of them is 90 degrees. What kind of angle is the other?

board.text: Linear pair: one angle is 90°. The other?

beats.say: A straight line is a half turn. So the two angles of a linear pair always add up to 180 degrees.

board.text: Linear pair: the two angles add up to 180°

beats.say: One angle is 90. Which sum gives us the other one?

ask.ifNot: The two angles share 180 degrees. Take away the 90 we know, and what is left is the other angle.

beats.say: 180 minus 90 is 90. So the other angle is 90 degrees as well.
Now, what do we call an angle of exactly 90 degrees?

ask.ifNot: Acute is less than 90 degrees and obtuse is more than 90. Exactly 90 degrees, like the corner of your notebook, has its own name.

beats.say: A right angle. So the other angle is a right angle too.

board.text: The other angle is a right angle

beats.say: Check: 90 plus 90 is 180, a whole straight line. Picture a pole standing straight up on flat ground: a square corner on each side.
So for any linear pair, take the angle you know away from 180, then name what is left.
Picture a compass. We want the angle between North and West.
A compass is a full circle. How many degrees are there in a full turn?

ask.ifNot: 180 degrees is only a half turn, a straight line. All the way round, back to where you started, is twice that.

beats.say: 360 degrees. And the 4 main directions, North, East, South and West, cut that circle into 4 equal parts.

board.text: N, E, S, W: 4 equal parts

beats.say: So each part is 360 divided by 4. That is 90 degrees, a quarter turn.
Now, North and West. Are they next-door neighbours on the compass, or is there another main direction between them?

ask.ifNot: Go round the compass in order: North, East, South, West, and back to North. West and North come one straight after the other.

beats.say: They are neighbours. So turning from North to West is exactly 1 quarter turn.
The angle between North and West is 90 degrees. A right angle.
Check with the half-way direction, North-West. From North to North-West is 45 degrees, and from North-West to West is another 45. Together, 90.
So for the main compass directions, neighbours are always a quarter turn apart: 90 degrees.
An angle is bigger than 90 degrees but smaller than 180 degrees. What is it called?

board.text: An angle between 90° and 180° is called ...?

beats.say: Let's line up the angle names by size. The smallest kind is sharp and pointy, less than 90 degrees. That is an acute angle.
Exactly 90 degrees is the square corner, like the corner of your notebook. What is that one called?

ask.ifNot: A straight angle is a flat line, 180 degrees. The square corner, exactly 90 degrees, is the right angle.

beats.say: A right angle. And exactly 180 degrees is a flat, straight line, called a straight angle.
Our angle sits between those two. Wider than a square corner, but not yet flat. Like a book opened wide, or a hand fan.
Which name fills that gap?

ask.ifNot: Acute is the small, sharp one, under 90 degrees. Right is exactly 90. The wide one, between 90 and 180, has a different name.

beats.say: Obtuse. An angle between 90 degrees and 180 degrees is an obtuse angle.
A way to remember: acute is a cute little angle. Obtuse is the big, wide one.
So learn the two fence posts, 90 and 180. Below 90 is acute, and between them is obtuse.
Two angles add up to 140 degrees, and one of them is 85 degrees. We want the supplementary angle of the smaller one. That is two jobs.

board.text: Supplementary angle of the smaller one = ?

beats.say: First job: find the other angle. Which sum does that?

ask.ifNot: The two angles together make 140. We know one is 85, so the other is what is left of the 140.

beats.say: 140 minus 85. Take away 80 to get 60, then 5 more to get 55. The other angle is 55 degrees.
So the two angles are 85 degrees and 55 degrees. The smaller one is 55.
Second job: the supplementary angle of 55. What must 55 and its partner add up to?

ask.ifNot: 140 was the total of the first two angles, and that job is done. Supplementary partners always make a straight line, 180 degrees.

beats.say: So the partner is 180 minus 55. 180 minus 50 is 130, and 5 more off is 125.
Check: 55 plus 125 is 180. Yes, a straight line.
Two traps here. One is to stop at 55, which is only the first job. The other is to use the 85: that gives 95, the partner of the bigger angle.
For a two-job question, underline what is really being asked, and do the jobs one at a time.
Here is an equilateral triangle, and each side is 5.3 centimetres. We want the perimeter, the distance all the way round.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, each side 5.3 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 5.3 centimetres, 3 times over. A quicker way to write that is 3 times 5.3.
To multiply, split 5.3 into 5 and 0.3. 3 times 5 is 15, and 3 times 0.3 is 0.9.
Put the two pieces together. 15 plus 0.9 is 15.9, so the perimeter is 15.9 centimetres.
Careful not to lose the decimal part. 3 times 5 alone gives 15, but those 3 lots of 0.3 count too.
Check by sharing it back out. 15.9 divided by 3 is 5.3, the side we started with.
So for any shape with equal sides, the perimeter is the number of sides times one side.
A square has a perimeter of 16 centimetres. We want the length of one side.
The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 16?

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 sides, and all 4 are the same length.

beats.say: So 4 equal sides, put end to end, make 16 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides together make 16. To get back to one side, we share 16 equally among 4, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: 16 divided by 4. Well, 4 times 4 is 16, so each side is 4 centimetres.
Careful not to just halve it. Half of 16 is 8, but a square has 4 sides, not 2.
Let's check by going back round. 4 times 4 is 16, the perimeter. It works.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 40 centimetres and a length of 12 centimetres. We need its breadth.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 40 cm, length 12 cm. Breadth = ?

beats.say: Walk round a rectangle and you pass a length, a breadth, another length and another breadth. So the perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths.
So what does half of the perimeter give us?

ask.ifNot: Half of the walk round takes you along one length and one breadth. So half the perimeter is length plus breadth.

beats.say: Half of 40 is 20. So the length and the breadth together make 20.
The length is 12. So the breadth is 20 minus 12, which is 8 centimetres.
Here is the trap. Take both lengths off the 40 and you get 16. But that is two breadths, so it still has to be halved.
Check: 12 plus 8 is 20, and twice 20 is 40. It matches the perimeter.
So to find a missing side of a rectangle, halve the perimeter, then take away the side you know.
A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 54 centimetres. We want the length of one side.

board.text: Regular hexagon, perimeter 54 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 54?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So 6 equal sides, put end to end, make 54 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 6 equal sides together make 54. To get back to one side, we share 54 equally among 6, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: 54 divided by 6. Well, 6 times 9 is 54, so each side is 9 centimetres.
A trap here is to answer 6, the number of sides. The 6 is what we divide by. The side is what comes out, 9.
Let's check by going back round. 6 times 9 is 54, the perimeter. It works.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
This rectangle is twice as long as it is wide, and its perimeter is 42 centimetres. We want both the length and the breadth.
Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length is 2 parts, because it is 2 times as long.
Going all the way round the rectangle, how many parts do we pass?

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 3 parts. But the walk round passes two lengths and two breadths, so it is 3 parts, twice over.

beats.say: 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6 parts. And those 6 parts together are the whole perimeter, 42 centimetres.
So one part is 42 divided by 6, which is 7. That is the breadth: 7 centimetres.
The length is 2 parts. 2 times 7 is 14 centimetres.
The trap is to share 42 among 3 parts only. That forgets we pass every side twice on the way round.
Check: 14 plus 7 is 21, and twice 21 is 42. That is the perimeter, so it all fits.
The plan to keep: turn the sides into parts, count the parts round the whole edge, and divide the perimeter by that.
A square with a perimeter of 20 centimetres. We want its area.
Area needs the side, and all we have is the perimeter. So this takes two steps: first the side, then the area.
A square has 4 equal sides. How do we get one side from the perimeter?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides add up to the perimeter. So one side is the perimeter shared among 4.

beats.say: 20 divided by 4 is 5. Each side is 5 centimetres.
Now for the area of the square. Which sum is it?

ask.ifNot: Area counts the little squares inside: 5 rows, with 5 in each row. That is side times side. 4 times the side only takes us back to the perimeter.

beats.say: 5 times 5 is 25. The area is 25 square centimetres.
Don't stop at 5, that is only the side. And notice that the perimeter, 20, and the area, 25, are different numbers, measuring different things.
Check the first step: 4 sides of 5 make 20, the perimeter we were given.
So from perimeter to area in a square: divide by 4 for the side, then multiply the side by itself.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 50 centimetres, and its length is 5 centimetres more than its breadth. We want the area, so first we need both sides.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 50 cm, length = breadth + 5 cm

beats.say: Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Half of 50 is 25.
The length is a breadth with 5 extra. If we take that extra 5 away from the 25, what is left?

ask.ifNot: Without its extra 5, the length is exactly as long as the breadth. So what is left is one breadth, and another breadth.

beats.say: 25 minus 5 is 20, and that is two breadths.
So one breadth is half of 20, which is 10. And the length is 10 plus 5, which is 15.
Now the area, which is length times breadth. 15 times 10 is 150 square centimetres.
Two traps to dodge. Don't stop at the sides, because the question asks for the area. And don't halve the 25 straight away: the extra 5 has to come off first.
Check: 15 plus 10 is 25, and twice 25 is 50. And 15 is 5 more than 10. Both clues fit.
So: halve the perimeter, take off the extra, and halve again for the shorter side. Then it is length times breadth.
A square with an area of 441 square centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter needs the side. And the area of a square is side times side. So we want a number that, multiplied by itself, makes 441.
Let's get close first. 20 times 20 is 400. So what can we say about the side?

ask.ifNot: 400 is smaller than 441. So the side has to be a bit bigger than 20.

beats.say: 441 ends in 1, and 1 times 1 is 1. So let's try 21. 21 times 21 is 441, so the side is 21 centimetres.
Now the perimeter. A square has 4 equal sides, so which sum do we want?

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is the walk round all 4 sides. Each side is 21, so it is 4 times 21.

beats.say: 4 times 21 is 84. The perimeter is 84 centimetres.
Two things to watch. 21 is only the side, so don't stop there. And a perimeter is a length, so it is 84 centimetres, not square centimetres.
Check by going backwards. 84 divided by 4 is 21, and 21 times 21 is 441, the area we were given.
Two steps to keep: the area tells you the side, and 4 times the side is the perimeter.
A rectangle with an area of 98 square centimetres, and its length is double its breadth. We want the perimeter, so we need the sides.

board.text: Rectangle: area 98 sq cm, length = 2 × breadth

beats.say: Here is a picture that helps. If the length is double the breadth, the rectangle is really two equal squares, side by side.
The two squares together have an area of 98. So what is the area of one square?

ask.ifNot: Two equal squares share the 98 between them. So each one is half of 98.

beats.say: Half of 98 is 49. So each square has an area of 49.
Which number, multiplied by itself, makes 49? 7 times 7. So the breadth is 7 centimetres, and the length is double that, 14.
Now the perimeter, 2 lengths and 2 breadths. 14 plus 7 is 21, and twice 21 is 42 centimetres.
Don't stop at 7, or 14, or 21. Those are steps on the way. The question asks for the whole walk round, and that is 42.
Check the area clue: 14 times 7 is 98. It fits.
So when you are given an area, find the sides first. Once you have the sides, the perimeter is easy.
The distance all the way round an equilateral triangle is 23.1 centimetres. How long is each side?

board.text: Equilateral triangle, perimeter 23.1 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 23.1?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So 3 equal sides, put end to end, make 23.1 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 3 equal sides together make 23.1. To get back to one side, we share 23.1 equally among 3, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: To divide 23.1 by 3, split it into 21 and 2.1. 21 divided by 3 is 7, and 2.1 divided by 3 is 0.7.
7 plus 0.7 is 7.7. Each side is 7.7 centimetres.
Don't drop the decimal part. A side of just 7 would give a perimeter of only 21, and ours is 23.1.
Check: 3 sides of 7.7 make 23.1. That is the perimeter we were given.
The rule to keep: count the equal sides, then divide the perimeter by that number.
An isosceles triangle with a perimeter of 26 centimetres. Each of its two equal sides is 8 centimetres, and we want the third side.

board.text: Equal sides 8 cm each. Third side = ?

beats.say: Isosceles means two sides are equal, and congruent is just another word for equal. So the sides are 8, 8, and one we do not know yet.
What should we work out first?

ask.ifNot: There are two equal sides, and both are part of the perimeter. So first find how much the two of them make together.

beats.say: 8 plus 8 is 16. That is how much of the perimeter the two equal sides use up.
The rest belongs to the third side. 26 minus 16 is 10 centimetres.
The trap is taking away only one 8. That gives 18, but there are two equal sides to take off, not one.
Check by adding all three sides. 8 plus 8 plus 10 is 26. It matches the perimeter.
The plan to keep: perimeter, minus all the sides you already know, leaves the side you want.
Here is a square, and each side is 4.6 centimetres. We want the perimeter, the distance all the way round.
How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 sides, and all 4 are the same length.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 4.6 centimetres, 4 times over. A quicker way to write that is 4 times 4.6.
To multiply, split 4.6 into 4 and 0.6. 4 times 4 is 16, and 4 times 0.6 is 2.4.
Put the two pieces together. 16 plus 2.4 is 18.4, so the perimeter is 18.4 centimetres.
Now look at the units. A perimeter is a length, so it stays in centimetres. Square centimetres are for area, and nothing here was changed to millimetres.
Check by sharing it back out. 18.4 divided by 4 is 4.6, the side we started with.
So for any shape with equal sides, the perimeter is the number of sides times one side.
This is an equilateral triangle with every side 5.4 centimetres long. The perimeter is how far it is all the way round.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, each side 5.4 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 5.4 centimetres, 3 times over. A quicker way to write that is 3 times 5.4.
To multiply, split 5.4 into 5 and 0.4. 3 times 5 is 15, and 3 times 0.4 is 1.2.
Put the two pieces together. 15 plus 1.2 is 16.2, so the perimeter is 16.2 centimetres.
Two things to watch. A triangle has 3 sides, not 4. And a perimeter is a length, so it is in centimetres, not square centimetres.
Let's check. Share 16.2 equally among the 3 sides, and each one gets 5.4. That is our side.
So for any shape with equal sides, the perimeter is the number of sides times one side.
A square has a perimeter of 24.4 centimetres. We want the length of one side.
The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 24.4?

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 sides, and all 4 are the same length.

beats.say: So 4 equal sides, put end to end, make 24.4 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides together make 24.4. To get back to one side, we share 24.4 equally among 4, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: To divide 24.4 by 4, split it into 24 and 0.4. 24 divided by 4 is 6, and 0.4 divided by 4 is 0.1.
6 plus 0.1 is 6.1. Each side is 6.1 centimetres.
Now the units. The perimeter was in centimetres, so the side is in centimetres too. Not millimetres, and not square units, which are for area.
Let's check by going back round. 4 times 6.1 is 24.4, the perimeter. It works.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 48 centimetres and a length of 14 centimetres. We need its breadth.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 48 cm, length 14 cm. Breadth = ?

beats.say: Walk round a rectangle and you pass a length, a breadth, another length and another breadth. So the perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths.
So what does half of the perimeter give us?

ask.ifNot: Half of the walk round takes you along one length and one breadth. So half the perimeter is length plus breadth.

beats.say: Half of 48 is 24. So the length and the breadth together make 24.
The length is 14. So the breadth is 24 minus 14, which is 10 centimetres.
Here is the trap. Take both lengths off the 48 and you get 20. But that is two breadths, so it still has to be halved. And keep the unit: centimetres, like the question.
Check: 14 plus 10 is 24, and twice 24 is 48. It matches the perimeter.
So to find a missing side of a rectangle, halve the perimeter, then take away the side you know.
A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 72 centimetres. We want the length of one side.

board.text: Regular hexagon, perimeter 72 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 72?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So 6 equal sides, put end to end, make 72 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 6 equal sides together make 72. To get back to one side, we share 72 equally among 6, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: 72 divided by 6. Well, 6 times 12 is 72, so each side is 12 centimetres.
Careful with the 6 times table. 6 times 10 is 60, and 2 more sixes take us up to 72. So each side is 12.
Check: 6 sides of 12 make 72. That is the perimeter we were given.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
A square with a perimeter of 36 centimetres. We want its area.
Area needs the side, and all we have is the perimeter. So this takes two steps: first the side, then the area.
A square has 4 equal sides. How do we get one side from the perimeter?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides add up to the perimeter. So one side is the perimeter shared among 4.

beats.say: 36 divided by 4 is 9. Each side is 9 centimetres.
Now for the area of the square. Which sum is it?

ask.ifNot: Area counts the little squares inside: 9 rows, with 9 in each row. That is side times side. 4 times the side only takes us back to the perimeter.

beats.say: 9 times 9 is 81. The area is 81 square centimetres.
Careful not to do something quick with the 36, like doubling it. The area always comes from the side, and 9 times 9 is exactly 81.
Check the first step: 4 sides of 9 make 36, the perimeter we were given.
So from perimeter to area in a square: divide by 4 for the side, then multiply the side by itself.
