A rectangle with a perimeter of 40 centimetres, and its length is 8 centimetres more than its breadth. We want the area, so first we need both sides.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 40 cm, length = breadth + 8 cm

beats.say: Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Half of 40 is 20.
The length is a breadth with 8 extra. If we take that extra 8 away from the 20, what is left?

ask.ifNot: Without its extra 8, the length is exactly as long as the breadth. So what is left is one breadth, and another breadth.

beats.say: 20 minus 8 is 12, and that is two breadths.
So one breadth is half of 12, which is 6. And the length is 6 plus 8, which is 14.
Now the area, which is length times breadth. 14 times 6 is 84 square centimetres.
Careful not to multiply the numbers in the question. 40 is a perimeter and 8 is a difference, so 40 times 8 means nothing here. We need the two sides first.
Check: 14 plus 6 is 20, and twice 20 is 40. And 14 is 8 more than 6. Both clues fit.
So: halve the perimeter, take off the extra, and halve again for the shorter side. Then it is length times breadth.
A square with an area of 676 square centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter needs the side. And the area of a square is side times side. So we want a number that, multiplied by itself, makes 676.
Let's get close first. 25 times 25 is 625. So what can we say about the side?

ask.ifNot: 625 is smaller than 676. So the side has to be a bit bigger than 25.

beats.say: 676 ends in 6, and 6 times 6 ends in 6. So let's try 26. 26 times 26 is 676, so the side is 26 centimetres.
Now the perimeter. A square has 4 equal sides, so which sum do we want?

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is the walk round all 4 sides. Each side is 26, so it is 4 times 26.

beats.say: 4 times 26 is 104. The perimeter is 104 centimetres.
Mind the units. Area is in square centimetres, but a perimeter is a length. So the answer is 104 centimetres, plain centimetres.
Check by going backwards. 104 divided by 4 is 26, and 26 times 26 is 676, the area we were given.
Two steps to keep: the area tells you the side, and 4 times the side is the perimeter.
The length of this rectangle is twice its breadth, and the perimeter is 78 centimetres. We need the length and the breadth.
Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length is 2 parts, because it is 2 times as long.
Going all the way round the rectangle, how many parts do we pass?

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 3 parts. But the walk round passes two lengths and two breadths, so it is 3 parts, twice over.

beats.say: 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6 parts. And those 6 parts together are the whole perimeter, 78 centimetres.
So one part is 78 divided by 6, which is 13. That is the breadth: 13 centimetres.
The length is 2 parts. 2 times 13 is 26 centimetres.
The trap is to share 78 among 3 parts only. That makes both sides twice too big, because we pass every side twice on the way round.
Check: 26 plus 13 is 39, and twice 39 is 78. That is the perimeter, so it all fits.
So when one side is so many times the other, count the parts all the way round, find one part, and build the sides from it.
An equilateral triangle has a perimeter of 29.1 centimetres. We want the length of one side.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, perimeter 29.1 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 29.1?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So 3 equal sides, put end to end, make 29.1 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 3 equal sides together make 29.1. To get back to one side, we share 29.1 equally among 3, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: To divide 29.1 by 3, split it into 27 and 2.1. 27 divided by 3 is 9, and 2.1 divided by 3 is 0.7.
9 plus 0.7 is 9.7. Each side is 9.7 centimetres.
Careful with the whole part. 3 times 9 is 27, so the side starts with 9, not with 8 or 7.
Let's check by going back round. 3 times 9.7 is 29.1, the perimeter. It works.
The rule to keep: count the equal sides, then divide the perimeter by that number.
A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 42 centimetres. We want the total of just 5 of its sides.

board.text: Regular hexagon, perimeter 42 cm. Sum of 5 sides = ?

beats.say: First, how many equal sides does a regular hexagon have?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So 6 equal sides make 42. One side is 42 divided by 6, which is 7 centimetres.
We want 5 of the sides, not all 6. What is the quickest way to get that?

ask.ifNot: 5 sides is all 6 sides with one side left out. So we can take one side, 7, away from the whole perimeter.

beats.say: 42 minus 7 is 35. The 5 sides add up to 35 centimetres.
We can also multiply. 5 sides of 7 centimetres is 35. Two ways, one answer.
The trap is dividing 42 by 5. The 42 belongs to all 6 sides, so we must find one side first.
So with a regular shape, always find one side first. After that you can build any number of sides you like.
Here is a regular hexagon, and each side is 6.1 centimetres. We want the perimeter, the distance all the way round.

board.text: Regular hexagon, each side 6.1 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 6.1 centimetres, 6 times over. A quicker way to write that is 6 times 6.1.
To multiply, split 6.1 into 6 and 0.1. 6 times 6 is 36, and 6 times 0.1 is 0.6.
Put the two pieces together. 36 plus 0.6 is 36.6, so the perimeter is 36.6 centimetres.
Don't drop the little 0.1. It is on all 6 sides, so together it adds 0.6. The answer is 36.6, not just 36.
Check by sharing it back out. 36.6 divided by 6 is 6.1, the side we started with.
The rule to keep: when every side is equal, count the sides and multiply by the length of one.
A triangle with sides 3.2, 4.6 and 5.3 centimetres. The perimeter is the walk all the way round, so we add the three sides.

board.text: Triangle: sides 3.2 cm, 4.6 cm, 5.3 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Add the whole numbers first. 3 plus 4 plus 5 is 12.
Now the tenths: 2 tenths, 6 tenths and 3 tenths. How many tenths is that altogether?

ask.ifNot: Add them like ordinary numbers. 2 plus 6 is 8, and 3 more makes 11. So there are 11 tenths.

beats.say: 11 tenths is more than one whole. It is 1 whole and 1 tenth, which we write as 1.1. This is the step that often gets dropped.
12 plus 1.1 is 13.1. The perimeter is 13.1 centimetres.
Check by adding in order. 3.2 plus 4.6 is 7.8, and 7.8 plus 5.3 is 13.1 again.
So with decimals, add the wholes, add the tenths, and when the tenths go past 10, carry a whole across.
Thrice means 3 times. So this rectangle is 3 times as long as it is wide, and its perimeter is 64 centimetres. We want the breadth.
Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length is 3 parts, because it is 3 times as long.
Going all the way round the rectangle, how many parts do we pass?

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 4 parts. But the walk round passes two lengths and two breadths, so it is 4 parts, twice over.

beats.say: 3 plus 1 plus 3 plus 1 is 8 parts. And those 8 parts together are the whole perimeter, 64 centimetres.
So one part is 64 divided by 8, which is 8. And one part is the breadth: 8 centimetres.
The length is 3 parts, so 3 times 8 is 24 centimetres. We were not asked for it, but it helps us check.
Two traps here. Sharing 64 among 4 parts forgets we pass every side twice. And the question wants the breadth, not the length.
Check: 24 plus 8 is 32, and twice 32 is 64. That is the perimeter, so it all fits.
The plan to keep: turn the sides into parts, count the parts round the whole edge, and divide the perimeter by that.
An isosceles triangle with a perimeter of 32 centimetres. Each of its two equal sides is 9 centimetres, and we want the third side.

board.text: Equal sides 9 cm each. Third side = ?

beats.say: Isosceles means two sides are equal, and congruent is just another word for equal. So the sides are 9, 9, and one we do not know yet.
What should we work out first?

ask.ifNot: There are two equal sides, and both are part of the perimeter. So first find how much the two of them make together.

beats.say: 9 plus 9 is 18. That is how much of the perimeter the two equal sides use up.
The rest belongs to the third side. 32 minus 18 is 14 centimetres.
Don't stop at 18. That is the two equal sides together, not the third side. The third side is what is left of the perimeter.
Check by adding all three sides. 9 plus 9 plus 14 is 32. It matches the perimeter.
The plan to keep: perimeter, minus all the sides you already know, leaves the side you want.
A rectangle with a length of 1.2 metres and a breadth of 50 centimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Rectangle: length 1.2 m, breadth 50 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Before we multiply anything, look at the units. What do you notice?

choices: one is metres, one is centimetres
ask.ifNot: Read the two measurements again. The length is in metres, but the breadth is in centimetres. They do not match yet.

beats.say: The answer is wanted in square centimetres, so let's turn the length into centimetres. 1 metre is 100 centimetres.
So 1.2 metres is 1.2 times 100, which is 120 centimetres.
Now both sides are in centimetres, and area is length times breadth. 12 times 5 is 60, and the two zeros go on the end: 6000 square centimetres.
Here is the trap. Multiply 1.2 by 50 straight away and you get 60. But that mixes metres with centimetres, so it means nothing.
So before any area sum, make the units match. Then it is just length times breadth.
A square whose area and perimeter are the very same number. We have to find its side.
Write the two rules side by side. Area is side times side. Perimeter is 4 times the side.
Let's try a small square and watch. With side 2, the area is 2 times 2, which is 4. The perimeter is 4 times 2, which is 8. Not equal.
Look at the two rules again. Both multiply the side by something. When will they give the same answer?

ask.ifNot: One rule multiplies the side by the side, the other multiplies it by 4. They agree when those two are the same, so the side must be 4.

beats.say: Try 4. The area is 4 times 4, which is 16. The perimeter is 4 times 4, which is 16. Equal!
What about 0? The numbers do match, but a square with side 0 is no square at all. So we leave that one out.
And bigger squares? With side 5, the area is 25 but the perimeter is only 20. From here on the area runs ahead, so 4 is the only answer.
So when a question gives a rule but no numbers, write the formulas side by side and test small numbers.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 50 centimetres. Its length is 3 over 2 times its breadth, and we want the area.
3 over 2 times sounds hard, so let's make it easy. Cut the breadth into 2 equal parts. Then the length is 3 of those same parts.
Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Half of 50 is 25.
One length and one breadth together: how many parts is that?

ask.ifNot: The length is 3 parts and the breadth is 2 parts. Together that is 3 plus 2.

beats.say: 3 plus 2 is 5 parts, and they make 25. So one part is 25 divided by 5, which is 5 centimetres.
The breadth is 2 parts: 2 times 5 is 10. The length is 3 parts: 3 times 5 is 15.
Area is length times breadth. 15 times 10 is 150 square centimetres.
Check both clues. Twice 15 plus 10 is 50, the perimeter. And 15 is one and a half times 10. Everything fits.
So when one side is a fraction of the other, turn the sides into equal parts. Find one part, and the rest follows.
Two playgrounds. One is a rectangle, 25 metres by 20 metres. The other is a square with sides of 22 metres. Which one is bigger?
A bigger playground means more room to play. Which measurement tells us that?

ask.ifNot: Room to run about is the flat space inside the edges. That is the area.

beats.say: The rectangle first. 25 times 20 is 500 square metres.
Now the square, 22 times 22. Take it in two bites: 22 times 20 is 440, and 22 times 2 is 44.
440 plus 44 is 484 square metres.
500 is more than 484. So the rectangular playground is the bigger one.
Don't judge by the side lengths. 22 looks big next to 20, but the rectangle has that long 25. Only working out both areas settles it.
So to compare two shapes for size, find the area of each one, then compare the two numbers.
A plot of land is 16 metres long and 10 metres wide. Each square metre costs 1000 rupees. What does the whole plot cost?

board.text: Plot 16 m × 10 m. 1 sq m costs Rs. 1000. Cost = ?

beats.say: The price is for each square metre. So what must we find first?

ask.ifNot: Square metres measure the flat surface of the plot, and that is its area.

beats.say: Area is length times breadth. 16 times 10 is 160 square metres.
Picture 160 squares, each one metre by one metre, and every one of them costs 1000 rupees. So the cost is 160 times 1000.
To multiply by 1000, write 160 and put three zeros after it. That makes 1,60,000 rupees.
Careful with the trap. 16 times 1000 is only 16000. That leaves out the breadth altogether.
Check by dividing back. 1,60,000 divided by 1000 is 160, the area we found.
So for a cost on land or floors, find the area first, then multiply by the price of one square metre.
A ground 30 metres long and 20 metres wide has to be levelled. The charge is 5 rupees for every square metre.

board.text: Ground 30 m × 20 m. Levelling: Rs. 5 per sq m. Cost = ?

beats.say: We pay for every square metre of ground. So which sum comes first?

ask.ifNot: The number of square metres is the area of the ground. For a rectangle, that is length times breadth.

beats.say: 30 times 20. 3 times 2 is 6, and the two zeros go on the end: 600 square metres.
Careful: 600 is the area, not the cost. Each of those 600 square metres costs 5 rupees.
6 times 5 is 30, so 600 times 5 is 3000. The levelling costs 3000 rupees.
Check by sharing the money back out. 3000 rupees divided by 5 rupees is 600 square metres, the area we found.
So it is always two steps: the area first, then area times the rate.
A square with an area of 144 square centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter needs the side. And the area of a square is side times side. So we want a number that, multiplied by itself, makes 144.
Let's get close first. 10 times 10 is 100. So what can we say about the side?

ask.ifNot: 100 is smaller than 144. So the side has to be a bit bigger than 10.

beats.say: 144 ends in 4, and 2 times 2 is 4. So let's try 12. 12 times 12 is 144, so the side is 12 centimetres.
Now the perimeter. A square has 4 equal sides, so which sum do we want?

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is the walk round all 4 sides. Each side is 12, so it is 4 times 12.

beats.say: 4 times 12 is 48. The perimeter is 48 centimetres.
Careful not to divide 144 by 4, and don't stop at 12. The side comes first, then all 4 sides. And the answer is a length, in centimetres.
Check by going backwards. 48 divided by 4 is 12, and 12 times 12 is 144, the area we were given.
Two steps to keep: the area tells you the side, and 4 times the side is the perimeter.
A triangle with an area of 5 square centimetres and a height of 2 centimetres. We want its base. It is isosceles, but that does not change the area rule.

board.text: Triangle: area 5 sq cm, height 2 cm. Base = ?

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
Put in what we know. 5 equals half, times the base, times 2.
Look at the half and the 2 on that line. What is half of 2?

ask.ifNot: Half of 2 means 2 split into two equal parts. Each part is 1.

beats.say: So the half and the 2 together make just 1. And 1 times the base is simply the base.
That leaves 5 equals the base. The base is 5 centimetres.
Check it in the rule. Half of 5 times 2 is half of 10, which is 5. That is our area.
The trap is to forget the half and say 5 divided by 2. The steady way is: double the area, then divide by the height.
So for a missing base, double the area and divide by the height.
A room has a floor 5 metres long and 4 metres wide. Its four walls have a total area of 108 square metres. How high is the room?

board.text: Floor 5 m × 4 m. Four walls: 108 sq m. Height = ?

beats.say: Imagine unfolding the four walls and laying them flat in a row. They make one long rectangle, exactly as tall as the room.
How long is that strip of walls?

ask.ifNot: The walls stand on the edges of the floor, all the way round. So the strip is as long as the walk round the floor, its perimeter.

beats.say: The floor's perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths. 5 plus 4 is 9, and twice 9 is 18 metres.
So the strip is 18 metres long, and its area is 108. Length times height gives area.
The height is 108 divided by 18. Now 18 times 6 is 108, so the room is 6 metres high.
Check wall by wall. Two walls are 5 by 6, which is 30 each. Two are 4 by 6, which is 24 each. And 30, 30, 24 and 24 make 108.
The trap is dividing 108 by the floor area, 20. The walls stand on the floor's edges, so it is the perimeter we need.
So the area of four walls is the perimeter of the floor times the height. Divide to get the height back.
One side of a square grows by 50 percent, and the other shrinks by 50 percent. It becomes a rectangle. Is its area bigger, smaller, or the same?

board.text: Square: one side + 50%, the other side − 50%
New area: bigger, smaller or the same?

beats.say: No numbers are given, so let's choose an easy square. Say each side is 10. Its area is 10 times 10, which is 100.
50 percent means half. So what is 50 percent of 10?

ask.ifNot: 50 percent is the same as half. And half of 10 is 5.

beats.say: One side grows by 5: 10 plus 5 is 15. The other shrinks by 5: 10 minus 5 is 5.
One side went up by 5 and the other came down by 5. What do you think happens to the area?

ask.ifNot: It feels as if up 5 and down 5 should cancel out. But area multiplies the sides, so let's work it out and see.

beats.say: The new rectangle is 15 times 5, which is 75. And 75 is less than 100.
So the rectangle's area is smaller than the square's.

board.text: The new area is smaller than the square

beats.say: That is the trap: the same percent up and down does not cancel. One side became one and a half times as long, but the other became only half. Together that makes just three quarters of the square.
So when a question gives no numbers, pick easy ones and try it. The sums will show you what really happens.
A hall is 5 metres long and 4 metres wide. It is covered with square tiles of side 25 centimetres. How many tiles are needed?

board.text: Hall 5 m × 4 m, square tiles of side 25 cm. Tiles = ?

beats.say: Metres and centimetres are mixed, so first we make them match. 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so the hall is 500 centimetres by 400 centimetres.
How many 25 centimetre tiles fit in one row along the 500 centimetre length?

ask.ifNot: Four 25s make 100. There are 5 hundreds in 500, so that is 4 times 5, which is 20 tiles.

beats.say: 500 divided by 25 is 20 tiles in a row. And across the breadth, 400 divided by 25 is 16 rows.
So the floor is a grid of tiles: 16 rows, with 20 tiles in each row. 20 times 16 is 320 tiles.
Check it with areas. The floor is 500 times 400, which is 200000 square centimetres. One tile is 25 times 25, which is 625.
And 200000 divided by 625 is 320. The same answer both ways.
The trap is using 5 and 4 with 25 without changing units. Metres and centimetres must never be mixed in one sum.
So for tiles: same units first, count how many fit along each side, then multiply.
A wire 100 centimetres long is bent into a square. Then the same wire makes a rectangle, 5 centimetres longer and 5 centimetres narrower than the square.

board.text: Wire 100 cm, bent into a square
Rectangle: length = side + 5 cm, breadth = side − 5 cm

beats.say: The wire goes all the way round the square, so 100 centimetres is its perimeter. One side is 100 divided by 4, which is 25.
The area of the square is 25 times 25, which is 625 square centimetres.
Now the rectangle. Its length is 5 more than 25, and its breadth is 5 less than 25. What are they?

ask.ifNot: Both sides change. 25 plus 5 is 30 for the length, and 25 minus 5 is 20 for the breadth.

beats.say: So the rectangle is 30 by 20, and 30 times 20 is 600 square centimetres.
The difference is 625 minus 600, which is 25 square centimetres.
Don't answer 625 or 600. Those are the two areas, and the question wants the gap between them.
Notice something. Both shapes use the same wire: twice 30 plus 20 is 100 too. Yet the square holds more, by exactly 5 times 5.
So: the perimeter gives the side, the side gives each area, and then we subtract.
A triangle with a base of 5.2 centimetres and a height of 2.9 centimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Triangle: base 5.2 cm, height 2.9 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
A smart move is to halve one of the numbers first. Which one halves more easily?

ask.ifNot: 5.2 ends in an even digit, so it halves neatly. 2.9 ends in an odd digit, so its half would be messier.

beats.say: Half of 5.2 is 2.6. So the area is 2.6 times 2.9.
Leave the decimal points out for a moment: 26 times 29. Now 26 times 30 is 780, and taking away one 26 leaves 754.
Time to put the point back. 2.6 and 2.9 have one decimal place each. So how many decimal places does the answer have?

ask.ifNot: Count the decimal places in both numbers: one, and one more. Together that makes 2 decimal places in the answer.

beats.say: So 754 becomes 7.54. The area is 7.54 square centimetres.
Does that look right? Half of 5 times 3 is 7 and a half, so 7.54 is sensible. And area is in square centimetres, not plain centimetres.
So for a triangle: halve the easy number, multiply, then count the decimal places.
A square with each side 6.1 centimetres. We want its area.
Which sum gives the area of a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk round the edge, which is the perimeter. Area is the space inside: side times side.

beats.say: That is the trap in this question. 4 times 6.1 is 24.4, but that is the perimeter, a length.
So we need 6.1 times 6.1. Leave the points out for now: 61 times 61. Well, 61 times 60 is 3660, and one more 61 makes 3721.
Each 6.1 has one decimal place. So where does the point go in 3721?

ask.ifNot: One decimal place and one more make two. So count two digits from the right, and put the point there.

beats.say: That gives 37.21. The area is 37.21 square centimetres.
A quick sense check: 6 times 6 is 36, and 6.1 is a little more than 6. So a little more than 36 is just right.
So for the area of a square, multiply the side by itself, then count the decimal places in the answer.
A rectangle with a length of 1.1 centimetres and a breadth of 30 centimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Rectangle: length 1.1 cm, breadth 30 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Both sides are already in centimetres, so we can multiply straight away. Area is length times breadth.
1.1 is 1 whole and 1 tenth. What is 1 tenth of 30?

ask.ifNot: A tenth means divide by 10. And 30 divided by 10 is 3.

beats.say: So split the sum in two. 1 times 30 is 30, and 0.1 times 30 is 3.
30 plus 3 is 33. The area is 33 square centimetres.
Here is another way to see it. 11 times 30 is 330, and one decimal place brings that back to 33.
Watch the decimal point: it is 33, not 330. And we multiplied centimetres by centimetres, so the answer is in square centimetres.
So for an area with a decimal, split the decimal into its whole and its tenths, multiply each, and add.
A triangle with an area of 120 square centimetres and a base of 40 centimetres. We want its height.

board.text: Triangle: area 120 sq cm, base 40 cm. Height = ?

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
Put in what we know. Half of the base is half of 40, which is 20. So 20 times the height is 120.
20 times the height is 120. So how do we find the height?

ask.ifNot: 20 times something gives 120. To undo the times, we divide 120 by 20.

beats.say: 120 divided by 20 is 6. The height is 6 centimetres.
Now look at the choices: none of them says 6 centimetres. A height is a length, so which unit could be right?

ask.ifNot: Square units are for area. A height is a length, so it needs a plain length unit, like millimetres.

beats.say: 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. So 6 centimetres is 6 times 10, which is 60 millimetres.
Check it in the rule. Half of 40 is 20, and 20 times 6 is 120. And mind the trap: 120 divided by 40 gives 3, which forgets the half.
So for a missing height: halve the base, divide the area by that, and then check which unit the answer is wanted in.
A square with a perimeter of 52 millimetres. We want its area.
Area needs the side, and all we have is the perimeter. So this takes two steps: first the side, then the area.
A square has 4 equal sides. How do we get one side from the perimeter?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides add up to the perimeter. So one side is the perimeter shared among 4.

beats.say: 52 divided by 4 is 13. Each side is 13 millimetres.
Now for the area of the square. Which sum is it?

ask.ifNot: Area counts the little squares inside: 13 rows, with 13 in each row. That is side times side. 4 times the side only takes us back to the perimeter.

beats.say: 13 times 13. Take it in two bites: 13 times 10 is 130, and 13 times 3 is 39.
130 plus 39 is 169. The area is 169 square millimetres.
Look at the units. The side is in millimetres, so the area is in square millimetres. Not square centimetres, and not plain millimetres.
Check the first step: 4 sides of 13 make 52, the perimeter we were given.
So from perimeter to area in a square: divide by 4 for the side, then multiply the side by itself.
We are counting the numbers from 100 to 300 that 9 divides exactly. Those are the numbers in the 9 times table.

board.text: From 100 to 300: how many are divisible by 9?

spec.note: Multiples of 9 from 100 to 300

beats.say: Writing them all out would take ages. So we find the first one and the last one, and count smartly.
9 times 11 is 99, which is just too small. 9 times 12 is 108. So 108 is the first.
Now the last one. Divide 300 by 9: it goes 33 times, with a bit left over. 9 times 33 is 297, and one more step gives 306, which is past 300. So 297 is the last.
So we want the 12th number in the table, up to the 33rd. How many numbers is that, counting both ends?

ask.ifNot: Taking away gives 21, but that is only the number of jumps from the first to the last. We count the first one too, so we add 1.

beats.say: 33 minus 12 is 21 jumps. Add 1 for the number we started on. That makes 22.
The plus 1 is the trap here. Think of counting from 2 to 4: that is 2, 3, 4, which is three numbers. And 4 minus 2, plus 1, is 3.
So 22 numbers from 100 to 300 are divisible by 9.
Remember: first multiple, last multiple, subtract their places in the table, then add 1 because both ends count.
We want to count the odd numbers from 20 to 50. Counting them one by one would take a while, so let us be clever.

board.text: Odd numbers from 20 to 50: how many?

beats.say: Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. 20 and 50 are both even, so the first odd number is 21 and the last is 49.
Odd and even numbers take turns. So in any 10 numbers in a row, how many are odd?

ask.ifNot: Odd and even take turns, so exactly half of them are odd. Half of 10 is 5.

beats.say: Look at the 10 numbers from 21 to 30. The odd ones are 21, 23, 25, 27 and 29. That is 5 of them.
From 21 to 50 there are 3 lots of ten like that. So we need 3 lots of 5.
3 times 5 is 15. So there are 15 odd numbers.
Let us check another way. From 21 to 49 we jump in twos. 49 minus 21 is 28, and half of 28 is 14 jumps.
Careful here: 14 jumps touch 15 numbers, because the starting number counts too. So it is 15 again.
So the plan: find the first and last odd number, then count in tens, 5 odd numbers for every ten.
We want to count the odd numbers from 50 to 90. Counting them one by one would take a while, so let us be clever.

board.text: Odd numbers from 50 to 90: how many?

beats.say: Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9. 50 and 90 are both even, so the first odd number is 51 and the last is 89.
Odd and even numbers take turns. So in any 10 numbers in a row, how many are odd?

ask.ifNot: Odd and even take turns, so exactly half of them are odd. Half of 10 is 5.

beats.say: Look at the 10 numbers from 51 to 60. The odd ones are 51, 53, 55, 57 and 59. That is 5 of them.
From 51 to 90 there are 4 lots of ten like that. So we need 4 lots of 5.
4 times 5 is 20. So there are 20 odd numbers.
Let us check another way. From 51 to 89 we jump in twos. 89 minus 51 is 38, and half of 38 is 19 jumps.
Careful here: 19 jumps touch 20 numbers, because the starting number counts too. So it is 20 again.
So the plan: find the first and last odd number, then count in tens, 5 odd numbers for every ten.
We want the supplement of 89 degrees. Supplementary angles are two angles that sit side by side on a straight line. Here is the picture.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 89, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 89.

beats.say: The whole is 180 and one piece is 89. Which sum finds the missing piece?
Let's take 89 away in two easy hops. First the 80: 180 take away 80 leaves 100.
Now the 9 that is left: 100 take away 9 leaves 91. So 180 minus 89 is 91.
So the supplement is 91 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 89 plus 91 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.
A triangle has 3 angles. We are told 2 of them: 41 degrees and 40 degrees. Let's hunt for the third.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 40 plus 40 is 80. Then 1 more makes 81.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 81 away from 180.

beats.say: So 81 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 81 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 80: that leaves 100. Then take away 1 more: 99.
So the third angle is 99 degrees. Found it!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 41, 40 and 99. They make 180, just as they should. And notice: 99 degrees is a wide angle, an obtuse one. A triangle can have just 1 of those.
Remember the plan: add the 2 angles you have, and take that from 180. What is left is the third angle.
Our angle is 71 degrees, and we want its supplementary partner. The two angles lie together along a straight line, like this.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 71, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 71.

beats.say: We know the whole, 180, and one part, 71. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 71 away in two easy hops. First the 70: 180 take away 70 leaves 110.
Now the 1 that is left: 110 take away 1 leaves 109. So 180 minus 71 is 109.
So the supplement is 109 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 71 plus 109 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.

board.text: Lines cross: one angle is 22°. Opposite angle = ?

beats.say: Two straight lines cross and make 4 angles. One of them is 22 degrees. We want the angle vertically opposite: the one straight across the crossing point.
I have called the two angles next door p and q. Now, a straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees.
Look at 22 degrees and its neighbour, p. They sit side by side on one straight line. So p is what is left of 180.
Let's take 22 away in two easy hops. First the 20: 180 take away 20 leaves 160.
Now the 2 that is left: 160 take away 2 leaves 158. So 180 minus 22 is 158.

ask.ifNot: p and the mystery angle share a straight line, so together they make 180 degrees. We take p, which is 158, away from 180.

beats.say: So p is 158 degrees. Now look at p and our mystery angle. They sit side by side on the other straight line. So what is the mystery angle?
Let's take 158 away in two easy hops. First the 150: 180 take away 150 leaves 30.
Now the 8 that is left: 30 take away 8 leaves 22. So 180 minus 158 is 22.
22 degrees. Exactly the angle we started with! That always happens: angles straight across from each other are equal.
So next time you can say it straight away: the vertically opposite angle is equal, 22 degrees. The slip to watch for is giving 158, which is the neighbour on the line.

board.text: Angles in the ratio 3 : 1 : 1. Largest angle = ?

beats.say: The angles of this triangle are in the ratio 3 to 1 to 1. We want the largest angle.
A ratio is a way of sharing. Think of equal parts: the first angle gets 3 parts, the second gets 1 part, and the third gets 1 part.

ask.ifNot: Count every part of every angle. Add the 3 ratio numbers: 3, 1 and 1.

beats.say: How many equal parts are there altogether?
3 plus 1 plus 1 makes 5. So there are 5 equal parts in all.
Now the fact about every triangle: its 3 angles add up to 180 degrees. So these 5 parts share 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Sharing equally means dividing. 180 degrees shared among 5 equal parts is 180 divided by 5.

beats.say: So how big is 1 part?
180 divided by 5 is 36. Multiply back to be sure: 5 times 36 is 180. So 1 part is 36 degrees.
Careful: 36 degrees is only 1 part, not the answer. The largest angle has the most parts, 3 of them. 3 times 36 is 108.
So the largest angle is 108 degrees.
Let's check with all 3 angles: 108, 36 and 36. Together they make 180. It works.
So with a ratio: add the parts, divide 180 by that to get 1 part, then multiply by the parts you need.

board.text: On a straight line: x° and 56°. x = ?

beats.say: Here is a straight line with two angles sitting on it. One is 56 degrees. The other is called x, and we want its size.

ask.ifNot: The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand where the two angles meet. You face along the line, then turn to face the other way. That is a half turn. So how much do the two angles make together?
A half turn is 180 degrees. So x, plus 56, equals 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So x is 180 take away 56.

beats.say: 180 is the whole, and 56 is one part of it. x is the other part. How do we find x?
Let's take 56 away in two easy hops. First the 50: 180 take away 50 leaves 130.
Now the 6 that is left: 130 take away 6 leaves 124. So 180 minus 56 is 124.
So x equals 124. The other angle is 124 degrees.
Check: 124 plus 56 makes 180, one whole straight line. It fits.
Remember: a straight line is 180 degrees. Know one angle on it, and 180 minus that angle gives you the other.
Our numbers go 20, 35, 50, 65. What comes next? Let's find out together.
Start with the first two numbers. How far is it from 20 up to 35?

ask.ifNot: Count on from 20 up to 35. 35 take away 20 leaves 15.

beats.say: 35 minus 20 is 15. So the first jump is plus 15.

spec.note: Every jump is the same size

beats.say: Now check the next pair. 50 minus 35 is 15 as well. The jump never changes: it is always 15.
So how do we get the number after 65?

ask.ifNot: This pattern grows by adding, and the jump is always 15. So we add 15 to 65, just once.

beats.say: 65 plus 15 is 80. So the next number is 80.
Quick check. From 65 to 80 is a jump of 15, the same as all the others. It fits.
Remember the three moves. Measure a jump, check the other jumps match, then make one more jump from the last number.
This pattern begins 6, 12, 18, and goes on and on. Each number in it is called a term. We are after the 10th term.
First, the jump. 12 minus 6 is 6, and 18 minus 12 is 6 too. So each term is 6 more than the one before.

spec.note: Every jump is the same size

beats.say: We could keep adding 6 all the way, but that is slow. To go from the 1st term to the 10th term, how many jumps do we make?

ask.ifNot: Count on your fingers. From the 1st term to the 2nd is 1 jump. From the 1st to the 3rd is 2 jumps. The jumps are always 1 fewer than the term number.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. The 1st term needs no jump at all. So the jumps are 1 fewer than 10, which is 9.
Let's test that on a term we can see. The 3rd term should be the 1st term plus 2 jumps. 6 plus 2 times 6 is 18. It matches.
Now, 9 jumps of 6. 9 times 6 is 54. So the jumps carry us 54 forward.
We have 54 from the jumps. What do we do with it?

ask.ifNot: The jumps begin at the 1st term, which is 6. So the 54 must be added on to 6.

beats.say: 6 plus 54 is 60. So the 10th term is 60.
Here is the plan to keep. Find the jump. Count 1 fewer jump than the term number. Multiply, then add the 1st term.
We want the supplement of 25 degrees. Supplementary angles are two angles that sit side by side on a straight line. Here is the picture.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 25, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 25.

beats.say: The whole is 180 and one piece is 25. Which sum finds the missing piece?
Let's take 25 away in two easy hops. First the 20: 180 take away 20 leaves 160.
Now the 5 that is left: 160 take away 5 leaves 155. So 180 minus 25 is 155.
So the supplement is 155 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 25 plus 155 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.

board.text: Rectangle: length 26 cm, breadth 20 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 26 centimetres long and 20 centimetres broad. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 20 rows of 26, so we multiply 26 by 20.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 20 rows, with 26 in every row. So the area is length times breadth.
20 is 2 tens. So first we find 26 times 2. That is 52.
26 times 20 is 10 times as big as that. So it is 520.
There it is: the area is 520 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 520 squares shared into 20 rows gives 26 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the breadth, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Rectangle: length 14 cm, breadth 7 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 14 centimetres long and 7 centimetres broad. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two breadths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a breadth, then another length and another breadth. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one breadth first. 14 plus 7 is 21.
Careful: 21 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two breadths, so we double it. 2 times 21 is 42.
There it is: the perimeter is 42 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 14, 7, 14, 7. Together they make 42.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the breadth, then double.

Look at these numbers. 3, 6, 12, 24, 48. They grow fast! One more is hiding at the end.
Let's try the jumps first. They are 3, then 6, then 12. The jump keeps changing, so this is not a plain adding pattern.
When adding does not fit, try times. Which of these rules works at every step?

ask.ifNot: Adding 3 works for the first step, but not for the next one. Multiplying works every time: 3 times 2 is 6, and 6 times 2 is 12.

beats.say: 3 times 2 is 6. 6 times 2 is 12. 12 times 2 is 24. Each number is double the one before.
So we multiply the last number by 2. 48 times 2 is 96. The next number is 96.
Let's check by going backwards. 96 divided by 2 takes us back to 48. It fits.
Keep this in mind. If adding does not fit a pattern, test times. Find the multiplier, then use it on the last number.
Here is our pattern: 3, 7, 11, 15, and then a gap. Let's find the number that fills it.
To find the rule, we measure a jump. How much bigger is 7 than 3?

spec.note: Every jump is the same size

board.text: Triangle: base 12 cm, height 4 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Here is a triangle. Its base is 12 centimetres and its height is 4 centimetres. We want its area, the space inside it.

spec.note: The triangle is half of the rectangle

beats.say: Picture a rectangle drawn round the triangle, with the same base and the same height. The triangle fills exactly half of that rectangle.

ask.ifNot: The area of a rectangle is its length times its breadth. Adding the 2 numbers does not give the space inside.

beats.say: So let's find the rectangle first. Which sum gives the area of the whole rectangle?
12 times 4 is 48. That is the whole rectangle.

ask.ifNot: The triangle covers half of the rectangle, so its area is half of 48. We divide by 2.

beats.say: Here comes the step that is easy to forget. The triangle is only half of the rectangle. So what do we do with 48?
Half of 48 is 24.
So the area of the triangle is 24 square centimetres.
So for the area of a triangle: multiply the base by the height, then take half. Stopping at 48 is the classic slip.
Here is a triangle. 2 of its angles are 30 degrees and 37 degrees. We need to find the third one.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 30 plus 30 is 60. Then 7 more makes 67.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 67 away from 180.

beats.say: The 2 known angles take 67 degrees out of the 180. What is left for the third angle?
Take 67 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 60: that leaves 120. Then take away 7 more: 113.
The hidden angle is 113 degrees.
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 30, 37 and 113. They make 180, just as they should. And notice: 113 degrees is a wide angle, an obtuse one. A triangle can have just 1 of those.
Remember the plan: add the 2 angles you have, and take that from 180. What is left is the third angle.
This triangle is keeping a secret. We know 2 angles, 76 degrees and 58 degrees, and the third is hidden.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

Let's add in 2 small steps. 76 plus 50 is 126. Then 8 more makes 134.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 134 away from 180.

Take 134 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 130: that leaves 50. Then take away 4 more: 46.
So the third angle is 46 degrees. There it is!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 76, 58 and 46. They make 180, just as they should.
So for a missing angle in a triangle: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.

We are counting the numbers from 1 to 101 that 5 divides exactly. Those are the numbers in the 5 times table.

board.text: From 1 to 101: how many are divisible by 5?

spec.note: Multiples of 5 from 1 to 101

beats.say: Writing them all out would take ages. So we find the first one and the last one, and count smartly.
The first is easy: 5 itself, which is 5 times 1.
Now the last one. Divide 101 by 5: it goes 20 times, with a bit left over. 5 times 20 is 100, and one more step gives 105, which is past 101. So 100 is the last.
So our numbers are 5 times 1, 5 times 2, and so on, up to 5 times 20. How many numbers is that?

ask.ifNot: We are counting 1, 2, 3 and so on, up to 20. Counting from 1 up to 20 gives exactly 20 numbers.

beats.say: Counting from 1 up to 20 gives 20 numbers. So 20 numbers from 1 to 101 are divisible by 5.
Careful with the end. 101 is not in the 5 times table, so the count stops at 100.
So here is the plan: find the last multiple, and see which number in the table it is. That number is the count.

So x equals 57. The other angle is 57 degrees.

board.text: Angles in the ratio 4 : 2 : 4. Largest angle = ?

board.text: Rectangle: length 13 cm, breadth 6 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 13 centimetres long and 6 centimetres broad. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 6 rows of 13, so we multiply 13 by 6.

The squares sit in 6 rows, with 13 in every row. So the area is length times breadth.

board.text: Triangle: base 16 cm, height 20 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: The triangle is half of the rectangle

ask.ifNot: The area of a rectangle is its length times its breadth. Adding the 2 numbers does not give the space inside.

ask.ifNot: The triangle covers half of the rectangle, so its area is half of 320. We divide by 2.

Half of 320 is 160.
So the area of the triangle is 160 square centimetres.
So for the area of a triangle: multiply the base by the height, then take half. Stopping at 320 is the classic slip.
This pattern begins 4, 7, 10, and goes on and on. Each number in it is called a term. We are after the 10th term.

I have called the two angles next door p and q. Now, a straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees.

board.text: On a straight line: x° and 27°. x = ?

beats.say: Two angles share a straight line. One is 27 degrees and the other is a mystery, called x. Let's find x.

ask.ifNot: The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand where the two angles meet. You face along the line, then turn to face the other way. That is a half turn. So how much do the two angles make together?
A half turn is 180 degrees. So x, plus 27, equals 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So x is 180 take away 27.

beats.say: 180 is the whole, and 27 is one part of it. x is the other part. How do we find x?
Let's take 27 away in two easy hops. First the 20: 180 take away 20 leaves 160.
Now the 7 that is left: 160 take away 7 leaves 153. So 180 minus 27 is 153.
So x equals 153. The other angle is 153 degrees.
Check: 153 plus 27 makes 180, one whole straight line. It fits.
So angles on a straight line always make 180 degrees. Take the one you know away from 180, and you have the other.

The 3 angles of any triangle make 180 degrees together. So all 12 parts together are 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Sharing equally means dividing. 180 degrees shared among 12 equal parts is 180 divided by 12.

beats.say: So how big is 1 part?
180 divided by 12 is 15. Multiply back to be sure: 12 times 15 is 180. So 1 part is 15 degrees.
Careful: 15 degrees is only 1 part, not the answer. The largest angle has the most parts, 5 of them. 5 times 15 is 75.
So the largest angle is 75 degrees.
Let's check with all 3 angles: 60, 45 and 75. Together they make 180. It works.
So with a ratio: add the parts, divide 180 by that to get 1 part, then multiply by the parts you need.

Divisible by 3 means the number is in the 3 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 3.

ask.ifNot: 102 is past 100, and 96 is not the last one we can reach. The last multiple of 3 inside the range is 99.

beats.say: Start at the top end. What is the biggest multiple of 3 that is not more than 100?
3 times 33 is 99. One more step gives 102, and that is past 100.
Look at the 3 times table from its very start. 99 is multiple number 33. So up to 100 there are 33 multiples of 3.
But our range only starts at 50. 3 times 16 is 48, still too small. The next one, 51, is the first one inside.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 48, and 48 is 3 times 16. So exactly 16 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 33 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
So we take 16 away from 33, and 17 are left.
Check another way. From 51 to 99 is 48. That is 16 jumps of 3, and 16 jumps join 17 numbers.
So 17 numbers from 50 to 100 are divisible by 3.
The plan: find the last multiple, count from the start of the table, then take away the ones that are too small.
The numbers start 1, 3, 5, and keep going. Our job is to find the 20th one without writing them all out.
First, see how it grows. What is the jump from each number to the next?

ask.ifNot: Subtract neighbours: 3 minus 1 is 2, and 5 minus 3 is 2 again. So the jump is plus 2.

beats.say: Plus 2, every single time. A sequence that climbs by the same jump each time is called an arithmetic sequence.
We can't write out all 20 terms, so let's count jumps instead. The 2nd term is 1 jump from the start. The 3rd term is 2 jumps.
See the pattern in the table? So how many jumps take us to the 20th term?

ask.ifNot: Look at the table again. The jumps are always 1 fewer than the term number, because the 1st term needs no jump at all. So the 20th term needs 19 jumps.

beats.say: 19 jumps, and each jump is 2. 19 times 2 is 38.
Now start at 1, the first term, and add all those jumps. 1 plus 38 is 39. So the 20th term is 39.
Let's test the idea on a term we already know. The 3rd term is 2 jumps from 1: 1 plus 2 times 2 is 5. And 5 is right there in our list.
The plan: find the jump, count the jumps, which is always 1 fewer than the term number, multiply, then add the first term.
Here is a line of numbers: 5, 10, 20, 40, and then a gap. We need the number that comes next.
Let's write the jumps underneath. From 5 to 10 is plus 5. From 10 to 20 is plus 10. From 20 to 40 is plus 20.
The jumps are not the same: they keep growing. So adding is not the rule. What takes each number to the next one?

ask.ifNot: Adding the same amount does not work here, because the jumps change. But double each number and you get the next one, every time.

beats.say: Each number is double the one before it. 5 times 2 is 10. 10 times 2 is 20. 20 times 2 is 40.
So what comes after 40?

ask.ifNot: Don't add the last jump again. The rule is double, so we double 40.

beats.say: 40 times 2 is 80. So the next number is 80.
Read it back: 5, 10, 20, 40, 80. Each one is double the one before. It fits.
So when the jumps keep growing, try multiplying instead of adding.
Add 1, 3, 5, and every number in the pattern up to 29. That is a long sum, so we will look for a short cut.
First, the jump. 3 minus 1 is 2, and 5 minus 3 is 2. So the numbers climb by 2 each time.
How many numbers are in the list? From 1 up to 29 is a climb of 28. In jumps of 2, that is 14 jumps.
14 jumps. So how many numbers are there?

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3 numbers. There is always 1 more number than jumps.

beats.say: 1 more than the jumps: 15 numbers in all.
Now the clever bit. Add the first and the last: 1 plus 29 is 30. Then the second and the second last: 3 plus 27 is 30 again!
Every pair makes 30. So write the list twice, once forwards and once backwards, and we get 15 pairs of 30. 15 times 30 is 450.
But 450 has every number counted twice. What do we do to get the real sum?

ask.ifNot: We wrote the list two times, so 450 is double the sum. Halving it brings us back.

beats.say: Half of 450 is 225. So the sum is 225.
Does the trick really work? Try just the first 3 numbers. 1 plus 3 plus 5 is 9. The trick says: 1 plus 5 is 6, times 3, then halved. That is 9 too.
So, to add a long, evenly spaced list: count the numbers, add the first and the last, multiply, and halve.

beats.say: Start at the top end. What is the biggest multiple of 5 that is not more than 150?
5 times 30 is exactly 150. It lands right on the end of our range, so it counts.
Look at the 5 times table from its very start. 150 is multiple number 30. So up to 150 there are 30 multiples of 5.
Careful here: 100 itself is in the 5 times table, so it counts. The ones that are too small stop at 95, which is 5 times 19.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 95, and 95 is 5 times 19. So exactly 19 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 30 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
30 take away 19 leaves 11.

ask.ifNot: 20 itself is even, and it is inside the range, so it counts. Our list starts right at 20.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first even number in the range?
So we start at 20. And the last one is 70 itself, because 70 is even.
Even numbers go up in jumps of 2: 20, 22, 24 and so on, all the way to 70.
From 20 to 70 is 50. Each jump is 2, so that is 25 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 25 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
One more than the jumps: 25 plus 1 is 26. That extra 1 is our starting number.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 even ones. From 20 up to 70 there are 5 runs of 10, plus 70 itself, which is even. That gives 26 again.
So there are 26 even numbers from 20 to 70.

board.text: Sum of the first 14 even numbers = ?

beats.say: We need to add up the first 14 even numbers. That is a long sum, so let's find a clever way.
Even numbers go 2, 4, 6 and so on. Each one is 2 times its position in the list, so the last one is 2 times 14, which is 28.
Here is the trick. Add the first and the last: 2 plus 28 makes 30.

ask.ifNot: 4 plus 26 is 30 again. One number went up by 2 and the other came down by 2, so the total did not change.

beats.say: Now the second and the second last: 4 and 26. What do they make?
Yes, 30 again. Every pair, working inwards from the two ends, makes 30.
14 numbers make 7 pairs, because each pair uses up 2 numbers.
7 pairs of 30: 7 times 30 is 210.
Check another way. Write the list twice, once forwards and once backwards. That makes 14 columns of 30, and half of that is 210.
So the sum of the first 14 even numbers is 210.
Pair the ends, count the pairs, multiply. That trick turns a long sum into a short one.

ask.ifNot: Don't add the last jump again. The rule is double, so we double 8.

beats.say: 8 times 2 is 16. So the next number is 16.
Read it back: 2, 4, 8, 16. Each one is double the one before. It fits.
So when the jumps keep growing, try multiplying instead of adding.

First, the jump. 11 minus 7 is 4, and 15 minus 11 is 4. So the numbers climb by 4 each time.
How many numbers are in the list? From 7 up to 63 is a climb of 56. In jumps of 4, that is 14 jumps.
14 jumps. So how many numbers are there?

ask.ifNot: We wrote the list two times, so 1050 is double the sum. Halving it brings us back.

The short cut: how many numbers, times first plus last, then halve. Just remember to count the numbers, not the jumps.

board.text: A book has 75 pages. How many digits?

beats.say: A book with 75 pages. Every page has its number printed on it, and we are counting all the digits in those numbers.
Careful: this is not the same as counting pages. Page 5 uses 1 digit, but page 75 uses 2.

ask.ifNot: Page 10 already needs 2 digits, a 1 and a 0. And there is no page 0. So the 1 digit pages are 1 to 9.

beats.say: So we sort the pages by how many digits they use. Which pages use just 1 digit?

board.text: Sum of the first 23 odd numbers = ?

beats.say: The first 23 odd numbers, all added together. Before the big sum, let's try some tiny ones and watch what happens.
The first odd number on its own is 1. The first 2 odd numbers, 1 plus 3, make 4. And 4 is 2 times 2.

ask.ifNot: Add them up: 1, 3, 5 and 7. Then compare with 4 times 4. They match.

So the first 23 odd numbers must add up to 23 times 23.
Split it to make it easy. 23 times 20 is 460. 23 times 3 is 69. Together that is 529.
Check with pairs. The last odd number is 45. First plus last, 1 plus 45, is 46. Forwards and backwards gives 23 columns of 46, and half of that is 529.
So the sum of the first 23 odd numbers is 529.
The first so many odd numbers always add up to that number times itself. A pattern worth remembering!

16 once more. Keep stepping inwards from both ends, and every pair makes 16.
15 is an odd count, so one number is left alone in the middle. It is half of 16, which is 8. The rest make 7 pairs.
7 pairs of 16, plus the middle 8, makes 120.
Check another way. Write the list twice, once forwards and once backwards. That makes 15 columns of 16, and half of that is 120.

Pair the ends, count the pairs, multiply. That trick turns a long sum into a short one.

board.text: Odd numbers from 10 to 50: how many?

beats.say: We want to know how many odd numbers there are from 10 to 50. Both ends count, if they are odd.

ask.ifNot: 10 is even, so it does not count. The very next number, 11, is the first odd one.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first odd number in the range?
So we start at 11. And the last one is 49, because 50 is even.
Odd numbers go up in jumps of 2: 11, 13, 15 and so on, all the way to 49.
From 11 to 49 is 38. Each jump is 2, so that is 19 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 19 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
19 jumps join 20 numbers. The extra 1 is the number we started on.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 odd ones. From 10 up to 50 there are 4 runs of 10. The 50 left at the end is even, so it adds nothing. 20 again.
So there are 20 odd numbers from 10 to 50.
Find the two ends, count the jumps between them, then add 1 for the starting number. That works every time.

board.text: Odd numbers from 1 to 51: how many?

beats.say: From 1 to 51, how many of the numbers are odd? Let's count them without writing every one.

ask.ifNot: 1 itself is odd, and it is inside the range, so it counts. Our list starts right at 1.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first odd number in the range?
So we start at 1. And the last one is 51 itself, because 51 is odd.
Odd numbers go up in jumps of 2: 1, 3, 5 and so on, all the way to 51.
From 1 to 51 is 50. Each jump is 2, so that is 25 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 25 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
One more than the jumps: 25 plus 1 is 26. That extra 1 is our starting number.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 odd ones. From 1 up to 51 there are 5 runs of 10, plus 51 itself, which is odd. That gives 26 again.
So there are 26 odd numbers from 1 to 51.

board.text: Sum of the first 7 odd numbers = ?

beats.say: The first 7 odd numbers, all added together. Before the big sum, let's try some tiny ones and watch what happens.
The first odd number on its own is 1. The first 2 odd numbers, 1 plus 3, make 4. And 4 is 2 times 2.
The first 3 odd numbers: 1 plus 3 plus 5 makes 9. That is 3 times 3. Interesting!

ask.ifNot: Add them up: 1, 3, 5 and 7. Then compare with 4 times 4. They match.

beats.say: So what do you think the first 4 odd numbers, 1, 3, 5 and 7, add up to?
Yes, 4 times 4. Look at the picture: each new odd number wraps round the square like a letter L, and makes the next bigger square.
So the first 7 odd numbers must add up to 7 times 7.
And 7 times 7 is 49.
Check with pairs. The last odd number is 13. First plus last, 1 plus 13, is 14. Forwards and backwards gives 7 columns of 14, and half of that is 49.
So the sum of the first 7 odd numbers is 49.
So, count how many odd numbers there are, and multiply that count by itself. Isn't that neat?

board.text: Sum of the first 14 natural numbers = ?

beats.say: We need to add up the first 14 natural numbers. That is a long sum, so let's find a clever way.
Natural numbers are the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3 and so on. The first 14 of them end at 14.
Do not start adding from the left. Join the two ends instead: 1 plus 14 makes 15.

ask.ifNot: 2 plus 13 is 15 again. One number went up by 1 and the other came down by 1, so the total did not change.

beats.say: Now the second and the second last: 2 and 13. What do they make?
Yes, 15 again. Every pair, working inwards from the two ends, makes 15.
14 numbers make 7 pairs, because each pair uses up 2 numbers.
7 pairs of 15: 7 times 15 is 105.
Check another way. Write the list twice, once forwards and once backwards. That makes 14 columns of 15, and half of that is 105.
So the sum of the first 14 natural numbers is 105.
Whenever numbers go up in equal steps, pair the first with the last. Every pair gives the same total.

board.text: From 50 to 250: how many are divisible by 5?

beats.say: From 50 to 250, some numbers can be divided by 5 exactly. Our job is to count them.
Divisible by 5 means the number is in the 5 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 5.

ask.ifNot: 250 itself is in the 5 times table, and it is inside our range. So 250 is the last one.

beats.say: Let's find the far end first. Which is the last multiple of 5 that does not go past 250?
5 times 50 is exactly 250. It lands right on the end of our range, so it counts.
Look at the 5 times table from its very start. 250 is multiple number 50. So up to 250 there are 50 multiples of 5.
Careful here: 50 itself is in the 5 times table, so it counts. The ones that are too small stop at 45, which is 5 times 9.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 45, and 45 is 5 times 9. So exactly 9 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 50 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
So we take 9 away from 50, and 41 are left.
Check another way. From 50 to 250 is 200. That is 40 jumps of 5, and 40 jumps join 41 numbers.
So 41 numbers from 50 to 250 are divisible by 5.
So, count the multiples up to the top end, then remove the ones below the bottom end. No long lists needed.

board.text: Sum of the first 17 even numbers = ?

ask.ifNot: 4 plus 32 is 36 again. One number went up by 2 and the other came down by 2, so the total did not change.

beats.say: Now the second and the second last: 4 and 32. What do they make?

17 is an odd count, so one number is left alone in the middle. It is half of 36, which is 18. The rest make 8 pairs.

Check another way. Write the list twice, once forwards and once backwards. That makes 17 columns of 36, and half of that is 306.

board.text: Triangle: base 20 cm, height 7 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Here is our triangle. Its base is 20 centimetres and its height is 7 centimetres. We want its area, the flat space inside.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides is for the walk round the edge. The space inside a rectangle is its length times its breadth.

beats.say: Counting squares inside a triangle is awkward. So let me box it in: a rectangle around the triangle, with the same base and the same height. How do we find the area of that rectangle?
The area of a rectangle is its length times its breadth. Here that means base times height.
20 times 7 is 140.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing once more. The triangle covers only half of the dashed rectangle. So we need half of 140.

beats.say: Now look closely. The two corner pieces outside the triangle fit together to make another triangle, just the same size. So what do we do with 140?
So the rule for a triangle is: half of base times height.
Half of 140 is 70. And see how it is written: a half, times 20, times 7.

spec.note: Area = 70 sq. cm

beats.say: So the area of the triangle is 70 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area counts little squares.
A quick check: two triangles of 70 make 140, the whole rectangle. It fits.
The method in one line: half of base times height. If you stop at base times height, you have found the whole rectangle, not the triangle.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Here is our circle. Its radius, from the centre out to the edge, is 14 centimetres. We want the circumference, and we are told to use 22 over 7 for pi.
Circumference is the walk all the way round the circle. And here is a lovely fact: for every circle, that walk is a little more than 3 times the distance straight across. That number is pi.

ask.ifNot: The radius only goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter goes right across, through the centre. That is 2 radii, so 2 times 14.

beats.say: We were given the radius, 14. So what is the distance straight across, the diameter?
The diameter is 2 radii: 2 times 14 is 28 centimetres. That is why the rule is often written as 2 times pi times the radius.
Now we need 22 over 7, times 28. Divide by the 7 first, because 28 is in the 7 times table: 28 divided by 7 is 4.
Then multiply by the 22. 22 times 4 is 88.

spec.note: Circumference = 88 cm

beats.say: So the circumference is 88 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because it is a length, a walk round the edge.
Does that make sense? 3 times 28 is 84, and our answer, 88, is a little more than that. Just as pi promised.
So: circumference is 2 times pi times the radius. The slip to watch for is forgetting to double the radius, which gives only half the walk.

board.text: Rectangle: length 25 cm, breadth 5 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle. The length is 25 centimetres and the breadth is 5 centimetres. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter is a walk all the way round the edge, back to where you started. Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so there are 2 lengths and 2 breadths. Let me label all 4 sides.

ask.ifNot: 25 plus 5 only gets us halfway, along one length and one breadth. The walk goes along all 4 sides. And 25 times 5 would be the space inside, the area.

beats.say: Which sum takes us all the way round?
Let's walk it. One length and one breadth: 25 plus 5 is 30. That is halfway round.
The other two sides are the same again, so we double it: 30 plus 30 is 60.
That is where the rule comes from: add the length and the breadth, then double.

spec.note: Perimeter = 60 cm

beats.say: So the perimeter is 60 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because a perimeter is a length.
Check with the whole walk: 25 plus 5 plus 25 plus 5 makes 60.
The method in one line: perimeter is 2 times, length plus breadth. Do not stop after adding just two sides.
Here is 43 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplementary angle is the other piece of that line, the one marked with a question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a corner, a right angle.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 43 degrees, plus our missing angle, makes 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 43.

beats.say: We know the whole, 180, and one part, 43. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 43 away in two easy hops. First the 40: 180 take away 40 leaves 140.
Now the 3 that is left: 140 take away 3 leaves 137. So 180 minus 43 is 137.
So the supplementary angle is 137 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 43 plus 137 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So for a supplementary angle, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.
Here is our triangle. Two of its angles are 41 degrees and 71 degrees. The third one, at the top, is our mystery.

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So the 3 angles of a triangle always make 180 degrees.

beats.say: Here is something you can try with paper. Tear the 3 corners off any triangle and put them side by side. They always make a straight line. So how much do the 3 angles make together?

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: A straight line is a half turn, 180 degrees. So the 3 angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees.
First, how much have the two angles we know used up? 41 plus 71 is 112.

ask.ifNot: Both known angles have to come off the 180, not just one of them. Together they are 112, so it is 180 take away 112.

beats.say: So 112 of the 180 degrees is gone. What sum finds the third angle?
Let's take 112 away in two easy hops. First the 110: 180 take away 110 leaves 70.
Now the 2 that is left: 70 take away 2 leaves 68. So 180 minus 112 is 68.
So the third angle is 68 degrees. Into the drawing it goes.
Check: 41 plus 71 plus 68 makes 180. All three together make the straight line.
So for any triangle: add the two angles you know, then take the total away from 180. The slip to watch for is taking away only one of them.

board.text: On a straight line: x° and 116°. x = ?

beats.say: Here is a straight line with two angles sitting on it. One is 116 degrees. The other is called x, and we want to know its size.

ask.ifNot: The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand where the two angles meet. Facing along the line one way, then turning to face the other way, is a half turn. So how much do the two angles make together?
A half turn is 180 degrees. So x, plus 116, equals 180. Now it is an equation.

ask.ifNot: To undo plus 116, we take away 116. And to keep the two sides level, we take it from both sides.

beats.say: We want x on its own. What do we do about the plus 116?
To undo plus 116, we take 116 away, from both sides.
Let's take 116 away in two easy hops. First the 110: 180 take away 110 leaves 70.
Now the 6 that is left: 70 take away 6 leaves 64. So 180 minus 116 is 64.
So x equals 64. The other angle is 64 degrees.
Check: 64 plus 116 makes 180, a full straight line. It fits.
So angles on a straight line always make 180 degrees. Take the one you know away from 180, and you have the other.

board.text: Lines cross: one angle is 108°. Opposite angle = ?

beats.say: Two straight lines cross and make 4 angles. One of them is 108 degrees. We want the angle vertically opposite: the one straight across the crossing point.
I have called the two angles next door p and q. Now, here is what we know about a straight line: it is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees.
Look at 108 degrees and its neighbour, p. They sit side by side on one straight line. Let's take 108 away in two easy hops. First the 100: 180 take away 100 leaves 80.
Now the 8 that is left: 80 take away 8 leaves 72. So 180 minus 108 is 72.

ask.ifNot: p and the mystery angle share a straight line, so together they make 180 degrees. We take p, which is 72, away from 180.

beats.say: So p is 72 degrees. Now look at p and our mystery angle. They sit side by side on the other straight line. So what is the mystery angle?
Let's take 72 away in two easy hops. First the 70: 180 take away 70 leaves 110.
Now the 2 that is left: 110 take away 2 leaves 108. So 180 minus 72 is 108.
108 degrees. Exactly the angle we started with! That always happens: angles straight across from each other are equal.
So next time you can say it straight away: the vertically opposite angle is equal, 108 degrees. The slip to watch for is giving 72, which is the neighbour on the line.

board.text: Sum of the first 20 odd numbers = ?

beats.say: Add up the first 20 odd numbers: 1, 3, 5 and so on. Let's start small and hunt for a pattern.
The first odd number on its own is 1. The first 2 odd numbers, 1 plus 3, make 4. And 4 is 2 times 2.

The series is 48, 51, 57, 69, and then a star. We must find the number hiding behind the star.

spec.note: How big is each jump? What comes next?

beats.say: Find the jumps. 51 minus 48 is 3. 57 minus 51 is 6. 69 minus 57 is 12.
The jumps are 3, 6 and 12. How do they grow?

choices: each is double the one before
ask.ifNot: 3 to 6 could be adding 3. But 6 to 12 is not adding 3. Doubling fits both: double 3 is 6, and double 6 is 12.

beats.say: The jumps double each time. So the next jump is double 12, which is 24. The trap is to use an old jump again.
69 plus 24 is 93. So the star stands for 93.
Read the jumps once more: 3, 6, 12, 24. Each one is double the last. It fits.
When the jumps are not steady, check whether they grow by adding or by multiplying. Here they doubled.
We want the difference between 9.07 and 7.9.

spec.note: How much longer is the top bar?

beats.say: The word difference tells us what to do. What is it?

ask.ifNot: The difference is how far apart two numbers are. To find it, we take the smaller one away from the bigger one.

beats.say: 9.07 has two digits after the point, and 7.9 has only one. So write 7.9 as 7.90, and put the points in line.
Start at the hundredths. 7 take away 0 is 7.
Now the tenths: 0 take away 9. We cannot do that. So what do we do?

ask.ifNot: 0 tenths is less than 9 tenths, so we borrow 1 whole from the 9 ones. One whole is the same as 10 tenths.

beats.say: Now we have 10 tenths, and 10 take away 9 is 1. In the ones, 8 are left after the borrowing, and 8 take away 7 is 1.
So the difference is 1.17.
Check by adding back: 7.90 plus 1.17 makes 9.07. Line up the points, fill the gap with a zero, and remember what you borrowed.
In how many ways can 98 be written as one number times another? Each way is a pair of factors of 98.

spec.note: How many pairs multiply to 98?

beats.say: Every number has the pair made with 1. So the first way is 1 times 98.
98 is even, so 2 divides it. Half of 98 is 49. The second way is 2 times 49.
Keep going in order. Which of these numbers divides 98 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 5 needs a last digit of 0 or 5. 3 needs a digit sum in the 3 times table. Neither works for 98. But 7 goes in exactly.

beats.say: 7 times 14 is 98. That is a third way. And 3, 4, 5 and 6 do not divide 98 at all.
The next factors are 14 and 49, and both are already on the board as partners. So there are no new pairs. 98 can be written in 3 ways.
The trap is 6. That is how many factors 98 has. But each way uses two factors, so six factors make three pairs.
Nine numbers to add on the left, a times sum on the right, and a box between them. We find each side, then pick the sign.
Adding nine numbers one by one is slow. Here is a trick: make pairs. What do 1 and 9 make?

ask.ifNot: 1 plus 9 is 10. And tens are lovely to add.

beats.say: 1 and 9 make 10. So do 2 and 8, 3 and 7, and 4 and 6. That is four tens, which is 40.
The 5 in the middle has no partner. Add it on: 40 plus 5 is 45. The left side is 45.
Right side. 5 times 7 is 35.
Compare 45 with 35. Which is true?

ask.ifNot: 45 has 4 tens and 35 has only 3 tens. So 45 is bigger, and the open mouth of the sign faces the 45.

beats.say: 45 is greater than 35. So the sign in the box is the greater than sign.
So: work out both sides first, then compare. And when you add a long list, hunt for pairs that make 10.
Each of these numbers has two 6s. We want the number where one 6 is worth 1000 times the other 6.

board.text: One 6 worth 1000 times the other 6: in which number?

beats.say: Each seat is worth 10 times the seat on its right. So how many seats apart must the two 6s be?

ask.ifNot: One seat apart is 10 times. Two seats is 100 times. Three seats is 1000 times. So the 6s must be 3 seats apart.

board.text: 1 seat left: 10 times      2 seats left: 100 times

beats.say: 10 times 10 times 10 is 1000. So we look for two 6s that are 3 seats apart.
Take 576006. One 6 is in the thousands, worth 6000. The other is in the ones, worth 6. Yes, 3 seats apart!
Now the trap. Do not stop at the first one that fits! One of the choices is All of them, so we must test the others too.
In 567060 the 6s are worth 60000 and 60. That fits as well.
In 657600 the 6s are worth 600000 and 600. That fits too.
All three numbers work. So the answer is: All of them.
Remember: when All of them is a choice, test every number before you decide.
A typist types every prime number between 1 and 100. How many times does she press the 2 key? We need the primes that have a 2 in them.

board.text: Primes from 1 to 100: how many times is 2 typed?

beats.say: A 2 can sit in the ones place or in the tens place. Take the ones place first. Any number that ends in 2 is even.
Which is the only prime number that ends in 2?

ask.ifNot: 12 and 22 are even, so 2 divides them and they are not prime. The only even prime is 2 itself.

beats.say: So the ones place gives us one 2: the prime number 2.
Now the tens place: the numbers from 20 to 29. The even ones are not prime. That leaves the odd ones: 21, 23, 25, 27 and 29.
Careful here. 21 is 3 times 7. 25 is 5 times 5. 27 is 3 times 9. None of those is prime.
23 and 29 are prime, and each has one 2. So the primes with a 2 are 2, 23 and 29. That is 3 times.
The trap is counting numbers like 12 and 22. They have a 2 in them, but they are not prime. And do not forget the prime 2 itself.
We are told m is 21 and n is 3. We also know that m equals n times p. We must find m divided by p.
One letter has no value yet: p. So first we find p. Let's put the numbers we know into m equals n times p.
21 equals 3 times p. So what is p?

ask.ifNot: Which number times 3 makes 21? In the 3 times table, 3 times 7 is 21. So p is 7.

beats.say: 3 times 7 is 21, so p equals 7.
Careful: 7 is one of the choices, but it is only p. The question asks for m divided by p.
m is 21 and p is 7. So which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: m is 21 and p is 7. So m divided by p is 21 divided by 7.

beats.say: 21 divided by 7 is 3. So m divided by p equals 3.
