Notice something neat. The answer 3 is the same as n. That is because 21 is 3 times 7, so dividing by 7 brings back the 3.
So put in the numbers you know, find the missing letter, and then do what the question asks.
Three fractions in one line. One quarter, plus two thirds, take away one half.
The bottoms are 4, 3 and 2. Which number do all three go into?

ask.ifNot: 4 times 3 is 12, and 2 goes into 12 as well. 8 does not work, because 3 does not go into 8.

beats.say: So we change every fraction into twelfths. One quarter is 3 over 12, because 4 times 3 is 12.
Two thirds is 8 over 12: we multiply the top and bottom by 4. And one half is 6 over 12.
Now they are all twelfths. We work with the tops only, and each sign stays with its own number.
3 plus 8, then take away 6. What is it?

ask.ifNot: 3 and 8 make 11. Then 11 take away 6 leaves 5.

beats.say: 3 and 8 make 11, and 11 take away 6 is 5. So the answer is 5 over 12.
With several fractions: one bottom number for all, change each one, then add and subtract the tops.
The bottle holds 150 millilitres of syrup, and 25 millilitres are taken each day. How many days will it last?
Each day uses up one lot of 25. So what do we need to find?

ask.ifNot: Every day takes one lot of 25 out of the bottle. So we count how many lots of 25 fit into 150.

beats.say: That is a division. 150 divided by 25.
Let us count up in 25s, one for each day. 25, 50, 75, 100.
Keep going. 125, 150. We have reached the full bottle. That was 6 lots of 25.
So 150 divided by 25 is 6. The syrup lasts for 6 days.
Check by multiplying. 6 times 25 is 150. It fits.
So when something is used up in equal amounts, divide the total by the amount used each time.
Sarika was born in 2006 and Surya was born in 2013. In which year will Sarika be twice the age of Surya?

board.text: Sarika was born in 2006. Surya was born in 2013.
In which year is Sarika twice as old as Surya?

beats.say: First, how much older is Sarika? 2013 minus 2006 is 7. Sarika is 7 years older, and she always will be.
When Sarika is twice Surya's age, Surya is 1 block and Sarika is 2 blocks. Sarika's extra block is the gap.
The gap is 7 years. So how old is Surya when Sarika is twice his age?

ask.ifNot: The extra block is the gap, which is 7. Surya's block is the same size. So Surya is 7.

beats.say: Surya is 7, and Sarika is 7 plus 7, which is 14. And 14 is twice 7.
Now, in which year is Surya 7 years old? He was born in 2013, so add 7. 2013 plus 7 is 2020.
So the year is 2020.
Check with Sarika. 2020 minus 2006 is 14. So in 2020 she is 14 and Surya is 7. Exactly twice.
What about 2019, one year earlier? Then they would be 13 and 6, and twice 6 is 12, not 13. So only 2020 works.
The gap between two ages never changes. When one is double the other, the younger one's age equals the gap.
57 over 17. The top is bigger than the bottom, so this is more than 1 whole. Let's write it as a mixed number.
Every 17 seventeenths make 1 whole. So how many seventeens fit into 57? Pick the one that fits and gets closest.

ask.ifNot: 68 is more than 57, so 4 times is too many. 51 fits, and it is closer to 57 than 34 is.

beats.say: 17 times 3 is 51. So we have 3 wholes.
How many seventeenths are left over?

ask.ifNot: We need 57 take away 51. Count up from 51 to 57: that is 6.

beats.say: 57 take away 51 is 6. Those 6 are still seventeenths, so the bottom stays 17.
So 57 over 17 is 3 wholes, and 6 over 17.
Check: 3 times 17 is 51, and 6 more is 57. It works.
So: divide the top by the bottom. The answer is the whole part, and the remainder goes on top of the same bottom.
Three baskets, A, B and C. We only know C for sure: it has 22 oranges. So we start there and build up.
Basket A has 16 more than C. 22 plus 16 is 38. So A has 38 oranges.
Now basket B. Read carefully: B has 12 more than the sum of A and C. So what must we find first?

ask.ifNot: The sum of A and C means A and C added together. B is compared with both baskets together, not with one of them.

beats.say: This is the trap in the question. B is compared with A and C together. 38 plus 22 is 60.
B has 12 more than that. 60 plus 12 is 72. So B has 72 oranges.
Now add all three baskets. We already know that A and C make 60. So we need 60 plus 72.
60 plus 72 is 132. The fruit seller bought 132 oranges.
So: start from the basket you know, build the others one at a time, and read each clue slowly.
Three numbers, each with a hidden digit: a star, a heart and a third symbol. 11 divides all three. Then we build the greatest number from the hidden digits.

spec.note: 11 divides the number in each row.

beats.say: The test for 11 with three digits: add the first and last digits, then take away the middle one. The result must be 0 or 11.
First number. 5 plus 7 is 12. Take away the star, and we need 0 or 11. One digit cannot bring 12 all the way down to 0, so it must leave 11.
12 take away 1 is 11. So the star is 1. The number is 517, which is 11 times 47.
Second number: 5, 7, heart. The middle digit is 7. So 5 plus the heart, take away 7, must be 0. What is the heart?

ask.ifNot: 5 plus the heart must equal 7, so that taking 7 away leaves 0. And 5 plus 2 is 7.

beats.say: The heart is 2. The number is 572, which is 11 times 52.
Third number. The hidden digit plus 9, take away 5. That is the hidden digit plus 4, which can never be 0. So it must be 11.
7 plus 4 is 11, so the hidden digit is 7. The number is 759, which is 11 times 69.
The hidden digits are 1, 2 and 7. What is the greatest number we can make from them?

ask.ifNot: For the greatest number, put the biggest digit first, then the next biggest. That is 7, then 2, then 1.

beats.say: Biggest digit first: 7, then 2, then 1. The greatest number is 721.
One trap: the 9 is printed in the question. It is not a hidden digit, so it cannot be used in the answer.

board.text: Facing South, then North-East. How did he turn?

beats.say: A man faces south. Later he faces north-east. We have to say how he turned: how many degrees, and which way round.
The 8 compass directions share a full turn of 360 degrees. So each step from one direction to the next is 360 divided by 8, which is 45 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Anticlockwise from south we pass south-east, then east, and then we reach north-east. That is 3 steps.

beats.say: Let's go anticlockwise from south first. That is the opposite way to clock hands. How many steps is it to north-east?
South-east, east, north-east. 3 steps of 45 make 135 degrees, anticlockwise.
Now the other way, clockwise. South-west, west, north-west, north, north-east. That is 5 steps, and 5 times 45 is 225 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The size matches, but the direction does not. 135 clockwise from south passes south-west and west, and stops at north-west. The way round matters.

beats.say: So there are two true ways to say it: 135 anticlockwise, or 225 clockwise. Now the trap. One choice says 135 clockwise. Is that true?

board.text: 135° clockwise from S ends at NW

beats.say: The right size, but the other way round, so it lands on north-west. And none of the choices says 225 clockwise.
So the true statement is: he turned 135 degrees in the anticlockwise direction.
With turning questions, always check two things: how far, and which way round.
Find the H C F of 65 and 91. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 65 and 91 exactly.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number that goes into both. These numbers have only a few factors, so let's list them all.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 65: 1 times 65 and 5 times 13. So the factors of 65 are 1, 5, 13 and 65.
Now 91. Its pairs are 1 times 91 and 7 times 13. So the factors of 91 are 1, 7, 13 and 91.
Here is the important part. Run a finger along both lists. What is the biggest number that shows up in both?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 13. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 13. Careful: 65 is in its own list, but it does not divide 91, so it is out.
The picture shows it too: the shared factors sit in the middle. So the H C F of 65 and 91 is 13.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 65 divided by 13 is 5, and 91 divided by 13 is 7. Nothing is left over either time.
Remember the three moves: list the factors, spot the common ones, pick the biggest. And the H C F is never bigger than the smaller number.
Radhika bought 24 fruits. She bought three times as many oranges as bananas. Let's first find how many of each she bought.
For every 1 banana there are 3 oranges. So the fruits come in groups of 4: 3 oranges and 1 banana.
How many groups of 4 are there in 24 fruits?

ask.ifNot: Each group has 4 fruits: 3 oranges and 1 banana. 24 divided by 4 is 6. So there are 6 groups.

beats.say: 6 groups. So she bought 6 bananas, and 3 times 6, which is 18 oranges.
Now the accident. She took home 15 fruits, so she dropped 24 minus 15. That is 9 fruits.
She dropped twice as many oranges as bananas. So the dropped fruits come in groups of 3: 2 oranges and 1 banana.
9 fruits were dropped, in groups of 3. How many oranges were dropped?

ask.ifNot: 9 divided by 3 is 3 groups. Each group has 2 oranges, so 3 groups have 6 oranges. The other 3 are bananas.

beats.say: So 6 oranges fell. She had bought 18 oranges. 18 minus 6 is 12.
Let's check. At home she has 12 oranges, and 6 minus 3, that is 3 bananas. 12 plus 3 is 15. It works!
Watch the traps. 9 is all the dropped fruits, and 6 is the dropped oranges. The question asks for the oranges at home, which is 12.
4 friends, A, B, C and D, are playing chess. Each of them plays 2 games with every other player. How many games is that altogether?

board.text: A, B, C, D. 2 games with every other. Total?

beats.say: A game needs 2 players. So first let's find all the pairs of players. Start with A: A and B, A and C, A and D.
Now B. The pair B and A is already on our list, written as A B. So which new pairs does B make?

ask.ifNot: B with A is the same pair as A with B. So the new ones are B with C, and B with D.

beats.say: B gives B C and B D. And the last new pair is C and D.
Count the pairs: 3, then 2, then 1. That makes 6 pairs.
Every pair plays 2 games. 6 times 2 is 12.
So 12 games were played altogether.
Remember: a game belongs to a pair of players. List the pairs in order, count them, then multiply by the games each pair plays.
We write the Roman numerals from 1 to 20, and count every V we write.

board.text: Roman numerals I to XX: how many times is V written?

beats.say: First, 1 to 10. The numerals with a V are I V, V, V I, V I I and V I I I. Those are 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8.
What about 9? Is there a V in the numeral for 9?

choices: Yes, 9 is V I I I I
ask.ifNot: A letter is never written 4 times in a row. 9 is 1 less than 10, so it is I X, with no V at all.

beats.say: 9 is I X, so there is no V there. That gives 5 Vs from 1 to 10.
From 11 to 20 the same pattern repeats with an X in front: X I V, X V, X V I, X V I I and X V I I I.
Careful: the sneaky ones are I V and X I V, where the V hides behind an I. And X I X and X X have no V at all.
So 5 plus 5 makes 10.
So: write out the pattern for 1 to 10, then see how it repeats for the next ten.
m is 5 and n is 7. One of four expressions is worth exactly 70. We test them one by one.
First, 5 m plus 7 n. 5 times 5 is 25. 7 times 7 is 49. And 25 plus 49 is 74. Close, but not 70.
Next, 7 m plus 5 n. What is 7 m when m is 5?

ask.ifNot: 7 m means 7 times m. And m is 5. So it is 7 times 5.

beats.say: 7 times 5 is 35. And 5 n is 5 times 7, which is 35 too. 35 plus 35 is 70. That is the one!
Let's make sure about the others. They both have a minus sign. 7 m minus 5 n is 35 minus 35, which is 0.
And 5 m minus 7 n would take 49 away from 25. That cannot reach 70 either.
So the expression worth 70 is 7 m plus 5 n.
The first one used the very same numbers, but paired them differently. Which number multiplies which letter matters. The answer is 7 m plus 5 n.
P stands for an odd number. We want the 17th odd number that comes after it.
Try a real odd number first, say 1. The odd numbers after 1 are 3, 5, 7 and so on.
How big is each jump from one odd number to the next?

ask.ifNot: Between two odd numbers there is always an even number, and we jump over it. From 1 to 3 is a jump of 2.

beats.say: Each jump is 2. So the 1st odd number after P is P plus 2. The 2nd is P plus 4. The 3rd is P plus 6.
See the pattern? For the 17th odd number after P, how many jumps of 2 do we make?

ask.ifNot: The 1st one took 1 jump. The 2nd took 2 jumps. The 3rd took 3. So the 17th takes 17 jumps.

beats.say: 17 jumps of 2. 17 times 2 is 34.
So the 17th odd number after P is P plus 34.
The trap is to add just 17. But an odd number plus 17 is even, so that cannot be right. Each step is worth 2, so we add 34.

board.text: Isosceles triangle with one angle of 80°.
Which CANNOT be another of its angles?

beats.say: One angle of an isosceles triangle is 80 degrees. One of these 4 sizes can never be another angle of the triangle. Which?
An isosceles triangle has 2 equal angles, the twins, and 1 odd angle. The question does not say whether the 80 is a twin or the odd one. So we try both.
Case 1: the 80 is a twin. Then the angles are 80, 80 and one more. 80 plus 80 is 160.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles add up to 180. The twins use 160 of it, so 20 is left.

beats.say: What is the third angle in this case?
20 degrees. So in case 1 the other angles are 80 and 20. Both of those can appear.
Case 2: the 80 is the odd one. Then the twins share the rest. 180 minus 80 is 100.

ask.ifNot: 2 equal angles share 100 between them. Half of 100 is 50.

beats.say: The twins share 100 equally. How big is each one?
50 each. So in case 2 the other angles are 50 and 50.

board.text: 70° cannot be one of the angles

beats.say: There are no more cases. The other angles can only be 80, 20 or 50. The one that never shows up is 70 degrees.
With an isosceles triangle, always ask: is the angle I know a twin, or the odd one? Then work through both cases.

board.text: Rectangle 4 cm by 1 cm, cut into 4 equal squares.

spec.note: Cut into 4 equal squares

beats.say: A rectangle 4 centimetres long and 1 centimetre broad is cut into 4 equal squares. How much more is the total perimeter of the squares than the perimeter of the rectangle?
First the squares. The rectangle is 1 centimetre broad, so each square has a side of 1 centimetre. Its perimeter is 4 times 1, which is 4.
There are 4 squares. 4 times 4 is 16 centimetres in all.
Now the rectangle. Length plus breadth is 4 plus 1, which is 5. Double it: 10 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Each cut opens up two fresh edges, one on each side of the cut. Those edges were hidden inside the rectangle before.

beats.say: The squares have 16 and the rectangle has 10. The pieces are the same paper! So why do the squares have more?
Every cut makes new edges. So the squares have more perimeter. 16 minus 10 is 6.
The squares have 6 centimetres more.
Check with the cuts. 3 cuts, each making 2 new edges of 1 centimetre. 3 times 2 is 6. It matches!
Read the last words of the question carefully. It asks how much more, so we find both totals and subtract.
12 friends want pizza, and each one can eat one third of a pizza. How many pizzas should they order?

board.text: 12 friends, each eats 1/3 of a pizza

beats.say: Here is one pizza cut into thirds. How many friends can 1 pizza feed?

ask.ifNot: One pizza has 3 thirds, and each friend eats 1 third. So 1 pizza feeds 3 friends.

beats.say: 3 thirds make 1 whole pizza. So every pizza feeds 3 friends.
There are 12 friends, in groups of 3. How do we find the number of pizzas?

ask.ifNot: We are counting how many groups of 3 there are in 12. Counting equal groups is dividing.

beats.say: 12 divided by 3 is 4. They should order 4 pizzas.
Check: 4 pizzas give 4 times 3 thirds, which is 12 thirds. One third for each of the 12 friends.
Did 3 tempt you? 3 is how many friends one pizza feeds, not how many pizzas. Always ask what your number is counting.
The shopkeeper has 6 gross of pencils, and each box holds one dozen. How many boxes does he fill?

board.text: 6 gross of pencils.   Each box holds 1 dozen.

beats.say: First, what is a gross?

ask.ifNot: A gross is 12 dozen. That is 12 lots of 12.

beats.say: A gross is 12 dozen. Let us write that down.
Now look. Each box holds exactly one dozen. So one gross fills 12 boxes.
He has 6 gross. Which sum gives the number of boxes?

ask.ifNot: Each gross fills 12 boxes, and there are 6 gross. So we need 6 lots of 12.

beats.say: 6 times 12. 6 times 10 is 60, and 6 times 2 is 12. Together, 72.
So 72 boxes will be packed.
We could have counted every pencil. 6 gross is 864 pencils, and 864 divided by 12 is 72 as well. But thinking in dozens was much quicker.
So when the units match, like dozens and boxes of a dozen, work in those units. 72 boxes it is.
In 2016, Republic Day was on a Tuesday. In which year would Republic Day fall on a Sunday?

board.text: Republic Day 2016 = Tuesday. Sunday in which year?

spec.note: Republic Day, year by year

beats.say: Republic Day is the 26th of January. From one year to the next it usually moves on 1 day, because 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day.
But 2016 is a leap year, and its 29th of February comes after the 26th of January. So from Republic Day 2016 to Republic Day 2017, how far does the day move?

ask.ifNot: The leap day sits between the two Republic Days, so that stretch has 366 days. The day moves on by 2.

beats.say: Tuesday plus 2 is Thursday. So Republic Day 2017 is a Thursday. This is the step that is easy to miss.
Now ordinary steps of 1. 2018 gives Friday, and 2019 gives Saturday.
2020 is a leap year too. From January 2019 to January 2020, do we pass a 29th of February?

ask.ifNot: The leap day of 2020 is in February 2020, after Republic Day. It is not between our two dates, so the day moves just 1.

beats.say: So Saturday moves on by 1 to Sunday. Republic Day 2020 is a Sunday.
It is not the leap year itself that matters, but where its 29th of February sits. Between the two dates, move 2. Otherwise, move 1.
Four pairs of numbers. Which pair has the greatest L C M? We must work out all four before we choose.

board.text: Which pair has the greatest LCM?

beats.say: Every pair has 15 in it. So write out the 15 times table just once, and use it four times.
15 and 25. The first number in the list that 25 divides is 75, because 25 times 3 is 75.
15 and 20: the first one is 60, because 20 times 3 is 60. 15 and 12: also 60, because 12 times 5 is 60.
Now 15 and 18. Which is the first number in the list that 18 divides?

ask.ifNot: 18 times 5 is 90. None of the earlier numbers in the list is in the 18 times table.

beats.say: 18 times 5 is 90. So the L C M of 15 and 18 is 90, the greatest of the four.
Here is the trap. 25 is the biggest partner, so it looks like the winner. But 25 shares the factor 5 with 15, and that keeps their L C M down to 75.

board.text: Square and equilateral triangle: equal perimeter.

beats.say: A square and an equilateral triangle have equal perimeters. Which shape has the longer side?
There are no numbers here, so let's choose our own. Say both perimeters are 12 centimetres. 12 is easy to share.
The square shares 12 among 4 equal sides. 12 divided by 4 is 3.

ask.ifNot: The triangle has 3 equal sides, so we share 12 into 3 parts, not 4.

beats.say: The triangle shares the same 12 among only 3 sides. What is each side of the triangle?
12 divided by 3 is 4. So the triangle's side is 4 centimetres.
3 is less than 4. The square's side is shorter than the triangle's side.
Why? It is like sharing a chocolate bar. Share the same bar among more friends, and each piece is smaller.

board.text: Side of square < side of triangle

beats.say: So the true statement is: side of square is less than side of triangle.
When a question has no numbers, try an easy number of your own. Then look for the reason behind what you see.
Four numbers, all made from a 2 and a 3. We must find the smallest and the greatest, and then add those two.
The digits are the same each time, but they sit in different places. Let's give every number four digits after the point.
Which number is the greatest?

ask.ifNot: 2.3 is the only one with a whole number part. All the others are less than 1.

beats.say: 2.3 has 2 wholes, so it is the greatest. It is also the shortest number here, so do not judge by length.
And which number is the smallest?

ask.ifNot: The more zeros there are straight after the point, the smaller the number. 0.0023 has two zeros before its 2.

beats.say: The smallest is 0.0023, and the greatest is 2.3.

spec.note: The smallest is 0.0023 and the greatest is 2.3

beats.say: Now add them. Write 2.3 as 2.3000, so the points line up. The 2 and the 3 of 0.0023 drop into the last two places.
So the sum is 2.3023.
Keep the zeros in their places when you add, or the digits slip. Same number of places first, then compare, then add.
The hall has as many rows as there are chairs in each row, and every chair is filled. Which of these could be the number of men?

board.text: Rows = chairs in each row. How many men?

spec.note: Rows = chairs in each row

beats.say: Think of a small hall: 5 rows of 5 chairs hold 25 men. So what kind of number is the number of men?

ask.ifNot: Men equals rows times chairs in a row, and those two are the same. So it is a number times itself: a square number.

beats.say: So we are looking for a square number. Let us test each choice against squares we know.
131: 11 times 11 is 121 and 12 times 12 is 144. 131 falls in between, so it is not a square.
275: 16 times 16 is 256 and 17 times 17 is 289. In between again, so not a square.
Now try 18. 18 times 18 is 324. That is one of our choices!

spec.note: 18 rows of 18 chairs

beats.say: Careful with 325. It is only 1 more than 324, but a full hall needs an exact square. One extra man would have no chair.
So the number of men can be 324.
So: equal rows and columns means a square number. Test each choice by squeezing it between two squares.
Two mystery numbers. Each has three digits. One ends in 7 and the other ends in 8. Which choice could be their product?
We cannot multiply, because we do not know the numbers. But we can be detectives. Here are the four choices.
Clue one. The last digit of a product comes only from the last digits of the two numbers. So what must this product end in?

ask.ifNot: 7 times 8 is 56, and 56 ends in 6. So the product must end in 6.

beats.say: It must end in 6. So 10552 is out, because it ends in 2.
Clue two: the size. Each number has three digits, so each is at least 100. And 100 times 100 is 10000, which has five digits.
So the product has at least five digits. 9786 has only four, so it is too small. Cross it off.
Each number is also less than 1000. And 1000 times 1000 is 1000000, which has seven digits. So our product has fewer than seven digits.
9950006 has seven digits, so it is too big. Cross it off.
Only one choice is left. It ends in 6 and it is the right size. So the product can be 308256.
The key idea: you can rule answers out without multiplying. Check the last digit, and check how many digits there should be.
We need to write 1946 the Roman way. Romans had no place seats like ours, so first we break the number into parts.
Split it by place: 1000, 900, 40 and 6.
Here are the 7 Roman letters and what each one is worth. Keep them in view.

spec.note: and V = 5, I = 1

beats.say: 1000 is simply M.
Now the 900. How do the Romans write 900?

ask.ifNot: C in front of M takes 100 away from 1000, which leaves 900. C after M would add 100 on instead.

beats.say: 900 is 100 less than 1000, so the smaller letter goes in front: C M.
40 is 10 less than 50, so the smaller letter goes in front: X L. 6 is 5 and 1 more, so we write V I.
Now join the parts in order, biggest first: M, C M, X L, V I.
Check the tens carefully. X X X is only 30. For 40 we need X L.
So the plan for any number: split it by place, write each part in Roman letters, then join them from left to right.
We need the supplementary angle to 57 and a quarter degrees.

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do two supplementary angles add up to?
So we take 57 and a quarter away from 180. A mixed number is easier in two bites: first the whole number, then the quarter.
First the 57. 180 take away 50 is 130, and 7 more away leaves 123.

ask.ifNot: We are taking away, so the answer drops just below 123. Break one whole into 4 quarters and take 1 quarter off. That leaves 122 and three quarters.

beats.say: The quarter still has to come off. What is a quarter less than 123?
Take one whole from 123, leaving 122, and cut that whole into 4 quarters. Take 1 quarter away, and three quarters are left.
So the supplementary angle is 122 and three quarters degrees.
Check by adding. 57 and 122 make 179. A quarter and three quarters make 1 more. 180 exactly.
The slip to watch for is adding the quarter back on, instead of taking it off. Whole number first, then the fraction, and both are taken away.
Here is our sum. Plus, times, minus and divide, all in one line. The BODMAS rule tells us the order.
Which two jobs go first?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide go before plus and minus. So 5 times 4, and 6 divided by 2, go first.

beats.say: Box them both. Notice that the divide only touches the 6 just in front of it, not the whole sum.
5 times 4 is 20. And 6 divided by 2 is 3.
Write the sum again, with 20 and 3 where the boxes were.
Left to right now. 6 plus 20 is 26.
And 26 take away 3 is 23.
The trap is going straight along from the left, with 6 plus 5 first. That gives a different answer. Times and divide must jump the queue.
So: times and divide first, then plus and minus from left to right.
How many factors does 84 have? A factor of 84 is a number that divides 84 exactly, with nothing left over.
Factors always come with a partner. The two partners multiply to make 84. Start with the easy pair: 1 times 84.
Next we try 2. 84 is even, so 2 is a factor. What is its partner?

ask.ifNot: The partner is the number we multiply 2 by to make 84. Half of 84 is 42, so the partner of 2 is 42.

beats.say: 2 times 42 is 84. That is our second pair.
Keep going in order: try 3, then 4, then 5, and so on. We get 3 times 28 and 4 times 21.
Carry on the same way: 6 times 14 and 7 times 12. 5 does not divide 84, so we skip it.
When do we stop? The next factor after 7 is 12, and 12 is already on the board as a partner. So the pairs would only repeat.
Now count. We have 6 pairs, and each pair gives 2 different factors. How many factors is that?

ask.ifNot: Each pair holds 2 factors, and there are 6 pairs. So we double 6.

beats.say: 6 pairs, 2 factors in each, makes 12. So 84 has 12 factors. Here they all are, in order.
So to count factors: write the pairs in order, stop when they start to repeat, and count 2 for each pair. Your turn next!
Which of the choices is the same as 11.11 kilograms? Let's turn 11.11 kilograms into kilograms and grams, then compare.
Split the number at the decimal point. 11 whole kilograms, and 0.11 of a kilogram.
The 11 kilograms are easy. But what is 0.11 kilograms in grams? Remember, 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

ask.ifNot: Multiply 0.11 by 1000. The digits slide 3 places to the left, so 0.11 becomes 110.

beats.say: 0.11 times 1000 is 110. So 0.11 kilograms is 110 grams.
Here is the trap. 11 kilograms 11 grams looks just like 11.11. But 11 grams is only 0.011 kilograms.
So 11.11 kilograms is 11 kilograms 110 grams.
The method: split at the decimal point, keep the whole kilograms, and change only the decimal part into grams.
This is a chain. x is 3. But y is given using x, and z is given using x and y. So we find the letters first, in order.

board.text: x = 3,  y = x − 1,  z = x + y

beats.say: We know x. Which letter can we find next?

ask.ifNot: z needs both x and y, and we do not have y yet. But y needs only x, and we know x. So y comes next.

beats.say: y is x minus 1. 3 minus 1 is 2. So y is 2.
Now z is x plus y. 3 plus 2 is 5. So z is 5. It is x and y added together, not x on its own.
Now the big expression. 6 x is 6 times 3, which is 18. 3 y is 3 times 2, which is 6. 5 z is 5 times 5, which is 25.
We have 18, 6 and 25. How do they go together?

ask.ifNot: Each part keeps the sign in front of it. 3 y has a minus in front, and 5 z has a plus. So it is 18, minus 6, plus 25.

beats.say: Left to right. 18 minus 6 is 12. And 12 plus 25 is 37.
So the value is 37. In a chain, find each letter in order. Then swap them all in, and keep every sign in its place.
We need to write this number name in figures. Let us take it one piece at a time.

board.text: One lakh one thousand one hundred ten = ?

beats.say: One lakh is a 1 followed by 5 zeros.
One thousand is 1,000. And one hundred ten is 110.
Now add the three pieces together.
Look at the thousands. They have 2 seats, but there is only one thousand. What goes in those 2 seats?

ask.ifNot: One thousand needs a 1 in the thousands seat. The ten-thousands seat is empty, so it gets a 0 to hold the place.

beats.say: That 0 is a place holder. Leave it out, or put a 1 there, and the number changes.
So the number is 1,01,110. Without the commas, that is 101110.
Check: it has 6 digits, just as a lakh number should.
Three of these numbers can be made by adding two primes. One cannot. We test each one.
5 is 2 plus 3. 7 is 2 plus 5. Remember, 2 is a prime number. So both of those can be made.
12 is 5 plus 7, and both are prime. So 12 can be made too.
Now 11. It is odd. Two odd primes add up to an even number, so to make 11, one of the primes has to be 2, the only even prime.
11 minus 2 is 9. Is 9 a prime number?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 3 is 9. So 9 has a factor other than 1 and itself, and it is not prime.

beats.say: 9 is 3 times 3, so it is not prime. There is no other way to try. So 11 is not the sum of two primes.
The trap: 11 is a prime number itself. But that does not mean it can be split into two primes.
M N is a 2-digit number with tens digit M and units digit N. N M is the same two digits swapped. We want the biggest possible difference.

board.text: M and N: different digits, not zero

beats.say: To make a difference big, the first number should be as big as we can make it, and the second as small as we can.
For a big M N, the tens digit M should be the biggest digit there is, 9.
Now N should be as small as the rules allow. What is the smallest N we may use?

ask.ifNot: 0 is the smallest digit, but the question says the digits are not zero. So the smallest N allowed is 1.

beats.say: This is the trap. The digits are non zero, so N cannot be 0. The smallest it can be is 1.
So M N is 91 and N M is 19.
91 minus 19 is 72.
A pattern to notice: the difference is always 9 times the gap between the digits. The gap here is 8, and 9 times 8 is 72.
Four fractions, all very close to 1. Which is the largest?
Look closely. In every fraction, the top is just 1 less than the bottom. So each one is a whole with one piece missing.
17 over 18 is 1 whole with which piece missing?

ask.ifNot: A whole is 18 over 18, and we have 17 of them. So 1 piece of size 1 over 18 is missing.

beats.say: So each fraction is 1 whole, take away one small piece.
Here is the key idea. The largest fraction has the smallest piece missing. Which missing piece is the smallest?

ask.ifNot: Cut a whole into 20 pieces and each piece is tiny. More pieces, smaller pieces. So 1 over 20 is the smallest.

beats.say: 1 over 20 is the smallest piece, like the thinnest slice of a cake. Take the thinnest slice away, and the most cake is left.
So 19 over 20 is the closest to 1, and it is the largest.
When every fraction is one piece short of a whole, compare the missing pieces. Smallest gap, largest fraction.
500 sheets of paper make a pile 5 centimetres thick. Mr. Deepak's big stack is 1 metre 22.5 centimetres thick. How many sheets are in it?

board.text: Stack: 1 m 22.5 cm. How many sheets?

beats.say: First, let's make the stack's thickness all centimetres. 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so the stack is 100 plus 22.5. That is 122.5 centimetres.
Now, 500 sheets fill 5 centimetres. So how many sheets fit in just 1 centimetre?

ask.ifNot: Share the 500 sheets equally over the 5 centimetres. That is 500 divided by 5.

beats.say: 500 divided by 5 is 100. So every centimetre of the stack holds 100 sheets.
The stack is 122.5 centimetres thick, so we need 122.5 times 100. Times 100 slides the digits 2 places to the left.
So there were 12250 sheets in all.
Does that make sense? 100 centimetres alone would hold 10000 sheets, so a bit more than that is just right.
The plan: find how many fit in 1 centimetre, then multiply by the number of centimetres.
A man walks 66 kilometres in 6 days. Each day he walks 4 kilometres less than the day before. How far does he walk on the 6th day?

board.text: 66 km in 6 days. Each day 4 km less.

beats.say: We don't know how far he walked on any single day. So here is the plan: compare every day with day 6, the shortest walk of all.
Day 5 is 4 kilometres more than day 6. So how much more than day 6 is day 4?

ask.ifNot: Day 4 is 4 more than day 5, and day 5 is 4 more than day 6. That is 4 and 4, which makes 8.

beats.say: So day 5 is 4 more than day 6. Day 4 is 8 more. Then 12 more, 16 more, and day 1 is 20 more.

spec.note: Every day compared with day 6

beats.say: Add up all the extra: 4 plus 8 plus 12 plus 16 plus 20. That is 60 kilometres of extra walking.
Now take that extra 60 away from the total. What does the leftover stand for?

ask.ifNot: Without the extras, every one of the 6 days is as short as day 6. So what is left is 6 equal walks.

beats.say: 66 take away 60 leaves 6 kilometres. That is 6 equal walks, so each one is 1 kilometre.
So on the 6th day he walked just 1 kilometre.
Check. The six days were 21, 17, 13, 9, 5 and 1 kilometres. Add them up and you get 66. It works.
The trap is to share 66 equally among 6 days. The days are not equal! Compare every day with the one you want, then take away the extras.
Ajay rolls three dice. The three numbers multiply to make 90. What do they add up to? Remember, a die only shows 1 to 6.
Break 90 into its prime factors: 2 times 3 times 3 times 5.
Look at the 5. Could it join with another prime on one die? 5 times 2 is 10, and 5 times 3 is 15.

ask.ifNot: A die only goes up to 6. 10 and 15 are both too big, so the 5 must sit on a die by itself.

beats.say: So one die shows 5. The other two dice must multiply to make 90 divided by 5, which is 18.
How can two dice make 18? 2 times 9 would need a 9, and a die has no 9. So it must be 3 times 6.
The dice show 3, 5 and 6. Check: 3 times 5 times 6 is 90.
Add them up. 3 plus 5 plus 6 is 14.
Only one set of dice fits, so we do have enough information. The key was that a die stops at 6.
Mrs. Joshi's groceries cost 39.46 rupees. She gives the cashier a 50 rupee note. How much comes back?

spec.note: Groceries, and the change

beats.say: Which sum gives the change?

ask.ifNot: The change is what is left of the 50 rupees after the bill is paid. So we take the bill away from 50.

beats.say: Shopkeepers do this by counting up. We go from 39.46 up to 40 first, and then from 40 up to 50.
How far is it from 39.46 up to 40?

ask.ifNot: Look at the part after the point, 0.46. Together, 0.46 and 0.54 make exactly 1 whole rupee. With 0.44 we would stop a little short of 40.

beats.say: From 39.46 up to 40 is 0.54.

spec.note: Count up from 39.46 to 40

beats.say: And from 40 up to 50 is 10 more.
Put the two jumps together: 10 and 0.54. The cashier returns 10.54 rupees.
Check: 39.46 plus 10.54 makes 50. And it makes sense: 39.46 is nearly 40, so the change should be just over 10.
This sum should come to 40. As it stands, it does not. One bracket will fix it, and we must find where it goes.
First, with no bracket. Times first: 5 times 7 is 35. Then 35 plus 3, take away 10, is 28. Too small.
We need a bigger answer, 40. So the 5 should multiply something bigger than 7. Which bracket makes that happen?

ask.ifNot: A bracket round 5 times 7 changes nothing, because times goes first anyway. A bracket round 7 plus 3 makes the 5 multiply 10 instead of 7.

beats.say: Try it. Bracket first: 7 plus 3 is 10.
Then the times. 5 times 10 is 50.
Then the minus. 50 take away 10 is 40. That is our number!
So the bracket goes round 7 plus 3.
One more choice to check. A bracket round 7 plus 3 minus 10 is worth 0, and 5 times 0 is 0. No good.
The key idea: the bracket has to make the adding happen before the multiplying. So it goes round 7 plus 3.

board.text: Each has perimeter 24 cm. Perimeter of new figure = ?

spec.note: Each triangle's perimeter is 24 cm. The dashed side is shared.

beats.say: 2 equilateral triangles of the same size are joined along a side. Each triangle had a perimeter of 24 centimetres. What is the perimeter of the new figure?
First we need the length of one side. An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides, and they add up to 24.

ask.ifNot: The perimeter, 24, is shared equally among 3 sides. So each side is 24 divided by 3.

beats.say: How long is each side?
8 centimetres. Every side of both triangles is 8 centimetres long.
Now look at the picture. The triangles are joined along one full side. That dashed side is inside the figure now. It is not part of the edge any more.
Count the sides. 2 triangles have 6 sides in all.

ask.ifNot: Each triangle gives up 1 side at the join. There are 2 triangles, so 2 sides are hidden, even though they look like 1 line.

beats.say: The join hides some sides inside the figure. How many?
2 sides, one from each triangle. 6 minus 2 leaves 4 sides on the outside.
4 sides of 8 centimetres each. 4 times 8 is 32. The perimeter of the new figure is 32 centimetres.
The trap is to add 24 and 24 and say 48. The join costs 2 sides of 8, so take 16 away from 48, and you get 32 again.
Karan buys some 5 paise stamps and some 10 paise stamps. Together they cost 55 paise.
In a second plan, he buys the same 5 paise stamps, but twice as many 10 paise stamps. That would cost 1 rupee and 5 paise.

board.text: Twice the 10 paise stamps: Rs. 1 and 5 paise

beats.say: 1 rupee is 100 paise. So how many paise is 1 rupee and 5 paise?

ask.ifNot: 1 rupee is 100 paise. Add the 5 paise, and we get 105 paise.

beats.say: So the first plan costs 55 paise and the second costs 105 paise. The second costs 50 paise more.
What did that extra 50 paise pay for?

choices: a second lot of 10 paise stamps
ask.ifNot: Only one thing changed: the 10 paise stamps were doubled. So the extra 50 paise paid for a second lot of 10 paise stamps.

beats.say: The second lot is the same size as the first lot. So the 10 paise stamps he really bought cost 50 paise. That is 5 stamps.
Now back to the first plan. Out of 55 paise, 50 paise went on 10 paise stamps. So only 5 paise is left.
5 paise is left for the 5 paise stamps. How many stamps is that?

ask.ifNot: Each stamp costs 5 paise, and there is only 5 paise to spend. So that buys just 1 stamp.

beats.say: So Karan bought 1 stamp of 5 paise.
Let's check. 50 paise and 5 paise make 55. With the 10 paise stamps doubled, 100 paise and 5 paise make 105. It works!
Careful: the 5 we found first was the number of 10 paise stamps. The 5 paise stamps came to just 1.
Here is a long list: 1, 8, 15, 22, 29, all the way up to 113. How many numbers are in it? Let's count without writing them all.
First the jump. 8 minus 1 is 7, and 15 minus 8 is 7 too. Each term is 7 more than the one before.
How far is it from the first term to the last? 113 minus 1 is 112.
That distance of 112 is covered in jumps of 7. How do we find the number of jumps?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many 7s fit into 112. That is a division.

beats.say: Split 112 into 70 and 42. 70 divided by 7 is 10. 42 divided by 7 is 6. So there are 16 jumps.
There are 16 jumps. So how many terms are there?

ask.ifNot: Think small. 1 jump joins 2 numbers. 2 jumps join 3 numbers. There is always 1 more number than jumps.

beats.say: Here is the trap. Jumps sit between the terms, and the first term is there before any jump. So we add 1.
Check with the start of the list. From 1 to 29 is 4 jumps, and there are 5 terms. One more than the jumps. So there are 17 terms in all.
So the plan is: last take away first, divide by the jump to count the jumps, and add 1 to count the terms.
All Fools' Day in 2017 was on a Saturday. On what day does Teachers' Day fall in the same year?

board.text: All Fools' Day 2017 = Saturday. Teachers' Day = ?
All Fools' Day: 1 April.  Teachers' Day: 5 September

beats.say: All Fools' Day is the 1st of April, and Teachers' Day is the 5th of September. We need the number of days from one to the other, month by month.
April has 30 days. How many days are left in April after the 1st?

ask.ifNot: We start on the 1st, so that day is already used. 30 minus 1 leaves 29 more days in April.

beats.say: April gives 29 days. Then May 31, June 30, July 31, August 31, and 5 days of September.
Add them up. 29 plus 31 plus 30 is 90. Add 31 and 31 to get 152. And 5 more makes 157 days.
Every 7 days brings Saturday back again. So what really matters about 157?

choices: the days left after full weeks
ask.ifNot: Full weeks bring us back to Saturday, so they change nothing. Only the days left over move the day on.

beats.say: 22 times 7 is 154. So 157 days is 22 weeks, with 3 days left over.
The 22 weeks bring us back to Saturday. Then 3 more days: Sunday, Monday, Tuesday.
Teachers' Day fell on a Tuesday.
Count the days between the dates, take out the full weeks, and count on the days that are left.
Here is our equation. 12 x, minus 40, equals 2 x. The x is on both sides.
Think of x as a bag of marbles. 12 bags, with 40 marbles taken out, weigh the same as 2 bags.
Let's take 2 bags off each side. How many x are left on the left?

ask.ifNot: 12 x take away 2 x leaves 10 x. We are taking away here, not adding.

beats.say: We take 2 x from both sides. The right side is now 0. The left is 10 x, minus 40.
If 10 x, minus 40, leaves nothing, then 10 x must be exactly 40.
10 times x is 40. So what is x?

ask.ifNot: To undo times 10, we divide by 10. And 40 divided by 10 is 4.

beats.say: 40 divided by 10 is 4. So x equals 4.
Let's check. Left: 12 times 4 is 48, and 48 minus 40 is 8. Right: 2 times 4 is 8. Both sides are 8!
So gather the x on one side first. After that it is a simple times fact.
Here is a sum with a twist. 2 metres, plus 2 decimetres, plus 15 centimetres. Each length has its own unit.
Can we just add 2 and 2 and 15? Not yet. What must we do first?

ask.ifNot: Lengths can only be added when they are in the same unit. The choices are in centimetres, so let's change everything into centimetres.

beats.say: Start with the metres. 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so 2 metres is 200 centimetres.
Now the decimetres. A decimetre is 10 centimetres, so 2 decimetres is 20 centimetres.
The 15 centimetres are already centimetres. Now everything matches, so we can add. 200 plus 20 is 220.
And 15 more makes 235. So the total is 235 centimetres.
Remember: same units first, then add. Never just push the numbers together.
What is the smallest number we can add to 267 times 348, so that 5 divides the total? Good news: we do not need the whole product.
A number is divisible by 5 only when it ends in 0 or 5. So all that matters is the last digit of the product.
The last digit of a product comes from the two ones digits. Here they are 7 and 8, and 7 times 8 is 56. So what digit does the product end in?

ask.ifNot: 7 times 8 is 56, and 56 ends in 6. So the whole product ends in 6.

beats.say: The product ends in 6. Counting on from 6, the next ending that 5 likes is 0. And 6 needs 4 more to reach 10.
So the smallest number to add is 4.
Let's check with the full product. 267 times 348 is 92,916. Add 4, and we get 92,920. It ends in 0, so 5 divides it.
The trap is adding 5. That would make the number end in 1. For the 5 test, only the last digit matters.
A student should have written 9.7, but he wrote 0.97. By how much was his number off?

spec.note: How far apart are the two numbers?

beats.say: How do we find how far apart the two numbers are?

ask.ifNot: How far off means the difference between them. We take the smaller number away from the bigger one.

beats.say: First a quick guess. 9.7 is nearly 10, and 0.97 is nearly 1. So the gap should be somewhere near 9.
Now exactly. Write 9.7 as 9.70, so both numbers have two digits after the point.
Here is a clever way. 0.97 is nearly 1, so take away a whole 1 first. That gives 8.70. But how much too much did we take?

ask.ifNot: 1 is just 3 hundredths more than 0.97. So we took away 0.03 too much.

beats.say: We took 0.03 too much, so we give it back. 8.70 and 0.03 make 8.73.
So his number was off by 8.73.
Check: 0.97 plus 8.73 makes 9.70. And 8.73 is near our guess of 9, so the decimal point is in the right place.
5 years ago, the ages of a mother and her daughter added up to 5 x. We want the sum of their ages 5 years hence. Hence means from now.

spec.note: A mother and her daughter

beats.say: There are three moments: 5 years ago, today, and 5 years hence. We will walk forward one step at a time.
From 5 years ago to today, the mother gets 5 years older. What about the daughter?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for both of them. Each one has 5 more birthdays. So the daughter is 5 years older as well.

beats.say: Two people, each 5 years older. So the sum grows by 5 plus 5, which is 10. Today the sum is 5 x plus 10.
Is 5 x plus 10 our answer?

ask.ifNot: The question asks for 5 years hence, which is 5 years after today. So far we have only reached today.

beats.say: From today to 5 years hence, both grow 5 years older again. The sum grows by another 10.
So 5 years hence, the sum of their ages will be 5 x plus 20.
Two traps. Count the years for both people, not just one. And go all the way from 5 years ago to 5 years hence. That is 10 years for each of them, so 20 in all.
Find the L C M of 48 and 54. L C M means lowest common multiple: the first number that both 48 and 54 reach when you count up in their tables.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 54?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 54 is 54 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 54, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: The simplest way is to count up in both tables until they meet. Count up in 48s: 48, 96, 144, 192, 240, 288, 336, 384, 432.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 48 and 54?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 432 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: There it is. 432 is the first number in both lists, so the L C M is 432.
Let's check. 432 divided by 48 is 9, and 432 divided by 54 is 8. Both divide exactly, so 432 really is a multiple of each.
One trap to watch for. Multiplying 48 by 54 gives 2592. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 432 gets there first.
So for an L C M: count up in both tables, and the first number in both is the answer. Your turn next!

board.text: In 300 seconds the minute hand moves ___ degrees

beats.say: In 300 seconds, how many degrees does the minute hand of a clock move?

ask.ifNot: There are 60 seconds in a minute. 60 times 5 is 300, so 300 seconds is 5 minutes.

beats.say: The minute hand works in minutes, not seconds. So first, how many minutes is 300 seconds?
300 divided by 60 is 5. So we are really asking: how far does the minute hand move in 5 minutes?
In 60 minutes the minute hand goes right round the clock once. That is a full turn, 360 degrees.
So in 1 minute it turns 360 divided by 60. That is 6 degrees each minute.

ask.ifNot: Each minute is 6 degrees, and there are 5 minutes, so it is 5 times 6. 30 degrees is the size of a whole gap between two numbers, not of 1 minute.

beats.say: 5 minutes, at 6 degrees each minute. Which sum tells us how far?
5 times 6 is 30. The minute hand moves 30 degrees.
And that makes sense. In 5 minutes the minute hand goes from one number to the next, like from 12 to 1. That gap is 360 divided by 12, which is 30 as well.
So change the seconds to minutes first. Then it is 6 degrees for every minute.

spec.note: The length is 2 breadths

beats.say: The length of a rectangle is twice its breadth, and both are natural numbers. Which of these can be its perimeter: 232, 138, 334 or 146?

ask.ifNot: Each length counts as 2 breadths. So we add 2 and 1 and 2 and 1.

beats.say: Let's count the perimeter in breadths. One length is 2 breadths. Walk round: 2, then 1, then 2, then 1. How many breadths is that?
2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6. So the perimeter is 6 breadths. It must be in the 6 times table!

board.text: 6 times table: even, and in the 3 times table

beats.say: A number in the 6 times table is even, and also in the 3 times table. All four choices are even, so we test for 3.
Here is a handy test for 3: add the digits. For 232, 2 plus 3 plus 2 is 7. 7 is not in the 3 times table, so 232 is out.
For 138, 1 plus 3 plus 8 is 12. 12 is in the 3 times table. So 138 works!
Check the other two. 3 plus 3 plus 4 is 10, and 1 plus 4 plus 6 is 11. Neither is in the 3 times table.
So the perimeter can be 138 centimetres.
Let's make sure. 138 divided by 6 is 23. So the breadth is 23 and the length is 46. Both natural numbers.
The big idea: turn the whole perimeter into breadths. Then you know which times table it must be in. Only 138 fits.
An equilateral triangle. Each side is 7 m minus 2 n. We want its perimeter.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: How many equal sides does an equilateral triangle have?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides. So there are 3 equal sides.

beats.say: So the perimeter is 3 times one side. 3 times, 7 m minus 2 n.
The 3 multiplies each part. First, 3 times 7 m is 21 m.
Then 3 times 2 n is 6 n.
What sign goes between 21 m and 6 n?

ask.ifNot: In each side, 2 n is taken away. Three sides means it is taken away three times. So 6 n is still taken away.

beats.say: So the perimeter is 21 m minus 6 n.
Test it with m as 1 and n as 1. One side is 7 minus 2, which is 5, and 3 sides make 15. Our answer gives 21 minus 6, also 15.
m and n are different letters, so they never join into one term. Multiply each by 3, and keep the minus.
Which movement of the minute hand takes 50 minutes? The choices use Roman numerals, the kind you see on old clocks.

board.text: Which move of the minute hand takes 50 minutes?
IX to III     X to VI     IV to XII     VI to IV

beats.say: Let's turn the Roman numerals into our numbers. So the choices are 9 to 3, 10 to 6, 4 to 12, and 6 to 4.
How long does the minute hand take to go from one number to the next?

ask.ifNot: When the minute hand moves from the 12 to the 1, the time is 5 past. So each step from one number to the next is 5 minutes.

beats.say: Each step is 5 minutes. 50 divided by 5 is 10, so 50 minutes is 10 steps.
Count the steps for each choice, always going forwards. From 9 round to 3: 3 steps up to 12, then 3 more. That is 6 steps.
From 10 on to 6: 2 steps to reach 12, then 6 more. That is 8 steps. From 4 to 12 is 8 steps as well.
From 6 on to 4: 6 steps up to 12, then 4 more steps to reach the 4. That is 10 steps!
10 steps of 5 minutes make 50 minutes. So the answer is 6 to 4, the last choice.
Clock hands only move forwards. When the hand passes 12, count up to 12 first, and then carry on.
P stands for an even number. We want the 3rd even number before it.
Try a real even number first, say 20. The even numbers before 20 are 18, 16 and 14.
How big is each jump back?

ask.ifNot: Even numbers are 2 apart, with an odd number in between. From 20 back to 18 is a jump of 2.

beats.say: Each jump back takes away 2. So before P come P minus 2, then P minus 4, then P minus 6.
Which one is the 3rd even number before P?

ask.ifNot: Count along the list: 1st, 2nd, 3rd. Three jumps of 2 take away 6. And before means smaller, so we subtract.

beats.say: 3 jumps of 2 is 6. So it is P minus 6.
Check with 20. The 3rd even number before 20 was 14. And 20 minus 6 is 14.
Before means go back, so we take away. And each even step is worth 2, not 1. That gives P minus 6.
The letter d stands for one digit. We want to know for how many digits the number 2.00d5 is greater than 2.005.

board.text: How many values of d work?

beats.say: 2.00d5 has four digits after the point. So write 2.005 with four digits as well, by adding a zero at the end.
Now compare from the left, one place at a time. The ones match. The tenths match. The hundredths match. The first place that can differ is the thousandths: d against 5.
If d is bigger than 5, our number is greater. How many digits are bigger than 5?

ask.ifNot: The digits bigger than 5 are 6, 7, 8 and 9. Count them: there are 4.

beats.say: So 6, 7, 8 and 9 all work. But we are not finished. What if d is 5 itself?
With d as 5, the number is 2.0055. How does it compare with 2.0050?

ask.ifNot: The first three places after the point match. So look at the last place: 5 against 0. 5 is more, so 2.0055 is greater.

beats.say: That is the trap. When d is 5 the thousandths are level, but the last digit, 5, beats the 0. So 5 works too.
And if d is 4, we get 2.0045, which is less than 2.0050. Smaller digits are no good either.
So d can be 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9. That is 5 values.
Give both numbers the same number of places, compare from the left, and always test the digit that makes them level.
115 over 8. A big top number! We will turn it into a mixed number.
Every 8 eighths make a whole, so we divide 115 by 8. Let's do it in two bites. First, 8 times 10 is 80.
We have used 80 of the 115. How many are left?

ask.ifNot: We need 115 take away 80. Check by adding: 80 plus 35 is 115.

beats.say: 115 take away 80 is 35. Now, how many eights fit into 35? 8 times 4 is 32.
So altogether 8 fits 10 times, and then 4 more times. That is 14 wholes.
And what is left over after the 32?

ask.ifNot: We need 35 take away 32. Count up from 32 to 35: that is 3.

beats.say: 35 take away 32 is 3. Those 3 are eighths. So 115 over 8 is 14, and 3 over 8.
Check: 8 times 14 is 112, and 3 more is 115. It works.
For a big top number, divide in easy bites: the tens first, then the rest. What is left over goes on top.
A sum with a bracket at the end. Brackets go first, so we begin inside it.
Inside the bracket: 2 times 4 minus 15 divided by 3. Which jobs go first in there?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, times and divide go before minus. So 2 times 4, and 15 divided by 3, go first.

beats.say: 2 times 4 is 8. And 15 divided by 3 is 5.
Finish the bracket. 8 take away 5 is 3. So the bracket is worth 3.
Now outside the bracket: 9 minus 3 times 2 plus 3. Careful, this is the trap. What goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before minus, even though the minus is written first. So 3 times 2 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 2 is 6. Now the sum is 9 minus 6 plus 3.
Left to right. 9 take away 6 is 3. Then 3 plus 3 is 6.
One more trap. The sign in front of the bracket is a plus. So the bracket's 3 is added at the end, not taken away.
So: bracket first, then times and divide, then plus and minus from left to right.
We have 7 kilograms and 70 grams, and we want one decimal number in kilograms.
The 7 kilograms stay. Only the 70 grams need changing. 1000 grams make 1 kilogram, so we divide 70 by 1000.
What is 70 divided by 1000?

ask.ifNot: Dividing by 1000 slides the digits 3 places to the right. The 7 lands in the hundredths place.

beats.say: 70 divided by 1000 is 0.07. The 7 sits in the hundredths place.
Careful, this is where many people slip. 0.70 kilograms would be 700 grams, ten times too much. And 0.007 would be just 7 grams.
Now add the 7 whole kilograms. 7 plus 0.07 is 7.07.
So 7 kilograms 70 grams is 7.07 kilograms.
Remember: grams to kilograms, divide by 1000, and watch where each digit lands.
In 978652 we want the place value of the 7, the place value of the 5, and then the difference between them.

board.text: 978652: place value of 7 − place value of 5 = ?

spec.note: Find the 7 and the 5

beats.say: Count from the right: 2 ones, 5 tens, 6 hundreds, 8 thousands, and then the 7. Which place is the 7 in?

ask.ifNot: After the thousands comes the ten-thousands place. The 7 is the fifth digit from the right, so it sits there.

beats.say: So the 7 is worth 70000.
The 5 is in the tens place, so it is worth 50.
Difference means subtract. So we need 70000 minus 50.
Borrowing across all those zeros is fiddly. Try this instead: 70000 minus 100 is 69900. Then give back 50.
So the difference is 69950.
Careful: 70050 is what you get by adding. The word difference always means take away.
A watch gains 2 minutes every hour. It is set correctly at 8:00 a.m. What time will this watch show at 8:00 p.m. the same day?

board.text: Watch gains 2 minutes every hour. Correct at 8:00 am.
What does it show at 8:00 pm?

spec.note: Real time 8:00 p.m. The watch gains 2 minutes every hour

beats.say: How many hours is it from 8:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m.?

ask.ifNot: From 8 in the morning to 8 at night, the hour hand goes exactly once round the clock. That takes 12 hours.

beats.say: From 8 in the morning to 8 at night is 12 hours.
The watch gains 2 minutes in every one of those hours. 12 times 2 is 24 minutes.
The watch has gained 24 minutes. So do we add them to 8:00 p.m., or take them away?

ask.ifNot: A watch that gains runs fast. It is ahead of the real time, so it shows a later time. We add.

beats.say: Gains means the watch is ahead. So it shows 24 minutes after 8:00 p.m. Taking the minutes away is the trap here.
The watch shows 8:24 p.m.
Count the hours, multiply by the gain, and then ask yourself: is the watch ahead or behind?
Three Roman numerals. Only a numeral that follows every rule is correctly written. So let us check each one against the rules.

board.text: Which Roman numeral is correctly written?

beats.say: Rule one: a letter may be repeated at most 3 times in a row.

board.text: Rule 1: a letter repeats at most 3 times

beats.say: Look at M C C C C I V. Does it follow rule one?

ask.ifNot: Count the Cs. There are 4 in a row, and that breaks the rule.

beats.say: 4 Cs in a row, so that one is out. 400 should be written C D.
Rule two: V, L and D are never put in front of a bigger letter to take away.

board.text: Rule 2: V, L, D never go in front to take away

beats.say: In C D V L I I, the V stands in front of L. That breaks rule two, so it is out as well.
Now C D L X V I. C D is 400, then L is 50, X is 10, V is 5 and I is 1. Every part follows the rules. It is 466.
So do not rush to None of these. Test each numeral against the rules, one at a time.
For each pair, we square both numbers and add. We want a total that is itself a square number.

board.text: Sum of the squares of which two is a square?

beats.say: 2 and 3: the squares are 4 and 9, and together they make 13. Not a square.
5 and 6: 25 plus 36 is 61. And 4 and 6: 16 plus 36 is 52.
7 times 7 is 49 and 8 times 8 is 64. So are 52 and 61 squares?

ask.ifNot: 52 and 61 are both more than 49 and less than 64. No whole number lies between 7 and 8, so neither is a square.

beats.say: Now 6 and 8: 36 plus 64 is 100.
And 100 is 10 times 10. A square! So the pair is 6 and 8.
Notice: 6, 8 and 10 are the famous 3, 4 and 5, doubled. 9 plus 16 is 25 as well.

spec.note: Perimeter = 14 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of a square is 14 centimetres. What could one side measure?
A square has 4 equal sides, so we share 14 among 4. Half of 14 is 7, and half of 7 is 3.5.
So the side is 3.5 centimetres. That is 3 whole centimetres and half a centimetre more.

ask.ifNot: 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. Half a centimetre is half of 10.

beats.say: But 3.5 centimetres is not written like that in the choices. How many millimetres make half a centimetre?
Half of 10 is 5. So half a centimetre is 5 millimetres.
One side is 3 centimetres and 5 millimetres.
Careful with one choice: 3.5 millimetres. The number looks right, but the unit is far too small. Always read the unit.
Check: 4 sides of 3.5 make 14. It fits.
How many different isosceles triangles have whole-number sides and a perimeter of 23?
An isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides, the twins, and a third side. Twin plus twin plus third side makes 23.
Let's list in order, starting with the longest twins. Twins of 11: 11 plus 11 is 22, so the third side is 1.
Twins of 10: the third side is 3. Twins of 9: the third side is 5. Twins of 8: the third side is 7. These all close easily, because the twins are the longest sides.
Twins of 7: the third side is 9. Now the third side is the longest, so we must test. 7 plus 7 is 14, more than 9. It closes.

ask.ifNot: 12 is more than 11, even if only just. So the twins can meet above the long side. It is a very flat triangle, but a real one.

beats.say: Twins of 6: the third side is 11. 6 plus 6 is 12. Does it close?
It just fits, because 12 is more than 11.

ask.ifNot: 10 is less than 13. The twins are too short to reach across the long side, so there is no triangle.

beats.say: Twins of 5: the third side is 13. 5 plus 5 is 10. Does it close?
It does not. And shorter twins would be even worse. So the list stops here.
Count the triangles: twins of 11, 10, 9, 8, 7 and 6. That makes 6 triangles.
List in order, and test the ones where the third side is the longest. That is where the list comes to an end.
Here is a series: 24, 39, 53, 66, 78, and on it goes. Which number will be 10th? Let's find the rule first.
Look at the jumps between neighbours. They are 15, then 14, then 13, then 12.
The jumps are not the same. So what is happening to them?

ask.ifNot: Read the jumps again: 15, 14, 13, 12. Each one is 1 less than the one before.

beats.say: So the next jumps are 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7. Count carefully: 78 is the 5th term, so we need 5 more jumps to reach the 10th.
The 6th term is 78 plus 11, which is 89. The 7th is 89 plus 10, which is 99.
The 8th is 99 plus 9, which is 108. Don't stop there! The 9th is 108 plus 8, which is 116.
One jump is left. Which jump takes us from the 9th term to the 10th?

ask.ifNot: The jumps we listed were 11, 10, 9, 8 and 7. We have used four of them, so the last one is 7.

beats.say: 116 plus 7 is 123. So the 10th term is 123.
So the plan is: find the pattern in the jumps, then step forward, naming each term as you go, until you reach the one you want.
We count the square numbers that have 2 digits and are even.
First list every 2-digit square. Start at 4 times 4, which is 16, and stop before 10 times 10, which is 100.
Which numbers give an even square?

ask.ifNot: Even times even is even, and odd times odd is odd. So only even numbers give even squares.

beats.say: Even times even is even. So the even squares come from 4, 6 and 8.
That is 16, 36 and 64. So there are 3 of them.
Careful: 6 is the count of all the 2-digit squares. The question wants only the even ones.
And 4 and 100 are even squares too, but they do not have 2 digits.
Four times sums joined by plus and minus. We could work out each one. But first, look closely. Which number keeps coming back?

ask.ifNot: Every part has a 7 in it: 11 times 7, 13 times 7, 7 times 6 and 2 times 7.

beats.say: Every part has a 7. So each part is just a number of sevens: 11 sevens, 13 sevens, 6 sevens and 2 sevens.
So we can simply count sevens. But careful: one lot is taken away. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Look at the sign in front of 7 times 6. It is a minus. So those 6 sevens are taken away.

beats.say: 11 plus 13 is 24. Take away 6 to get 18. Add 2 to get 20. So there are 20 sevens altogether.
20 sevens. 2 times 7 is 14, so 20 times 7 is 140.
Let us check the long way. The four products are 77, 91, 42 and 14. The 42 is the one that is taken away.
77 plus 91 is 168. Take away 42 to get 126. Add 14 to get 140. The same answer.
So when the same number sits in every part, count how many of it you have. And watch for the minus: that part is taken away.

board.text: Which pair of angles is complementary?

beats.say: Here are 4 pairs of angles. Only one pair is complementary, and we have to find it.

ask.ifNot: Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. A square corner is a right angle, and that is 90 degrees.

beats.say: What must two complementary angles add up to?
So we add each pair and look for 90. 30 and 30 make 60. Too small. 40 and 30 make 70. Still too small.

ask.ifNot: 80 from the tens, and 10 more from the ones. 80 and 10 make 90.

beats.say: Next pair: 22 and 68. Add the ones first: 2 and 8 make 10. Then the tens: 20 and 60 make 80. What is the total?
22 plus 68 is exactly 90. That is our pair.
Let's make sure of the last one too. 34 and 66: 4 and 6 make 10, and 30 and 60 make 90, so that is 100. Too big.
So the complementary pair is 22 degrees and 68 degrees.
Complementary means the two angles fill a square corner exactly. So add the pair, and look for 90 on the dot.
Two ribbons, 84 metres and 108 metres long. Both are cut into pieces of the same length, with nothing left over. How long can each piece be?

board.text: Ribbons: 84 m and 108 m. Equal pieces, none left.

spec.note: Equal pieces, as long as possible.

beats.say: The piece length must divide 84 exactly, and 108 exactly. We want the greatest such length. What is that?

ask.ifNot: A length that divides both ribbons exactly is a common factor. The greatest one is the highest common factor.

beats.say: So we want the H C F. Here are the factors of 84. We will test them on 108, starting from the big end.
84, 42, 28, 21 and 14 do not divide 108. It is not in any of their tables. Cross them out.
Next is 12. Does 12 divide 108 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 12 times 9 is 108. So 12 divides 108 exactly.

beats.say: 12 times 9 is 108, and 12 times 7 is 84. So each piece can be 12 metres long: 7 pieces from one ribbon, and 9 from the other.
Watch the traps. 6 divides both ribbons, but it is not the greatest. And 14 divides only 84, so the longer ribbon would have some left over.
How many factors does 30 have? A factor of 30 is a number that divides 30 exactly, with nothing left over.
Here is a neat trick. Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 30. The first pair is easy: 1 times 30.
Next we try 2. 30 is even, so 2 is a factor. What is its partner?

ask.ifNot: The partner is the number we multiply 2 by to make 30. Half of 30 is 15, so the partner of 2 is 15.

beats.say: 2 times 15 is 30. That is our second pair.
Keep going in order: try 3, then 4, then 5, and so on. We get 3 times 10 and 5 times 6. 4 does not divide 30, so we skip it.
When do we stop? The next factor after 5 is 6, and 6 is already on the board as a partner. So the pairs would only repeat.
Now count. We have 4 pairs, and each pair gives 2 different factors. How many factors is that?

ask.ifNot: Each pair holds 2 factors, and there are 4 pairs. So we double 4.

beats.say: 4 pairs, 2 factors in each, makes 8. So 30 has 8 factors. Here they all are, in order.
Remember the plan: go up in order, 1, 2, 3 and so on, and write each pair that works. Then count the numbers in the pairs.
m stands for some even number and n stands for some odd number. We must find which of the 4 expressions is always odd.

board.text: m is even, n is odd. Which is always odd?

beats.say: We do not know m and n, so let us test with easy numbers. Take m as 2 and n as 1.
First, 3 m plus 4 n. 3 times 2 is 6, 4 times 1 is 4, and 6 plus 4 is 10. That is even.
Now m plus 3 n. With m as 2 and n as 1, what do we get?

ask.ifNot: 3 n is 3 times 1, which is 3. Then 2 plus 3 is 5.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 is 5, and 5 is odd. That looks like our answer.
Check the other two. 5 m plus 6 n is 10 plus 6, which is 16. And 5 m n is 5 times 2 times 1, which is 10. Both are even.
Why does it always work? m is even. 3 n is odd times odd, which is odd. And even plus odd is always odd.
So the answer is m plus 3 n.
The key idea: anything times an even number is even. So look for the expression with exactly one odd part.
A rectangle is 2 a plus 5 b centimetres long, and 7 centimetres wide. We want its perimeter.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Walk all the way round a rectangle. What do you pass?

ask.ifNot: A rectangle has 4 sides. The top and the bottom are both lengths. The left and the right are both breadths.

beats.say: So the perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths.
Two lengths first. Double each part of 2 a plus 5 b. 2 times 2 a is 4 a. 2 times 5 b is 10 b.
Now the breadths. The breadth is 7. What do two breadths make?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 breadths, one on each side. 7 and 7 make 14.

beats.say: 2 times 7 is 14.
Now add. 4 a, 10 b and 14 are three different kinds, so they just stand side by side.
Every side is counted, so the length and the breadth are both doubled. The perimeter is 4 a plus 10 b plus 14.
Three statements, and we check each one by the rules. Maybe one is true. Maybe none is. Let us find out.

board.text: Which one is correct by the BODMAS rule?

beats.say: First: 2 times 7 minus 5 equals 4. Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before minus. So 2 times 7 comes first.

beats.say: 2 times 7 is 14, and 14 take away 5 is 9, not 4. So the first one is not true.
Second: 5 plus 5 times 25 equals 250. Times first again. 5 times 25 is 125.
Then 5 plus 125 is 130, not 250. Not true. The 250 comes from adding 5 and 5 first, and that breaks the rule.
Third: bracket 18 plus 7, divided by 7, equals 19. Bracket first: 18 plus 7 is 25.
25 divided by 7 is 3, with 4 left over. That is nowhere near 19. Not true.
All three are crossed off. So the answer is none of these.
Each statement hid a trap: it did the jobs in a different order from the rule. Brackets first, then times and divide, then plus and minus.
Here are four decimals. Which one is the smallest?
Each one is made of 7s and zeros. What matters is the place where each 7 sits. Let's give them all three digits after the point.
In which number does the 7 sit in the smallest place?

ask.ifNot: After the point the places get smaller and smaller: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. In 0.007 the 7 is in the thousandths, the smallest place here.

beats.say: Read them all as thousandths: 7, then 70, then 7070, then 700. The smallest of those is 7.
One of the four is far bigger than all the rest. Which one?

ask.ifNot: 7.07 is the only one with whole ones in front of the point. All the others are less than 1.

beats.say: 7.07 has 7 whole ones, so it is the biggest by far. And the smallest is 0.007.

spec.note: 7 thousandths is the least

beats.say: A decimal is not smaller just because it is shorter. 0.07 is shorter than 0.007, but it is ten times as big. Look at the place, not the length.
Two mystery numbers with three digits each. One ends in 8, the other ends in 7. Which choice could be their product?
We cannot multiply mystery numbers. But we can be detectives and rule choices out. Here they are.
Clue one: the last digit. The last digit of a product comes only from the last digits of the two numbers. What is 8 times 7?

ask.ifNot: 8 times 7 is 56. So the product must end in 6.

beats.say: 8 times 7 is 56, so the product must end in 6. But 11558 ends in 8. Cross it off.
The other three all end in 6. So now we need clue two: the size.
The smallest the two numbers can be is 108 and 107. 108 times 100 is 10800, and 108 times 7 is 756.
Together that is 11556. So the product is at least 11556. But 10556 is smaller than that. Cross it off.
Both numbers are less than 1000, and 1000 times 1000 is 1000000. So the product is less than that. 9995006 is far bigger. Cross it off.
Only 36846 is left. It ends in 6 and it is the right size.
The sneaky one was 10556. It ends in 6, but it is just too small. So check the last digit and the size, both.
Here is 7.256 in a place-value chart. We want the place value of the digit 5.

board.text: Place value of the digit 5 in 7.256 = ?

beats.say: The first place after the point is the tenths place. Which digit is sitting there?

ask.ifNot: Find the decimal point, then look at the very next digit. It is the 2.

beats.say: After the tenths come the hundredths, and then the thousandths. So we have 2 tenths, 5 hundredths and 6 thousandths.

spec.note: The 5 is in the hundredths place

beats.say: So the 5 stands for 5 hundredths. How do we write 5 hundredths as a fraction?

ask.ifNot: Hundredths means parts out of 100. So 5 hundredths is 5 over 100.

beats.say: The place value of the 5 is 5 over 100.
If the 5 were on the left of the point, it would be worth far more. Here it is after the point, in the second place, so it is only 5 hundredths.
After the point, count the places: tenths, hundredths, thousandths. The name of the place gives you the bottom of the fraction.
8.05 kilograms is a decimal way of writing some kilograms and some grams. Which ones?
Split it at the point. 8 whole kilograms, and 0.05 of a kilogram.
1 kilogram is 1000 grams. So to turn 0.05 kilograms into grams, we multiply by 1000.
What is 0.05 times 1000?

ask.ifNot: Times 1000 slides the digits 3 places to the left. So 0.05 becomes 50.

beats.say: 0.05 times 1000 is 50. So 0.05 kilograms is 50 grams.
Watch the 0 after the point. 0.5 kilograms would be 500 grams, but we have 0.05, which is ten times smaller.
So 8.05 kilograms is 8 kilograms 50 grams.
The method: split at the point, keep the whole kilograms, and change the decimal part into grams.
At a meeting there were 21 more women than men. Altogether there were 105 people. We want the number of women.
Look at the bars. The women's bar is the same as the men's bar, with 21 extra on the end.
If we set the 21 extra women aside, what can we say about the people left?

ask.ifNot: Without the 21 extra, the two bars are the same length. So the people left are men and women in equal numbers.

beats.say: 105 minus 21 is 84. These 84 people are two equal groups.
Half of 84 is 42. So there were 42 men.
Careful: 42 is the men. How do we get the women?

ask.ifNot: There are 21 more women than men. So we add the 21 back on to 42.

beats.say: 42 plus 21 is 63. So there were 63 women.
Let's check. 63 women and 42 men make 105 people. And 63 is 21 more than 42. It works!
So set the extra aside, halve what is left, and then give the extra back to the bigger group.
Four Roman numerals, and we want the largest. But be careful: not all of them are proper numerals.

board.text: Which Roman numeral has the largest value?

beats.say: Look at X X X X I X. It has X four times in a row. Is that allowed?

choices: No, at most 3 in a row
ask.ifNot: A Roman letter may be repeated at most 3 times in a row. Four Xs break the rule, so this is not a proper numeral.

beats.say: So X X X X I X is out. The proper way to write 49 is X L I X.
X X L I V puts two Xs in front of the L. Only one smaller letter may stand in front of a bigger one. So it is out too.
Now the two proper ones. X X X I X is three tens and a nine. That is 39.
X X V I I I is two tens, a five and three ones. That is 28.
39 is more than 28. So the largest is X X X I X.
The trap is to pick the longest numeral, or the one that looks biggest. Check the rules first, then compare the values.
The teacher joins every pair of points on a circle and gets 15 line segments, the most possible. How many points were on the circle?
We do not know the number of points, so let's build up from small cases. 2 points give just 1 segment.
Add a 3rd point. It can be joined to both of the points already there. How many segments now?

ask.ifNot: There was 1 segment. The new point adds 2 more, one to each old point. 1 plus 2.

beats.say: 1 plus 2 is 3. Here is the pattern: each new point joins all the points already there.
A 4th point adds 3 more, which makes 6. A 5th point adds 4 more, which makes 10.
We want 15, and we are at 10. A 6th point adds 5 more. 10 plus 5 is 15. There it is!
So there were 6 points on the circle.
Check another way: 6 points, each joined to 5 others, is 30. Halve it, since each segment was counted twice. 15.
Four pairs of fractions. Three pairs are equal in value, and one pair is not. We must find the odd pair.
First pair: 15 over 20 and 9 over 12. Divide 15 and 20 by 5. Divide 9 and 12 by 3. Both become three quarters, so this pair is equal.
Second pair: two thirds and 16 over 24. Divide 16 and 24 by 8, and we get two thirds. Equal again.
Third pair: 33 over 55 and 15 over 25. Divide the first by 11 and the second by 5. Both become 3 over 5. Equal.
Last pair: 7 over 25 and 15 over 50. To get from 25 to 50, we double. So what should the top, 7, become?

ask.ifNot: Whatever we do to the bottom, we do to the top. The bottom was doubled, and double 7 is 14.

beats.say: Double 7 is 14. So 7 over 25 equals 14 over 50, not 15 over 50.
So the pair that is not equivalent is 7 over 25 and 15 over 50.
To test a pair: simplify both, or change one to the other's bottom. If the tops then differ, they are not equal.
A watch falls slow by 30 seconds in every hour. It is set to the correct time at 8:00 a.m. What time would it show at 10 p.m. the same day?

board.text: Watch loses 30 seconds every hour. Correct at 8:00 am.
What does it show at 10:00 pm?

spec.note: Real time 10 p.m. The watch loses 30 seconds every hour

beats.say: First count the hours. Stop at noon on the way. From 8 to noon is 4 hours, and from noon to 10 is 10 hours. That is 14 hours.

board.text: 8 am → noon: 4 hours.   noon → 10 pm: 10 hours

beats.say: The watch loses 30 seconds each hour, and 30 seconds is half a minute. So in 14 hours, how many minutes does it lose?

ask.ifNot: Two half minutes make 1 whole minute. So 14 half minutes make 7 whole minutes.

beats.say: 14 times 30 seconds is 420 seconds. 60 seconds make a minute, and 420 divided by 60 is 7 minutes.
A slow watch is behind the real time. So we take the 7 minutes away from 10:00 p.m. We do not add them.
7 minutes before 10 o'clock: 60 minus 7 is 53. So the watch shows 53 minutes past 9.
The watch shows 9:53 p.m.
Seconds lost each hour add up. Change them into minutes, then step back from the real time.
A four-digit number: 8, star, 2, star. Both stars are the same digit, and 9 divides the number exactly. Which digit is the star?

spec.note: Both stars are the same digit.

beats.say: The test for 9: add up all the digits. If the total is in the 9 times table, then 9 divides the number.
The digits we know are 8 and 2. They add up to 10.
The two stars are the same digit. So together they add up to double that digit, and a double is always an even number.
The total must land in the 9 times table: 18 or 27. For that, the stars must add 8 or 17. Which of those can two equal digits make?

ask.ifNot: Two equal digits always add up to an even number. 17 is odd, so it must be 8.

beats.say: The two stars add up to 8, and half of 8 is 4. So each star is 4.
Let's check. The digits add up to 18, which is in the 9 times table. And the number is 8,424, which is 9 times 936.
One trap: 8 is what the two stars add up to together. It is not one star. Share it equally between the two.
A bracket, a divide, a plus and a times. Brackets go first, so we begin inside.
Inside the bracket: 19 plus 3 times 2. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Even inside a bracket, times goes before plus. So 3 times 2 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 2 is 6, and 19 plus 6 is 25. The bracket is worth 25.
Now we have 25 divided by 5, plus 4 times 3. Here is the trap. What happens to the plus?
