beats.say: 15 goes in the centre. And the magic constant is always 3 times the centre.
3 times 15 is 45. So the magic constant is 45.
Check another way. Pair the ends: 11 and 19 make 30. There are 4 pairs like that, which makes 120. The 15 in the middle brings it to 135.
Three rows share the 135 equally. 135 divided by 3 is 45. The same answer.
The trap is to stop at 135. That is the sum of all nine numbers. One line is a third of it.
The numbers are 2, 6, 12, 20, 30. Which number comes next?

spec.note: How big is each jump? What comes next?

beats.say: Measure the jumps. 2 to 6 is 4. 6 to 12 is 6. 12 to 20 is 8. 20 to 30 is 10.
The jumps are 4, 6, 8, 10. What will the next jump be?

ask.ifNot: The jumps go up by 2 each time: 4, 6, 8, 10. So the next jump is 12.

beats.say: The jumps grow by 2 each time. So the next jump is 12, not 10 again.
30 plus 12 is 42. So the next number is 42.
Here is another way to see these numbers. 2 is 1 times 2. 6 is 2 times 3. 12 is 3 times 4. So the 6th number is 6 times 7, which is 42 again.
When the jumps change, look for the pattern in the jumps. And if you can find a second way, use it to check.
We are told two facts and asked for the next one: 14 times 14. We can simply work it out.
Split one of the 14s into 10 and 4.
First piece. What is 14 times 10?

ask.ifNot: 14 tens is 140. Multiplying by 10 puts a 0 on the end.

beats.say: 14 times 10 is 140. Now 14 times 4: 10 times 4 is 40, and 4 times 4 is 16, so 56.
Add the two pieces. 140 plus 56 is 196.
Now look at the pattern in the question. From 144 to 169 is a jump of 25.
From 169 to 196 is a jump of 27. The jump grew by 2.
So the trap is adding 25 again. The jump gets 2 bigger each time. The answer is 196.
Three blue balls balance two red balls. And one red ball balances three green balls. How many green balls balance the three blue ones?

spec.note: Three blue = two red. One red = three green

beats.say: Blue and green are never compared directly. Red is the bridge between them. So let's swap the reds for greens.
3 blues are worth 2 reds. Each red is worth 3 greens. So what are 2 reds worth?

ask.ifNot: One red is 3 greens. So two reds are 3 greens, and 3 greens more.

beats.say: 2 reds are 2 lots of 3 greens. 2 times 3 is 6.
So 3 blues balance 2 reds, and 2 reds balance 6 greens. That means 3 blues balance 6 greens.
The slip is to multiply the 3 blues by the 3 greens and say 9. But the 3 greens belong to each red, and there are only 2 reds.
When two things are not compared directly, find the thing that links them, and swap it for its equal.
All nine numbers in a 3 by 3 magic square add up to 72. What is the number in the centre?

board.text: All nine numbers add up to 72.  Centre = ?

spec.note: All nine numbers add up to 72. Centre = ?

beats.say: The square has 3 rows, and in a magic square the rows have equal sums. So how do we find the sum of one row?

ask.ifNot: The 3 rows have equal sums and share the 72. So one row is 72 divided by 3.

beats.say: Split 72 into 60 and 12. 60 divided by 3 is 20, and 12 divided by 3 is 4. So each row adds up to 24.
Now, the centre. What part of a row total is the centre number?

ask.ifNot: A row total is always 3 times the centre. So the centre is one third of the row total.

beats.say: 24 divided by 3 is 8. So the centre number is 8.
Careful: 24 is the sum of one row, not the centre. We had to divide by 3 twice.
Check: all nine boxes add up to 9 times the centre, and 9 times 8 is 72. So you could also divide 72 by 9 straight away.

board.text: Rectangle: length 7 cm, width 4 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 7 centimetres long and 4 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Imagine an ant walking round the rectangle until it is back where it started.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 7 plus 4 is 11.
Careful: 11 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two widths, so we double it. 2 times 11 is 22.
So the perimeter is 22 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 7, 4, 7, 4. Together they make 22.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.

board.text: Rectangle: length 13 cm, width 8 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Here is our rectangle. It is 13 centimetres long and 8 centimetres wide, and we want its perimeter.
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 13 plus 8 is 21.
Careful: 21 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two widths, so we double it. 2 times 21 is 42.
So the perimeter is 42 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 13, 8, 13, 8. Together they make 42.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.
A cross has 5 in the centre. The numbers 1, 3, 7 and 9 go at the four ends, so that both lines through the centre have the same sum. Which number is opposite 1?

board.text: Both lines have the same sum.  Opposite 1 = ?

spec.note: 3, 7 and 9 go at the other ends. Both lines have the same sum

beats.say: Each line is one end, the 5, and the opposite end. Both lines share the 5. So the two ends of one line must add up to the same as the two ends of the other.
So split 1, 3, 7 and 9 into two pairs with equal sums. Which pairs?

ask.ifNot: 1 plus 9 is 10, and 3 plus 7 is 10. Those are the two equal pairs.

beats.say: 1 plus 9 is 10, and 3 plus 7 is 10. So 1 and 9 sit at the two ends of one line.
One line is 1, 5, 9, and the other is 3, 5, 7. Both add up to 15.

spec.note: Both lines add up to 15

beats.say: So the number opposite 1 is 9.
When two lines share a middle number, forget the middle. Just make the ends of each line add up to the same amount.
A magic square has 6, 15 and 3 in its first row. We want two things: the magic constant, and the number in the centre.

spec.note: Find the magic constant and the centre number

beats.say: The magic constant is the sum of any row. Add the first row: 6 plus 15 plus 3 is 24.
Now the centre. How do we get it from the magic constant, 24?

choices: pick a number from the first row
ask.ifNot: The magic constant is always 3 times the centre. So the centre is the constant divided by 3.

beats.say: 24 divided by 3 is 8. So the centre is 8.
Here is the trap. The centre is a new number. It is not 6, 15 or 3 from the first row, and it is not 24 itself.
So the constant is 24 and the centre is 8.
Here is the finished square, with 8 in the centre. Every row, column and diagonal makes 24.

spec.note: Every line adds up to 24

beats.say: One full row gives you the magic constant. Divide that by 3 and you have the centre.
A, B and C are three numbers. We know them only in pairs: A plus B is 10, B plus C is 15, and A plus C is 11. We want all three added together.
We can't see any single letter. So let's add all three sums together: 10 plus 15 plus 11 is 36.
In that total of 36, how many times is each letter counted?

ask.ifNot: A is in the first sum and the third. B is in the first and the second. C is in the second and the third. Each letter appears twice.

beats.say: So 36 is two lots of A plus B plus C. Every letter was counted twice.

board.text: A + B + B + C + A + C = 36

beats.say: So halve it. Half of 36 is 18. The trap is to stop at 36, which counts every letter twice.
Check. C is 18 take away 10, which is 8. A is 18 take away 15, which is 3. B is 18 take away 11, which is 7. And 3 plus 7 is 10, as the first clue says.
So A plus B plus C is 18. When you only know things in pairs, add all the pairs and see how many times each one was counted.
Rohan makes a 3 by 3 magic square from 9 odd numbers in a row, starting from 5. Which number goes in the centre?

board.text: 9 odd numbers in a row, starting from 5.  Centre = ?

beats.say: Odd numbers go up in 2s. Starting from 5, the nine of them are 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 19 and 21.
The centre of the magic square holds the middle number of this list. Which is it?

ask.ifNot: The middle of nine numbers is the 5th one, with four before it and four after it. Count along: 5, 7, 9, 11, and then 13.

beats.say: The 5th number is 13. It has four numbers before it and four after it.
Check. The magic constant would be 3 times 13, which is 39. And the smallest, middle and largest numbers do add up to 39.
So the number in the centre is 13.
Careful: 9 is how many numbers there are, not the answer. Write the list out and find the one in the middle.
What an odd list! Every number is just one digit, repeated. And one of the numbers has gone missing from the middle.
Don't try to subtract these giants. Look at which digit each one uses: 9, then 7, then the gap, then 3, then 1.
So which digit does the missing term use?

ask.ifNot: The digits go down by 2 each time: 9, 7, then 5, then 3, then 1.

beats.say: The digit is 5. Now count how many times each digit is written. Seven 9s. Six 7s. Then the gap. Then four 3s and three 1s.
So how many 5s does the missing term have?

ask.ifNot: The lengths go 7, 6, then the gap, then 4, 3. They go down by 1 each time, so the gap has 5 digits.

beats.say: The digit is 5 and it is written 5 times. So the missing term is five 5s in a row.
Two things had to be right at once: the digit and the length. Four 5s or six 5s would have the right digit, but not the right length.
So with odd-looking numbers, ask how each one is built. Here it was the digit used, and how many times.
The sequence is 416, 525, 636, 749. What comes next? Let's measure the jumps.
525 minus 416 is 109. 636 minus 525 is 111. 749 minus 636 is 113.
Here is the thing to spot. Are the jumps all the same?

ask.ifNot: Look closely: 109, 111, 113. Each jump is 2 more than the one before.

beats.say: The jumps look alike, but they are not the same. They grow by 2. So the next jump is 115.
749 plus 115. Add 100 to get 849. Then add 15 to get 864.
So the next term is 864.
There is a second way to see it. The first digits go 4, 5, 6, 7. And the last two digits are 4 times 4, 5 times 5, 6 times 6, 7 times 7.
So next comes 8, followed by 8 times 8, which is 64. That makes 864 again. Two ways, one answer.
Jumps that look nearly the same may still be changing. Work each one out exactly before you decide on the rule.
Let us multiply 14 by 6. The sign is times, so we want 14 lots of 6, not 14 plus 6.
14 is easier in two pieces. Split it into 10 and 4.

spec.note: Split 14 into 10 and 4

beats.say: First the tens piece. What is 10 times 6?

ask.ifNot: 6 tens is 60. Multiplying by 10 moves every digit one place to the left.

beats.say: 10 times 6 is 60. That is the tens piece done.
Now the ones piece. 4 times 6 is 24.
Add the two pieces. 60 and 24 make 84.
So 14 times 6 equals 84.
The plan: break the big number up, multiply each piece, and add the pieces.
Here is our sum. 12 plus 20. Look at the sign first. It is a plus, so we add.
20 is a round number, full tens and no ones. So we only need to split the 12, into 10 and 2.
Add the tens first. What is 20 plus 10?

ask.ifNot: 2 tens and 1 ten make 3 tens. And 3 tens is 30.

beats.say: 2 tens and 1 ten make 3 tens. That is 30.
Now bring in the 2 ones. 30 and 2 make 32.
So 12 plus 20 equals 32.
Let us check by going backwards. 32 take away 20 brings us back to 12.
So add the tens first, then drop the ones in.
The list is 2, 6, 12, 20, a question mark, 42, 56. The missing number sits in the middle.
Start with the jumps we can see. 2 to 6 is 4. 6 to 12 is 6. 12 to 20 is 8.
The jumps are 4, 6, 8. So what is the jump into the missing number?

ask.ifNot: Each jump is 2 bigger than the last. After 8 comes 10.

beats.say: The jumps grow by 2, so the next jump is 10. And 20 plus 10 is 30.
Now test it with the numbers after the gap. The next jumps should be 12 and 14.
30 plus 12 is 42. And 42 plus 14 is 56. Both fit the list perfectly.
So the missing number is 30.
When the gap is in the middle, the numbers after it are a free check. Use them!
Here is the sequence: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125. Each number is much bigger than the last. Let's find the next one.
Try the jumps first: 7, then 19, then 37, then 61. No easy pattern there. So let's look at each number on its own.
Think about the 8. Which of these makes 8?

ask.ifNot: 2 times 2 is 4, and 4 times 2 is 8. So 8 is 2 used three times in a multiplication.

beats.say: 1 times 1 times 1 is 1. 2 times 2 times 2 is 8. 3 times 3 times 3 is 27. Each counting number is used three times.
It carries on. 4 times 4 times 4 is 64, and 5 times 5 times 5 is 125.
So what do we work out for the next term?

ask.ifNot: The numbers used so far are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Next is 6, and it is used three times: 6 times 6 times 6.

beats.say: Careful: 6 times 6 is 36, but we are not done. That is only two 6s. Now 36 times 6: 30 sixes are 180, and 6 sixes are 36.
180 plus 36 is 216. So the next number is 216.
So when the jumps give no clue, look at how each number is built. These are the cube numbers: a number used three times.
Here are five terms: 53, 56, 62, 71, 83. Two more are missing at the end. Let's find them both.
Measure the jumps. 53 to 56 is 3. 56 to 62 is 6. Then 9, then 12.
The jumps are 3, 6, 9, 12. What will the next two jumps be?

ask.ifNot: 3, 6, 9, 12 are the multiples of 3. The jump grows by 3 every time, so next come 15 and then 18.

beats.say: The jumps go up by 3 each time. So the next two are 15 and 18. The trap is to use 15 twice.
83 plus 15 is 98. That is the first new term.
Now the jump grows again. 98 plus 18 is 116. That is the second new term.
So the next two terms are 98 and 116.
So: find the jumps, see how the jumps grow, and let them keep growing for each new term you add.
Here are the numbers: 525, 438, a gap, 264, 177, 90. Let's find the one that fell out.

spec.note: How big are the jumps? Find the missing number

beats.say: The numbers are going down. Find the drop from 525 to 438. 525 minus 438 is 87.
One pair is not enough to be sure of the rule. Which other pair can we use to check the drop?

ask.ifNot: We need two numbers that are next-door neighbours, with no gap between them. 264 and 177 are neighbours.

beats.say: 264 minus 177 is 87. And 177 minus 90 is 87 again. So every drop is 87.
Now take 87 away from 438. Take away 80 first to get 358. Then take away 7 to get 351.
So the missing number is 351.
Does the drop after the gap fit too? 351 take away 87 is 264. Yes, that is the very next number in the list.
So when a number is missing in the middle, use the neighbours you can see to find the jump, and test your answer on both sides.
The series is 37, 39, 42, 47, 54, then a hidden number, then 78.
Find the jumps. 37 to 39 is 2. Then 3, then 5, then 7.
The jumps are 2, 3, 5, 7. Think about which family these numbers belong to. What comes next?

ask.ifNot: If these were the odd numbers, 2 would not be there. 2, 3, 5 and 7 are prime numbers. 9 is 3 times 3, so it is not prime. The next prime is 11.

beats.say: This is the trap. 2, 3, 5, 7 look as if 9 should follow. But they are the primes, and 9 is 3 times 3. So the next jump is 11.
54 plus 11 is 65.
Now test it with the last number. The prime after 11 is 13, and 65 plus 13 is 78. That is exactly the last number in the series.
So the hidden number is 65.
And if we had used 9? 54 plus 9 is 63. Then we would need a jump of 15 to reach 78, and that fits no pattern.
When jumps look almost like a pattern you know, check carefully which family they really belong to. Then test with the numbers that follow.
Let us add 88 and 50. Look at the sign first. It is a plus, so we add.
50 is a round number, full tens and no ones. So we only need to split the 88, into 80 and 8.
Add the tens first. What is 50 plus 80?

ask.ifNot: 5 tens and 8 tens make 13 tens. And 13 tens is 130.

beats.say: 5 tens and 8 tens make 13 tens. That is 130.
Now bring in the 8 ones. 130 and 8 make 138.
So 88 plus 50 is 138.
A quick check. 138 take away 50 is 88, right where we started. It fits.
So add the tens first, then drop the ones in.
Let us multiply 98 by 23. Look at the sign first. It is times, so we multiply.
That is a big one, so we break it into two smaller jobs. Split 23 into 20 and 3.

spec.note: Split 23 into 20 and 3

beats.say: Start with the tens piece, 20. First, 98 times 2. 90 times 2 is 180, and 8 times 2 is 16. Together that makes 196.
20 is 2 tens. So what is 98 times 20?

ask.ifNot: 20 is ten times 2. So the answer is ten times 196, which is 196 with a 0 on the end.

beats.say: Ten times 196 is 1960. That is the first piece done.
Now the ones piece. 98 times 3. 90 times 3 is 270, and 8 times 3 is 24. Together that makes 294.
Now put the two pieces together. 1960 and 294 make 2254.
So 98 times 23 equals 2254.
A quick check on the last digit. 8 times 3 is 24, which ends in 4. Our answer ends in 4 too.
So the plan is: split one number into tens and ones, multiply each piece, then add.
The sequence starts 53, 60, 68, 77. We want the 10th term, so first we need the rule.
Look at the jumps. 53 to 60 is 7. 60 to 68 is 8. 68 to 77 is 9.
How do the jumps change?

ask.ifNot: Read them again: 7, 8, 9. Each jump is 1 more than the one before.

beats.say: 77 is the 4th term. To reach the 10th we need 6 more jumps: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 15. Counting them is the tricky part.
The 5th term is 77 plus 10, which is 87. The 6th is 87 plus 11, which is 98.
The 7th is 98 plus 12, which is 110. The 8th is 110 plus 13, which is 123. Don't stop there, it is only the 8th!
The 9th term is 123 plus 14, which is 137.
One jump is left. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We listed six jumps: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15. Five are used, so the last is 15.

beats.say: 137 plus 15 is 152. So the 10th term is 152.
When jumps keep changing, walk forward one term at a time and label each term. That way you stop at exactly the right one.
Here are five terms: 4, 7, 11, 18, 29. Two more belong at the end. Let's find them.
Try the jumps: 3, then 4, then 7, then 11. They don't grow in a steady way. So the jumps are not the key here.
Here is the idea that unlocks it. Look at 4, 7 and 11. How can you make 11 from the two numbers before it?

ask.ifNot: Just add the two numbers before it. 4 plus 7 is 11.

beats.say: 4 plus 7 is 11. 7 plus 11 is 18. 11 plus 18 is 29. Each term is the sum of the two terms before it.
So the next term is the last two added together. 18 plus 29 is 47.
Now for the second new term. Which two numbers do we add this time?

ask.ifNot: Always the two newest terms. Now those are 29 and 47.

beats.say: Careful: use the two newest terms. 29 plus 47 is 76.
So the next two terms are 47 and 76.
So if the jumps look messy, test whether each term is made from the two before it. That was the secret here.
Our terms are fractions: 1 fifth, 2 fifths, 4 fifths, 7 fifths, 11 fifths. We want the next one.
Every fraction has the same bottom number, 5. So where is the pattern hiding?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number never changes. Only the top numbers move: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11.

beats.say: Look only at the tops: 1, 2, 4, 7, 11. The jumps between them are 1, 2, 3 and 4.
So what is the next jump?

ask.ifNot: The jumps go 1, 2, 3, 4. Each is 1 more than the last, so the next is 5.

beats.say: 11 plus 5 is 16. So the next term is 16 fifths.
The choices are mixed numbers, so let's change it. 5 fifths make 1 whole. So 15 fifths make 3 wholes, and 1 fifth is left over.
So the next term is 3 and 1 fifth.
Careful: 11 fifths is the same as 2 and 1 fifth. That is the last term we were given, not the next one.
With fractions that share a bottom number, find the pattern in the tops. Then write the answer in the form the question wants.
The series is 0.25, 0.50, 1, 1.75, a hidden number, and then 4. Decimals this time, but the idea is the same.
Find the jumps. 0.50 minus 0.25 is 0.25. 1 minus 0.50 is 0.50. 1.75 minus 1 is 0.75.
The jumps are 0.25, 0.50, 0.75. What is the next jump?

ask.ifNot: Each jump is 0.25 more than the last. And 0.75 plus 0.25 makes exactly 1 whole.

beats.say: The jumps grow by 0.25 each time. 0.75 plus 0.25 is 1 whole. So the next jump is 1.
Test it with the last number. The jump after 1 is 1.25. And 2.75 plus 1.25 is 4. It matches!
So the hidden number is 2.75.
Decimals follow the same plan as whole numbers. Find the jumps, see how they change, and check with the numbers that follow.
Let us take 7 away from 49. The sign is a minus, so we are taking away, not adding.
49 is 40 and 9. Let us split it into its tens and its ones.
There are enough ones to take 7 from. So only the ones change. What is 9 take away 7?

ask.ifNot: Start at 9 and hop back 7. You land on 2.

beats.say: 9 ones take away 7 ones leaves 2 ones.
The tens have not changed, so put them back. 40 and 2 make 42.
There it is. 49 minus 7 leaves 42.
Check by adding back. 42 plus 7 makes 49, the number we started with.
So when there are enough ones, keep the tens and just take away from the ones.
Five numbers: 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71. One of them does not belong with the others. Which one?
They all end in 1, and they go up in tens. So the pattern is not the clue. Think instead about what kind of numbers they are. 31 and 41 are prime.
Let's test 51 for 3, by adding its digits. 5 plus 1 is 6. Is 6 in the 3 times table?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 2 is 6. So the digit sum is in the 3 times table, and that means 3 divides 51.

beats.say: So 3 divides 51. In fact 51 is 3 times 17. It is not prime!
Now the others. Their digits add up to 4, 5, 7 and 8. None of those is in the 3 times table. They are odd, they do not end in 5, and 7 skips them all. They are prime.
Four primes, and one number that is not. So 51 does not belong.
The trap is that 51 looks prime. It is odd and it ends in 1. But adding the digits shows that 3 divides it.
Our terms are 3, 7, 11, 15, 19. Let's find the one that comes next.
Start with the first two. How big is the jump from 3 to 7?

ask.ifNot: Count on from 3: 4, 5, 6, 7. That is 4 steps. Or 7 take away 3 is 4.

beats.say: 7 minus 3 is 4. Now check the others. 11 minus 7 is 4, and 15 minus 11 is 4. Every jump is 4.

spec.note: Every jump is the same size

beats.say: So the rule is: add 4 each time.
The last term is 19. 19 plus 4 is 23. So the next term is 23.
Quick check. From 19 to 23 is a jump of 4, the same as all the others. It fits.
Find the jump, check that it never changes, then add it once more. That is the whole plan.
The numbers are 3, 6, 12, 24, 48. What comes next?
Try the jumps: 3, then 6, then 12, then 24. They are not steady. But look, the jumps are growing just like the numbers themselves.
So adding is not the rule. Which move works at every step?

ask.ifNot: Adding 3 works only once. Doubling works every time: double 3 is 6, and double 6 is 12.

beats.say: 3 times 2 is 6. 6 times 2 is 12. 12 times 2 is 24. 24 times 2 is 48. Each number is double the one before.
So we double 48. Double 40 is 80, and double 8 is 16. Together that makes 96.
The trap is to add the last jump, 24, once more. But the jumps double too. The next jump is 48, and 48 plus 48 is 96.
When the jumps keep growing fast, test for multiplying. Here each number is double the one before.
The numbers are 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Let's work out what comes next.
Let's look at how each number is made. 4 is 2 times 2. 9 is 3 times 3.
So how is 16 made?

ask.ifNot: 4 times 4 is 16. Each number in the list is a counting number multiplied by itself.

beats.say: And 1 is 1 times 1, 16 is 4 times 4, and 25 is 5 times 5. These are called the square numbers.
We have used 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Next comes 6, multiplied by itself. Careful: not 5 times 6. 6 times 6 is 36.
Check with the jumps: 3, 5, 7, 9. They grow by 2, so the next jump is 11. And 25 plus 11 is 36. The same answer.
So the next number is 36. When you see 1, 4, 9, 16, think square numbers: each counting number times itself.
The numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21. What comes next?
Measure the jumps. 1 to 3 is 2. 3 to 6 is 3. Then 4, then 5, then 6.
The jumps are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. What will the next jump be?

ask.ifNot: Each jump is 1 more than the one before. After 6 comes 7.

beats.say: The jump grows by 1 every time. So the next jump is 7, not 6 again.
21 plus 7 is 28. So the next number is 28.
These numbers have a nice secret. 3 is 1 plus 2. 6 is 1 plus 2 plus 3. 10 is 1 plus 2 plus 3 plus 4. Each one adds the next counting number.
When the jumps are not the same, look at the jumps themselves. Here they simply count up: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.
The terms are 2, 5, 14, 41. Only four of them, and they grow fast. Let's find the next.
Find the jumps. 5 minus 2 is 3. 14 minus 5 is 9. 41 minus 14 is 27.
The jumps are 3, 9 and 27. How do they grow?

ask.ifNot: 3 to 9 could be adding 6. But 9 plus 6 is not 27. Times 3 fits both: 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 times 3 is 27.

beats.say: This is the thing to spot. The jumps don't grow by adding. Each jump is 3 times the one before. So the next jump is 27 times 3, which is 81.
41 plus 81 is 122. So the next term is 122.
Here is a second way to see it. Each term is 3 times the one before, take away 1. 2 times 3 is 6, and 6 take away 1 is 5.
Try it on the last term. 41 times 3 is 123, and 123 take away 1 is 122. Both ways agree.
When the jumps are not steady, ask if they are multiplied each time. And a second way to the same answer is the best check.
The terms are 1, 2, 6, 24, 120. They grow faster and faster. What is next?
Adding can't keep up with growth like this, so think times. 1 times 2 is 2. 2 times 3 is 6.
Now from 6 to 24. 6 times what makes 24?

ask.ifNot: 6 times 4 is 24. We are multiplying here, not adding.

beats.say: 6 times 4 is 24, and 24 times 5 is 120. Look at the multipliers: 2, 3, 4, 5.
So what do we multiply by next?

ask.ifNot: The multiplier goes up by 1 each time: 2, 3, 4, 5. So the next one is 6.

beats.say: 120 times 6. 100 sixes are 600 and 20 sixes are 120. Together that is 720.
So the next term is 720. The trap is to use an old multiplier again. Here the multiplier itself keeps growing.
In some patterns you multiply by a different number each time. Then look for the pattern in the multipliers.
Each letter is worth its place in the alphabet: A is 1, B is 2, C is 3, and so on. We want the letters of the word MATH added up.

spec.note: A = 1, B = 2, C = 3 and so on. Add the four letters

beats.say: Count along the alphabet. A is 1. H is the 8th letter. Keep going to 10 for J, and M is the 13th letter.

board.text: A B C D E F G H I J K L M

beats.say: T comes later. After M come N, O, P, Q, R and S, which are 14, 15, 16, 17, 18 and 19. So what is T?

ask.ifNot: S is 19, and T comes straight after S. So T is 20.

beats.say: T is the 20th letter. So the four letters are worth 13, 1, 20 and 8.
Now add them. 13 plus 1 is 14. Add 20 to get 34. Add 8 to get 42.
So the letters of MATH add up to 42.
It is easy to be one place out when counting letters. Two handy markers: J is the 10th letter and T is the 20th.
The numbers are 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21. One more belongs at the end.
Try the jumps: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. That is strange. The jumps look just like the list itself, one step behind!
That is a big clue. Look at 2, 3 and 5. How is 5 made from the two numbers before it?

ask.ifNot: Add the two numbers just before it. 2 plus 3 is 5.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 is 5. 3 plus 5 is 8. 5 plus 8 is 13. 8 plus 13 is 21. Each number is the sum of the two before it.
So add the last two numbers in the list, 13 and 21. Careful: use both of them, not 21 and an old jump.
13 plus 21 is 34. So the missing number is 34.
This is a famous pattern. When the jumps look odd, test whether each number is the two before it added together.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a minus, a times and a plus.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: It is tempting to start on the left. But multiplying always goes first, so 6 times 3 is our first job.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding and taking away. So we box the 6 times 3. It goes first.
6 times 3 is 18. Write 18 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 29 take away 18.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 29 take away 18 is 11.
And now the plus. 11 plus 5 is 16.
Did you spot the trap? Going left to right from the very start would mean taking away before multiplying, and that gives a different number.
The rule: multiply first. Then add and take away in order, from left to right.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a minus, a times and a plus.
Where do we begin?

ask.ifNot: It is tempting to start on the left. But multiplying always goes first, so 3 times 9 is our first job.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding and taking away. So we box the 3 times 9. It goes first.
3 times 9 is 27. So 27 goes where the box was. The rest of the sum stays the same.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 46 take away 27.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 46 take away 27 is 19.
And now the plus. 19 plus 12 is 31.
Did you spot the trap? Going left to right from the very start would mean taking away before multiplying, and that gives a different number.
The rule: multiply first. Then add and take away in order, from left to right.
Here are six numbers: 2, 5, 10, 17, 28, 37. Five follow a rule and one does not. Let's catch it.

spec.note: One number breaks the pattern. Look at the jumps

beats.say: Measure the jumps. They are 3, then 5, then 7, then 11, then 9.
Most of those jumps go up nicely. Which two look out of order?

ask.ifNot: 3, 5, 7 go up by 2 each time. Next should come 9 and then 11. But here they come as 11 and then 9.

beats.say: Both of those jumps touch 28. The jump into 28 is too big, and the jump out of it is too small. So 28 is the one that breaks the pattern.
What should be there instead? 17 plus 9 is 26. And then 26 plus 11 is 37, which matches the last number.
Here is another way to see it. Each number is a square number plus 1. 1 times 1 plus 1 is 2. 2 times 2 plus 1 is 5. 3 times 3 plus 1 is 10.
Then 5 times 5 plus 1 is 26, not 28. So the number that does not belong is 28.
To find the odd one out, look at the jumps. The number sitting between two jumps that don't fit is the culprit.
The terms are 4, 12, 36, 108. Let's find the next term.
From 4 to 12 we could add 8, or we could multiply by 3. Which of these also works from 12 to 36?

ask.ifNot: Adding 8 to 12 does not give 36. But 12 times 3 is 36. So the rule is times 3.

beats.say: 4 times 3 is 12. 12 times 3 is 36. 36 times 3 is 108. Each term is 3 times the one before.
So the next term is 108 times 3. 100 threes are 300, and 8 threes are 24.
300 plus 24 is 324. So the next term is 324.
Check by going backwards. 324 divided by 3 is 108. It fits.
One step can fool you, because adding and multiplying may both fit it. Always test your rule on a second step.
This time we are given the rule: n times, n plus 1. Here n is the place of the term: 1 for the 1st, 2 for the 2nd, and so on.
Let's test the rule. The 1st term is 1 times 2. The 2nd is 2 times 3. The 3rd is 3 times 4. Each is the place number times the number just after it.
So for the 10th term, which two numbers do we multiply?

ask.ifNot: Here n is 10. And n plus 1 is the number just after it, which is 11.

beats.say: n is 10, and the number just after it is 11. Careful: 9 times 10 would be the 9th term, not the 10th.
10 times 11 is 110. So the 10th term is 110.
Check the rule on the last term we can see. The 6th term should be 6 times 7, which is 42. Yes, it matches.
When a rule uses n, put the place number in for n. Then you can jump straight to any term without listing them all.
The numbers are 729, 243, 81, 27, 9. They shrink quickly. What comes next?
Look at the small end, where the numbers are easy. Which rule works at every step?

ask.ifNot: 27 take away 18 is 9, but 81 take away 18 is not 27. Dividing by 3 works every time.

beats.say: 27 divided by 3 is 9. 81 divided by 3 is 27. 243 divided by 3 is 81. Each number is the one before it, divided by 3.
So divide the last number by 3. 9 divided by 3 is 3.
The trap is to subtract. 9 take away 3 is 6, but this pattern divides. It never takes away.
Check by going back up. 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 times 3 is 27. It fits.
So the next number is 3. When numbers shrink fast, test for dividing, and start with the small numbers where it is easy to see.
What a tangle: 1, 1, 2, 4, 3, 9, 4, 16, 5, and then a gap. It goes up and down, so one simple rule won't do.
Read every second number, starting from the very first. What do you get?

ask.ifNot: Start at the first number and skip one each time: 1, then 2, then 3, then 4, then 5.

beats.say: Two patterns are woven together. One is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. The numbers in between are 1, 4, 9, 16.
Look at each pair. 2 is followed by 4. 3 is followed by 9. 4 is followed by 16. Each in-between number is the number before it, times itself.
The gap comes straight after the 5. So what goes there?

ask.ifNot: The gap belongs to the in-between pattern. It is the number just before it, times itself. That is 5 times 5.

beats.say: The gap is not the next counting number. It belongs to the in-between pattern. 5 times 5 is 25.
So the next term is 25. When a list zigzags, split it into two patterns, and work out which one the gap belongs to.
Which of these is a leap year: 2100, 1900, 2024 or 2023?
There are two rules. Rule 1: a leap year divides exactly by 4. Rule 2: a year ending in two zeros must divide exactly by 400 instead.

board.text: Rule 2: ends in 00 → must divide by 400

beats.say: Start with 2023. It is an odd number, so it cannot divide by 4. Out it goes.
Now 2100 and 1900. They both end in two zeros. Which test must they pass?

ask.ifNot: Years that end in two zeros are special. Dividing by 4 is not enough for them. They must divide exactly by 400.

beats.say: 5 times 400 is 2000. 2100 is 100 more than that, and 1900 is 100 less. So neither one divides exactly by 400. This is the trap.
That leaves 2024. It does not end in two zeros, so Rule 1 is enough. 24 is 4 times 6, so 2024 divides exactly by 4.
The leap year is 2024.
Test the easy rule first: does it divide by 4? But if the year ends in two zeros, it has to divide by 400.
How many days are there from the 1st of March to the 1st of May, including both dates?

board.text: 1st March to 1st May, counting both dates = ? days

spec.note: Both dates are counted

beats.say: We count every day of March, every day of April, and then the 1st of May.

board.text: all of March + all of April + 1st May

beats.say: How many days does March have?

ask.ifNot: Think of the rhyme: 30 days have September, April, June and November. March is not in it, so March has 31 days.

beats.say: March has 31 days. The 1st of March is counted, so we take all 31.
April is in the rhyme, so it has 30 days.
Both dates are included, so the 1st of May counts too. That is 1 more day. Leaving it out is the trap.
Add the three parts. 31 plus 30 plus 1 is 62.
There are 62 days.
When both end dates are included, make sure the last date gets counted.
The 1st of January 2023 was a Sunday. What day was the 1st of January 2024?

spec.note: 1st January, one year on

beats.say: From the 1st of January 2023 to the 1st of January 2024 is the whole of the year 2023. So we need to know how many days 2023 has.
Is 2023 a leap year?

ask.ifNot: A leap year divides exactly by 4. 2023 is an odd number, so it cannot. It is an ordinary year.

beats.say: 2023 is an ordinary year, with 365 days.
A week is 7 days. 52 weeks make 364 days. So 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day more.
After 52 full weeks it is Sunday again. Then 1 more day makes it Monday.
The 1st of January 2024 was a Monday.
2024 is a leap year, but its extra day comes later, in February 2024. The days we counted were all in 2023.
So an ordinary year moves a date on by exactly 1 day of the week.
The 1st of January 2024 was a Monday. What day was the 1st of January 2025?

spec.note: 1st January, one year on

beats.say: Between these two dates lies the whole of the year 2024. So first we ask: how many days does 2024 have?
Is 2024 a leap year?

ask.ifNot: A leap year divides exactly by 4. 24 is 4 times 6, so 2024 divides exactly by 4. It is a leap year.

beats.say: 2024 is a leap year. So it has 366 days, one more than an ordinary year.
52 weeks make 364 days. So 366 days is 52 weeks and 2 days more.
After 52 full weeks it is Monday again. Then 2 more days: Tuesday, Wednesday.
The 1st of January 2025 was a Wednesday.
An ordinary year moves a date on 1 day. A leap year moves it on 2. Forget the leap day and you would stop at Tuesday.
Republic Day in 1993 was on a Tuesday. On which day did it fall in 1997?

spec.note: Republic Day, four years on

beats.say: Republic Day is the 26th of January. From 1993 to 1997 is 4 years, so we take 4 steps.
An ordinary step moves the day on by 1, because 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day.
So 1994 gives Wednesday, 1995 gives Thursday, and 1996 gives Friday.
1996 is a leap year. Its 29th of February comes after Republic Day 1996 and before Republic Day 1997. So how far does the last step move the day?

ask.ifNot: The leap day is inside that last stretch, so it has one extra day. The day moves on by 2.

beats.say: Friday plus 2 is Sunday. Saturday gets skipped.
Republic Day 1997 was a Sunday.
Check by adding the steps: 1 plus 1 plus 1 plus 2 is 5. And 5 days after Tuesday is Sunday.
Step one year at a time. Move 1 day, or 2 days when a 29th of February lies in between.
In 2007, Republic Day fell on a Friday. On what day was it celebrated in 2008?

spec.note: Republic Day, one year on

beats.say: Republic Day is the 26th of January. So we go from the 26th of January 2007 to the 26th of January 2008.
2008 is a leap year. Its leap day is the 29th of February 2008. Does that day come between our two dates?

ask.ifNot: February comes after January. So the 29th of February 2008 is later than the 26th of January 2008. It is outside our stretch.

beats.say: The leap day comes later, so it does not count here. Only 365 days pass.
52 weeks are 364 days. So 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day.
The day moves on by 1. Friday becomes Saturday.
The trap is to see a leap year and jump 2 days straight away. Always check where the 29th of February sits.
The 14th of February 1992 was a Friday. What day did the 13th of February 1993 fall on?
The dates are almost one year apart. So first jump exactly one year, to the 14th of February 1993. Then step back one day.
1992 is a leap year. Is its 29th of February inside our one year jump?

board.text: 1992 is a leap year: it has a 29 February

ask.ifNot: The 29th comes after the 14th in the same February. So the leap day is inside our jump.

beats.say: So the jump is 366 days long, which is 52 weeks and 2 days. The day moves on by 2.
Friday plus 2 is Sunday. So the 14th of February 1993 is a Sunday.
But we want the 13th, one day earlier. The day before Sunday is Saturday. Stopping at Sunday is the trap.
The 13th of February 1993 was a Saturday.
Jump a whole year first. Then fix the last day or two by counting.
In a certain year, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday each came 5 times in July. Which date fell on a Sunday?

board.text: July: Wednesday, Thursday, Friday come 5 times.

beats.say: July has 31 days. 4 full weeks are 28 days, so there are 3 extra days.
The days that come 5 times are the days of the 29th, 30th and 31st. And those fall on the same days as the 1st, 2nd and 3rd.
Wednesday, Thursday and Friday come 5 times. So what day is the 1st of July?

ask.ifNot: The three days come in order, on the 1st, 2nd and 3rd. The first of the three is Wednesday, so the 1st is a Wednesday.

beats.say: The 1st is a Wednesday, the 2nd a Thursday, the 3rd a Friday. Seeing this is the key to the whole question.
Carry on. The 4th is a Saturday, and the 5th is the first Sunday.
Add 7 each time to find the other Sundays: the 5th, 12th, 19th and 26th.
Among the choices, the Sunday is the 26th of July.
In a month of 31 days, the days that come 5 times tell you the day of the 1st. After that, just add sevens.
Gandhi Jayanti, the 2nd of October, was on a Wednesday. On which day did Children's Day, the 14th of November, fall that year?

spec.note: Count the days from Gandhi Jayanti to Children's Day

beats.say: We need the number of days from the 2nd of October to the 14th of November. October has 31 days.
How many days are left in October after the 2nd?

ask.ifNot: Take the 2 days that are gone away from 31. 31 minus 2 is 29.

beats.say: 31 minus 2 is 29. Then come 14 days of November. 29 plus 14 is 43 days.
Every 7 days we come back to Wednesday. 6 times 7 is 42, so 43 days is 6 weeks and 1 day.
6 weeks later it is Wednesday again. 1 more day makes it Thursday.
Children's Day fell on a Thursday.
Check by hopping in sevens. The Wednesdays are October 2, 9, 16, 23 and 30, then November 6 and 13. So the 14th is a Thursday.
Count the days between, take out the full weeks, and count on what is left.
In 2020, Republic Day, the 26th of January, fell on a Sunday. On which day was Independence Day, the 15th of August, that year?

spec.note: The year is 2020

beats.say: We count the days from the 26th of January to the 15th of August, month by month. January has 31 days, and 31 minus 26 leaves 5.
Next comes February 2020. How many days does it have?

ask.ifNot: 2020 divides exactly by 4, so it is a leap year. In a leap year February has 29 days.

beats.say: 2020 is a leap year, so February has 29. Then March 31, April 30, May 31, June 30, July 31, and 15 days of August.
Add one row at a time. The first row makes 95. The second row makes 107. Together that is 202 days.
Now take out the full weeks. 28 times 7 is 196, and 202 minus 196 leaves 6 days.
So we want 6 days after Sunday. Here is a quick way: 6 days forward is 1 day short of a full week. Which day is that?

ask.ifNot: 7 days after Sunday is Sunday again. 6 days is one day less, so it is the day before Sunday. That is Saturday.

beats.say: 6 days after Sunday is Saturday. Independence Day 2020 was a Saturday.
Count the days, remember the leap February, take out the weeks, and count on what is left.
How many minutes are there in 3 hours 45 minutes?
How many minutes are there in 1 hour?

ask.ifNot: An hour has 60 minutes. The minute hand passes 60 little marks to go once round the clock.

beats.say: One hour is 60 minutes.
So 3 hours are 3 lots of 60. 3 times 60 is 180 minutes.
Don't stop there! There are still 45 extra minutes to add.
180 plus 45. Add the 40 first to get 220, then 5 more makes 225.
There are 225 minutes in 3 hours 45 minutes.
Change the hours into minutes, then add the minutes you already had.
A movie starts at 2:40 p.m. and ends at 5:10 p.m. How long is the movie?

board.text: Movie: 2:40 pm to 5:10 pm. How long?

spec.note: How long is the movie?

beats.say: Let's count up in easy jumps, stopping at the full hours on the way.
First jump: from 2:40 up to 3:00. How many minutes is that?

ask.ifNot: An hour has 60 minutes. 40 of them are gone, and 60 minus 40 leaves 20.

beats.say: 60 minus 40 is 20. So the first jump is 20 minutes.
Second jump: from 3:00 to 5:00 is 2 hours.
Last jump: from 5:00 to 5:10 is 10 minutes.
Put the jumps together. 2 hours, and 20 minutes plus 10 minutes, which is 30 minutes.
The movie is 2 hours 30 minutes long.
You cannot take 40 minutes from 10 minutes, so jumping up is easier than subtracting.
What is 3:45 p.m. in 24-hour time?
In 24-hour time, the hours do not start again after 12 noon. They carry on: 13, 14, 15, and so on.
So for a p.m. time, what do we do to the hours?

ask.ifNot: 12 hours have already gone by before noon. So for a p.m. time, we add 12 to the hours.

beats.say: 3 plus 12 is 15.
The minutes stay just the same, 45.
Check: 15 minus 12 is 3, so 15:45 is 3:45 p.m. For p.m., add 12 to the hours and leave the minutes alone.
How many odd days are there in 400 years?
Odd days are the days left over when full weeks are taken out. An ordinary year is 52 weeks and 1 day, so it has 1 odd day. A leap year has 2.

board.text: Ordinary year: 1 odd day.  Leap year: 2 odd days

beats.say: So we must know how many of the 400 years are leap years. Every 4th year would give 400 divided by 4, which is 100.
But years ending in two zeros are special. In 400 years there are 4 of them. How many of those 4 are really leap years?

ask.ifNot: A year ending in two zeros is a leap year only if it divides by 400. Only 1 of the 4 does. The other 3 are ordinary.

beats.say: So 3 of our 100 are not leap years after all. 100 minus 3 is 97 leap years. And 400 minus 97 is 303 ordinary years.
Count the odd days. The ordinary years give 303. The leap years give 97 times 2, which is 194. Together that is 497.
Now take out the full weeks. 7 times 71 is 497, exactly. Nothing is left over!
So there are 0 odd days in 400 years.
That is why the calendar repeats itself every 400 years. Count the odd days, then take out the sevens.
A Cricket World Cup began on the 17th of March, a Wednesday. The final was on the second Sunday in May. On what date was the final?

board.text: 17th March = Wednesday. Final: second Sunday in May.

spec.note: The final is on the second Sunday in May

beats.say: If we know the day of the 1st of May, the rest is easy. So let's count the days from the 17th of March to the 1st of May.
March has 31 days. How many days of March are left after the 17th?

ask.ifNot: Take the 17 days that have gone away from 31. 31 minus 17 is 14.

beats.say: 31 minus 17 is 14. Then come all 30 days of April, and 1 day of May. 14 plus 30 plus 1 is 45 days.
6 times 7 is 42. So 45 days is 6 weeks and 3 days.
6 weeks later it is Wednesday again. Then 3 more days: Thursday, Friday, Saturday. So the 1st of May is a Saturday.
The 1st of May is a Saturday, so the 2nd is a Sunday. Is that the Sunday we want?

choices: no, that is the first Sunday
ask.ifNot: The 2nd of May is the very first Sunday of the month. The final is on the second Sunday, one week later.

beats.say: The first Sunday is the 2nd. Add 7 to reach the second Sunday. 2 plus 7 is 9.
The final was on the 9th of May.
Find the day of the 1st of the month, find the first Sunday, then add sevens.
In 2003, April Fools' Day, the 1st of April, was on a Tuesday. On which day was it in 2004?

spec.note: 1st April, one year on

beats.say: From the 1st of April 2003 to the 1st of April 2004 is one full year. Usually a year moves the day on by 1. But let's check for a leap day.
2004 is a leap year. Its leap day is the 29th of February 2004. Is that between April 2003 and April 2004?

ask.ifNot: February 2004 comes after April 2003 and before April 2004. So the leap day is inside our year.

beats.say: The leap day is inside, so this stretch has 366 days, one more than usual.
52 weeks make 364 days. So 366 days is 52 weeks and 2 days.
Full weeks bring us back to Tuesday. Only the 2 extra days matter: Tuesday, then Wednesday, then Thursday.
In 2004, April Fools' Day was on a Thursday.
This is the trap: an ordinary year moves the day by 1, but a leap day in between makes it 2.
In 2019, New Year, the 1st of January, fell on a Tuesday. On which day was Christmas, the 25th of December, in the same year?

spec.note: The year is 2019

beats.say: Counting through every month would take a long time. Here is a smarter way: use the end of the year.
2019 is an ordinary year with 365 days. So the 31st of December, the last day, is 364 days after the 1st of January.
52 times 7 is 364. So 364 days is exactly 52 weeks. What day is the 31st of December, then?

ask.ifNot: Exactly 52 full weeks, with no days left over, bring us back to the same day. So the 31st of December is a Tuesday too.

beats.say: An ordinary year ends on the same day it begins. So the 31st of December 2019 is a Tuesday.
Now hop back 7 days from the 31st. 31 minus 7 is 24. So the 24th of December is a Tuesday too.
Christmas is the day after the 24th. The day after Tuesday is Wednesday.
Check another way. Christmas is 6 days before the 31st, so it is 364 minus 6, which is 358 days after New Year. 51 times 7 is 357, so 1 day is left over.
An ordinary year starts and ends on the same day of the week. That one fact saves a lot of counting.
The 9th of April 1990 was a Monday. Which days occurred five times in that month?

board.text: 9th April 1990 = Monday. Which days came 5 times?

spec.note: April 1990. Which days came five times?

beats.say: April has 30 days. 4 full weeks are 28 days. So how many extra days does April have?

ask.ifNot: 4 weeks are 28 days. 30 minus 28 leaves 2 extra days.

beats.say: 30 minus 28 is 2. In 4 full weeks every day comes 4 times, and the 2 extra days get a 5th turn.
The extra dates are the 29th and 30th. They are exactly 28 days after the 1st and 2nd, so they fall on the same days.
So let's find the 1st. Monday the 9th, back 7 days, is Monday the 2nd.
The 2nd is a Monday. So what day is the 1st?

ask.ifNot: The 1st is the day before the 2nd. And the day before Monday is Sunday.

beats.say: The 1st is a Sunday. So the 29th is a Sunday, and the 30th is a Monday.
Check: the Mondays fall on the 2nd, 9th, 16th, 23rd and 30th. Five of them.
With 30 days, only 2 days can come five times. So a choice with three days cannot be right.
A train departs at 09:45 and the journey takes 4 hours 35 minutes. At what time does it arrive?

spec.note: Departs at 09:45. When does it arrive?

beats.say: Add the hours first. 9 plus 4 is 13, so 09:45 plus 4 hours is 13:45.
Now the minutes. 45 plus 35 is 80 minutes.
A clock never shows 80 minutes. So what do we do with them?

ask.ifNot: 60 minutes make 1 hour. So 80 minutes is 1 hour and 20 minutes, and the hour gets carried over.

beats.say: 80 minutes is 1 hour and 20 minutes. Carry the 1 hour: 13 plus 1 is 14. So the time is 14:20.
The choices use the 12-hour clock. 14 is more than 12, so it is p.m., and 14 minus 12 is 2.
The train arrives at 2:20 p.m.
Add hours, add minutes, and when the minutes reach 60 or more, trade 60 of them for 1 hour. Carry it just once.
How many days are there from the 15th of August to the 2nd of October, not counting the 15th of August?

board.text: 15th August to 2nd October, not counting 15th August

spec.note: 15th August itself is not counted

beats.say: We count in three parts: the rest of August, all of September, and the start of October.

board.text: rest of August + September + start of October

beats.say: August has 31 days. We leave out the 15th. So how many days are there from the 16th to the 31st?

board.text: August has 31 days: count the 16th to the 31st

ask.ifNot: Take away the first 15 days of August. 31 minus 15 is 16, and those are the days from the 16th to the 31st.

beats.say: 31 minus 15 is 16. August gives 16 days.
September has 30 days, and all of them count.
In October we count the 1st and the 2nd. Take care: the 15th of August is left out, but the 2nd of October is counted.
Add the three parts. 16 plus 30 plus 2 is 48.
There are 48 days.
Read which end dates are counted, then go month by month.
Teachers' Day, the 5th of September, 2016 was a Monday. On which day was Christmas celebrated that year?

spec.note: Count the days from Teachers' Day to Christmas

beats.say: Christmas is the 25th of December. Count the days from the 5th of September. September has 30 days, and 30 minus 5 leaves 25.
Then October has 31 days, November has 30, and December gives 25.
Add them in pairs. 25 plus 31 is 56, and 30 plus 25 is 55. 56 plus 55 is 111 days.
Now take out the full weeks. Which is the biggest lot of sevens that fits into 111?

ask.ifNot: 16 sevens make 112, which is 1 too many. So 15 sevens, 105, is the most that fits.

beats.say: 15 times 7 is 105. And 111 minus 105 leaves 6 days.
6 days after Monday. That is 1 day short of a full week, so it is the day just before Monday: Sunday.
Christmas 2016 was on a Sunday.
Count the days between, take out the full weeks, and move on by what is left.
Rahul celebrated his 5th birthday on the 3rd of August 2014, which was a Sunday. Which birthday will fall on a Thursday?

board.text: Which birthday falls on a Thursday?

spec.note: 5th birthday: 3rd August 2014, a Sunday

beats.say: Each year the birthday moves on 1 day of the week. But if a 29th of February lies in between, it moves on 2.

board.text: No leap day: + 1.    29 February in between: + 2

beats.say: The 6th birthday is in August 2015. No leap day lies in between, so Sunday becomes Monday.
The 7th birthday is in August 2016. 2016 is a leap year, and February comes before August. How far does the day move?

ask.ifNot: The 29th of February 2016 lies between August 2015 and August 2016. So the day moves on by 2.

beats.say: Monday plus 2 is Wednesday. So the 7th birthday is a Wednesday.
The 8th birthday is in 2017. No leap day this time, so Wednesday becomes Thursday.
There is our Thursday. It is Rahul's 8th birthday.
Go one birthday at a time. Move 1 day, or 2 days when a leap day lies in between.
How many seconds are there in 2 hours?
We go in two steps: hours to minutes, and then minutes to seconds.
One hour has 60 minutes. So 2 hours have 2 times 60, which is 120 minutes.
Each of those 120 minutes has 60 seconds. So what do we work out?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 120 minutes holds 60 seconds. 120 lots of 60 means we multiply.

beats.say: 120 times 60. First, 12 times 6 is 72. Then put the two zeros back: 7200.
There are 7200 seconds in 2 hours.
Check: 1 hour is 60 times 60, which is 3600 seconds. Double that is 7200.
Stopping at 120 is the trap, because those are only minutes. Hours to minutes, then minutes to seconds: multiply by 60 each time.
A normal year has how many odd days?

board.text: A normal year has ? odd days

beats.say: Odd days are the days left over after we take out all the full weeks.

board.text: Odd days = days left after the full weeks

beats.say: A normal year has 365 days, and a week has 7 days.
52 weeks make 364 days. So how many days of the year are left over?

ask.ifNot: The year has 365 days, and the full weeks use up 364 of them. 365 minus 364 leaves 1 day.

beats.say: 365 minus 364 is 1. So a normal year is 52 weeks and 1 day.
A normal year has 1 odd day.
That 1 odd day is why your birthday moves on by one day of the week each year. In a leap year it moves by 2.
In the year 2000, Gandhi Jayanti, the 2nd of October, fell on a Monday. In which year after 2000 was it first on a Sunday?

board.text: 2nd October 2000 = Monday. Sunday in which year?

spec.note: 2nd October, year by year

beats.say: From one 2nd of October to the next, the day usually moves on by 1, because 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day.
2000 was a leap year, but its leap day was in February, before October. So it does not matter here.
So 2001 gives Tuesday, 2002 gives Wednesday, and 2003 gives Thursday.
Now from October 2003 to October 2004. The 29th of February 2004 lies in between. What happens to the day?

ask.ifNot: The leap day adds one extra day to that stretch. So the day jumps on by 2 instead of 1.

beats.say: Thursday plus 2 is Saturday. So 2004 gives Saturday. Friday is skipped, and that is the trap!
One more ordinary year, and Saturday becomes Sunday. That is 2005.
Go one year at a time. Move 1 day, and jump 2 when a 29th of February lies in between.

board.text: More than 90° but less than 180°: called?

beats.say: Here is an angle that is more than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees. What is it called?
Angle names go by size. The small ones, less than 90, are acute. Exactly 90, the square corner, is a right angle.
Now jump to the far end. An angle that opens past a straight line, more than 180, is called reflex.

ask.ifNot: Acute is for angles under 90, and reflex is for angles over 180. The name for the ones in between is obtuse.

beats.say: Our angle is wider than the square corner, but it has not opened out flat. Which name is left for it?
Obtuse. An angle between 90 and 180 degrees is an obtuse angle.
Obtuse means blunt. An acute angle is sharp, like a pencil tip. An obtuse angle is blunt and wide, like a book lying nearly flat.
So, in order of size: acute, right, obtuse, straight, reflex. Obtuse sits between the square corner and the straight line.
What kind of angle is 250 degrees? Here it is. It is a big one.
To name an angle, we compare it with the fence posts. 90 is a right angle, 180 is a straight line, and 360 is a full turn.

ask.ifNot: Look at the hundreds. 180 has 1 hundred and 250 has 2 hundreds. So 250 is the bigger number.

beats.say: Is 250 more than 180, or less?
More than 180. So the angle has opened past a straight line. It cannot be obtuse, because obtuse stops at 180.
But 250 is less than 360, so it is not a full turn either. It is not a complete angle.

ask.ifNot: A straight angle is exactly 180, and a complete angle is exactly 360. Anything in between those two is a reflex angle.

beats.say: Past a straight line, but short of a full turn. What do we call an angle like that?
So 250 degrees is a reflex angle.
A reflex angle is the long way round. Whenever the size is between 180 and 360, the angle is reflex.

board.text: Which instrument is used to measure an angle?

beats.say: Open your geometry box. Which of these tools is used to measure an angle?

ask.ifNot: Centimetres are for lengths and grams are for weights. The size of an angle, how far it opens, is measured in degrees.

beats.say: First, what are angles measured in?
Degrees. So we need a tool that has degrees marked on it. Let's check each tool's job.
A compass holds a pencil and draws circles. A pair of dividers has two sharp points, for comparing lengths. No degrees on either.

board.text: Set square: a few fixed angles

beats.say: A set square has a few fixed corners, so it helps to draw some angles. But it cannot measure any angle you like.

ask.ifNot: The half circle with the degree marks is the protractor. A ruler measures length, and a compass draws circles.

beats.say: One tool is left. It is a half circle, with degrees marked all round its curved edge, from 0 to 180. What is it called?
The protractor. That is the tool that measures an angle.
Each tool has its own job. A ruler for lengths, a compass for circles, and a protractor for angles.
We want the complementary angle of 67 and a half degrees.

ask.ifNot: Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. A square corner is a right angle, and that is 90 degrees.

beats.say: What do two complementary angles add up to?
So we take 67 and a half away from 90. Let's do it in two bites: the whole 67 first, then the half.
90 take away 67. 90 take away 60 is 30, and 7 more away leaves 23.

ask.ifNot: We are taking away, so the answer goes just below 23. Half way back from 23 towards 22 is 22 and a half.

beats.say: The half still has to come off. What is half less than 23?
Half less than 23 is 22 and a half.
So the complementary angle is 22 and a half degrees.
Check. 67 and 22 make 89. The two halves make 1 more. 90 exactly.
Whole number first, then the half. Both are taken away, so the answer ends up just below 23, not above it.
A triangle has 3 angles. We are told 2 of them: 75 degrees and 67 degrees. Let's hunt for the third.
Here is the fact that unlocks every triangle. Its 3 angles always add up to 180 degrees.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: So 2 angles are known and 1 is missing. What is our first move?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 75 plus 60 is 135. Then 7 more makes 142.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 142 away from 180.

beats.say: So 142 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
180 minus 142. Take off 140 first, which leaves 40. Then take off the last 2, and we land on 38.
So the third angle is 38 degrees. There it is!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 75, 67 and 38. They make 180, just as they should.
Remember the plan: add the 2 angles you have, and take that from 180. What is left is the third angle.
This triangle is keeping a secret. We know 2 angles, 36 degrees and 74 degrees, and the third is hidden.
Here is the fact that unlocks every triangle. Its 3 angles always add up to 180 degrees.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Add the tens first. 36 plus 70 is 106. Now the 4 that is left: that makes 110.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 110 away from 180.

beats.say: So 110 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 110 away from 180. That leaves 70. So the third angle is 70 degrees.
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 36, 74 and 70. They make 180, just as they should.
Remember the plan: add the 2 angles you have, and take that from 180. What is left is the third angle.
We want the supplementary angle of 55 degrees. Here is 55 degrees on a straight line, with its partner beside it.

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do two supplementary angles add up to?
So 55 and its partner make 180. The partner is 180 take away 55.

ask.ifNot: 130 take away 5 is 125. It must end up below 130, because we are taking away.

beats.say: Take the 50 away first. 180 take away 50 is 130. Then the 5. What is 130 take away 5?
125. So 180 take away 55 is 125.
The supplementary angle is 125 degrees.
Check: 55 and 125. The two 5s make 10, and 50 and 120 make 170. 170 and 10 is 180.
The tempting slip is 35. That is 90 take away 55, the complementary angle. S for supplementary, S for straight line: 180.
Here is 10 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplement is the other piece of that line, the one with the question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 10, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 10.

beats.say: The whole is 180 and one piece is 10. Which sum finds the missing piece?
180 take away 10 leaves 170.
So the supplement is 170 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 10 plus 170 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.
This question has two parts. First we find x. Then we find the supplement of x.

ask.ifNot: 90 is the whole and 35 is one part. To find the other part, take 35 away from 90.

beats.say: x and 35 make 90. So x is the missing piece of a square corner. Which sum finds it?
90 take away 30 is 60, and 5 more away is 55. So x is 55 degrees.
Careful. 55 is x, but the question does not stop there. It asks for the supplement of x.

ask.ifNot: We want the supplement of x, and x is 55. So we take 55 away from 180. 180 take away 35 would be the supplement of the other angle.

beats.say: A supplement is the partner that makes a straight line, 180 degrees. So which sum do we need now?
180 take away 50 is 130, and 5 more away is 125.
So the supplement of x is 125 degrees.
Check: 55 and 125 make 180. And in a two part question, read the last line again before you choose.

board.text: Supplement of an angle = 125°. Its complement = ?

beats.say: We are not told the angle. We are told its supplement, 125 degrees. And we are asked for its complement.

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So first we must find the angle itself. An angle and its supplement make how much together?
So the angle is 180 take away 125. Count up from 125: 5 more gets to 130, and 50 more gets to 180. That is 55.

ask.ifNot: The complement belongs to the angle itself, which is 55. Complementary angles make 90, so take 55 away from 90.

beats.say: Now for what the question asks: the complement of this angle. A complement is the partner that makes a square corner. Which sum is it?
90 take away 55 is 35.
So the complement is 35 degrees.
Check both. 55 and 125 make 180: that is the supplement. 55 and 35 make 90: that is the complement.
One choice says the angle has no complement. That only happens when an angle is 90 or more. Ours is 55, so it has one. Find the angle first, then its partner.

board.text: Two lines cross. Pairs of opposite angles = ?

beats.say: Two lines cross, like the letter X. How many pairs of vertically opposite angles do they make?
Two crossing lines make 4 angles round the crossing point. I have called them a, b, c and d.

ask.ifNot: b and d are next door to a, one on each side. The one straight across the crossing point is c.

beats.say: Vertically opposite angles face each other across the crossing point. Which angle is straight across from a?
a faces c. That is one pair.
Two angles are left, b and d. They face each other too. That is a second pair.
Every angle is in a pair now. So there are 2 pairs of vertically opposite angles.
The slip to avoid is saying 4. That is the number of angles. They match up across the point, 2 by 2, so there are 2 pairs.

board.text: Lines intersect: one angle is 70°. Opposite = ?

beats.say: Two lines cross, and one of the angles is 70 degrees. We want the angle opposite to it, straight across the crossing point.

ask.ifNot: Two angles side by side on a straight line make a half turn together. A half turn is 180 degrees.

beats.say: Look at the angle next door, called p. It shares a straight line with the 70. What do two angles on a straight line make together?
So p is 180 take away 70, which is 110.

ask.ifNot: 180 take away 110 leaves 70. You can check: 110 and 70 make 180.

beats.say: Now p and our mystery angle share the other straight line. So the mystery angle is 180 take away 110. What is that?
70. The very same as the angle we started with!
That always happens. Angles straight across a crossing are called vertically opposite, and they are always equal.
So next time there is nothing to work out: the opposite angle is equal. 110 is the neighbour on the line, not the angle across.
Here is 85 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplement is the other piece of that line, the one with the question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 85, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 85.

beats.say: The whole is 180 and one piece is 85. Which sum finds the missing piece?
Let's take 85 away in two easy hops. First the 80: 180 take away 80 leaves 100.
Now the 5 that is left: 100 take away 5 leaves 95. So 180 minus 85 is 95.
So the supplement is 95 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 85 plus 95 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.

board.text: Linear pair: one angle is 65°. The other = ?

beats.say: Two angles form a linear pair, and one of them is 65 degrees. We want the other one.

ask.ifNot: Two angles side by side on a straight line make a half turn together. A half turn is 180 degrees.

beats.say: The word linear has line inside it. A linear pair is two angles side by side on a straight line. So what do they add up to?
So 65, plus the other angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: 5 less than 120 is 115. We are taking away, so we land below 120.

beats.say: We need 180 take away 65. First take away 60, which leaves 120. Then take 5 more. What is left?
115. So 180 take away 65 is 115.
The other angle is 115 degrees.
Check: 65 and 115. 60 and 110 make 170, and the two 5s make 10 more. 180.
The two angles of a linear pair do not have to be equal. They just have to make a straight line together: 180 degrees.

board.text: Angle between the hands at 3 o'clock = ?

beats.say: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand at 3 o'clock? Here is the clock.

ask.ifNot: Share 360 among the 12 gaps. 12 times 30 is 360, so each gap is 30 degrees.

beats.say: The 12 numbers cut the clock face into 12 equal gaps, and all the way round is a full turn of 360 degrees. So how big is one gap?
360 divided by 12 is 30. Each gap is 30 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps: 12 to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3. That is 3 gaps.

beats.say: At 3 o'clock the minute hand points straight up at the 12, and the hour hand points at the 3. How many gaps are between them?
3 gaps of 30 make 90 degrees.
So the angle is 90 degrees.
And look at the clock. The hands make a perfect square corner, and 90 degrees is a right angle. Count the gaps, then times by 30.
What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand at 9:30? This one has a catch.
Each gap between two numbers on a clock is 30 degrees, because 360 shared among 12 gaps is 30.

ask.ifNot: The hour hand keeps moving all the time. In half an hour it goes half of the way from the 9 to the 10.

beats.say: At half past, the minute hand points at the 6. Now the catch. Where is the hour hand at half past 9?
Halfway between the 9 and the 10. So we count in two parts. First, from the 6 to the 9. That is 3 gaps, and 3 times 30 is 90.
Then the extra half gap, past the 9. Half of 30 is 15.
Add the two parts. 90 and 15 make 105.
So the angle is 105 degrees.
90 is the trap. That is what you get if you leave the hour hand on the 9. At half past, the hour hand is always half a gap further on.
We want the supplement of 165 degrees. Supplementary angles are two angles that sit side by side on a straight line. Here is the picture.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Picture yourself standing where the two angles meet. You face along the line, then turn to face the other way. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 165, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 165.

beats.say: We know the whole, 180, and one part, 165. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 165 away in two easy hops. First the 160: 180 take away 160 leaves 20.
Now the 5 that is left: 20 take away 5 leaves 15. So 180 minus 165 is 15.
So the supplement is 15 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 165 plus 15 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So the two partners make 180. Take the angle you have away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.

board.text: At which time is the angle between the hands obtuse?

beats.say: At which of these 4 times do the clock hands make an obtuse angle? We need to test each time.

ask.ifNot: Obtuse means wider than a right angle, 90 degrees, but not yet a straight line, 180 degrees.

beats.say: First, what makes an angle obtuse?
On a clock, each gap between two numbers is 30 degrees. So 90 degrees is 3 gaps, and 180 degrees is 6 gaps. We want more than 3 gaps, but fewer than 6.
Start with the o'clock times. At 10 o'clock the minute hand points straight up, and the hour hand is on the 10, only 2 gaps away. 60 degrees. That is acute.
At 6 o'clock the hands are 6 gaps apart, pointing opposite ways. Exactly 180. That is a straight angle, and an obtuse angle must be less than 180.

ask.ifNot: By half past, the hour hand has gone half of the way to the next number. So it is halfway between the 3 and the 4.

beats.say: Now half past 3. The minute hand is on the 6. Careful: where is the hour hand?
So from the hour hand to the 6 is 2 and a half gaps. 60, and 15 more, is 75 degrees. Acute again. Leaving the hand on the 3 would give 90, and that is the trap.
That leaves 4 o'clock. The hands are 4 gaps apart, and 4 times 30 is 120. More than 90, and less than 180.
So the angle is obtuse at 4 o'clock.
For each time: find both hands, count the gaps, and times by 30. Then name the angle.

board.text: When do the hands form a straight angle (180°)?

beats.say: When do the two hands of a clock form a straight angle, 180 degrees? We have three times to test.

ask.ifNot: 6 times 30 is 180. So the hands must be exactly 6 gaps apart, half way round the clock from each other.

beats.say: A straight angle means the hands point in exactly opposite directions. Each gap between two numbers on a clock is 30 degrees. So 180 degrees is how many gaps?
6 gaps of 30 make 180. So we want the hands exactly 6 gaps apart.
At 6 o'clock the minute hand points straight up, and the hour hand is exactly on the 6, straight down. 6 gaps apart. A perfect straight line.

choices: No, it has moved towards the 4
ask.ifNot: The hour hand never stops. After 45 minutes it has gone three quarters of the way from the 3 to the 4.

beats.say: Now 3:45. The minute hand is on the 9, and the 9 is opposite the 3. But is the hour hand still on the 3?
It has crept most of the way to the 4. So the hands are not exactly opposite any more.
It is the same story at 9:15. The minute hand is on the 3, opposite the 9. But the hour hand has moved a little past the 9. Close to a straight line, but not exact.
So the hands form a straight angle only at 6 o'clock.
All of these was the trap. It only looks true if the hour hand waits on its number. It never does, except exactly on the hour.
A triangle has 3 angles. We are told 2 of them: 34 degrees and 60 degrees. Let's hunt for the third.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 60 plus 30 is 90. Then 4 more makes 94.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 94 away from 180.

beats.say: The 2 known angles take 94 degrees out of the 180. What is left for the third angle?
180 minus 94. Take off 90 first, which leaves 90. Then take off the last 4, and we land on 86.
So the third angle is 86 degrees. Found it!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 34, 60 and 86. They make 180, just as they should.
Remember the plan: add the 2 angles you have, and take that from 180. What is left is the third angle.
Here is a triangle. 2 of its angles are 63 degrees and 87 degrees. We need to find the third one.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Add the tens first. 63 plus 80 is 143. Now the 7 that is left: that makes 150.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 150 away from 180.

beats.say: The 2 known angles take 150 degrees out of the 180. What is left for the third angle?
Take 150 away from 180. That leaves 30. So the third angle is 30 degrees.
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 63, 87 and 30. They make 180, just as they should.
Remember the plan: add the 2 angles you have, and take that from 180. What is left is the third angle.

board.text: At which time is the angle between the hands greatest?

beats.say: At which of these 4 times is the angle between the clock hands the greatest? We have to compare them.
Every gap between two numbers on a clock is the same size, 30 degrees. So to begin with we can just count gaps. The most gaps wins.
9 o'clock is the easy one. The hour hand is exactly on the 9 and the minute hand is on the 12. That is 3 gaps.

ask.ifNot: From halfway past the 4, it is half a gap to reach the 5, and then one more gap to the 6. That is 1 and a half gaps.

beats.say: At half past 4, the minute hand is on the 6. The hour hand is halfway between the 4 and the 5. So how many gaps is it from there to the 6?
1 and a half gaps. That is small. Not our winner.
Now the two quarter past times. In 15 minutes, a quarter of an hour, the hour hand creeps a quarter of a gap forward. That little creep decides everything.
At 12:15 the minute hand is on the 3. The hour hand has crept a little past the 12, towards the 3. So the angle shrinks: a bit less than 3 gaps.

ask.ifNot: From the 3 to the 6 is 3 gaps. The hour hand has moved on past the 6, further from the 3. So the angle has grown a little.

beats.say: At 6:15 the minute hand is on the 3 again. But the hour hand has crept past the 6, away from the 3. Is the angle bigger or smaller than 3 gaps?
A bit more than 3 gaps. That beats 9 o'clock, which is exactly 3.
So the greatest angle is at 6:15.
3 gaps are exactly 90 degrees. So 6:15 is just past a right angle, and 12:15 is just short of one.
The hour hand's small creep matters. Always ask which way it creeps: towards the other hand, or away from it.

board.text: At 1 o'clock the angle is 30°. Complementary angle at?

beats.say: At 1 o'clock the hands are 30 degrees apart. We want the time when the angle is complementary to that.

ask.ifNot: Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. A square corner is a right angle, and that is 90 degrees.

beats.say: First find the angle we are looking for. Complementary angles add up to how much?
So the angle we want is 90 take away 30. That is 60 degrees.

ask.ifNot: 30 and 30 make 60. So 60 degrees is 2 gaps.

beats.say: On a clock, each gap between two numbers is 30 degrees. That is why 1 o'clock gives 30: the hands are 1 gap apart. How many gaps make 60?
2 gaps of 30 make 60. So we need the hands 2 gaps apart.
