On the hour, the minute hand points straight up. The hour hand must be 2 gaps away from it, and that is on the 2. So the time is 2 o'clock.
Check the other times. 5 o'clock and 7 o'clock are both 5 gaps from the top, 150 degrees. 6 o'clock is 180, a straight line. None of them is 60.
Two steps: first find the angle you need, then turn it into gaps on the clock.
Our angle is 27 degrees, and we want its complementary partner. The two angles fit snugly into one square corner, like this.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles fit inside a square corner, and a square corner is a quarter turn. That makes 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Picture the corner of your notebook. That square corner is a right angle, a quarter of a full turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. So 27, plus our missing angle, makes 90.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 90 take away 27.

beats.say: We know the whole, 90, and one part, 27. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 27 away in two easy hops. First the 20: 90 take away 20 leaves 70.
Now the 7 that is left: 70 take away 7 leaves 63. So 90 minus 27 is 63.
So the complement is 63 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 27 plus 63 makes 90. It fits exactly.
So the two partners make 90. Take the angle you have away from 90. To remember which is which: C for complementary, C for corner. S for supplementary, S for straight line.
A triangle has 3 angles. We are told 2 of them: 27 degrees and 41 degrees. Let's hunt for the third.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: So 2 angles are known and 1 is missing. What is our first move?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 27 plus 40 is 67. Then 1 more makes 68.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 68 away from 180.

beats.say: So 68 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 68 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 60: that leaves 120. Then take away 8 more: 112.
So the third angle is 112 degrees. Found it!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 27, 41 and 112. They make 180, just as they should. And notice: 112 degrees is a wide angle, an obtuse one. A triangle can have just 1 of those.
Remember the plan: add the 2 angles you have, and take that from 180. What is left is the third angle.
We want the complement of 85 degrees. Complementary angles are two angles that fit together to make a right angle, like the corner of a page. Here is the picture.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles fit inside a square corner, and a square corner is a quarter turn. That makes 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Picture the corner of your notebook. That square corner is a right angle, a quarter of a full turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. So 85, plus our missing angle, makes 90.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 90 take away 85.

beats.say: The whole is 90 and one piece is 85. Which sum finds the missing piece?
Let's take 85 away in two easy hops. First the 80: 90 take away 80 leaves 10.
Now the 5 that is left: 10 take away 5 leaves 5. So 90 minus 85 is 5.
So the complement is 5 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 85 plus 5 makes 90. It fits exactly.
So to find a complement, take the angle away from 90. To remember which is which: C for complementary, C for corner. S for supplementary, S for straight line.
What is the angle between north-east and south? Here is the compass.
North, east, south and west are the 4 main directions. They share a full turn of 360 degrees equally. So from one to the next is a quarter turn, 90 degrees.

ask.ifNot: North-east is halfway between two directions that are 90 apart. Half of 90 is 45.

beats.say: North-east sits exactly halfway between north and east. So how far is it from north-east round to east?
Half of 90 is 45. That is the first part of the turn.
Then from east on to south is one more quarter turn, 90 degrees.
Add the two parts. 45 and 90 make 135.
So the angle between north-east and south is 135 degrees.
The slip is to stop at 90 and forget the first little piece, from north-east to east. Walk round the compass one stop at a time, and add as you go.

board.text: How many degrees does the hour hand move in one hour?

beats.say: How many degrees does the hour hand of a clock move in one hour?

ask.ifNot: The hour hand is the slow one. It points at each of the 12 numbers in turn, one number each hour. So once round takes 12 hours.

beats.say: Think about the hour hand's whole trip. How long does it take to go once all the way round the clock?
12 hours for one full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The 360 degrees are shared equally among 12 hours. Sharing means dividing, so it is 360 divided by 12.

beats.say: It moves steadily, so each hour gets an equal share. Which sum gives the share for 1 hour?
360 divided by 12. 12 times 3 is 36, so 12 times 30 is 360. The answer is 30.

board.text: The hour hand moves 30° in one hour

beats.say: So the hour hand moves 30 degrees in one hour.
You can see it on a clock. In one hour the hour hand goes from one number to the next, say from 2 to 3. That gap is 30 degrees.
Do not mix it up with the minute hand. That one is fast: it does the whole 360 in one hour. The hour hand does just 30.
Here is 8 degrees, drawn inside a right angle. Its complement is the other piece of that corner, the one with the question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles fit inside a square corner, and a square corner is a quarter turn. That makes 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Picture the corner of your notebook. That square corner is a right angle, a quarter of a full turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. So 8, plus our missing angle, makes 90.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 90 take away 8.

beats.say: The whole is 90 and one piece is 8. Which sum finds the missing piece?
90 take away 8 leaves 82.
So the complement is 82 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 8 plus 82 makes 90. It fits exactly.
So to find a complement, take the angle away from 90. To remember which is which: C for complementary, C for corner. S for supplementary, S for straight line.

board.text: How many degrees does the minute hand move in 1 minute?

beats.say: How many degrees does the minute hand of a clock move in 1 minute?

ask.ifNot: There are 60 minutes in 1 hour. So the minute hand takes 60 minutes to go once round.

beats.say: The minute hand goes once all the way round the clock in 1 hour. How many minutes is that?
60 minutes for one full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees.
Each minute gets an equal share of the 360. So we divide 360 by 60.

ask.ifNot: 6 times 6 is 36. So 36 divided by 6 is 6.

beats.say: Here is a trick. Cross off a zero from each number. 360 divided by 60 is the same as 36 divided by 6. And what is 36 divided by 6?

board.text: The minute hand moves 6° in 1 minute

beats.say: 6. So the minute hand moves 6 degrees in 1 minute.
Check: 60 minutes, at 6 degrees each. 60 times 6 is 360, the full turn.
Do not mix it up with 30 degrees. That is the gap between two numbers, and the minute hand takes 5 whole minutes to cross it. 5 times 6 is 30.

board.text: Complementary angles in the ratio 2:3. Smaller = ?

beats.say: Two complementary angles are in the ratio 2 to 3. We want the smaller angle.

ask.ifNot: Complementary angles fit together into a square corner. A square corner is a right angle, and that is 90 degrees.

beats.say: What do two complementary angles add up to?
A ratio of 2 to 3 means the 90 is cut into equal parts. The smaller angle gets 2 parts and the larger angle gets 3 parts.

ask.ifNot: 2 parts for one angle and 3 parts for the other. 2 and 3 make 5 parts altogether.

beats.say: How many equal parts are there altogether?
5 parts share 90 degrees. So one part is 90 divided by 5. 5 tens are 50 and 5 eights are 40, so 5 times 18 is 90. One part is 18.
The smaller angle is 2 parts. 2 times 18 is 36.
So the smaller angle is 36 degrees.
Check. The larger angle is 3 parts, 3 times 18, which is 54. And 36 and 54 make 90.
54 is waiting in the choices as a trap. It is the larger angle. Always look back to see which one the question asks for.
Here is 118 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplement is the other piece of that line, the one with the question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Picture yourself standing where the two angles meet. You face along the line, then turn to face the other way. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 118, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 118.

beats.say: The whole is 180 and one piece is 118. Which sum finds the missing piece?
Let's take 118 away in two easy hops. First the 110: 180 take away 110 leaves 70.
Now the 8 that is left: 70 take away 8 leaves 62. So 180 minus 118 is 62.
So the supplement is 62 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 118 plus 62 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.
Two supplementary angles differ by 40 degrees. So one is 40 bigger than the other. We want the larger one.

ask.ifNot: Supplementary angles sit side by side on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do two supplementary angles add up to?
So the two angles make 180 together. Now look at the two bars. The larger angle is the smaller one, with an extra 40 on the end.

ask.ifNot: Without its extra 40, the larger bar is exactly as long as the smaller bar. So we are left with two equal angles.

beats.say: Suppose we cut that extra 40 off the larger angle. What are we left with?
Two equal angles. And together they make 180 take away 40, which is 140.
Two equal angles sharing 140. Each one is half of 140, which is 70. That is the smaller angle.
Here is the trap. The question asks for the larger angle. So give the 40 back. 70 and 40 make 110.
So the larger angle is 110 degrees.
Check both facts. 70 and 110 make 180, so they are supplementary. And 110 take away 70 is 40.
So when you know the total and the difference: take off the difference, halve, then add the difference back for the bigger one.

board.text: Angles at a point: 110°, 85° and x°. x = ?

beats.say: Three angles meet at a point. Two of them are 110 degrees and 85 degrees, and the third is x. We want x.

ask.ifNot: All the way round a point is a full turn, and a full turn is 360 degrees. 180 is only half way round, a straight line.

beats.say: The three angles go all the way round the point, with no gaps. How much is a turn all the way round?
A full turn is 360. So 110, plus 85, plus x, makes 360.
First add the two angles we know. 110 and 80 is 190, and 5 more makes 195.

ask.ifNot: 360 is the whole turn, and 195 is the part we know. Take the part from the whole: 360 take away 195.

beats.say: 195 of the 360 is used up. x is whatever is left. Which sum finds it?
360 take away 195. Take away 200 first, which leaves 160. But that took 5 too many, so give 5 back: 165.
So x equals 165.
Check: 195 and 165 make 360. A full turn.
Angles round a point make 360. Angles on a straight line make 180. Look at which picture you have before you start.
Our angle is 55 degrees, and we want its complementary partner. The two angles fit snugly into one square corner, like this.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles fit inside a square corner, and a square corner is a quarter turn. That makes 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a book or a door. Turning through it is a quarter turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. So 55, plus our missing angle, makes 90.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 90 take away 55.

beats.say: The whole is 90 and one piece is 55. Which sum finds the missing piece?
Let's take 55 away in two easy hops. First the 50: 90 take away 50 leaves 40.
Now the 5 that is left: 40 take away 5 leaves 35. So 90 minus 55 is 35.
So the complement is 35 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 55 plus 35 makes 90. It fits exactly.
So to find a complement, take the angle away from 90. To remember which is which: C for complementary, C for corner. S for supplementary, S for straight line.
This triangle is keeping a secret. We know 2 angles, 39 degrees and 79 degrees, and the third is hidden.
Here is the fact that unlocks every triangle. Its 3 angles always add up to 180 degrees.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: So 2 angles are known and 1 is missing. What is our first move?
Add the tens first. 39 plus 70 is 109. Now the 9 that is left: that makes 118.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 118 away from 180.

beats.say: So 118 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 118 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 110: that leaves 70. Then take away 8 more: 62.
The hidden angle is 62 degrees.
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 39, 79 and 62. They make 180, just as they should.
That is the whole method. Add what you know, then find how far it is from 180.

board.text: On a straight line: x°, 2x° and 3x°. x = ?

beats.say: Three angles sit on a straight line. They are x, 2 x and 3 x. We want to find x.

ask.ifNot: Angles side by side on a straight line make a half turn together. A half turn is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do the angles on a straight line add up to?
So x, plus 2 x, plus 3 x, equals 180.

ask.ifNot: Do not forget the first x. It is 1 slice by itself. 1 and 2 and 3 make 6 slices.

beats.say: Think of x as one equal slice. Then 2 x is 2 slices, and 3 x is 3 slices. How many slices are there in all?
1 and 2 and 3 make 6. So 6 x equals 180.
6 slices make 180, so one slice is 180 divided by 6. 6 times 30 is 180, so x is 30.
Check. The three angles are 30, 60 and 90. Add them up, and they make 180. A straight line.
So count how many x there are altogether, then share the 180 among them.

board.text: Angle between the clock hands at 4:30 = ?

beats.say: What is the angle between the clock hands at 4:30? Here is the clock.
The 12 numbers cut the full turn of 360 degrees into 12 equal gaps. So each gap is 30 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The hour hand keeps moving. In half an hour it goes half of the way from the 4 to the 5.

beats.say: At half past 4 the minute hand is on the 6. Where is the hour hand?
Halfway between the 4 and the 5. That is the catch. If it were still on the 4, we would count 2 gaps to the 6 and say 60. But it has moved.
From where it really is, it is half a gap up to the 5, and then one whole gap from the 5 to the 6.
Half a gap is half of 30, which is 15. One whole gap is 30.
15 and 30 make 45.
So the angle is 45 degrees.
At half past any hour, the hour hand sits halfway between two numbers. Start counting from there, not from the number.

board.text: Facing North, turns clockwise through 225°. Now?

beats.say: A person faces north and turns clockwise through 225 degrees. Which way is he facing now?

ask.ifNot: A half turn makes you face the opposite way. The opposite of north is south.

beats.say: 225 is a big turn, so let's break it up. A half turn is 180 degrees. From north, where does a half turn take you?
South. That uses up 180 of the 225. 225 take away 180 leaves 45 still to turn.
The 8 compass directions are 45 degrees apart, because 360 shared among 8 is 45. So 45 degrees is exactly one more step.

ask.ifNot: Clockwise goes north, east, south, west. So after south we are heading towards west, and the direction between south and west is south-west.

beats.say: So from south, go one more step clockwise. Which direction comes next?
South-west. He is facing south-west.
Or count steps. 225 is 5 steps of 45: north-east, east, south-east, south, south-west. The same answer.
South-east is the trap. You land there if you count too few steps. Go round one stop at a time, the way clock hands move.

board.text: Each angle of an equilateral triangle = ?

spec.note: All three angles are equal

beats.say: How big is each angle of an equilateral triangle?
Equilateral means all 3 sides are equal. And when all the sides are equal, all the angles are equal too.

ask.ifNot: The 3 corners of a triangle fit along a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do the 3 angles of any triangle add up to?
180 degrees. So 3 equal angles share 180 between them.

ask.ifNot: Sharing equally means dividing. 180 shared among 3 angles is 180 divided by 3.

beats.say: How do we share 180 equally among 3 angles?
180 divided by 3 is 60. Multiply back to be sure: 3 times 60 is 180.
So each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60 degrees.
And this never changes. A tiny equilateral triangle and a huge one both have 3 angles of 60 degrees.

spec.note: An equilateral triangle. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: An equilateral triangle has a side of 7 centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter is the walk all the way round. Equilateral means all 3 sides are equal, so every side is 7 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: The walk goes along all 3 sides, and each one is 7. So we add 7 three times.

beats.say: Which sum gives the walk all the way round?
7 plus 7 plus 7. That is 3 lots of 7, and 3 times 7 is 21.
So the perimeter is 21 centimetres.
Watch out for 7 times 7. That makes 49, and it has nothing to do with walking round a triangle.
And 4 times 7 would be right for a square, which has 4 sides. A triangle has only 3.
For any equilateral triangle, the perimeter is 3 times the side. Here that is 21.

board.text: Rectangle: length 8 cm, width 3 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 8 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 3 rows of 8, so we multiply 8 by 3.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 3 rows, with 8 in every row. So the area is length times width.
8 times 3 means 3 lots of 8. 8 plus 8 plus 8 makes 24.
There it is: the area is 24 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 24 squares shared into 3 rows gives 8 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.
2 angles of a triangle are 35 degrees and 65 degrees. Let's find the third.
Every triangle keeps one rule: its 3 angles add up to 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: We need to know how much of the 180 is used already. So we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: What do we do with the 2 angles we know?
35 plus 65. 30 and 60 make 90. 5 and 5 make 10. And 90 plus 10 is 100.

ask.ifNot: 100 is the 2 known angles together. The third angle is what is left of the 180.

beats.say: 100 is one of the choices. Is it the third angle?
180 minus 100 is 80. The third angle is 80 degrees.
Check: 35 plus 65 plus 80 makes 180. It works.
So: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.
A triangle has 3 angles. We are told 2 of them: 52 degrees and 59 degrees. Let's hunt for the third.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: So 2 angles are known and 1 is missing. What is our first move?
Add the tens first. 52 plus 50 is 102. Now the 9 that is left: that makes 111.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 111 away from 180.

beats.say: The 2 known angles take 111 degrees out of the 180. What is left for the third angle?
Take 111 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 110: that leaves 70. Then take away 1 more: 69.
The hidden angle is 69 degrees.
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 52, 59 and 69. They make 180, just as they should.
So for a missing angle in a triangle: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.
We want the complement of 43 degrees. Complementary angles are two angles that fit together to make a right angle, like the corner of a page. Here is the picture.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles fit inside a square corner, and a square corner is a quarter turn. That makes 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a book or a door. Turning through it is a quarter turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. So 43, plus our missing angle, makes 90.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 90 take away 43.

beats.say: The whole is 90 and one piece is 43. Which sum finds the missing piece?
Let's take 43 away in two easy hops. First the 40: 90 take away 40 leaves 50.
Now the 3 that is left: 50 take away 3 leaves 47. So 90 minus 43 is 47.
So the complement is 47 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 43 plus 47 makes 90. It fits exactly.
So to find a complement, take the angle away from 90. To remember which is which: C for complementary, C for corner. S for supplementary, S for straight line.

board.text: Two angles: 28° and 45°. What type of triangle?

spec.note: What type of triangle is it?

beats.say: 2 angles of a triangle are 28 degrees and 45 degrees. What type of triangle is it?
Both angles we can see are acute, small and sharp. It is tempting to say acute-angled straight away. But a triangle has 3 angles.
So find the third angle first. 28 plus 45: 28 plus 40 is 68, and 5 more is 73.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees. So the third angle is 180 minus 73.

beats.say: The 2 known angles make 73. What is the third angle?
180 minus 73. Take away 70 to get 110, then 3 more to get 107.

ask.ifNot: 107 is bigger than 90. An angle bigger than a right angle is called obtuse.

beats.say: The third angle is 107 degrees. What kind of angle is that?
Obtuse. And one obtuse angle makes the whole triangle obtuse-angled.
It is not isosceles, because 28, 45 and 107 are all different. And 2 angles were enough to decide, because they give us the third.
Never judge a triangle by the 2 angles you can see. The third may be the big one.

board.text: Which lengths can be the sides of a triangle?

beats.say: Which of these sets of lengths can be the sides of a triangle?
Think of 3 sticks. They make a triangle only if the 2 shorter ones, put together, are longer than the longest. Otherwise they cannot meet.
A: 2 plus 5 is 7, and the longest side is 9. 7 is less than 9, so the short sides cannot reach each other.
So already we know that all of these cannot be the answer.

ask.ifNot: The 2 short sides together are exactly as long as the long side. They can only lie flat along it. Equal is not enough.

beats.say: C: 1 plus 5 is 6, and the longest side is 6 as well. Is that a triangle?
Flat, so not a triangle.
B: 6 plus 8 is 14, and the longest side is 12. 14 is more than 12, so these sides can meet.
So the lengths that make a triangle are 6, 8 and 12 centimetres.
The test in one line: add the 2 shorter sides. More than the longest, a triangle. Equal or less, no triangle.

board.text: Which are the angles of an isosceles triangle?

beats.say: Which of these sets are the angles of an isosceles triangle?
An isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides. And equal sides always come with equal angles. So we are looking for a set with a matching pair.

ask.ifNot: Look at set D: 30, 75 and 75. The 75 is there twice.

beats.say: Look along each set. Which set has an angle that appears twice?
Set D. The 75 appears twice.
A, B and C each have 3 different angles. Those triangles are scalene.
Let's make sure D is a real triangle. 75 plus 75 is 150, and 30 more makes 180. It is.
So the angles of an isosceles triangle are 30, 75 and 75 degrees.
For isosceles, hunt for the twins: 2 angles exactly the same.
Here is a triangle. 2 of its angles are 61 degrees and 26 degrees. We need to find the third one.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Add the tens first. 61 plus 20 is 81. Now the 6 that is left: that makes 87.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 87 away from 180.

beats.say: So 87 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 87 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 80: that leaves 100. Then take away 7 more: 93.
So the third angle is 93 degrees. There it is!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 61, 26 and 93. They make 180, just as they should. And notice: 93 degrees is a wide angle, an obtuse one. A triangle can have just 1 of those.
So for a missing angle in a triangle: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.

board.text: Right-angled triangle. One acute angle = 27°. Other = ?

spec.note: A right-angled triangle. Find the other acute angle.

beats.say: One acute angle of a right-angled triangle is 27 degrees. What is the other acute angle?
A right-angled triangle has one angle of 90 degrees. And the 3 angles of any triangle add up to 180.

ask.ifNot: Take the right angle out of the total. 180 minus 90 leaves 90 for the 2 acute angles.

beats.say: So what do the 2 acute angles add up to?
90. In a right-angled triangle the 2 acute angles always share 90. That is a handy shortcut.
One of them is 27. So the other is 90 minus 27. Take away 20 to get 70, then 7 more to get 63.
So the other acute angle is 63 degrees.
Check: 90 plus 27 plus 63 makes 180.
In a right-angled triangle, the 2 acute angles add up to 90. Just take the one you know away from 90.
Here is a triangle. 2 of its angles are 52 degrees and 73 degrees. We need to find the third one.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: So 2 angles are known and 1 is missing. What is our first move?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 52 plus 70 is 122. Then 3 more makes 125.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 125 away from 180.

beats.say: So 125 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 125 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 120: that leaves 60. Then take away 5 more: 55.
So the third angle is 55 degrees. Found it!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 52, 73 and 55. They make 180, just as they should.
That is the whole method. Add what you know, then find how far it is from 180.

board.text: Right-angled isosceles triangle. Each equal angle = ?

spec.note: Right-angled and isosceles: the two ? angles are equal

beats.say: A triangle is right-angled and isosceles at the same time. How big is each of its equal angles?
This triangle has 2 names. Right-angled tells us one angle is 90 degrees. Isosceles tells us 2 angles are equal.

ask.ifNot: 2 angles of 90 make 180 already. That would leave nothing for the third angle.

beats.say: Could the right angle be one of the equal pair?
So the right angle is the odd one, and the other 2 angles are the equal pair.
The 3 angles make 180. Take away the 90, and 90 is left for the equal pair.

ask.ifNot: Equal shares means halving. Half of 90 is 45.

beats.say: 2 equal angles share 90. How big is each one?
Half of 90 is 45. Each of the equal angles is 45 degrees.
Check: 90 plus 45 plus 45 makes 180. You can make this triangle by folding a square from corner to corner.
One name gave us the 90. The other name told us to halve what was left.
Here is 6 degrees, drawn inside a right angle. Its complement is the other piece of that corner, the one with the question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles fit inside a square corner, and a square corner is a quarter turn. That makes 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Picture the corner of your notebook. That square corner is a right angle, a quarter of a full turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. So 6, plus our missing angle, makes 90.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 90 take away 6.

beats.say: The whole is 90 and one piece is 6. Which sum finds the missing piece?
90 take away 6 leaves 84.
So the complement is 84 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 6 plus 84 makes 90. It fits exactly.
So the two partners make 90. Take the angle you have away from 90. To remember which is which: C for complementary, C for corner. S for supplementary, S for straight line.

board.text: Which is NOT a type of triangle?

beats.say: 3 of these are real types of triangle. 1 can never exist. Which?

board.text: Acute: less than 90°. Obtuse: more than 90°.

beats.say: Each name has 2 parts, one about angles and one about sides. A type is real if we can find 3 angles that fit both parts. Let's try to build each one.
A: acute-angled isosceles. Try 70, 70 and 40. All less than 90, 2 are equal, and they make 180. Real.
B: obtuse-angled isosceles. Try 100, 40 and 40. One angle is above 90, and 2 are equal. Real.
D: acute-angled scalene. Try 50, 60 and 70. All different, and all less than 90. Real.

ask.ifNot: All 3 angles of an equilateral triangle are equal, and they share 180. So each one is 60.

beats.say: Now C: right-angled equilateral. How big is every angle of an equilateral triangle?
60, every one of them. But right-angled needs an angle of 90. An angle cannot be 60 and 90 at once!
And 3 angles of 90 would make 270, far more than 180.
So a right-angled equilateral triangle is not a type of triangle.
To test a type of triangle, try to build one. If the 2 parts of the name fight each other, it cannot exist.

board.text: Which are the angles of an obtuse-angled scalene triangle?

beats.say: Which set gives the angles of an obtuse-angled scalene triangle?
2 things must both be true. Obtuse-angled: one angle is more than 90. Scalene: all 3 sides are different, and so all 3 angles are different.

ask.ifNot: In A and B the biggest angle is exactly 90. That is a right angle, not an obtuse one. C has 120 and D has 150.

beats.say: First test: obtuse. Which sets have an angle bigger than 90?
C and D. In A and B the biggest angle is exactly 90, so those are right-angled triangles.

ask.ifNot: The 15 is there twice. 2 equal angles make a triangle isosceles, not scalene.

beats.say: Second test: scalene. Look at D: 150, 15 and 15. Are all 3 different?
D has twins, so it is isosceles. Out.
C: 40, 120 and 20. 120 is obtuse, and all 3 are different. They add up to 180, so it is a real triangle.
So the angles are 40, 120 and 20 degrees.
When a name has 2 parts, test one part at a time, and cross off as you go.

board.text: Exterior angle next to the third angle = ?

spec.note: Find the exterior angle next to the third angle

beats.say: 2 interior angles of a triangle are 55 degrees and 70 degrees. We want the exterior angle next to the third angle.
Interior angles are the ones inside the triangle. An exterior angle is made outside, when one side is stretched on past a corner.
First find the third inside angle. 55 plus 70 is 125, and 180 minus 125 is 55.
So the third interior angle is 55. Now stretch a side past that corner. The inside angle and the outside angle sit side by side on a straight line.

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees.

beats.say: What do 2 angles on a straight line add up to?
180. So the exterior angle is 180 minus 55. Take away 50 to get 130, then 5 more to get 125.
So the exterior angle is 125 degrees.
Did you spot it? 125 is also 55 plus 70, the other 2 inside angles added together. That always happens with an exterior angle.
The trap is 110. That is the outside angle next to the 70, which is a different corner. The one we want, next to the third angle, is 125.
We want the complement of 84 degrees. Complementary angles are two angles that fit together to make a right angle, like the corner of a page. Here is the picture.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles fit inside a square corner, and a square corner is a quarter turn. That makes 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: Picture the corner of your notebook. That square corner is a right angle, a quarter of a full turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. So 84, plus our missing angle, makes 90.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 90 take away 84.

beats.say: The whole is 90 and one piece is 84. Which sum finds the missing piece?
Let's take 84 away in two easy hops. First the 80: 90 take away 80 leaves 10.
Now the 4 that is left: 10 take away 4 leaves 6. So 90 minus 84 is 6.
So the complement is 6 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 84 plus 6 makes 90. It fits exactly.
So the two partners make 90. Take the angle you have away from 90. To remember which is which: C for complementary, C for corner. S for supplementary, S for straight line.

board.text: Exterior angle = 130°. One opposite interior angle = 50°.

spec.note: The exterior angle at the bottom right corner is 130°

beats.say: An exterior angle of a triangle is 130 degrees. One of the opposite interior angles is 50 degrees. What is the other one?
An exterior angle sits outside the triangle, next to one corner. The 2 opposite interior angles are the inside angles at the other 2 corners.
Start with the inside angle right beside the exterior angle. Together they lie on a straight line, so they make 180. 180 minus 130 is 50.
So that inside angle is 50, and we are told another inside angle is 50 as well. And the 3 inside angles make 180.

ask.ifNot: The 2 inside angles we know are 50 and 50, which make 100. Take 100 away from 180.

beats.say: What is the last inside angle?
80 degrees. 50 plus 50 is 100, and 180 minus 100 is 80.
Now look at this. The 2 opposite angles, 50 and 80, add up to 130. That is exactly the exterior angle!
It is always true: an exterior angle equals the 2 opposite interior angles added together. So the quick way is 130 minus 50, which is 80.
Either way, the other angle is 80 degrees.
Here is 12 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplement is the other piece of that line, the one with the question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Picture yourself standing where the two angles meet. You face along the line, then turn to face the other way. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 12, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 12.

beats.say: We know the whole, 180, and one part, 12. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 12 away in two easy hops. First the 10: 180 take away 10 leaves 170.
Now the 2 that is left: 170 take away 2 leaves 168. So 180 minus 12 is 168.
So the supplement is 168 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 12 plus 168 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So the two partners make 180. Take the angle you have away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.

board.text: Isosceles triangle. Each base angle = 70°. Vertex angle = ?

beats.say: In an isosceles triangle each base angle is 70 degrees. We want the vertex angle.
An isosceles triangle has 2 equal base angles at the bottom, and 1 vertex angle at the top, between the equal sides.

ask.ifNot: An isosceles triangle has 2 base angles, and they are equal. So there are 2 angles of 70.

beats.say: Each base angle is 70. How many base angles are there?
2 of them. Together they make 70 plus 70, which is 140.
The 3 angles of a triangle make 180. So the vertex angle is whatever is left.
180 minus 140 is 40. The vertex angle is 40 degrees.
The trap is to take away only one 70 and say 110. Both base angles have to come off.
Check: 70 plus 70 plus 40 makes 180. So for the vertex angle, double the base angle and take it from 180.
This triangle is keeping a secret. We know 2 angles, 75 degrees and 74 degrees, and the third is hidden.
Every triangle, big or small, keeps one rule. Its 3 angles together make exactly 180 degrees.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: We know 2 of the 3 angles. What should we do with them first?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 75 plus 70 is 145. Then 4 more makes 149.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 149 away from 180.

beats.say: The 2 known angles take 149 degrees out of the 180. What is left for the third angle?
Take 149 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 140: that leaves 40. Then take away 9 more: 31.
The hidden angle is 31 degrees.
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 75, 74 and 31. They make 180, just as they should.
So for a missing angle in a triangle: add the 2 angles you know, then take the total away from 180.
We want the supplement of 169 degrees. Supplementary angles are two angles that sit side by side on a straight line. Here is the picture.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Picture yourself standing where the two angles meet. You face along the line, then turn to face the other way. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 169, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 169.

beats.say: We know the whole, 180, and one part, 169. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 169 away in two easy hops. First the 160: 180 take away 160 leaves 20.
Now the 9 that is left: 20 take away 9 leaves 11. So 180 minus 169 is 11.
So the supplement is 11 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 169 plus 11 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.

board.text: Isosceles triangle. Vertex angle = 50°. Each base angle = ?

spec.note: The two base angles marked ? are equal

beats.say: The vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is 50 degrees. How big is each base angle?
The vertex angle is at the top. The 2 base angles at the bottom are equal, like twins.

ask.ifNot: Take the vertex angle out of the 180. What is left belongs to the 2 base angles.

beats.say: The 3 angles of a triangle make 180. So what do the 2 base angles share?
130. That is both base angles together.

ask.ifNot: The 2 base angles are equal, and they share 130. So each one is half of 130.

beats.say: So how big is each base angle?
Half of 130. Half of 100 is 50, and half of 30 is 15. 50 plus 15 is 65.
So each base angle is 65 degrees.
Check: 50 plus 65 plus 65 makes 180.
When you know the vertex angle: take it from 180, then halve what is left.
Here is 72 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplement is the other piece of that line, the one with the question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 72, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 72.

beats.say: We know the whole, 180, and one part, 72. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 72 away in two easy hops. First the 70: 180 take away 70 leaves 110.
Now the 2 that is left: 110 take away 2 leaves 108. So 180 minus 72 is 108.
So the supplement is 108 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 72 plus 108 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So the two partners make 180. Take the angle you have away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.

board.text: The side opposite the right angle is called the ...?

spec.note: What is the highlighted side called?

beats.say: In a right-angled triangle, what do we call the side opposite the right angle?
A right-angled triangle has one square corner. 2 sides meet at that corner. The third side does not touch it: it lies across from the right angle.

ask.ifNot: In any triangle the longest side lies opposite the biggest angle. Here the biggest angle is the right angle.

beats.say: Look at the highlighted side. Compared with the other 2 sides, it is...
The longest. The biggest angle always faces the longest side, and the right angle is the biggest angle in this triangle.

board.text: Side opposite the right angle: hypotenuse

beats.say: This special longest side has a special name: the hypotenuse.

board.text: Base and height: meet at the right angle

beats.say: What about the other words? The base and the height are the 2 sides that meet at the right angle.
And a median is a line from a corner to the middle of the opposite side. It is not a side at all.
So the side opposite the right angle is called the hypotenuse.
Hypotenuse is a long word for a long side: the longest side of a right-angled triangle.

board.text: Axes of symmetry of a scalene triangle = ?

spec.note: A scalene triangle: all three sides are different

beats.say: How many axes of symmetry does a scalene triangle have?
An axis of symmetry is a fold line. Fold the shape along it, and the 2 halves match exactly.

spec.note: Equal sides fold onto each other

beats.say: In a triangle, a fold line goes through a corner. For the halves to match, the 2 sides that meet at that corner must land on each other. So they must be equal.

ask.ifNot: Scalene is the name for a triangle whose 3 sides are all different lengths.

beats.say: Now, what does scalene mean?
No sides are equal. So at every corner, a longer side would be folded onto a shorter one. The halves can never match.
No pair of equal sides means no fold line at all. A scalene triangle has 0 axes of symmetry.
Compare the others. An isosceles triangle has 1 fold line, through the corner between its equal sides. An equilateral triangle has 3.
So the number of fold lines tells you how many sides match. For a scalene triangle, that is 0.

board.text: Triangle with sides 8 cm, 11 cm, 15 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: A triangle has sides of 8, 11 and 15 centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter is the walk all the way round the triangle, along every side.

ask.ifNot: Walking round means going along one side, then the next, then the last. The distances add up.

beats.say: So what do we do with the 3 lengths?
Add them. Start with 8 plus 11, which is 19.
Then 19 plus 15. 19 plus 10 is 29, and 5 more is 34.
So the perimeter is 34 centimetres.
Check by adding in another order. 15 plus 11 is 26, and 26 plus 8 is 34. The same answer.
Perimeter always means add. Multiplying the sides gives a huge number that means nothing here.

board.text: Rectangle: length 29 cm, width 14 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 29 centimetres long and 14 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 14 rows of 29, so we multiply 29 by 14.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 14 rows, with 29 in every row. So the area is length times width.
29 times 14 looks hard, but we can do it in two small parts. Think of 14 as 10 and 4.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 29 times 10 is 290. And 29 times 4 is 116. Now we put the two parts together. What is 290 plus 116?
290 plus 116 makes 406.
So the area is 406 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 406 squares shared into 14 rows gives 29 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. For area we multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the distance round the edge.

board.text: Rectangle: length 5 cm, width 3 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Here is our rectangle. It is 5 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide, and we want its perimeter.
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 5 plus 3 is 8.
Don't stop at 8. That is just one length and one width, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 8 is 16.
So the perimeter is 16 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 5, 3, 5, 3. Together they make 16.
Remember the plan. Length plus width takes you halfway round. Double it for the whole perimeter.
We have a square with sides of 6 centimetres. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side goes round the edge. That is the perimeter. The little squares inside sit in 6 rows of 6, so we multiply 6 by 6.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the square filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
In a square the length and the width are the same. That gives 6 rows of 6 little squares. So area is side times side.
From the times tables, 6 times 6 is 36.
There it is: the area is 36 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 36 squares shared into 6 rows gives 6 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any square: multiply the side by itself, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Perimeter 36 cm. Two sides: 12 cm and 9 cm. Third side = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = 36 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of a triangle is 36 centimetres. 2 of its sides are 12 centimetres and 9 centimetres. How long is the third side?
The perimeter is all 3 sides added together. So 12, plus 9, plus the missing side, makes 36.

ask.ifNot: First find how much of the perimeter the 2 known sides use up. Add 12 and 9.

beats.say: What should we do first?
12 plus 9 is 21. The 2 known sides use up 21 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 21 is the 2 known sides together. The third side is what is still needed to reach 36.

beats.say: 21 is one of the choices. Is it the third side?
36 minus 21. Take away 20 to get 16, then 1 more to get 15.
So the third side is 15 centimetres.
Check: 12 plus 9 plus 15 makes 36. It works.
To find a missing side: add the sides you know, then take that from the perimeter.

board.text: Rectangle: length 29 cm, width 15 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 29 centimetres long and 15 centimetres wide. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 29 plus 15 is 44.
Don't stop at 44. That is just one length and one width, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 44 is 88.
So the perimeter is 88 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 29, 15, 29, 15. Together they make 88.
Remember the plan. Length plus width takes you halfway round. Double it for the whole perimeter.

board.text: Right-angled triangle with legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: A right-angled triangle has legs of 6 centimetres and 8 centimetres. We want its area.

spec.note: Two of the triangles make a rectangle

beats.say: The legs are the 2 sides that meet at the right angle. Put 2 of these triangles together and they make a rectangle, 6 by 8.

ask.ifNot: The area of a rectangle is its length times its breadth. Adding gives a length, not the space inside.

beats.say: What is the area of that rectangle?
6 times 8 is 48. That is the whole rectangle.

ask.ifNot: 2 equal triangles fill the rectangle. So one triangle is half of 48.

beats.say: Our triangle is one of the 2 equal halves. So what is its area?
Half of 48 is 24. The area of the triangle is 24 square centimetres.
The 10 in the choices is the length of the third, slanted side of this triangle. That is a length, not an area.
For a right-angled triangle: multiply the 2 legs, then halve.

board.text: A median joins a vertex to the ____ of the opposite side.

beats.say: A median of a triangle joins a vertex to a special point of the opposite side. Which point?
A vertex is a corner. Every corner of a triangle has an opposite side: the one side that it does not touch.
A median is a line from a corner across to its opposite side. But it does not land just anywhere. Listen to the word: median sounds like middle.

ask.ifNot: Median and middle come from the same idea. A median lands exactly in the middle of the opposite side.

beats.say: So where on the opposite side does a median land?
Exactly in the middle. It cuts that side into 2 equal parts, like the 2 parts of 5 centimetres here.

board.text: Middle point of a side = midpoint

beats.say: The point in the middle of a side has its own name: the midpoint.
If the line went to an end point of the side, it would just run along a side of the triangle. That is no median.
So a median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side.
Median, middle, midpoint. The 3 words belong together.

board.text: How many medians does a triangle have?

beats.say: How many medians does a triangle have?
A median is a line from a corner of the triangle to the middle of the opposite side. Here is one.

ask.ifNot: Tri means 3. A triangle has 3 corners and 3 sides.

beats.say: How many corners does a triangle have?
3 corners. And each corner has exactly 1 opposite side, the side it does not touch.
So from each corner we can draw exactly 1 median. 3 corners, 1 median each: 3 medians.
So a triangle has 3 medians.
Why not 6? Because each corner gives only 1 median, not 2.
A lovely fact for later: all 3 medians cross at one single point, the balance point of the triangle.

board.text: Angles: 40°, 60°, 80°. Which side is the longest?

spec.note: Which side is the longest?

beats.say: A triangle has angles of 40, 60 and 80 degrees. Which of its sides is the longest?
Think of an angle as an open mouth. The wider the mouth opens, the longer the side it has to stretch across.

board.text: Biggest angle faces the longest side

beats.say: So the biggest angle faces the longest side, and the smallest angle faces the shortest side.

ask.ifNot: Compare the 3 numbers. 80 is more than 60, and 60 is more than 40.

beats.say: Which is the biggest angle here?
80 degrees. So the longest side is the one opposite the 80. Opposite means across from it: the side that angle does not touch.
So the longest side is the side opposite 80 degrees.
And the side opposite 40 is the shortest. The side opposite 60 is in between.
Could all the sides be equal? Only if all the angles were equal, and these are not.
Big angle, long side. Small angle, short side. Here the 80 wins.

board.text: Can a triangle have two right angles?

beats.say: Can a triangle have 2 right angles? Let's try to build one and see what happens.
A right angle is 90 degrees, a square corner.

ask.ifNot: Each right angle is 90. And 90 plus 90 is 180.

beats.say: 2 right angles together make how much?
180 degrees.
But the 3 angles of a triangle add up to 180 altogether. The 2 right angles have used up all of it.

ask.ifNot: 180 minus 180 is 0. Nothing at all is left.

beats.say: So how much is left for the third angle?
0 degrees. An angle of 0 is no corner at all! The 2 sides would stand straight up, side by side, and never meet.
Making the triangle bigger, or its sides longer, changes nothing. The angles still have to add up to 180.
And a right-angled isosceles triangle has only 1 right angle. Its angles are 90, 45 and 45.
So the answer is no. 90 plus 90 is 180, and that leaves 0 for the third angle.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, perimeter 45 cm. Each side = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = 45 cm

beats.say: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 45 centimetres. How long is each side?
Equilateral means 3 equal sides. Together the 3 sides make the perimeter, 45.

ask.ifNot: The 45 is shared equally among 3 sides. Sharing equally means dividing, and there are 3 sides.

beats.say: How do we find 1 side?
45 divided by 3. Split 45 into 30 and 15. 30 divided by 3 is 10, and 15 divided by 3 is 5. 10 plus 5 is 15.
So each side is 15 centimetres.
Check: 15 plus 15 plus 15 makes 45.
2 slips to dodge. Multiplying by 3 makes one side longer than the whole perimeter. And dividing by 2 forgets that a triangle has 3 sides.
Perimeter of an equilateral triangle, divided by 3, gives the side.

board.text: Right-angled triangle: base 12 cm, area 42 cm². Height = ?

spec.note: Area = 42 cm²

beats.say: A right-angled triangle has a base of 12 centimetres and an area of 42 square centimetres. What is its height?
We know how to go forwards: the area is half of base times height. This time we go backwards, from the area to the height.

ask.ifNot: Twice means 2 lots. 42 plus 42 is 84.

beats.say: The triangle is half of a rectangle with the same base and height. So the rectangle's area is twice 42. What is twice 42?
84. So the base times the height is 84.

ask.ifNot: To undo times 12, we divide by 12. So the height is 84 divided by 12.

beats.say: 12 times what makes 84?
84 divided by 12 is 7, because 12 times 7 is 84.
So the height is 7 centimetres.
Check forwards: 12 times 7 is 84, and half of 84 is 42. That matches the area.
The trap is 42 divided by 12, which gives 3.5. That forgets the half. Double the area first, then divide by the base. That gives 7.
Here is our square. Each side is 22 centimetres long, and we want its area.

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side goes round the edge. That is the perimeter. The little squares inside sit in 22 rows of 22, so we multiply 22 by 22.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the square filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
A square is as wide as it is long. So there are 22 rows, with 22 little squares in every row. The area is side times side.
Let's make 22 times 22 easier. We split 22 into 20 and 2, and do one part at a time.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 22 times 20 is 440. And 22 times 2 is 44. Now we put the two parts together. What is 440 plus 44?
Add them up: 440 plus 44 is 484.
So the area is 484 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 484 squares shared into 22 rows gives 22 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any square: multiply the side by itself, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Sum of all angles of a quadrilateral = ?

beats.say: What do all the angles of a quadrilateral add up to? Let's work it out instead of just remembering it.
Here's a fact you know: the three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: One straight cut from corner to corner splits the shape into two pieces, and each piece has three sides.

spec.note: One diagonal cuts the shape into 2 triangles

beats.say: Now draw one diagonal across the quadrilateral, from corner to corner. How many triangles does it make?
2 triangles. And together their angles make up all four angles of the quadrilateral.
Each triangle gives 180. So we need 2 times 180, which is 360.
The angles of a quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees.
A square is a good check. It has 4 right angles of 90 degrees, and 4 times 90 is 360.
So remember: a quadrilateral is two triangles stuck together, and two lots of 180 make 360.
Our angle is 18 degrees, and we want its complementary partner. The two angles fit snugly into one square corner, like this.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles fit inside a square corner, and a square corner is a quarter turn. That makes 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line.

beats.say: A right angle is a square corner, like the corner of a book or a door. Turning through it is a quarter turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. So 18, plus our missing angle, makes 90.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 90 take away 18.

beats.say: We know the whole, 90, and one part, 18. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 18 away in two easy hops. First the 10: 90 take away 10 leaves 80.
Now the 8 that is left: 80 take away 8 leaves 72. So 90 minus 18 is 72.
So the complement is 72 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 18 plus 72 makes 90. It fits exactly.
So to find a complement, take the angle away from 90. To remember which is which: C for complementary, C for corner. S for supplementary, S for straight line.
We want the supplement of 98 degrees. Supplementary angles are two angles that sit side by side on a straight line. Here is the picture.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Picture yourself standing where the two angles meet. You face along the line, then turn to face the other way. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 98, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 98.

beats.say: The whole is 180 and one piece is 98. Which sum finds the missing piece?
Let's take 98 away in two easy hops. First the 90: 180 take away 90 leaves 90.
Now the 8 that is left: 90 take away 8 leaves 82. So 180 minus 98 is 82.
So the supplement is 82 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 98 plus 82 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.
Here is a triangle. 2 of its angles are 32 degrees and 73 degrees. We need to find the third one.
Start with the one thing we know about every triangle. The 3 angles add up to 180 degrees, every time.

choices: take the small one from the big one
ask.ifNot: We want to know how much of the 180 degrees is used up already. So first we add the 2 angles we know.

beats.say: So 2 angles are known and 1 is missing. What is our first move?
Let's add in 2 small steps. 32 plus 70 is 102. Then 3 more makes 105.

ask.ifNot: The 3 angles share 180 degrees between them. So the third angle is what is left when we take 105 away from 180.

beats.say: So 105 degrees are used up by the 2 angles we know. How do we find the third angle?
Take 105 away from 180 in 2 small steps. First take away 100: that leaves 80. Then take away 5 more: 75.
So the third angle is 75 degrees. Found it!
Good mathematicians check. Add all 3 angles: 32, 73 and 75. They make 180, just as they should.
That is the whole method. Add what you know, then find how far it is from 180.

board.text: Rectangle (not a square): axes of symmetry = ?

spec.note: A rectangle that is not a square

beats.say: How many axes of symmetry does a rectangle have, if it is not a square?

board.text: Axis of symmetry = a fold line that matches

beats.say: An axis of symmetry is a fold line. Fold along it, and one half lands exactly on the other half.

spec.note: Fold top onto bottom: the halves match

beats.say: Take a sheet of paper. Fold it so the top edge meets the bottom edge. The halves match. That is 1 axis.

spec.note: Fold left onto right: the halves match again

beats.say: Now fold it so the left edge meets the right edge. The halves match again. That is 2.

ask.ifNot: Try it with a sheet of paper. The corners stick out past each other, because the long side and the short side are different.

beats.say: What about folding corner to corner, along a diagonal? Will the halves match?

spec.note: Corner to corner: the halves do not land on each other

beats.say: The corners don't land on each other, because the length and the breadth are different. So the diagonals are not axes.
A rectangle that is not a square has 2 axes of symmetry.
A square has 4, because its diagonals work as well. That is why the question says not a square.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: We have a square with sides of 4 centimetres. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Count the sides of the square in the picture. There are 4 of them, each 4 centimetres. So the walk is 4 lots of 4.

beats.say: A square has 4 sides, and they are all the same length. So which sum gives the whole walk?
4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times the side.
4 lots of 4. From the times tables, 4 times 4 is 16.
So the perimeter is 16 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking the four sides one at a time. 4, 4, 4, 4. Together they make 16.
Remember the plan. 4 times the side is the perimeter. Side times side is the area. Don't mix them up!

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: A square has a side of 11 centimetres. What is its perimeter?

ask.ifNot: Walk round the square: 4 sides, each 11 centimetres. So we need 4 lots of 11.

beats.say: Perimeter is the distance all the way round. A square has 4 equal sides. So which sum do we need?
4 lots of 11.
4 times 10 is 40, and 4 times 1 is 4. Together that makes 44.
The perimeter is 44 centimetres.
Careful: 11 times 11 gives the area, the space inside. We wanted the distance round the edge.
Check by walking: 11, 11, 11 and 11 make 44.
Look at this square. Every side is 8 centimetres. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side goes round the edge. That is the perimeter. The little squares inside sit in 8 rows of 8, so we multiply 8 by 8.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the square filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
A square is as wide as it is long. So there are 8 rows, with 8 little squares in every row. The area is side times side.
8 times 8 is 64. That one is straight from the times tables.
There it is: the area is 64 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 64 squares shared into 8 rows gives 8 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any square: multiply the side by itself, and give the answer in square units.
A square has a side of 9 metres. What is its area?
Area is the space inside. For a square it is side times side. So we need 9 times 9.
9 times 9 is 81.

ask.ifNot: Metres measure a length, like the side of the square. Area counts squares, so it is measured in square metres.

beats.say: Now watch out. Two of the choices say 81! One says 81 metres. The other says 81 square metres. Which one is an area?
Area is counted in squares, each 1 metre by 1 metre. So the area is 81 square metres.
Another trap: 4 times 9 is 36. That is the perimeter, the distance round the edge.
So for area: side times side, and always say square units. Here that is 81 square metres.

board.text: Rectangle: length 12 cm, breadth 7 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: A rectangle is 12 centimetres long and 7 centimetres broad. What is its perimeter?
Perimeter is the walk all the way round. First, one length and one breadth: 12 plus 7 is 19.

choices: No, it is only halfway round
ask.ifNot: A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two breadths. 12 plus 7 walks along just two of them.

beats.say: Is 19 the whole perimeter?
19 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two breadths, so we double it.
2 times 19 is 38.
The perimeter is 38 centimetres.
Check by walking all four sides: 12, 7, 12 and 7 make 38.
Careful not to multiply 12 by 7. That gives the area. For perimeter we add the sides.

board.text: Rectangle: length 15 cm, breadth 8 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: A rectangle is 15 centimetres long and 8 centimetres broad. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides takes you along the edge. Rows of squares are counted by multiplying: 15 times 8.

beats.say: Area is the space inside: 8 rows of little squares with 15 in each row. Which sum counts them?
So we need 15 times 8. Let's split 15 into 10 and 5.
10 times 8 is 80. And 5 times 8 is 40.
Don't stop at 80! That is only part of the rectangle. Add the other part: 80 plus 40 is 120.
The area is 120 square centimetres.
Check by going backwards: 120 shared into 8 rows gives 15 in each row.
For area, multiply length by breadth. If the sum is big, split one number and add the parts.

board.text: Rectangle: length 6 cm, width 3 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 6 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 3 rows of 6, so we multiply 6 by 3.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 3 rows of squares, and 6 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
6 times 3 means 3 lots of 6. 6 plus 6 plus 6 makes 18.
So the area is 18 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 18 squares shared into 3 rows gives 6 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. For area we multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the distance round the edge.

board.text: Square: perimeter and area are the same number.

beats.say: A square's perimeter and its area are the same number. What is its side? The choices are 8, 6 and 4.
The perimeter is 4 times the side. The area is the side times the side. We can simply test each choice.
Try 8. The perimeter is 4 times 8, which is 32. The area is 8 times 8, which is 64. Not the same.
Try 6. The perimeter is 24 and the area is 36. Closer, but still not the same.

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is 4 times 4. The area is 4 times 4 as well. Both sums are the same.

beats.say: The area is still too big, so we go smaller. For a side of 4, what are the perimeter and the area?
4 times 4 is 16 for the perimeter, and 4 times 4 is 16 for the area. They match!
The side of the square is 4.
Can you see why? Perimeter is 4 times the side and area is side times the side. They agree when the side itself is 4.

board.text: Rectangle: length 14 cm, width 6 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 14 centimetres long and 6 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 6 rows of 14, so we multiply 14 by 6.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 6 rows of squares, and 14 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
14 times 6 looks hard, but we can do it in two small parts. Think of 14 as 10 and 4.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 10 times 6 is 60. And 4 times 6 is 24. Now we put the two parts together. What is 60 plus 24?
60 plus 24 makes 84.
So the area is 84 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 84 squares shared into 6 rows gives 14 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. For area we multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the distance round the edge.

board.text: Rectangle: length 13 cm, width 3 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 13 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 13 plus 3 is 16.
Don't stop at 16. That is just one length and one width, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 16 is 32.
So the perimeter is 32 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 13, 3, 13, 3. Together they make 32.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.

board.text: Which pair can be the length and breadth?

spec.note: Perimeter = 32 m

beats.say: A rectangle has a perimeter of 32 metres. Which pair can be its length and breadth?

ask.ifNot: 32 is all four sides. One length and one breadth is half of the way round, so we halve 32.

beats.say: The perimeter is two lengths and two breadths. So one length and one breadth must add up to what?
Half of 32 is 16. A pair fits only if it adds up to 16.
Test 18 and 14. They add up to 32. Careful, that's the trap! 32 is the whole perimeter, not half. This pair is too big.
Test 8 and 7. They add up to 15. That is 1 short of 16. So close, but no.
Test 10.5 and 5.5. The two halves make 1 whole, and 10 plus 5 is 15. So that is 16. It fits!
So the length and breadth can be 10.5 metres and 5.5 metres.
Sides don't have to be whole numbers. Halve the perimeter, then look for the pair that adds up to it: 10.5 and 5.5.

board.text: Rectangle: length 19 cm, width 16 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 19 centimetres long and 16 centimetres wide. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Imagine an ant walking round the rectangle until it is back where it started.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 19 plus 16 is 35.
Don't stop at 35. That is just one length and one width, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 35 is 70.
There it is: the perimeter is 70 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 19, 16, 19, 16. Together they make 70.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: This rectangle's sides are written with letters. The length is 2 m plus 5 n. The breadth is m minus 3 n. We want the perimeter.
Letters don't change the plan. Perimeter is still length plus breadth, then doubled.
First add the length and the breadth. Collect the m's together: 2 m and 1 more m make 3 m.

ask.ifNot: The breadth has minus 3 n, so we take 3 n away from the 5 n. 5 take away 3 is 2.

beats.say: Now the n's. We have 5 n, and then minus 3 n. What is left?
5 n take away 3 n leaves 2 n. So length plus breadth is 3 m plus 2 n. That is halfway round.
Now double everything. 2 times 3 m is 6 m. And 2 times 2 n is 4 n.
Careful: the 2 multiplies both parts, the 3 m and the 2 n. Doubling only one of them is the classic slip.
So the perimeter is 6 m plus 4 n.
With letters or with numbers, the plan is the same: add the two sides, then double.

spec.note: Perimeter = 40 cm

beats.say: This rectangle's sides use a letter, a. The length is 3 a minus 5 and the breadth is a plus 5. The perimeter is 40 centimetres. We must find a.
Start with what we know about perimeters. Length plus breadth is half of the perimeter. Half of 40 is 20.

ask.ifNot: Minus 5 means take 5 away. Plus 5 puts 5 back. So together they do nothing at all.

beats.say: Now add the length and the breadth. 3 a and 1 more a make 4 a. But what happens to the minus 5 and the plus 5?
Minus 5 and plus 5 cancel. So length plus breadth is just 4 a.
Here's the trap: 4 a is only halfway round. So 4 a equals 20, not 40.
4 times what makes 20? We divide 20 by 4.
20 divided by 4 is 5. So a is 5.
Check. The length is 3 times 5 minus 5, which is 10. The breadth is 5 plus 5, which is 10 too.
10 plus 10 is 20, and double 20 is 40. That is our perimeter, so a equals 5 works!

board.text: Field: 350 m long, 120 m wide. Sam runs 10 rounds.

spec.note: Ten rounds of the field = ?

beats.say: Sam ran ten rounds of a rectangular field, 350 metres long and 120 metres wide. What total distance did Sam run?
One round is the perimeter of the field. One length and one width: 350 plus 120 is 470.

choices: No, it is half a round
ask.ifNot: 350 plus 120 takes Sam along one long side and one short side. He is at the opposite corner, only halfway round.

beats.say: Is 470 metres one full round?
470 is only halfway. Double it for a full round: 2 times 470 is 940 metres.
Sam ran ten rounds. 10 times 940 is 9400 metres.
Now look at the choices. 9400 metres isn't there, but some are in kilometres. 1000 metres make 1 kilometre.
9400 divided by 1000 is 9.4. So Sam ran 9.4 kilometres.
Three things to watch here: double for the full round, times 10 for ten rounds, and change the unit at the end.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 21 centimetres. We want its area, using 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 21 times 21.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 21 divided by 7 is 3.
So we have 22 times 3 times 21. 22 times 3 is 66.
Now 66 times 21. Split 21 into 20 and 1.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 66 times 20 is 1320. 66 times 1 is 66. What do the two parts make together?
1320 plus 66 makes 1386.
There it is: the area is 1386 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because it is an area.
Does that look sensible? 21 times 21 is 441. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 441 is 1323, so 1386 fits.
Remember: area is pi times radius times radius. The rule with the 2 in it is for the circumference.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 35 centimetres. We want its circumference, using 22 over 7 for pi.
Circumference means the distance right round the edge of the circle. Think of an ant walking once round the rim.

ask.ifNot: For going round the circle we need the 2 as well. Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius, and the radius goes in just once.

beats.say: The rule is 2 times pi times the radius. Which sum is that for our circle?
Here's a trick to keep the numbers small. Divide the 35 by the 7 first. 35 divided by 7 is 5.
Now it is just 2 times 22 times 5. First, 2 times 22 is 44.
Then 44 times 5 is 220.
So the circumference is 220 centimetres.
Does that look sensible? The circle is 70 centimetres across. Going round is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 70 is 210, so 220 fits.
So for a circumference: 2 times pi times the radius. And divide by the 7 first to keep the sum small.

board.text: Length + breadth = 12 cm. Length − breadth = 2 cm.

spec.note: Length + breadth = 12 cm. They differ by 2 cm

beats.say: The length and breadth of a rectangle add up to 12 centimetres, and they differ by 2 centimetres. We want the area.
Careful: 12 and 2 are not the sides. They are the sum and the difference. First we must find the two sides.
The length is the breadth and 2 more. So take that extra 2 away from 12. What is left is two equal breadths.

ask.ifNot: 10 is two equal breadths together. Halve it to get one breadth.

beats.say: Two breadths make 10. So what is one breadth?
Half of 10 is 5. The breadth is 5 centimetres. The length is 2 more, which is 7.
Check the clues: 7 plus 5 is 12, and 7 minus 5 is 2. Both fit.
Now the area: 7 times 5 is 35.
The area is 35 square centimetres.
