So with a sum and a difference: take the difference off, halve what is left, and you have the smaller side.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: We have a square with sides of 9 centimetres. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Count the sides of the square in the picture. There are 4 of them, each 9 centimetres. So the walk is 4 lots of 9.

beats.say: A square has 4 sides, and they are all the same length. So which sum gives the whole walk?
4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times the side.
That is 4 lots of 9, and 4 times 9 is 36.
There it is: the perimeter is 36 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking the four sides one at a time. 9, 9, 9, 9. Together they make 36.
So, for the perimeter of any square: multiply the side by 4.
Four shapes: a square, an equilateral triangle, a rectangle and a rhombus. Which one has the least perimeter?
We can't tell by looking, so we work out all four. The square has 4 sides of 5.5 centimetres. 4 times 5.5 is 22.
The equilateral triangle has 3 sides of 6 centimetres. 3 times 6 is 18.
The rectangle is 5 centimetres by 3 centimetres. 5 plus 3 is 8, and double is 16.

ask.ifNot: A rhombus is like a square that has been pushed over. All 4 of its sides are equal.

beats.say: Last, the rhombus, with a side of 5 centimetres. How many equal sides does a rhombus have?
4 equal sides. 4 times 5 is 20.
Now compare: 22, 18, 16 and 20. The smallest is 16.

board.text: Least: the rectangle, 5 cm by 3 cm

beats.say: So the least perimeter belongs to the rectangle, 5 centimetres by 3 centimetres.
The triangle has the fewest sides, but that didn't make it the smallest. Work each one out before you compare.

board.text: Triangle's perimeter = perimeter of a square of side 6 cm

spec.note: An equilateral triangle has the same perimeter. Its side = ?

beats.say: An equilateral triangle has the same perimeter as a square of side 6 centimetres. What is the side of the triangle?
Start with the shape we know. The square has 4 sides of 6 centimetres. 4 times 6 is 24.

ask.ifNot: The triangle shares its 24 centimetres equally among 3 sides. So we divide 24 by 3.

beats.say: The triangle has the same perimeter, 24 centimetres. An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides. So how do we find one side?
24 divided by 3 is 8.
Each side of the triangle is 8 centimetres.
Notice that 8 is more than 6. The triangle has fewer sides to share the same perimeter, so each side is longer.
Check: 3 sides of 8 make 24, the same as the square.
Look at this square. Every side is 19 centimetres. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side goes round the edge. That is the perimeter. The little squares inside sit in 19 rows of 19, so we multiply 19 by 19.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the square filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
A square is as wide as it is long. So there are 19 rows, with 19 little squares in every row. The area is side times side.
19 times 19 looks hard, but we can do it in two small parts. Think of 19 as 10 and 9.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 19 times 10 is 190. And 19 times 9 is 171. Now we put the two parts together. What is 190 plus 171?
Add them up: 190 plus 171 is 361.
There it is: the area is 361 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 361 squares shared into 19 rows gives 19 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. Side times side is the area. 4 times the side is the perimeter. Don't mix them up!

board.text: Area of square = area of a rectangle 16 cm by 4 cm

spec.note: A square has the same area. Perimeter of the square = ?

beats.say: A square has the same area as a rectangle 16 centimetres long and 4 centimetres broad. We want the perimeter of the square.
Three steps here: the rectangle's area, then the square's side, then the square's perimeter. First, 16 times 4 is 64.

ask.ifNot: Try the times tables. 8 times 8 is 64. Halving 64 or dividing it by 4 does not give the side.

beats.say: The square's area is also 64. Area is side times side. Which number times itself makes 64?
8 times 8 is 64. So the side of the square is 8 centimetres.
Don't stop here! 8 is the side, but the question asks for the perimeter.
A square has 4 equal sides. 4 times 8 is 32.
The perimeter of the square is 32 centimetres.
Same area links the two shapes. From the area we find the side, and from the side we find the perimeter.

board.text: Perimeter of square = perimeter of a rectangle 16 cm by 4 cm

spec.note: A square has the same perimeter. Area of the square = ?

beats.say: A square has the same perimeter as a rectangle 16 centimetres long and 4 centimetres broad. We want the area of the square.
First the rectangle's perimeter. 16 plus 4 is 20. That is halfway round, so double it: 40.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 equal sides. Share the 40 centimetres among all 4 of them.

beats.say: The square's perimeter is also 40 centimetres. How long is each side of the square?
40 divided by 4 is 10. The side of the square is 10 centimetres.
Now the area: side times side. 10 times 10 is 100.
The area of the square is 100 square centimetres.
Here's something neat. The rectangle's area is 16 times 4, only 64. Same perimeter, but the square holds more.
Same perimeter links the two shapes. From the perimeter we find the side, then side times side gives 100.

board.text: Rectangle: length 12 cm, width 11 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Here is our rectangle. It is 12 centimetres long and 11 centimetres wide, and we want its perimeter.
Perimeter means the distance right round the outside. Picture yourself walking along every edge, back to the start.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 12 plus 11 is 23.
Don't stop at 23. That is just one length and one width, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 23 is 46.
There it is: the perimeter is 46 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 12, 11, 12, 11. Together they make 46.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.

board.text: Rectangle: length 25 cm, width 16 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 25 centimetres long and 16 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 16 rows of 25, so we multiply 25 by 16.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
The squares sit in 16 rows, with 25 in every row. So the area is length times width.
25 times 16 looks hard, but we can do it in two small parts. Think of 16 as 10 and 6.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 25 times 10 is 250. And 25 times 6 is 150. Now we put the two parts together. What is 250 plus 150?
Add them up: 250 plus 150 is 400.
There it is: the area is 400 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 400 squares shared into 16 rows gives 25 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. For area we multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the distance round the edge.

board.text: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are: ?

beats.say: In a parallelogram, what is true about the opposite sides?

ask.ifNot: Say it slowly: parallel, o, gram. The name begins with the word parallel.

beats.say: Listen to the name: parallelogram. Which word can you hear hiding inside it?
Parallel! Opposite sides run in the same direction, like railway tracks, and never meet.

spec.note: Each side is as long as the side facing it

beats.say: Now look at their lengths. In the picture, compare the top side with the bottom side, and the left side with the right side.
Each side is exactly as long as the side facing it. So opposite sides are equal as well.
So in a parallelogram, opposite sides are parallel and equal.
Two facts, and both are true. Don't settle for a choice that gets only one of them right.

board.text: In a rhombus, the axes of symmetry are: ?

spec.note: A rhombus

beats.say: A rhombus has axes of symmetry. Which lines are they?

board.text: Axis of symmetry = a fold line that matches

beats.say: An axis of symmetry is a fold line. Fold along it, and one half lands exactly on the other.

choices: No, an angle is not a line
ask.ifNot: An angle is a corner, the turn between two sides. We can only fold along a line.

beats.say: So an axis has to be a line we can fold along. Could an angle be an axis of symmetry?
Right, angles are out. Now try folding along a side. Nothing lands on anything, so the sides are out too.

spec.note: A rhombus folds onto itself in 2 ways

beats.say: Now fold the rhombus corner to corner, along a diagonal. All four sides are equal, so the two halves match exactly.

spec.note: The fold lines are its two diagonals

beats.say: The other diagonal works in the same way. So a rhombus has 2 axes of symmetry, and they are its diagonals.
Remember the paper test: if you can fold along the line and the halves match, it is an axis of symmetry.
Four statements about shapes. Only one is true. Let's test each one.
Every rhombus is a square? A rhombus has four equal sides, but it can lean over like a diamond. Then it has no right angles. Not true.
Every parallelogram is a rectangle? A parallelogram can lean over too. A rectangle needs four right angles. Not true.

choices: No, it is longer than it is wide
ask.ifNot: A door is much taller than it is wide. A square needs all four sides to be the same length.

beats.say: Every rectangle is a square? Think of a door. It is a rectangle, but are its four sides equal?
A long rectangle is not a square. So that one is not true either.
Every square is a rectangle? A rectangle only needs four right angles. Does every square have four right angles? Yes, always!

board.text: Every square is a rectangle: TRUE

beats.say: So the true statement is: every square is a rectangle. A square is a special rectangle, one with equal sides.
The trick with the word every: hunt for one shape that breaks the rule. If you find one, the statement is not true.

board.text: Rectangle: length 26 cm, width 24 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Here is our rectangle. It is 26 centimetres long and 24 centimetres wide, and we want its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 24 rows of 26, so we multiply 26 by 24.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 24 rows of squares, and 26 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
26 times 24 looks hard, but we can do it in two small parts. Think of 24 as 20 and 4.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 26 times 20 is 520. And 26 times 4 is 104. Now we put the two parts together. What is 520 plus 104?
520 plus 104 makes 624.
There it is: the area is 624 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 624 squares shared into 24 rows gives 26 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Exactly one pair of parallel sides. It is called a: ?

spec.note: Exactly one pair of parallel sides

beats.say: A quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides. What is it called?
Parallel sides run in the same direction and never meet, like railway tracks. Let's count the parallel pairs in each shape.
A parallelogram has two pairs: top with bottom, and left with right. A rhombus has two pairs as well.

ask.ifNot: Picture a kite in the sky. Its sides all slant in different directions, so none of them are parallel.

beats.say: What about a kite? Its equal sides sit next to each other. Does a kite usually have any parallel sides?
A kite usually has no parallel sides at all.
That leaves the trapezium. Its top and bottom are parallel, but its other two sides are not. Exactly one pair!
So the shape is a trapezium.
The word exactly matters. Two pairs is too many. We want one pair and no more.

board.text: A kite has how many axes of symmetry?

spec.note: A kite

beats.say: Here is a kite. How many axes of symmetry does it have?

spec.note: Two short sides together, two long sides together

beats.say: A kite has two short sides that meet at one end, and two long sides that meet at the other end.

spec.note: Fold along this line: one half lands on the other

beats.say: An axis of symmetry is a fold line where the two halves match. Fold the kite along its length, from one end corner to the other.
One half lands exactly on the other. Short side on short side, long side on long side. That is 1 axis.

ask.ifNot: One part has the two short sides and the other part has the two long sides. When you fold, a short side lands on a long side.

beats.say: Now fold it the other way, across the middle, joining the two side corners. Do the halves match?

spec.note: This fold puts a short side on a long side

beats.say: A short side would land on a long side. So that fold does not match.

spec.note: 1 axis of symmetry

beats.say: A kite has just 1 axis of symmetry.
A rhombus has 2 and a square has 4. The kite, with its two different pairs of sides, has only the one.
Three angles of a quadrilateral are 90 degrees, 85 degrees and 110 degrees. What is the fourth angle?
The key fact: the four angles of a quadrilateral always add up to 360 degrees.
Add the three we know. 90 plus 85 is 175. Then 175 plus 110 is 285.

ask.ifNot: The fourth angle is whatever is left of the 360 after the other three. To find what is left, we subtract.

beats.say: Three angles use up 285 of the 360 degrees. What do we do to find the fourth?
360 minus 285. From 285 up to 300 is 15, and from 300 up to 360 is 60. 15 and 60 make 75.
The fourth angle is 75 degrees.
Check: 90, 85, 110 and 75 add up to 360.
Add the three you know, then take the total from 360. And add carefully: most slips happen in the adding.
The area of a square is 144 square centimetres. What is its side?
Area of a square is side times side. So we need a number that, multiplied by itself, gives 144.
Careful: this is not 144 divided by 4. Dividing by 4 is for a perimeter. Here we hunt for a number times itself.

ask.ifNot: 100 is less than 144. We need more area, so we need a longer side.

beats.say: Start with an easy one. 10 times 10 is 100. Is the side bigger or smaller than 10?
Bigger. Try 11: 11 times 11 is 121. Still too small.
Try 12: 12 times 12 is 144. That's it!
The side of the square is 12 centimetres.
To go from area back to the side, ask: which number times itself gives the area? Try, check, and adjust.

board.text: Rectangle: length 23 cm, width 7 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 23 centimetres long and 7 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 7 rows of 23, so we multiply 23 by 7.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 7 rows of squares, and 23 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
23 times 7 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 23 into 20 and 3.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 20 times 7 is 140. And 3 times 7 is 21. Now we put the two parts together. What is 140 plus 21?
140 plus 21 makes 161.
So the area is 161 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 161 squares shared into 7 rows gives 23 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Rectangle: area = 96 cm², length = 12 cm. Breadth = ?

beats.say: A rectangle has an area of 96 square centimetres and a length of 12 centimetres. What is its breadth?
Length times breadth gives the area. So 12 times the breadth is 96.

ask.ifNot: Multiplying made the 96. To go backwards from a multiplication, we divide.

beats.say: We know the answer to a multiplication and one of its numbers. How do we find the missing number?
Divide the area by the length: 96 divided by 12. Think: 12 times 8 is 96.
The breadth is 8 centimetres.
Check: 12 times 8 is 96. That is the area we were given.
A breadth of 8 makes sense: it must be a small number, because 12 lots of it make only 96.

spec.note: The diagonals AC and BD

beats.say: What is true about the two diagonals of a square?

board.text: Equal?  Cut in half?  Right angles?

beats.say: A diagonal joins opposite corners. A square has two of them, and they cross in the middle. We'll check three things.

spec.note: Like a rectangle: AC and BD are equal

beats.say: First: are they the same length? A square looks the same when you turn it. So one diagonal can't be longer than the other.

ask.ifNot: The crossing point is the very middle of the square. So it is the middle of each diagonal too.

beats.say: Second: bisect means cut exactly in half. The diagonals cross at the centre of the square. Does each one cut the other in half?
Yes. Each diagonal cuts the other exactly in half. They bisect each other.

spec.note: Like a rhombus: they cut each other in half at 90°

beats.say: Third: look at the corner where they cross. It is a square corner, a right angle.

board.text: Equal, and bisect at right angles

beats.say: So the diagonals of a square are equal, and they bisect each other at right angles.
A square gets the best of both: equal diagonals like a rectangle, and a right angle crossing like a rhombus.

board.text: Rectangle: length 28 cm, width 26 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 28 centimetres long and 26 centimetres wide. How far is it all the way round?
Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Imagine an ant walking round the rectangle until it is back where it started.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 28 plus 26 is 54.
Careful: 54 is only halfway round. There are two lengths and two widths, so we double it. 2 times 54 is 108.
There it is: the perimeter is 108 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 28, 26, 28, 26. Together they make 108.
Remember the plan. Length plus width takes you halfway round. Double it for the whole perimeter.

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this square. Every side is 19 centimetres. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Imagine an ant walking round the square until it is back where it started.

ask.ifNot: Count the sides of the square in the picture. There are 4 of them, each 19 centimetres. So the walk is 4 lots of 19.

beats.say: A square has 4 sides, and they are all the same length. So which sum gives the whole walk?
4 equal sides, so the perimeter is 4 times the side.
4 times 19 is a big sum, so let's break it into two easy ones. Split 19 into 10 and 9.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 4 times 10 is 40. And 4 times 9 is 36. Now we put the two parts together. What is 40 plus 36?
40 plus 36 makes 76.
There it is: the perimeter is 76 centimetres. It is a length, so the unit is just centimetres.
Let's check by walking the four sides one at a time. 19, 19, 19, 19. Together they make 76.
So, for the perimeter of any square: multiply the side by 4.

board.text: All points equidistant from a fixed point called the: ?

spec.note: Every point on the circle is this far from one fixed point

beats.say: A circle is all the points that are the same distance from one fixed point. What is that fixed point called?
Equidistant is a long word. It just means the same distance away.

ask.ifNot: The rope keeps the goat the same distance from the post all the time. That makes a perfectly round path.

beats.say: Think of a goat tied to a post by a rope. It walks round as far out as the rope lets it. What shape is its path?
A circle! The goat is always the same distance from the post. So the post is the fixed point, right in the middle.
That middle point of a circle is called the centre.
And the rope? Its length is the radius. Careful: the radius is a distance, but the question asks for a point.
So: the centre is the point in the middle. The radius is how far the circle is from it.
The radius of a circle is 9.5 centimetres. What is its diameter?
The diameter goes right across the circle through the centre. That is one radius, then another radius.

ask.ifNot: The diameter is the longer one. It is made of two radii, so we need 2 lots of 9.5.

beats.say: So what do we do to 9.5?
Double it. 2 times 9 is 18. And 2 times 0.5 is two halves, which make 1.
18 plus 1 is 19.
The diameter is 19 centimetres.
Don't let the decimal worry you. Double the whole part, double the half, and put them together.

board.text: The longest chord of a circle is called the: ?

beats.say: What is the longest chord of a circle called?

board.text: Chord: straight line, two points on the circle

beats.say: A chord is a straight line joining two points on the circle.

ask.ifNot: A circle is widest right across its middle. So the longest chord is the one that passes through the centre.

beats.say: A chord near the edge is short. As it slides towards the middle it grows. Where is it longest?

spec.note: A chord is longest when it passes through the centre

beats.say: Through the centre. No chord can be longer than that one.
A chord through the centre is called the diameter.
Watch the other names. An arc is curved, and the circumference goes round. A radius stops at the centre, so it is not a chord.
So the diameter is a chord, and it is the longest one a circle can have.

board.text: How many axes of symmetry does a circle have?

beats.say: How many axes of symmetry does a circle have?

board.text: Axis of symmetry = a fold line that matches

beats.say: An axis of symmetry is a fold line. Fold along it, and the two halves match exactly.

board.text: top to bottom: yes.  side to side: yes.

beats.say: Take a paper circle. Fold it top to bottom, through the centre. The halves match. Now fold it side to side. They match again.

ask.ifNot: A circle is equally round everywhere. However you turn it, a fold through the centre gives two equal halves.

beats.say: Now tilt the fold a little, still through the centre. Do the halves still match?

spec.note: Every diameter cuts the circle into two matching halves

beats.say: They do! Any fold through the centre works. Every diameter is an axis of symmetry.
And how many diameters are there? You can keep tilting the line a tiny bit more, for ever. There is no end to them.
So a circle has an infinite number of axes of symmetry. Infinite means without end.
A square has 4 and a rectangle has 2. The circle beats them all, because it is the same in every direction.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Find the circumference of a circle with radius 21 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is the distance round the circle. It is pi times the diameter.

ask.ifNot: The diameter is two radii, end to end. So we double 21.

beats.say: We are given the radius, 21. So what is the diameter?
Double 21 is 42. Careful not to skip this step: pi times the radius alone gives only half of the way round.
Now 22 over 7, times 42. Let the 7 divide first: 42 divided by 7 is 6.
That leaves 22 times 6. 20 times 6 is 120, and 2 times 6 is 12. Together, 132.
The circumference is 132 centimetres.
Does it look sensible? Going round is a bit more than 3 times the diameter. 3 times 42 is 126, so 132 fits.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 28 centimetres. We want its area, using 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 28 times 28.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 28 divided by 7 is 4.
So we have 22 times 4 times 28. 22 times 4 is 88.
Now 88 times 28. Split 28 into 20 and 8.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 88 times 20 is 1760. 88 times 8 is 704. What do the two parts make together?
1760 plus 704 makes 2464.
There it is: the area is 2464 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because it is an area.
Does that look sensible? 28 times 28 is 784. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 784 is 2352, so 2464 fits.
So for the area of a circle: pi times radius times radius. No 2 in it, and the answer is in square units.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 14 centimetres. We want its circumference, using 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is the distance all the way round the circle. It is like a perimeter, but for a round shape.

ask.ifNot: For going round the circle we need the 2 as well. Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius, and the radius goes in just once.

beats.say: The rule is 2 times pi times the radius. Which sum is that for our circle?
Before we multiply, let's make it easy. The 7 underneath divides into 14. 14 divided by 7 is 2.
Now it is just 2 times 22 times 2. First, 2 times 22 is 44.
Then 44 times 2 is 88.
So the circumference is 88 centimetres.
Does that look sensible? The circle is 28 centimetres across. Going round is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 28 is 84, so 88 fits.
Remember the plan: 2 times pi times the radius. Don't leave out the 2, and let the 7 divide first.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 28 centimetres. We want its circumference, using 22 over 7 for pi.
Circumference means the distance right round the edge of the circle. Think of an ant walking once round the rim.

ask.ifNot: For going round the circle we need the 2 as well. Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius, and the radius goes in just once.

beats.say: The rule is 2 times pi times the radius. Which sum is that for our circle?
Here's a trick to keep the numbers small. Divide the 28 by the 7 first. 28 divided by 7 is 4.
Now it is just 2 times 22 times 4. First, 2 times 22 is 44.
Then 44 times 4 is 176.
So the circumference is 176 centimetres.
Does that look sensible? The circle is 56 centimetres across. Going round is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 56 is 168, so 176 fits.
So for a circumference: 2 times pi times the radius. And divide by the 7 first to keep the sum small.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: This circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. Our job is to find its circumference. For pi we use 22 over 7.
Circumference means the distance right round the edge of the circle. Think of an ant walking once round the rim.

ask.ifNot: For going round the circle we need the 2 as well. Circumference is 2 times pi times the radius, and the radius goes in just once.

beats.say: The rule is 2 times pi times the radius. Which sum is that for our circle?
Here's a trick to keep the numbers small. The 7 underneath and the radius 7 cancel each other. 7 divided by 7 is 1.
Now it is just 2 times 22 times 1. 2 times 22 is 44, and 44 times 1 is still 44.
So the circumference is 44 centimetres.
Does that look sensible? The circle is 14 centimetres across. Going round is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 14 is 42, so 44 fits.
So for a circumference: 2 times pi times the radius. And divide by the 7 first to keep the sum small.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Find the circumference of a circle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is pi times the diameter.

ask.ifNot: Read the question once more. It says diameter 14 centimetres. So there is no need to double it.

beats.say: Look carefully at what we are given. Is 14 the radius or the diameter?
It is already the diameter. That's the trap: don't double it again! We just need 22 over 7, times 14.
Let the 7 divide first. 14 divided by 7 is 2.
That leaves 22 times 2, which is 44.
The circumference is 44 centimetres.
Sensible? A bit more than 3 times the diameter. 3 times 14 is 42, so 44 fits.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: This circle has a radius of 35 centimetres. Our job is to find its area. For pi we use 22 over 7.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 35 times 35.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 35 divided by 7 is 5.
So we have 22 times 5 times 35. 22 times 5 is 110.
Now 110 times 35. Split 35 into 30 and 5.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 110 times 30 is 3300. 110 times 5 is 550. What do the two parts make together?
3300 plus 550 makes 3850.
So the area is 3850 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area measures the space inside.
Does that look sensible? 35 times 35 is 1225. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 1225 is 3675, so 3850 fits.
So for the area of a circle: pi times radius times radius. No 2 in it, and the answer is in square units.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Here is a circle with a radius of 14 centimetres. We want its area, using 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 14 times 14.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 14 divided by 7 is 2.
So we have 22 times 2 times 14. 22 times 2 is 44.
Now 44 times 14. Split 14 into 10 and 4.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 44 times 10 is 440. 44 times 4 is 176. What do the two parts make together?
440 plus 176 makes 616.
There it is: the area is 616 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because it is an area.
Does that look sensible? 14 times 14 is 196. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 196 is 588, so 616 fits.
So for the area of a circle: pi times radius times radius. No 2 in it, and the answer is in square units.

spec.note: Circumference = 440 m

beats.say: The circumference of a circle is 440 metres. Find its radius. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter. Think of it in parts: if the diameter is 7 parts, the circumference is 22 of the same parts.

ask.ifNot: 22 equal parts make 440. To find one part, share 440 into 22.

beats.say: The circumference, 440, is 22 parts. So how big is one part?
440 divided by 22 is 20. One part is 20 metres.
The diameter is 7 parts. 7 times 20 is 140 metres.
Stop! Is 140 our answer? The question asks for the radius, and 140 is the diameter.
The radius is half the diameter. Half of 140 is 70.
The radius is 70 metres.
Check: the diameter is 140. 140 divided by 7 is 20, and 22 times 20 is 440. It fits.

spec.note: Circumference = 176 m

beats.say: The circumference of a round park is 176 metres. Find its diameter. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The circumference is 22 over 7 times the diameter. In parts: when the diameter is 7 parts, the circumference is 22 parts.
So 22 parts make 176. One part is 176 divided by 22. 22 times 8 is 176, so one part is 8.

ask.ifNot: The diameter is 7 of those parts. So we need 7 lots of 8.

beats.say: One part is 8 metres. How do we get the diameter?
7 times 8 is 56.
The diameter of the park is 56 metres.
This time the question wants the diameter, so we stop here. Halving would give the radius, which nobody asked for.
Check: 56 divided by 7 is 8, and 22 times 8 is 176. It fits.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Find the area of a circle with radius 7 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The rule with the 2 is for the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
22 over 7, times 7, times 7. The radius goes in twice, and there is no 2.
One of the 7s cancels the 7 underneath. That leaves 22 times 7.
22 times 7: 20 times 7 is 140, and 2 times 7 is 14. Together, 154.
The area is 154 square centimetres.
Remember: radius times radius for area, and the answer is in square units. 154 for a radius of 7 is a number worth knowing.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Find the area of a circle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The area rule is pi times the radius times the radius. But look at what we are given.

ask.ifNot: The radius is half of the diameter. Half of 14 is what we need.

beats.say: We have the diameter, and the rule needs the radius. What is the radius?
Half of 14 is 7. That's the trap here: using 14 in the rule would make the area far too big.
Now 22 over 7, times 7, times 7. One 7 cancels the 7 underneath, leaving 22 times 7.
22 times 7: 20 times 7 is 140, and 2 times 7 is 14. Together, 154.
The area is 154 square centimetres.
Before using any circle rule, check: have I got the radius or the diameter? Then change it if you need to.

board.text: Track: radius 35 m. Distance in 3 laps = ? (π = 22/7)

spec.note: One lap is once round the track. 3 laps = ?

beats.say: A circular track has a radius of 35 metres. How far does a runner go in 3 laps? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

ask.ifNot: The runner goes round the edge of the circle. The distance round the edge is the circumference.

beats.say: One lap is once round the track. Which measure of a circle is that?
One lap is the circumference: pi times the diameter. The diameter is double the radius: 2 times 35 is 70.
Now 22 over 7, times 70. Let the 7 divide first: 70 divided by 7 is 10.
22 times 10 is 220. So one lap is 220 metres.
Don't stop at one lap! The runner goes round 3 times. 3 times 220 is 660.
The runner goes 660 metres.
Always read to the end of the question. First one lap, then as many laps as it asks for.

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: This circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. Our job is to find its area. For pi we use 22 over 7.
The area is the space inside the circle. The rule is pi times the radius times the radius.

ask.ifNot: The 2 belongs to the circumference, the distance round. For the space inside, the radius is used twice: pi times 7 times 7.

beats.say: Which sum is that for our circle?
Careful: the radius goes in twice, and there is no 2 in this rule. Now let the 7 divide first. 7 divided by 7 is 1.
So we have 22 times 1 times 7. 22 times 1 is just 22.
Now 22 times 7. Split 22 into 20 and 2.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 20 times 7 is 140. 2 times 7 is 14. What do the two parts make together?
140 plus 14 makes 154.
So the area is 154 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area measures the space inside.
Does that look sensible? 7 times 7 is 49. A circle's area is a bit more than 3 times that. 3 times 49 is 147, so 154 fits.
So for the area of a circle: pi times radius times radius. No 2 in it, and the answer is in square units.
5 points are marked on a circle. A chord is a straight line joining 2 of the points. How many chords can we draw?

board.text: 5 points on a circle. How many chords?

beats.say: Let's name the points A, B, C, D and E. From A we can draw chords to B, C, D and E. That is 4.

spec.note: From A: chords to B, C, D and E. That is 4 chords

beats.say: Now B. How many new chords can B make?

ask.ifNot: B joins C, D and E. The chord from B to A is already drawn, so it is not new.

beats.say: B gives 3 new chords. C gives 2 new ones, to D and E. D gives 1 new one, to E.

board.text: From B: 3   From C: 2   From D: 1

beats.say: And E? Every chord from E is already there. So we add: 4 plus 3 plus 2 plus 1.
That is 10. So 10 chords can be drawn.
The trap is 5 times 4, which is 20. That counts each chord twice, once from each end. Half of 20 is 10 again.

board.text: A diameter cuts a circle into 2 equal parts.

spec.note: The diameter cuts the circle into two equal parts

beats.say: A diameter divides a circle into two equal parts. What is each part called?

spec.note: A diameter passes through the centre

beats.say: A diameter passes straight through the centre. So the piece on one side is exactly the same as the piece on the other.

ask.ifNot: When something is shared into 2 equal parts, each part is one half.

beats.say: Two equal parts. So what fraction of the circle is each part?

board.text: each part = half of the circle

spec.note: Each part is exactly half of the circle

beats.say: Each part is half of the circle.
There is a little word that means half: semi. You may know it from semi final, the match halfway to the final.

spec.note: Half of a circle is a semicircle

beats.say: So half of a circle is called a semicircle.
An arc is only a piece of the curved edge, and a quarter circle is one of four parts. Half a circle is a semicircle.

board.text: Wheel: diameter 28 cm. Turns to cover 440 cm = ?

spec.note: How many full turns to cover 440 cm?

beats.say: A wheel has a diameter of 28 centimetres. How many complete turns will it make to cover 440 centimetres? Use 22 over 7 for pi.

ask.ifNot: In one turn the whole rim is laid out along the ground. The length of the rim is the circumference.

beats.say: Picture the wheel rolling. In one full turn, every bit of its rim touches the ground once. So how far does it move in one turn?
One turn moves the wheel forward by one circumference. That is pi times the diameter: 22 over 7, times 28.
Let the 7 divide first: 28 divided by 7 is 4. Then 22 times 4 is 88.
So each turn covers 88 centimetres. Careful: 88 is not the answer. It is the distance for one turn.
How many 88s fit into 440? 88 times 5 is 440.
The wheel makes 5 complete turns.
For rolling wheels: one turn is one circumference. Then divide the whole distance by that.

board.text: Same centre, different radii. These circles are called: ?

beats.say: Circles that have the same centre but different radii have a special name. What is it?
Different radii means different sizes: a small circle, a bigger one, a bigger one still.

choices: No, those mean the same size
ask.ifNot: Equal and congruent both mean exactly the same size. These circles have different radii, so they are different sizes.

beats.say: So could they be called equal circles, or congruent circles?
No. Those names are for circles of the same size. What is special here is that they all share one centre.
Think of a target board, or the ripples when a stone drops into a pond. Rings inside rings, all round one middle point.
Circles like that are called concentric circles. Con means together, and centric is about the centre.
So: same centre, different sizes, concentric. Listen for the word centre hiding inside the name.

spec.note: Area = 616 cm²

beats.say: The area of a circle is 616 square centimetres. Find its radius. Use 22 over 7 for pi.
The area is 22 over 7, times the radius, times the radius. We know the area, so we work backwards.
To undo 22 over 7, we divide by 22 and then multiply by 7. First, 616 divided by 22 is 28.
Then 28 times 7 is 196. So radius times radius is 196.

ask.ifNot: Halving 196 will not do it. We need a number times itself. 10 times 10 is 100 and 20 times 20 is 400, so it lies between 10 and 20.

beats.say: Careful: 196 is not the radius. It is the radius times itself. Which number times itself makes 196?
It is between 10 and 20. Try 14: 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 4 is 56. Together, 196. Yes!
The radius is 14 centimetres.
Working backwards from an area: undo the pi, then find the number that multiplies by itself. Two steps, not one.

board.text: Circle: radius 7 cm. Which number is larger:

spec.note: Which number is larger: circumference or area?

beats.say: A circle has a radius of 7 centimetres. Looking just at the numbers, which is larger: its circumference or its area?
We can't guess, so we work out both. Circumference first: 2 times 22 over 7 times 7.
The 7s cancel, leaving 2 times 22. The circumference is 44.

ask.ifNot: Area is pi times the radius times the radius. The radius goes in twice, and there is no 2.

beats.say: Now the area. Which sum do we need?
22 over 7, times 7, times 7. One 7 cancels, leaving 22 times 7, which is 154.
Compare the two numbers. 154 is greater than 44.
So the area is the larger number: 154 is greater than 44.
One is in centimetres and the other in square centimetres, so we only compare the numbers, just as the question says.

board.text: How many radii and diameters can a circle have?

spec.note: A radius can go to any point on the circle

beats.say: How many radii and how many diameters can a circle have?

ask.ifNot: Pick any point on the circle and join it to the centre. That is a radius too. Every point gives one.

beats.say: A radius joins the centre to a point on the circle. We usually draw just one. But could we draw another, to a different point?
Yes! Every point on the circle gives a radius. And between any two points there are always more points. There is no end to them.

spec.note: A diameter can point in any direction

beats.say: Now diameters. A diameter is a straight line through the centre. Turn it a tiny bit, and you have a new diameter.
You can keep turning it by smaller and smaller amounts, for ever. So there is no end to the diameters either.
The word for no end is infinite. A circle has infinite radii and infinite diameters.
We draw one radius or one diameter to keep pictures tidy. But the circle really has endlessly many of each.

spec.note: Cut along the diameter. Perimeter of one half = ?

beats.say: Find the perimeter of a semicircle with diameter 14 centimetres. Use 22 over 7 for pi.

choices: a curved edge and a straight edge
ask.ifNot: Half a roti has a round side and a flat side where it was cut. The perimeter goes along both.

beats.say: A semicircle is half a circle, like half a roti. Walk all the way round its edge. What kinds of edge do you walk along?
A curved edge and a straight edge. That's the trap in this question: people forget the straight edge.

spec.note: Whole circle: 22/7 × 14 = 44 cm

beats.say: The curved edge is half of the whole circle's circumference. The whole circle: 22 over 7 times 14. 14 divided by 7 is 2, and 22 times 2 is 44.

spec.note: Curved edge of the half: 44 ÷ 2 = 22 cm

beats.say: Half of 44 is 22. So the curved edge is 22 centimetres.

spec.note: Straight edge: the diameter, 14 cm

beats.say: The straight edge is the diameter itself: 14 centimetres.
Add the two edges. 22 plus 14 is 36.
The perimeter of the semicircle is 36 centimetres.
Perimeter means all the way round. For a semicircle that is the curve and the flat side together.
We have a square with sides of 12 centimetres. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side goes round the edge. That is the perimeter. The little squares inside sit in 12 rows of 12, so we multiply 12 by 12.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the square filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
In a square the length and the width are the same. That gives 12 rows of 12 little squares. So area is side times side.
12 times 12 looks hard, but we can do it in two small parts. Think of 12 as 10 and 2.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 12 times 10 is 120. And 12 times 2 is 24. Now we put the two parts together. What is 120 plus 24?
120 plus 24 makes 144.
So the area is 144 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 144 squares shared into 12 rows gives 12 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. Side times side is the area. 4 times the side is the perimeter. Don't mix them up!

board.text: Rectangle: length 21 cm, width 16 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 21 centimetres long and 16 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its area.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 16 rows of 21, so we multiply 21 by 16.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 16 rows of squares, and 21 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
Let's make 21 times 16 easier. We split 16 into 10 and 6, and do one part at a time.

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly, one place at a time. Let's write it down together.

beats.say: 21 times 10 is 210. And 21 times 6 is 126. Now we put the two parts together. What is 210 plus 126?
Add them up: 210 plus 126 is 336.
There it is: the area is 336 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area is counted in little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 336 squares shared into 16 rows gives 21 in each row. It fits!
So, for the area of any rectangle: multiply the length by the width, and give the answer in square units.

board.text: Rectangle: length 29 cm, width 20 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Look at this rectangle: 29 centimetres long and 20 centimetres wide. Our job is to find its perimeter.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round the edge. Imagine an ant walking round the rectangle until it is back where it started.

ask.ifNot: Look at the picture again. A rectangle has four sides: two lengths and two widths. The walk must go along all four of them.

beats.say: The walk goes along a length, then a width, then another length and another width. Which sum gives the whole walk?
Let's add one length and one width first. 29 plus 20 is 49.
Don't stop at 49. That is just one length and one width, halfway round. Double it: 2 times 49 is 98.
So the perimeter is 98 centimetres. Plain centimetres this time, because a perimeter is a distance.
Let's check by walking all four sides, one at a time. 29, 20, 29, 20. Together they make 98.
So, for the perimeter of any rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.
In a pictograph, one apple picture stands for 5 apples. Monday shows 3 apple pictures. How many apples were sold?

spec.note: Each picture stands for 5 apples

beats.say: The part that says one picture is 5 apples is called the key. Always read the key first.
Monday has 3 pictures, each worth 5. What do we work out?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 3 pictures stands for 5 apples. So we need 3 lots of 5, and that is 3 times 5.

beats.say: 3 times 5 is 15. Or count in fives, once for each picture: 5, 10, 15.
15 apples were sold.
3 is only the number of pictures. Use the key to turn pictures into apples.
In a bar graph, what does the tallest bar represent?

board.text: In a bar graph, the tallest bar shows ...?

beats.say: Let's make a tiny bar graph to see. Say three friends have 3, 7 and 5 stickers.
In a bar graph, each bar is drawn as tall as its number. So 3 gets a short bar, and 7 gets a tall one.
Whose bar is the tallest?

ask.ifNot: The bigger the number, the taller the bar. 7 is the biggest number, so Bina's bar is the tallest.

beats.say: Bina's bar is the tallest, because 7 is the largest number.
So the tallest bar always represents the largest value.
And the shortest bar shows the smallest value. In a bar graph, height tells you how big.
What is the mean of 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24?

spec.note: Average = ?

beats.say: Mean is another word for average, the fair share. Add all the numbers, then divide by how many there are.
Add them one at a time. 12 plus 15 is 27. Add 18 to get 45. Add 21 to get 66. And 24 more makes 90.
The total is 90. What do we divide it by?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers: 12, 15, 18, 21, 24. There are 5 of them, so we share the total 5 ways.

beats.say: 90 divided by 5 is 18.
The mean is 18.
Here is something pretty. These numbers go up in equal steps of 3, so the mean is simply the middle one, 18.
For any mean: add everything up, then divide by how many numbers there are.
What is the mode of 3, 5, 7, 5, 9, 5, 2?
The mode is the number that appears most often. Think of it as the most popular number in the list.

board.text: Mode = the number that appears most often

beats.say: So we count how many times each number shows up. 3 appears once. 7 once. 9 once. 2 once.
How many times does 5 appear?

ask.ifNot: Point at each 5 in the list. There is one in second place, one in fourth place and one in sixth place. That is 3.

beats.say: 5 appears 3 times. That is more than any other number.
The mode is 5.
The mode is not the biggest number, and it is not the first one. It is the one you see the most.
What is the range of 14, 8, 22, 5 and 17?

spec.note: Range = ?

beats.say: The range tells us how spread out the numbers are. It is the biggest number minus the smallest.
Which are the biggest and the smallest numbers here?

ask.ifNot: Look through the whole list. Nothing is bigger than 22, and nothing is smaller than 5.

beats.say: The biggest is 22 and the smallest is 5.
22 minus 5 is 17.
The range is 17.
The range is a gap, so we subtract. Adding the biggest and the smallest is the slip to watch for.
In a pictograph, one smiley face stands for 10 students. A row shows 2 full faces and half a face. How many students is that?

board.text: 1 picture = 10 students. Row: 2 full pictures and a half.

spec.note: Each full picture stands for 10 students

beats.say: Start with the 2 full faces. 2 times 10 is 20.
Now the half face. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Half a picture stands for half of 10 students. Half of 10 is 5.

beats.say: Half of 10 is 5. So the half face stands for 5 students.
20 plus 5 is 25.
The row represents 25 students.
A half picture is worth half the key. Do the full pictures first, then the part picture.
Bar A shows 45 and Bar B shows 30. What is the difference?

spec.note: Difference = ?

beats.say: What does the word difference tell us to do?

ask.ifNot: The difference is the gap between two numbers. We find a gap by taking the smaller from the bigger.

beats.say: Difference means how far apart. So take the smaller from the bigger: 45 minus 30.
4 tens take away 3 tens is 1 ten, and the 5 ones stay. That is 15.
The difference is 15.
On the graph, Bar A stands 15 higher than Bar B. Check: 30 plus 15 is 45.
If you toss a coin, how likely is it that you get a head?

board.text: Toss a coin. Getting a head is ...?

beats.say: A coin has 2 sides: heads on one, tails on the other. When it lands, one of the 2 sides faces up.
Is a head certain to come up?

ask.ifNot: Certain means it happens every single time. But a coin can also land on tails.

beats.say: So a head is not certain. And it is not impossible either, because heads do come up.
The two sides are just alike. Nothing makes one side luckier than the other. So each has the same chance: 1 out of 2.

board.text: Heads: 1 out of 2.    Tails: 1 out of 2

beats.say: Getting a head is equally likely as tails.
That is why tossing a coin is a fair way to decide who goes first.
A table shows: Monday 12, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 18, Thursday 10, Friday 20. What is the total?

board.text: Mon 12, Tue 15, Wed 18, Thu 10, Fri 20. Total = ?

spec.note: Total = ?

beats.say: Five numbers to add. Don't just go from left to right. Look for friendly pairs first.
Which number pairs with 12 to make a round number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the ones digits. 2 and 8 make 10. So 12 and 18 go together to make a round number.

beats.say: 12 and 18 make 30.
10 and 20 are already round. Together they make 30 as well.
Now everything: 30 plus 30 is 60, and the 15 that is left makes 75.
The total is 75.
Pair up numbers that make tens, and tick each one off so that none is left out.
The average of 5 numbers is 20. Four of the numbers are 15, 22, 18 and 25. Find the 5th.

spec.note: Find the missing number

beats.say: If the average of 5 numbers is 20, they add up to the same as five 20s. 5 times 20 is 100.
Now add the four we know. 15 and 25 make 40. 22 and 18 make 40. Together that is 80.
The total must be 100, and four numbers make 80. So how do we find the fifth number?

ask.ifNot: The fifth number fills the gap between 80 and the full total of 100. So we subtract.

beats.say: 100 minus 80 is 20.
The fifth number is 20.
It is the same as the average! That is because the other four already average 20: 80 divided by 4 is 20.
Average times count gives the total. The missing number is the total minus the rest.
What do we call an event that will definitely happen?

board.text: An event that will definitely happen is called ...?

beats.say: In maths we have special words for how sure we are that something will happen. Let's line them up.
Impossible means it can never happen, like a cow jumping over the moon. Unlikely means it probably will not happen.
Try this one. The sun will rise tomorrow morning. How sure are we?

ask.ifNot: The sun rises every single morning. There is no doubt about it at all.

beats.say: When there is no doubt at all, and the event will definitely happen, we call it certain.
An event that will definitely happen is called certain.
Uncertain is the opposite: it means we are not sure. Definitely and certain go together.
In a pie chart, cricket takes up one quarter of the circle. What is the angle of that slice?

board.text: Cricket takes up 1/4 of the pie chart. Angle = ?

spec.note: Cricket takes up 1/4 of the circle. Angle = ?

beats.say: A pie chart is a full circle. All the way round a circle is 360 degrees.
We want one quarter of the circle. What do we do to 360?

ask.ifNot: A quarter means one of 4 equal parts. To find one of 4 equal parts, we divide by 4.

beats.say: 360 divided by 4. Half of 360 is 180, and half of 180 is 90.
The angle is 90 degrees.
90 degrees is a right angle, like the corner of a square. So a quarter slice of a pie chart always has a square corner.
Find the median of 7, 3, 9, 5 and 11.

spec.note: Median = ?

beats.say: The median is the middle number. But only after the numbers are lined up in order, from smallest to biggest.

board.text: Median = the middle number, once in order

beats.say: The list is 7, 3, 9, 5, 11. Right now the number in the middle of it is 9. So is 9 the median?

choices: no, put them in order first
ask.ifNot: The list is not in order yet. The median is the middle number only once the numbers go from smallest to biggest.

beats.say: Put them in order: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11.
Now cross off one from each end. 3 and 11 go. Then 5 and 9 go. The one left standing is 7.
The median is 7.
Order first, then find the middle. With 5 numbers, the middle one is the third.
36 books need to be shown in a pictograph. If each symbol stands for 6 books, how many symbols are needed?
Each symbol holds 6 books. So we are packing 36 books into groups of 6.
How do we find the number of groups of 6 in 36?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many 6s fit into 36. Finding how many fit is a division.

beats.say: Count in sixes: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36. That took 6 steps. So 36 divided by 6 is 6.
6 symbols are needed.
Check by multiplying back: 6 symbols of 6 books make 36 books. To go from books to symbols, divide by the key.
A bar graph has this scale: 1 centimetre stands for 20 students. A bar is 3.5 centimetres tall. How many students does it show?

board.text: Scale: 1 cm = 20 students. The bar is 3.5 cm tall.

spec.note: 1 cm stands for 20 students

beats.say: 3.5 means 3 and a half. So split the bar into 3 whole centimetres and half a centimetre.
The 3 whole centimetres: 3 times 20 is 60 students.
And what does the half centimetre stand for?

ask.ifNot: A whole centimetre stands for 20 students. Half a centimetre stands for half of 20, which is 10.

beats.say: Half of 20 is 10.
60 plus 10 is 70.
The bar shows 70 students.
Check: 3.5 times 20 is 70. Use the scale on the whole part and on the half part, then add.
A car goes 240 kilometres in 4 hours. Average speed means: how far does it go in one hour, if every hour is the same?
So we share the 240 kilometres equally among the 4 hours. Which sum is that?

ask.ifNot: Sharing equally means dividing. So we need 240 divided by 4.

beats.say: Speed is distance divided by time.
24 divided by 4 is 6. So 240 divided by 4 is 60.
So the car goes 60 kilometres in each hour. Its average speed is 60 kilometres an hour.
Check. 4 hours at 60 kilometres each hour makes 240 kilometres. It fits.
So to find speed, divide the distance by the time.
How likely is it to roll a 7 on a standard die?

board.text: Rolling a 7 on a standard die is ...?

beats.say: A standard die is a cube with 6 faces. The faces show 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
Look at the faces. Is there a 7 anywhere?

ask.ifNot: The faces stop at 6. Read them again: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. There is no 7.

beats.say: There is no face with a 7. So however many times you roll, a 7 can never come up.
Unlikely would mean it can happen, just not often. But this can never happen at all. The word for that is impossible.
Rolling a 7 is impossible.
Before you decide how likely something is, list everything that can happen. If it is not on the list, it is impossible.
Here are ten marks: 8, 9, 8, 10, 9, 8, 7, 9, 8, 10. What is the frequency of 8?
Frequency is just a grown-up word for how many times. So we ask: how many times does the mark 8 appear?
Go along the list and ring every 8. Slowly, so that we miss none.
Count the rings. How many 8s are there?

ask.ifNot: The 8s are in first place, third place, sixth place and ninth place. That makes 4.

beats.say: There are 4 rings. So the frequency of 8 is 4.
For comparison, 9 appears 3 times and 10 appears 2 times. Mark each one as you count, so nothing is counted twice.
The average of 4 numbers is 25. Three of the numbers are 20, 30 and 22. Find the fourth.

spec.note: Find the missing number

beats.say: The average of 4 numbers is 25. What must the 4 numbers add up to?

ask.ifNot: An average of 25 means the total is the same as four 25s. 4 times 25 is 100.

beats.say: 4 times 25 is 100. The four numbers add up to 100.
Add the three we know. 20 plus 30 is 50, and 22 more is 72.
The fourth number is the rest. 100 minus 72 is 28.
The fourth number is 28.
Check: 72 plus 28 is 100, and 100 divided by 4 is 25.
Average times count gives the total. Then take away the numbers you know.
Look at this. 3 x, plus 1, plus 2 x, plus 2. Four pieces, and some of them can be joined together. Let's find out which.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 3 x is 3 boxes, and 2 x is 2 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: First the x family. 3 lots of x and 2 more lots of x make 5 lots of x.
Now the plain numbers. 1 plus 2 makes 3.
So we have 5 x and 3. Here is where many people slip. Can we join those two into one piece?

ask.ifNot: 5 x means 5 lots of a hidden number. 3 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 5 x plus 3. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Good mathematicians check. If x were 1, the long one would be 3 plus 1 plus 2 plus 2. That is 8. The short one is 5 plus 3, and that is 8 too.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own number. That gave us 5 x plus 3.
We know that x is 4. We want the value of 2 x, plus 3, minus 8.
Look at 2 x. The 2 and the x are side by side. When x is 4, what does that mean?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 2 x means 2 times x. Here that is 2 times 4.

beats.say: So the x goes, and 4 takes its place. Now it reads 2 times 4, plus 3, minus 8.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 2 times 4 comes first. The 3 must not be added to the 4.

beats.say: 2 times 4 is 8. So now we have 8, plus 3, minus 8.
Now we go left to right. 8 plus 3 is 11. The sign before the 8 is a minus, so we take it away. 11 minus 8 is 3.
So when x is 4, the whole thing is worth 3. The plan: swap the letter for its number, multiply first, then work left to right.
Two equal fractions, but one top number is hiding. 3 over 8 equals something over 24.
Here is 3 over 8 as a bar: 8 pieces, 3 shaded. Underneath is the very same bar, cut into 24 smaller pieces.
Start with the bottoms. What was 8 multiplied by to make 24?

ask.ifNot: Use the 8 times table. 8 times 3 is 24, so the bottom was multiplied by 3.

beats.say: 8 times 3 is 24. In the picture, that means every piece was cut into 3 smaller pieces.
So to keep the two fractions equal, what must happen to the top?

ask.ifNot: Every shaded piece was cut into 3 as well. So the top must be multiplied by the same number, 3.

beats.say: The top gets the same treatment. 3 times 3 is 9.
So 3 over 8 equals 9 over 24. The missing number is 9.
Check with the picture. The same amount of bar is shaded in both. Only the size of the pieces changed.
The rule to keep: top and bottom always get multiplied by the same number.
Nikhil is 39 and Diya is 32. We want the sum of their ages, but after 6 years.
The word after means we go forward in time, so ages go up. After 6 years Nikhil will be 39 plus 6, which is 45.
Now Diya. What do we do with Diya's age?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everybody. Diya also grows 6 years older, so we add 6 to 32 as well.

beats.say: Diya grows older as well. 32 plus 6 is 38.
Sum means add. So add the two new ages: 45 plus 38 makes 83.
So after 6 years, their ages will add up to 83.
Here is a quick check. Today they add up to 71. Each of them gains 6 years, so we add 6 twice. We reach 83 again.
Remember the trap: adding the years only once. Two people grow older, so the sum grows twice as much.
Arjun buys 9 sharpeners, and each sharpener costs 8 rupees. Arjun hands over 97 rupees. We want to know how much money comes back.

board.text: 9 sharpeners at Rs.8 each. Pays Rs.97. Change = ?

spec.note: 9 sharpeners at Rs.8 each, then the change

beats.say: Look at the bar. The whole bar is the money Arjun paid. The sharpeners take up part of it, and the change is the piece at the end. What do we need to find first?

ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper wants money for all 9 sharpeners, not just one. So first we find what all of them cost together.

beats.say: 9 sharpeners at 8 rupees each is 9 lots of 8. From our tables, 9 times 8 is 72.
So the sharpeners cost 72 rupees altogether. That is the part of the bar that stays in the shop.
Arjun paid 97 rupees, and the bill is 72 rupees. How do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is the money left over after the bill is paid. So we take the bill away from the money paid.

beats.say: Count up from 72 to 97: that is a jump of 25. So 97 take away 72 is 25.
So the change is 25 rupees. That is what Arjun gets back.
Let's check. The bill, 72, plus the change, 25, makes 97. That is exactly what Arjun paid.
Remember the plan for change: multiply to find the bill, then subtract the bill from the money paid.
Here is what we know. 24 pencils cost 216 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one pencil.
Every pencil costs the same. So how do we find the cost of one?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 216 rupees equally among 24 pencils. Sharing equally means dividing.

beats.say: Sharing 216 rupees equally among 24 pencils is a division. 216 divided by 24.
To divide, think of times. 24 times what number makes 216?
Try 10 first, because it is easy. 24 times 10 is 240. That is a little too big.
It is too big by exactly one lot of 24, because 240 take away 24 is 216. So we need 9 lots, not 10.
So 216 divided by 24 is 9. One pencil costs 9 rupees.
Does that make sense? One pencil must cost much less than all 24 together, and 9 is much less than 216. Yes.
The plan: the cost of one is the total cost divided by the number of things.
Tara buys 9 notebooks, and each notebook costs 5 rupees. Tara hands over 70 rupees. We want to know how much money comes back.

board.text: 9 notebooks at Rs.5 each. Pays Rs.70. Change = ?

spec.note: 9 notebooks at Rs.5 each, then the change

beats.say: The long bar is all the money Tara paid. Part of it pays for the notebooks, and the piece with the question mark is the change. So, what should we find first?

ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper wants money for all 9 notebooks, not just one. So first we find what all of them cost together.

beats.say: We need 9 lots of 5. 9 times 5 is 45.
So the whole bill is 45 rupees. That much stays with the shopkeeper.
Tara paid 70 rupees, and the bill is 45 rupees. How do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is the money left over after the bill is paid. So we take the bill away from the money paid.

beats.say: Take the bill away from the money paid. 70 take away 45 leaves 25.
So Tara gets 25 rupees back.
Let's check. The bill, 45, plus the change, 25, makes 70. That is exactly what Tara paid.
Remember the plan for change: multiply to find the bill, then subtract the bill from the money paid.
Here is a long expression. 9 x, plus 1, plus 5 x, plus 2. Simplify means write it shorter, without changing what it is worth.
Some of these pieces belong together. The ones with an x are one family. The plain numbers are another family. Which two are from the same family?

ask.ifNot: Look for the letter. 9 x and 5 x both have an x, so they are one family. 1 has no x at all.

beats.say: First the x family. 9 lots of x and 5 more lots of x make 14 lots of x.
Next, the numbers with no letter. 1 and 2 together make 3.
So we have 14 x and 3. Here is where many people slip. Can we join those two into one piece?

ask.ifNot: 14 x means 14 lots of a hidden number. 3 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: So the short form is 14 x plus 3. Same value, fewer pieces.
Let's test it. Pretend x is 1. The long one is 9 plus 1 plus 5 plus 2, which is 17. The short one is 14 plus 3, also 17. They match.
So to simplify: gather the x terms, gather the plain numbers, and keep the two families apart. Our answer is 14 x plus 3.
Look at this. 5 x, plus 8, plus 6 x, minus 5. Four pieces, and some of them can be joined together. Let's find out which.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 5 x is 5 boxes, and 6 x is 6 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: First the x family. 5 lots of x and 6 more lots of x make 11 lots of x.
Now the plain numbers. Careful: the sign in front of a number belongs to that number. So this is 8 minus 5, which is 3.
So we have 11 x and 3. Here is where many people slip. Can we join those two into one piece?

ask.ifNot: 11 x means 11 lots of a hidden number. 3 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: So the short form is 11 x plus 3. Same value, fewer pieces.
Good mathematicians check. If x were 1, the long one would be 5 plus 8 plus 6 minus 5. That is 14. The short one is 11 plus 3, and that is 14 too.
So to simplify: gather the x terms, gather the plain numbers, and keep the two families apart. Our answer is 11 x plus 3.
A bottle holds 20 litres of water. Each glass takes 300 millilitres. How many glasses can we fill?

board.text: 20 litres. Glasses of 300 ml. How many?

beats.say: Look at the units: litres for the bottle, millilitres for the glasses. So what is our first job?

ask.ifNot: We cannot match litres against millilitres straight away. Let's turn the litres into millilitres, so both are in the same unit.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. So 20 litres is 20000 millilitres.
Now, how many lots of 300 fit into 20000? Take two zeros off both numbers. It is the same as 200 divided by 3.
3 times 60 is 180, and 3 times 6 is 18 more. So 3 times 66 is 198. How much of the 200 is left over?

ask.ifNot: Count on from 198 up to 200. That little bit is what is left over.

beats.say: So 66 glasses get filled, and a little water is left. 300 times 66 is 19800, which leaves 200 millilitres.
Careful here: 200 millilitres is not enough for another glass of 300. So we do not count it.
So 66 full glasses can be filled.
Remember: make the units the same first, then see how many full lots fit. A part of a glass does not count.

board.text: Rectangle: length 9 cm, width 5 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 9 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 5 rows of 9, so we multiply 9 by 5.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 5 rows of squares, and 9 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
From the times tables, 9 times 5 is 45.
So the area is 45 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 45 squares shared into 5 rows gives 9 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. For area we multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the distance round the edge.
Here is our sum. 3 over 8, plus 1 over 8.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 8 equal pieces. The first has 3 shaded, and the second has 1.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all eighths. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, lots of children slip here. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, eighths. Adding more eighths does not change their size, so the bottom stays 8.

beats.say: So adding is just counting. 3 pieces, and 1 piece more, is 4 pieces.
4 over 8 is right, but we can make it simpler. What is the biggest number that divides both 4 and 8?

ask.ifNot: 4 goes into 8, and the top is 4 itself. So 4 is the biggest number that goes into both.

beats.say: So we divide the top and the bottom by 4. 4 divided by 4 is 1, and 8 divided by 4 is 2.
So 3 over 8 plus 1 over 8 is one half, in its simplest form.
Quick check with the picture. Count the shaded pieces in the first two bars: 3 and 1 make 4. It matches.
So when the bottom numbers match: add the tops, keep the bottom, and then make it simpler if you can.

board.text: Rectangle: length 12 cm, width 10 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: We have a rectangle, 12 centimetres long and 10 centimetres wide. How much space is inside it?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides measures along the edges, not the inside. The little squares sit in 10 rows of 12, so we multiply 12 by 10.

beats.say: Area means the space inside. Picture the rectangle filled with little squares, each 1 centimetre wide. Which sum counts them all?
There are 10 rows of squares, and 12 squares in each row. That is why area is length times width.
12 times 10 is 12 tens, and 12 tens is 120.
So the area is 120 square centimetres. We say square centimetres because we counted little squares.
Let's check by going backwards. 120 squares shared into 10 rows gives 12 in each row. It fits!
Remember the plan. For area we multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the distance round the edge.
Two equal fractions, but one top number is hiding. 1 over 5 equals something over 20.
Here is 1 over 5 as a bar: 5 pieces, 1 shaded. Underneath is the very same bar, cut into 20 smaller pieces.
Start with the bottoms. What was 5 multiplied by to make 20?

ask.ifNot: Use the 5 times table. 5 times 4 is 20, so the bottom was multiplied by 4.

beats.say: 5 times 4 is 20. In the picture, that means every piece was cut into 4 smaller pieces.
So to keep the two fractions equal, what must happen to the top?

ask.ifNot: Every shaded piece was cut into 4 as well. So the top must be multiplied by the same number, 4.

beats.say: The top gets the same treatment. 1 times 4 is 4.
So 1 over 5 equals 4 over 20. The missing number is 4.
Check with the picture. The same amount of bar is shaded in both. Only the size of the pieces changed.
The rule to keep: top and bottom always get multiplied by the same number.
We want the square root of 576. That means: which number, times itself, makes 576?
20 times 20 is 400, and 30 times 30 is 900. Our 576 lies in between, so the answer is between 20 and 30.
Now a clever clue. 576 ends in 6. Which last digit gives a square that ends in 6?

ask.ifNot: Square each digit and look at the last digit of the result. Only 4 or 6 gives a square that ends in 6.

beats.say: 4 times 4 is 16. 6 times 6 is 36. Both end in 6. So we try 24 or 26.
Try 24. 24 times 20 is 480, and 24 times 4 is 96. Together that is 576. That is our number!
So the square root of 576 is 24.
Careful: a square root is not a half. Half of 576 is 288. But 288 times just 2 is already 576, so 288 times itself is far too big.
So remember: a square root undoes squaring. Ask yourself which number, times itself, gives 576.
4 x, plus 7, plus 3 x, plus 8. That is a lot to say! Let's tidy it up, so it says the same thing in fewer pieces.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 4 x is 4 boxes, and 3 x is 3 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: First the x family. 4 lots of x and 3 more lots of x make 7 lots of x.
Next, the numbers with no letter. 7 and 8 together make 15.
So we have 7 x and 15. Here is where many people slip. Can we join those two into one piece?

ask.ifNot: 7 x means 7 lots of a hidden number. 15 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 7 x plus 15. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Good mathematicians check. If x were 1, the long one would be 4 plus 7 plus 3 plus 8. That is 22. The short one is 7 plus 15, and that is 22 too.
So to simplify: gather the x terms, gather the plain numbers, and keep the two families apart. Our answer is 7 x plus 15.
Here is a little number game. Start with 12. Multiply it by 2. Then add 8.
There are two jobs to do. Which one comes first?

ask.ifNot: Do the jobs in the order they are given. The first job is to multiply 12 by 2. The adding comes after.

beats.say: First job: multiply. 12 times 2. 10 times 2 is 20, and 2 times 2 is 4. Together that makes 24.
Careful now. The add 8 is done to our new number, 24. It is not added to the 2 we multiplied by.
Second job: add 8. 24 plus 8 is 32.
Let us write the whole game on one line. 12 times 2, plus 8, equals 32.
One job at a time, in order. Multiply first, then add.
Here is our story. Aarav has 36 marbles, and one quarter of them go to a friend. How many does Aarav keep?
Let's draw the 36 marbles. The bottom number is 4, so we share them into 4 equal groups.
How many marbles are in each group?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 36 marbles equally into 4 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 36 divided by 4.

beats.say: 36 divided by 4 is 9. So each group holds 9 marbles.
Aarav gives away 1 of those groups, so 9 marbles go to the friend.
Careful now. Read the question again: it asks how many are left. So what do we do with the 9?

ask.ifNot: 9 is how many marbles went to the friend. Aarav started with 36, so what is left is 36 take away 9.

beats.say: 36 take away 9 leaves 27. Aarav keeps 27 marbles.
Let's check with the picture. 3 groups were not given away, and 3 times 9 is 27. It matches.
The plan: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top, and then check what the question is really asking for.
We have a drum with 10 litres of water, and glasses that hold 250 millilitres each. Let's find how many glasses it fills.

board.text: 10 litres. Glasses of 250 ml. How many?

beats.say: One amount is in litres and the other is in millilitres. What must we do before we share the water out?

ask.ifNot: We cannot match litres against millilitres straight away. Let's turn the litres into millilitres, so both are in the same unit.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. So 10 litres is 10000 millilitres.
Now think about just 1 litre, which is 1000 millilitres. How many glasses of 250 does it fill?

ask.ifNot: Count up in steps of 250 until you reach 1000. The number of steps is the number of glasses.

beats.say: 4 glasses of 250 make 1000. So every litre fills 4 glasses.
We have 10 litres, and each one fills 4 glasses. 10 times 4 is 40.
So 40 glasses can be filled.
Let's check. 40 glasses of 250 millilitres make 10000 millilitres. That is the whole drum, so it fits.
Remember: make the units the same first, then see how many lots fit.
A tank holds 10 litres of water. Each glass takes 250 millilitres. How many glasses can we fill?

board.text: 10 litres. Glasses of 250 ml. How many?

beats.say: One amount is in litres and the other is in millilitres. What must we do before we share the water out?

ask.ifNot: We cannot match litres against millilitres straight away. Let's turn the litres into millilitres, so both are in the same unit.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. So 10 litres is 10000 millilitres.
Now think about just 1 litre, which is 1000 millilitres. How many glasses of 250 does it fill?

ask.ifNot: Count up in steps of 250 until you reach 1000. The number of steps is the number of glasses.

beats.say: 4 glasses of 250 make 1000. So every litre fills 4 glasses.
We have 10 litres, and each one fills 4 glasses. 10 times 4 is 40.
So 40 glasses can be filled.
Let's check. 40 glasses of 250 millilitres make 10000 millilitres. That is the whole tank, so it fits.
Litres into millilitres first, then share. That plan works for every question like this.
Vivek is 30 and Meera is 24. We want the sum of their ages, but after 4 years.
The word after means we go forward in time, so ages go up. After 4 years Vivek will be 30 plus 4, which is 34.
Now Meera. What do we do with Meera's age?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everybody. Meera also grows 4 years older, so we add 4 to 24 as well.

beats.say: Meera grows older as well. 24 plus 4 is 28.
Now we add the two new ages. 34 plus 28 is 62.
