Aarav has 90 marbles and gives away 2 over 5 of them. We want to know how many are left.
Let's draw all 90 marbles as one long bar. The bottom number is 5, so we cut it into 5 equal parts.
So how many marbles does one part hold?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 90 marbles equally into 5 parts. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 90 divided by 5.

beats.say: 90 divided by 5 is 18. So each part holds 18 marbles.
Aarav gives away 2 of those parts. 2 times 18 is 36 marbles.
Careful now. Read the question again: it asks how many are left. So what do we do with the 36?

ask.ifNot: 36 is how many marbles went to the friend. Aarav started with 90, so what is left is 90 take away 36.

beats.say: 90 minus 36 is 54. So Aarav has 54 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. 3 parts were not given away, and 3 times 18 is 54. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
We need two thirds of 36. Let's work it out together.
A picture helps. These are 36 counters, and the bottom number, 3, says share them into 3 equal groups.
What do we do to the 36 first?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number, 3, tells us how many equal groups to make. Sharing into 3 equal groups means dividing by 3.

beats.say: 36 divided by 3 is 12. So each group holds 12.
Now the top number, 2. It tells us how many of those groups to take. So what is two thirds of 36?

ask.ifNot: One group is 12, and the top number says take 2 of them. So we need 2 times 12.

beats.say: 2 groups of 12. 2 times 12 is 24.
There it is. Two thirds of 36 is 24.
Let's check our groups were fair. 3 groups of 12 should give back 36, and 3 times 12 is 36. They were.
So, for a fraction of an amount: divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top number.
Which is greater, 1 over 6 or 6 over 8? Let's find out.
Here they are as two bars of the same length. The first is cut into 6 pieces with 1 shaded. The second is cut into 8 pieces with 6 shaded.
Can we just compare the top numbers, 1 and 6?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, the bigger top always wins
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Sixths and eighths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 6 and 8 both go into, and the smallest one is 24.
For 1 over 6, the bottom was multiplied by 4, so the top must be too. 1 times 4 is 4, so 1 over 6 is 4 over 24.
And for 6 over 8, the bottom was multiplied by 3, so the top must be too. 6 times 3 is 18, so 6 over 8 is 18 over 24.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all twenty-fourths. Which is greater, 4 over 24 or 18 over 24?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 18 pieces is more than 4 pieces.

beats.say: 18 pieces beat 4 pieces. And 18 over 24 is only another name for 6 over 8, so 6 over 8 is the greater fraction.
The picture agrees. The bar for 6 over 8 has more of it shaded.
Keep this plan. Same bottom number first, and only then compare the tops.
Which is greater, 4 over 8 or 1 over 5? Let's find out.
Here they are as two bars of the same length. The first is cut into 8 pieces with 4 shaded. The second is cut into 5 pieces with 1 shaded.
Can we just compare the top numbers, 4 and 1?

choices: Yes, the bigger top always wins
No, the pieces are different sizes
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Eighths and fifths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 8 and 5 both go into, and the smallest one is 40.
For 4 over 8, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 5 as well: 4 times 5 is 20. That makes 20 over 40.
And for 1 over 5, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 8 as well: 1 times 8 is 8. That makes 8 over 40.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all fortieths. Which is greater, 20 over 40 or 8 over 40?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 20 pieces is more than 8 pieces.

beats.say: 20 pieces beat 8 pieces. And 20 over 40 is only another name for 4 over 8, so 4 over 8 is the greater fraction.
The picture agrees. The bar for 4 over 8 has more of it shaded.
Keep this plan. Same bottom number first, and only then compare the tops.
Here is our sum. 5 over 10, plus 6 over 10.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 10 equal pieces. The first has 5 shaded, and the second has 6.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all tenths. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, this is the classic slip. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, tenths. Adding more tenths does not change their size, so the bottom stays 10.

beats.say: So we only count the pieces. 5 pieces and 6 pieces make 11 pieces.
11 over 10. The top is bigger than the bottom, and that is fine. It means more than 1 whole: one full bar, and 1 more piece.
Can we make 11 over 10 simpler? 11 and 10 share no factor except 1, so it is already in its simplest form.
So 5 over 10 plus 6 over 10 is 11 over 10.
Let's check against the picture. 5 shaded pieces, and 6 more, is 11 pieces. Just what we wrote.
Remember it like this. Same size pieces? Just count them: add the tops, and the bottom stays as it is.
Here is our story. Vivek has 72 marbles, and one quarter of them go to a friend. How many does Vivek keep?
Let's draw all 72 marbles as one long bar. The bottom number is 4, so we cut it into 4 equal parts.
How many marbles are in each part?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 72 marbles equally into 4 parts. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 72 divided by 4.

beats.say: 72 divided by 4 is 18. So each part holds 18 marbles.
Vivek gives away 1 of those parts, so 18 marbles go to the friend.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 18?

ask.ifNot: 18 is how many marbles went to the friend. Vivek started with 72, so what is left is 72 take away 18.

beats.say: 72 minus 18 is 54. So Vivek has 54 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. 3 parts were not given away, and 3 times 18 is 54. It matches.
The plan: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top, and then check what the question is really asking for.
We need one third of 60. Let's work it out together.
Let's draw it. Here are 60 counters. The bottom number, 3, tells us to share them into 3 equal groups.
What do we do to the 60 first?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number, 3, tells us how many equal groups to make. Sharing into 3 equal groups means dividing by 3.

beats.say: 60 divided by 3 is 20. So each group holds 20.
The top number is 1, so we take just 1 of those groups.
So one third of 60 is 20.
Let's check our groups were fair. 3 groups of 20 should give back 60, and 3 times 20 is 60. They were.
So, for a fraction of an amount: divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top. When the top is 1, the dividing does it all.
Two fractions, 4 over 7 and 5 over 6. We want the greater one.
A picture first. Two equal bars: the top one cut into 7 with 4 shaded, the bottom one cut into 6 with 5 shaded.
Can we just compare the top numbers, 4 and 5?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, the bigger top always wins
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Sevenths and sixths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 7 and 6 both go into, and the smallest one is 42.
For 4 over 7, the bottom was multiplied by 6, so the top must be too. 4 times 6 is 24, so 4 over 7 is 24 over 42.
And for 5 over 6, the bottom was multiplied by 7, so the top must be too. 5 times 7 is 35, so 5 over 6 is 35 over 42.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all forty-seconds. Which is greater, 24 over 42 or 35 over 42?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 35 pieces is more than 24 pieces.

beats.say: 35 pieces beat 24 pieces. And 35 over 42 is only another name for 5 over 6, so 5 over 6 is the greater fraction.
The picture agrees. The bar for 5 over 6 has more of it shaded.
Keep this plan. Same bottom number first, and only then compare the tops.
Here is our sum. 2 over 5, plus 1 over 5.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 5 equal pieces. The first has 2 shaded, and the second has 1.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all fifths. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, this is the classic slip. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, fifths. Adding more fifths does not change their size, so the bottom stays 5.

beats.say: So we only count the pieces. 2 pieces and 1 piece make 3 pieces.
Can we make 3 over 5 simpler? 3 and 5 share no factor except 1, so it is already in its simplest form.
So 2 over 5 plus 1 over 5 is 3 over 5.
Let's check against the picture. 2 shaded pieces, and 1 more, is 3 pieces. Just what we wrote.
Remember it like this. Same size pieces? Just count them: add the tops, and the bottom stays as it is.
Priya has 36 marbles and gives away three quarters of them. We want to know how many are left.
Let's draw the 36 marbles. The bottom number is 4, so we share them into 4 equal groups.
So how many marbles does one group hold?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 36 marbles equally into 4 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 36 divided by 4.

beats.say: 36 divided by 4 is 9. So each group holds 9 marbles.
The top number is 3, so 3 groups go to the friend. 3 times 9 is 27 marbles.
Careful now. Read the question again: it asks how many are left. So what do we do with the 27?

ask.ifNot: 27 is how many marbles went to the friend. Priya started with 36, so what is left is 36 take away 27.

beats.say: 36 take away 27 leaves 9. Priya keeps 9 marbles.
Let's check with the picture. Just 1 group was not given away, and one group is 9 marbles. It matches.
The plan: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top, and then check what the question is really asking for.
One half equals something over 6. Let's find the missing top number.
Here is one half as a bar: 2 pieces, 1 shaded. Underneath is the very same bar, cut into 6 smaller pieces.
Start with the bottoms. What was 2 multiplied by to make 6?

ask.ifNot: Use the 2 times table. 2 times 3 is 6, so the bottom was multiplied by 3.

beats.say: 2 times 3 is 6. In the picture, that means every piece was cut into 3 smaller pieces.
So to keep the two fractions equal, what must happen to the top?

ask.ifNot: Every shaded piece was cut into 3 as well. So the top must be multiplied by the same number, 3.

beats.say: The top gets the same treatment. 1 times 3 is 3.
So one half equals 3 over 6. The missing number is 3.
Check with the picture. The same amount of bar is shaded in both. Only the size of the pieces changed.
So for equal fractions: whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by the same number.
Look at 99307. We want to compare two digits: the 9 in the ten-thousands place and the 9 in the thousands place.

board.text: In 99307: (9 in ten-thousands) is ? times (9 in thousands)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 9 in the ten-thousands place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 9 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 90000.

beats.say: The ten-thousands place is worth 10000, and 9 times 10000 is 90000.
Now the 9 in the thousands place. That seat is worth 1000, so 9 times 1000 is 9000.
How many times means: how many lots of 9000 fit into 90000? Which sum finds that?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 9000 fit into 90000, and that is a division.

beats.say: A neat trick: cross off the same number of zeros from both. Here that is 3 zeros from each, leaving 90 divided by 9.
90 divided by 9 is 10.
So the 9 in the ten-thousands place is worth 10 times the 9 in the thousands place.
Good mathematicians check. 9000 times 10 takes us back to 90000.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second. And notice: each seat is worth 10 times the seat on its right.
Here is our number, 12645. We want the place value of the 6 in the hundreds place.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens and hundreds.
Our 6 sits in the hundreds place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens and hundreds. The hundreds place is worth 100.

beats.say: Place value is the digit times what its seat is worth. So we multiply 6 by 100.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 6 times 100 is 600. So this 6 is worth 600.
Careful: 6 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 600.
A quick check: 600 is 6 followed by 2 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So remember: find the seat, then multiply the digit by what the seat is worth.
This is 68457. Let us find out how much the 4 in the hundreds place stands for.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens and hundreds.
Our 4 sits in the hundreds place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens and hundreds. The hundreds place is worth 100.

beats.say: Place value is the digit times what its seat is worth. So we multiply 4 by 100.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 4 times 100 is 400. So this 4 is worth 400.
Careful: 4 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 400.
A quick check: 400 is 4 followed by 2 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So the plan is: find the seat, then multiply the digit by the worth of that seat.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a divide, a plus and a times.
One of these three signs has to wait until the very end. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times both go before plus. So the plus is the one that waits until the end.

beats.say: Dividing and multiplying go before adding. So we box 18 divided by 6, and we box 3 times 6.
First box. 18 divided by 6 is 3, because 6 times 3 is 18.
Second box. 3 times 6 is 18.
Put each answer where its box was, with the plus still in between.
Now the plus gets its turn. 3 plus 18 is 21.
The trap here is going straight along from left to right. The 3 must not be added until the times is done.
So remember: divide and multiply first, then add.
We need the L C M of 15 and 9. That is the lowest common multiple: the first number that is in the 15 times table and in the 9 times table.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 15?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 15 is 15 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 15, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: Let's write out both tables and watch for a match. First the 15s: 15, 30, 45.
Now count up in 9s: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 15 and 9?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 45 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: 45 is in both lists, and nothing before it is. So the L C M is 45.
Let's check. 45 divided by 15 is 3, and 45 divided by 9 is 5. Both divide exactly, so 45 really is a multiple of each.
One trap to watch for. Multiplying 15 by 9 gives 135. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 45 gets there first.
That is the idea of an L C M: the first meeting point of the two tables. Write out the multiples and look for the first match.
Two ratios are equal here. 7 to 8 is the same as 35 to x. Our job is to find x.
Equal ratios are made by multiplying both numbers by the same number. So look at the two first numbers, 7 and 35.
What was 7 multiplied by to become 35?

ask.ifNot: Say the 7 times table until you reach 35. 7 times 5 is 35.

beats.say: 7 times 5 is 35. So the multiplier is 5.
Careful here. We do not add anything. The second number, 8, must be multiplied by the very same 5.
8 times 5 is 40. So x is 40.
Let us check. 7 to 8 became 35 to 40. Both numbers were multiplied by 5, so the two ratios are equal.
So with equal ratios, find the multiplier from the pair you know, then use it on the other pair.
The average of 5 numbers is 60. We know 4 of them: 54, 59, 49, 54. We must find the missing one.
Here is the key. If the average of 5 numbers is 60, the numbers add up to the same as 5 lots of 60.
So how do we find the total of all 5 numbers?

ask.ifNot: If each of the 5 numbers were 60, the total would be 5 lots of 60. So we multiply.

beats.say: 60 times 5 is 300. All 5 numbers together make 300.
Now add the 4 numbers we know. 54 plus 59 is 113. Add 49 to get 162, and 54 more makes 216.
The missing number is whatever is left. 300 minus 216 is 84.
The missing number is 84.
Check: 216 plus 84 is 300, and 300 divided by 5 is 60. It works.
So: average times count gives the total. Then take away what you know.
The average of 6 numbers is 50. Then a new number, 64, joins them. What is the new average?

board.text: Average of 6 numbers is 50. A new number 64 joins.

beats.say: We do not know what the 6 numbers are. But we do not need to! Their total is enough.
6 numbers with an average of 50 add up to the same as 6 lots of 50. 50 times 6 is 300.
Now the new number joins the pot. 300 plus 64 is 364.
We must share the new total. How many numbers are there now?

ask.ifNot: There were 6 numbers, and 1 more joined. 6 plus 1 is 7. Forgetting to count the new one is the classic slip.

beats.say: There are 7 numbers now. 364 divided by 7 is 52, because 7 times 52 is 364.
The new average is 52.
The new number, 64, is bigger than the old average, 50. So it pulled the average up a little. That makes sense.
Go through the total every time. Find it, add the new number, and share it among one more.
We want the average of these five numbers: 55, 79, 65, 57, 84.
The average is the fair share. Imagine putting all the numbers into one pot, and then sharing the pot out equally.
First the total. We add one number at a time. 55 plus 79 is 134. Add 65 to get 199.
Keep going. Add 57 to get 256, and 84 more makes 340.
So the pot holds 340. How many shares do we cut it into?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers in the list. There are 5 of them, so the total is shared 5 ways.

beats.say: 340 divided by 5 is 68, because 5 times 68 is 340.
So the average is 68.
Does it look sensible? The smallest number is 55 and the biggest is 84, and 68 sits between them. An average always does.
So for any average: add everything up, then divide by how many numbers there are.
Here are four numbers: 61, 48, 73, 62. Let's find their average.
The average is the fair share. Imagine putting all the numbers into one pot, and then sharing the pot out equally.
First the total. 61 plus 48 is 109. Add 73 to get 182, and 62 more makes 244.
So the pot holds 244. How many shares do we cut it into?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers in the list. There are 4 of them, so the total is shared 4 ways.

beats.say: 244 divided by 4 is 61, because 4 times 61 is 244.
So the average is 61.
Does it look sensible? The smallest number is 48 and the biggest is 73, and 61 sits between them. An average always does.
Two steps every time: find the total, then share it by the count.
We want the average of these six numbers: 19, 60, 55, 42, 53, 41.
The average is the fair share. Imagine putting all the numbers into one pot, and then sharing the pot out equally.
First the total. We add one number at a time. 19 plus 60 is 79. Add 55 to get 134.
Keep going. Add 42 to get 176. Add 53 to get 229, and 41 more makes 270.
So the pot holds 270. How many shares do we cut it into?

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers in the list. There are 6 of them, so the total is shared 6 ways.

beats.say: 270 divided by 6 is 45, because 6 times 45 is 270.
So the average is 45.
Does it look sensible? The smallest number is 19 and the biggest is 60, and 45 sits between them. An average always does.
So for any average: add everything up, then divide by how many numbers there are.
Here is our equation. 7 x, minus 8, equals 34. The x is a hidden number, and we are going to find it.
When a number sits next to x, it means times. So x was multiplied by 7, then someone took away 8, and the answer was 34.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the minus 8. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo minus 8, we add 8.

beats.say: And the rule of the balance is: what we do to one side, we do to the other. So I write plus 8 under both.
On the left, only 7 x is left. On the right, 34 plus 8 is 42. So 7 x equals 42.
Don't stop here! 42 is in the list of answers, but it is what 7 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 7, we divide by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7. 7 times 6 is 42, so 42 divided by 7 is 6.
That means x is 6. We found the number that was hiding.
Let's check. Put 6 in place of x. 7 times 6 is 42, and 42 minus 8 is 34. It works!
Every equation like this works the same way. Undo the last thing first, and keep both sides level.
Here is our equation. 5 x, plus 1, equals 41. The x is a hidden number, and we are going to find it.
5 x means 5 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 5, then added 1, and got 41.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance, and every move must keep it level. What should our first move be?

ask.ifNot: We undo the last thing first, and that is the plus 1. Its opposite is taking away 1. The dividing comes after that.

beats.say: To undo plus 1, we take away 1. And to keep the balance level, we do it to both sides.
Now the left side is just 5 x. And 41 minus 1 makes 40. So 5 times x is 40.
Careful: 40 is one of the choices, but 40 is 5 x, not x. So, what undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 5. 5 times 8 is 40, so 40 divided by 5 is 8.
So x equals 8. The mystery is solved.
Good mathematicians always check. 5 times 8 is 40, and 40 plus 1 is 41. Both sides match.
So the plan is to work backwards. First undo the adding or taking away. Then undo the times.
We are hunting for the number whose digits add up to 22. Digit sum simply means: add up the digits.

board.text: Which number has a digit sum of 22?

beats.say: Let us try the first one, 54913. What do its digits add up to?

ask.ifNot: Add them one at a time: 5 plus 4 plus 9 plus 1 plus 3. That makes 22.

beats.say: 5 plus 4 plus 9 plus 1 plus 3 makes 22. That is the 22 we are looking for!
Now 43148. 4 plus 3 plus 1 plus 4 plus 8 makes 20. That is less than 22, so not this one.
Now 41608. 4 plus 1 plus 6 plus 0 plus 8 makes 19. That is less than 22, so not this one.
Next, 19149. 1 plus 9 plus 1 plus 4 plus 9 makes 24. That is more than 22, so not this one.
So the number with a digit sum of 22 is 54913.
A tip for next time: a zero adds nothing, so you can skip over it. And check every choice, so nothing surprises you.
Here is 42338. Two digits are marked: the 2 in the thousands place and the 8 in the units place. We must compare what they are worth.

board.text: In 42338: (2 in thousands) is ? times (8 in units)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 2 in the thousands place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 2 sits in the thousands place, so it is worth 2000.

beats.say: The thousands place is worth 1000, and 2 times 1000 is 2000.
Now the 8 in the units place. That seat is worth just 1, so this 8 is worth 8.
How many times means: how many lots of 8 fit into 2000? Which sum finds that?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 8 fit into 2000, and that is a division.

beats.say: We need the number that, times 8, makes 2000. That number is 250, because 250 times 8 is 2000.
So the 2 in the thousands place is worth 250 times the 8 in the units place.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a divide, a plus and a times.
One of these three signs has to wait until the very end. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times both go before plus. So the plus is the one that waits until the end.

beats.say: Dividing and multiplying go before adding. So we box 24 divided by 6, and we box 4 times 6.
First box. 24 divided by 6 is 4, because 6 times 4 is 24.
Second box. 4 times 6 is 24.
Put each answer where its box was, with the plus still in between.
Now the plus gets its turn. 4 plus 24 is 28.
The trap here is going straight along from left to right. The 4 must not be added until the times is done.
The rule: do the dividing and the multiplying first. The adding comes last.
Look at this one. 3 x, minus 10, equals 14. Our job is to find the number that x stands for.
3 x means 3 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 3, then took away 10, and got 14.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance, and every move must keep it level. What should our first move be?

ask.ifNot: We undo the last thing first, and that is the minus 10. Its opposite is adding 10. The dividing comes after that.

beats.say: To undo minus 10, we add 10. And to keep the balance level, we do it to both sides.
On the left, only 3 x is left. On the right, 14 plus 10 is 24. So 3 x equals 24.
Don't stop here! 24 is in the list of answers, but it is what 3 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 3?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 3, we divide by 3.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 3. 3 times 8 is 24, so 24 divided by 3 is 8.
So x equals 8. The mystery is solved.
Good mathematicians always check. 3 times 8 is 24, and 24 minus 10 is 14. Both sides match.
So the plan is to work backwards. First undo the adding or taking away. Then undo the times.
Here is our equation. 6 x, plus 18, equals 42. The x is a hidden number, and we are going to find it.
6 x means 6 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 6, then added 18, and got 42.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance, and every move must keep it level. What should our first move be?

ask.ifNot: We undo the last thing first, and that is the plus 18. Its opposite is taking away 18. The dividing comes after that.

beats.say: To undo plus 18, we take away 18. And to keep the balance level, we do it to both sides.
Now the left side is just 6 x. And 42 minus 18 makes 24. So 6 times x is 24.
Careful: 24 is one of the choices, but 24 is 6 x, not x. So, what undoes times 6?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 6, we divide by 6.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 6. 6 times 4 is 24, so 24 divided by 6 is 4.
So x equals 4. The mystery is solved.
Let's check. Put 4 in place of x. 6 times 4 is 24, and 24 plus 18 is 42. It works!
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
We need the L C M of 9 and 3. That is the lowest common multiple: the first number that is in the 9 times table and in the 3 times table.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 9?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 9 is 9 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 9, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: Look closely at these two numbers. 9 is in the 3 times table: 3 times 3 is 9.
So where do the two tables first meet?

ask.ifNot: 9 is the very first number in its own table, and we just saw it is in the 3 times table too. So the two tables first meet at 9.

beats.say: Here are both tables. 9 is in each of them. Nothing smaller can be, because 9 is where its own table starts. So the L C M is 9.
One trap to watch for: do not just multiply them. 3 times 9 is 27. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one.

Put each answer where its box was, with the plus still in between.

Here is our number, 77108. We want the place value of the 1 in the hundreds place.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens and hundreds.
Our 1 sits in the hundreds place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens and hundreds. The hundreds place is worth 100.

beats.say: To get the place value, we multiply the digit by the worth of its seat. That is 1 times 100.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 1 times 100 is just 100. So this 1 is worth 100.
Careful: 1 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 100.
A quick check: 100 is 1 followed by 2 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So remember: find the seat, then multiply the digit by what the seat is worth.
Look at 33276. We want to compare two digits: the 3 in the ten-thousands place and the 2 in the hundreds place.

board.text: In 33276: (3 in ten-thousands) is ? times (2 in hundreds)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 3 in the ten-thousands place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 3 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 30000.

beats.say: The ten-thousands place is worth 10000, and 3 times 10000 is 30000.
Now the 2 in the hundreds place. That seat is worth 100, so 2 times 100 is 200.
Now, how many times. That asks how many lots of 200 fit into 30000. Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 200 fit into 30000, and that is a division.

beats.say: A neat trick: cross off the same number of zeros from both. Here that is 2 zeros from each, leaving 300 divided by 2.
Dividing by 2 is halving. Half of 300 is 150.
So the 3 in the ten-thousands place is worth 150 times the 2 in the hundreds place.
Check by multiplying back: 200 times 150 is 30000. It works.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a minus.
So, which bit goes first?

Find the L C M of 12 and 10. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we looking for?

Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 12 and 10?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 60 is in both, and nothing before it is.

One trap to watch for. Multiplying 12 by 10 gives 120. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 60 gets there first.

Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 12?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 12 is 12 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 12, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: Look closely at these two numbers. 12 is in the 6 times table: 6 times 2 is 12.
So where do the two tables first meet?

ask.ifNot: 12 is the very first number in its own table, and we just saw it is in the 6 times table too. So the two tables first meet at 12.

beats.say: Here are both tables. 12 is in each of them. Nothing smaller can be, because 12 is where its own table starts. So the L C M is 12.
One trap to watch for: do not just multiply them. 6 times 12 is 72. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one.
So here is a shortcut worth keeping. When one number is a multiple of the other, the bigger number is the L C M straight away.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a plus and a times.
Where do we begin?

beats.say: Times goes before plus, so put a box round 2 times 4.
2 times 4 is 8. So 8 goes where the box was, and the rest stays the same.
Now the plus. 12 plus 8 is 20.
Careful with the trap here. Adding 12 and 2 first, just because they come first, gives a different number. The 2 belongs to the times.
The rule: multiply before you add, wherever the times sign sits.
One of these numbers has digits that add up to 18. Digit sum just means we add the digits together.

board.text: Which number has a digit sum of 18?

beats.say: Let us try the first one, 35481. What do its digits add up to?

ask.ifNot: Add them one at a time: 3 plus 5 plus 4 plus 8 plus 1. That makes 21.

beats.say: 3 plus 5 plus 4 plus 8 plus 1 makes 21. That is more than 18, so not this one.

Which part do we work out first?

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding and taking away. So we box the 3 times 1. It goes first.
3 times 1 is just 3. So 3 goes where the box was. The rest of the sum stays the same.
Just a minus and a plus now. Which one comes first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 25 take away 3.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 25 take away 3 is 22.
And now the plus. 22 plus 1 is 23.

Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a minus.
Which part do we work out first?

Here is our equation. 5 x, minus 11, equals 44. The x is a hidden number, and we are going to find it.
5 x means 5 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 5, then took away 11, and got 44.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the minus 11. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo minus 11, we add 11.

beats.say: So 11 goes on. But if we did that on one side only, the balance would tip. So we do it to both sides.
On the left, only 5 x is left. On the right, 44 plus 11 is 55. So 5 x equals 55.
Don't stop here! 55 is in the list of answers, but it is what 5 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 5. 5 times 10 is 50, and one more 5 makes 55. So 55 divided by 5 is 11.
So x equals 11. The mystery is solved.
Let's check. Put 11 in place of x. 5 times 11 is 55, and 55 minus 11 is 44. It works!
So the plan is to work backwards. First undo the adding or taking away. Then undo the times.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a plus.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus. So 28 times 8 is our first job. The 15 has to wait.

So 224 goes where the box was. The plus 15 is still there.
Now the plus. 224 plus 15 is 239.
Careful with one thing. The 15 is not part of the times. It is only added on after the multiplying is done.
So remember: times first, then plus or minus.

So, which bit goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 2 times 8.

Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 79 take away 16.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 79 take away 16 is 63.
And now the plus. 63 plus 4 is 67.
Did you spot the trap? Going left to right from the very start would mean taking away before multiplying, and that gives a different number.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.

board.text: Which number has a digit sum of 23?

beats.say: Let us try the first one, 6855. What do its digits add up to?

ask.ifNot: Add them one at a time: 6 plus 8 plus 5 plus 5. That makes 24.

beats.say: 6 plus 8 plus 5 plus 5 makes 24. That is more than 23, so not this one.

Find the H C F of 72 and 60. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 72 and 60 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both: that is our target. To find it, we split each number into prime factors, its building blocks.
Take 72. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 three times, then 3, and 3 is left. So 72 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 3.
Take 60. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 twice, then 3, and 5 is left. So 60 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 72 and 60 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have two 2s and a 3. Careful: 72 has three 2s, but 60 has only two 2s. So only two 2s are shared.
The middle of the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 2 times 3 is 12. So the H C F is 12.

spec.note: The middle holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 72 divided by 12 is 6, and 60 divided by 12 is 5, with nothing left over. And 6 and 5 share no factor except 1, so nothing bigger works.
So the plan for an H C F of bigger numbers: break both into primes, keep only the primes they share, and multiply those. Your turn next!
Three signs in one sum: a minus, a times and a plus. The trick is knowing where to start.
Where do we begin?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 2 times 7.

2 times 7 is 14. Write 14 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Just a minus and a plus now. Which one comes first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 69 take away 14.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 69 take away 14 is 55.
One job left, the plus. 55 and 1 make 56.
Did you spot the trap? Going left to right from the very start would mean taking away before multiplying, and that gives a different number.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.

We need the H C F of 65 and 91. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both, with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 65?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 65, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. These numbers have only a few factors, so we list every factor of each one. Then we look for the biggest number in both lists.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 65: 1 times 65 and 5 times 13. So the factors of 65 are 1, 5, 13 and 65.
Do the same for 91. The pairs are 1 times 91 and 7 times 13. That gives the factors of 91: 1, 7, 13 and 91.
Now look along both lists. Which is the biggest number that is in both of them?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 13. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 13. Careful: 65 is in its own list, but it does not divide 91, so it is out.
The picture shows it too: the shared factors sit in the middle. So the H C F of 65 and 91 is 13.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 65 divided by 13 is 5, and 91 divided by 13 is 7. Nothing is left over either time.
So the plan for an H C F like this one: list the factors of each number, find the ones in both lists, and take the biggest. Your turn next!
Find the H C F of 6 and 4. H C F means highest common factor: the biggest number that divides both 6 and 4 exactly.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 4?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 4, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: So how do we find it? We write down all the factors of each number. Then we pick the biggest one they share.

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 2. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 2. Careful: 4 is in its own list, but it does not divide 6, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 2, so the H C F is 2.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 4 divided by 2 is 2. Nothing is left over either time.
That is the whole method. Write both lists of factors, look for the numbers in both, and the biggest of those is the H C F.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a divide, a plus and a times.

Look at 89956. We want to compare two digits: the 9 in the thousands place and the 5 in the tens place.

board.text: In 89956: (9 in thousands) is ? times (5 in tens)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 9 sits in the thousands place, so it is worth 9000.

Now the 5 in the tens place. That seat is worth 10, so 5 times 10 is 50.

Priya has 136 marbles and splits them into two groups, in the ratio 3 to 5. We want the larger group.

board.text: Priya shares 136 marbles in the ratio 3 : 5

beats.say: A ratio of 3 to 5 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One group gets 3 parts and the other gets 5.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One group has 3 parts and the other has 5. Put them together, so add: 3 plus 5.

beats.say: 3 plus 5 is 8. There are 8 equal parts.
Now share 136 into 8 equal parts. 136 divided by 8 is 17. So one part is 17.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the larger group. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The larger group goes with the larger number of the ratio. Of 3 and 5, that is 5.

beats.say: 5 parts of 17 each. 5 times 17 is 85. So the larger group is 85 marbles.
Let us check. The other group is 3 parts, which is 51. And 51 plus 85 is 136. Nothing is lost.

Find the L C M of 16 and 9. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we looking for?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

ask.ifNot: Try dividing each one by 9. It only goes in exactly when we reach 144.
