Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a plus and a times.
Where do we begin?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus, even though the plus is written first. So we begin with 2 times 4.

beats.say: Times goes before plus, so put a box round 2 times 4.
2 times 4 is 8. Write 8 in its place, and copy the rest just as it was.
Now the plus. 20 plus 8 is 28.
Careful with the trap here. Adding 20 and 2 first, just because they come first, gives a different number. The 2 belongs to the times.
So remember: times first, then the plus.
One of these numbers has digits that add up to 25. Digit sum just means we add the digits together.

board.text: Which number has a digit sum of 25?

beats.say: Let us try the first one, 968. What do its digits add up to?

ask.ifNot: Add them one at a time: 9 plus 6 plus 8. That makes 23.

beats.say: 9 plus 6 plus 8 makes 23. That is less than 25, so not this one.
Next, 898. 8 plus 9 plus 8 makes 25. There it is, 25!
Then 634. 6 plus 3 plus 4 makes 13. That is less than 25, so not this one.
Then 720. 7 plus 2 plus 0 makes 9. That is less than 25, so not this one.
So the number with a digit sum of 25 is 898.
A tip for next time: a zero adds nothing, so you can skip over it. And check every choice, so nothing surprises you.
This is 22049. Let us find out how much the 2 in the thousands place stands for.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Careful: 22049 has more than one 2. We only want the one sitting in the thousands place.
Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens, hundreds and thousands.

board.text: From right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands

beats.say: Our 2 is in the thousands seat. What is the thousands place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. The thousands place is worth 1000.

beats.say: To get the place value, we multiply the digit by the worth of its seat. That is 2 times 1000.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 2 times 1000 is 2000. So this 2 is worth 2000.
Careful: 2 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 2000.
A quick check: 2000 is 2 followed by 3 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So the plan is: find the seat, then multiply the digit by the worth of that seat.
Here is 19741. Two digits are marked: the 7 in the hundreds place and the 1 in the units place. We must compare what they are worth.

board.text: In 19741: (7 in hundreds) is ? times (1 in units)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 7 in the hundreds place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 7 sits in the hundreds place, so it is worth 700.

beats.say: The hundreds place is worth 100, and 7 times 100 is 700.
Now the 1 in the units place. That seat is worth just 1, so this 1 is worth 1.
Now, how many times. That asks how many lots of 1 fit into 700. Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 1 fit into 700, and that is a division.

beats.say: Dividing by 1 changes nothing. So 700 divided by 1 is 700.
So the 7 in the hundreds place is worth 700 times the 1 in the units place.
Check by multiplying back: 1 times 700 is 700. It works.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second.
195 is cut into two shares, in the ratio 5 to 8. We want the smaller one.
A ratio of 5 to 8 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One share gets 5 parts and the other gets 8.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One share has 5 parts and the other has 8. Put them together, so add: 5 plus 8.

beats.say: 5 plus 8 is 13. There are 13 equal parts.
Now share 195 into 13 equal parts. 195 divided by 13 is 15. So one part is 15.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the smaller share. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The smaller share goes with the smaller number of the ratio. Of 5 and 8, that is 5.

beats.say: 5 parts of 15 each. 5 times 15 is 75. So the smaller share is 75.
Let us check. The other share is 8 parts, which is 120. And 75 plus 120 is 195. Nothing is lost.
Three small steps every time. Count the parts. Find one part. Multiply by the parts you need.
75 toffees, two groups, in the ratio 1 to 4. Let us find how many are in the larger group.

board.text: Meera shares 75 toffees in the ratio 1 : 4

beats.say: A ratio of 1 to 4 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One group gets 1 part and the other gets 4.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One group has 1 part and the other has 4. Put them together, so add: 1 plus 4.

beats.say: 1 plus 4 is 5. There are 5 equal parts.
Now share 75 into 5 equal parts. 75 divided by 5 is 15. So one part is 15.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the larger group. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The larger group goes with the larger number of the ratio. Of 1 and 4, that is 4.

beats.say: 4 parts of 15 each. 4 times 15 is 60. So the larger group is 60 toffees.
Let us check. The other group is 1 part, which is 15. And 15 plus 60 is 75. Nothing is lost.
Three small steps every time. Count the parts. Find one part. Multiply by the parts you need.
Find the H C F of 26 and 91. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 26 and 91 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both: that is our target. Let's write down every factor of each number.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 26: 1 times 26 and 2 times 13. So the factors of 26 are 1, 2, 13 and 26.
Now 91. Its pairs are 1 times 91 and 7 times 13. So the factors of 91 are 1, 7, 13 and 91.
Here is the important part. Run a finger along both lists. What is the biggest number that shows up in both?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 13. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 13. Careful: 26 is in its own list, but it does not divide 91, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 13, so the H C F is 13.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 26 divided by 13 is 2, and 91 divided by 13 is 7. Nothing is left over either time.
So the plan for an H C F like this one: list the factors of each number, find the ones in both lists, and take the biggest. Your turn next!
Find the L C M of 4 and 12. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: Look closely at these two numbers. 12 is in the 4 times table: 4 times 3 is 12.
So where do the two tables first meet?

ask.ifNot: 12 is the very first number in its own table, and we just saw it is in the 4 times table too. So the two tables first meet at 12.

beats.say: Here are both tables. 12 is in each of them. Nothing smaller can be, because 12 is where its own table starts. So the L C M is 12.
One trap to watch for: do not just multiply them. 4 times 12 is 48. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one.
So here is a shortcut worth keeping. When one number is a multiple of the other, the bigger number is the L C M straight away.
Two ratios are equal here. 6 to 10 is the same as 18 to x. Our job is to find x.
Equal ratios are made by multiplying both numbers by the same number. So look at the two first numbers, 6 and 18.
What was 6 multiplied by to become 18?

ask.ifNot: Say the 6 times table until you reach 18. 6 times 3 is 18.

beats.say: 6 times 3 is 18. So the multiplier is 3.
Careful here. We do not add anything. The second number, 10, must be multiplied by the very same 3.
10 times 3 is 30. So x is 30.
Let us check. 6 to 10 became 18 to 30. Both numbers were multiplied by 3, so the two ratios are equal.
So with equal ratios, find the multiplier from the pair you know, then use it on the other pair.
150 is cut into two shares, in the ratio 3 to 7. We want the smaller one.
A ratio of 3 to 7 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One share gets 3 parts and the other gets 7.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One share has 3 parts and the other has 7. Put them together, so add: 3 plus 7.

beats.say: 3 plus 7 is 10. There are 10 equal parts.
Now share 150 into 10 equal parts. 150 divided by 10 is 15. So one part is 15.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the smaller share. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The smaller share goes with the smaller number of the ratio. Of 3 and 7, that is 3.

beats.say: 3 parts of 15 each. 3 times 15 is 45. So the smaller share is 45.
Let us check. The other share is 7 parts, which is 105. And 45 plus 105 is 150. Nothing is lost.
Three small steps every time. Count the parts. Find one part. Multiply by the parts you need.
Find the H C F of 16 and 20. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 16 and 20 exactly.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number that goes into both. These numbers have only a few factors, so let's list them all.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 16: 1 times 16, 2 times 8 and 4 times 4. So the factors of 16 are 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16.
Do the same for 20. The pairs are 1 times 20, 2 times 10 and 4 times 5. That gives the factors of 20: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10 and 20.
Now look along both lists. Which is the biggest number that is in both of them?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1, 2 and 4. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 4. Careful: 16 is in its own list, but it does not divide 20, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 4, so the H C F is 4.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 16 divided by 4 is 4, and 20 divided by 4 is 5. Nothing is left over either time.
So the plan for an H C F like this one: list the factors of each number, find the ones in both lists, and take the biggest. Your turn next!
Neha has 85 toffees and splits them into two groups, in the ratio 1 to 4. We want the larger group.

board.text: Neha shares 85 toffees in the ratio 1 : 4

beats.say: A ratio of 1 to 4 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One group gets 1 part and the other gets 4.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One group has 1 part and the other has 4. Put them together, so add: 1 plus 4.

beats.say: 1 plus 4 is 5. There are 5 equal parts.
Now share 85 into 5 equal parts. 85 divided by 5 is 17. So one part is 17.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the larger group. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The larger group goes with the larger number of the ratio. Of 1 and 4, that is 4.

beats.say: 4 parts of 17 each. 4 times 17 is 68. So the larger group is 68 toffees.
Let us check. The other group is 1 part, which is 17. And 17 plus 68 is 85. Nothing is lost.
Three small steps every time. Count the parts. Find one part. Multiply by the parts you need.
30 is cut into two shares, in the ratio 2 to 3. We want the smaller one.
A ratio of 2 to 3 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One share gets 2 parts and the other gets 3.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One share has 2 parts and the other has 3. Put them together, so add: 2 plus 3.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 is 5. There are 5 equal parts.
Now share 30 into 5 equal parts. 30 divided by 5 is 6. So one part is 6.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the smaller share. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The smaller share goes with the smaller number of the ratio. Of 2 and 3, that is 2.

beats.say: 2 parts of 6 each. 2 times 6 is 12. So the smaller share is 12.
Let us check. The other share is 3 parts, which is 18. And 12 plus 18 is 30. Nothing is lost.
So for sharing in a ratio: add to count the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for the share you want.
Let's put it on the board. 2 x, minus 10, equals 12. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
2 x means 2 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 2, then took away 10, and got 12.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance. To find x we work backwards, and undo the last thing first. Which was done last?

ask.ifNot: Read it from left to right. First x was multiplied by 2. After that came the minus 10. So the minus 10 was last, and we undo it first.

beats.say: We undo taking away by adding. So I add 10 to both sides, and the balance stays level.
On the left, only 2 x is left. On the right, 12 plus 10 is 22. So 2 x equals 22.
Careful: 22 is one of the choices, but 22 is 2 x, not x. So, what undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2. 2 times 10 is 20, and one more 2 makes 22. So 22 divided by 2 is 11.
So x equals 11. The mystery is solved.
Good mathematicians always check. 2 times 11 is 22, and 22 minus 10 is 12. Both sides match.
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a plus and a times.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: It is tempting to start on the left. But multiplying always goes before adding, so 8 times 4 is our first job.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding. So we box the 8 times 4. It goes first.
8 times 4 is 32. Write 32 in its place, and copy the rest just as it was.
One job left, the adding. 30 and 32 make 62.
Careful with the trap here. Adding 30 and 8 first, just because they come first, gives a different number. The 8 belongs to the times.
The rule: multiply before you add, wherever the times sign sits.
Look at 97486. Our job is to find what the 7 in the thousands place is really worth.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens, hundreds and thousands.

board.text: From right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands

beats.say: Our 7 sits in the thousands place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. The thousands place is worth 1000.

beats.say: Place value is the digit times what its seat is worth. So we multiply 7 by 1000.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 7 times 1000 is 7000. So this 7 is worth 7000.
Careful: 7 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 7000.
A quick check: 7000 is 7 followed by 3 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So remember: find the seat, then multiply the digit by what the seat is worth.
Look at 67666. We want to compare two digits: the 6 in the units place and the 6 in the tens place.

board.text: In 67666: (6 in units) is ? times (6 in tens)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 6 in the units place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 6 sits in the units place, so it is worth 6.

beats.say: The units place is worth just 1, so this 6 is worth 6.
Now the 6 in the tens place. That seat is worth 10, so 6 times 10 is 60.
How many times means we divide the first value by the second. Which sum is that?

ask.ifNot: The question starts with the 6 in the units place, so its value goes first: 6 divided by 60.

beats.say: 6 is smaller than 60, so the answer is less than 1. 60 is 10 times 6, so 6 is one tenth of 60. One tenth is written 0.1.
So the 6 in the units place is worth only 0.1 times the 6 in the tens place. It is the smaller one!
Check: one tenth of 60 is 6. It works.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second. And each seat is worth 10 times the seat on its right.
Let's put it on the board. 2 x, plus 19, equals 31. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
2 x means 2 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 2, then added 19, and got 31.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the plus 19. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 19, we take away 19.

beats.say: So 19 comes off. But if we did that on one side only, the balance would tip. So we do it to both sides.
On the left, only 2 x is left. On the right, 31 minus 19 is 12. So 2 x equals 12.
Don't stop here! 12 is in the list of answers, but it is what 2 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2. 2 times 6 is 12, so 12 divided by 2 is 6.
So x equals 6. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. 2 times 6 is 12, and 12 plus 19 is 31. Both sides match.
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Let's put it on the board. 7 x, plus 13, equals 83. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
7 x means 7 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 7, then added 13, and got 83.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance. To find x we work backwards, and undo the last thing first. Which was done last?

ask.ifNot: Read it from left to right. First x was multiplied by 7. After that came the plus 13. So the plus 13 was last, and we undo it first.

beats.say: We undo adding by taking away. So I take 13 from both sides, and the balance stays level.
Now the left side is just 7 x. And 83 minus 13 makes 70. So 7 times x is 70.
Don't stop here! 70 is in the list of answers, but it is what 7 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 7, we divide by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7. 7 times 10 is 70, so 70 divided by 7 is 10.
So x equals 10. The mystery is solved.
Let's check. Put 10 in place of x. 7 times 10 is 70, and 70 plus 13 is 83. It works!
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Let's put it on the board. 7 x, plus 8, equals 43. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
7 x means 7 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 7, then added 8, and got 43.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance, and every move must keep it level. What should our first move be?

ask.ifNot: We undo the last thing first, and that is the plus 8. Its opposite is taking away 8. The dividing comes after that.

beats.say: To undo plus 8, we take away 8. And to keep the balance level, we do it to both sides.
On the left, only 7 x is left. On the right, 43 minus 8 is 35. So 7 x equals 35.
Careful: 35 is one of the choices, but 35 is 7 x, not x. So, what undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 7, we divide by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7. 7 times 5 is 35, so 35 divided by 7 is 5.
So x equals 5. There is our hidden number!
Let's check. Put 5 in place of x. 7 times 5 is 35, and 35 plus 8 is 43. It works!
Every equation like this works the same way. Undo the last thing first, and keep both sides level.
Let's put it on the board. 5 x, plus 19, equals 59. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
5 x means 5 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 5, then added 19, and got 59.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the plus 19. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 19, we take away 19.

beats.say: And the rule of the balance is: what we do to one side, we do to the other. So I write minus 19 under both.
On the left, only 5 x is left. On the right, 59 minus 19 is 40. So 5 x equals 40.
Don't stop here! 40 is in the list of answers, but it is what 5 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 5. 5 times 8 is 40, so 40 divided by 5 is 8.
So x equals 8. There is our hidden number!
Let's check. Put 8 in place of x. 5 times 8 is 40, and 40 plus 19 is 59. It works!
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a plus and a times.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus, even though the plus is written first. So we begin with 6 times 4.

beats.say: Times goes before plus, so put a box round 6 times 4.
6 times 4 is 24. So 24 goes where the box was, and the rest stays the same.
Now the plus. 26 plus 24 is 50.
Careful with the trap here. Adding 26 and 6 first, just because they come first, gives a different number. The 6 belongs to the times.
The rule: multiply before you add, wherever the times sign sits.
We need the H C F of 30 and 45. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both, with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 30?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 30, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. These numbers have only a few factors, so we list every factor of each one. Then we look for the biggest number in both lists.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 30: 1 times 30, 2 times 15, 3 times 10 and 5 times 6. So the factors of 30 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15 and 30.
Now 45. Its pairs are 1 times 45, 3 times 15 and 5 times 9. So the factors of 45 are 1, 3, 5, 9, 15 and 45.
Here is the important part. Run a finger along both lists. What is the biggest number that shows up in both?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1, 3, 5 and 15. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 15. Careful: 30 is in its own list, but it does not divide 45, so it is out.
The picture shows it too: the shared factors sit in the middle. So the H C F of 30 and 45 is 15.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 30 divided by 15 is 2, and 45 divided by 15 is 3. Nothing is left over either time.
That is the whole method. Write both lists of factors, look for the numbers in both, and the biggest of those is the H C F.
Look at 90447. We want to compare two digits: the 9 in the ten-thousands place and the 4 in the tens place.

board.text: In 90447: (9 in ten-thousands) is ? times (4 in tens)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 9 in the ten-thousands place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 9 sits in the ten-thousands place, so it is worth 90000.

beats.say: The ten-thousands place is worth 10000, and 9 times 10000 is 90000.
Now the 4 in the tens place. That seat is worth 10, so 4 times 10 is 40.
How many times means: how many lots of 40 fit into 90000? Which sum finds that?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 40 fit into 90000, and that is a division.

beats.say: A neat trick: cross off the same number of zeros from both. Here that is 1 zero from each, leaving 9000 divided by 4.
Dividing by 4 is halving twice. Half of 9000 is 4500, and half of 4500 is 2250.
So the 9 in the ten-thousands place is worth 2250 times the 4 in the tens place.
Good mathematicians check. 40 times 2250 takes us back to 90000.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a divide, a plus and a times.
One of these three signs has to wait until the very end. Which one?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times both go before plus. So the plus is the one that waits until the end.

beats.say: Dividing and multiplying go before adding. So we box 18 divided by 2, and we box 2 times 2.
First box. 18 divided by 2 is 9, because 2 times 9 is 18.
Second box. 2 times 2 is 4.
Put each answer where its box was, with the plus still in between.
Now the plus gets its turn. 9 plus 4 is 13.
Careful with the trap. Do not add in the middle first. The plus joins the two boxes, so it comes last.
So remember: divide and multiply first, then add.
Look at 71411. Our job is to find what the 1 in the thousands place is really worth.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Careful: 71411 has more than one 1. We only want the one sitting in the thousands place.
Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens, hundreds and thousands.

board.text: From right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands

beats.say: Our 1 is in the thousands seat. What is the thousands place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. The thousands place is worth 1000.

beats.say: To get the place value, we multiply the digit by the worth of its seat. That is 1 times 1000.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 1 times 1000 is just 1000. So this 1 is worth 1000.
Careful: 1 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 1000.
A quick check: 1000 is 1 followed by 3 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So the plan is: find the seat, then multiply the digit by the worth of that seat.
Let's put it on the board. 6 x, plus 5, equals 17. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
6 x means 6 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 6, then added 5, and got 17.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the plus 5. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 5, we take away 5.

beats.say: And the rule of the balance is: what we do to one side, we do to the other. So I write minus 5 under both.
On the left, only 6 x is left. On the right, 17 minus 5 is 12. So 6 x equals 12.
Don't stop here! 12 is in the list of answers, but it is what 6 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 6?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 6, we divide by 6.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 6. 6 times 2 is 12, so 12 divided by 6 is 2.
That means x is 2. We found the number that was hiding.
Let's check. Put 2 in place of x. 6 times 2 is 12, and 12 plus 5 is 17. It works!
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Find the L C M of 12 and 5. L C M means lowest common multiple: the first number that both 12 and 5 reach when you count up in their tables.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 12?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 12 is 12 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 12, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: Counting up in 5s would take a long time. Here is a quicker way: count up in the bigger number, 12, and test each one.
Which is the first number in the list that 5 divides exactly?

ask.ifNot: A number in the 5 times table ends in 0 or 5. Look along the list for the first one that does.

beats.say: Numbers in the 5 times table end in 0 or 5, and 60 is the first in our list that does. And yes, 5 times 12 is 60. So the L C M is 60.
Let's check. 60 divided by 12 is 5, and 60 divided by 5 is 12. Both divide exactly.
Did you notice? The L C M is just 12 times 5. That happens when the two numbers share no factor except 1.
Remember the trick: write the multiples of the bigger number, and test each with the smaller one. The first that works is the L C M.
Let's put it on the board. 7 x, minus 2, equals 82. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
7 x means 7 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 7, then took away 2, and got 82.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance. To find x we work backwards, and undo the last thing first. Which was done last?

ask.ifNot: Read it from left to right. First x was multiplied by 7. After that came the minus 2. So the minus 2 was last, and we undo it first.

beats.say: We undo taking away by adding. So I add 2 to both sides, and the balance stays level.
On the left, only 7 x is left. On the right, 82 plus 2 is 84. So 7 x equals 84.
Don't stop here! 84 is in the list of answers, but it is what 7 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 7, we divide by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7. 7 times 10 is 70. That leaves 14, and 7 times 2 is 14. So 84 divided by 7 is 10 and 2 more, which is 12.
That means x is 12. We found the number that was hiding.
Good mathematicians always check. 7 times 12 is 84, and 84 minus 2 is 82. Both sides match.
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a plus and a times.
Where do we begin?

ask.ifNot: It is tempting to start on the left. But multiplying always goes before adding, so 7 times 4 is our first job.

beats.say: Times goes before plus, so put a box round 7 times 4.
7 times 4 is 28. So 28 goes where the box was, and the rest stays the same.
One job left, the adding. 20 and 28 make 48.
Careful with the trap here. Adding 20 and 7 first, just because they come first, gives a different number. The 7 belongs to the times.
The rule: multiply before you add, wherever the times sign sits.
Find the H C F of 24 and 60. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 24 and 60 exactly.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number that goes into both. Listing every factor would be slow, so we break each number into prime factors instead.
24 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 24 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3.
60 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 60 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 24 and 60 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have two 2s and a 3. Careful: 24 has three 2s, but 60 has only two 2s. So only two 2s are shared.
The middle of the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 2 times 3 is 12. So the H C F is 12.

spec.note: The middle holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 24 divided by 12 is 2, and 60 divided by 12 is 5. Both divide exactly, and 2 and 5 have nothing more in common.
Remember the three moves: split into primes, ring what is shared, multiply. And the H C F is never bigger than the smaller number.
We need the H C F of 55 and 44. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both, with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 44?

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 44, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. These numbers have only a few factors, so we list every factor of each one. Then we look for the biggest number in both lists.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 55: 1 times 55 and 5 times 11. So the factors of 55 are 1, 5, 11 and 55.
Do the same for 44. The pairs are 1 times 44, 2 times 22 and 4 times 11. That gives the factors of 44: 1, 2, 4, 11, 22 and 44.
Here is the important part. Run a finger along both lists. What is the biggest number that shows up in both?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 11. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 11. Careful: 44 is in its own list, but it does not divide 55, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 11, so the H C F is 11.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Let's check. 55 divided by 11 is 5, and 44 divided by 11 is 4. Nothing is left over either time.
So the plan for an H C F like this one: list the factors of each number, find the ones in both lists, and take the biggest. Your turn next!
Look at this one. 4 x, minus 8, equals 20. Our job is to find the number that x stands for.
When a number sits next to x, it means times. So x was multiplied by 4, then someone took away 8, and the answer was 20.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance. To find x we work backwards, and undo the last thing first. Which was done last?

ask.ifNot: Read it from left to right. First x was multiplied by 4. After that came the minus 8. So the minus 8 was last, and we undo it first.

beats.say: We undo taking away by adding. So I add 8 to both sides, and the balance stays level.
On the left, only 4 x is left. On the right, 20 plus 8 is 28. So 4 x equals 28.
Don't stop here! 28 is in the list of answers, but it is what 4 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 4?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 4, we divide by 4.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 4. 4 times 7 is 28, so 28 divided by 4 is 7.
So x equals 7. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. 4 times 7 is 28, and 28 minus 8 is 20. Both sides match.
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Here is 69697. Two digits are marked: the 9 in the thousands place and the 6 in the hundreds place. We must compare what they are worth.

board.text: In 69697: (9 in thousands) is ? times (6 in hundreds)

spec.note: Compare the two marked digits

beats.say: Start with the 9 in the thousands place. What is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right. This 9 sits in the thousands place, so it is worth 9000.

beats.say: The thousands place is worth 1000, and 9 times 1000 is 9000.
Now the 6 in the hundreds place. That seat is worth 100, so 6 times 100 is 600.
Now, how many times. That asks how many lots of 600 fit into 9000. Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: Taking away tells us how much more. How many times asks how many lots of 600 fit into 9000, and that is a division.

beats.say: A neat trick: cross off the same number of zeros from both. Here that is 2 zeros from each, leaving 90 divided by 6.
6 times 15 is 90. So 90 divided by 6 is 15.
So the 9 in the thousands place is worth 15 times the 6 in the hundreds place.
Good mathematicians check. 600 times 15 takes us back to 9000.
So the plan: find what each digit is worth, then divide the first by the second.
Here is our number, 62121. We want the place value of the 1 in the hundreds place.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Careful: 62121 has more than one 1. We only want the one sitting in the hundreds place.
Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens and hundreds.
Our 1 sits in the hundreds place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens and hundreds. The hundreds place is worth 100.

beats.say: Place value is the digit times what its seat is worth. So we multiply 1 by 100.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 1 times 100 is just 100. So this 1 is worth 100.
Careful: 1 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 100.
A quick check: 100 is 1 followed by 2 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So remember: find the seat, then multiply the digit by what the seat is worth.
Here is our equation. 2 x, minus 4, equals 2. The x is a hidden number, and we are going to find it.
2 x means 2 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 2, then took away 4, and got 2.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance, and every move must keep it level. What should our first move be?

ask.ifNot: We undo the last thing first, and that is the minus 4. Its opposite is adding 4. The dividing comes after that.

beats.say: The opposite of minus 4 is plus 4. What we do to one side, we do to the other, so I write it under both.
Now the left side is just 2 x. And 2 plus 4 makes 6. So 2 times x is 6.
Careful: 6 is one of the choices, but 6 is 2 x, not x. So, what undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2. 2 times 3 is 6, so 6 divided by 2 is 3.
So x equals 3. There is our hidden number!
Let's check. Put 3 in place of x. 2 times 3 is 6, and 6 minus 4 is 2. It works!
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Here is our equation. 2 x, plus 1, equals 9. The x is a hidden number, and we are going to find it.
2 x means 2 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 2, then added 1, and got 9.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance, and every move must keep it level. What should our first move be?

ask.ifNot: We undo the last thing first, and that is the plus 1. Its opposite is taking away 1. The dividing comes after that.

beats.say: To undo plus 1, we take away 1. And to keep the balance level, we do it to both sides.
On the left, only 2 x is left. On the right, 9 minus 1 is 8. So 2 x equals 8.
Careful: 8 is one of the choices, but 8 is 2 x, not x. So, what undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2. 2 times 4 is 8, so 8 divided by 2 is 4.
That means x is 4. We found the number that was hiding.
Good mathematicians always check. 2 times 4 is 8, and 8 plus 1 is 9. Both sides match.
So the plan is to work backwards. First undo the adding or taking away. Then undo the times.
Here is our number, 66933. We want the place value of the 6 in the ten-thousands place.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Careful: 66933 has more than one 6. We only want the one sitting in the ten-thousands place.
Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands.

board.text: From right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands

beats.say: Our 6 sits in the ten-thousands place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands. The ten-thousands place is worth 10000.

beats.say: Place value is the digit times what its seat is worth. So we multiply 6 by 10000.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 6 times 10000 is 60000. So this 6 is worth 60000.
Careful: 6 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 60000.
A quick check: 60000 is 6 followed by 4 zeros, one for each seat to its right. So the plan is: find the seat, then multiply the digit by the worth of that seat.
Find the L C M of 14 and 6. L C M means lowest common multiple: the first number that both 14 and 6 reach when you count up in their tables.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 14?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of 14 is 14 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 14, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: The simplest way is to count up in both tables until they meet. Count up in 14s: 14, 28, 42.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 14 and 6?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 42 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: There it is. 42 is the first number in both lists, so the L C M is 42.
Let's check. 42 divided by 14 is 3, and 42 divided by 6 is 7. Both divide exactly, so 42 really is a multiple of each.
One trap to watch for. Multiplying 14 by 6 gives 84. That is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 42 gets there first.
So for an L C M: count up in both tables, and the first number in both is the answer. Your turn next!
Here is our sum. Two signs in it: a times and a minus.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus. So 16 times 9 is our first job. The 10 has to wait.

beats.say: Times always goes before plus and minus. This time it is also first in line, so we start on the left.
16 times 9. 10 times 9 is 90, and 6 times 9 is 54. Together that makes 144.
So 144 goes where the box was. The minus 10 is still there.
Now the minus. 144 take away 10 is 134.
Careful with one thing. The 10 is not part of the times. It is only taken away after the multiplying is done.
So remember: times first, then plus or minus.
Look at this one. 5 x, minus 4, equals 56. Our job is to find the number that x stands for.
When a number sits next to x, it means times. So x was multiplied by 5, then someone took away 4, and the answer was 56.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the minus 4. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo minus 4, we add 4.

beats.say: So 4 goes on. But if we did that on one side only, the balance would tip. So we do it to both sides.
Now the left side is just 5 x. And 56 plus 4 makes 60. So 5 times x is 60.
Don't stop here! 60 is in the list of answers, but it is what 5 x is worth, not x. What undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 5. 5 times 10 is 50. That leaves 10, and 5 times 2 is 10. So 60 divided by 5 is 10 and 2 more, which is 12.
That means x is 12. We found the number that was hiding.
Good mathematicians always check. 5 times 12 is 60, and 60 minus 4 is 56. Both sides match.
Every equation like this works the same way. Undo the last thing first, and keep both sides level.
Find the H C F of 12 and 10. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 12 and 10 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both: that is our target. Let's write down every factor of each number.
Factors come in pairs that multiply to make 12: 1 times 12, 2 times 6 and 3 times 4. So the factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
Now 10. Its pairs are 1 times 10 and 2 times 5. So the factors of 10 are 1, 2, 5 and 10.
Here is the important part. Run a finger along both lists. What is the biggest number that shows up in both?

ask.ifNot: It has to be in both lists, not just one. Check each number against the other list, and take the biggest one that is in both.

beats.say: The numbers in both lists are 1 and 2. These are the common factors, and the biggest is 2. Careful: 10 is in its own list, but it does not divide 12, so it is out.
In the picture, the middle part holds the factors they share. The biggest one there is 2, so the H C F is 2.

spec.note: The middle holds the common factors.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 12 divided by 2 is 6, and 10 divided by 2 is 5. Both divide exactly.
Remember the three moves: list the factors, spot the common ones, pick the biggest. And the H C F is never bigger than the smaller number.
Here is our number, 93939. We want the place value of the 3 in the tens place.

spec.note: How much is the marked digit worth?

beats.say: Careful: 93939 has more than one 3. We only want the one sitting in the tens place.
Every digit has a seat. Counting from the right, the seats are ones, tens and hundreds.
Our 3 sits in the tens place. How much is that place worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the seats from the right once more: ones, tens and hundreds. The tens place is worth 10.

beats.say: To get the place value, we multiply the digit by the worth of its seat. That is 3 times 10.

board.text: Place value = digit × value of its place

beats.say: 3 times 10 is 30. So this 3 is worth 30.
Careful: 3 by itself is only the face value. The place value also counts the seat, and that is why we get 30.
A quick check: 30 is 3 followed by 1 zero, one for each seat to its right. So remember: find the seat, then multiply the digit by what the seat is worth.
Here is our sum. It has three signs in it: a minus, a times and a plus.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Times goes before plus and minus, even when it sits in the middle. So we begin with 3 times 9.

beats.say: Times is the boss here. It goes before plus and minus, so put a box round 3 times 9.
3 times 9 is 27. Write 27 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Just a minus and a plus now. Which one comes first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 27 take away 27.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 27 take away 27 leaves nothing at all. That is 0.
And now the plus. 0 plus 1 is 1.
Did you spot the trap? Going left to right from the very start would mean taking away before multiplying, and that gives a different number.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Look at the signs here. A minus, then a times, then a plus.
Which part do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: It is tempting to start on the left. But multiplying always goes first, so 2 times 5 is our first job.

beats.say: Multiplying goes before adding and taking away. So we box the 2 times 5. It goes first.
2 times 5 is 10. Write 10 in its place, and copy everything else just as it was.
Now only a minus and a plus are left. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we go from left to right, just like reading. The minus comes first: 35 take away 10.

beats.say: Left to right, just like reading. 35 take away 10 is 25.
One job left, the plus. 25 and 5 make 30.
The trap in this sum is the minus at the front. It looks like the place to start, but the times must go first.
So remember: times first, then plus and minus from left to right.
Let's put it on the board. 8 x, plus 5, equals 29. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
8 x means 8 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 8, then added 5, and got 29.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance. To find x we work backwards, and undo the last thing first. Which was done last?

ask.ifNot: Read it from left to right. First x was multiplied by 8. After that came the plus 5. So the plus 5 was last, and we undo it first.

beats.say: We undo adding by taking away. So I take 5 from both sides, and the balance stays level.
On the left, only 8 x is left. On the right, 29 minus 5 is 24. So 8 x equals 24.
Careful: 24 is one of the choices, but 24 is 8 x, not x. So, what undoes times 8?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 8, we divide by 8.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 8. 8 times 3 is 24, so 24 divided by 8 is 3.
So x equals 3. There is our hidden number!
Let's check. Put 3 in place of x. 8 times 3 is 24, and 24 plus 5 is 29. It works!
Every equation like this works the same way. Undo the last thing first, and keep both sides level.
Let's put it on the board. 6 x, minus 9, equals 21. A number is hiding behind the x. Let's go and find it.
When a number sits next to x, it means times. So x was multiplied by 6, then someone took away 9, and the answer was 21.
Think of a balance. Both sides are worth the same. To get x alone, we first undo the minus 9. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners. Each one undoes the other. So to undo minus 9, we add 9.

beats.say: So 9 goes on. But if we did that on one side only, the balance would tip. So we do it to both sides.
On the left, only 6 x is left. On the right, 21 plus 9 is 30. So 6 x equals 30.
Careful: 30 is one of the choices, but 30 is 6 x, not x. So, what undoes times 6?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 6, we divide by 6.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 6. 6 times 5 is 30, so 30 divided by 6 is 5.
So x equals 5. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. 6 times 5 is 30, and 30 minus 9 is 21. Both sides match.
Remember the order. Clear the plus or minus first, then divide. And do the same to both sides each time.
Kavya has 136 toffees and splits them into two groups, in the ratio 3 to 5. We want the larger group.

board.text: Kavya shares 136 toffees in the ratio 3 : 5

beats.say: A ratio of 3 to 5 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One group gets 3 parts and the other gets 5.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One group has 3 parts and the other has 5. Put them together, so add: 3 plus 5.

beats.say: 3 plus 5 is 8. There are 8 equal parts.
Next, the size of one part. 136 divided by 8 is 17. Each part is 17.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the larger group. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The larger group goes with the larger number of the ratio. Of 3 and 5, that is 5.

beats.say: 5 parts of 17 each. 5 times 17 is 85. So the larger group is 85 toffees.
Let us check. The other group is 3 parts, which is 51. And 51 plus 85 is 136. Nothing is lost.
So for sharing in a ratio: add to count the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for the group you want.
60 books, two groups, in the ratio 1 to 4. Let us find how many are in the larger group.

board.text: Arjun shares 60 books in the ratio 1 : 4

beats.say: A ratio of 1 to 4 means the whole lot is cut into equal parts. One group gets 1 part and the other gets 4.
So first, how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: One group has 1 part and the other has 4. Put them together, so add: 1 plus 4.

beats.say: 1 plus 4 is 5. There are 5 equal parts.
Next, the size of one part. 60 divided by 5 is 12. Each part is 12.
Careful now, this is where slips happen. We want the larger group. How many parts does it have?

ask.ifNot: The larger group goes with the larger number of the ratio. Of 1 and 4, that is 4.

beats.say: 4 parts of 12 each. 4 times 12 is 48. So the larger group is 48 books.
Let us check. The other group is 1 part, which is 12. And 12 plus 48 is 60. Nothing is lost.
So for sharing in a ratio: add to count the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for the group you want.
Here is 44324. We are comparing two 4s: one in the thousands place, and one in the units place.

ask.ifNot: It is 4 in the thousands column, so it stands for 4 lots of 1000. That makes 4000.

beats.say: Here they are in the chart. Start with the 4 in the thousands column. What is it worth?
4 times 1000 is 4000. So that 4 is worth 4000.
Now the other 4 in the units place. There it is worth just itself: 4.

ask.ifNot: 'How many times' asks how many lots of 4 fit into 4000. Fitting in means dividing the place values, not taking away.

beats.say: The question says 'how many times'. So which sum do we need?
4000 divided by 4 is 1000. Both digits are 4, so only their columns make the difference.
Check it by going backwards: 1000 times 4 gives back 4000. It works.
So the 4 in the thousands place is worth 1000 times the 4 in the units place.
Find each place value first, then divide. And when the digits are the same, only their columns matter.
We are hunting for the number whose digits add up to 17. Here are the four to choose from.

ask.ifNot: Digit sum is just what it says. Take each digit of the number and add them all together.

beats.say: First, what does 'digit sum' ask us to do?
So we test the numbers one at a time. A tip: a zero adds nothing, so you can skip straight over any zeros.
Try 97045. 9 plus 7 plus 0 plus 4 plus 5 makes 25. That is too big, so we cross it out.
Take 74821. 7 plus 4 plus 8 plus 2 plus 1 makes 22. Not 17 either, so out it goes.
Look at 10784. 1 plus 0 plus 7 plus 8 plus 4 makes 20, which is too big. Cross it out.

ask.ifNot: Go one digit at a time: 6, 4, 4, 0, 3. Keep a running total as you go.

beats.say: Now 64403. Add its digits yourself before I do. What do you get?
6 plus 4 plus 4 plus 0 plus 3 makes 17. We have found it!
So the number with a digit sum of 17 is 64403.
Digit sum means add the digits, nothing more. Test each choice calmly and cross out the ones that miss.
This is 13773. One of its digits, the 7 in the tens place, has a value for us to find.
Count the columns from the right: units, tens. Careful, this number has more than one 7. We want the one in the tens column.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called tens, so each one in it stands for 10.

beats.say: A digit in the tens column counts tens. So what is each one in that column worth?
Our digit says there are 7 of those. 7 times 10 makes 70.
Careful: 7 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 70. The zero on the end is there because 1 more place sits to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 10000 plus 3000 plus 700 plus 70 plus 3. There is our 70, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 7 in the tens place is 70.
So, find the column, then multiply the digit by what the column is worth. That works for any number.
Let's write 99035 on the board. Two digits matter here: the 9 in the ten-thousands place and the 3 in the tens place.

ask.ifNot: It is 9 in the ten-thousands column, so it stands for 9 lots of 10000. That makes 90000.

beats.say: Here they are in the chart. Start with the 9 in the ten-thousands column. What is it worth?
9 times 10000 is 90000. So that 9 is worth 90000.
Now the 3 in the tens place. 3 times 10 is 30.

ask.ifNot: 'How many times' asks how many lots of 30 fit into 90000. Fitting in means dividing the place values, not taking away.

beats.say: The question says 'how many times'. So which sum do we need?
90000 divided by 30 is 3000.
Good mathematicians check. 3000 times 30 is 90000, just as it should be.
So the 9 in the ten-thousands place is worth 3000 times the 3 in the tens place.
The plan: find each place value first, then divide. Never just divide the digits as they look.
One of these four numbers has a digit sum of 22. Let's find out which.

ask.ifNot: Digit sum is just what it says. Take each digit of the number and add them all together.

beats.say: First, what does 'digit sum' ask us to do?
So we test the numbers one at a time. A tip: a zero adds nothing, so you can skip straight over any zeros.

ask.ifNot: Go one digit at a time: 6, 7, 9, 0. Keep a running total as you go.

beats.say: Start with 6790. Add its digits yourself before I do. What do you get?
6 plus 7 plus 9 plus 0 makes 22. We have found it!
Let's make sure of the others. First 3962. 3 plus 9 plus 6 plus 2 makes 20. That is too small, so we cross it out.
Then 7183. 7 plus 1 plus 8 plus 3 makes 19. Not 22 either, so out it goes.
And last, 9379. 9 plus 3 plus 7 plus 9 makes 28, which is too big. Cross it out.

Remember the order: undo the plus 2 first, then undo the times 4. And every move is made on both sides.

beats.say: The first number in both tables: that is our target. Counting up in 16s and 15s would take a while. So we build the L C M from prime factors instead, the building blocks of each number.
Take 16. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 three times, and 2 is left. So 16 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 2.
Take 15. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 3, and 5 is left. So 15 is 3 times 5.
Here is the important part. Both 16 and 15 must fit inside the L C M. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in either number. Which of these does that?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 16 and all of 15, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: four 2s from 16, and the 3 and the 5 from 15. These two share no prime at all, so every prime goes in.
In the picture, the L C M is everything, counted once. 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 5 is 240. So the L C M is 240.

spec.note: The L C M uses every prime in the picture, once each.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 240 divided by 16 is 15, and 240 divided by 15 is 16, with nothing left over.
So for an L C M with bigger numbers: split both into primes, then take each prime the most times it appears in one number. Multiply, and you are done!
Which of these numbers is divisible by 12? We could do four long divisions. But there is a quicker way: a divisibility rule.
12 is 4 times 3. So what must be true of a number that 12 divides?

ask.ifNot: 2 and 6 overlap, because 6 already has a 2 inside it. But 4 and 3 share nothing, so passing both of those tests means 12 divides the number.

beats.say: Two tests, then. For 4, the last two digits must be in the 4 times table. For 3, the digits must add up to a multiple of 3.

board.text: Rule for 12: pass the 4 test and the 3 test

beats.say: First, 3596. Its last two digits make 96, and 96 is 4 times 24. So it passes the test for 4.
Now the test for 3. 3 plus 5 plus 9 plus 6 makes 23. 23 is 3 times 7, plus 2 left over, so 3596 is out.
Next, 1452. Its last two digits make 52, and 52 is 4 times 13. So it passes the test for 4.
Now the test for 3. 1 plus 4 plus 5 plus 2 makes 12. Is 12 in the 3 times table?

ask.ifNot: 12 is 3 times 4, so yes, it is in the 3 times table.

beats.say: So 1452 passes both tests. Ring it!
A careful mathematician tests the rest too. Now 8879. It ends in 9, so it is odd. 4 will not go into an odd number, so 12 cannot either.
Last one: 1799. It ends in 9, so it is odd. 4 will not go into an odd number, so 12 cannot either.
Only 1452 passed, so that is our answer. And the division agrees: 1452 divided by 12 is 121, with nothing left over.
So for 12, run two tests: the last two digits for 4, and the digit sum for 3. It must pass both.
Find the H C F of 75 and 45. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 75 and 45 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both 75 and 45: that is our target. To find it, we split each number into its prime factors.
75 is odd, so 2 will not go in. Try 3 next, and 3 does go in. Keep splitting, and 75 is 3 times 5 times 5.
45 is odd, so 2 will not go in. Try 3 next, and 3 does go in. Keep splitting, and 45 is 3 times 3 times 5.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 75 and 45 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Ring them on the board. Both lines have a 3 and a 5. Careful: 45 has two 3s, but 75 has only one 3. So only one 3 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 3 times 5 is 15. So the H C F is 15.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 75 divided by 15 is 5, and 45 divided by 15 is 3. Both divide exactly, and 5 and 3 have nothing more in common.
Remember the three moves: split into primes, ring what is shared, multiply. And the H C F is never bigger than the smaller number.
Find the L C M of 18 and 10. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: So we want the first number that both tables reach. We could count up both tables, but with 18 and 10 that is a long walk. Prime factors get us there faster.
Take 18. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, then 3, and 3 is left. So 18 is 2 times 3 times 3.
10 is even, so 2 comes out first. That leaves 5, so 10 is 2 times 5.
Now the key idea. The L C M must contain all of 18 and all of 10. So we take each prime the most times it appears in one number. Which of these builds the L C M?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 18 and all of 10, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: the 2 and two 3s from 18, and the 5 from 10. Careful: we do not add the 2 in 10 on top, because the 2 from 18 already covers it.
In the picture, the L C M is everything, counted once. 2 times 3 times 3 times 5 is 90. So the L C M is 90.

spec.note: The L C M uses every prime in the picture, once each.

beats.say: Let's check. 90 divided by 18 is 5, and 90 divided by 10 is 9. Both divide exactly, so 90 is a multiple of each.
So for an L C M with bigger numbers: split both into primes, then take each prime the most times it appears in one number. Multiply, and you are done!
We need the L C M of 18 and 15. That is the lowest common multiple: the first number that is in the 18 times table and in the 15 times table.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 18?

choices: No, 18 has to fit into it
ask.ifNot: A multiple of 18 is 18 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 18, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: With small numbers like these we can just write out both tables and watch for a match. First the 18s: 18, 36, 54, 72, 90, 108.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 18 and 15?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 90 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: There it is. 90 is the first number in both lists, so the L C M is 90.
Let's check. 90 divided by 18 is 5, and 90 divided by 15 is 6. Both divide exactly, so 90 really is a multiple of each.
One trap to watch for. Multiplying 18 by 15 gives 270, which is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 90 gets there first.
So for small numbers: count up in both tables, and the first number in both is the L C M. Your turn next!
Which of these numbers is divisible by 11? We could do four long divisions. But there is a quicker way: a divisibility rule.
The rule for 11 is a neat one. Add the 1st and 3rd digits. Then add the 2nd and 4th digits.

board.text: Add the 1st and 3rd digits. Add the 2nd and 4th.

beats.say: If the two totals are equal, or exactly 11 apart, then 11 divides the number.

board.text: Totals equal, or 11 apart: divisible by 11

beats.say: First, 5753. The 1st and 3rd digits, 5 and 5, make 10. The 2nd and 4th, 7 and 3, make 10 as well. Does 5753 pass?

choices: Yes, the totals fit the rule
ask.ifNot: The totals are 10 and 10. The rule wants them equal, or exactly 11 apart, and these fit.

beats.say: The two totals match, so 5753 passes. Ring it!
A careful mathematician tests the rest too. Next, 9810. The 1st and 3rd digits make 10, and the 2nd and 4th make 8. Not equal, and not 11 apart, so 9810 is out.
Now 2190. The 1st and 3rd digits make 11, and the 2nd and 4th make 1. Not equal, and not 11 apart, so 2190 is out.
Last one: 9906. The 1st and 3rd digits make 9, and the 2nd and 4th make 15. Not equal, and not 11 apart, so 9906 is out.
Only 5753 passed, so that is our answer. And the division agrees: 5753 divided by 11 is 523, with nothing left over.
So for 11, add every other digit to make two totals. Equal totals, or totals 11 apart, mean 11 divides the number.
Find the H C F of 84 and 70. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 84 and 70 exactly.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number that goes into both 84 and 70. The plan: break each number into prime factors, its building blocks.
Take 84. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 twice, then 3, and 7 is left. So 84 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 7.
70 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 70 is 2 times 5 times 7.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 84 and 70 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Let's ring them. Both lines have a 2 and a 7. Careful: 84 has two 2s, but 70 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 7 is 14. So the H C F is 14.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 84 divided by 14 is 6, and 70 divided by 14 is 5. Both divide exactly, and 6 and 5 have nothing more in common.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.
Find the L C M of 20 and 7. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: The first number in both tables: that is our target. We could count up both tables, but with 20 and 7 that is a long walk. Prime factors get us there faster.
20 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 20 is 2 times 2 times 5.
7 is a prime number already. It cannot be split, so we leave it just as it is.
Here is the important part. Both 20 and 7 must fit inside the L C M. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in either number. Which of these does that?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 20 and all of 7, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: two 2s and the 5 from 20, and 7 itself. These two share no prime at all, so every prime goes in.
In the picture, the L C M is everything, counted once. 2 times 2 times 5 times 7 is 140. So the L C M is 140.

spec.note: The L C M uses every prime in the picture, once each.

beats.say: Let's check. 140 divided by 20 is 7, and 140 divided by 7 is 20. Both divide exactly, so 140 is a multiple of each.
Remember the difference. For an H C F we keep only the shared primes. For an L C M we take every prime, the most times it appears.
Siya has 55 stickers and shares them into two groups, in the ratio 2 is to 3. We want to know how many are in the larger group.

board.text: 55 stickers in the ratio 2 : 3. Larger group = ?

beats.say: First, what are we given? A total of 55, and a ratio, 2 is to 3. And what are we asked for? Just the larger group.
Let's draw the ratio. 2 is to 3: one bar with 2 equal parts, and one bar with 3. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 2 and 3 together make 5 parts.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 is 5. So the whole 55 is cut into 5 equal parts.
Now for the step where slips happen. How do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 55 fills all 5 parts, not just the 3 parts of one bar. So we divide 55 by 5.

beats.say: 55 divided by 5 is 11. Now we can write 11 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 11

beats.say: We want the larger group, and that is 3 parts. 3 times 11 makes 33.
So 33 stickers are in the larger group.
Let's check. The smaller group is 2 times 11, which is 22. And 22 plus 33 is 55, just what we started with.
So, to share in a ratio: count the parts, find what one part is worth, then take as many parts as you need.
Read it with me: 7 is to 12, equals 42 is to x. It says the two ratios are the same, and it hides one number behind x.
What do we have? A complete ratio, 7 is to 12. The second ratio shows only its first number, 42. We must find its partner.
Compare the two first numbers, 7 and 42. What happened to 7 to turn it into 42?

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 7 times 6 gives 42, so it was multiplied by 6.

beats.say: 42 divided by 7 is 6. So the first number was multiplied by 6.
For the two ratios to stay equal, what must we do to the second number, 12?

ask.ifNot: Whatever was done to the first number must be done to the second. 7 was multiplied by 6, so 12 is multiplied by 6 as well.

beats.say: 12 times 6 is 72. Careful: we multiply here. Adding would break the ratio.
So x is 72. There is our missing number!
Let's check. Divide 42 and 72 by 6, and we get 7 and 12 again. The two ratios match.
So in a proportion, find what the first number was multiplied by, then do the very same to the second.
110 is being shared out in the ratio 3 is to 7. We are after the smaller share.

board.text: Divide 110 in the ratio 3 : 7. Smaller share = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 110 to share. The ratio is 3 is to 7. And the question only wants the smaller share.
Let's draw the ratio. 3 is to 7: one bar with 3 equal parts, and one bar with 7. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 3 and 7 together make 10 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 7 is 10. So the whole 110 is cut into 10 equal parts.
Now for the step where slips happen. How do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 110 fills all 10 parts, not just the 7 parts of one bar. So we divide 110 by 10.

beats.say: 110 divided by 10 is 11. Now we can write 11 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 11

beats.say: The smaller share has 3 of these parts. 3 times 11 is 33.
So 33 is the smaller share.
Let's check. The larger share is 7 times 11, which is 77. And 33 plus 77 is 110, just what we started with.
That is the whole method. Total parts first, then one part, then the share the question asks for.
Here is our story. 80 toffees, split into two groups in the ratio 3 is to 5. How many toffees land in the larger group?

board.text: 80 toffees in the ratio 3 : 5. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Before any sum, let's be sure what we know. The total is 80. The ratio is 3 is to 5. And we want the larger group only.
A ratio of 3 is to 5 means this. One side gets 3 equal parts, and the other gets 5 parts of the very same size. Here they are as two bars.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 3 and 5 together make 8 parts.

beats.say: 3 and 5 make 8. That means the 80 is spread over 8 equal parts.
Here comes the turning point. Which sum tells us what a single part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 80 fills all 8 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 80 by 8.

beats.say: 80 divided by 8 is 10. So every single part is worth 10 toffees.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 10

beats.say: We want the larger group, and that is 5 parts. 5 times 10 makes 50.
So 50 toffees are in the larger group.
Let's check. The smaller group is 3 times 10, which is 30. And 30 plus 50 is 80, just what we started with.
Remember the three moves. Add the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for the share you want.
Read it with me: 2 is to 12, equals 6 is to x. It says the two ratios are the same, and it hides one number behind x.
Before any sum, look at what is given. The first ratio is whole: 2 is to 12. The second has its first number, 6, and a gap where x sits.
Compare the two first numbers, 2 and 6. What happened to 2 to turn it into 6?

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 2 times 3 gives 6, so it was multiplied by 3.

beats.say: 6 divided by 2 is 3. So the first number was multiplied by 3.
For the two ratios to stay equal, what must we do to the second number, 12?

ask.ifNot: Whatever was done to the first number must be done to the second. 2 was multiplied by 3, so 12 is multiplied by 3 as well.

beats.say: 12 times 3 is 36. Careful: we multiply here. Adding would break the ratio.
That makes x equal to 36.
Now check it. Shrink 6 is to 36 by dividing both by 3. Out comes 2 is to 12, the ratio we began with.
So in a proportion, find what the first number was multiplied by, then do the very same to the second.
Let's write it on the board. 4 x, minus 3, equals 9. The x is a mystery number, and our job is to work out what it is.
The two sides are worth the same, like a level see-saw. To get x alone we undo things, last one first. The minus 3 was done last. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners: each one undoes the other. So to undo minus 3, we add 3.

beats.say: So 3 goes on. But if we only did that on the left, the balance would tip. So we add 3 to both sides.
On the left, minus 3 and plus 3 cancel each other out. On the right, 9 plus 3 makes 12.
It is tempting to stop here and say 12. But that is 4 x, and we want just x. 4 x means 4 times x. What undoes times 4?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 4, we divide by 4.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide both by 4.
12 divided by 4 is 3. So x equals 3. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 3 back in place of x. 4 times 3 is 12, and 12 minus 3 is 9. It works.
We undid things in reverse: first the minus, then the times. Keep the balance level, and the hidden number always comes out.
Look at this one. 5 x, plus 11, equals 41. We want x standing all on its own, so we can see what it is worth.
Both sides of an equation weigh the same, like a balance, and every move has to keep it level. So what is our first move?

ask.ifNot: If we divided first, the 11 would have to be divided as well, and that gets messy. It is easier to clear the plus 11 first, by doing the opposite.

beats.say: We take 11 from both sides. Minus is the opposite of plus, so that clears the plus 11 away.
On the left the plus 11 has gone, and only 5 x is there. On the right, 41 minus 11 is 30. So 5 x equals 30.
It is tempting to stop here and say 30. But that is 5 x, and we want just x. 5 x means 5 times x. What undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 5.
30 divided by 5 is 6. So x equals 6. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 6 back in place of x. 5 times 6 is 30, and 30 plus 11 is 41. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Here is our equation. 7 x, minus 10, equals 67. Somewhere behind that x a number is hiding, and we are going to find it.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 7 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 7 x has a minus 10 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: To undo minus 10, we add 10. And to keep the balance level, we add it to both sides.
On the left, minus 10 and plus 10 cancel each other out. On the right, 67 plus 10 makes 77.
Careful, we are not finished. 77 is what 7 x is worth, not x. How do we get from 7 lots of x down to one x?

ask.ifNot: 7 x is 7 equal lots of x. To find one lot, we share 77 into 7 equal parts. That is dividing by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7.
77 divided by 7 is 11. So x equals 11. Found it!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 11 back in place of x. 7 times 11 is 77, and 77 minus 10 is 67. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Here is our equation. 2 x, minus 9, equals 15. Somewhere behind that x a number is hiding, and we are going to find it.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 2 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 2 x has a minus 9 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: To undo minus 9, we add 9. And to keep the balance level, we add it to both sides.
On the left, minus 9 and plus 9 cancel each other out. On the right, 15 plus 9 makes 24.
It is tempting to stop here and say 24. But that is 2 x, and we want just x. 2 x means 2 times x. What undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2.
24 divided by 2 is 12. So x equals 12. Found it!
Let's test it in the equation we started with. 2 times 12 is 24. Then 24 minus 9 gives 15, just as it should.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
5 x, plus 17, equals 57. Someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 5, then added 17, and got 57. Let's work backwards and find that number.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 5 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 5 x has a plus 17 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: The opposite of plus 17 is minus 17. Whatever we do to one side we do to the other, so I write it under both.
On the left the plus 17 has gone, and only 5 x is there. On the right, 57 minus 17 is 40. So 5 x equals 40.
Careful, we are not finished. 40 is what 5 x is worth, not x. How do we get from 5 lots of x down to one x?

ask.ifNot: 5 x is 5 equal lots of x. To find one lot, we share 40 into 5 equal parts. That is dividing by 5.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide both by 5.
40 divided by 5 is 8. So x equals 8. Found it!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 8 back in place of x. 5 times 8 is 40, and 40 plus 17 is 57. It works.
Remember the order: undo the plus 17 first, then undo the times 5. And every move is made on both sides.
Kavya has 104 marbles and shares them into two groups, in the ratio 3 is to 5. We want to know how many are in the larger group.

board.text: 104 marbles in the ratio 3 : 5. Larger group = ?

Let's draw the ratio. 3 is to 5: one bar with 3 equal parts, and one bar with 5. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 3 and 5 together make 8 parts.
