ask.ifNot: The 104 fills all 8 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 104 by 8.

beats.say: 104 divided by 8 is 13. So every single part is worth 13 marbles.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 13

beats.say: We want the larger group, and that is 5 parts. 5 times 13 makes 65.
So 65 marbles are in the larger group.
Let's check. The smaller group is 3 times 13, which is 39. And 39 plus 65 is 104, just what we started with.

Here is a proportion. 3 is to 5, equals 9 is to x. Two ratios that are equal, with one number, x, in hiding.

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 3 times 3 gives 9, so it was multiplied by 3.

beats.say: The smaller share has 3 of these parts. 3 times 7 is 21.
So the smaller share is 21. There it is!
Let's check. The larger share is 5 times 7, which is 35. And 21 plus 35 is 56, just what we started with.

Here is our story. 76 toffees, split into two groups in the ratio 1 is to 3. How many toffees land in the larger group?

board.text: 76 toffees in the ratio 1 : 3. Larger group = ?

A ratio of 1 is to 3 means this. One side gets 1 equal part, and the other gets 3 parts of the very same size. Here they are as two bars.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 1 and 3 together make 4 parts.

beats.say: 1 and 3 make 4. That means the 76 is spread over 4 equal parts.
Here comes the turning point. Which sum tells us what a single part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 76 fills all 4 parts, not just the 3 parts of one bar. So we divide 76 by 4.

beats.say: 76 divided by 4 is 19. So every single part is worth 19 toffees.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 19

beats.say: The larger group has 3 of these parts. 3 times 19 is 57.
So 57 toffees are in the larger group.

ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: With small numbers like these we can just write out both tables and watch for a match. First the 6s: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number that goes into both 24 and 42. The plan: break each number into prime factors, its building blocks.
24 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 24 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3.
Take 42. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, then 3, and 7 is left. So 42 is 2 times 3 times 7.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 24 and 42 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have a 2 and a 3. Careful: 24 has three 2s, but 42 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 3 is 6. So the H C F is 6.

beats.say: Let's check. 24 divided by 6 is 4, and 42 divided by 6 is 7, with nothing left over. And 4 and 7 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.

The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 3 times 3 is 9. So the H C F is 9.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 45 divided by 9 is 5, and 63 divided by 9 is 7, with nothing left over. And 5 and 7 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
So the plan for any H C F: break both numbers into primes, keep only the primes they share, and multiply those. Your turn next!
Find the L C M of 8 and 7. L C M stands for lowest common multiple: the first number both 8 and 7 will reach when you count up in their tables.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 8?

choices: No, 8 has to fit into it
ask.ifNot: A multiple of 8 is 8 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 8, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: Counting up in 8s and 7s would take a while. So we build the L C M from prime factors instead, the building blocks of each number.
Take 8. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 twice, and 2 is left. So 8 is 2 times 2 times 2.
7 is a prime number already. It cannot be split, so we leave it just as it is.
Here is the important part. Both 8 and 7 must fit inside the L C M. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in either number. Which of these does that?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 8 and all of 7, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: three 2s from 8, and 7 itself. These two share no prime at all, so every prime goes in.
In the picture, the L C M is everything, counted once. 2 times 2 times 2 times 7 is 56. So the L C M is 56.

spec.note: The L C M uses every prime in the picture, once each.

beats.say: Let's check. 56 divided by 8 is 7, and 56 divided by 7 is 8. Both divide exactly, so 56 is a multiple of each.

beats.say: Picture yourself standing where the two angles meet. You face along the line, then turn to face the other way. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 50, plus our missing angle, makes 180.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 50.

beats.say: We know the whole, 180, and one part, 50. How do we find the other part?
180 take away 50 leaves 130.
So the supplement is 130 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 50 plus 130 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So to find a supplement, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.

Look at this one. 3 x, plus 13, equals 73. Our job is to find the number that x stands for.
3 x means 3 times x. So someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 3, then added 13, and got 73.
Both sides are worth the same, like a level balance. To find x we work backwards, and undo the last thing first. Which was done last?

ask.ifNot: Read it from left to right. First x was multiplied by 3. After that came the plus 13. So the plus 13 was last, and we undo it first.

beats.say: We undo adding by taking away. So I take 13 from both sides, and the balance stays level.
Now the left side is just 3 x. And 73 minus 13 makes 60. So 3 times x is 60.
We are not done yet: 60 is 3 times x, not x. What undoes times 3?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. What times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 3, we divide by 3.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 3. 6 divided by 3 is 2, so 60 divided by 3 is 20.
So x equals 20. There is our hidden number!
Let's check. Put 20 in place of x. 3 times 20 is 60, and 60 plus 13 is 73. It works!
So the plan is to work backwards. First undo the adding or taking away. Then undo the times.

We are counting the factors of 24. A factor is a number that goes into 24 exactly, with nothing left over.
Factors always come with a partner. The two partners multiply to make 24. Start with the easy pair: 1 times 24.
Next we try 2. 24 is even, so 2 is a factor. What is its partner?

ask.ifNot: The partner is the number we multiply 2 by to make 24. Half of 24 is 12, so the partner of 2 is 12.

beats.say: 2 times 12 is 24. That is our second pair.
Keep going in order: try 3, then 4, then 5, and so on. We get 3 times 8 and 4 times 6.
When do we stop? The next factor after 4 is 6, and 6 is already on the board as a partner. So the pairs would only repeat.
Now count. We have 4 pairs, and each pair gives 2 different factors. How many factors is that?

ask.ifNot: Each pair holds 2 factors, and there are 4 pairs. So we double 4.

beats.say: 4 pairs, 2 factors in each, makes 8. So 24 has 8 factors. Here they all are, in order.
So to count factors: write the pairs in order, stop when they start to repeat, and count 2 for each pair. Your turn next!

Here is our question. 13 over 15, plus two thirds.
Let's draw them. One bar is cut into 15 pieces, with 13 shaded. The other is cut into 3 pieces, with 2 shaded.
Look at the pieces. Can we add 13 over 15 and two thirds straight away?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, add tops and add bottoms
ask.ifNot: Look at the two bars. Thirds are much bigger pieces than fifteenths. We can only add when the pieces are the same size.

beats.say: So let's turn the thirds into fifteenths. 3 times 5 is 15, so each piece gets cut into 5 smaller pieces.
Whatever we do to the bottom, we do to the top. 2 times 5 is 10, so two thirds is the same as 10 over 15.
Now both are fifteenths, so we just count. 13 pieces and 10 pieces make 23. The bottom stays 15.
23 over 15. The top is bigger than the bottom, and that is fine. It means more than 1 whole: one full bar, and 8 more pieces.
So 13 over 15 plus two thirds is 23 over 15.
Let's check by taking away. 23 over 15, take away 10 over 15, is 13 over 15 again. It works.
So when the bottom numbers are different: make the pieces the same size first. Then count the tops, and keep the bottom.
Here is our question. 13 over 15, take away 2 over 5.
Let's draw them. One bar is cut into 15 pieces, with 13 shaded. The other is cut into 5 pieces, with 2 shaded.
Look at the pieces. Can we take 2 over 5 away from 13 over 15 straight away?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
ask.ifNot: Look at the two bars. Fifths are much bigger pieces than fifteenths. We can only take away when the pieces are the same size.

beats.say: So let's turn the fifths into fifteenths. 5 times 3 is 15, so each piece gets cut into 3 smaller pieces.
Whatever we do to the bottom, we do to the top. 2 times 3 is 6, so 2 over 5 is the same as 6 over 15.
Now both are fifteenths, so we just count. 13 pieces, take away 6 pieces, leaves 7. The bottom stays 15.
So 13 over 15 take away 2 over 5 is 7 over 15.
Let's check by adding back. 7 over 15, plus 6 over 15, is 13 over 15. It works.
The plan to keep: same bottom number first. Only then do we work with the tops.
We are adding two fractions. 3 over 10, plus 7 over 10.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 10 equal pieces. The first has 3 shaded, and the second has 7.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all tenths. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, lots of children slip here. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, tenths. Adding more tenths does not change their size, so the bottom stays 10.

beats.say: So adding is just counting. 3 pieces, and 7 pieces more, is 10 pieces.
We have 10 over 10: every single piece of the bar. What is that worth?

ask.ifNot: When all 10 of the 10 pieces are shaded, the whole bar is full. So 10 over 10 is 1 whole.

beats.say: 10 over 10 is exactly 1. So 3 over 10 plus 7 over 10 is 1 whole.
Let's check against the picture. 3 shaded pieces, and 7 more, is 10 pieces. Just what we wrote.
So when the bottom numbers match: add the tops, keep the bottom, and then make it simpler if you can.
Here is our question. 9 over 10, take away 3 over 10.
Let's draw it. One bar cut into 10 equal pieces, with 9 of them shaded. We are going to take 3 of those shaded pieces away.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all tenths. So when we take some away, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, tenths. Taking some away does not change their size, so the bottom stays 10.

beats.say: So taking away is just counting. Start with 9 pieces, remove 3, and 6 are left.
6 over 10 is right, but we can make it simpler. What is the biggest number that divides both 6 and 10?

ask.ifNot: Try the times tables. 2 goes into 6, and 2 goes into 10, and nothing bigger goes into both.

beats.say: So we divide the top and the bottom by 2. 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 10 divided by 2 is 5.
So 9 over 10 take away 3 over 10 is 3 over 5, in its simplest form.
Let's check by adding back. 6 pieces, plus the 3 we took away, is 9 pieces again. It works.
So when the bottom numbers match: subtract the tops, keep the bottom, and then make it simpler if you can.

Find the L C M of 24 and 56. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we looking for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: Let's write out both tables and watch for a match. First the 24s: 24, 48, 72, 96, 120, 144, 168.

Careful, we are not finished. 40 is what 2 x is worth, not x. How do we get from 2 lots of x down to one x?

ask.ifNot: 2 x is 2 equal lots of x. To find one lot, we share 40 into 2 equal parts. That is dividing by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2.
40 divided by 2 is 20. So x equals 20. Found it!
Does it really work? Swap the x for 20. 2 times 20 is 40, and 40 plus 27 is 67. Both sides match.
Remember the order: undo the plus 27 first, then undo the times 2. And every move is made on both sides.
Let's write it on the board. 2 x, plus 30, equals 54. The x is a mystery number, and our job is to work out what it is.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 2 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 2 x has a plus 30 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: To undo plus 30, we take away 30. And to keep the balance level, we take it from both sides.
On the left the plus 30 has gone, and only 2 x is there. On the right, 54 minus 30 is 24. So 2 x equals 24.
It is tempting to stop here and say 24. But that is 2 x, and we want just x. 2 x means 2 times x. What undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: We divide the left by 2 and, to keep it fair, the right by 2 too.
24 divided by 2 is 12. So x equals 12. There is our hidden number!
Let's test it in the equation we started with. 2 times 12 is 24. Then 24 plus 30 gives 54, just as it should.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Here is our sum. 1 over 11, plus 8 over 11.

We need the H C F of 12 and 18. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both of them with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 12?

choices: No, it has to fit into 12
ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 12, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: So how do we find it? We split each number into its prime factors, the smallest building blocks it is made of.
12 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 12 is 2 times 2 times 3.
Take 18. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, then 3, and 3 is left. So 18 is 2 times 3 times 3.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 12 and 18 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have a 2 and a 3. Careful: 12 has two 2s, but 18 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 3 is 6. So the H C F is 6.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 12 divided by 6 is 2, and 18 divided by 6 is 3. Both divide exactly, and 2 and 3 have nothing more in common.
So the plan for any H C F: break both numbers into primes, keep only the primes they share, and multiply those. Your turn next!

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 14 divided by 7 is 2, and 49 divided by 7 is 7. Both divide exactly, and 2 and 7 have nothing more in common.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.

Find the L C M of 16 and 28. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we hunting for?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: The first number in both tables: that is our target. We could count up both tables, but with 16 and 28 that is a long walk. Prime factors get us there faster.
Take 16. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 three times, and 2 is left. So 16 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 2.
Take 28. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 twice, and 7 is left. So 28 is 2 times 2 times 7.
Here is the important part. Both 16 and 28 must fit inside the L C M. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in either number. Which of these does that?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 16 and all of 28, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: four 2s from 16, and the 7 from 28. Careful: we do not add the two 2s in 28 on top, because the four 2s from 16 already cover them.

Find the L C M of 42 and 49. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: So we want the first number that both tables reach. Counting up in 42s and 49s would take a while. So we build the L C M from prime factors instead, the building blocks of each number.
42 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 42 is 2 times 3 times 7.
Take 49. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 7, and 7 is left. So 49 is 7 times 7.
Here is the important part. Both 42 and 49 must fit inside the L C M. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in either number. Which of these does that?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 42 and all of 49, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: the 2 and the 3 from 42, and two 7s from 49. Careful: we do not add the 7 in 42 on top, because the two 7s from 49 already cover it.

spec.note: The L C M uses every prime in the picture, once each.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 294 divided by 42 is 7, and 294 divided by 49 is 6, with nothing left over.
So for an L C M with bigger numbers: split both into primes, then take each prime the most times it appears in one number. Multiply, and you are done!

500 students in all, and 50 per cent are girls. How many girls is that?
Per cent means out of every 100. So 50 per cent girls means 50 girls in every 100 students.
Careful: that does not mean 50 girls altogether. It is 50 in every 100, and here there are 500 students.
50 out of every 100. Which fraction is that?

ask.ifNot: 50 is half of 100. So 50 per cent is the same as one half.

beats.say: One half. So we simply halve the number. Half of 500 is 250.

spec.note: 2 equal pieces: each is 50%

beats.say: So there are 250 girls.
Check it another way. 500 is 5 hundreds, and each hundred gives 50. 5 times 50 is 250. Same answer.
So remember: 50 per cent is one half. Just halve the number. Now you try one!
The test is out of 1000 marks, and the student scored 20 per cent. We want the actual marks.
Per cent means out of every 100. So scoring 20 per cent means getting 20 marks for every 100 marks in the test.
Careful: that does not mean 20 marks altogether. It is 20 for every 100, and this test has 1000 marks.
Let us start from an easy one. What is 10 per cent of 1000?

ask.ifNot: 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10, not by 100. 1000 divided by 10 is 100.

beats.say: One tenth of 1000 is 100, so 10 per cent is 100. Look at the bar: it is 1 of the 10 equal pieces.

spec.note: 10 equal pieces: each is 10%

beats.say: 20 per cent is 2 lots of 10 per cent. 2 times 100 is 200.
So the student scored 200 marks.
Check it another way. 1000 is 10 hundreds, and each hundred gives 20. 10 times 20 is 200. Same answer.
So remember: per cent means out of every 100. Find 10 per cent by dividing by 10, then build the per cent you need from it. Your turn next!

board.text: Triangle: base 15 cm, height 17 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Look at this triangle. The base, along the bottom, is 15 centimetres. The height, straight up, is 17 centimetres. How much space is inside?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides is for the walk round the edge. The space inside a rectangle is its length times its breadth.

beats.say: Counting squares inside a triangle is awkward. So let me box it in: a rectangle around the triangle, with the same base and the same height. How do we find the area of that rectangle?
The area of a rectangle is its length times its breadth. Here that means base times height.

Someone puts 500 rupees in a bank at 12 per cent simple interest, and leaves it for 5 years. How much is there at the end? That is called the amount.

board.text: Rs.500 at 12% simple interest for 5 years

beats.say: 12 per cent means 12 out of every 100. So every 100 rupees earns 12 rupees in one year.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.12 in 1 year

beats.say: So how many hundreds are in 500? 500 divided by 100 is 5. That is 5 hundreds.

spec.note: Each 100 earns Rs.12 in a year

beats.say: Each of the 5 hundreds earns 12 rupees in a year. So which sum gives the interest for one year?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 5 hundreds earns 12 rupees. So that is 12 rupees, 5 times over: 5 times 12.

beats.say: 5 times 12 is 60. That is what one year earns: 60 rupees of interest.
Simple interest is steady. It earns the same 60 rupees every single year. Look at the table, one year at a time.
So we need 60, 5 times over. 5 times 60 is 300. That is the interest for all 5 years.
Grown-ups write this as a formula. The starting money is the principal. Simple interest is principal, times rate, times time in years, divided by 100.
Put our numbers in. 500 times 12 times 5, divided by 100, comes to 300. The same answer, so we can trust it.
Now, careful. The question asks for the amount after 5 years. Is 300 the amount?

choices: No: take it away from Rs.500
ask.ifNot: 300 rupees is only the interest, the extra money. The amount is everything in the bank: the 500 rupees put in at the start, plus the interest.

beats.say: 500 plus 300 is 800. So the amount after 5 years is 800 rupees.
So: find what one year earns, multiply by the number of years, and for the amount, add the interest back on to the money at the start. Now you try one!

beats.say: 7 per cent means 7 out of every 100. So every 100 rupees earns 7 rupees in one year.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.7 in 1 year

beats.say: So how many hundreds are in 500? 500 divided by 100 is 5. That is 5 hundreds.

spec.note: Each 100 earns Rs.7 in a year

beats.say: Each of the 5 hundreds earns 7 rupees in a year. So which sum gives the interest for one year?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 5 hundreds earns 7 rupees. So that is 7 rupees, 5 times over: 5 times 7.

beats.say: 5 times 7 is 35. That is what one year earns: 35 rupees of interest.
The lovely thing about simple interest: every year earns exactly the same, 35 rupees. Here it is, a year at a time.
The money stays for 2 years, so the 35 comes twice. 35 twice is 70. That is the interest for both years.
Here is the same idea as a formula. The money at the start is called the principal. Simple interest is principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100.
Put our numbers in. 500 times 7 times 2, divided by 100, comes to 70. The same answer, so we can trust it.
Now, careful. The question asks for the amount after 2 years. Is 70 the amount?

choices: No: take it away from Rs.500
ask.ifNot: 70 rupees is only the interest, the extra money. The amount is everything in the bank: the 500 rupees put in at the start, plus the interest.

beats.say: 500 plus 70 is 570. So the amount after 2 years is 570 rupees.
Three moves. Interest for one year, then for all the years, and then add it to the starting money to get the amount. Now you try one!
